title_en: Deepen Investment Ties as Chinese Delegation Explores Coffee, Industry and Tourism Opportunities
excerpt_en: Uganda, China April 13, 2026 - A high-level Chinese business delegation is currently in Uganda to explore investment opportunities in coffee production, industrial infrastructure, and tourism, as Kampala strengthens its economic partnership with China. The visit forms part of the
body_en:
Uganda, China April 13, 2026 - A high-level Chinese business delegation is currently in Uganda to explore investment opportunities in coffee production, industrial infrastructure, and tourism, as Kampala strengthens its economic partnership with China.
The visit forms part of the Uganda-China Coffee Investment and Destination Tour 2026, a coordinated initiative aimed at expanding trade, investment flows, and market linkages between the two countries. The delegation arrived this week and will remain in Uganda from April 10 to 23, 2026.
The mission is being facilitated by Uganda’s diplomatic missions in Beijing and Guangzhou, and brings together representatives from several major Chinese companies, including firms operating in manufacturing, infrastructure, agriculture, and tourism.
During their stay, investors are expected to tour key industrial zones such as the Sino-Uganda Mbale Industrial Park, Liao Shen Industrial Park, and Namanve Industrial Park, where they will assess potential opportunities in manufacturing, infrastructure development, and export-oriented production.
A central focus of the visit is Uganda’s coffee sector, one of the country’s top foreign exchange earners. Delegates will engage directly with producers at the Ankole Coffee Producers Cooperative Union and visit a coffee processing facility in Bushenyi to observe the full value chain from production to export.
The programme also includes an extensive tourism component designed to showcase Uganda’s natural attractions. The delegation is scheduled to visit Bwindi Impenetrable National Park, Queen Elizabeth National Park, Rwenzori Mountains National Park, and the Source of the Nile, highlighting the country’s biodiversity and tourism potential.
Officials say the combined investment and tourism exposure is intended to position Uganda as a competitive destination for both foreign direct investment and international tourism, particularly targeting Asian markets.
The Uganda-China Coffee Investment and Destination Tour reflects broader efforts to deepen bilateral cooperation in agro-industrialisation, tourism development, mineral-based industrialisation, and science and technology.
Government authorities in Kampala say the initiative is expected to enhance market access for Ugandan exports, attract new investment inflows, and strengthen long-term economic cooperation between Uganda and China.
body_fr:
Ouganda, Chine, 13 avril 2026 - Une délégation commerciale chinoise de haut niveau est actuellement en Ouganda pour explorer les opportunités d'investissement dans la production de café, les infrastructures industrielles et le tourisme, alors que Kampala renforce son partenariat économique avec la Chine.
La visite fait partie du Tour d'investissement et de destination du café Ouganda-Chine 2026, une initiative coordonnée visant à développer le commerce, les flux d'investissement et les liens commerciaux entre les deux pays. La délégation est arrivée cette semaine et restera en Ouganda du 10 au 23 avril 2026.
La mission est facilitée par les missions diplomatiques ougandaises à Pékin et Guangzhou et rassemble des représentants de plusieurs grandes entreprises chinoises, notamment des entreprises opérant dans les secteurs de la fabrication, des infrastructures, de l’agriculture et du tourisme.
Au cours de leur séjour, les investisseurs devraient visiter des zones industrielles clés telles que le parc industriel sino-ougandais de Mbale, le parc industriel de Liao Shen et le parc industriel de Namanve, où ils évalueront les opportunités potentielles dans les domaines de la fabrication, du développement des infrastructures et de la production orientée vers l'exportation.
L’un des thèmes centraux de la visite est le secteur du café ougandais, l’une des principales sources de devises du pays. Les délégués dialogueront directement avec les producteurs de l'Union coopérative des producteurs de café d'Ankole et visiteront une installation de transformation du café à Bushenyi pour observer toute la chaîne de valeur, de la production à l'exportation.
Le programme comprend également un vaste volet touristique conçu pour mettre en valeur les attractions naturelles de l’Ouganda. La délégation devrait visiter le parc national impénétrable de Bwindi, le parc national Queen Elizabeth, le parc national des monts Rwenzori et la source du Nil, mettant en valeur la biodiversité et le potentiel touristique du pays.
Les responsables affirment que l'exposition combinée aux investissements et au tourisme vise à positionner l'Ouganda comme une destination compétitive à la fois pour les investissements directs étrangers et le tourisme international, en ciblant particulièrement les marchés asiatiques.
La tournée d'investissement et de destination du café Ouganda-Chine reflète des efforts plus larges visant à approfondir la coopération bilatérale dans les domaines de l'agro-industrialisation, du développement du tourisme, de l'industrialisation basée sur les minéraux, ainsi que de la science et de la technologie.
Les autorités gouvernementales de Kampala affirment que cette initiative devrait améliorer l'accès au marché pour les exportations ougandaises, attirer de nouveaux flux d'investissements et renforcer la coopération économique à long terme entre l'Ouganda et la Chine.

title_en: United States Urges DRC to Dismantle FDLR, Warns of Possible SanctionsApril 16, 2026 ; The United States has called on the government of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) to urgently dismantle the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), warning that continued inaction could lead to sanctions.
excerpt_en: The message was reiterated on April 15, 2026, by U.S. Deputy Permanent Representative to the United Nations, Tammy Bruce, during a United Nations Security Council session focused on peace and stability in the Great Lakes region. The discussion also featured remarks from Rwanda’s
body_en:
The message was reiterated on April 15, 2026, by U.S. Deputy Permanent Representative to the United Nations, Tammy Bruce, during a United Nations Security Council session focused on peace and stability in the Great Lakes region.
The discussion also featured remarks from Rwanda’s Deputy Permanent Representative to the UN, Robert Kayinamura, who stated that the FDLR remains active in eastern DRC and continues to pose a regional security threat. He also linked the group to its historical origins tied to the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi, calling for its complete dismantlement.
US position on peace commitments
The U.S. delegation emphasized that the DRC must fulfill its commitments under the peace agreement signed with Rwanda in June 2025, which included provisions for dismantling the armed group. Washington noted that implementation has been delayed despite the agreement.
U.S. officials argued that the continued presence of the FDLR contributes to mistrust between parties and fuels instability in eastern Congo.
“The DRC government must honor its commitments and quickly eliminate the FDLR, at least in the areas it controls. Eliminating these long-standing security concerns is essential to ending the cycle of mistrust that has caused war for many years,” Tammy Bruce said.
Ongoing dispute over presence of armed group
The DRC government has previously argued that FDLR elements are not primarily located in areas under its direct control, stating that some are in territories affected by ongoing conflict involving other armed actors in the east.
However, U.S. officials countered that FDLR presence has also been reported in government-controlled areas, reinforcing the need for immediate action.
Warning of possible sanctions
The United States also warned that it is prepared to use available diplomatic and economic measures if parties are seen to be obstructing peace efforts, including the possibility of targeted sanctions.
The statement reflects growing international pressure on actors in the region to accelerate implementation of existing peace commitments as instability persists in eastern DRC.

title: Rubavu Mayor Says FDLR Deceived Residents Into Selling Land, as Hundreds Return from Eastern DRC
excerpt: April 17, 2026 - Authorities in Rubavu District say some residents were misled into selling their property by members of the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), who allegedly convinced them that they would soon take control of Rwanda. The remarks were made by R
title_en: Rubavu Mayor Says FDLR Deceived Residents Into Selling Land, as Hundreds Return from Eastern DRC
excerpt_en: April 17, 2026 - Authorities in Rubavu District say some residents were misled into selling their property by members of the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), who allegedly convinced them that they would soon take control of Rwanda. The remarks were made by R
body_en:
April 17, 2026 - Authorities in Rubavu District say some residents were misled into selling their property by members of the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), who allegedly convinced them that they would soon take control of Rwanda.
The remarks were made by Rubavu Mayor Mulindwa Prosper on April 16, 2026, during the reception of Rwandan nationals who had returned from the Democratic Republic of Congo after being held in areas controlled by the armed group.
Return of civilians from eastern DRC
A total of 403 returnees-including 280 children, 105 women, and 18 men-entered Rwanda through the La Corniche border crossing between Rubavu and Goma. They were subsequently transferred to a temporary reception facility in Nyarushishi, Rusizi District, where they are receiving initial assistance.
The group is part of civilians who had been living in eastern DRC and were recently assisted in returning through coordination involving humanitarian actors.
Allegations of exploitation and misinformation
Mayor Mulindwa warned returnees to remain cautious of misinformation and what he described as manipulation by armed groups operating in eastern Congo.
He stated that some individuals had been persuaded to sell land and assets under the belief that armed groups would soon take control of Rwanda, leaving them impoverished as a result.
“The people you have been with were deceiving some Rwandans into believing they would attack and take over the country, encouraging them to sell their land and fall into poverty through false promises and harmful narratives,” he said.
He urged returnees to rely on official institutions and to share accurate information with relatives who remain outside the country, encouraging voluntary return.
Testimonies from returnees
Some returnees described difficult living conditions in eastern DRC, citing insecurity and lack of access to basic livelihoods.
One returnee, 25-year-old Niyonsenga Segasore, said life in the DRC was marked by fear and instability, making daily survival difficult.
Another returnee, 18-year-old Uwase Jeannette, said insecurity had severely affected agricultural activities, making it impossible to sustain livelihoods.
Reintegration support
Authorities confirmed that returnees are receiving reintegration assistance upon arrival, including financial support and basic supplies to help them restart their lives.
Officials say the program is part of ongoing efforts to facilitate the voluntary return and reintegration of Rwandans from conflict-affected areas in eastern DRC.

title: Rwanda-DRC Tensions Rise After Minister Accuses Congolese Spokesperson of Hate Speech
excerpt: Kigali, April 9, 2026 - Rwanda’s Minister of National Unity and Civic Engagement, Jean-Damascène Bizimana, has accused the Congolese government spokesperson, Patrick Muyaya, of promoting hate speech targeting Tutsi communities, escalating already strained relations between Rwanda
title_en: Rwanda-DRC Tensions Rise After Minister Accuses Congolese Spokesperson of Hate Speech
excerpt_en: Kigali, April 9, 2026 - Rwanda’s Minister of National Unity and Civic Engagement, Jean-Damascène Bizimana, has accused the Congolese government spokesperson, Patrick Muyaya, of promoting hate speech targeting Tutsi communities, escalating already strained relations between Rwanda
body_en:
Kigali, April 9, 2026 - Rwanda’s Minister of National Unity and Civic Engagement, Jean-Damascène Bizimana, has accused the Congolese government spokesperson, Patrick Muyaya, of promoting hate speech targeting Tutsi communities, escalating already strained relations between Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
The remarks were made during commemorations marking the 32nd anniversary of the Genocide against the Tutsi, where Bizimana alleged that Muyaya had previously described Tutsis as “murderers” during a televised appearance on Télé 50.
Muyaya swiftly rejected the accusation, stating on the social media platform X that the claims were “a lie told on the day of remembrance.”
In response, Bizimana reiterated his position, referencing a July 2024 interview in which Muyaya discussed the long-running conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo. The Rwandan minister argued that such statements contribute to dangerous narratives, warning that “genocide is always preceded by hate speech.”
He also criticized what he described as broader rhetoric from certain Congolese officials, drawing parallels with past figures accused of incitement. Bizimana cited historical examples to underline the potential consequences of inflammatory discourse, particularly in a region marked by recurring tensions and armed conflict.
The dispute comes amid ongoing instability in eastern DRC, where fighting involving armed groups, including the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda and the AFC/M23 coalition, continues to fuel diplomatic friction between Kinshasa and Kigali.
Muyaya has also recently commented on the presence and role of armed groups in the region, reportedly questioning the effectiveness of military approaches to addressing the FDLR, a group historically linked to individuals involved in the 1994 genocide.
The exchange highlights the sensitivity of public discourse around ethnicity and conflict in the Great Lakes region, where accusations of hate speech and genocide denial carry significant political and historical weight.

The facility, developed by Yaobai Cement Uganda, is located in Moroto and represents an investment of more than US$300 million. Officials describe it as one of the largest industrial projects in northern Uganda, with the potential to reshape the country’s manufacturing landscape.
The commissioning ceremony is expected to draw a wide range of stakeholders, including government officials, private sector leaders, development partners, and cultural representatives from across the Karamoja sub-region and beyond.
Industrial Boost for Karamoja
The project is widely seen as a turning point for Karamoja, a region historically associated with insecurity and underdevelopment but now increasingly opening up to investment, infrastructure, and economic opportunities.
At its initial phase, the plant is producing more than 6,000 tonnes of clinker per day, significantly boosting Uganda’s domestic production capacity.
Officials estimate the facility will reduce the country’s reliance on imported clinker by more than 2.5 million tonnes annually, easing pressure on foreign exchange and strengthening local supply chains.
Impact on Construction and Local Economy
Industry stakeholders say increased domestic production is expected to stabilise cement supply and potentially lower prices over time, providing a boost to Uganda’s rapidly expanding construction sector.
Beyond industrial output, the project is already generating tangible benefits for local communities. Residents in and around Moroto are experiencing increased economic activity, improved household incomes, and expanded employment opportunities linked to the factory and its supporting infrastructure.
Symbol of Economic Transformation
The launch also highlights Karamoja’s evolving role in Uganda’s broader industrialisation agenda, as the region positions itself as a new frontier for investment and development.
Officials say the project reflects growing investor confidence in Uganda’s economic prospects and underscores government efforts to promote inclusive growth by extending industrial development to previously underserved regions.

title: Security Intensifies Crackdown on Illegal Mining in Kassanda
excerpt: Kassanda April 12, 2026 - Security agencies in Uganda’s Wamala Region have intensified operations against illegal mining activities in Kassanda District following a directive from the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Development ordering the suspension of operations under Explorati
title_en: Security Intensifies Crackdown on Illegal Mining in Kassanda
excerpt_en: Kassanda April 12, 2026 - Security agencies in Uganda’s Wamala Region have intensified operations against illegal mining activities in Kassanda District following a directive from the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Development ordering the suspension of operations under Explorati
body_en:
Kassanda April 12, 2026 - Security agencies in Uganda’s Wamala Region have intensified operations against illegal mining activities in Kassanda District following a directive from the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Development ordering the suspension of operations under Exploration Licence No. 00459.
The enforcement exercise, code-named Operation Safisha, is being jointly conducted by the Police Mineral Protection Unit and the Wamala Regional Police Command to restore order and ensure compliance with mining regulations.
According to regional police spokesperson Lameck Kigozi, the licence in question had been issued to Mugobwa Katugo Small Scale Miners strictly for exploration within a 0.34 square kilometre area in Bubali, Kitumbi Sub-county. However, authorities allege that the operators exceeded the scope of the permit by engaging in full-scale extraction without the required mining licence.
“This was purely an exploration licence. The law requires that after exploration, findings must be submitted to the Ministry before an extraction licence is granted. Unfortunately, this procedure was ignored, and illegal extraction commenced,” Kigozi said.
Following this breach, the Ministry ordered an immediate suspension of all activities, prompting the launch of the enforcement operation aimed at demobilising miners and clearing the site. Authorities say operators were initially given a two-week ultimatum to vacate the area and remove equipment, but several failed to comply.
“Despite the grace period given, some operators remained defiant. That is why security forces have now moved in to fully enforce the directive,” Kigozi added.
The crackdown involves multiple security units, including the Field Force Unit, the Criminal Investigations Directorate (CID), and Crime Intelligence teams, tasked with monitoring and investigating any related criminal activity.
Authorities have also warned both local and foreign nationals involved in the mining activities-including individuals from neighbouring countries such as the Democratic Republic of Congo, Rwanda, Burundi, Tanzania, Kenya, and South Sudan-to vacate the area peacefully.
Kigozi cautioned against illegal scavenging in abandoned mining pits, locally known as “okwekyokola,” describing it as both unlawful and dangerous, with several fatalities already reported.
“This kind of activity has already claimed lives due to poor safety practices. Security will remain on the ground to ensure no one returns to the pits. These areas will be backfilled to prevent further incidents,” he said.
He urged aggrieved parties to pursue legal remedies through the Ministry rather than resisting enforcement.
“If you feel dissatisfied, the law provides avenues for appeal. You can formally engage the Ministry and apply for an extraction licence through the right procedures,” he added.
Authorities say the operation marks a decisive step toward regulating the mining sector in Kassanda, improving safety standards, and ensuring compliance with Uganda’s legal framework for mineral exploitation.

title: Des étudiants indiens célèbrent le souvenir du génocide avec un hommage artistique
excerpt: New Delhi, le 7 avril 2026 - Des étudiants de plusieurs écoles indiennes ont présenté des œuvres d'art illustrant l'histoire du génocide perpétré contre les Tutsi, dans le cadre des commémorations marquant son 32e anniversaire. L'exposition s'est tenue le matin du 7 avril lors d'une cérémonie officielle de commémoration
title_en: Indian Students Mark Genocide Remembrance with Artistic Tribute
excerpt_en: New Delhi, 7 April 2026 - Students from several schools in India have presented artworks depicting the history of the Genocide against the Tutsi, as part of commemorations marking its 32nd anniversary. The exhibition was held on the morning of 7 April during an official remembran
body_en:
New Delhi, 7 April 2026 - Students from several schools in India have presented artworks depicting the history of the Genocide against the Tutsi, as part of commemorations marking its 32nd anniversary.
The exhibition was held on the morning of 7 April during an official remembrance event, where the artworks were displayed and interpreted to invited guests. Organizers said the initiative aimed to educate young people and promote reflection on the consequences of genocide and the importance of remembrance.
Among those attending were Jacqueline Mukangira, as well as Darrin Farrant and members of the diplomatic and educational community. The guests were guided through the exhibition, with students explaining the themes and messages behind their work.
April 7 is observed globally as the International Day of Reflection on the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda, marking the start of a period of commemoration for victims of the 1994 atrocities.
In Rwanda, the annual National Week of Mourning has officially begun, launching 100 days of remembrance activities held across the country and within the global Rwandan community.
body_fr:
New Delhi, le 7 avril 2026 - Des étudiants de plusieurs écoles indiennes ont présenté des œuvres d'art illustrant l'histoire du génocide perpétré contre les Tutsi, dans le cadre des commémorations marquant son 32e anniversaire.
L'exposition a eu lieu le matin du 7 avril lors d'un événement commémoratif officiel, au cours duquel les œuvres d'art ont été exposées et interprétées devant des invités. Les organisateurs ont déclaré que l'initiative visait à éduquer les jeunes et à promouvoir la réflexion sur les conséquences du génocide et l'importance du souvenir.
Parmi les participants figuraient Jacqueline Mukangira, ainsi que Darrin Farrant et des membres de la communauté diplomatique et éducative. Les invités ont été guidés à travers l'exposition, les étudiants expliquant les thèmes et les messages derrière leur travail.
Le 7 avril est célébré dans le monde entier comme la Journée internationale de réflexion sur le génocide perpétré contre les Tutsi au Rwanda en 1994, marquant le début d'une période de commémoration pour les victimes des atrocités de 1994.
Au Rwanda, la Semaine nationale annuelle de deuil a officiellement commencé, lançant 100 jours d'activités de commémoration organisées à travers le pays et au sein de la communauté rwandaise mondiale.

title_en: South Sudan Speaker Calls Emergency Sitting as Pressure Mounts Over Her Removal
excerpt_en: Juba April 7, 2026 - South Sudan’s Speaker of Parliament, Jemma Nunu Kumba, has summoned Members of Parliament and government ministers to an extraordinary sitting, as political pressure intensifies following a ruling party move to remove her from office. The emergency session, s
body_en:
Juba April 7, 2026 - South Sudan’s Speaker of Parliament, Jemma Nunu Kumba, has summoned Members of Parliament and government ministers to an extraordinary sitting, as political pressure intensifies following a ruling party move to remove her from office.
The emergency session, scheduled for April 8, comes days after the ruling Sudan People’s Liberation Movement (SPLM) voted to withdraw confidence in her leadership and recommended her dismissal to President Salva Kiir.
Parliamentary spokesperson Oliver Mori Benjamin confirmed the summons, describing the session as unprecedented and instructing all lawmakers and ministers to attend.
“We are in the operations room in Parliament, although it is a holiday. All Members of Parliament and ministers are required to attend this sitting without fail. The agenda will be communicated, but as you are aware, there have been political developments,” he said.
The developments stem from an internal dispute within the SPLM, where a caucus meeting chaired by President Kiir on March 31 reportedly resulted in a unanimous vote of no confidence against Kumba. Lawmakers subsequently recommended her removal, forwarding the decision to the president, who also serves as party chairman.
Reports suggest that a leadership change in Parliament could occur within days, with potential successors already under discussion within party ranks.
In response, the Speaker’s office has challenged the process, stating that Kumba was not given an opportunity to respond to the allegations during the caucus meeting and that no formal parliamentary procedure was followed.
“The Office of the Speaker has taken note of the concerns raised and stands ready to address these matters through appropriate institutional processes,” the statement said.
The emergency sitting places Kumba in the unusual position of convening a session that could ultimately determine her political future.
At the center of the dispute are allegations of financial misconduct raised in a petition by a group of SPLM lawmakers. The claims include funds linked to regional parliamentary games, procurement expenditures, and alleged irregular payments for services. The allegations have not been independently verified, and Kumba has not publicly addressed them in detail.
The controversy has intensified divisions within the ruling party and raised broader concerns about governance and accountability in South Sudan’s legislature.
Analysts say the situation reflects deeper fractures within the SPLM as the country approaches planned elections later in 2026, pointing to a possible realignment of political power within the unity government.
Kumba, who became South Sudan’s first female Speaker in 2021, now faces one of the most significant challenges of her political career, with the outcome of the emergency sitting expected to shape both parliamentary leadership and the wider balance of power in the country.
body_fr:
Juba, le 7 avril 2026 - La présidente du Parlement du Soudan du Sud, Jemma Nunu Kumba, a convoqué les membres du Parlement et les ministres du gouvernement à une séance extraordinaire, alors que la pression politique s'intensifie suite à la décision du parti au pouvoir de la destituer.
La session d’urgence, prévue pour le 8 avril, intervient quelques jours après que le Mouvement populaire de libération du Soudan (SPLM) au pouvoir a voté en faveur du retrait de confiance dans ses dirigeants et a recommandé sa destitution au président Salva Kiir.
Le porte-parole parlementaire Oliver Mori Benjamin a confirmé la convocation, qualifiant la session de sans précédent et ordonnant à tous les législateurs et ministres d'y assister.
"Nous sommes dans la salle des opérations du Parlement, bien que ce soit un jour férié. Tous les députés et ministres sont tenus d'assister à cette séance sans faute. L'ordre du jour sera communiqué, mais comme vous le savez, il y a eu des développements politiques", a-t-il déclaré.
Ces développements découlent d'un conflit interne au sein du SPLM, où une réunion du caucus présidée par le président Kiir le 31 mars aurait abouti à un vote unanime de censure contre Kumba. Les législateurs ont ensuite recommandé sa destitution, transmettant la décision au président, qui est également président du parti.
Des rapports suggèrent qu'un changement de direction au Parlement pourrait avoir lieu d'ici quelques jours, les successeurs potentiels étant déjà en discussion au sein des rangs du parti.
En réponse, le bureau du Président a contesté le processus, affirmant que Kumba n’avait pas eu la possibilité de répondre aux allégations lors de la réunion du caucus et qu’aucune procédure parlementaire formelle n’avait été suivie.
"Le Bureau du Président a pris note des préoccupations soulevées et se tient prêt à résoudre ces questions par le biais de processus institutionnels appropriés", indique le communiqué.
La séance d'urgence place Kumba dans la position inhabituelle de convoquer une session qui pourrait en fin de compte déterminer son avenir politique.
Au centre du conflit se trouvent les allégations de mauvaise conduite financière soulevées dans une pétition déposée par un groupe de législateurs du SPLM. Les réclamations comprennent des fonds liés à des jeux parlementaires régionaux, des dépenses d'achat et des paiements irréguliers présumés pour des services. Les allégations n’ont pas été vérifiées de manière indépendante et Kumba ne les a pas abordées publiquement en détail.
La controverse a intensifié les divisions au sein du parti au pouvoir et soulevé des préoccupations plus larges concernant la gouvernance et la responsabilité au sein de l’Assemblée législative du Soudan du Sud.
Les analystes affirment que la situation reflète des fractures plus profondes au sein du SPLM à l’approche des élections prévues plus tard en 2026, ce qui laisse présager un possible réalignement du pouvoir politique au sein du gouvernement d’unité.
Kumba, qui est devenue la première femme présidente du Soudan du Sud en 2021, est désormais confrontée à l’un des défis les plus importants de sa carrière politique, le résultat de la séance d’urgence devant façonner à la fois la direction parlementaire et l’équilibre plus large des pouvoirs dans le pays.

title: Le Premier ministre sénégalais critique les interventions militaires mondiales à la Conférence de Dakar
excerpt: 12 avril 2026 - Le Premier ministre sénégalais, Ousmane Sonko, a vivement critiqué les récentes interventions militaires occidentales, affirmant qu'elles ont contribué à l'instabilité mondiale plutôt qu'à la paix. Ses remarques ont été prononcées lors d'une conférence internationale sur la souveraineté des États.
title_en: Senegalese Prime Minister Criticizes Global Military Interventions at Dakar Conference
excerpt_en: April 12, 2026 - The Senegalese Prime Minister, Ousmane Sonko, has sharply criticized recent Western military interventions, stating that they have contributed to global instability rather than peace. His remarks were delivered during an international conference on state sovereig
body_en:
April 12, 2026 - The Senegalese Prime Minister, Ousmane Sonko, has sharply criticized recent Western military interventions, stating that they have contributed to global instability rather than peace. His remarks were delivered during an international conference on state sovereignty held in Dakar on April 9, 2026.
Speaking at the forum, Sonko argued that recent and historical military campaigns led by Western powers have failed to achieve their stated objectives and have instead left long-term political and humanitarian consequences in several regions.
He cited conflicts including Vietnam, Iraq, Afghanistan, Libya, and Syria as examples of what he described as unsuccessful attempts to reshape political outcomes through military force.
According to the Prime Minister, similar dynamics are now being observed in the ongoing tensions involving Iran, where military pressure has not produced the intended political results. He suggested that despite escalating confrontation, diplomatic engagement is gradually becoming the preferred path for the parties involved.
“The goal of overthrowing the Iranian regime has not been achieved. It still exists and has, in some respects, become stronger than before,” Sonko stated during his address.
The Prime Minister also directly criticized US President Donald Trump, linking him to what he described as destabilizing global policies. He argued that the current trajectory of international relations reflects a pattern in which powerful states impose decisions under the banner of democracy, often without regard for national sovereignty.
“Donald Trump is not a person who wants peace. He is a person who is concerned with disrupting the stability of people,” he said.
Sonko further stated that continued reliance on military solutions should be reconsidered, urging a shift toward dialogue and cooperation in resolving international disputes. He emphasized that unilateral interventions by powerful nations should give way to approaches that respect the sovereignty and independent choices of states.
He concluded that sustainable peace can only be achieved through negotiation rather than military confrontation, given the far-reaching consequences of modern conflicts on global stability.
body_fr:
12 avril 2026 - Le Premier ministre sénégalais, Ousmane Sonko, a vivement critiqué les récentes interventions militaires occidentales, affirmant qu'elles ont contribué à l'instabilité mondiale plutôt qu'à la paix. Ses remarques ont été prononcées lors d'une conférence internationale sur la souveraineté des États tenue à Dakar le 9 avril 2026.
S'exprimant lors du forum, Sonko a affirmé que les campagnes militaires récentes et historiques menées par les puissances occidentales n'ont pas réussi à atteindre leurs objectifs déclarés et ont au contraire entraîné des conséquences politiques et humanitaires à long terme dans plusieurs régions.
Il a cité les conflits du Vietnam, de l’Irak, de l’Afghanistan, de la Libye et de la Syrie comme exemples de ce qu’il a décrit comme des tentatives infructueuses de remodeler les résultats politiques par la force militaire.
Selon le Premier ministre, une dynamique similaire est désormais observée dans les tensions actuelles impliquant l'Iran, où la pression militaire n'a pas produit les résultats politiques escomptés. Il a suggéré qu'en dépit de l'escalade de la confrontation, l'engagement diplomatique devient progressivement la voie privilégiée par les parties concernées.
"L'objectif de renverser le régime iranien n'a pas été atteint. Il existe toujours et est, à certains égards, devenu plus fort qu'avant", a déclaré Sonko lors de son discours.
Le Premier ministre a également directement critiqué le président américain Donald Trump, le liant à ce qu’il a qualifié de politique mondiale déstabilisatrice. Il a fait valoir que la trajectoire actuelle des relations internationales reflète un modèle selon lequel des États puissants imposent des décisions sous la bannière de la démocratie, souvent sans égard à la souveraineté nationale.
"Donald Trump n'est pas une personne qui veut la paix. C'est une personne qui souhaite perturber la stabilité des gens", a-t-il déclaré.
Sonko a en outre déclaré que le recours continu aux solutions militaires devrait être reconsidéré, appelant à une évolution vers le dialogue et la coopération dans la résolution des différends internationaux. Il a souligné que les interventions unilatérales des nations puissantes devraient céder la place à des approches respectueuses de la souveraineté et des choix indépendants des États.
Il a conclu qu’une paix durable ne peut être obtenue que par la négociation plutôt que par la confrontation militaire, compte tenu des conséquences considérables des conflits modernes sur la stabilité mondiale.

title_en: Danish Companies Target Uganda’s Agriculture and Manufacturing Sectors as Investment Ties Deepen
excerpt_en: Kampala April 9, 2026 - Denmark is stepping up efforts to expand its commercial footprint in Uganda, with a renewed focus on attracting investment and supporting Danish firms already operating in the country, according to Ambassador Signe Winding Alberg. She made the remarks duri
body_en:
Kampala April 9, 2026 - Denmark is stepping up efforts to expand its commercial footprint in Uganda, with a renewed focus on attracting investment and supporting Danish firms already operating in the country, according to Ambassador Signe Winding Alberg.
She made the remarks during a visit to Uganda’s State House Investors Protection Unit, underscoring strengthening bilateral economic relations anchored in trade, investment, and sustainable development.
Alberg highlighted growing Danish interest in sectors such as agriculture, food processing, and safety technologies. She cited examples including a Danish-linked pineapple processing facility that adds value to Ugandan agricultural produce, as well as Fire Express, which is introducing modern fire safety solutions in the country.
“We remain very committed to strengthening the Danish business community here in Uganda to deepen our commercial engagement,” Alberg said. “We have a very active business community that is growing here, and we value Uganda as an investment destination for foreign investors.”

title_en: Burundi Confirms Death of Communications Minister Gabby Bugaga in Road AccidentApril 16, 2026 ; The Government of Burundi has confirmed the death of the Minister of Communications and Information, Gabby Bugaga, who died in a road accident in the early hours of April 16, 2026, in Bujumbura City.
excerpt_en: The announcement was made by government spokesperson Jérôme Niyonzima, who dismissed speculation surrounding the circumstances of the incident and described the death as an accident. According to official information, the minister’s body was discovered at around 2:00 a.m. inside
body_en:
The announcement was made by government spokesperson Jérôme Niyonzima, who dismissed speculation surrounding the circumstances of the incident and described the death as an accident.
According to official information, the minister’s body was discovered at around 2:00 a.m. inside his vehicle, a Toyota Hilux, parked in a palm grove in the Kivoga area near a roadside in Bujumbura.
Authorities noted that the minister was traveling alone at the time of the incident and was not accompanied by security personnel, a situation considered unusual for a senior government official in Burundi.
“The Republic of Burundi is deeply saddened to inform the public and the international community of the sudden death of Minister Gabby Bugaga, who died in a road accident in the early hours of this morning, April 16, 2026,” Niyonzima said in an official statement.
President Évariste Ndayishimiye expressed condolences to the family of the deceased and to the nation, praising the late minister’s public service.
“May God receive him and reward him for the courage, diligence, and dedication he demonstrated in serving the country,” the president said.
Bugaga had previously built a career in journalism at the national broadcaster RTNB before serving in several public institutions, including the Senate and the National Independent Electoral Commission (CENI). He was appointed Minister of Communications and Information in August 2025.

title: Rwanda Among Countries Set to Receive Long-Acting HIV Prevention Drug
excerpt: April 15, 2026 - Rwanda is among a group of countries expected to benefit from the expanded rollout of a long-acting HIV prevention drug as part of a global initiative led by the United States and the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria. The program aims to make t
title_en: Rwanda Among Countries Set to Receive Long-Acting HIV Prevention Drug
excerpt_en: April 15, 2026 - Rwanda is among a group of countries expected to benefit from the expanded rollout of a long-acting HIV prevention drug as part of a global initiative led by the United States and the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria. The program aims to make t
body_en:
April 15, 2026 - Rwanda is among a group of countries expected to benefit from the expanded rollout of a long-acting HIV prevention drug as part of a global initiative led by the United States and the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria.
The program aims to make the drug, Lenacapavir, accessible to at least three million people by 2028. Developed by Gilead Sciences, the treatment has already been introduced in nine African countries, with plans underway to extend distribution to an additional 12 nations.
Alongside Rwanda, the next phase of the rollout is expected to include countries such as Dominican Republic, Fiji, Indonesia, Morocco, and Thailand.
The Global Fund signed an agreement with Gilead in July 2025 to supply at least two million doses of the drug over a five-year period to low- and middle-income countries.
Humanitarian organization Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) welcomed the initiative but cautioned that current distribution levels remain insufficient compared to global demand.
Lenacapavir is administered via injection twice a year and is designed to prevent HIV infection by inhibiting the virus’s ability to replicate in the body. Health experts highlight its potential advantage over daily oral preventive treatments, as its long-acting formulation may improve adherence among patients.
Global health stakeholders say the expansion of access to such treatments could play a significant role in reducing new HIV infections, particularly in regions with high prevalence rates.

title: President Kagame Promotes Over 5,700 Police Officers

title_en: President Kagame Promotes Over 5,700 Police Officers
excerpt_en: Kigali, Rwanda April 9, 2026 - Rwandan President Paul Kagame has approved the promotion of 5,741 officers within the Rwanda National Police, in a sweeping move affecting multiple ranks across the institution. According to an official announcement released on Thursday, five senior
body_en:
Kigali, Rwanda April 9, 2026 - Rwandan President Paul Kagame has approved the promotion of 5,741 officers within the Rwanda National Police, in a sweeping move affecting multiple ranks across the institution.
According to an official announcement released on Thursday, five senior officers were elevated to the rank of Commissioner of Police (CP): Emmanuel Karasi, Bertin Mutezintare, Jean Népomucène Mbonyumuvunyi, Barthélemy Rugwizangoga, and Fidèle Mugengana.
Ten officers were promoted to the rank of Assistant Commissioner of Police (ACP), including Claude Bizimana, Adolphe Nyagatare, Rango Ndoli, Callixte Kalisa, Vincent Habintwali Bihigi, Antoine Munyampundu, Faustin Kalimba, Hodali Rwanyindo, Christian Safari, and Alexis Nyamwasa.
The promotions span both senior and junior ranks. Among senior officers, five were elevated from Senior Superintendent of Police (SSP) to Commissioner of Police (CSP), 94 from Superintendent of Police (SP) retained or advanced within their rank, and 161 officers moved from Chief Inspector of Police (CIP) to SP. Additionally, 574 officers were promoted from Inspector of Police (IP) to CIP, while 17 advanced from Assistant Inspector of Police (AIP) to IP.
At the junior level, 282 officers were promoted from Staff Sergeant (S/SGT) to Chief Sergeant (C/SGT), while 763 advanced from Sergeant (SGT) to Staff Sergeant. A total of 1,886 corporals (CPL) were promoted to sergeant, and 1,949 police constables (PC) advanced to corporal.
The Rwanda National Police stated that the promotions are part of ongoing efforts to strengthen institutional capacity and recognize merit within the force.

title: Ndayishimiye Denies Attacks on Rwanda as Cross-Border Security Tensions Persist
excerpt: Bujumbura April 19, 2026 - Burundian President Évariste Ndayishimiye has reiterated that no armed attacks have been launched against Rwanda from Burundian territory, rejecting long-standing accusations from Kigali regarding cross-border militancy. In an interview with Yaga Burund
title_en: Ndayishimiye Denies Attacks on Rwanda as Cross-Border Security Tensions Persist
excerpt_en: Bujumbura April 19, 2026 - Burundian President Évariste Ndayishimiye has reiterated that no armed attacks have been launched against Rwanda from Burundian territory, rejecting long-standing accusations from Kigali regarding cross-border militancy. In an interview with Yaga Burund
body_en:
Bujumbura April 19, 2026 - Burundian President Évariste Ndayishimiye has reiterated that no armed attacks have been launched against Rwanda from Burundian territory, rejecting long-standing accusations from Kigali regarding cross-border militancy.
In an interview with Yaga Burundi, Ndayishimiye accused Rwanda of tolerating elements that he claims seek to destabilize Burundi, while insisting that Burundi does not permit its territory to be used for attacks against its neighbor.
“Rwanda does not agree with the criminals and bad people who come to attack Burundi. In other words, Rwanda opens the door for them, and they come to attack Burundi. Burundi never opens the door for someone who goes to attack Rwanda,” he said.
The Burundian leader suggested that greater border restrictions would be necessary to prevent infiltration, arguing that open movement across the frontier creates security risks. He questioned the effectiveness of current border controls, saying that individuals can sometimes evade security agencies and carry out attacks.
“If we opened them, you would find that they were attacking you right here,” he added, referring to the possibility of unrestricted movement between the two countries.
Since late 2023, Rwanda has repeatedly rejected allegations of supporting armed groups targeting Burundi, maintaining that it does not collaborate with organizations opposed to the Burundian government.
However, multiple armed incidents over the past years have been attributed by Rwandan authorities to groups such as the FLN, which Kigali says have operated from the Kibira forest area in Burundi. These include attacks in 2018 and 2019 in Nyaruguru and Nyamagabe districts, as well as an incident in May 2021 in Bweyeye Sector, Rusizi District.
Rwandan military officials have previously stated that FLN fighters involved in cross-border attacks were pushed back into Burundi through the Ruhwa River area, and that some of their equipment carried markings associated with Burundian military structures-an allegation Bujumbura has consistently denied.
Further incidents have also been reported in subsequent years, including an attack in Nyungwe Park in May 2022 that left civilians dead, according to Rwandan authorities.
The FLN and other armed groups, including RED-Tabara, have also been linked to operations in the wider Great Lakes region. In 2020, RED-Tabara fighters were captured in Rwanda after crossing from the Democratic Republic of Congo and later handed over to Burundi in 2021.
United Nations expert reports have previously indicated that relations between Rwanda and Burundi deteriorated further in late 2023, with allegations of indirect cooperation between Burundi and certain armed groups hostile to Rwanda, including the FLN and FDLR. Both Kigali and Bujumbura have denied supporting destabilization efforts against each other.
As tensions persist, both governments continue to publicly affirm their commitment to national security while exchanging accusations over the activities of armed groups operating in border regions.
Conclusion
The period from April 6 to 19, 2026, highlights a region shaped by a complex interplay of diplomatic engagement, historical remembrance, and persistent security challenges across East and Central Africa. Rwanda emerged as an active diplomatic actor, advancing bilateral cooperation through new agreements with partners such as Chad and Oman, reinforcing its strategic positioning on both the African and global stage.
However, these gains were tempered by continued instability in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, which remains a central concern for regional security. The launch of peace talks in Switzerland between the Congolese government and the AFC/M23 coalition marked a cautious step forward, but negotiations were overshadowed by mutual accusations of renewed hostilities, including drone strikes and civilian casualties. While confidence-building measures-such as the release of more than 400 detainees and the establishment of a ceasefire monitoring mechanism-offer tentative progress, deep divisions over territorial control, governance, and humanitarian access continue to undermine prospects for a durable settlement.
At the same time, Rwanda commemorated the 32nd anniversary of the Genocide against the Tutsi, a solemn moment that underscored the enduring importance of remembrance, national unity, and vigilance against hate speech and genocide ideology. These commemorations, observed both domestically and internationally, reaffirmed a collective commitment to preventing future atrocities. Nonetheless, reports of continued mobilization and ideological influence by the FDLR near border areas highlight the persistence of extremist narratives that threaten long-term stability.
Beyond the Great Lakes region, broader continental dynamics reflected a growing call for reform and self-determination. Advocacy for a more effective African Union, alongside debates on global representation and structural inequalities, signals renewed momentum toward strengthening Africa’s voice in international affairs. Yet, political developments such as constitutional reforms in Zimbabwe and leadership disruptions in Burundi illustrate the ongoing volatility that continues to shape governance across the continent.
In sum, the first half of April 2026 presents a region at a crossroads-marked by meaningful diplomatic and institutional progress, yet still constrained by entrenched conflicts and fragile political transitions. Rwanda’s trajectory reflects both the opportunities and limitations of this broader context, as sustained peace and stability will depend on continued regional cooperation, credible governance frameworks, and the ability to address the root causes of conflict.
By Jeff Buleli

Bujumbura April 19, 2026 - Burundian President Évariste Ndayishimiye has reiterated that no armed attacks have been launched against Rwanda from Burundian territory, rejecting long-standing accusations from Kigali regarding cross-border militancy.
In an interview with Yaga Burundi, Ndayishimiye accused Rwanda of tolerating elements that he claims seek to destabilize Burundi, while insisting that Burundi does not permit its territory to be used for attacks against its neighbor.
“Rwanda does not agree with the criminals and bad people who come to attack Burundi. In other words, Rwanda opens the door for them, and they come to attack Burundi. Burundi never opens the door for someone who goes to attack Rwanda,” he said.
The Burundian leader suggested that greater border restrictions would be necessary to prevent infiltration, arguing that open movement across the frontier creates security risks. He questioned the effectiveness of current border controls, saying that individuals can sometimes evade security agencies and carry out attacks.
“If we opened them, you would find that they were attacking you right here,” he added, referring to the possibility of unrestricted movement between the two countries.
Since late 2023, Rwanda has repeatedly rejected allegations of supporting armed groups targeting Burundi, maintaining that it does not collaborate with organizations opposed to the Burundian government.
However, multiple armed incidents over the past years have been attributed by Rwandan authorities to groups such as the FLN, which Kigali says have operated from the Kibira forest area in Burundi. These include attacks in 2018 and 2019 in Nyaruguru and Nyamagabe districts, as well as an incident in May 2021 in Bweyeye Sector, Rusizi District.
Rwandan military officials have previously stated that FLN fighters involved in cross-border attacks were pushed back into Burundi through the Ruhwa River area, and that some of their equipment carried markings associated with Burundian military structures-an allegation Bujumbura has consistently denied.
Further incidents have also been reported in subsequent years, including an attack in Nyungwe Park in May 2022 that left civilians dead, according to Rwandan authorities.
The FLN and other armed groups, including RED-Tabara, have also been linked to operations in the wider Great Lakes region. In 2020, RED-Tabara fighters were captured in Rwanda after crossing from the Democratic Republic of Congo and later handed over to Burundi in 2021.
United Nations expert reports have previously indicated that relations between Rwanda and Burundi deteriorated further in late 2023, with allegations of indirect cooperation between Burundi and certain armed groups hostile to Rwanda, including the FLN and FDLR. Both Kigali and Bujumbura have denied supporting destabilization efforts against each other.
As tensions persist, both governments continue to publicly affirm their commitment to national security while exchanging accusations over the activities of armed groups operating in border regions.
Conclusion
The period from April 6 to 19, 2026, highlights a region shaped by a complex interplay of diplomatic engagement, historical remembrance, and persistent security challenges across East and Central Africa. Rwanda emerged as an active diplomatic actor, advancing bilateral cooperation through new agreements with partners such as Chad and Oman, reinforcing its strategic positioning on both the African and global stage.
However, these gains were tempered by continued instability in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, which remains a central concern for regional security. The launch of peace talks in Switzerland between the Congolese government and the AFC/M23 coalition marked a cautious step forward, but negotiations were overshadowed by mutual accusations of renewed hostilities, including drone strikes and civilian casualties. While confidence-building measures-such as the release of more than 400 detainees and the establishment of a ceasefire monitoring mechanism-offer tentative progress, deep divisions over territorial control, governance, and humanitarian access continue to undermine prospects for a durable settlement.
At the same time, Rwanda commemorated the 32nd anniversary of the Genocide against the Tutsi, a solemn moment that underscored the enduring importance of remembrance, national unity, and vigilance against hate speech and genocide ideology. These commemorations, observed both domestically and internationally, reaffirmed a collective commitment to preventing future atrocities. Nonetheless, reports of continued mobilization and ideological influence by the FDLR near border areas highlight the persistence of extremist narratives that threaten long-term stability.
Beyond the Great Lakes region, broader continental dynamics reflected a growing call for reform and self-determination. Advocacy for a more effective African Union, alongside debates on global representation and structural inequalities, signals renewed momentum toward strengthening Africa’s voice in international affairs. Yet, political developments such as constitutional reforms in Zimbabwe and leadership disruptions in Burundi illustrate the ongoing volatility that continues to shape governance across the continent.
In sum, the first half of April 2026 presents a region at a crossroads-marked by meaningful diplomatic and institutional progress, yet still constrained by entrenched conflicts and fragile political transitions. Rwanda’s trajectory reflects both the opportunities and limitations of this broader context, as sustained peace and stability will depend on continued regional cooperation, credible governance frameworks, and the ability to address the root causes of conflict.

title: Uganda Links Teenage Pregnancies to Rising Fistula Cases, Expands Maternal Health Response
excerpt: Kampala April 19, 2026 - Uganda’s Ministry of Health has attributed the continued rise in obstetric fistula cases to high teenage pregnancy rates and delays in accessing emergency obstetric care, warning that most of the complications are preventable with timely medical intervent
title_en: Uganda Links Teenage Pregnancies to Rising Fistula Cases, Expands Maternal Health Response
excerpt_en: Kampala April 19, 2026 - Uganda’s Ministry of Health has attributed the continued rise in obstetric fistula cases to high teenage pregnancy rates and delays in accessing emergency obstetric care, warning that most of the complications are preventable with timely medical intervent
body_en:
Kampala April 19, 2026 - Uganda’s Ministry of Health has attributed the continued rise in obstetric fistula cases to high teenage pregnancy rates and delays in accessing emergency obstetric care, warning that most of the complications are preventable with timely medical intervention.
Commissioner for Maternal and Child Health Richard Mugahi said one in four pregnant women in Uganda is a teenager, with some as young as 12 to 14 years old, a trend he linked directly to increased childbirth complications.
“These are young girls whose bodies are not yet ready to carry a pregnancy, and this leads to complications like fistula, death of the baby, or even the mother,” Mugahi said.
Obstetric fistula, a severe childbirth injury caused by prolonged or obstructed labour, remains a significant health challenge in underserved communities, often leaving survivors with long-term physical and social consequences.
Mugahi noted that limited access to sexual and reproductive health information is a key driver of early pregnancies, calling for stronger education and awareness programs targeting adolescents.
Beyond social factors, he also highlighted systemic gaps in the health system, particularly delays in referring mothers with complications from lower-level facilities to higher-level care centres. He warned that such delays often result in life-threatening conditions, including uterine rupture, fistula, or death.
In response, the government-working with the United Nations Population Fund and the Government of Iceland-is scaling up maternal health interventions in high-burden regions.
These include the construction of a Health Centre IV in Namayingo District, recruitment of additional health workers, improved medical equipment supply, and enhanced training for emergency obstetric care.
The programme also supports surgical repair for fistula survivors and provides reintegration support, including income-generating activities aimed at helping affected women rebuild their lives.
“Addressing both the social drivers and the health system gaps is critical if we are to eliminate fistula in Uganda,” Mugahi said.
The initiative was formalized during a signing ceremony in Kampala involving Iceland’s Head of Mission Hildigunnur Engilbertsdóttir and Kristine Blokhus.
The programme will focus on regions including Acholi, West Nile, Bukedi, Karamoja, and Busoga, targeting improvements in adolescent health education, reproductive health services, and response mechanisms for gender-based violence.
Engilbertsdóttir described obstetric fistula as both a public health and human rights issue, emphasizing that it reflects broader gaps in health system capacity.
“Fistula happens when a health system lacks the capacity to meet the full spectrum of reproductive health needs of women and girls. It is a human rights and gender equality issue,” she said.
Officials say the combined interventions are expected to strengthen maternal healthcare delivery, reduce preventable injuries, and improve outcomes for vulnerable women and girls across Uganda.

title: IGP Byakagaba Transfers 433 Police Officers in Major Nationwide Reshuffle
excerpt: Kampala April 17, 2026 - The Inspector General of Police, Abas Byakagaba, has announced a major reshuffle involving 433 officers across the Uganda Police Force, with immediate effect. The transfers affect multiple directorates and units, including Welfare, Production and Sports;
title_en: IGP Byakagaba Transfers 433 Police Officers in Major Nationwide Reshuffle
excerpt_en: Kampala April 17, 2026 - The Inspector General of Police, Abas Byakagaba, has announced a major reshuffle involving 433 officers across the Uganda Police Force, with immediate effect. The transfers affect multiple directorates and units, including Welfare, Production and Sports;
body_en:
Kampala April 17, 2026 - The Inspector General of Police, Abas Byakagaba, has announced a major reshuffle involving 433 officers across the Uganda Police Force, with immediate effect.
The transfers affect multiple directorates and units, including Welfare, Production and Sports; Human Resources Administration; the Chief Political Commissariat; Human Resource Development; Fire and Rescue Services; the Professional Standards Unit; Traffic Police; and the Criminal Investigations Directorate (CID).
Senior officers have been reassigned to strategic positions, including postings to the Inspector General’s office, Interpol, legal services, finance, and specialized operational units.
Among the key appointments, Senior Commissioner of Police Geoffrey Chombe has been posted to the Inspector General’s office, while Commissioner Alison Agaba has been assigned to Interpol. Commissioner John William Okalany has been deployed to the Human Rights and Legal Services Directorate, and Commissioner Richard Arumadri has been transferred to the Finance Department.
Assistant Commissioner of Police Richard Mugwisagye has been named Deputy Commander of the Professional Standards Unit.
The reshuffle also includes officers recently trained at the Oliver Reginald Tambo Leadership School in Kaweweta, with several receiving new postings across regions. Former Kampala Central Police Station operations commander, Assistant Superintendent of Police Ivan Nduhura, has been deployed to West Nile as Police Legal Officer.
Other notable changes include Commissioner Enock Baine, now heading the Police Duty Free Scheme and Supermarkets, and Assistant Commissioner Grace Ewiku, appointed Head of Crop Production in the Agriculture Police.
In specialized units, Senior Superintendent Bashir Siriba has been appointed Coordinator of the National Drowning Prevention Program within the Marine Unit, while Senior Superintendent Ahmed Kimera Seguya has been moved to the Railways Unit as Head of Operations.
Regional commands have also been significantly affected. Senior Superintendent Diana Nyamisango has been appointed Regional Police Commander for Katonga Region, while other officers have been reassigned across Kigezi, Busoga East, Kidepo, and other regional formations.
In the Traffic Directorate, multiple senior officers have been redeployed, including new appointments in vehicle inspection and transport monitoring sections.
The reshuffle also includes officers in the CID, where 132 personnel have been moved. Assistant Commissioner Moses Taremwa has been appointed Acting Commissioner of the Trafficking in Persons Department, while Assistant Commissioner Peter Muwonge has been reassigned to inspection duties at CID headquarters in Kibuli. Assistant Commissioner Charles Mutungi has been posted to the Uganda Anti-Money Laundering Task Force.
Authorities say the changes are part of ongoing efforts to strengthen efficiency, accountability, and operational effectiveness within the police force, following leadership training and institutional reviews.

title: Les qualifications pour la Coupe du monde de la RDC alimentent les efforts renouvelés de Tshisekedi pour reconquérir les territoires de l’Est
excerpt: Kinshasa, 6 avril 2026 - Le président Félix Tshisekedi a exprimé un regain d'optimisme quant à la reprise des territoires détenus par l'AFC/M23 dans l'est de la République démocratique du Congo, liant sa confiance à la vague d'unité nationale suscitée par la récente qualification du pays à la Coupe du monde. T
title_en: DRC World Cup Qualification Fuels Tshisekedi’s Renewed Push to Reclaim Eastern Territories
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, 6 April 2026 - President Félix Tshisekedi has expressed renewed optimism about retaking territories held by the AFC/M23 in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, linking his confidence to a wave of national unity sparked by the country’s recent World Cup qualification. T
body_en:
Kinshasa, 6 April 2026 - President Félix Tshisekedi has expressed renewed optimism about retaking territories held by the AFC/M23 in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, linking his confidence to a wave of national unity sparked by the country’s recent World Cup qualification.
The Congolese national football team secured its place in the tournament on 31 March with a narrow 1-0 victory over Jamaica national football team, marking the country’s first qualification in 52 years. Celebrations erupted nationwide, including in conflict-affected areas such as Goma, where residents joined in festivities despite ongoing control by rebel forces.
Speaking on 5 April during a ceremony in Kinshasa honoring the national team, Tshisekedi pointed to the celebrations in the east as a sign of enduring national cohesion. “You have seen the images. In these areas controlled by the enemy there is joy, and we will soon take them back because of this strength, because of this pride,” he said.
The president’s remarks come amid continued tensions with the AFC/M23, which maintains control over parts of North and South Kivu provinces. The group has rejected any suggestion of withdrawal, warning that it would respond forcefully to any military offensive.
Previous attempts by government forces to retake lost territories have largely been unsuccessful, with the AFC/M23 often managing to repel advances and, in some cases, expand its positions. International observers continue to emphasize the need for a political solution to the conflict.
Peace talks between Kinshasa and the AFC/M23 are expected to resume later this month, with discussions set to take place in Switzerland after being relocated from Doha.
Despite these developments, both sides appear to be moving cautiously, raising concerns that without tangible political progress, hostilities could reignite and intensify in the coming weeks.
body_fr:
Kinshasa, 6 avril 2026 - Le président Félix Tshisekedi a exprimé un regain d'optimisme quant à la reprise des territoires détenus par l'AFC/M23 dans l'est de la République démocratique du Congo, liant sa confiance à la vague d'unité nationale suscitée par la récente qualification du pays à la Coupe du monde.
L’équipe nationale congolaise de football a assuré sa place dans le tournoi le 31 mars grâce à une victoire serrée 1-0 contre l’équipe nationale de football de la Jamaïque, marquant la première qualification du pays en 52 ans. Des célébrations ont eu lieu dans tout le pays, y compris dans les zones touchées par le conflit, comme Goma, où les habitants se sont joints aux festivités malgré le contrôle continu des forces rebelles.
S'exprimant le 5 avril lors d'une cérémonie à Kinshasa en l'honneur de l'équipe nationale, Tshisekedi a qualifié les célébrations dans l'Est de signe d'une cohésion nationale durable. "Vous avez vu les images. Dans ces zones contrôlées par l'ennemi, il y a de la joie, et nous les reprendrons bientôt à cause de cette force, à cause de cette fierté", a-t-il déclaré.
Les remarques du président interviennent dans un contexte de tensions persistantes avec l’AFC/M23, qui maintient le contrôle de certaines parties des provinces du Nord et du Sud-Kivu. Le groupe a rejeté toute suggestion de retrait, avertissant qu'il répondrait avec force à toute offensive militaire.
Les précédentes tentatives des forces gouvernementales pour reprendre les territoires perdus ont largement échoué, l’AFC/M23 parvenant souvent à repousser les avancées et, dans certains cas, à étendre ses positions. Les observateurs internationaux continuent de souligner la nécessité d'une solution politique au conflit.
Les pourparlers de paix entre Kinshasa et l'AFC/M23 devraient reprendre plus tard ce mois-ci, les discussions devant avoir lieu en Suisse après avoir été transférées de Doha.
Malgré ces évolutions, les deux parties semblent agir avec prudence, ce qui fait craindre que sans progrès politiques tangibles, les hostilités pourraient reprendre et s’intensifier dans les semaines à venir.

title: Le député élu Fungaroo appelle à l'unité de l'opposition avant la 12e législature
excerpt: Kampala, le 6 avril 2026 - Hassan Kaps Fungaroo, député élu du comté d'Obongi, a appelé à une plus grande unité entre les partis d'opposition et a exhorté les Ougandais à rester optimistes quant à la prochaine 12e législature, qui devrait prendre forme en mai 2026. S'exprimant lors de la matinée B du NBS
title_en: MP-Elect Fungaroo Urges Opposition Unity Ahead of 12th Parliament
excerpt_en: Kampala April 6, 2026 - Obongi County Member of Parliament-elect Hassan Kaps Fungaroo has called for greater unity among opposition parties and urged Ugandans to remain optimistic about the incoming 12th Parliament, set to take shape in May 2026. Speaking during the NBS Morning B
body_en:
Kampala April 6, 2026 - Obongi County Member of Parliament-elect Hassan Kaps Fungaroo has called for greater unity among opposition parties and urged Ugandans to remain optimistic about the incoming 12th Parliament, set to take shape in May 2026.
Speaking during the NBS Morning Breeze program on Monday, the Forum for Democratic Change (FDC) politician expressed confidence that the new legislature would improve on the performance of its predecessor.
“I want to assure Ugandans that the 12th Parliament will be better. My optimism is that as human beings, we always seek to improve. People should have hope in the 12th Parliament and not dismiss it,” Fungaroo said.
He emphasized the importance of the relationship between the Executive and Parliament, describing it as central to effective governance. Fungaroo pointed to the role of the presidency under Yoweri Kaguta Museveni in shaping how Parliament operates.
“How does the Executive look at Parliament? How will the President see Parliament? That’s the big picture,” he noted.
Fungaroo also highlighted internal divisions within the opposition during the 11th Parliament, which he said weakened its ability to hold the government accountable. He cited tensions among opposition parties, particularly toward the National Unity Platform (NUP), as a key challenge.
“What I saw in the 11th Parliament was some form of resentment from some Opposition parties towards NUP. That was a mistake. We never accepted certain realities and this led to a weaker opposition,” he said.
The MP-elect reaffirmed his commitment to remaining in the opposition, stressing the need to strengthen oversight and accountability mechanisms.
“I have chosen to be in the Opposition offering checks and balances,” he added.
Fungaroo further called for a collaborative approach within the new Parliament, urging citizens to support lawmakers in their legislative work.
“In the 12th Parliament, we are going to work as a team, and we need the support of the citizens of Uganda,” he said.
Uganda’s 12th Parliament is expected to comprise 556 Members of Parliament, including representatives of special interest groups. The legislature will be dominated by the ruling National Resistance Movement (NRM), alongside independents and members from parties such as NUP, the Uganda People’s Congress (UPC), FDC, the Democratic Party (DP), the People’s Front for Freedom (PFF), and the Alliance for National Transformation (ANT).
The size of the House has sparked renewed debate over its sustainability, with critics warning that maintaining more than 550 MPs could strain public finances. Others have questioned whether such numbers are necessary for effective representation.
Analysts have also raised concerns about the capacity of the incoming Parliament, noting that nearly 80 percent of its members are newcomers. Some observers warn that the high turnover could affect the quality of debate and legislative scrutiny if not supported by strong institutional frameworks and a clear commitment to public service.
body_fr:
Kampala, le 6 avril 2026 - Hassan Kaps Fungaroo, député élu du comté d'Obongi, a appelé à une plus grande unité entre les partis d'opposition et a exhorté les Ougandais à rester optimistes quant à la prochaine 12e législature, qui devrait prendre forme en mai 2026.
S'exprimant lundi lors de l'émission Morning Breeze du NBS, le politicien du Forum pour le changement démocratique (FDC) s'est dit convaincu que la nouvelle législature améliorerait les performances de son prédécesseur.
"Je veux assurer aux Ougandais que le 12ème Parlement sera meilleur. Mon optimisme est qu'en tant qu'êtres humains, nous cherchons toujours à nous améliorer. Les gens devraient avoir de l'espoir dans le 12ème Parlement et ne pas le rejeter", a déclaré Fungaroo.
Il a souligné l'importance de la relation entre l'exécutif et le Parlement, la décrivant comme essentielle à une gouvernance efficace. Fungaroo a souligné le rôle de la présidence sous Yoweri Kaguta Museveni dans l'élaboration du fonctionnement du Parlement.
"Comment l'Exécutif regarde-t-il le Parlement ? Comment le Président verra-t-il le Parlement ? C'est une vue d'ensemble", a-t-il noté.
Fungaroo a également souligné les divisions internes au sein de l'opposition au cours de la 11e législature, qui, selon lui, ont affaibli sa capacité à demander des comptes au gouvernement. Il a cité les tensions entre les partis d'opposition, en particulier à l'égard de la Plateforme d'unité nationale (NUP), comme un défi majeur.
"Ce que j'ai vu lors de la 11e législature, c'est une forme de ressentiment de la part de certains partis d'opposition à l'égard du NUP. C'était une erreur. Nous n'avons jamais accepté certaines réalités et cela a conduit à une opposition plus faible", a-t-il déclaré.
Le député élu a réaffirmé son engagement à rester dans l'opposition, soulignant la nécessité de renforcer les mécanismes de contrôle et de responsabilisation.
« J’ai choisi d’être dans l’opposition en proposant des freins et contrepoids », a-t-il ajouté.
Fungaroo a en outre appelé à une approche collaborative au sein du nouveau Parlement, exhortant les citoyens à soutenir les législateurs dans leur travail législatif.
« Au cours de la 12e législature, nous allons travailler en équipe et nous avons besoin du soutien des citoyens ougandais », a-t-il déclaré.
Le 12e Parlement ougandais devrait comprendre 556 députés, dont des représentants de groupes d’intérêts spéciaux. La législature sera dominée par le Mouvement de résistance nationale (NRM) au pouvoir, aux côtés d'indépendants et de membres de partis tels que le NUP, le Congrès du peuple ougandais (UPC), le FDC, le Parti démocrate (DP), le Front populaire pour la liberté (PFF) et l'Alliance pour la transformation nationale (ANT).
La taille de la Chambre a suscité un nouveau débat sur sa viabilité, les critiques avertissant que le maintien de plus de 550 députés pourrait mettre à rude épreuve les finances publiques. D’autres se demandent si de tels chiffres sont nécessaires pour une représentation efficace.
Les analystes ont également exprimé leurs inquiétudes quant à la capacité du nouveau Parlement, notant que près de 80 pour cent de ses membres sont de nouveaux venus. Certains observateurs préviennent que ce roulement élevé pourrait affecter la qualité du débat et du contrôle législatif s’il n’est pas soutenu par des cadres institutionnels solides et un engagement clair en faveur du service public.
