title: Jamaica Praises Rwandan Forces for Post-Cyclone Relief Efforts
excerpt: Kingston, 17 March 2026 – The Jamaican Armed Forces have expressed gratitude to the Rwanda Defence Forces (RDF) for their contribution to recovery efforts following the devastation caused by Cyclone Melissa. The storm, which struck in October 2025, killed 45 people and left more
title_en: Jamaica Praises Rwandan Forces for Post-Cyclone Relief Efforts
excerpt_en: Kingston, 17 March 2026 – The Jamaican Armed Forces have expressed gratitude to the Rwanda Defence Forces (RDF) for their contribution to recovery efforts following the devastation caused by Cyclone Melissa. The storm, which struck in October 2025, killed 45 people and left more
body_en:
Kingston, 17 March 2026 – The Jamaican Armed Forces have expressed gratitude to the Rwanda Defence Forces (RDF) for their contribution to recovery efforts following the devastation caused by Cyclone Melissa.
The storm, which struck in October 2025, killed 45 people and left more than 15 missing, according to humanitarian data. It also damaged 450 schools and over 120,000 homes, affecting more than 626,000 people.
In response, Rwanda deployed 100 military engineers in January 2026 to assist with rebuilding homes and infrastructure in affected areas, including Trelawny and St. James.
In a message shared publicly, the Jamaican military praised the Rwandan troops for their commitment and sacrifice. “We will not forget the work you did during one of the greatest disasters in our recent history,” the statement read.
Officials noted that the presence of the Rwandan forces helped restore hope among affected communities, highlighting the impact of rebuilding efforts on families who had lost their homes.
After completing a two-month mission, the RDF contingent, led by Col Moses Kayigamba, returned to Rwanda on 16 March 2026, where they were received by military leadership in Kigali.
Beyond reconstruction work, the Rwandan team also carried out community service activities, including cleaning and supporting the Blessed Assurance Children’s Home, which cares for children with disabilities.
The mission has been widely seen as a sign of growing cooperation and solidarity between Rwanda and Jamaica in times of crisis.

title: Modeste Bahati Lukwebo Resigns as Second Vice-President of the Senate, Cites Desire to Avoid Power Struggle
excerpt: Kinshasa, March 18, 2026 – Modeste Bahati Lukwebo officially resigned from his position as Second Vice-President of the Senate on Wednesday, March 18, the day after a petition for his removal was filed by Senator Dany Kabongo Bondanya (UDPS) and signed by multiple elected officia
title_en: Modeste Bahati Lukwebo Resigns as Second Vice-President of the Senate, Cites Desire to Avoid Power Struggle
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, March 18, 2026 – Modeste Bahati Lukwebo officially resigned from his position as Second Vice-President of the Senate on Wednesday, March 18, the day after a petition for his removal was filed by Senator Dany Kabongo Bondanya (UDPS) and signed by multiple elected officia
body_en:
Kinshasa, March 18, 2026 – Modeste Bahati Lukwebo officially resigned from his position as Second Vice-President of the Senate on Wednesday, March 18, the day after a petition for his removal was filed by Senator Dany Kabongo Bondanya (UDPS) and signed by multiple elected officials.
In an interview following the submission of his resignation letter to Senate President Jean-Michel Sama Lukonde Kyenge, Bahati Lukwebo explained his decision:
“I figured there was no point in getting into a power struggle with my colleagues. In any case, when you receive a mandate, you have to be prepared to leave it at any time. Because there were misunderstandings following my statement, I thought I had been understood when I said that much work is needed on the individual, their mentality, and their behavior if we hope for the text to be properly implemented.”
The petition and public criticism had raised grievances against Bahati Lukwebo, including allegations of incompetence, lack of respect for institutions, and controversial remarks regarding a potential constitutional revision.
“I thought I had explained myself clearly, but there you have it. By nature, I don’t like confrontation, so I preferred to submit my resignation today,” he added.
The resignation also follows internal distancing within his own political platform, the AFDC-A, whose members had urged him to accept the political consequences of the controversy.
Bahati Lukwebo, who served as Senate President from 2019 to 2024, had held the position of Second Vice-President since the 2023 legislative elections. His departure closes a chapter marked by recent political tension within the Sacred Union of the Nation (USN) coalition.

title: Two Years After Amendment 5: Progress on Infrastructure Amid Persistent Criticism
excerpt: Kinshasa March 18, 2026 – Two years after the renegotiation of the Sicomines agreement between the Democratic Republic of Congo and a consortium of Chinese companies, progress on infrastructure is visible, but criticism from civil society and experts remains. The Congolese govern
title_en: Two Years After Amendment 5: Progress on Infrastructure Amid Persistent Criticism
excerpt_en: Kinshasa March 18, 2026 – Two years after the renegotiation of the Sicomines agreement between the Democratic Republic of Congo and a consortium of Chinese companies, progress on infrastructure is visible, but criticism from civil society and experts remains. The Congolese govern
body_en:
Kinshasa March 18, 2026 – Two years after the renegotiation of the Sicomines agreement between the Democratic Republic of Congo and a consortium of Chinese companies, progress on infrastructure is visible, but criticism from civil society and experts remains. The Congolese government recently announced a technical and financial audit of the project, renewing debate over whether the nation is truly benefiting from its mineral wealth.
A Renegotiation Presented as a Turning Point
Signed in March 2024, Amendment 5 to the original 2008 Sicomines agreement aimed to correct long-standing imbalances. The agreement included increased infrastructure investment, greater involvement of Gécamines in marketing mining production, and a more structured institutional framework for energy projects such as the Busanga Dam.
Visible Infrastructure Gains
Some improvements are evident on the ground. Along National Route 1, between Nguba and Lubudi, formerly muddy roads have been paved, easing travel and trade. Four bridges are under construction on this 142-kilometer section, part of an 850-kilometer road network planned to connect Nguba to Mbuji-Mayi by 2027. Drivers and local traders note positive effects on transportation and commerce.
Persistent Concerns and Discrepancies
Despite these visible gains, many projects remain incomplete, and the cost of some works appears inflated. Reports highlight discrepancies such as Boulevard du 30 Juin in Kinshasa, billed at $142 million despite estimates of $28 million, and Triomphal Boulevard, billed at $61 million versus an actual $5 million.
Financial Mechanisms Under Scrutiny
Analysts also question the financial structure of Amendment 5. The fixed annual contribution formula limits the DRC’s benefits if copper prices rise while exposing the state to losses if prices fall. Critics argue this mechanism diminishes the potential gains from the country’s mineral wealth.
Electricity and Tax Exemptions
The Busanga Dam, a key component of the partnership, primarily powers mining facilities, with minimal electricity directed to households. Tax exemptions granted to Sicomines are estimated to have cost the state hundreds of millions of dollars annually, with projections suggesting losses could reach $7 billion over the remaining life of the project.
Audit Could Clarify Accountability
The government’s announced audit aims to clarify resource allocation, project costs, and financial mechanisms. Experts hope the process will identify irregularities and ensure the partnership delivers tangible benefits to Congolese citizens.
Public Debate Continues
Two years after Amendment 5, the question remains: who truly benefits from the Sicomines partnership? While some infrastructure improvements are apparent, civil society, analysts, and local stakeholders continue to call for renegotiation and greater accountability to ensure the DRC maximizes the value of its mineral resources.

title: Goma and Bukavu’s Judicial System Crumbles Amid Ongoing Eastern DRC Conflict
excerpt: March 14, 2026 – The judicial infrastructure in Goma and Bukavu has been devastated by the ongoing war in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, as the AFC/M23 rebellion, allegedly backed by Rwanda, clashes with government forces. A UN report covering 2025 reveals that the destruc
title_en: Goma and Bukavu’s Judicial System Crumbles Amid Ongoing Eastern DRC Conflict
excerpt_en: March 14, 2026 – The judicial infrastructure in Goma and Bukavu has been devastated by the ongoing war in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, as the AFC/M23 rebellion, allegedly backed by Rwanda, clashes with government forces. A UN report covering 2025 reveals that the destruc
body_en:
March 14, 2026 – The judicial infrastructure in Goma and Bukavu has been devastated by the ongoing war in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, as the AFC/M23 rebellion, allegedly backed by Rwanda, clashes with government forces.
A UN report covering 2025 reveals that the destruction of courts and prisons led to the loss of nearly all case files, including 36 serious crime cases, 11 of which involved conflict-related sexual violence.
The report also highlights a rise in inter-ethnic tensions and hate speech, particularly against the Tutsi and Banyamulenge communities. Thirteen incidents were documented, six of which met international standards for hate speech, directly targeting Kinyarwanda-speaking populations.
Despite these challenges, the UN continued its humanitarian and rights programs. Through the “Digital Identification for All” initiative, a campaign promoting birth registration reached three million people in Kinshasa, registering 174,439 children and increasing the birth registration rate in Masina from 28% in 2023 to 68% in 2025.
The UN also organized 93 training and awareness sessions, reaching nearly 5,000 participants, including civil society representatives, human rights defenders, government officials, media professionals, and security personnel.
Human rights observers warn that abuses continue amid escalating violence in North Kivu and South Kivu, compounded by a shortage of humanitarian aid. Civilians remain at risk as hostilities persist, including reports of drone strikes. The government denies targeting civilians.
On the diplomatic front, the Washington process is addressing tensions between Kinshasa and Kigali, while the Doha process focuses on resolving the conflict with AFC/M23. Despite formal progress, both initiatives face obstacles in producing tangible results, fueling mistrust and ongoing fighting.

March 14, 2026 – The judicial infrastructure in Goma and Bukavu has been devastated by the ongoing war in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, as the AFC/M23 rebellion, allegedly backed by Rwanda, clashes with government forces.
A UN report covering 2025 reveals that the destruction of courts and prisons led to the loss of nearly all case files, including 36 serious crime cases, 11 of which involved conflict-related sexual violence.
The report also highlights a rise in inter-ethnic tensions and hate speech, particularly against the Tutsi and Banyamulenge communities. Thirteen incidents were documented, six of which met international standards for hate speech, directly targeting Kinyarwanda-speaking populations.
Despite these challenges, the UN continued its humanitarian and rights programs. Through the “Digital Identification for All” initiative, a campaign promoting birth registration reached three million people in Kinshasa, registering 174,439 children and increasing the birth registration rate in Masina from 28% in 2023 to 68% in 2025.
The UN also organized 93 training and awareness sessions, reaching nearly 5,000 participants, including civil society representatives, human rights defenders, government officials, media professionals, and security personnel.
Human rights observers warn that abuses continue amid escalating violence in North Kivu and South Kivu, compounded by a shortage of humanitarian aid. Civilians remain at risk as hostilities persist, including reports of drone strikes. The government denies targeting civilians.
On the diplomatic front, the Washington process is addressing tensions between Kinshasa and Kigali, while the Doha process focuses on resolving the conflict with AFC/M23. Despite formal progress, both initiatives face obstacles in producing tangible results, fueling mistrust and ongoing fighting.

Walikale March 11, 2026 — Heavy clashes erupted Wednesday morning, March 11, in Mikumbi, located in the Luberike area of Walikale Territory, between the Armed Forces of the DRC (FARDC), supported by Wazalendo militia, and AFC/M23 rebels.
The confrontation reportedly began around 9:00 a.m. after an attack by AFC/M23 forces on government positions. The exchange of fire has suspended traffic on the Mungazi-Kashebere road, a vital route in the region.
Fighting continued in the vicinity of Mikumbi until early afternoon. Local authorities and security sources warned civilians to remain vigilant and avoid the area while the situation develops.

title: Several Civilians Killed and Village Burned in Major ADF Attack in Babesua
excerpt: Mambasa, Ituri March 17, 2026 – Islamist militants from the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) carried out a deadly attack on the evening of March 16 in Babesua, a village 12 kilometers from Badengaido, in Ituri province. At least ten civilians were killed, and numerous homes and veh
title_en: Several Civilians Killed and Village Burned in Major ADF Attack in Babesua
excerpt_en: Mambasa, Ituri March 17, 2026 – Islamist militants from the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) carried out a deadly attack on the evening of March 16 in Babesua, a village 12 kilometers from Badengaido, in Ituri province. At least ten civilians were killed, and numerous homes and veh
body_en:
Mambasa, Ituri March 17, 2026 – Islamist militants from the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) carried out a deadly attack on the evening of March 16 in Babesua, a village 12 kilometers from Badengaido, in Ituri province. At least ten civilians were killed, and numerous homes and vehicles were burned.
Journalists on the scene reported unbearable images of bodies lying on the ground and the village completely destroyed. The attack also targeted rangers of the Okapi Wildlife Reserve (RFO), some of whom sought refuge inside the forest.
The New Congolese Civil Society has called on authorities to resume joint FARDC-UPDF operations in the area, citing the vast territory of Mambasa (covering 54% of Ituri) and the limited presence of soldiers.
This attack comes days after another ADF assault on the Muchacha and Mavuvu mining sites on the night of March 11–12, which killed at least 17 people. The Islamic State claimed responsibility, releasing images showing burning trucks, tractors, and camps.
The Muchacha region connects to Badengaido, Niania, and the Okapi Wildlife Reserve, forming part of the Kivu-Kinshasa Green Corridor, a strategic route supplying Kisangani and Kinshasa with essential agricultural products.

title: Rwanda Delivers Presidential Message to Senegal Amid OIF Diplomacy
excerpt: Dakar, 18 March 2026 – Rwanda’s Minister of Sports, Nelly Mukazayire, has delivered a message from President Paul Kagame to Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye during an official visit aimed at strengthening bilateral and multilateral cooperation. According to Senegal’s pr
title_en: Rwanda Delivers Presidential Message to Senegal Amid OIF Diplomacy
excerpt_en: Dakar, 18 March 2026 – Rwanda’s Minister of Sports, Nelly Mukazayire, has delivered a message from President Paul Kagame to Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye during an official visit aimed at strengthening bilateral and multilateral cooperation. According to Senegal’s pr
body_en:
Dakar, 18 March 2026 – Rwanda’s Minister of Sports, Nelly Mukazayire, has delivered a message from President Paul Kagame to Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye during an official visit aimed at strengthening bilateral and multilateral cooperation.
According to Senegal’s presidency, the meeting focused on shared priorities within the Organisation internationale de la Francophonie (OIF), particularly in the areas of youth and economic development.
Discussions also highlighted efforts to support the candidacy of Louise Mushikiwabo for another term as Secretary-General of the OIF. Rwanda has been actively engaging partners to back her re-election bid.
Prior to her visit to Senegal, Minister Mukazayire traveled to Mauritania, where she met President Mohamed Ould Cheikh El Ghazouani to seek support for the same candidacy.
President Kagame re-nominated Mushikiwabo in January 2026. She has led the OIF since 2019 and began her second term in November 2022, positioning her for a potential third term.
Rwanda and Senegal maintain longstanding diplomatic ties, reinforced by regular high-level exchanges. In recent months, both countries have signed cooperation agreements covering sectors such as agriculture, health, and development.
The latest diplomatic engagement underscores Rwanda’s continued efforts to consolidate regional and international partnerships, particularly within Francophone institutions.

title: Fitch Affirms Rwanda’s Economic Outlook Despite Regional Tensions
excerpt: Kigali, 14 March 2026 – Fitch Ratings, the American-British credit rating agency, has reaffirmed confidence in Rwanda’s economy, maintaining its ‘B+ rating with a stable outlook’ and projecting continued growth despite regional security and political challenges. In its latest ass
title_en: Fitch Affirms Rwanda’s Economic Outlook Despite Regional Tensions
excerpt_en: Kigali, 14 March 2026 – Fitch Ratings, the American-British credit rating agency, has reaffirmed confidence in Rwanda’s economy, maintaining its ‘B+ rating with a stable outlook’ and projecting continued growth despite regional security and political challenges. In its latest ass
body_en:
Kigali, 14 March 2026 – Fitch Ratings, the American-British credit rating agency, has reaffirmed confidence in Rwanda’s economy, maintaining its ‘B+ rating with a stable outlook’ and projecting continued growth despite regional security and political challenges.
In its latest assessment released on 13 March 2026, Fitch indicated that Rwanda’s economy is expected to remain resilient, with growth projected to exceed 7% in the 2026/2027 fiscal year.
The agency acknowledged that earlier concerns over reduced external financing, driven by regional tensions and strained diplomatic relations with countries such as the United Kingdom, Canada, and Belgium, had weighed on the outlook. However, it noted that confidence has rebounded since April 2025.
According to the report, international partners continued to support Rwanda, providing nearly $1 billion in funding by June 2025. Fitch expects external financing to remain strong, with foreign loans projected to approach $1 billion in 2026/2027, largely on low-interest, long-term terms.
Fitch also downplayed the potential economic impact of recent U.S. sanctions on the Rwandan military, stating that these measures are unlikely to significantly affect the broader economy. “The loans are directed to the government, not the military, and are concessional in nature,” the agency noted.
However, the report highlighted rising public debt, which could reach 79% of GDP by 2027, driven by major investments such as the Bugesera International Airport project and the expansion of RwandAir.
Key sectors expected to sustain growth include infrastructure development, agriculture, and tourism, with the new airport seen as a critical driver of economic expansion.
Fitch further commended Rwanda’s efforts to reduce the budget deficit, noting that fiscal reforms, including the introduction of new tax measures, are improving domestic revenue. The deficit is projected to decline to 3.6% of GDP by 2026/2027, down from 5.9% in 2024/2025.
Overall, the agency concluded that Rwanda’s economic fundamentals remain strong, supported by prudent fiscal management and sustained international support, even as regional uncertainties persist.

title: Rwandan Minister Warns of Persistent Genocide Ideology, Accuses Habyarimana Family of Influence
excerpt: Kigali, Rwanda March 9, 2026 — Rwanda’s Minister of Youth and Arts Development, Jean Nepo Abdallah Utumatwishima, has warned that the ideology behind the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi remains present, cautioning against efforts to downplay or distort its legacy. Speaking at Lyc
title_en: Rwandan Minister Warns of Persistent Genocide Ideology, Accuses Habyarimana Family of Influence
excerpt_en: Kigali, Rwanda March 9, 2026 — Rwanda’s Minister of Youth and Arts Development, Jean Nepo Abdallah Utumatwishima, has warned that the ideology behind the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi remains present, cautioning against efforts to downplay or distort its legacy. Speaking at Lyc
body_en:
Kigali, Rwanda March 9, 2026 — Rwanda’s Minister of Youth and Arts Development, Jean Nepo Abdallah Utumatwishima, has warned that the ideology behind the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi remains present, cautioning against efforts to downplay or distort its legacy.
Speaking at Lycée de Kigali during the launch of the third phase of the Ndi Umunyarwanda program in schools, the minister said the spread of genocide ideology continues to be fueled in part by narratives linked to the family of former President Juvénal Habyarimana.
The Ndi Umunyarwanda program—implemented in collaboration with the Ministry of Education Rwanda, the Ministry of Youth and Arts Development, the Ministry of National Unity and Civic Engagement, and the Unity Club Intwararumuri—aims to strengthen historical awareness among students and counter misinformation about Rwanda’s past.
Utumatwishima said that, more than three decades after the genocide, its underlying ideology persists in subtle forms, including within families.
“You will often hear people attempting to absolve their relatives or conceal the truth about what happened, which contributes to the continued spread of this ideology,” he said.
He specifically cited members of the Habyarimana family, including Agathe Kanziga, accusing them of promoting narratives that deny or minimize the former president’s role in events leading up to the genocide.
“They claim innocence and attempt to mislead public opinion, even expressing ambitions to return and lead the country, while refusing to acknowledge historical responsibility,” he added.
The minister further alleged that such narratives are not limited to rhetoric, warning of potential links between individuals associated with the former regime and the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda, an armed group operating in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo and composed in part of individuals linked to the 1994 genocide.
“This is not something to take lightly. It goes beyond words and can translate into actions that threaten national security,” he said.
The remarks come amid heightened concerns expressed by President Paul Kagame, who recently criticized what he described as the continued presence and reception of individuals linked to the former regime in Kinshasa.
“The son of the former president and others continue to visit Kinshasa to expand collaboration with the FDLR, and they are being welcomed,” Kagame said during a meeting with diplomats on March 6.
Rwandan authorities say initiatives such as Ndi Umunyarwanda remain critical in educating younger generations and preventing the resurgence of divisive ideologies.

title: Rwandan Security Forces Support Education in Mozambique
excerpt: Cabo Delgado, Mozambique, 16 March 2026 – Rwandan Security Forces deployed in Cabo Delgado Province have donated school supplies to students at Buji Primary School, in collaboration with local authorities, as part of ongoing efforts to support communities affected by conflict. Th
title_en: Rwandan Security Forces Support Education in Mozambique
excerpt_en: Cabo Delgado, Mozambique, 16 March 2026 – Rwandan Security Forces deployed in Cabo Delgado Province have donated school supplies to students at Buji Primary School, in collaboration with local authorities, as part of ongoing efforts to support communities affected by conflict. Th
body_en:
Cabo Delgado, Mozambique, 16 March 2026 – Rwandan Security Forces deployed in Cabo Delgado Province have donated school supplies to students at Buji Primary School, in collaboration with local authorities, as part of ongoing efforts to support communities affected by conflict.
The donation, made on 16 March 2026, will benefit 525 students at the school, located in Mocímboa da Praia District.
School principal Lahaia Tomé expressed gratitude for the continued support, noting its positive impact on both the school and the wider community. The district’s Director of Education, Salmo Bacary, also praised the initiative, highlighting the role of Rwandan forces not only in restoring security but also in supporting the education sector.
This contribution follows a similar project earlier in March, when Rwandan forces handed over a newly renovated school building in Macomia District. The facility, which includes three classrooms and two offices, was completed in three months after construction had been halted due to terrorist attacks, and now serves 150 students.
Lt Col Frank Rwabugande, in charge of civil-military relations, said the initiative reflects a broader commitment to promoting education and strengthening ties with local communities. “This school is not just a building, but a symbol of unity and cooperation between the people of Rwanda and Mozambique,” he said.
Since July 2021, Rwandan and Mozambican security forces have worked together to combat insurgent groups in Cabo Delgado, restoring stability in areas previously affected by violence. The improved security situation has enabled displaced residents to return home and allowed the gradual restoration of basic services, including infrastructure and electricity.

title_en: Senator Dany Kabongo Files Petition Against Senate Vice-President Modeste Bahati for Alleged Incompetence
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, March 16, 2026 – Senator Dany Kabongo has officially filed a petition against Modeste Bahati Lukwebo, the Second Vice-President of the Senate, citing alleged incompetence in the exercise of his duties. The initiative reportedly garnered 83 signatures from fellow parliam
body_en:
Kinshasa, March 16, 2026 – Senator Dany Kabongo has officially filed a petition against Modeste Bahati Lukwebo, the Second Vice-President of the Senate, citing alleged incompetence in the exercise of his duties. The initiative reportedly garnered 83 signatures from fellow parliamentarians.
Kabongo, a member of the Sacred Union of the Nation (USN), accuses Bahati, leader of the Alliance of Democratic Forces of Congo and Allies (AFDC-A), of failing to properly consult the Head of State, President Félix Tshisekedi, before making public statements on sensitive political issues, including constitutional discussions.
Bahati had previously appeared in the media, suggesting the opening of a debate on constitutional matters. This statement was perceived by some colleagues as a lack of respect toward the President. In response, Bahati issued an apology on March 10, asserting that his words had been misinterpreted and clarifying that he was not opposed to constitutional revision, but rather advocating for an internal debate within the USN.
The petition underscores rising tensions within the Senate and the ruling coalition, drawing attention to the scrutiny senior officials face over their public remarks.

title: National Assembly Affirms Vigilance Over Washington Accords and Investment Opportunities
excerpt: Kinshasa March 18, 2026 – The Speaker of the National Assembly, Aimé Boji Sangara, assured Parliament and the public that upcoming discussions on the ratification of the Washington Accords between the Democratic Republic of Congo and Rwanda, as well as the Strategic Partnership A
title_en: National Assembly Affirms Vigilance Over Washington Accords and Investment Opportunities
excerpt_en: Kinshasa March 18, 2026 – The Speaker of the National Assembly, Aimé Boji Sangara, assured Parliament and the public that upcoming discussions on the ratification of the Washington Accords between the Democratic Republic of Congo and Rwanda, as well as the Strategic Partnership A
body_en:
Kinshasa March 18, 2026 – The Speaker of the National Assembly, Aimé Boji Sangara, assured Parliament and the public that upcoming discussions on the ratification of the Washington Accords between the Democratic Republic of Congo and Rwanda, as well as the Strategic Partnership Agreement with the United States, will be conducted responsibly, without compromising national sovereignty or restricting other international investments.
Speaking at the opening of the March 2026 ordinary session, Boji emphasized that these agreements aim to strengthen the DRC’s capacity, promote transparent management of strategic resources, and foster mutually beneficial partnerships. “Our country remains open to all investors of good faith. Beyond mining, there are considerable opportunities in agriculture, industrial processing, tourism, energy, and telecommunications,” he said.
The Washington Accords, signed under U.S. auspices on June 27, 2025, and December 4, 2025, seek to end the cycle of insecurity in eastern DRC and encourage regional economic integration. Parliament is expected to review and vote on the ratification bills, as well as consider the draft law on the Inga Dam project during the current session.
Boji reassured that the National Assembly will act with “vigilance and responsibility” to ensure the agreements serve both national security and the long-term prosperity of the Congolese people.
The accords are part of a broader international framework designed to foster peace, regional stability, and economic growth in the Great Lakes region, while enabling DRC to attract additional foreign investment and develop local industries.

excerpt: Walikale, North Kivu March 16, 2026 – The General Staff of the 34th Military Region announced the arrest of two Wazalendo commanders accused of indiscipline and acts of violence severely affecting civilians. The arrested leaders are Kirikicho Mirimba, alias Mwana Mayi, of the COP
title_en: Two Wazalendo Commanders Arrested in Walikale for “Uncivil and Anti-Patriotic” Acts
excerpt_en: Walikale, North Kivu March 16, 2026 – The General Staff of the 34th Military Region announced the arrest of two Wazalendo commanders accused of indiscipline and acts of violence severely affecting civilians. The arrested leaders are Kirikicho Mirimba, alias Mwana Mayi, of the COP
body_en:
Walikale, North Kivu March 16, 2026 – The General Staff of the 34th Military Region announced the arrest of two Wazalendo commanders accused of indiscipline and acts of violence severely affecting civilians.
The arrested leaders are Kirikicho Mirimba, alias Mwana Mayi, of the COPACO (Coalition of Patriots in Congo) movement, and Musubao Kalimba, alias Kasilasi. Military authorities cited their “uncivil and anti-patriotic behavior,” which contradicts the mission of the Volunteers for the Defense of the Homeland (VDP).
The commanders have been engaged in fratricidal clashes for nearly 17 months, with serious consequences for both their groups and the civilian population. Despite mediation efforts by traditional authorities and local leaders, confrontations continued.
The most recent clashes, between February 15–18, 2026, in the Tushunguti and Zirhalo areas of the Buhavu chiefdom in Kalehe territory, South Kivu, resulted in 14 civilian deaths, 7 serious injuries, 7 cases of sexual violence, and numerous instances of looting.
The army stated that these actions have strayed from the VDP’s original mission. Both commanders, described as repeat offenders, will now answer to competent authorities under the jurisdiction of the 34th Military Region.

body_en:
Walikale March 11, 2026 — Tensions erupted on Tuesday, March 10, in Mungazi, located in the Luberike area of Walikale Territory, following a deadly confrontation between a FARDC soldier and members of the Wazalendo militia. The clash left three Wazalendo fighters dead.
The incident reportedly stemmed from a misunderstanding between the soldier and the group of militia members, though the exact cause of the dispute remains unclear. During the altercation, the soldier opened fire, killing all three Wazalendo fighters instantly.
The situation was brought under control within hours, but the gunfire caused panic among the local population. The soldier involved was detained by military authorities and is currently under questioning.
The three victims were buried locally on Wednesday morning. This incident is part of a pattern of clashes in Mungazi, where previous confrontations between FARDC soldiers and Wazalendo fighters in 2025 also resulted in deaths and injuries.

Walikale, North Kivu – March 16, 2026 – Cases of rape and looting were reported on March 13, 2026, along the Tuonane-Busurungi road in the Waloa Loanda group, Walikale territory.
According to local authorities, unidentified armed men intercepted civilians on the road. Several women were raped, while money and belongings were stolen. Administrative sources in the Wanianga sector confirmed the attacks.
Security services have launched investigations to identify the perpetrators and bring them before judicial authorities. Victims are receiving treatment at local health facilities.
The assaults occurred in March, a month dedicated to defending and promoting women’s rights, raising serious concerns about the persistent insecurity in rural areas of Walikale territory.

title: Denis Sassou Nguesso Re-Elected President of Congo-Brazzaville
excerpt: Brazzaville, 18 March 2026 – Denis Sassou Nguesso has been re-elected president of the Republic of Congo, securing a fifth term with 94.82% of the vote following elections held on 15 March 2026. The 82-year-old leader, representing the Congolese Labour Party, defeated six other c
title_en: Denis Sassou Nguesso Re-Elected President of Congo-Brazzaville
excerpt_en: Brazzaville, 18 March 2026 – Denis Sassou Nguesso has been re-elected president of the Republic of Congo, securing a fifth term with 94.82% of the vote following elections held on 15 March 2026. The 82-year-old leader, representing the Congolese Labour Party, defeated six other c
body_en:
Brazzaville, 18 March 2026 – Denis Sassou Nguesso has been re-elected president of the Republic of Congo, securing a fifth term with 94.82% of the vote following elections held on 15 March 2026.
The 82-year-old leader, representing the Congolese Labour Party, defeated six other candidates. His closest challenger, Mabio Mavoungou Zinga, received 1.48% of the vote.
The results, announced by national authorities, extend Sassou Nguesso’s rule, which has spanned nearly four decades since he first came to power in 1979. Although he briefly lost power in 1992, he returned to leadership in 1997 following a civil war.
Opposition candidates have a five-day window to file appeals, which will be reviewed by the Constitutional Court before the final results are confirmed.
A constitutional amendment adopted in 2015 removed presidential term limits and age restrictions, enabling Sassou Nguesso to run for additional terms.
The Republic of Congo, located in Central Africa, borders Gabon, Cameroon, the Central African Republic, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and has a population of over six million people.

title: Rwanda Cooperation Initiative Generates Rwf19 Billion from Study Tours
excerpt: Kigali, 13 March 2026 – The Rwanda Cooperation Initiative (RCI) has generated nearly Rwf19 billion since its establishment in 2018, driven by thousands of international visitors seeking to learn from Rwanda’s development model and innovations. The announcement was made by RCI Dir
title_en: Rwanda Cooperation Initiative Generates Rwf19 Billion from Study Tours
excerpt_en: Kigali, 13 March 2026 – The Rwanda Cooperation Initiative (RCI) has generated nearly Rwf19 billion since its establishment in 2018, driven by thousands of international visitors seeking to learn from Rwanda’s development model and innovations. The announcement was made by RCI Dir
body_en:
Kigali, 13 March 2026 – The Rwanda Cooperation Initiative (RCI) has generated nearly Rwf19 billion since its establishment in 2018, driven by thousands of international visitors seeking to learn from Rwanda’s development model and innovations.
The announcement was made by RCI Director General Patricie Uwase during a partners’ meeting aimed at improving the quality of services offered to visiting delegations.
Uwase revealed that around 10,000 visitors from over 70 countries, including 45 African nations, have participated in study tours in Rwanda. These visits, which combine knowledge exchange and tourism, have become a growing source of revenue and international engagement.
“In Rwanda, we have many solutions others can learn from, but we must improve how we present and package them,” Uwase said, emphasizing the need to integrate practical demonstrations and business components into presentations.
However, an internal audit found that only 15% of the 297 partner institutions were able to clearly present their services. Gaps included weak program design, limited practical exposure, and insufficient integration of tourism experiences for visitors.
Dr. Willy Mugenzi, Director of Operations at RCI, noted that some visitors expressed dissatisfaction due to a mismatch between expectations and delivery. He stressed the importance of moving beyond theory: “It is not enough to explain achievements; visitors need to see how solutions work in practice, including the challenges faced and how they were overcome.”
Partners are now being encouraged to adopt a more transparent and hands-on approach, showcasing both successes and challenges to enhance credibility and learning outcomes.
Vividi Karangwa Immaculée, Director General of Hope and Homes for Children, acknowledged that institutions previously focused mainly on positive outcomes, often overlooking challenges. “Visitors come to learn, not just to admire success. We are now committed to sharing our experiences more fully, while maintaining a constructive approach,” she said.
Established in 2018, the RCI serves as a platform to promote Rwanda’s homegrown solutions, particularly across Africa, by facilitating knowledge sharing, innovation transfer, and capacity building.

Uwase revealed that around 10,000 visitors from over 70 countries, including 45 African nations, have participated in study tours in Rwanda. These visits, which combine knowledge exchange and tourism, have become a growing source of revenue and international engagement.
“In Rwanda, we have many solutions others can learn from, but we must improve how we present and package them,” Uwase said, emphasizing the need to integrate practical demonstrations and business components into presentations.
However, an internal audit found that only 15% of the 297 partner institutions were able to clearly present their services. Gaps included weak program design, limited practical exposure, and insufficient integration of tourism experiences for visitors.
Dr. Willy Mugenzi, Director of Operations at RCI, noted that some visitors expressed dissatisfaction due to a mismatch between expectations and delivery. He stressed the importance of moving beyond theory: “It is not enough to explain achievements; visitors need to see how solutions work in practice, including the challenges faced and how they were overcome.”
Partners are now being encouraged to adopt a more transparent and hands-on approach, showcasing both successes and challenges to enhance credibility and learning outcomes.
Vividi Karangwa Immaculée, Director General of Hope and Homes for Children, acknowledged that institutions previously focused mainly on positive outcomes, often overlooking challenges. “Visitors come to learn, not just to admire success. We are now committed to sharing our experiences more fully, while maintaining a constructive approach,” she said.
Established in 2018, the RCI serves as a platform to promote Rwanda’s homegrown solutions, particularly across Africa, by facilitating knowledge sharing, innovation transfer, and capacity building.

body_en:
Kigali, 13 March 2026 – The Kicukiro Primary Court has ordered 30 days of detention for Mike Habinshuti, a former advisor to Rwandan artist Bruce Melodie, as investigations continue into alleged cocaine trafficking.
Habinshuti was arrested on 18 February 2026 and is suspected of involvement in the purchase and distribution of illegal drugs.
According to preliminary findings, he is alleged to have bought cocaine worth 3,970,000 Rwandan francs between November and December 2025. Investigators claim the substances were sourced from a Nigerian supplier identified as James Ogbu and later distributed to various clients.
Habinshuti was previously known in the local entertainment industry for his association with Bruce Melodie, although the two are no longer working closely.
He had also been mentioned in sports management circles, notably within Rayon Sports, where he was appointed deputy director in November 2025 before the committee was later dissolved.
The case remains under investigation as authorities continue efforts to combat drug trafficking and related criminal activities.

title_en: Rwanda Defence Forces Return from Jamaica Mission

body_en:
Kigali, 16 March 2026 – The Rwanda Defence Forces (RDF) team of engineers has returned to Kigali after completing a mission in Jamaica to assist with repairs of infrastructure and houses damaged by Cyclone Melissa.
The team arrived at Kigali International Airport on Monday morning, concluding a 60-day mission that began on 14 January 2026.
Welcoming them, the Chief of Defence Forces, Gen Maj Alex Kagame, praised the soldiers for their dedication, professionalism, and teamwork. “The RDF culture and values were very clear. We have not heard anything negative from them during their time in Jamaica. Please give them a round of applause,” he said.
During the mission, RDF personnel focused on repairing infrastructure and homes in Montego Bay, Province of St James, earning appreciation from local residents.
The Chief of Defence Staff of Jamaica, Vice Admiral Antonette Wemyss-Gorman, commended the RDF for their work. “They are sincere, professional, and have done a lot in a short time. They spent time with the community and have not caused any issues. We are very proud of these peacekeepers,” she said.
Vice Admiral Wemyss-Gorman emphasized that the collaboration would continue to strengthen the relationship between Rwanda and Jamaica. “The people you helped will not forget the RDF under President Kagame’s leadership. We will continue working to preserve this good relationship,” she added.

title: Kinshasa Seeks Strong EU Response to Rwanda-Backed AFC/M23 Rebellion
excerpt: Strasbourg, March 12–13, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo, represented by Minister of Foreign Affairs Thérèse Kayikwamba Wagner, engaged with Members of the European Parliament (MEPs) to discuss the security and humanitarian crisis in eastern DRC, particularly the ongoing
title_en: Kinshasa Seeks Strong EU Response to Rwanda-Backed AFC/M23 Rebellion
excerpt_en: Strasbourg, March 12–13, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo, represented by Minister of Foreign Affairs Thérèse Kayikwamba Wagner, engaged with Members of the European Parliament (MEPs) to discuss the security and humanitarian crisis in eastern DRC, particularly the ongoing
body_en:
Strasbourg, March 12–13, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo, represented by Minister of Foreign Affairs Thérèse Kayikwamba Wagner, engaged with Members of the European Parliament (MEPs) to discuss the security and humanitarian crisis in eastern DRC, particularly the ongoing hostilities involving the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 rebellion. The meeting was chaired by Belgian MEP Hilde Vautmans and included the EU Special Representative for the Great Lakes Region, Johan Borgstam, via videoconference.
Key Points from Kinshasa’s Appeal
Minister Kayikwamba Wagner emphasized that the conflict in eastern DRC has claimed over six million lives, making it one of the deadliest crises since World War II.
She denounced repeated violations of peace agreements and called for stronger international mobilization, including diplomatic pressure, regional mediation via the African Union, and concrete commitments from global partners.
The Congolese government specifically highlighted Rwanda’s continued support for the AFC/M23 as a major factor fueling instability.
EU Engagement and Advocacy
The non-profit United Front for the DRC urged the European Union to move beyond declarations, calling for:
Protection of civilians and promotion of peace and security in the Great Lakes region.
Respect for DRC territorial integrity.
Concrete actions against armed groups destabilizing eastern DRC, particularly Rwanda-backed rebels.
Dr. Audrey Mundine, president of the United Front for the DRC, stressed that the EU’s credibility in international law and human rights is at stake if it fails to act decisively.
Context and Challenges
Hostilities between AFC/M23 and government forces continue in North Kivu and South Kivu, including the increased use of drones, which both sides accuse the other of deploying against civilians.
International mediation processes—the Washington process (Kinshasa–Kigali) and the Doha process (Kinshasa–AFC/M23)—have recorded some progress on paper but struggle to produce tangible results on the ground, contributing to ongoing mistrust and violence.
Humanitarian needs are growing, with international aid funding falling short amid escalating hostilities.

title: MP Questions Deputy Prime Minister on Fuel Supply Amid Middle East Crisis
excerpt: Kinshasa March 16, 2026 – Congolese National Deputy Flory Mapamboli Posa submitted a written question to the Deputy Prime Minister in charge of the National Economy regarding the potential impact of the Middle East crisis on the Democratic Republic of Congo’s fuel supply. The par
title_en: MP Questions Deputy Prime Minister on Fuel Supply Amid Middle East Crisis
excerpt_en: Kinshasa March 16, 2026 – Congolese National Deputy Flory Mapamboli Posa submitted a written question to the Deputy Prime Minister in charge of the National Economy regarding the potential impact of the Middle East crisis on the Democratic Republic of Congo’s fuel supply. The par
body_en:
Kinshasa March 16, 2026 – Congolese National Deputy Flory Mapamboli Posa submitted a written question to the Deputy Prime Minister in charge of the National Economy regarding the potential impact of the Middle East crisis on the Democratic Republic of Congo’s fuel supply.
The parliamentary inquiry, formally submitted under Article 180 of the National Assembly’s Rules of Procedure, addresses concerns stemming from recent disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz and the Suez Canal—two key global petroleum transit routes responsible for approximately 20% and 10% of daily oil consumption, respectively.
During a recent Council of Ministers meeting, the government assessed the effects of these disruptions on national fuel availability. Officials indicated that current stock levels are sufficient to meet the country’s needs until June and presented a series of measures designed to maintain the balance of the fuel supply system and limit budgetary impacts over the short, medium, and long term.
The National Assembly’s Bureau will now review the submission to ensure its admissibility before forwarding it to the Deputy Prime Minister for response.

title: Three Kidnapped Teachers Freed After Ransom Payment

title_en: Three Kidnapped Teachers Freed After Ransom Payment
excerpt_en: Rutshuru March 14, 2026 — Three of the five teachers abducted earlier this week in Busanza, in Rutshuru Territory, have been released after a ransom payment, while two others remain in captivity, according to local education authorities. The victims were kidnapped on March 11 by
body_en:
Rutshuru March 14, 2026 — Three of the five teachers abducted earlier this week in Busanza, in Rutshuru Territory, have been released after a ransom payment, while two others remain in captivity, according to local education authorities.
The victims were kidnapped on March 11 by unidentified armed men in two separate incidents targeting teachers and school officials traveling along key roads in the area. According to Félix Gakiza, spokesperson for the local teachers’ union, approximately $1,000 was paid to secure the release of three of the hostages.
Those freed were part of a group of five education workers, including a school principal, a deputy headmaster, and several teachers from different primary schools in the Busanza area. The remaining two victims are still being held by their captors.
The first abduction occurred on the Kinyandonyi–Rugarama road in Mutego, where two school officials and their driver were intercepted while returning from Kiwanja. A second incident took place hours later on the Kitagoma–Kidandari road, where three other educators, including a school director, were kidnapped.
The teachers’ union strongly condemned the attacks, highlighting the growing insecurity targeting educators in conflict-affected zones. “Teachers are apolitical actors and deserve protection,” Gakiza stressed, calling on security forces to guarantee their safety as they continue working under increasingly difficult and dangerous conditions.
These incidents underscore the persistent security challenges in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, where civilians, including education personnel, remain vulnerable to kidnappings and armed violence.

title: Drone Strikes Hit Goma, International Reactions Pour In
excerpt: Goma DRC March 11, 2026 — The city of Goma, capital of North Kivu Province and currently under AFC/M23 rebel control, was struck by drone attacks early Wednesday morning. The strikes, attributed by the AFC/M23 rebellion to the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FAR
title_en: Drone Strikes Hit Goma, International Reactions Pour In
excerpt_en: Goma DRC March 11, 2026 — The city of Goma, capital of North Kivu Province and currently under AFC/M23 rebel control, was struck by drone attacks early Wednesday morning. The strikes, attributed by the AFC/M23 rebellion to the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FAR
body_en:
Goma DRC March 11, 2026 — The city of Goma, capital of North Kivu Province and currently under AFC/M23 rebel control, was struck by drone attacks early Wednesday morning. The strikes, attributed by the AFC/M23 rebellion to the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC), caused material damage and at least three deaths, including a French UNICEF aid worker, as well as two other civilians.
The Himbi neighborhood, near Lake Kivu, was particularly affected, with homes and civilian infrastructure damaged. The city has been controlled by the AFC/M23 since January 2025 and serves as the rebellion’s operational headquarters in North and South Kivu provinces.
Rebel Response
Bertrand Bisimwa, deputy coordinator of AFC/M23, condemned the strikes, accusing the Kinshasa government of violating the ceasefire and deploring the silence of international partners. He described the attacks as part of a campaign to “decapitate the revolution” and force an escalation of regional conflict.
Corneille Nangaa, political coordinator of AFC/M23, specified that the strikes were allegedly targeting the leadership of the rebellion and key political figures, including General Sultani Makenga, Bertrand Bisimwa, and Freddy Kaniki. He affirmed the rebellion’s commitment to protecting civilians in areas under its control and warned that any escalation would be the responsibility of Kinshasa.
International Reactions
Belgium :Maxime Patrick Robert Albert Prévot, Belgian Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister, condemned the attacks as a violation of the ceasefire, emphasizing that such strikes against humanitarian workers are rising. “The drone attack in Goma claimed the lives of a humanitarian worker and civilians. The guns must fall silent. Let’s negotiate,” he said on X, offering condolences to the victims’ families.
European Union :  Commissioner Hadja Lahbib, responsible for Crisis Preparedness and Equality, called for respect for international humanitarian law and protection of humanitarian personnel. “All parties must respect their commitments. Humanitarian workers must never be targeted,” she warned.
France :President Emmanuel Macron confirmed the death of the French UNICEF aid worker and urged all parties to respect international humanitarian law. “These aid workers are committed to saving lives in a precarious and dangerous environment,” he said, offering condolences to the family, colleagues, and loved ones of the deceased.
United Nations : The UN mission in the DRC (MONUSCO) strongly condemned the escalation, describing the attacks as deeply concerning and reiterating that targeting UN personnel could constitute war crimes under the Rome Statute. Bruno Lemarquis, Acting Head of MONUSCO, called for a swift, independent investigation into the drone strikes and urged both parties to prioritize political dialogue to protect civilians.
International Contact Group (ICG) :  Earlier, on March 5, members of the ICG, including Belgium, Denmark, the EU, France, Germany, the Netherlands, Sweden, Switzerland, the UK, and the USA, had expressed concern over ceasefire violations in eastern DRC, highlighting the use of drones in military operations that endanger civilians. They stressed that there is no military solution to the conflict and called for urgent negotiations.
Context
The strikes come amid ongoing diplomatic efforts, including the Washington and Doha processes, supported by the African Union. Despite these initiatives, tensions remain high between Kinshasa and Kigali, as well as between Kinshasa and the AFC/M23, limiting progress on the ground.
The attacks also reignite concern over humanitarian security, as the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) had recorded a decrease in incidents affecting aid workers in January 2026, but the Goma attack demonstrates that risks remain severe.

body_en:
Goma, North Kivu March 16, 2026 – At least thirteen Wazalendo fighters were killed and three captured during an overnight attack in the Mugunga neighborhood in western Goma, according to AFC/M23 officials.
The Wazalendo militiamen, coming from Virunga National Park, reportedly entered the city with the aim of looting population property, especially food supplies. Clashes with AFC/M23 patrols triggered an exchange of heavy and light weapons fire, causing widespread fear among residents.
Residents reported a restless night, with a bomb explosion at the CCLK roundabout damaging shops and bars and causing a fire. Witnesses described the incident as terror-inducing, reflecting the growing security concerns in Goma and surrounding areas.
The attack comes amid ongoing tensions following recent drone strikes on the city, which killed three people, including a French UNICEF employee. AFC/M23 and the government have publicly blamed each other for the drone strikes, while the Paris anti-terrorism prosecutor's office has opened an investigation.
The security situation in Goma remains highly volatile, with residents and authorities on alert after the escalation of violence.

title: Residents Flee Bembele Village Amid Fears of Armed Presence
excerpt: Bafwasende, Tshopo March 23, 2026 – Residents of Bembele village, located 76 kilometers from Bafwasende, have begun fleeing their homes following reports of suspected armed men in nearby forests. Since March 23, families have been moving toward Nia-Nia (Ituri) and Bafwasende town
title_en: Residents Flee Bembele Village Amid Fears of Armed Presence
excerpt_en: Bafwasende, Tshopo March 23, 2026 – Residents of Bembele village, located 76 kilometers from Bafwasende, have begun fleeing their homes following reports of suspected armed men in nearby forests. Since March 23, families have been moving toward Nia-Nia (Ituri) and Bafwasende town
body_en:
Bafwasende, Tshopo March 23, 2026 – Residents of Bembele village, located 76 kilometers from Bafwasende, have begun fleeing their homes following reports of suspected armed men in nearby forests.
Since March 23, families have been moving toward Nia-Nia (Ituri) and Bafwasende town, though the exact number of displaced people remains unknown.
Local sources report that farmers spotted armed individuals, triggering fears of a possible ADF presence, especially after recent deadly attacks in Mambasa, where at least 50 people were killed in Muchacha and Babesua.
The renewed insecurity has already forced more than 7,000 people to flee Mambasa, many now living in precarious conditions with host families in Bafwasende and surrounding areas.
The situation highlights growing concerns over the spread of violence and the humanitarian impact of ongoing armed group activity in eastern DRC.
Conclusion
The period from March 9 to 22, 2026, revealed the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) at a pivotal crossroads, navigating ambitious national development projects amid persistent security and political challenges.
On the security front, eastern provinces remain volatile. Despite international mediation efforts through the Washington and Doha tracks, which enabled gestures such as the release of over 5,000 FARDC soldiers, tangible improvements for local populations remain limited. Clashes involving the AFC/M23, Wazalendo militias, and the ADF continue, with civilian communities bearing the brunt of the violence. Humanitarian crises persist, exemplified by the destruction of judicial infrastructure in Goma and Bukavu and continued displacement.
Politically, the landscape is marked by polarization and high-stakes maneuvering. Resignations of senior parliamentary figures, such as Modeste Bahati Lukwebo, and rising opposition debates over constitutional amendments underscore a tense road toward 2028 electoral cycles. Meanwhile, legal reforms and institutional strengthening, including the establishment of the Economic and Financial Criminal Court, signal efforts to improve governance and combat corruption.
Economically, the DRC is pursuing strategic modernization, from infrastructure projects under Amendment 5 of the Sicomines agreement to the launch of a national gold refinery in Kalemie. Investments in energy, notably the Inga III development program, reflect a drive to transform the country into a continental energy hub. Yet these advances coexist with setbacks: the precarious state of Congo Airways, deadly landslides in Lualaba and Masisi, and the ongoing risks posed by irregular migration routes highlight continued vulnerabilities.
Overall, March 2026 underscores a nation striving for progress but constrained by conflict and institutional fragility. While the DRC lays foundations for long-term economic growth, energy expansion, and administrative modernization, persistent security threats and political tensions threaten to undermine these gains. Sustained stability will demand robust governance, inclusive dialogue, transparent resource management, and effective enforcement of the rule of law to ensure that economic and social progress reaches all Congolese citizens.
By Glad Musema
Jeff Buleli

title: Rwanda and Djibouti Explore Expanded Bilateral Cooperation
excerpt: Djibouti, 16 March 2026 – Rwanda and Djibouti have held high-level talks aimed at strengthening and expanding bilateral cooperation across key sectors. Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation, Ambassador Olivier Nduhungirehe, was received by his Djiboutian counterpar
title_en: Rwanda and Djibouti Explore Expanded Bilateral Cooperation
excerpt_en: Djibouti, 16 March 2026 – Rwanda and Djibouti have held high-level talks aimed at strengthening and expanding bilateral cooperation across key sectors. Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation, Ambassador Olivier Nduhungirehe, was received by his Djiboutian counterpar
body_en:
Djibouti, 16 March 2026 – Rwanda and Djibouti have held high-level talks aimed at strengthening and expanding bilateral cooperation across key sectors.
Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation, Ambassador Olivier Nduhungirehe, was received by his Djiboutian counterpart, Abdoulkader Houssein Omar, where both sides discussed opportunities to deepen collaboration in areas of mutual interest.
According to Djibouti’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Rwandan minister is also expected to meet the President of Djibouti and deliver a special message from President Paul Kagame.
Relations between the two countries have remained stable over the years, supported by a joint ministerial commission that meets regularly to explore new avenues of cooperation.
In November 2025, Rwanda and Djibouti signed nine cooperation agreements covering sectors such as sports, health, family development, and diplomatic training. Existing agreements also span trade, air transport, technology, investment protection, and visa facilitation for diplomats.
As part of this partnership, Djibouti has allocated 60 hectares of land to Rwanda, including plots near the port and in a commercial zone, while Rwanda has provided Djibouti with 10 hectares in an industrial zone in Masoro.

title: Rwandan Parliament Calls for Stronger Measures Against Illegal Mining
excerpt: Kigali, 13 March 2026 – The House of Representatives has urged authorities to address illegal mining in a lasting and comprehensive manner, citing its growing threat to public safety and the environment. The issue was raised during the presentation of an analytical report by the
title_en: Rwandan Parliament Calls for Stronger Measures Against Illegal Mining
excerpt_en: Kigali, 13 March 2026 – The House of Representatives has urged authorities to address illegal mining in a lasting and comprehensive manner, citing its growing threat to public safety and the environment. The issue was raised during the presentation of an analytical report by the
body_en:
Kigali, 13 March 2026 – The House of Representatives has urged authorities to address illegal mining in a lasting and comprehensive manner, citing its growing threat to public safety and the environment.
The issue was raised during the presentation of an analytical report by the Committee on Foreign Affairs and Security, which highlighted theft and illegal mining as key security challenges.
Deputy Tumukunde Hope Gasatura, Chairperson of the Committee, revealed that between 2020 and 2025, 1,335 cases of illegal mining were reported. Miners have been found operating in people’s fields, rivers, state forests, abandoned mines, and old mine sites, causing environmental damage and loss of property.
He identified several causes of illegal mining, including:
Growth of the mineral market and fraudulent traders
Residents with traditional knowledge of mineral locations
Mining in licensed areas without authorization
Unprotected abandoned or old mines
Youth dropping out of school and joining illegal mining due to financial incentives
Insufficient security personnel by mining companies
Minerals found in private fields and homes
Unauthorized local leaders or former workers exploiting mines
Lack of compliance with labor management and monitoring systems
Gasatura also noted that there are currently 994 unregulated mines across the country, posing risks of accidents, injuries, and deaths.
Deputy Niyorurema Jean Rene recommended the expedited cancellation of mining permits to curb illegal operations. Deputy Uwamahoro raised concerns about markets buying illegally mined minerals, calling for proper monitoring of the chain of custody.
MP Mukabunani Christine proposed the creation of a mining sector unit within the Private Sector Union to strengthen oversight, while MP Kanyandekwe Christine emphasized balancing worker health and safety in legally operating mines.
The Parliament has requested the Ministry of Local Government to present strategies to improve the Mining Task Force, and asked the Rwanda Development Board (RDB) to:
Expedite issuance of mining licenses
Improve monitoring of RMB contracts with companies
Prevent use of unethical subcontractors
Leverage the Inkomane system to track mining activities
The parliamentary push reflects a growing effort to curb illegal mining, protect communities, and ensure the responsible development of Rwanda’s mineral resources.

title_en: Nyarugenge Court Upholds 30-Day Detention for Barafinda Sekikubo Fred
excerpt_en: Kigali, 12 March 2026 – The Nyarugenge High Court has ruled that Barafinda Sekikubo Fred must remain in detention for 30 days, dismissing his appeal against the original detention order. The decision was read on 12 March 2026 in his absence. Barafinda, along with co-defendants Ma
body_en:
Kigali, 12 March 2026 – The Nyarugenge High Court has ruled that Barafinda Sekikubo Fred must remain in detention for 30 days, dismissing his appeal against the original detention order. The decision was read on 12 March 2026 in his absence.
Barafinda, along with co-defendants Mazimpaka Patrick, Nizeyimana Didier (Mucoma), Japhet Nkeramihigo, and Tumukunde, had challenged a prior ruling by the Kicukiro Primary Court, which ordered their detention on 3 March 2026.
The prosecution alleges that Barafinda, Mazimpaka, and Nkeramihigo conspired to create and broadcast YouTube interviews aimed at spreading rumors, inciting public dissent, and seeking protection from external donors who followed their content.
While Barafinda’s co-defendants were released on bail and prosecuted without detention on 9 March 2026, his own appeal for provisional release was argued by his brother in a closed-door hearing on the same day. The High Court ultimately rejected the appeal, confirming that Barafinda will remain in custody for the full 30-day period.
body_fr:
Kigali, 12 March 2026 – The Nyarugenge High Court has ruled that Barafinda Sekikubo Fred must remain in detention for 30 days, dismissing his appeal against the original detention order. The decision was read on 12 March 2026 in his absence.
Barafinda, along with co-defendants Mazimpaka Patrick, Nizeyimana Didier (Mucoma), Japhet Nkeramihigo, and Tumukunde, had challenged a prior ruling by the Kicukiro Primary Court, which ordered their detention on 3 March 2026.
The prosecution alleges that Barafinda, Mazimpaka, and Nkeramihigo conspired to create and broadcast YouTube interviews aimed at spreading rumors, inciting public dissent, and seeking protection from external donors who followed their content.
While Barafinda’s co-defendants were released on bail and prosecuted without detention on 9 March 2026, his own appeal for provisional release was argued by his brother in a closed-door hearing on the same day. The High Court ultimately rejected the appeal, confirming that Barafinda will remain in custody for the full 30-day period.

excerpt_en: South Kivu, 16 March 2026 – The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC), in coordination with Wazalendo armed groups, have closed the RN5 road linking Bukavu and Uvira, disrupting transport and trade in the region. The RN5 corridor, a vital route for movement of
body_en:
South Kivu, 16 March 2026 – The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC), in coordination with Wazalendo armed groups, have closed the RN5 road linking Bukavu and Uvira, disrupting transport and trade in the region.
The RN5 corridor, a vital route for movement of people and goods, connects communities in the Ruzizi Plain and Uvira territory. The closure has left traders and travelers stranded, raising concerns over the economic and humanitarian impact.
On the morning of 15 March 2026, traders traveling from Runingu to Sange were turned back by security forces. Reports indicate that passengers heading from Bukavu toward Uvira and the Ruzizi Valley were blocked and forced to gather at Sange, awaiting further instructions.
After hours of uncertainty, authorities informed residents that no vehicles, motorcycles, or pedestrians would be allowed to access Uvira from areas under the control of the AFC/M23 coalition.
Security Justification, Public Frustration
Officials say the decision was taken to maintain security in zones under government and allied control. However, many residents have expressed confusion and frustration, arguing that authorities should instead strengthen protection measures while allowing economic activities to continue.
The RN5 road had briefly resumed operations between December 2025 and January 2026, during a period when AFC/M23 forces controlled parts of the Ruzizi Plain and Uvira. Since their withdrawal in mid-January, traffic has significantly declined, with travelers forced to navigate areas controlled by opposing factions.
The latest closure highlights the ongoing instability in eastern DRC, where shifting control between armed groups continues to disrupt daily life, trade, and mobility for local populations.

title: AFC/M23 Accuses FARDC of Deadly Drone Attacks on Civilians in Minembwe
excerpt: Fizi Territory, South Kivu, March 22, 2026 — The AFC/M23 rebel coalition has accused the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) and allied groups of carrying out deadly drone strikes on civilian areas in Fizi Territory, resulting in casualties and displacement.
title_en: AFC/M23 Accuses FARDC of Deadly Drone Attacks on Civilians in Minembwe
excerpt_en: Fizi Territory, South Kivu, March 22, 2026 — The AFC/M23 rebel coalition has accused the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) and allied groups of carrying out deadly drone strikes on civilian areas in Fizi Territory, resulting in casualties and displacement.
body_en:
Fizi Territory, South Kivu, March 22, 2026 — The AFC/M23 rebel coalition has accused the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) and allied groups of carrying out deadly drone strikes on civilian areas in Fizi Territory, resulting in casualties and displacement.
In a statement released on March 22, AFC/M23 spokesman Lawrence Kanyuka said the attacks took place overnight between March 21 and 22, targeting several locations including Gakenke, Kalingi, and Minembwe Center.
Kanyuka alleged that the strikes were conducted using so-called “kamikaze drones” that dropped explosives in densely populated areas, leading to civilian deaths and destruction of property.
“These drones carried out indiscriminate attacks on civilians, killing people, destroying livelihoods, and forcing many to flee,” he said.
He added that the attacks triggered displacement and widespread fear among residents, with many seeking refuge in safer areas after the strikes.
The AFC/M23 spokesman further accused government forces of deliberately targeting populated zones and criticized what he described as inaction by the international community.
He called on Congolese citizens to remain vigilant, claiming that such attacks were being carried out openly without accountability.
There has been no immediate response from the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of the Congo regarding the allegations.
Conclusion
Rwanda’s Strategic Momentum Amid Regional Tensions (March 9–22, 2026)
Between March 9 and 22, 2026, Rwanda’s trajectory reflected a balance between active regional diplomacy, strong economic performance, and sustained internal development efforts, even as security challenges in the region persisted.
On the diplomatic front, Kigali maintained a proactive stance, advancing border discussions with Burundi and continuing demarcation efforts with neighboring states. At the same time, tensions linked to the ongoing conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo remained a central concern, particularly in relation to the implementation of the Washington Peace Accords. Rwanda also deepened international engagement, including military cooperation talks with Israel and expanded bilateral relations with Djibouti, Gabon, and Seychelles.
Economically, the country demonstrated resilience and forward-looking ambition. Tourism revenues surpassed Rwf 236.8 billion, while agricultural exports generated over Rwf 15 billion within a short period, underscoring sectoral productivity. Rwanda also pushed financial and technological innovation, notably through cross-border payment integration with Kenya and expanded investment in cybersecurity training and data-driven governance frameworks.
Domestically, efforts to strengthen social welfare and national cohesion remained prominent. Security institutions contributed to community development through projects valued at over Rwf 2.5 billion, including housing and educational infrastructure for vulnerable populations. Public health initiatives continued to expand access to primary care, while programs such as Ndi Umunyarwanda reinforced unity and addressed divisive ideologies, particularly among younger generations.
Overall, despite a complex and often volatile regional environment, Rwanda’s approach during this period highlighted a dual focus: managing external security pressures while advancing internal priorities centered on economic growth, technological progress, and inclusive social development.
By Jeff Buleli

title: Launch of Biometric Residence Cards for Foreigners
excerpt: Kinshasa – March 11, 2026 – The Kinshasa provincial government officially launched the issuance of biometric residence cards for foreign nationals residing in the city. The ceremony was held at Kinshasa City Hall, presided over by Provincial Minister Jeannot Canon Larose. The ini
title_en: Launch of Biometric Residence Cards for Foreigners
excerpt_en: Kinshasa – March 11, 2026 – The Kinshasa provincial government officially launched the issuance of biometric residence cards for foreign nationals residing in the city. The ceremony was held at Kinshasa City Hall, presided over by Provincial Minister Jeannot Canon Larose. The ini
body_en:
Kinshasa – March 11, 2026 – The Kinshasa provincial government officially launched the issuance of biometric residence cards for foreign nationals residing in the city. The ceremony was held at Kinshasa City Hall, presided over by Provincial Minister Jeannot Canon Larose.
The initiative aims to strengthen public security, improve identification of foreigners, and modernize administrative management of their stay. Minister Larose emphasized that the system ensures a secure, regulated, and harmonized integration of foreigners in the city.
Financial oversight is also a priority: Minister Magloire Kabemba highlighted that the system will help mobilize revenues to support the city-province’s operations.
Key features of the program:
Validity: 2 years, with fees by category:
Category A: US$250
Category B: US$200
Category C: US$100
Category D: US$50
Spouse-specific fees also apply.
Electronic verification: Agents equipped with smartphone-like devices can scan cards and check authenticity via a dedicated database.
Digital procedures: Applications can be submitted online to streamline processing.
The government called on foreign communities to raise awareness and ensure compliance with this new administrative measure.

title: DRC Launches First Pilot Gold Refinery in Kalemie
excerpt: Kalemie, Tanganyika – March 13, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo has inaugurated its first pilot gold refinery, marking a major milestone in the country’s efforts to process its mineral resources locally. The ceremony took place on Wednesday, March 11, with the attendance
title_en: DRC Launches First Pilot Gold Refinery in Kalemie
excerpt_en: Kalemie, Tanganyika – March 13, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo has inaugurated its first pilot gold refinery, marking a major milestone in the country’s efforts to process its mineral resources locally. The ceremony took place on Wednesday, March 11, with the attendance
body_en:
Kalemie, Tanganyika – March 13, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo has inaugurated its first pilot gold refinery, marking a major milestone in the country’s efforts to process its mineral resources locally. The ceremony took place on Wednesday, March 11, with the attendance of key government officials, including the Minister of Planning, Guylain Nyembo, Minister of Mines, Louis Watum Kabamba, and Minister of State Portfolio, Julie Shiku, alongside the Governor of Tanganyika Province and representatives of DRC Gold Trading S.A.
Named DRC Gold Refinery S.A., the facility has a production capacity of 500–600 kilograms of gold per month and manages the full value chain, from purchasing raw gold to refining and producing ingots. The refinery represents a strategic partnership between the state-owned DRC Gold Trading S.A. and Lunga Mining.
At the launch, the Minister of Mines emphasized that the refinery is a key step in President Félix Tshisekedi’s vision to transform the country’s natural resources into engines of economic development and national sovereignty.
“For the first time, the DRC can refine its own strategic minerals, ensuring fair prices and transparent conditions for artisanal miners, trading posts, and small to medium mining operations,” the minister said.
The refinery aims to produce gold with 99.9% purity, positioning the country as a competitive exporter of refined gold while creating local added value. Authorities also urged those involved in gold fraud or smuggling to use official channels established by the state through DRC Gold Trading S.A.
This initiative forms part of a broader reform of the Congolese gold sector, emphasizing transparency, traceability, and local processing, with the goal of ensuring that the nation fully benefits from its mineral wealth.
