title: Rwanda Partners with Japan to Strengthen Disaster Management
excerpt: Kigali, 13 March 2026 – Rwanda is learning from Japan to improve its ability to prevent and respond to disasters including earthquakes, floods, landslides, and lightning, which have historically caused loss of life, damaged infrastructure, and cost the country heavily in repairs.
title_en: Rwanda Partners with Japan to Strengthen Disaster Management
excerpt_en: Kigali, 13 March 2026 – Rwanda is learning from Japan to improve its ability to prevent and respond to disasters including earthquakes, floods, landslides, and lightning, which have historically caused loss of life, damaged infrastructure, and cost the country heavily in repairs.
body_en:
Kigali, 13 March 2026 – Rwanda is learning from Japan to improve its ability to prevent and respond to disasters including earthquakes, floods, landslides, and lightning, which have historically caused loss of life, damaged infrastructure, and cost the country heavily in repairs.
The knowledge exchange is taking place through a two-day conference in Kigali, which began on 12 March 2026. Activities showcased 12 Japanese companies offering technologies designed to prevent disasters before they occur and respond efficiently when they do.
Japan, situated near the Pacific Ocean, is among the world’s most disaster-prone nations, regularly affected by tsunamis and earthquakes. The conference also commemorates the over 15,900 people who died and the 2,500 still missing from the 11 March 2011 earthquake and tsunami in Japan.
According to Gen. Maj. (Rtd) Albert Murasira, Rwanda’s Minister of Disaster Management, researchers attending the conference, including those from the University of Rwanda, are studying Japanese approaches to early disaster detection, evacuation planning, and preventive measures. “These two days are for us to meet and learn how they work, but now the advantage is that schools and university researchers have also come, so they can continue research for Rwanda’s needs,” he said.
Japanese Ambassador to Rwanda, Kazuya Nakajo, emphasized the potential impact of Japanese technology on saving lives and supporting Rwanda’s economic growth. “I believe that Japanese technology and the NST2 development plan will play a role in preventing disasters and promoting continued economic growth in Rwanda. Together, we can deal with these disasters effectively,” he said.
Rwanda is already implementing programs such as tree planting to reduce landslides and erosion, alongside initiatives to combat deforestation. Japanese company Jibu Gaz One Ltd. showcased an innovative solution for providing affordable gas to low-income households. Traditionally sold in six-kilo cylinders, Jibu Gaz now offers 1, 2, or 3-kilo cylinders, costing 1,600 Rwandan francs per kilo, helping households avoid returning to charcoal or firewood, a key contributor to deforestation.

title: Kagame Urges Kigali Leaders to Eliminate Corruption and Improve Service Delivery
excerpt: Kigali, Rwanda March 23, 2026 – President Paul Kagame has called on leaders in the City of Kigali and across public institutions to urgently address persistent problems related to pollution, poor service delivery, and corruption, warning that failure to act will have serious cons
title_en: Kagame Urges Kigali Leaders to Eliminate Corruption and Improve Service Delivery
excerpt_en: Kigali, Rwanda March 23, 2026 – President Paul Kagame has called on leaders in the City of Kigali and across public institutions to urgently address persistent problems related to pollution, poor service delivery, and corruption, warning that failure to act will have serious cons
body_en:
Kigali, Rwanda March 23, 2026 – President Paul Kagame has called on leaders in the City of Kigali and across public institutions to urgently address persistent problems related to pollution, poor service delivery, and corruption, warning that failure to act will have serious consequences.
Speaking on Monday, March 23, at the conclusion of a high-level consultative meeting with government and local leaders, Kagame criticized what he described as a tolerance for “reduced” corruption rather than its total elimination.
“Why compare ourselves to countries where corruption is worse? Why accept so-called ‘petty corruption’?” he asked. “If you see services not being delivered properly and remain silent, you are complicit.”
The Rwandan leader stressed that silence in the face of corruption amounts to participation, urging officials to take responsibility and act decisively. He warned that negligence in public service delivery can have fatal consequences, citing the case of a woman who died after being denied care at a hospital due to administrative issues with her health insurance.
Kagame also highlighted visible shortcomings in urban management, pointing to poor sanitation, unmaintained public spaces, and unregulated construction in Kigali. He said he had personally observed dirt along roads and inconsistent urban planning, calling for immediate corrective measures.
“I still see dirt on the roads. I stop and ask those with me to remove it,” he said, emphasizing the need for practical, low-cost solutions, such as landscaping and better organization of residential and commercial areas.
The president urged city authorities to establish dedicated task forces, involving security services and urban planning officials, to ensure consistent enforcement and follow-up on identified issues. He expressed frustration at the slow pace of implementation, noting that similar directives had been issued for years.
Beyond urban governance, Kagame addressed broader social and economic challenges, including school dropouts, family instability, and agricultural productivity. He questioned why Rwanda has not yet achieved food self-sufficiency, pointing to gaps in awareness, production, and post-harvest management, particularly the lack of systems to preserve perishable goods.
He concluded with a firm warning: all identified problems must be resolved, or authorities themselves will be held accountable for inaction.

The Rwandan leader stressed that silence in the face of corruption amounts to participation, urging officials to take responsibility and act decisively. He warned that negligence in public service delivery can have fatal consequences, citing the case of a woman who died after being denied care at a hospital due to administrative issues with her health insurance.
Kagame also highlighted visible shortcomings in urban management, pointing to poor sanitation, unmaintained public spaces, and unregulated construction in Kigali. He said he had personally observed dirt along roads and inconsistent urban planning, calling for immediate corrective measures.
“I still see dirt on the roads. I stop and ask those with me to remove it,” he said, emphasizing the need for practical, low-cost solutions, such as landscaping and better organization of residential and commercial areas.
The president urged city authorities to establish dedicated task forces, involving security services and urban planning officials, to ensure consistent enforcement and follow-up on identified issues. He expressed frustration at the slow pace of implementation, noting that similar directives had been issued for years.
Beyond urban governance, Kagame addressed broader social and economic challenges, including school dropouts, family instability, and agricultural productivity. He questioned why Rwanda has not yet achieved food self-sufficiency, pointing to gaps in awareness, production, and post-harvest management, particularly the lack of systems to preserve perishable goods.
He concluded with a firm warning: all identified problems must be resolved, or authorities themselves will be held accountable for inaction.

body_en:
Maputo, Mozambique March 8, 2026 — Rwandan women living in Mozambique have been encouraged to take full advantage of opportunities created by their home country, during celebrations marking International Women's Day in the capital, Maputo.
The event, held at the Polana Serena Hotel, brought together more than 120 participants, including government officials and members of the Rwandan diaspora. Among those in attendance were Ministerial Advisor Kenneth Viagem Marizane, Dr. Anabela Inguane representing the Maputo City Council, and Rwanda’s Ambassador to Mozambique, Donat Ndamage.
Speaking at the gathering, Sangwa Aline, Commissioner for Women’s Development within the Rwandan community in Mozambique, emphasized the importance of empowering women to fully utilize available opportunities.
“Let us seize the opportunities our country has given us, build our confidence, and strengthen our capabilities,” she said.
Ambassador Ndamage highlighted Rwanda’s progress in promoting gender equality, noting the significant representation of women in leadership positions.
“We must continue to build a society characterized by equality, justice, and sustainable development, where women and girls play a full role in governance and social life,” he stated.
He pointed out that women currently make up 63 percent of Rwanda’s lower house of parliament, alongside growing representation at district leadership levels, while acknowledging that further progress is still needed.
The ambassador also commended the leadership of Paul Kagame and Francisco Daniel Chapo for their commitment to advancing gender equality and inclusion, underscoring the strong ties between Rwanda and Mozambique.
Mozambican official Kenneth Viagem Marizane praised the contributions of Rwandan women in the country, describing them as hardworking and impactful members of society.
The event featured cultural performances, including traditional Rwandan music and dance, celebrating the achievements of women, followed by a social gathering among attendees.

excerpt_en: Rubavu, Rwanda, 12 March 2026 – Rwanda welcomed 205 of its citizens who had been living in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), as they voluntarily returned home on Thursday, 12 March 2026. The returnees crossed the Rwanda-DRC border in Rubavu District, where they were receive
body_en:
Rubavu, Rwanda, 12 March 2026 – Rwanda welcomed 205 of its citizens who had been living in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), as they voluntarily returned home on Thursday, 12 March 2026.
The returnees crossed the Rwanda-DRC border in Rubavu District, where they were received by District Commissioner Ishimwe Pacifique, responsible for social welfare.
The majority of those returning were women and children born in the DRC. Many said they decided to come back after encouragement from colleagues who had returned earlier, aiming to rebuild their lives and pursue development.
Several of the returnees had been held hostage by FDLR fighters operating in the forests of eastern DRC. Since the AFC/M23 coalition gained control over parts of the region, security conditions have improved, allowing Rwandans to return safely with support from the UN Refugee Agency.
The initiative reflects ongoing efforts to assist citizens stranded abroad and facilitate their reintegration into Rwandan society.

title: Former Armed Group Members Repatriated from DRC Confront Genocide History in Rwanda
excerpt: Kigali, March 21, 2026 — A group of 244 individuals, largely former members of armed groups operating in the Democratic Republic of Congo, have undergone a civic and historical re-education program in Rwanda aimed at countering long-held extremist narratives and facilitating rein
title_en: Former Armed Group Members Repatriated from DRC Confront Genocide History in Rwanda
excerpt_en: Kigali, March 21, 2026 — A group of 244 individuals, largely former members of armed groups operating in the Democratic Republic of Congo, have undergone a civic and historical re-education program in Rwanda aimed at countering long-held extremist narratives and facilitating rein
body_en:
Kigali, March 21, 2026 — A group of 244 individuals, largely former members of armed groups operating in the Democratic Republic of Congo, have undergone a civic and historical re-education program in Rwanda aimed at countering long-held extremist narratives and facilitating reintegration into society.
The group, which includes ex-combatants linked to the FDLR as well as their families, recently returned to Rwanda and participated in guided visits to key historical sites. These included the Kigali Genocide Memorial and the Campaign Against Genocide Museum, where they were introduced to the history and consequences of the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi.
According to Rwanda’s National Demobilization and Reintegration Commission (RDRC), 173 of the returnees are former fighters, while the remainder are their spouses and children. A significant proportion—173 individuals—were born in the DRC, while 71 were born in Rwanda. The group is predominantly male, with 216 men among them.
The visits, held on March 20, form part of a broader reintegration program conducted at the Mutobo Demobilization Center in Musanze District. The initiative is designed to prepare returnees for civilian life, with completion expected by the end of March.
RDRC Chairperson Valérie Nyirahabineza said the inclusion of historical education marks a shift in the commission’s approach. She emphasized that many of the younger returnees, particularly those born in the DRC, had been exposed to distorted narratives about Rwanda and its history.
“In the past, most returnees had firsthand knowledge of the Genocide against the Tutsi,” she noted. “Today, many of these young people were born outside Rwanda and have grown up hearing falsehoods. It is essential that they see and understand the truth for themselves.”
Nyirahabineza added that discussions with the group revealed a widespread lack of awareness about the planning, execution, and aftermath of the genocide. She said the visits aim not only to inform but also to foster a sense of responsibility and encourage participation in national unity and remembrance programs.
Among the returnees is Mbare Amoni, who fled Rwanda as a child in 1994 and later joined the FDLR at age 25. He described harsh living conditions in eastern DRC and recounted fighting alongside the Armed Forces of the DRC (FARDC) before being pushed back by M23 rebels near Goma.
Amoni said his decision to return was influenced by contact with a former combatant who had already reintegrated. Reflecting on his visit to the memorial sites, he expressed shock at the historical realities presented, noting that they contradicted what he had long believed.
He also remarked on Rwanda’s development, saying it differed significantly from the image portrayed within armed groups. “What I saw here challenged everything we were told,” he said, adding that the experience, though difficult, was eye-opening.
Another participant, 25-year-old Ntakirutimana Faustin, born in the DRC, said he had never joined the FDLR but lived among its members and was influenced by their ideology. He explained that he grew up hearing that the group’s goal was to return to Rwanda and seize power.
Visiting Rwanda for the first time, Faustin described the country as “beautiful” and said learning about the Genocide against the Tutsi helped him reassess the beliefs he had held for years.
Authorities say such programs are critical in addressing the legacy of armed conflict and extremist indoctrination among returnees, particularly younger generations raised outside Rwanda.

title: ICRC Meets Defense Minister as Prisoner Exchange Process Moves Forward
excerpt: DRC March 13, 2026 — Efforts to advance the prisoner exchange process between the government of the Democratic Republic of Congo and the AFC/M23 rebellion received renewed attention following a meeting in Kinshasa between the Deputy Prime Minister of Defense and François Moreillo
title_en: ICRC Meets Defense Minister as Prisoner Exchange Process Moves Forward
excerpt_en: DRC March 13, 2026 — Efforts to advance the prisoner exchange process between the government of the Democratic Republic of Congo and the AFC/M23 rebellion received renewed attention following a meeting in Kinshasa between the Deputy Prime Minister of Defense and François Moreillo
body_en:
DRC March 13, 2026 — Efforts to advance the prisoner exchange process between the government of the Democratic Republic of Congo and the AFC/M23 rebellion received renewed attention following a meeting in Kinshasa between the Deputy Prime Minister of Defense and François Moreillon, head of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) delegation.
The discussions focused on the release and transfer of prisoners of war in eastern DRC within the framework of the Doha mediation process, where the ICRC acts as a neutral intermediary. The Congolese Defense Minister commended the organization’s humanitarian commitment and expressed support for its role in protecting the lives and dignity of victims of armed conflict.
François Moreillon подчеркнул that the ICRC has been active in the country for more than 40 years, working closely with national institutions, including the Ministry of Defense, and facilitating operations linked to detainees and international humanitarian law. He reiterated that the organization stands ready to assist in any transfer operation, provided there is agreement between all parties.
This meeting comes days after the AFC/M23 announced the release of more than 5,000 FARDC soldiers, captured on various frontlines and handed over to the ICRC in Rumangabo, located in Rutshuru Territory. According to the group, these soldiers are to be repatriated to Kinshasa under ICRC supervision.
The ICRC confirmed its readiness to facilitate this transfer, recalling its previous role in May 2025, when more than 1,300 disarmed soldiers were successfully transferred from Goma to Kinshasa.
The prisoner exchange forms part of broader confidence-building measures agreed upon within the Doha process, aimed at easing tensions and promoting dialogue. However, the process remains fragile. The AFC/M23 accuses Kinshasa of refusing to release detained fighters, including individuals allegedly arrested arbitrarily, and of continuing ceasefire violations.
Despite these challenges, the involvement of the ICRC represents a significant step toward de-escalation, although the success of the process will depend on mutual trust and the effective implementation of commitments by both sides in a context of ongoing conflict.

title: Sessanga Questions $13 Billion Defense Spending, Calls for Accountability
excerpt: Kinshasa, March 23, 2026 – Opposition leader Delly Sessanga sharply criticized the Félix Tshisekedi government, claiming that over $13 billion allocated to national defense and security between 2019 and 2025 failed to improve conditions on the ground. Speaking at a press conferen
title_en: Sessanga Questions $13 Billion Defense Spending, Calls for Accountability
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, March 23, 2026 – Opposition leader Delly Sessanga sharply criticized the Félix Tshisekedi government, claiming that over $13 billion allocated to national defense and security between 2019 and 2025 failed to improve conditions on the ground. Speaking at a press conferen
body_en:
Kinshasa, March 23, 2026 – Opposition leader Delly Sessanga sharply criticized the Félix Tshisekedi government, claiming that over $13 billion allocated to national defense and security between 2019 and 2025 failed to improve conditions on the ground.
Speaking at a press conference in Kinshasa, Sessanga highlighted that, despite significant budget increases—over 30% of national expenditures going to security and defense—and the declaration of a state of emergency in 2021, there has been “no visible strengthening of the defense apparatus” and “no lasting security for the population.”
He questioned the use of these funds, asking: “Where have all these resources committed to defense, security, and the war gone? Who benefits from these war funds? If they haven’t strengthened operational capabilities or restored territorial integrity, this could very well be hiding a war business.”
Sessanga accused the government of “instrumentalizing the war” to buy time and avoid accountability, warning that any delay in the CENI’s electoral roadmap could threaten the scheduled October 23, 2028 elections. He rejected proposals by some loyalists to extend President Tshisekedi’s mandate under the pretext of national security.
“Having fought alongside the people in the streets against the electoral postponement between 2016 and 2018, Félix Tshisekedi and his supporters cannot now become the architects of another postponement under the guise of war,” he said.
The opposition leader also criticized the stalled national dialogue, which was meant to serve as a platform for truth-telling about the country’s multifaceted crises and for consolidating national cohesion, noting that Angola had been mandated to facilitate consultations with Congolese political actors.

excerpt_en: Kananga, Kasai-Central March 22, 2026 – A total of 295 newly trained officers were formally inducted into the ranks of the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) during a swearing-in ceremony at the Kananga Military Academy on Saturday, March 21. The event was a
body_en:
Kananga, Kasai-Central March 22, 2026 – A total of 295 newly trained officers were formally inducted into the ranks of the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) during a swearing-in ceremony at the Kananga Military Academy on Saturday, March 21.
The event was attended by Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defense and Veterans Affairs, Guy Kabombo Muadiamvita, the Chief of the General Staff, Lieutenant General Jules Banza Mwilambwe, and several FARDC generals. The graduates represent the 37th ordinary session of the academy, which over three years trained nearly 400 cadets in applied and military sciences, as well as social and strategic military studies.
In his address, Minister Guy Kabombo Muadiamvita highlighted the importance of preparing officers capable of effectively responding to current security challenges. He stressed that the graduates must embody the strength and authority of the State, maintain discipline, and uphold the laws of the Republic in defense of the Congolese people.
“Your choice to join the leadership of your institution requires constant adaptation to the evolving socio-professional environment, the nation’s ambitions, and the legitimate demands of defending the national territory,” the Minister said. “You must be the reassuring face of defense and security, particularly where authority is questioned or challenged.”
The ceremony included military honors, the swearing-in of officers, and the formal presentation of rank insignia, confirming the graduates as second lieutenants. A military parade and group photo concluded the event, much to the delight of families in attendance.
This induction strengthens the FARDC at a critical time, as the army faces continued aggression from Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 forces, which occupy significant parts of North Kivu and South Kivu provinces. With these new officers, the FARDC aims to bolster its operational capacity and safeguard the territorial integrity of the Democratic Republic of Congo.

title: Former Energy Minister and Renowned Jurist Jeannot Matadi Nenga Ngamanda Dies at 76
excerpt: Kinshasa March 22, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo mourns the loss of Jeannot Matadi Nenga Ngamanda, former Minister of Energy and Water Resources, who passed away on March 22 at the age of 76. Born on September 14, 1949, in Kifumu, Ngamanda was a towering figure in both
title_en: Former Energy Minister and Renowned Jurist Jeannot Matadi Nenga Ngamanda Dies at 76
excerpt_en: Kinshasa March 22, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo mourns the loss of Jeannot Matadi Nenga Ngamanda, former Minister of Energy and Water Resources, who passed away on March 22 at the age of 76. Born on September 14, 1949, in Kifumu, Ngamanda was a towering figure in both
body_en:
Kinshasa March 22, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo mourns the loss of Jeannot Matadi Nenga Ngamanda, former Minister of Energy and Water Resources, who passed away on March 22 at the age of 76.
Born on September 14, 1949, in Kifumu, Ngamanda was a towering figure in both the Congolese legal and political spheres. He earned a doctorate in law from the University of Paris X-Nanterre, a law degree from the National University of Zaire, and a diploma in human rights from Columbia University, New York. He also held a bachelor’s degree in philosophy and literature from Lovanium University in Kinshasa.
A practicing lawyer since 1975, Ngamanda appeared before the Court of Cassation and the Council of State throughout his career. He was a member of the Standing Commission for the Reform of Congolese Law and held leadership positions within the legal profession, including President of the Kinshasa Bar Association, President of the Young Lawyers Association of Zaire, and Vice-President of the International Association of Young Lawyers.
In politics, he served as Minister of Energy and Water Resources under the Matata II government, was a member of parliament, and held the position of Second Vice-President of the National Assembly during the transitional period.
Ngamanda was also a prolific author, publishing several influential works on law and governance, including Private Judicial Law (2006), The Right to a Fair Trial (2002), The Question of Judicial Power in the Democratic Republic of Congo (2001), and Zaire: An Improbable Democracy (1997).
His passing marks the end of a distinguished career dedicated to law, justice, and public service, leaving a lasting legacy in Congolese legal and political life.

title: Islamic State-Linked ADF Fighters Launch Deadly Attack on Muchacha Mining Site
excerpt: Mambasa, Ituri March 15, 2026 – A deadly attack struck the Muchacha and Mavuvu mining sites on the night of March 11–12, carried out by Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) fighters linked to the Islamic State. The assault targeted operations run by the Chinese company Kimia Mining, le
title_en: Islamic State-Linked ADF Fighters Launch Deadly Attack on Muchacha Mining Site
excerpt_en: Mambasa, Ituri March 15, 2026 – A deadly attack struck the Muchacha and Mavuvu mining sites on the night of March 11–12, carried out by Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) fighters linked to the Islamic State. The assault targeted operations run by the Chinese company Kimia Mining, le
body_en:
Mambasa, Ituri March 15, 2026 – A deadly attack struck the Muchacha and Mavuvu mining sites on the night of March 11–12, carried out by Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) fighters linked to the Islamic State. The assault targeted operations run by the Chinese company Kimia Mining, leaving equipment destroyed and multiple casualties in its wake.
Images released by the Islamic State show trucks, tractors, and camps set ablaze, highlighting the scale of the destruction. More than a dozen people were killed, and around 100 civilians were taken hostage during the attack. The ADF also ambushed a Congolese army unit that arrived to intervene, resulting in the death of an officer and several soldiers.
The fighters involved are believed to belong to the Batike and Bapaitumba groups, two factions that have operated in the Bapere sector of North Kivu for over a year. Following previous clashes in Budhudea, the ADF relocated to new positions in Botambisi, Mapendano, and Mabuo, maintaining control over gold mining sites where they collect taxes and coordinate attacks.
Officials note that the ADF’s movement toward Muchacha was part of a search for new hideouts, evading Congolese and Ugandan military operations supported by Wazalendo trackers. The fighters crossed the Lenda River, entering Ituri territory, where they executed the coordinated assault.
Since June 2024, Bapere has hosted multiple ADF factions, including the group led by Abwakasi, notorious for its brutal and lethal operations. Analysts warn that the Muchacha region is strategically significant, forming part of the Kivu-Kinshasa Green Corridor, a critical route supplying Kisangani and Kinshasa with essential agricultural products, raising concerns about the ongoing threat to the region.

title: ADF Advance Toward Walese-Karo Raises Fears of Strategic Regrouping
excerpt: Mambasa, Ituri March 19, 2026 – Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) fighters have intensified their movement along the Kisangani axis, advancing from Bapere (Lubero) into the Okapi Wildlife Reserve following the recent attack on a Chinese mining site in Muchacha. On the night of March
title_en: ADF Advance Toward Walese-Karo Raises Fears of Strategic Regrouping
excerpt_en: Mambasa, Ituri March 19, 2026 – Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) fighters have intensified their movement along the Kisangani axis, advancing from Bapere (Lubero) into the Okapi Wildlife Reserve following the recent attack on a Chinese mining site in Muchacha. On the night of March
body_en:
Mambasa, Ituri March 19, 2026 – Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) fighters have intensified their movement along the Kisangani axis, advancing from Bapere (Lubero) into the Okapi Wildlife Reserve following the recent attack on a Chinese mining site in Muchacha.
On the night of March 17, the group attacked the Babesua patrol post, leaving at least 19 civilians dead, according to local reports. The attack has heightened fears among local leaders that the ADF is attempting to push toward the Walese-Karo region, a known stronghold of Musa Baluku, along the Mambasa–Isiro axis via Nduye.
Recent FARDC-UPDF operations reportedly targeted ADF positions in Walese-Karo, prompting concerns that the fighters are seeking to regroup or extract their leader. Local communities fear the group could bypass Epulu and Mambasa to reinforce Baluku before retreating to the Bapere forests, whose terrain offers a strategic advantage.
Observers note that such movements reflect a recurring ADF survival strategy, involving mobility and reinforcement between factions. Similar operations were reported after June 2024, when fighters moved across Bandulu, Bilulu, and Midede to support units under pressure from joint military offensives.
The evolving situation underscores the fluid and adaptive nature of ADF operations, raising concerns over regional security and the risk of further attacks along key corridors in eastern DRC.

title: Minister Nduhungirehe Condemns International Hypocrisy Over DRC Conflict
excerpt: Kigali, 12 March 2026 – Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation, Ambassador Olivier Nduhungirehe, has denounced what he described as the bias and hypocrisy of the international community regarding the ongoing war in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). Speakin
title_en: Minister Nduhungirehe Condemns International Hypocrisy Over DRC Conflict
excerpt_en: Kigali, 12 March 2026 – Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation, Ambassador Olivier Nduhungirehe, has denounced what he described as the bias and hypocrisy of the international community regarding the ongoing war in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). Speakin
body_en:
Kigali, 12 March 2026 – Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation, Ambassador Olivier Nduhungirehe, has denounced what he described as the bias and hypocrisy of the international community regarding the ongoing war in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).
Speaking after the death of French national Karine Buisset in a drone strike in Goma on 11 March 2026, Minister Nduhungirehe criticized the global response, noting that while many countries and organizations expressed sorrow, no accountability was demanded from those responsible.
“The international community stood united, blaming all parties and calling on the DRC government to establish an independent commission of inquiry,” he said, highlighting that the attack was carried out by DRC forces.
Minister Nduhungirehe questioned why, in other instances where DRC forces conducted attacks against civilians, particularly in Minembwe and Banyamulenge, the international community often remained silent. He added that even when calls for investigations were made, such as after the January 3, 2026 drone strike in Masisi that killed and injured many civilians, inquiries were never conducted.
“It is sad to see that today, not only have the principles of the United Nations and international law lost value, but human lives are sacrificed when powerful interests are threatened,” he stated.
The Minister further condemned the selective nature of international scrutiny. He pointed out that while attacks targeting Congolese Tutsi communities continue, and threats against Rwanda are made, the international community often chooses silence or partiality. Conversely, when Rwanda is accused of involvement in alleged killings, such claims are often amplified without verification.
Minister Nduhungirehe concluded by affirming Rwanda’s stance: while drone attacks and cross-border threats persist, the Rwandan army will continue to protect the nation and its citizens.

title_en: Joseph Kabila Calls for the Removal of Tshisekedi’s Regime
excerpt_en: Goma, North Kivu March 23, 2026 – Former President Joseph Kabila Kabange, who led the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) from 2001 to 2019, has publicly called for the removal of President Félix Tshisekedi’s government, denouncing it as acting illegally. The statement came during
body_en:
Goma, North Kivu March 23, 2026 – Former President Joseph Kabila Kabange, who led the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) from 2001 to 2019, has publicly called for the removal of President Félix Tshisekedi’s government, denouncing it as acting illegally. The statement came during an interview on March 20 with journalist Hubert Leclercq of Le Libre, conducted at Kabila’s residence in Goma, North Kivu province.
Kabila, who has been in eastern DRC since May 2025, has been accused by the authorities of collaborating with the AFC/M23 coalition, which controls Goma, and of undermining national security. He was sentenced to death in absentia by the Kinshasa government.
“When asked why I am in Goma, I said it is home. I received you in a house I bought in 1999. The relentless attacks on me and my political family began in 2019, before the birth of AFC/M23. I believe I have the right to work and communicate with all Congolese, with the aim of uniting the population and achieving peace,” Kabila told Le Libre.

title: Rwanda Launches Cybersecurity Training Center Targeting One Million Learners by 2030
excerpt: Kigali, March 21, 2026 — A new cybersecurity training and consultancy center aimed at strengthening digital skills across Africa has been launched in Rwanda, with an ambitious target of training more than one million people by 2030. The initiative, known as International Cybersec
title_en: Rwanda Launches Cybersecurity Training Center Targeting One Million Learners by 2030
excerpt_en: Kigali, March 21, 2026 — A new cybersecurity training and consultancy center aimed at strengthening digital skills across Africa has been launched in Rwanda, with an ambitious target of training more than one million people by 2030. The initiative, known as International Cybersec
body_en:
Kigali, March 21, 2026 — A new cybersecurity training and consultancy center aimed at strengthening digital skills across Africa has been launched in Rwanda, with an ambitious target of training more than one million people by 2030.
The initiative, known as International Cybersecurity Community for Africa (ICCA), was officially unveiled on March 20 by a consortium of international students specializing in technology.
ICCA Chief Executive Officer Petero Niyodusenga said the idea was born while he and his colleagues were studying in the United States, where they began informally teaching cybersecurity to fellow students.
“We realized there was a strong need to expand this knowledge to Africa,” he said, noting the continent’s rapid digital transformation and the growing importance of cybersecurity in both public and private sectors.
He pointed to Rwanda’s national development strategies, including National Strategy for Transformation phases, which emphasize infrastructure development and increased integration of technology across government services, businesses, and daily life.
“As digital adoption grows, so does the need for skilled professionals to protect systems and data,” Niyodusenga added.
Rwanda has set a national target of equipping one million people—primarily youth—with coding and basic technology skills by 2029, alongside training an additional 500,000 individuals in advanced digital competencies.
An official from the Ministry of ICT and Innovation, Grace Niwemukiza, stressed that achieving these goals will require strong collaboration across sectors.
“The government cannot achieve this alone,” Niwemukiza said. “Partnerships between public institutions, private companies, and initiatives like ICCA are essential to meet our national ambitions.”
The center plans to offer training to a wide range of beneficiaries, including university students, IT professionals, entrepreneurs, and corporate staff seeking to strengthen their cybersecurity capabilities.
Students have welcomed the initiative as a practical complement to academic learning. Carnegie Mellon University Africa student Aklile Mamo said the program would provide hands-on experience often missing from classroom instruction.
“Learning in school is important, but applying that knowledge in real-world situations is critical,” he said.
ICCA also aims to expand its reach beyond Rwanda, with plans to operate across multiple African countries, including Gabon, Republic of the Congo, Kenya, and Ethiopia, as part of a broader effort to build cybersecurity capacity across the continent.

title: 74 Burundians Voluntarily Return Home from Rwanda
excerpt: Bugesera, Rwanda, 12 March 2026 – Seventy-four Burundians, mostly men, who had sought refuge in Rwanda over the years, have voluntarily returned to their homeland, expressing gratitude for the peaceful environment they experienced during their stay. The group, comprising 30 women
title_en: 74 Burundians Voluntarily Return Home from Rwanda
excerpt_en: Bugesera, Rwanda, 12 March 2026 – Seventy-four Burundians, mostly men, who had sought refuge in Rwanda over the years, have voluntarily returned to their homeland, expressing gratitude for the peaceful environment they experienced during their stay. The group, comprising 30 women
body_en:
Bugesera, Rwanda, 12 March 2026 – Seventy-four Burundians, mostly men, who had sought refuge in Rwanda over the years, have voluntarily returned to their homeland, expressing gratitude for the peaceful environment they experienced during their stay.
The group, comprising 30 women and 44 men from 47 families, crossed the Rwanda-Burundi border at Nemba in Bugesera District. Sixty-two had been living in Mahama Camp in Kirehe District, while the remaining 12 resided in Kigali City.
The returnees were formally handed over to Burundian authorities, with representatives from the Ministry of Humanitarian Affairs (MINEMA) and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) accompanying them.
Jérémie Havugiyaremye, who spent 25 years in Rwanda, shared his experience: “Life in the camp was not easy, but I had no problems in Rwanda. My family in the camp is not ready to return yet, but I miss my country and want to start a new life there.” Havugiyaremye added that the decision to return was influenced by friends who had found their homeland safe.
Similarly, Oda Mariya, who had fled the 2015 unrest in Burundi and lived in Mahama Camp for 11 years, said, “I came back because peace has returned and our comrades encouraged us. I wanted to reunite with my family and live well.”
Karagire Gonzague, Director of Refugee Programs at MINEMA, noted that since 2020, over 31,000 Burundians have returned home voluntarily, with strong cooperation from Burundian authorities. “In 2022, Burundian representatives visited Mahama Camp and Kigali to encourage refugees to return. Last year, online discussions were also held to explain the benefits of repatriation,” he said.
These 74 returnees add to 115 others who returned in November 2025. MINEMA reports that over 50,000 Burundian refugees still remain in Rwanda, living in camps and urban areas.

title: 18 Migrants Killed in Boat Tragedy off Comoros Coast
excerpt: Mitsamiouli, Comoros, 20 March 2026 – At least 18 migrants have died after a boat capsized off the coast of the Comoros while attempting to reach the French-administered island of Mayotte. According to Comoros Security Minister Mohamed Ahmed Assoumani, the accident occurred durin
title_en: 18 Migrants Killed in Boat Tragedy off Comoros Coast
excerpt_en: Mitsamiouli, Comoros, 20 March 2026 – At least 18 migrants have died after a boat capsized off the coast of the Comoros while attempting to reach the French-administered island of Mayotte. According to Comoros Security Minister Mohamed Ahmed Assoumani, the accident occurred durin
body_en:
Mitsamiouli, Comoros, 20 March 2026 – At least 18 migrants have died after a boat capsized off the coast of the Comoros while attempting to reach the French-administered island of Mayotte.
According to Comoros Security Minister Mohamed Ahmed Assoumani, the accident occurred during the night of 18–19 March in the Mitsamiouli area. The victims included 16 nationals from the Democratic Republic of the Congo and two from Burundi.
The vessel was reportedly carrying 51 people, who had departed from Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, on a week-long journey toward Mayotte.
Following the accident, local residents and fishermen launched rescue efforts, managing to save 33 survivors, who were transported to a nearby hospital.
Authorities praised the swift response of the community. “Their lives were saved thanks to collective action and rapid intervention,” Assoumani said.
The United Nations Resident Coordinator in the Comoros, James Bot, attributed such incidents to human trafficking networks that exploit migrants by promising safe passage but abandoning them at sea.
He called for stronger regional cooperation, particularly between Comoros and Tanzania, to address the root causes of irregular migration and prevent further tragedies.
The accident underscores the ongoing risks faced by migrants attempting dangerous sea crossings in search of better opportunities.

title: Oakland Institute Criticizes Washington Agreement, Calls for Stronger Action Against Rwanda
excerpt: DRC March 13, 2026 — The Oakland Institute has sharply criticized the Washington Agreement, arguing that it contains “inherent contradictions” by allegedly rewarding Rwanda despite its continued involvement in the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. In a statement r
title_en: Oakland Institute Criticizes Washington Agreement, Calls for Stronger Action Against Rwanda
excerpt_en: DRC March 13, 2026 — The Oakland Institute has sharply criticized the Washington Agreement, arguing that it contains “inherent contradictions” by allegedly rewarding Rwanda despite its continued involvement in the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. In a statement r
body_en:
DRC March 13, 2026 — The Oakland Institute has sharply criticized the Washington Agreement, arguing that it contains “inherent contradictions” by allegedly rewarding Rwanda despite its continued involvement in the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
In a statement released on March 12, the organization called on the United States administration to take stronger measures to end what it describes as Rwandan aggression through the AFC/M23 rebellion, which it says fuels instability and illicit exploitation of natural resources at the expense of Congolese civilians.
The think tank also deemed U.S. sanctions imposed by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on the Rwandan Defence Forces (RDF) and several senior officials as insufficient, arguing they fail to counter the financial gains derived from the conflict.
According to the report, the RDF has played a decisive role in supporting the M23 rebellion, including in the capture of key areas such as Goma and Bukavu, as well as strategic mining sites. The organization highlights that control over resources—particularly coltan and gold—has enabled the rebels to generate significant revenues, including an estimated $800,000 per month from coltan taxation and up to $2 billion in gold exports in 2025.
The Oakland Institute further notes that Rwanda continues to receive substantial international financial support, including U.S. bilateral aid and major funding from the World Bank, raising concerns about policy contradictions. It points to infrastructure contracts allegedly linked to entities associated with the RDF, suggesting a nexus between military influence and economic interests.
Frédéric Mousseau, policy director at the institute, argued that Rwanda’s actions undermine the credibility of the Washington Agreement. “Rwanda’s violations and continued presence in the DRC highlight the contradictions of a so-called peace agreement that effectively grants access to Congolese resources while failing to ensure accountability,” he said, warning that such an approach cannot lead to lasting peace.
The report echoes earlier findings published in the institute’s study “Shafted: The Race for Critical Minerals in the DRC,” which cautioned that diplomatic initiatives may be used to advance resource interests under the guise of peacebuilding.
Diverging Positions
In response to the sanctions, Rwanda rejected the measures as “unilateral” and “distorting the facts”, arguing they unfairly target one side of the conflict. Kigali accused Kinshasa of violating ceasefire agreements through drone strikes and military offensives, and reiterated concerns over the presence of armed groups, including the FDLR, alongside Congolese forces.
On its part, the Congolese government welcomed the sanctions as a “clear signal” in support of sovereignty and territorial integrity, stressing the need for consistency between diplomatic commitments and realities on the ground. Authorities in Kinshasa maintain that ending support for armed groups and respecting international law are essential to stabilizing eastern DRC.
Fragile Diplomatic Progress
Despite ongoing diplomatic efforts, including the Washington and Doha processes supported by the African Union, progress remains limited on the ground. Persistent tensions between Kinshasa and Kigali, combined with renewed clashes in North and South Kivu, continue to undermine hopes for a sustainable resolution to the conflict.
The Oakland Institute’s critique adds to growing international debate over whether current diplomatic frameworks can effectively address the root causes of the conflict or risk entrenching existing power dynamics in the region.

The report echoes earlier findings published in the institute’s study “Shafted: The Race for Critical Minerals in the DRC,” which cautioned that diplomatic initiatives may be used to advance resource interests under the guise of peacebuilding.
Diverging Positions
In response to the sanctions, Rwanda rejected the measures as “unilateral” and “distorting the facts”, arguing they unfairly target one side of the conflict. Kigali accused Kinshasa of violating ceasefire agreements through drone strikes and military offensives, and reiterated concerns over the presence of armed groups, including the FDLR, alongside Congolese forces.
On its part, the Congolese government welcomed the sanctions as a “clear signal” in support of sovereignty and territorial integrity, stressing the need for consistency between diplomatic commitments and realities on the ground. Authorities in Kinshasa maintain that ending support for armed groups and respecting international law are essential to stabilizing eastern DRC.
Fragile Diplomatic Progress
Despite ongoing diplomatic efforts, including the Washington and Doha processes supported by the African Union, progress remains limited on the ground. Persistent tensions between Kinshasa and Kigali, combined with renewed clashes in North and South Kivu, continue to undermine hopes for a sustainable resolution to the conflict.
The Oakland Institute’s critique adds to growing international debate over whether current diplomatic frameworks can effectively address the root causes of the conflict or risk entrenching existing power dynamics in the region.

title_en: Youth from Goma and Bukavu Urge Inclusive Dialogue to Resolve Kivu Crisis
excerpt_en: Bukavu, March 22, 2026 – Around one hundred young leaders from Goma and Bukavu, including students and members of local youth committees, have called on the DRC government and the AFC-M23 movement to engage in sincere and inclusive dialogue to end decades of conflict in eastern D
body_en:
Bukavu, March 22, 2026 – Around one hundred young leaders from Goma and Bukavu, including students and members of local youth committees, have called on the DRC government and the AFC-M23 movement to engage in sincere and inclusive dialogue to end decades of conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
The appeal followed a two-day workshop held in Bukavu from March 14 to 15, organized by the Kivu Social Festival under the theme: “Youth of North and South Kivu: Catalysts for Peace, Resilience, and Participatory Governance.” The event aimed to position youth as central actors in peacebuilding and regional development.
In a final declaration, participants urged authorities and M23 leaders to “prioritize sincere and inclusive dialogue,” promote social cohesion, and combat all forms of community stigmatization. They also called on young people across Kivu and the DRC to actively participate in governance and peace processes.
Regional, African, and international organizations were asked to support peace efforts responsibly and impartially, ensuring lasting results. The youth pledged to resist divisive and tribal rhetoric, instead fostering hope, resilience, and reconstruction in their communities.
Blaise Rugusha, Director General of the Kivu Social Festival, highlighted the positive energy and creativity of Kivu’s youth, emphasizing that the region is defined not only by conflict but also by a generation determined to transform its future.
The workshop comes amid recent diplomatic progress. Following persistent tensions between the DRC and Rwanda, a March 17–18 meeting in Washington, D.C., mediated by the United States, produced “concrete measures” to accelerate the implementation of the Washington Peace Agreement. The International Conference on the Great Lakes Region (ICGLR) welcomed these commitments, noting they are a step toward reducing tensions and strengthening trust while respecting each country’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.

title: President Tshisekedi Demands “Urgent” Completion of Governance Framework for Inga III Project
excerpt: March 22, 2026 – President Félix Tshisekedi has called for the rapid finalization of the governance framework for the Grand Inga hydropower project, emphasizing its strategic importance in transforming the Democratic Republic of Congo into a continental energy powerhouse. Speakin
title_en: President Tshisekedi Demands “Urgent” Completion of Governance Framework for Inga III Project
excerpt_en: March 22, 2026 – President Félix Tshisekedi has called for the rapid finalization of the governance framework for the Grand Inga hydropower project, emphasizing its strategic importance in transforming the Democratic Republic of Congo into a continental energy powerhouse. Speakin
body_en:
March 22, 2026 – President Félix Tshisekedi has called for the rapid finalization of the governance framework for the Grand Inga hydropower project, emphasizing its strategic importance in transforming the Democratic Republic of Congo into a continental energy powerhouse.
Speaking at the 83rd Council of Ministers meeting on March 20 at the African Union City in Kinshasa, the President underscored the project’s potential to generate 42,000 MW, describing it as a “sovereign lever for industrialization, ecological transition, and social dignity” for the Congolese people.
“The Grand Inga project embodies a historic choice: to sustainably electrify the country, support youth employment, drive green growth based on a responsible mining industry, and assert the DRC’s energy leadership in Africa,” he said.
President Tshisekedi highlighted the critical role of world-class partnerships in realizing this vision. He recalled the World Bank’s approval of a US$1 billion loan for the Inga III development program on June 3, 2025, of which US$250 million is already available. He stressed that, with the financing agreements now in force as of February 2, 2026, the project’s governance framework must be finalized urgently.
To this end, he instructed relevant ministries—including Industry, National Education, Mines, Environment, Higher Education, Employment, and Water Resources and Electricity—and the Kongo Central provincial government to complete the necessary memoranda of understanding with the Agency for the Development and Promotion of the Grand Inga Project (ADPI-RDC) within 60 days. Signed protocols must be forwarded to donors no later than April 3, 2026.
The President also urged the government to review and finalize the Inga bill, aiming for adoption at the March 27 Council of Ministers meeting and submission to Parliament by March 31, 2026. This legislation is considered a key prerequisite for unlocking World Bank support. A progress report on these directives is expected within five days.
President Tshisekedi framed the Inga III program as central to addressing the country’s energy deficit, noting that only 21% of Congolese households currently have access to electricity. The project is a cornerstone of the National Energy Pact and aligns with Africa-wide initiatives, such as Mission 300, aimed at expanding energy access. By 2030, the government aims to increase electricity coverage to 62% of the population, leveraging Inga III to accelerate institutional reforms, infrastructure development, and private sector engagement.
The Inga III development program, structured in multi-phase investments, will also target local communities, job creation, and infrastructure, laying the foundation for sustainable energy growth well beyond 2030, according to the World Bank.

title: $1.9 Million Seized at N’djili Airport in High-Stakes Operation
excerpt: Kinshasa March 22, 2026 – Authorities in the Democratic Republic of Congo have seized approximately $1.9 million at N’djili International Airport, in a move described by the Minister of Justice and Keeper of the Seals, Guillaume Ngefa, as “lawful and complete.” According to an of
title_en: $1.9 Million Seized at N’djili Airport in High-Stakes Operation
excerpt_en: Kinshasa March 22, 2026 – Authorities in the Democratic Republic of Congo have seized approximately $1.9 million at N’djili International Airport, in a move described by the Minister of Justice and Keeper of the Seals, Guillaume Ngefa, as “lawful and complete.” According to an of
body_en:
Kinshasa March 22, 2026 – Authorities in the Democratic Republic of Congo have seized approximately $1.9 million at N’djili International Airport, in a move described by the Minister of Justice and Keeper of the Seals, Guillaume Ngefa, as “lawful and complete.”
According to an official directive sent to the Prosecutor General at the Court of Cassation, the interception was carried out amid suspicions that the funds were intended to be unlawfully manipulated or distributed, in clear violation of Congolese law.
The minister’s letter highlights that such actions could constitute serious offenses, including embezzlement of seized assets, corruption, obstruction of justice, and money laundering. Judicial authorities were instructed to seize the money immediately, place it under official seal in the presence of judicial police officers, and document the circumstances thoroughly, including the identification of all individuals involved.
Under the law on combating money laundering and terrorism financing, the funds are to be deposited with the Central Bank of Congo, and the reports transmitted to the National Financial Intelligence Unit (CENAREF). The Minister also demanded a full legal investigation to determine the origin of the funds, classify potential criminal actions, and hold responsible parties accountable.
“This is a highly sensitive matter for public order and the credibility of our institutions,” the minister stated, emphasizing that any attempt by officials to handle or dispose of the funds outside the legal framework will be prosecuted with the utmost rigor.
The authorities have committed to keeping the public informed of the progress of the case.

excerpt_en: Masisi March 14, 2026 — Intense fighting broke out early Saturday in Malemo, a village in the Bashali Mokoto area of Masisi Territory, pitting AFC/M23 rebels against Wazalendo fighters. According to local sources, the clashes began around 5:00 a.m. following an offensive launched
body_en:
Masisi March 14, 2026 — Intense fighting broke out early Saturday in Malemo, a village in the Bashali Mokoto area of Masisi Territory, pitting AFC/M23 rebels against Wazalendo fighters.
According to local sources, the clashes began around 5:00 a.m. following an offensive launched by Wazalendo forces on rebel-held positions along the Kalembe–Mpety axis. Since then, heavy and light weapons fire has been reported, with loud explosions echoing across the surrounding area.
The violence has triggered panic among civilians in nearby villages, many of whom have remained confined to their homes amid fears of further escalation.
These clashes come just 24 hours after similar fighting in Kashuga, located in the same Bashali Mokoto area, where Wazalendo forces also attacked AFC/M23 positions. The renewed offensives suggest mounting pressure on rebel strongholds in this part of Masisi.
As of midday Saturday, the situation remained highly volatile, with no confirmed casualty figures. Local sources in nearby Kalembe reported continued tension and uncertainty as fighting persisted.

body_en:
Rutshuru, North Kivu March 17, 2026 – A fragile return to calm was observed on March 17 in four villages of the Bwito chiefdom—Lusoa, Iyobora, Mirangi, and Chaala—after clashes between Wazalendo fighters and AFC/M23 rebels.
The fighting began around 4:00 a.m., when the Wazalendo launched coordinated attacks on rebel positions. Hours of heavy and light weapons fire followed, plunging the civilian population into fear.
The situation shifted after the arrival of AFC/M23 reinforcements from Birundule, forcing the Wazalendo to withdraw. The four villages are now under rebel control.

title: Rwanda, Israel Hold Talks to Strengthen Military Cooperation
excerpt: Kigali, March 12, 2026 — Rwanda and Israel have held high-level discussions aimed at deepening military cooperation, as both countries seek to reinforce security partnerships amid evolving regional challenges. The talks, held on March 11, brought together Rwanda’s Minister of Def
title_en: Rwanda, Israel Hold Talks to Strengthen Military Cooperation
excerpt_en: Kigali, March 12, 2026 — Rwanda and Israel have held high-level discussions aimed at deepening military cooperation, as both countries seek to reinforce security partnerships amid evolving regional challenges. The talks, held on March 11, brought together Rwanda’s Minister of Def
body_en:
Kigali, March 12, 2026 — Rwanda and Israel have held high-level discussions aimed at deepening military cooperation, as both countries seek to reinforce security partnerships amid evolving regional challenges.
The talks, held on March 11, brought together Rwanda’s Minister of Defense Juvenal Marizamunda and Chief of Defence Staff Mubarakh Muganga with Einat Weiss, Israel’s ambassador to Rwanda. The meeting was also attended by Brig. Gen. Patrick Karuretwa, Director General for International Military Cooperation at Rwanda’s Ministry of Defense.
According to the Rwandan Defence Force, discussions focused on issues of mutual interest and explored ways to further strengthen existing military ties between the two nations.
Rwanda and Israel maintain longstanding cooperation in defense and security, including joint training programs, knowledge sharing, and collaboration aimed at promoting regional and international stability. Their partnership also extends beyond the military sector into areas such as technology, education, healthcare, investment, and agriculture.
The renewed engagement comes at a time of heightened security concerns for both countries. Israel continues to face tensions in the Middle East, including conflict involving Hamas and broader regional dynamics linked to Iran.
For Rwanda, security challenges remain tied to instability in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, where authorities have repeatedly raised concerns over cooperation between Congolese forces and the FDLR armed group.
Officials from both sides emphasized the importance of sustained cooperation to address shared security concerns and contribute to broader peace and stability efforts.

Victoria, 20 March 2026 – Rwanda and Seychelles have held high-level discussions aimed at expanding cooperation across key sectors, including education, tourism, and agriculture.

Both sides also discussed improving service delivery, building institutional capacity, and sharing development experiences to advance sustainable development goals.
Vice President Pillay proposed the establishment of a joint mechanism to monitor the implementation of bilateral agreements and ensure effective follow-up.
The discussions build on existing cooperation between the two countries, including agreements reached during President Kagame’s 2023 visit to Seychelles, which covered areas such as health, investment, and security.
A visa waiver agreement between Rwanda and Seychelles also remains in place, facilitating travel and economic exchange between the two nations.

title: Rwanda Reports Decline in Attempted Bank Frauds Despite Rising Cyber Threats
excerpt: Kigali, 19 March 2026 – Rwanda recorded around 3,000 attempted bank frauds in 2025, down from 5,000 cases the previous year, according to the Central Bank. Governor Soraya Hakuziyaremye announced the figures during a press conference following discussions on monetary policy and f
title_en: Rwanda Reports Decline in Attempted Bank Frauds Despite Rising Cyber Threats
excerpt_en: Kigali, 19 March 2026 – Rwanda recorded around 3,000 attempted bank frauds in 2025, down from 5,000 cases the previous year, according to the Central Bank. Governor Soraya Hakuziyaremye announced the figures during a press conference following discussions on monetary policy and f
body_en:
Kigali, 19 March 2026 – Rwanda recorded around 3,000 attempted bank frauds in 2025, down from 5,000 cases the previous year, according to the Central Bank.
Governor Soraya Hakuziyaremye announced the figures during a press conference following discussions on monetary policy and financial stability, noting that while cyber-related threats persist, overall incidents have declined.
She confirmed that authorities are investigating a recent attempted fraud targeting Equity Bank Rwanda, adding that some of the affected funds have already been recovered.
Hakuziyaremye attributed many of the incidents to the growing use of digital financial services, which has introduced new vulnerabilities even as the sector modernizes.
“Cyber-related theft exists, but what matters is how we protect ourselves and respond when incidents occur,” she said, emphasizing the importance of prevention and accountability.
The Central Bank also indicated that mechanisms are in place to ensure that affected customers are reimbursed within a short period, with efforts underway to return funds within seven days in confirmed cases.
Rwanda’s financial sector includes 11 commercial banks, alongside microfinance institutions and SACCOs, all of which have strengthened cybersecurity measures in recent years.
Globally, cybercrime remains a growing challenge, with estimates suggesting that a cyberattack occurs every few seconds, underscoring the need for continued vigilance.

title: Goma Residents Protest Drone Strike, Call on AFC/M23 to “Liberate” DR Congo
excerpt: Goma, March 12, 2026 — Residents of Goma took to the streets on Thursday to protest a recent drone strike attributed to the army of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, condemning the attack and calling on the AFC/M23 coalition to expand its control across the country. The demon
title_en: Goma Residents Protest Drone Strike, Call on AFC/M23 to “Liberate” DR Congo
excerpt_en: Goma, March 12, 2026 — Residents of Goma took to the streets on Thursday to protest a recent drone strike attributed to the army of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, condemning the attack and calling on the AFC/M23 coalition to expand its control across the country. The demon
body_en:
Goma, March 12, 2026 — Residents of Goma took to the streets on Thursday to protest a recent drone strike attributed to the army of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, condemning the attack and calling on the AFC/M23 coalition to expand its control across the country.
The demonstration followed a drone strike carried out on March 11 in the Himbi neighborhood, where at least three civilians were killed, including Karine Buisset, a French national working for the UNICEF. Local residents reported that drones targeted residential areas, sparking outrage among the population.
Responding to a call from civil society groups, demonstrators gathered in large numbers, halting daily activities to denounce what they described as indiscriminate attacks on civilian areas in North and South Kivu. Protesters also expressed condolences to the families of those killed.
The AFC/M23 coalition condemned the strike, accusing the Congolese government of violating the ceasefire agreement reached in Doha, Qatar, and criticized the international community for what it described as silence in the face of escalating violence.
Some demonstrators accused President Félix Tshisekedi of pursuing military actions at the expense of civilian lives, alleging that ongoing operations reflect a determination to maintain power despite the human cost.
According to AFC/M23 spokesperson Lawrence Kanyuka, protesters called on the group to “remove Félix Tshisekedi from the entire country,” arguing that areas under government control have become centers of insecurity and violence.
Goma has been under the control of AFC/M23 since January 2025. The latest strike marks the first reported drone attack in the city in more than a year, heightening tensions in a region already affected by prolonged conflict.

body_en:
Uvira, 20 March 2026 – Fighting has resumed between the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (FARDC) and the AFC/M23 coalition in parts of the Ruzizi Valley, marking the end of a two-month lull in hostilities.
The renewed clashes come shortly after Congolese forces, supported by Wazalendo groups, closed the RN5 road linking Uvira and Bukavu, citing security concerns.
According to political analyst Tite Gatabazi, the AFC/M23 resumed combat following what it described as attacks on its positions. He added that the group also claims to be responding to violence targeting certain communities in the region.
Gatabazi suggested that the rebels retain significant operational capacity and could potentially attempt to advance toward Uvira town, particularly amid concerns over the current security situation.
The resurgence of fighting highlights ongoing instability in eastern DRC, despite recent diplomatic efforts aimed at reducing tensions and advancing peace agreements.

title: EAC Calls on AU to Strengthen Mediation Efforts in Eastern DRC
excerpt: Arusha, March 9, 2026 — The East African Community (EAC) has urged the African Union (AU) to mobilize adequate financial and logistical resources to support ongoing mediation efforts aimed at resolving the escalating crisis in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. The appeal foll
title_en: EAC Calls on AU to Strengthen Mediation Efforts in Eastern DRC
excerpt_en: Arusha, March 9, 2026 — The East African Community (EAC) has urged the African Union (AU) to mobilize adequate financial and logistical resources to support ongoing mediation efforts aimed at resolving the escalating crisis in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. The appeal foll
body_en:
Arusha, March 9, 2026 — The East African Community (EAC) has urged the African Union (AU) to mobilize adequate financial and logistical resources to support ongoing mediation efforts aimed at resolving the escalating crisis in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
The appeal follows the 25th Summit of Heads of State held on March 7 in Arusha, where regional leaders reviewed the deteriorating security and humanitarian situation marked by rising tensions between Democratic Republic of Congo and Rwanda, as well as continued clashes involving the AFC/M23 rebellion.
In its final communiqué, the Summit emphasized the urgency of reinforcing the AU-led mediation framework. “The Summit urged the African Union to provide the necessary financial and logistical resources to the African Union-led mediation process in eastern DRC to ensure a swift and sustained commitment to its conclusion,” the statement read.
The mediation process, aligned with parallel diplomatic tracks in Washington and Doha, is led by Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé, who serves as the AU’s designated mediator for the eastern DRC crisis. The current structure stems from a high-level meeting convened in January 2026 in Lomé, aimed at harmonizing peace initiatives.
Under this framework, Gnassingbé is supported by a Togolese mediation team drawn from the presidency and foreign affairs ministry. Five co-facilitators—former African heads of state—have been assigned key thematic roles: Olusegun Obasanjo oversees military and security issues, Sahle-Work Zewde handles humanitarian concerns, Uhuru Kenyatta leads dialogue with armed groups, Mokgweetsi Masisi manages regional economic cooperation, and Catherine Samba-Panza is responsible for civil society, reconciliation, and women’s issues.
A joint secretariat—bringing together the AU, EAC, Southern African Development Community (SADC), and International Conference on the Great Lakes Region (ICGLR)—has also been established to coordinate efforts, alongside international partners including the United Nations, the European Union, and Qatar.
Despite intensified diplomatic engagement, progress on the ground remains limited. The Washington track, backed by Donald Trump and endorsed by Félix Tshisekedi and Paul Kagame, has yet to translate into tangible security improvements. Mutual accusations between Kinshasa and Kigali over alleged violations continue to undermine trust and stability.
Meanwhile, the Doha negotiations—facilitated by Qatar between the Congolese government and the AFC/M23 rebellion—have slowed significantly. Key provisions, including the ceasefire mechanism, declaration of principles, and framework agreement, remain unimplemented, stalling efforts to address root causes of the conflict such as state authority and armed group reintegration.
This diplomatic impasse has contributed to renewed violent clashes in eastern DRC, further complicating an already fragile humanitarian situation. Calls for a national dialogue to complement international mediation efforts have also gone unanswered. President Tshisekedi maintains that such an initiative must be led exclusively by his office, despite mounting pressure from socio-political actors and recent proposals from religious groups.
As mediation efforts struggle to gain momentum, regional leaders warn that without stronger institutional backing and coordinated implementation, prospects for lasting peace in eastern DRC remain uncertain.

title: Delly Sesanga Condemns Any Attempt to Amend Constitution for Third Term
excerpt: Kinshasa, March 21, 2026 – Opposition leader Delly Sesanga issued a strong warning on Saturday against any efforts to amend the Constitution to allow President Félix Tshisekedi a third term. Speaking at a press conference in Kinshasa, Sesanga described such initiatives as a “seri
title_en: Delly Sesanga Condemns Any Attempt to Amend Constitution for Third Term
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, March 21, 2026 – Opposition leader Delly Sesanga issued a strong warning on Saturday against any efforts to amend the Constitution to allow President Félix Tshisekedi a third term. Speaking at a press conference in Kinshasa, Sesanga described such initiatives as a “seri
body_en:
Kinshasa, March 21, 2026 – Opposition leader Delly Sesanga issued a strong warning on Saturday against any efforts to amend the Constitution to allow President Félix Tshisekedi a third term.
Speaking at a press conference in Kinshasa, Sesanga described such initiatives as a “serious breach of the republican order” and called for citizen mobilization to prevent what he labeled an “act of institutional violence.”
“Those who want to change the Constitution are breaking our republican pact and taking to the bush against the Republic. They must be treated and fought as such by all means,” he said.
Sesanga emphasized the historical role of the Congolese people in defending freedoms and reiterated that no leader is above the Constitution. “Changing the Constitution, transforming mandates into unlimited terms, and disregarding all the requirements of the rule of law is not part of the Republic. Establishing a personal power structure is a challenge to the republican pact,” he added.
He went further, categorizing any move to amend the Constitution for a third term as “high treason” and a red line that cannot be crossed. Drawing parallels with past authoritarian periods, Sesanga denounced such actions as a repetition of the dictatorial excesses experienced under the Second Republic.
This statement comes amid ongoing speculation about a possible constitutional revision in the Democratic Republic of Congo, a topic already sparking strong reactions across political and civil society circles.

Sesanga emphasized the historical role of the Congolese people in defending freedoms and reiterated that no leader is above the Constitution. “Changing the Constitution, transforming mandates into unlimited terms, and disregarding all the requirements of the rule of law is not part of the Republic. Drawing parallels with past authoritarian periods, Sesanga denounced such actions as a repetition of the dictatorial excesses experienced under the Second Republic.

title: Congo Airways Faces Critical Challenges; President Tshisekedi Demands Realistic Recovery Plan
excerpt: March 22, 2026 – The national airline, Congo Airways SA, remains in a precarious state, posing legal, financial, and reputational risks for the state as a shareholder. Despite multiple government-led recovery efforts, the airline continues to struggle with operational inefficienc
title_en: Congo Airways Faces Critical Challenges; President Tshisekedi Demands Realistic Recovery Plan
excerpt_en: March 22, 2026 – The national airline, Congo Airways SA, remains in a precarious state, posing legal, financial, and reputational risks for the state as a shareholder. Despite multiple government-led recovery efforts, the airline continues to struggle with operational inefficienc
body_en:
March 22, 2026 – The national airline, Congo Airways SA, remains in a precarious state, posing legal, financial, and reputational risks for the state as a shareholder. Despite multiple government-led recovery efforts, the airline continues to struggle with operational inefficiencies, raising concerns over rising air travel costs in the Democratic Republic of Congo.
During the 83rd Council of Ministers meeting held on March 20 at the African Union City complex, President Félix Tshisekedi reviewed the findings of a joint investigation launched in December 2025. The mission, comprising the General Inspectorate of Finance (IGF), the High Council of the Portfolio, and the Civil Aviation Authority, assessed the company's administrative, financial, and operational management.
According to the report, Congo Airways continues to face serious operational problems, despite the emergency recovery plan initiated in 2023 and reinforced in 2024. The President stressed that, without rigorous planning and strengthened governance, these issues could undermine the airline’s fleet renewal process and jeopardize the strategic interests of the state.
“The situation is all the more concerning given that, in the absence of proper governance, it could compromise the renewal of the airline fleet recently acquired by the National Social Security Fund,” the meeting minutes note. President Tshisekedi also called for the state to meet its financial obligations, including outstanding taxes, to provide the company with the resources necessary for recovery.
The President instructed the Deputy Prime Minister, Minister of Transport and Communications, the Minister of Finance, and the Minister of State Enterprises, under the supervision of the Prime Minister, to develop a realistic, rigorously structured financial recovery plan. This plan must include internal controls, regulatory compliance, audits, human resource management, and systematic reporting to the State.
“These measures must underpin a profound restructuring of managerial governance, restore management discipline, strengthen executive accountability, and improve transparency,” President Tshisekedi emphasized. He also highlighted the need for a model ensuring financial sustainability, operational efficiency, and long-term competitiveness, safeguarding the state’s strategic interests.
This is not the government’s first attempt to revive Congo Airways. In 2024, a five-year business plan was proposed, including the acquisition of three A320 aircraft and measures to maintain the airline’s Air Operator Certificate (AOC) and IATA accreditation. A moratorium granted by the International Air Transport Association prevented the loss of these credentials.
The President warned that domestic air travel demand continues to rise, while supply remains insufficient. The underutilization of international routes has led to lost revenue for the country, despite Congo’s portfolio of over 52 international air traffic rights, many of which currently benefit foreign airlines.
With these challenges, the government now faces a pivotal moment: crafting a realistic recovery plan that restores Congo Airways’ operational viability while protecting the state’s financial and strategic interests.
