title: Etienne Davignon to Stand Trial for Role in Patrice Lumumba’s Assassination
excerpt: March 17, 2026 – Belgian courts have approved that Etienne Davignon will stand trial over his alleged involvement in the kidnapping and transfer of Patrice Lumumba, which ultimately led to the assassination of the first Prime Minister of independent Congo on January 17, 1961. Dav
title_en: Etienne Davignon to Stand Trial for Role in Patrice Lumumba’s Assassination
excerpt_en: March 17, 2026 – Belgian courts have approved that Etienne Davignon will stand trial over his alleged involvement in the kidnapping and transfer of Patrice Lumumba, which ultimately led to the assassination of the first Prime Minister of independent Congo on January 17, 1961. Dav
body_en:
March 17, 2026 – Belgian courts have approved that Etienne Davignon will stand trial over his alleged involvement in the kidnapping and transfer of Patrice Lumumba, which ultimately led to the assassination of the first Prime Minister of independent Congo on January 17, 1961.
Davignon, the last surviving of the eleven Belgians targeted in a war crimes complaint filed in 2011 by Lumumba’s children, will face proceedings following a decade-long investigation.
Speaking during a briefing in Brussels, members of the Lumumba family emphasized that the lawsuit is not about reparations, but about establishing legal accountability for colonial-era crimes.
"The primary objective of this lawsuit is for justice to be served for Patrice Lumumba, and to acknowledge that what he suffered was a crime," said Blandine Lumumba, wife of François Lumumba. "The consequences of this act continue to affect the family, and this justice will help heal wounds for both the family and the country."
The Belgian federal prosecutor’s office accuses Davignon of unlawfully detaining and transferring a prisoner of war, depriving him of a fair trial, and subjecting him to humiliating and degrading treatment, though no intent to kill has been established. At the time, Davignon was a young diplomat intern stationed in Kinshasa and Brazzaville, and his position allegedly allowed him knowledge of the planned arrest and transfer.
Lumumba was overthrown, arrested, and transferred to Katanga, where he was executed alongside Maurice M’Polo and Joseph Okito, amid Cold War tensions, regional secessions, and foreign interference.
Six grandchildren of Lumumba are participating in the proceedings as civil parties, seeking a public acknowledgment of Belgian responsibility and a debate on what they call a disastrous colonial crime.
The defense argued the case should be dismissed due to the statute of limitations, citing the extended time since the events. Davignon, a prominent figure in Belgian political and industrial circles after the 1960s, now faces a legal reckoning fueled by decades of historical research, including the work of historian Ludo De Witte, who documented Belgian civilian and military involvement in Lumumba’s execution.

title: Surrender of AFC/M23 Fighters Reported in Pinga
excerpt: Walikale March 13, 2026 — A group of AFC/M23 fighters who recently surrendered in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo has arrived in Pinga, located in Walikale Territory, following their defection from rebel ranks. The fighters, initially reported to have laid down their arms in
title_en: Surrender of AFC/M23 Fighters Reported in Pinga
excerpt_en: Walikale March 13, 2026 — A group of AFC/M23 fighters who recently surrendered in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo has arrived in Pinga, located in Walikale Territory, following their defection from rebel ranks. The fighters, initially reported to have laid down their arms in
body_en:
Walikale March 13, 2026 — A group of AFC/M23 fighters who recently surrendered in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo has arrived in Pinga, located in Walikale Territory, following their defection from rebel ranks.
The fighters, initially reported to have laid down their arms in Chanjikiro, in the Kisimba group, were transferred to Pinga on March 10. Local and administrative authorities confirmed their presence and indicated that they are currently being held under supervision pending further decisions regarding their status and reintegration process.
According to information gathered on the ground, the former combatants cited intensified military pressure from the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC), supported by the Wazalendo militia, as a key factor behind their surrender. They also pointed to harsh living conditions and internal suffering within the rebel movement.
This development comes amid escalating military operations and renewed clashes across Walikale, where government forces and their allies are seeking to reclaim rebel-held positions. The surrender is seen as a potential sign of strain within AFC/M23 ranks, as pressure continues to mount on multiple frontlines in North Kivu.

title_en: Death Toll Rises to 19 in ADF Attack on Babesua Village
excerpt_en: Mambasa, Ituri March 17, 2026 – The death toll from the ADF attack in Babesua village has risen to at least 19 civilians killed, following the assault on the evening of March 16. The village lies 12 kilometers from Badengaido, along the Kisangani road. A Red Cross team on the gro
body_en:
Mambasa, Ituri March 17, 2026 – The death toll from the ADF attack in Babesua village has risen to at least 19 civilians killed, following the assault on the evening of March 16. The village lies 12 kilometers from Badengaido, along the Kisangani road.
A Red Cross team on the ground confirmed the updated toll, reporting extensive destruction, including burned houses and a truck. The scale of the violence mirrors recent ADF attacks on the Muchacha and Mavuvu mining sites, which left at least 17 dead days earlier.
Despite ongoing joint military operations by the Congolese and Ugandan armies, the ADF militants continue to advance and carry out attacks.
According to the United Nations Joint Human Rights Office (UNJHRO), ADF fighters were responsible for 465 attacks in 2025, resulting in 1,749 victims, including women and children. Summary executions accounted for nearly half of these incidents.
The renewed violence in Mambasa territory is spreading fear to neighboring areas such as Bafwasende, where reports indicate population displacement as residents flee ongoing attacks.

title: Rwanda–Burundi: Catholic Bishops Express Hope for Reopening of Closed Borders
excerpt: Kigali March 12, 2026 — Catholic bishops from Rwanda and Burundi have expressed hope that land borders between the two countries, closed since January 2024, will soon reopen, allowing the resumption of cross-border travel and trade. The remarks came during a joint meeting of the
title_en: Rwanda–Burundi: Catholic Bishops Express Hope for Reopening of Closed Borders
excerpt_en: Kigali March 12, 2026 — Catholic bishops from Rwanda and Burundi have expressed hope that land borders between the two countries, closed since January 2024, will soon reopen, allowing the resumption of cross-border travel and trade. The remarks came during a joint meeting of the
body_en:
Kigali March 12, 2026 — Catholic bishops from Rwanda and Burundi have expressed hope that land borders between the two countries, closed since January 2024, will soon reopen, allowing the resumption of cross-border travel and trade.
The remarks came during a joint meeting of the two countries’ episcopal conferences held in Kigali from March 9 to 11, 2026. Discussions focused on strengthening cooperation and addressing challenges facing local populations, particularly Christian communities.
Speaking to the press, Joachim Ntahondereye, Bishop of Muyinga Diocese and President of the Catholic Bishops’ Conference of Burundi, urged believers not to lose hope despite the prolonged border closure. He emphasized that the situation is temporary, noting that “the reasons behind the closure will eventually come to an end,” and that people will once again be able to “travel and cooperate as before.”
He also encouraged those with the means to continue using air travel, which remains operational, as a way to maintain exchanges of ideas and promote development and peace between the two nations.
Meanwhile, Antoine Kambanda, Archbishop of Kigali and President of the Catholic Bishops’ Conference of Rwanda, highlighted the symbolic importance of the meeting. He noted that the Burundian delegation had arrived in Kigali by air, demonstrating that ties between the two countries remain intact despite ongoing tensions.
“This is strong evidence that we must work together to find solutions, in a spirit of understanding, because it is in our interest to live in harmony rather than in conflict,” he said.
Burundi closed its land borders citing security concerns. Although air traffic between the two countries has since resumed, trade and the movement of people remain significantly disrupted.

body_en:
Libreville, 19 March 2026 – Ambassador Parfait Busabiwa presented his credentials to President Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema to officially represent Rwanda in Gabon.
During the meeting at the Presidential Palace, President Nguema welcomed Amb. Busabiwa and praised the strong cooperation and friendship between Rwanda and Gabon, noting that previous agreements have been satisfactorily implemented.
Ambassador Busabiwa, delivering a message from President Paul Kagame, assured that he would work to strengthen ties between the two countries, particularly in trade, tourism, technology, and other sectors of mutual interest.
Rwanda and Gabon have collaborated through international organizations such as the African Union and the Francophonie. Recent milestones include a 2024 cooperation agreement on combating corruption and President Nguema’s visit to Rwanda in 2023 to discuss economic and educational partnerships.
The appointment of Amb. Busabiwa reinforces ongoing efforts to develop Rwanda–Gabon relations in education, trade, agriculture, and technology.

excerpt_en: Kigali, 13 March 2026 – Rwanda generated more than Rwf15 billion from agricultural and livestock exports between 9 and 13 March 2026, according to the National Agricultural Export Development Board (NAEB). During the five-day period, the country exported 8,300 tonnes of products,
body_en:
Kigali, 13 March 2026 – Rwanda generated more than Rwf15 billion from agricultural and livestock exports between 9 and 13 March 2026, according to the National Agricultural Export Development Board (NAEB).
During the five-day period, the country exported 8,300 tonnes of products, including coffee, tea, fruits, vegetables, flowers, cereals, and livestock products.
Coffee remained the top export, with 571 tonnes generating over Rwf5.4 billion, followed by tea exports of 649 tonnes worth more than Rwf2.7 billion.
Other exports included vegetables (431 tonnes), fruits (221 tonnes), and flowers (30 tonnes), contributing hundreds of millions of francs in revenue.
Rwanda also exported over 6,200 tonnes of additional agricultural products, alongside 248 tonnes of animal products, further boosting earnings.
Key export destinations included the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, the United Arab Emirates, France, Germany, and several African markets.
The figures highlight the continued importance of agriculture as a driver of export revenue and economic growth for Rwanda.

title: Rwanda Security Forces Launch Nationwide Welfare Projects Worth Rwf2.5 Billion
excerpt: Kigali, Rwanda March 10, 2026 — The Rwanda Defence Forces and the Rwanda National Police have launched a nationwide campaign of social welfare and development projects valued at more than Rwf2.5 billion, marking the 32nd anniversary of Rwanda’s liberation. The three-month initiat
title_en: Rwanda Security Forces Launch Nationwide Welfare Projects Worth Rwf2.5 Billion
excerpt_en: Kigali, Rwanda March 10, 2026 — The Rwanda Defence Forces and the Rwanda National Police have launched a nationwide campaign of social welfare and development projects valued at more than Rwf2.5 billion, marking the 32nd anniversary of Rwanda’s liberation. The three-month initiat
body_en:
Kigali, Rwanda March 10, 2026 — The Rwanda Defence Forces and the Rwanda National Police have launched a nationwide campaign of social welfare and development projects valued at more than Rwf2.5 billion, marking the 32nd anniversary of Rwanda’s liberation.
The three-month initiative, unveiled across multiple provinces, will focus on improving living conditions through interventions in healthcare, education, environmental protection, infrastructure, livestock distribution, and housing for vulnerable families.
In Kigali, the program was officially launched by Deputy Commissioner General Jeanne Chantal Ujeneza, who emphasized that security institutions must go beyond maintaining order to actively contribute to citizens’ well-being.
The Minister of Education, Joseph Nsengimana, praised the role of security forces in supporting key sectors such as education. Authorities announced that, in the capital alone, classrooms, sanitation facilities, and an Early Childhood Development (ECD) center in Ndera Sector will be constructed at a cost exceeding Rwf350 million.
Housing and Infrastructure Projects Across Provinces
In the Western Province, Police Commissioner Felix Namuhoranye, Governor Jean Bosco Ntibitura, and military officials launched the construction of 30 houses for vulnerable families in Nyabihu District.
“Protecting the country goes hand in hand with improving the welfare of its people,” Namuhoranye said, highlighting the practical impact of the initiative.
In the Southern Province, Defence Minister Juvenal Marizamunda and Governor Alice Kayitesi presided over the launch of new classroom construction at Kigese Technical Secondary School in Kamonyi District.
Marizamunda noted that the program strengthens cooperation between citizens, local authorities, and security institutions, stressing that sustainable security depends on development and public participation.
Healthcare and Connectivity in the North
In Northern Province, health-focused activities were launched at Byumba Teaching Hospital by State Minister Yvan Butera and senior military health officials. Services provided include surgery, pediatrics, dermatology, dentistry, and other specialized care, delivered jointly by military and civilian medical teams.
Meanwhile, authorities also launched the reconstruction of the Ryabazira bridge, a key link connecting communities in Musanze and Gakenke districts. Officials say the project will restore mobility, boost trade, and facilitate access to schools and markets.
Livelihood Support and Environmental Efforts in the East
In Eastern Province, the Permanent Secretary at the Ministry of Agriculture, Solange Uwituze, distributed livestock—including cows and goats—to 32 vulnerable families in Kayonza District to support income generation and food security.
Chief of Defence Staff Mubarakh Muganga joined residents in Gatsibo District for environmental activities, including tree planting, urging sustained community participation.
“These initiatives have expanded from short-term efforts to long-term programs aimed at providing practical solutions,” he said.

title: Former U.S. Official Questions DRC’s Commitment to Neutralizing FDLR
excerpt: Washington, 20 March 2026 – Former U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for African Affairs, Tibor Nagy, has expressed skepticism over the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s willingness to dismantle the FDLR armed group, a key condition in ongoing regional peace efforts. The remarks
title_en: Former U.S. Official Questions DRC’s Commitment to Neutralizing FDLR
excerpt_en: Washington, 20 March 2026 – Former U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for African Affairs, Tibor Nagy, has expressed skepticism over the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s willingness to dismantle the FDLR armed group, a key condition in ongoing regional peace efforts. The remarks
body_en:
Washington, 20 March 2026 – Former U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for African Affairs, Tibor Nagy, has expressed skepticism over the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s willingness to dismantle the FDLR armed group, a key condition in ongoing regional peace efforts.
The remarks come amid renewed diplomatic engagement between Rwanda and the DRC following a peace agreement signed in Washington on 27 June 2025, with U.S. support. The accord includes provisions for the neutralization of the FDLR and the eventual lifting of Rwanda’s security measures.
Although both countries ratified the agreement in December 2025 and recently recommitted to its implementation during talks held on 17–18 March 2026, progress remains limited.
Nagy argued that lasting peace in eastern DRC depends on concrete action against the FDLR, which Rwanda considers a major security threat. “It would be good to issue another joint peace declaration… but it all starts with Congo dismantling the FDLR,” he said, adding that he doubts Kinshasa’s willingness or ability to do so.
Rwanda has maintained that its security measures will remain in place until the group is effectively neutralized.
The ongoing stalemate highlights the challenges facing regional diplomacy, as both sides seek to balance security concerns and political commitments under the Washington peace framework.

Timbuktu Region, March 4, 2026 — The jihadist group Jama'at Nasr al‑Islam wal Muslimin (JNIM) has claimed responsibility for an improvised explosive device (IED) attack targeting Malian military forces and Russian fighters in northern Mali.
According to the group, the explosion struck a military vehicle on Wednesday morning along the Niafunké–Tonka road in the Timbuktu Region.
JNIM said the device targeted a convoy involving soldiers from the Malian Armed Forces and members of the Africa Corps, the Russian paramilitary formation operating alongside Malian forces.
No immediate official statement from the Malian authorities regarding casualties or damage was available at the time of reporting.
The attack comes amid continuing insurgent activity in northern and central Mali, where jihadist groups linked to al-Qaeda and the Islamic State frequently target security forces and their allies.

The three-hectare facility was described as a flagship project aimed at nurturing the potential of Mali’s youth. The ceremony highlighted remarks from President of the Transition Assimi Goïta, who emphasized that “youth is Mali’s greatest asset” and that the nation’s sovereignty and prosperity will be built through their commitment, discipline, and patriotism.
The Palace of Pioneers is expected to serve as a hub for educational programs, cultural activities, and events, reflecting Mali’s focus on youth development and civic engagement.

body_en:
Bamako, March 5, 2026 — Traders in Bamako staged protests on Thursday to denounce what they describe as worsening living and working conditions, citing a series of fires in local markets and growing insecurity in the Malian capital.
Demonstrators said several markets have recently been destroyed by fires, causing significant financial losses for vendors and raising concerns about the safety of commercial areas. Many traders claim the repeated incidents have left them vulnerable and without sufficient protection.
The protesters also warned that insecurity in the capital is increasingly affecting their daily activities, making it difficult to operate businesses and protect their goods.
In response, groups of traders gathered in the streets to voice their frustration and call on authorities to take urgent action to secure markets and prevent further incidents.
Organizers of the protest said they are preparing a large nationwide demonstration in the coming weeks aimed at pressuring the government to implement stronger security measures and guarantee the safety of traders and their businesses.

body_en:
Bamako, March 12, 2026 — General Assimi Goïta, President of the Transition and Head of State, presided over a ceremonial presentation of giant checks from the Local Mining Development Fund to nine municipalities on Thursday at Koulouba Palace.
The event was attended by Prime Minister Abdoulaye Maïga, the President of the National Transition Council, the Ministers of Territorial Administration, Mines, Economy and Finance, and other government and administrative officials, including the Minister-Commissioner in charge of mining affairs.
Goïta praised the government’s efforts in implementing a key recommendation from the National Refounding Conference by distributing the mining development funds to local communities.
According to Alousséni Sanou, Minister of Economy and Finance, the total allocation from the fund for the 2025 financial year amounts to over 18.4 billion CFA francs, aimed at supporting local development projects and strengthening the benefits of Mali’s mining sector for municipalities.

title_en: Mali’s Justice Minister Meets Bar Association President to Strengthen Judicial Dialogue
excerpt_en: Bamako, March 2026 — Mamoudou Kassogue, Minister of Justice and Human Rights, Keeper of the Seals, met with Souleymane Soumountera, President of the Malian Bar Association, to discuss shared challenges and opportunities within Mali’s judicial system. The meeting focused on key is
body_en:
Bamako, March 2026 — Mamoudou Kassogue, Minister of Justice and Human Rights, Keeper of the Seals, met with Souleymane Soumountera, President of the Malian Bar Association, to discuss shared challenges and opportunities within Mali’s judicial system.
The meeting focused on key issues including access to justice, modernization of judicial procedures, and capacity building for legal stakeholders. Soumountera presented the Bar Association’s vision for the coming years, highlighting priorities such as lawyer training, professional ethics, and the integration of digital tools to enhance efficiency and transparency in the justice system.
Minister Kassogue commended the quality of the discussions and reaffirmed his ministry’s commitment to maintaining constructive dialogue with the Bar Association, emphasizing that cooperation is essential to strengthen the rule of law and safeguard citizens’ rights.
The meeting reflects a shared commitment between Mali’s judicial authorities and legal professionals to create a more efficient, accessible, and citizen-focused justice system.

title_en: Mali’s Higher Education Minister Meets Orange Mali CEO to Discuss Digital Initiatives
excerpt_en: Bamako, March 12, 2026 — Professor Bouréma Kansaye, Mali’s Minister of Higher Education and Scientific Research, met with Mr. Leyti N’Diaye, the newly appointed CEO of Orange Mali, for an introductory visit on Thursday. During the meeting, Kansaye congratulated N’Diaye on his app
body_en:
Bamako, March 12, 2026 — Professor Bouréma Kansaye, Mali’s Minister of Higher Education and Scientific Research, met with Mr. Leyti N’Diaye, the newly appointed CEO of Orange Mali, for an introductory visit on Thursday.
During the meeting, Kansaye congratulated N’Diaye on his appointment and discussed potential areas of collaboration between the government and the telecommunications company.
Key topics included enhancing university connectivity, advancing the digitalization of higher education, developing digital libraries, and supporting the Digital University project, which seeks to modernize higher education and broaden access for students across Mali.
Officials described the discussions as a step toward strengthening partnerships between the public sector and private technology providers to advance Mali’s digital transformation in education.

title_en: 15th Ordinary Session of Mali’s National Institute for Judicial Training Opens
excerpt_en: Bamako, March 12, 2026 — The 15th Ordinary Session of the Board of Directors of the National Institute for Judicial Training (INFJ) “Maître Demba Diallo” opened on Thursday under the chairmanship of Dr. Boubacar Sidiki Diarrah, Secretary General of the Ministry of Justice and Hum
body_en:
Bamako, March 12, 2026 — The 15th Ordinary Session of the Board of Directors of the National Institute for Judicial Training (INFJ) “Maître Demba Diallo” opened on Thursday under the chairmanship of Dr. Boubacar Sidiki Diarrah, Secretary General of the Ministry of Justice and Human Rights.
The ceremony, held at the institute’s premises, was attended by members of the General Directorate and invited resource persons, including former Minister of Justice Hamidou Younoussa Maiga and former INFJ Board member Alassane Diallo.
In his address, Dr. Diarrah praised the institute’s management and staff for their achievements in 2025 and provided a positive assessment of the institute’s performance.
The 2026 session will review three key documents: the 2025 annual performance report, the 2026 annual performance plan, and the 2026 annual performance contract, which serve as essential tools for evaluating results and guiding future actions.
The Secretary General highlighted the importance of these sessions in ensuring effective management and the continued professional development of Mali’s judicial personnel.

title_en: BCEAO Governor Briefs President Goïta on Regional Economic Outlook
excerpt_en: Bamako, March 6, 2026 — Mali’s transitional president, General Assimi Goïta, received a delegation from the Central Bank of West African States (BCEAO) on Friday to discuss the state of the regional economy. The delegation was led by Jean-Claude Kassi Brou and met with the presid
body_en:
Bamako, March 6, 2026 — Mali’s transitional president, General Assimi Goïta, received a delegation from the Central Bank of West African States (BCEAO) on Friday to discuss the state of the regional economy.
The delegation was led by Jean-Claude Kassi Brou and met with the president at Koulouba, the presidential palace.
Discussions focused on the evolution of the West African Economic and Monetary Union (WAEMU) economies, with particular attention to Mali’s economic performance.
The BCEAO governor highlighted the delegation’s review of the regional economic situation and noted the strong performance of the Malian economy within the broader WAEMU framework.

title_en: Mali Marks International Women’s Day with Conference on Women’s Rights
excerpt_en: Bamako, March 12, 2026 — Mamoudou Kassogue, Mali’s Minister of Justice and Human Rights, Keeper of the Seals, co-chaired the opening of a conference-debate on Thursday at the Bamako International Conference Center (CICB) to celebrate International Women’s Day. Organized by the Ne
body_en:
Bamako, March 12, 2026 — Mamoudou Kassogue, Mali’s Minister of Justice and Human Rights, Keeper of the Seals, co-chaired the opening of a conference-debate on Thursday at the Bamako International Conference Center (CICB) to celebrate International Women’s Day.
Organized by the Network of African Women and Parliamentarians of Mali (REFAMP/Mali), the event focused on the theme: “Women’s and Girls’ Rights: Acting for a Safe and Equitable Future in a Resilient, Unified, and Sovereign Mali.” Minister Kassogue described the theme as highly relevant, highlighting the crucial role women play in shaping the country’s development and resilience.
In his address, the Minister paid tribute to the founders of REFAMP/Mali, noting that since its creation in 1996, the organization has played a key role in advocating for women’s empowerment and rights.
Before officially opening the ceremony, Kassogue assured participants of his and his ministry’s full commitment to supporting women in their ongoing efforts to protect and promote women’s rights across Mali.

title_en: Bamako Faces Fuel Shortages, Power Cuts, and Water Disruptions Amid Public Discontent
excerpt_en: Bamako, March 14, 2026 — The Malian capital is grappling with a severe fuel supply crisis, particularly affecting diesel, which has disrupted electricity and water services and fueled growing public frustration. The shortages, ongoing for approximately two weeks, follow a persist
body_en:
Bamako, March 14, 2026 — The Malian capital is grappling with a severe fuel supply crisis, particularly affecting diesel, which has disrupted electricity and water services and fueled growing public frustration. The shortages, ongoing for approximately two weeks, follow a persistent hydrocarbon supply instability after the Jama'at Nasr al-Islam wal Muslimin (JNIM) imposed a fuel embargo on the country in September 2025.
Residents report queues of up to three kilometers at gas stations, with trucks, buses, cars, and motorcycles waiting hours for diesel. While gasoline remains relatively available, the diesel shortage has worsened, echoing the crisis of last October and November when the armed embargo’s impact peaked.
The energy sector has been heavily affected, as Mali’s power plants rely on diesel. Many neighborhoods are now experiencing power outages exceeding 24 consecutive hours, while other areas receive electricity for only three to seven hours per day—far below the transitional authorities’ promise of roughly 19 hours of electricity daily during Ramadan.
Water supplies are also affected, as pumping stations depend on the national electricity grid operated by Énergie du Mali (EDM). Power outages have led to frequent water cuts in multiple districts, compounding public grievances.
Frustration has grown in the capital, expressed openly on social media and in traditional discussion forums known as “grins.” Citizens have also questioned taxes on mobile phone services and money transfers, introduced a year ago to fund energy sector improvements, citing a lack of transparency in the management of these funds. A widely shared social media slogan captures the mood:
“The blackness of night, the blackness of despair, the blackness of the new Mali, the blackness of propaganda.”
The government has attempted to downplay the crisis. Minister of Industry and Trade Moussa Alassane Diallo described the country’s petroleum supply as “regular,” attributing shortages to speculative practices and hoarding by some operators. Authorities have introduced measures such as limiting truck fuel to 600 liters per vehicle over 72 hours to better manage distribution.
Meanwhile, state media continue highlighting initiatives to distribute solar panels to artisans, promoted by President of the Transition Assimi Goïta as part of efforts to address the energy crisis. Despite these measures, observers warn that the fuel and electricity shortages highlight the fragility of Mali’s supply system, particularly amid ongoing security challenges and logistical difficulties, leaving the capital facing one of its most severe service crises in recent years.
Conclusion
The period from February 1 to March 15, 2026, illustrates a dual reality for Mali: a time of strategic diplomatic expansion alongside acute internal security and infrastructure challenges. While the transitional government has achieved notable international and legal milestones, the daily lives of citizens continue to be shaped by insecurity and disruptions to essential services.
Key Strategic Developments
Diplomatic Realignment: Mali has advanced a multipolar foreign policy, marked by high-level tributes to Iranian leadership, credential presentations in Kazakhstan, and strengthened cooperation with China.
Shifting Western Relations: Relations with the United States show signs of a pragmatic thaw, highlighted by the lifting of military sanctions and ongoing negotiations to resume intelligence-gathering flights.
Legal and Economic Milestones: Mali secured a major legal victory, with regional courts declaring the 2022 ECOWAS/WAEMU sanctions illegal. The government also advanced local development, including the allocation of 18.4 billion CFA francs from the Local Mining Development Fund to municipalities.
Persistent Challenges
Escalating Insecurity: Insurgent groups, including JNIM and the Azawad Army, have intensified attacks, using IEDs and drones against Malian forces and Africa Corps personnel. The seizure of key transport routes, such as Kayes-Bamako, underscores the ongoing struggle to maintain territorial control.
Humanitarian and Service Crisis: Bamako faces a severe fuel and diesel shortage, triggering widespread power and water outages. Public discontent has grown, with traders protesting fires, insecurity, and service disruptions across the capital.
Ultimately, the transitional authorities confront the challenge of transforming diplomatic and legal gains into tangible stability. The success of the National Strategy for Emergence (SNEDD 2024–2033) will hinge on securing strategic corridors, restoring reliable basic services, and addressing the urgent humanitarian and security needs of the population.
By Maïga Sidi Bonkana
(Boukari Zankey Sidi)
Jeff Buleli

Escalating Insecurity: Insurgent groups, including JNIM and the Azawad Army, have intensified attacks, using IEDs and drones against Malian forces and Africa Corps personnel. The seizure of key transport routes, such as Kayes-Bamako, underscores the ongoing struggle to maintain territorial control.
Humanitarian and Service Crisis: Bamako faces a severe fuel and diesel shortage, triggering widespread power and water outages. Public discontent has grown, with traders protesting fires, insecurity, and service disruptions across the capital.
Ultimately, the transitional authorities confront the challenge of transforming diplomatic and legal gains into tangible stability. The success of the National Strategy for Emergence (SNEDD 2024–2033) will hinge on securing strategic corridors, restoring reliable basic services, and addressing the urgent humanitarian and security needs of the population.

title: United States Nears Agreement with Mali to Resume Intelligence Flights

title_en: United States Nears Agreement with Mali to Resume Intelligence Flights
excerpt_en: Bamako, March 9, 2026 — The United States is reportedly close to reaching an agreement with Mali that would allow American aircraft and drones to resume intelligence-gathering operations over Malian territory, focusing on jihadist groups linked to al-Qaeda. The potential resumpti
body_en:
Bamako, March 9, 2026 — The United States is reportedly close to reaching an agreement with Mali that would allow American aircraft and drones to resume intelligence-gathering operations over Malian territory, focusing on jihadist groups linked to al-Qaeda.
The potential resumption of operations comes after Washington lifted sanctions against several high-ranking Malian officials, including the Defense Minister, who had previously faced restrictions for alleged ties to Russian mercenaries. The decision addresses a key demand from the Malian government and could pave the way for renewed security cooperation between the two countries.
Officials indicated that the U.S. is particularly motivated by the ongoing search for an American pilot, Kevin Rideout, 48, who was kidnapped in Niamey, Niger, while working with the missionary organization Serving In Mission. He is now believed to be held by armed groups linked to the Islamic State in the Sahel, and his recovery is a priority in Washington’s renewed engagement with Bamako.
The security situation in Mali remains precarious, with jihadist groups expanding in multiple regions and continuing attacks on roads, economic infrastructure, and some mining operations. The proposed agreement for intelligence flights is part of broader efforts to address these persistent threats.

The minister highlighted the longstanding friendship and cooperation between Mali and China, citing cultural and educational initiatives such as the Confucius Centre, which promotes Chinese language and culture, and the Luban Workshop, which supports professional training for young Malians.

title: Mali’s Transition President Meets Legal Team After Court Victory Over Regional Sanctions
excerpt: Bamako, March 2, 2026 — Mali’s transitional president Assimi Goïta received the legal team that represented the country before regional courts following a ruling that declared sanctions imposed on Mali in 2022 illegal. The meeting took place on Monday in Bamako and followed the J
title_en: Mali’s Transition President Meets Legal Team After Court Victory Over Regional Sanctions
excerpt_en: Bamako, March 2, 2026 — Mali’s transitional president Assimi Goïta received the legal team that represented the country before regional courts following a ruling that declared sanctions imposed on Mali in 2022 illegal. The meeting took place on Monday in Bamako and followed the J
body_en:
Bamako, March 2, 2026 — Mali’s transitional president Assimi Goïta received the legal team that represented the country before regional courts following a ruling that declared sanctions imposed on Mali in 2022 illegal.
The meeting took place on Monday in Bamako and followed the January 28 decision by the Court of Justice of the West African Economic and Monetary Union, which ruled in favor of Mali in its dispute with the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) and the West African Economic and Monetary Union (WAEMU).
The sanctions had been imposed during a tense political period in early 2022 after Mali’s military authorities delayed a transition to civilian rule.
During the audience, Goïta praised the legal team for their work defending the country’s interests in the case.
The delegation included Justice and Human Rights Minister Mahamadou Kassogué, along with lawyers Ousmane Mama Traoré, Fatoumata Sidibé Diarra, and Amadou Tiéoulé Diarra, who took part in the legal proceedings.
Human Rights Concerns Raised in Azawad
Separately, the association Kal Akal released a report on March 1 documenting alleged human rights violations in Azawad and central Mali.
According to the report, the group recorded 11 cases of executions and massacres, 13 cases of arrests and disappearances, and six incidents involving destruction and looting.
The organization said civilians were killed and that many communities had their livelihoods severely affected.
The report attributes most of the alleged violations to the Malian armed forces and allied Russian fighters linked to the Afrika Korps group.

excerpt_en: Bamako, March 13, 2026 — Thirty-one children of tanker truck drivers killed in terrorist attacks have officially been registered as Wards of the Nation in Mali, receiving their identity cards and bank accounts during a ceremony at the Prime Minister’s Office on Friday. The event
body_en:
Bamako, March 13, 2026 — Thirty-one children of tanker truck drivers killed in terrorist attacks have officially been registered as Wards of the Nation in Mali, receiving their identity cards and bank accounts during a ceremony at the Prime Minister’s Office on Friday.
The event was chaired by Prime Minister Abdoulaye Maïga and attended by the Ministers of Health and Social Development, Labor, Public Service and Social Dialogue, and Transport and Infrastructure.
In a departure from the usual schedule, which typically sees such ceremonies held in October under the President of the Transition, these children were registered and provided their cards ahead of time, in recognition of the government’s commitment to supporting families affected by terrorism.
The initiative aims to provide financial support and social protection to children who lost their parents in violent attacks, reinforcing the state’s efforts to care for victims of insecurity and their families.

The decision marks a potential easing of tensions between Mali’s transitional authorities and the United States, which had previously imposed restrictions following political and security developments in the country.

The meeting, held at the Ministry of Health, provided a platform for union leaders to present challenges faced by pharmacists in receiving timely payments under the Mandatory Health Insurance system.

title: Drone Attack in Gao Sparks Conflicting Reports Between Azawad Front and Malian Forces
excerpt: Gao, March 11, 2026 — The city of Gao witnessed a drone strike targeting the Gao military airport within the Firhoun Ag Alinsar camp, one of Mali’s major military installations, on Wednesday morning. The incident has generated conflicting accounts from the Azawad Liberation Front
title_en: Drone Attack in Gao Sparks Conflicting Reports Between Azawad Front and Malian Forces
excerpt_en: Gao, March 11, 2026 — The city of Gao witnessed a drone strike targeting the Gao military airport within the Firhoun Ag Alinsar camp, one of Mali’s major military installations, on Wednesday morning. The incident has generated conflicting accounts from the Azawad Liberation Front
body_en:
Gao, March 11, 2026 — The city of Gao witnessed a drone strike targeting the Gao military airport within the Firhoun Ag Alinsar camp, one of Mali’s major military installations, on Wednesday morning. The incident has generated conflicting accounts from the Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) and Malian military sources.
According to the FLA, the attack involved 25 kamikaze drones, causing significant casualties and material losses among Malian troops and Africa Corps forces stationed at the base. Sources close to the group added that the drones were deployed in two waves, with 18 drones in the first wave to overwhelm the Russian TOR-M2K air defense system, which intercepted 12 drones. A second wave, supported by mortar fire, reportedly damaged a Bayraktar TB2 drone command post, a Sukhoi-24 aircraft hangar, and several helicopters. The FLA claimed that 95% of the operation’s objectives had been achieved.
In contrast, the Malian army stated that a terrorist group had attempted a drone and projectile attack against its forces but reported no casualties or significant material damage. The army said a patrol was deployed to pursue the attackers and that investigations were ongoing to assess any possible damage outside the camp.
Russian elements of the Africa Corps have not issued an official statement, though unofficial channels suggested that the attack had no significant impact, with no losses reported among Russian personnel or within the base.
The incident highlights ongoing tensions and the persistent threat posed by drone and improvised attacks in northern Mali, while the differing accounts underscore the challenge of verifying operational impacts in conflict zones.

Bamako, March 6, 2026 — Mali’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, Abdoulaye Diop, on Friday received the outgoing Resident Representative of the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) in Mali, Maleye Diop, during a farewell audience marking the end of his diplomatic mission in the country.
During the meeting in Bamako, the Malian foreign minister praised the departing official for his professionalism, personal commitment, and innovative approach in supporting the UN agency’s development initiatives in Mali.
Diop highlighted the UNDP’s contributions to strengthening socio-economic governance, advancing institutional reforms, promoting innovative development financing, and supporting capacity-building efforts for development actors across the country.
For his part, Maleye Diop welcomed what he described as the Malian government’s strong commitment to cooperation with the UN agency. The outgoing representative also expressed gratitude to Malian authorities for their support throughout his tenure, describing Mali as a welcoming country committed to long-term development and economic emergence through a proactive strategic vision.

body_en:
Bandiagara, March 8, 2026 — Prime Minister Abdoulaye Maïga, representing President of the Transition Assimi Goïta, laid the foundation stone for a new Traditional Authority Building in Bandiagara on Sunday, providing the 19th administrative region with dedicated facilities for local traditional leaders.
The building will feature a vestibule, offices, guest rooms, and parking, and is scheduled for completion within ten months. Construction will be carried out by La Falaise du Mali, with the architectural firm ALDI overseeing the project.
Prime Minister Maïga praised the presidential initiative to equip all regions with formal spaces for traditional authorities, emphasizing their vital role in maintaining national stability and preserving cultural heritage.
The Bandiagara project follows similar initiatives in Koulikoro, Ségou, Koutiala, San, and Timbuktu, reinforcing the government’s commitment to supporting traditional leadership across Mali.

excerpt_en: Bamako, March 5, 2026 — The jihadist group Jama'at Nasr al-Islam wal Muslimin (JNIM) has reportedly established control over major routes connecting Kayes and Bamako, according to a video released by the group on March 5. The footage shows armed fighters stopping vehicles traveli
body_en:
Bamako, March 5, 2026 — The jihadist group Jama'at Nasr al-Islam wal Muslimin (JNIM) has reportedly established control over major routes connecting Kayes and Bamako, according to a video released by the group on March 5.
The footage shows armed fighters stopping vehicles traveling along the Kayes–Bamako and Nioro–Bamako roads, inspecting passengers and controlling who can continue their journey. Reports indicate that travelers originating from Kayes and Nioro are particularly affected, with some prevented from proceeding.
Local sources suggest that JNIM has maintained a presence and operational control over these routes since September 2025, raising ongoing concerns about security and the safe movement of civilians and goods.
Authorities have not yet provided an official response to the reported road closures and vehicle inspections. The situation underscores the persistent challenges posed by insurgent groups in Mali, especially along strategic transport corridors.

title: Malian Ambassador Presents Credentials to Kazakhstan’s President Tokayev
excerpt: Astana, March 4, 2026 — Mali’s Ambassador to Kazakhstan, Seydou Kamissoko, officially presented his credentials to President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev on Wednesday during a ceremony marking the start of his diplomatic mission in the Central Asian country. Kamissoko, who is based in M
title_en: Malian Ambassador Presents Credentials to Kazakhstan’s President Tokayev
excerpt_en: Astana, March 4, 2026 — Mali’s Ambassador to Kazakhstan, Seydou Kamissoko, officially presented his credentials to President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev on Wednesday during a ceremony marking the start of his diplomatic mission in the Central Asian country. Kamissoko, who is based in M
body_en:
Astana, March 4, 2026 — Mali’s Ambassador to Kazakhstan, Seydou Kamissoko, officially presented his credentials to President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev on Wednesday during a ceremony marking the start of his diplomatic mission in the Central Asian country.
Kamissoko, who is based in Moscow and concurrently accredited to Kazakhstan, delivered the credentials on behalf of Mali’s transitional authorities. Following the formal ceremony, the Malian diplomat held an audience with the Kazakh president.
During the meeting, Kamissoko conveyed the “warm greetings” of Mali’s transitional president, General Assimi Goïta, and briefed Tokayev on the political and security situation in Mali and within the broader confederal framework of the Sahel.
The ambassador reaffirmed his commitment to strengthening ties between Bamako and Astana, emphasizing cooperation grounded in solidarity, mutual respect, and shared interests.
Both sides highlighted the importance of expanding technical, economic, and trade cooperation across sectors of mutual interest, signaling a willingness to deepen bilateral relations.
Prior to the credential ceremony, Kamissoko had presented copies of his letters of credence on March 3 to Kazakhstan’s Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs, Alibek Kuantyrov. The two officials discussed avenues for enhancing political dialogue and boosting economic and cultural exchanges between the two countries.
Kamissoko’s appointment reflects Mali’s ongoing efforts to broaden its diplomatic engagement and develop partnerships beyond its traditional allies.

body_en:
Kidal Region, March 4, 2026 — The Azawad Army has claimed responsibility for two attacks targeting Malian forces and allied fighters south of Kidal, according to a statement released by the group.
The attacks reportedly took place on March 4 in the Adghar–Takalot area, where the armed group said it targeted a patrol of the Malian Armed Forces and fighters from the Afrika Korps, the Russian paramilitary force operating alongside Malian troops.

title: Bamako Pays Tribute to Iran’s Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei
excerpt: Bamako, March 5, 2026 — Mali’s Prime Minister, Major General Abdoulaye Maïga, paid tribute to Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Seyed Ali Khamenei, describing him as a “martyr of the sovereignty of peoples,” during a visit to the residence of Iran’s ambassador in Bamako on Thursday
title_en: Bamako Pays Tribute to Iran’s Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei
excerpt_en: Bamako, March 5, 2026 — Mali’s Prime Minister, Major General Abdoulaye Maïga, paid tribute to Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Seyed Ali Khamenei, describing him as a “martyr of the sovereignty of peoples,” during a visit to the residence of Iran’s ambassador in Bamako on Thursday
body_en:
Bamako, March 5, 2026 — Mali’s Prime Minister, Major General Abdoulaye Maïga, paid tribute to Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Seyed Ali Khamenei, describing him as a “martyr of the sovereignty of peoples,” during a visit to the residence of Iran’s ambassador in Bamako on Thursday.
Maïga signed the book of condolences following Khamenei’s reported death on February 28, 2026. The Malian leader was accompanied by Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation Minister Abdoulaye Diop during the visit.
In his message, delivered on behalf of Mali’s transitional president General Assimi Goïta, Maïga praised Khamenei for what he described as a lifelong struggle in defense of Iran’s sovereignty and the interests of its people.
“He died a martyr, defending until his last breath the higher interests of the Iranian state and people, in line with the vision of Ayatollah Khomeini,” the message stated.
According to Maïga, the passing of the Iranian leader leaves “an immense void,” but his political legacy and advocacy for what he called a “more just and multipolar world that respects identities” would continue to inspire those fighting for national independence and sovereignty.
The Malian government also extended condolences to Khamenei’s family and to the authorities and people of Iran, emphasizing solidarity between the two nations during the mourning period.
Maïga reaffirmed Mali’s support for Iran and praised Khamenei’s life as one dedicated to opposing injustice and defending the sovereignty of nations.
“We pray for the eternal rest of his soul and for all Iranian martyrs,” the prime minister concluded in the message.
The tribute highlights growing diplomatic ties between Mali’s transitional authorities and partners outside traditional Western alliances, particularly countries advocating a multipolar international order.

title: Malian Government Equips 14 Vocational Training Centers with 2 Billion CFA Investment
excerpt: Bamako, March 3, 2026 — The Malian government has provided new equipment worth 2 billion CFA francs to 14 vocational training centers across the country in an effort to strengthen technical education and boost employment opportunities. The handover ceremony was presided over on T
title_en: Malian Government Equips 14 Vocational Training Centers with 2 Billion CFA Investment
excerpt_en: Bamako, March 3, 2026 — The Malian government has provided new equipment worth 2 billion CFA francs to 14 vocational training centers across the country in an effort to strengthen technical education and boost employment opportunities. The handover ceremony was presided over on T
body_en:
Bamako, March 3, 2026 — The Malian government has provided new equipment worth 2 billion CFA francs to 14 vocational training centers across the country in an effort to strengthen technical education and boost employment opportunities.
The handover ceremony was presided over on Tuesday by Oumou Sall Seck, Minister of National Entrepreneurship, Employment, and Vocational Training.
According to the ministry, the equipment—fully financed through the national budget—aims to enhance the operational capacity of vocational institutions and improve practical training for young people.
The beneficiary centers are located in Sénou, Missabougou, Kéniéba, Keleya, Fana, Dioïla, Tominian, Saye, Yorosso, Yangasso, Sikasso, Bougouni, Yanfolila, and Badougou Djoliba.
Authorities say the equipment will support training in a wide range of technical and professional fields, including metal construction, building electricity, masonry, building painting, refrigeration and air conditioning, wood carpentry, tiling, automotive and motorcycle mechanics, photovoltaic electricity, electronics, as well as textile-related trades such as cutting, sewing, and dyeing.
The initiative is part of the government’s broader strategy to strengthen vocational education and equip young Malians with practical skills aligned with labor market needs.

title_en: JNIM Claims IED Attack on Malian Army and Russian Fighters Near Kidal
excerpt_en: Kidal Region, March 3, 2026 — The jihadist group Jama'at Nasr al-Islam wal Muslimin (JNIM) has claimed responsibility for another improvised explosive device (IED) attack targeting Malian and allied forces in northern Mali. According to the group, the explosion struck a Malian ar
body_en:
Kidal Region, March 3, 2026 — The jihadist group Jama'at Nasr al-Islam wal Muslimin (JNIM) has claimed responsibility for another improvised explosive device (IED) attack targeting Malian and allied forces in northern Mali.
According to the group, the explosion struck a Malian army armored vehicle on Tuesday evening in the village of Karouroukh, near Aguelhok in the Kidal Region.
JNIM said the attack targeted soldiers from the Malian Armed Forces along with members of the Africa Corps, the Russian paramilitary formation operating alongside Malian troops.
Following the explosion, a Malian military helicopter reportedly deployed to the scene near Aguelhok.
Initial reports indicate that several Russian fighters were killed and others wounded in the blast. The injured were reportedly evacuated to the city of Kidal for treatment.
There has been no immediate official confirmation from Malian authorities regarding the casualties. The incident underscores the continuing insurgent threat in northern Mali, where armed groups frequently target military convoys using roadside bombs.

title: Kinshasa Holds 65.2% of Bank Deposits, Central Bank Reports
excerpt: KINSHASA February 28, 2026 — Bank deposits in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) remain heavily concentrated in the capital, Kinshasa, accounting for 65.2% of total deposits, according to the latest economic outlook from the Central Bank of Congo (BCC). The report, covering e
title_en: Kinshasa Holds 65.2% of Bank Deposits, Central Bank Reports
excerpt_en: KINSHASA February 28, 2026 — Bank deposits in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) remain heavily concentrated in the capital, Kinshasa, accounting for 65.2% of total deposits, according to the latest economic outlook from the Central Bank of Congo (BCC). The report, covering e
body_en:
KINSHASA February 28, 2026 — Bank deposits in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) remain heavily concentrated in the capital, Kinshasa, accounting for 65.2% of total deposits, according to the latest economic outlook from the Central Bank of Congo (BCC).
The report, covering economic developments from February 13 to 20, 2026, shows that after Kinshasa, deposits are primarily held in Haut-Katanga (22.9%), Lualaba (4.0%), and North Kivu (2.7%). Total bank deposits reached $16.24 billion at the end of December 2025, marking a 3.4% increase from the previous month and a 10.2% year-on-year rise, largely driven by dollar-denominated deposits from households and private enterprises.
Households represent 35.8% of total deposits, while private businesses account for 31.8%. Sectorally, deposits come mostly from sectors outside public administration (39.2%), trade (21.7%), and extractive industries (14.5%).
Meanwhile, gross loans totaled $10.27 billion, up 2.5% month-on-month and 20.2% year-on-year, primarily due to increased lending to SMEs and the central government. Loans in foreign currency rose 2.5%, while local currency loans fell 1.7%.
The BCC notes that the formal financial system comprises 287 institutions, including 108 credit institutions, 137 financial companies, 39 insurance companies, two social security funds, and one guarantee fund. The banking sector includes 14 active banks with 445 service points (371 branches and 74 ATMs), representing 97% of financial sector assets.
The microfinance sector has 101 institutions, including 78 savings and credit cooperatives, 15 microfinance companies, and 8 microcredit enterprises, with 186 operating points representing roughly 3% of sector assets. Nearly 70% of microfinance institutions are concentrated in Kinshasa, North Kivu, and South Kivu.
The report underscores the continued dominance of Kinshasa in the country’s financial landscape, highlighting challenges for financial inclusion in other provinces.

title: DRC Inducts 2,500 New Magistrates to Strengthen Rule of Law
excerpt: Kinshasa, February 23, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo formally inducted 2,500 new magistrates into the national judiciary on Saturday, February 21, 2026, in a ceremony held at the Congress Hall of the People's Palace in Kinshasa. The event marked the conclusion of an int
title_en: DRC Inducts 2,500 New Magistrates to Strengthen Rule of Law
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, February 23, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo formally inducted 2,500 new magistrates into the national judiciary on Saturday, February 21, 2026, in a ceremony held at the Congress Hall of the People's Palace in Kinshasa. The event marked the conclusion of an int
body_en:
Kinshasa, February 23, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo formally inducted 2,500 new magistrates into the national judiciary on Saturday, February 21, 2026, in a ceremony held at the Congress Hall of the People's Palace in Kinshasa. The event marked the conclusion of an intensive three-month training program aimed at enhancing the efficiency, ethics, competence, and professional conduct of magistrates before their deployment across the country.
The Minister of Justice and Keeper of the Seals, Guillaume Ngefa, emphasized that this initiative represents a crucial step in strengthening the rule of law. “A magistrate is neither a tool of the powerful, nor a hostage to emotion, nor a prisoner of personal convictions. They are an impartial servant of the law, bound by strict neutrality and an equal distance from all parties,” he declared.
This graduating class completes the initial cohort of magistrates, already in office since 2023, all graduates of the national competitive examination held in October 2022 and dubbed the “Rule of Law” class.
During his address, Minister Ngefa reminded the new magistrates of the weight of their responsibilities: “In the exercise of your duties, you will be called upon to rule on matters of liberty, rights, property, and the honor of those seeking justice. These powers are delegated to you by the nation, within the limits set by the Constitution and the laws of the Republic.”
He stressed that integrity and probity are not merely personal virtues, but fundamental prerequisites for public trust in the justice system. Independence, he added, is not a privilege but an institutional guarantee that protects citizens against arbitrary power.
“You will face pressure, attempts at influence, and even threats, but these challenges cannot justify abandoning the principles upon which your oath is based. Fighting corruption, influence peddling, and unjustified delays is now both a professional obligation and a requirement for institutional performance,” Minister Ngefa stated.
The Minister also highlighted the need for digital transformation, streamlined procedures, expedited case processing, and transparent decision-making as essential elements of modern judicial governance. “Magistrates must be not only legal practitioners but also agents of transformation, demonstrating methodological rigor, quality decisions, and strict adherence to legal deadlines,” he said.
The deployment of these 2,500 magistrates is expected to address pressing challenges in multiple jurisdictions, including in field operations. Minister Ngefa reaffirmed the government’s commitment to supporting the judiciary with the necessary material and organizational resources to ensure effective performance.
The DRC Constitution of February 18, 2006, guarantees the independence of the judiciary from the legislative and executive branches, reinforcing the separation of powers as a cornerstone of democracy. The High Council of the Judiciary, responsible for managing appointments, promotions, disciplinary measures, and advisory functions, ensures the proper implementation of these principles.
“The mandate is clear: build a justice system worthy of the nation, protective of fundamental rights, firm against violations, and responsive to the legitimate expectations of the people,” concluded Minister Ngefa.

excerpt_en: MASISI, North Kivu – February 24, 2026 — Willy Ngoma, the military spokesperson for the AFC/M23 rebel group, was killed on Tuesday, February 24, 2026, during a drone strike attributed to the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) near Rubaya, a strategic mining
body_en:
MASISI, North Kivu – February 24, 2026 — Willy Ngoma, the military spokesperson for the AFC/M23 rebel group, was killed on Tuesday, February 24, 2026, during a drone strike attributed to the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) near Rubaya, a strategic mining area in Masisi territory, eastern DRC.
Ngoma’s death, confirmed by multiple sources within the rebel movement, marks the loss of a high-ranking member of AFC/M23, following the earlier killing of Magloire Paluku, amid escalating hostilities in eastern DRC. The increase in fighting coincides with intensified FARDC airstrikes, ground offensives by Wazalendo allies, and Angola’s perceived failure to enforce the ceasefire, according to the United Nations.
Prior to Ngoma’s death, Bertrand Bisimwa, the second-in-command of AFC/M23, accused the Kinshasa government of violating the ceasefire since signing the Strategic Partnership Agreement with the United States. In statements on social media, Bisimwa condemned what he described as “assassinations and massacres of innocent civilians with impunity,” denouncing the government’s disregard for the peace process.
Willy Ngoma had previously been sanctioned by the United States in 2023 for his role in serious human rights abuses, including murders and sexual violence against civilians, committed under the banner of the AFC/M23 rebel movement.
His death underscores the intensifying conflict in North Kivu, reflecting the volatile security situation in eastern DRC and the continuing struggle between government forces, allied militias, and armed rebel groups in the region.

body_en:
MASISI, North Kivu February 27, 2026 — The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) carried out an airstrike Thursday evening, February 26, targeting an AFC/M23 rebel position in Nyabiondo, Masisi territory.
Local sources reported that the strike occurred around 6:00 p.m. in the Isiro neighborhood, with a drone dropping bombs on the rebel camp. The resulting explosion was heard across surrounding areas, causing panic among residents. Civilians reportedly rushed into their homes immediately afterward, leaving the streets empty.
No official casualty figures have been released, but witnesses noted the presence of military personnel and equipment at the targeted position, suggesting potentially significant losses for the rebels.
This strike is part of intensified military operations by the FARDC in Masisi, aimed at weakening the operational capacity of the AFC/M23, which maintains active positions across several parts of North Kivu. By the end of 2025, at least three other rebel positions in Nyabiondo had already been destroyed by airstrikes, reflecting the army's increasing use of aerial firepower in this strategic area.
The security situation in Masisi remains tense, with civilians continuing to bear the brunt of repeated clashes between government forces and the AFC/M23 rebels.

body_en:
WALIKALE March 2, 2026 — Armed clashes persisted for a third consecutive day on Monday, March 2, in Kibati, located in the Luberike group of Walikale territory, North Kivu. The fighting pits the AFC/M23 rebels against the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC), supported by local Wazalendo fighters.
Following Sunday’s clashes, both sides reportedly share control of the town. Government forces and their Wazalendo allies hold the center of Kibati and two positions previously held by the rebels, while the AFC/M23 maintains two positions along the road to Kashebere, a strategic corridor for troop movements and supply lines.
Monday morning saw renewed fighting after rebel reinforcements arrived from Kashebere, with heavy and light weapons fire continuing to echo in the area.
The confrontations began on Saturday, February 28, when government forces launched an offensive to regain control of Kibati. The town is considered strategic due to its location along roads connecting multiple key towns in the territory.
As clashes continue, insecurity remains high, and local populations face ongoing disruptions to daily life and mobility in this volatile region of North Kivu.

title_en: Precarious Lull as AFC/M23 Consolidates Positions in Buhimba-Kazinga-Katoy Triangle
excerpt_en: NORTH KIVU March 4, 2026 — A temporary calm was reported on Wednesday, March 4, 2026, in the Buhimba-Kazinga-Katoy triangle, spanning Masisi and Walikale territories in North Kivu, following several days of intense clashes between AFC/M23 rebels and the FARDC, supported by Wazale
body_en:
NORTH KIVU March 4, 2026 — A temporary calm was reported on Wednesday, March 4, 2026, in the Buhimba-Kazinga-Katoy triangle, spanning Masisi and Walikale territories in North Kivu, following several days of intense clashes between AFC/M23 rebels and the FARDC, supported by Wazalendo forces.
Local sources indicate that fighting has been largely silent since Tuesday afternoon, after AFC/M23 recaptured Kazinga. This strategic area connects multiple localities in both Masisi and Walikale and has experienced significant population displacement due to recent hostilities.
Despite the lull, the situation remains highly volatile. Observers report that rebel reinforcements were seen moving from Nyabiondo and Kasopo towards Buhimba and Kazinga, and from Kasenyi towards Katoy. Security sources confirmed the movements but provided no details on the scale or objectives.
Analysts warn that these troop movements may signal the next phase of rebel offensives against government positions or attempts to seize additional surrounding localities, raising fears of a renewed escalation in fighting and a worsening humanitarian situation in this part of North Kivu.

title: Burundians Mourn as Ruhwa Border with Rwanda Remains Closed
excerpt: On March 5, 2026, residents of Cibitoke commune in Bujumbura Province, Burundi, expressed frustration and mourning after the Burundian government failed to reopen its border with Rwanda, breaking earlier promises. The border closure has severely affected trade and daily life. Bef
title_en: Burundians Mourn as Ruhwa Border with Rwanda Remains Closed
excerpt_en: On March 5, 2026, residents of Cibitoke commune in Bujumbura Province, Burundi, expressed frustration and mourning after the Burundian government failed to reopen its border with Rwanda, breaking earlier promises. The border closure has severely affected trade and daily life. Bef
body_en:
On March 5, 2026, residents of Cibitoke commune in Bujumbura Province, Burundi, expressed frustration and mourning after the Burundian government failed to reopen its border with Rwanda, breaking earlier promises.
The border closure has severely affected trade and daily life. Before the closure, Burundians exported fruits and vegetables such as lemons, oranges, mangoes, tangerines, and tomatoes to Rwanda, earning significant income. Residents now report higher costs for basic necessities in Burundi compared to Rwanda.
“While the border was still open, we used to export products to Rwanda… This money helped us survive,” said a local resident of Ruhwa village.
The closure has also split families, preventing Burundians and Rwandans who are blood relatives from visiting one another across the border.
The head of Ruhwa village, Nsengiyumva Révocat, highlighted the human impact, emphasizing that many families remain separated due to the government’s decision.
Burundians in Ruhwa are calling on their government to negotiate with Rwanda to reopen the border, restore trade, and allow familial visits, hoping to return to previous levels of economic and social interaction.

title: Rwanda Moves Toward Legalization of Virtual Assets
excerpt: On March 4, 2026, the Rwandan Cabinet approved a draft law regulating virtual assets, marking the first step toward legalizing their use in the country. The Ministry of Finance and Economic Planning defines virtual assets as electronic values that can be exchanged or transferred
title_en: Rwanda Moves Toward Legalization of Virtual Assets
excerpt_en: On March 4, 2026, the Rwandan Cabinet approved a draft law regulating virtual assets, marking the first step toward legalizing their use in the country. The Ministry of Finance and Economic Planning defines virtual assets as electronic values that can be exchanged or transferred
body_en:
On March 4, 2026, the Rwandan Cabinet approved a draft law regulating virtual assets, marking the first step toward legalizing their use in the country.
The Ministry of Finance and Economic Planning defines virtual assets as electronic values that can be exchanged or transferred digitally. These assets can be used for payments and investments, but do not include official currencies such as the Rwandan franc, US dollar, or euro.
The Ministry highlighted that virtual assets promote innovation and economic growth globally, but also pose risks, including potential misuse for corruption and illegal activities.
The draft law aims to protect Rwanda’s financial sector, control these risks, and support the sector’s development. It is aligned with international standards set by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) to prevent financial crime.
Once approved and enacted, the law will be published in the Official Gazette, and the Capital Market Authority (AMC) and the National Bank of Rwanda (BNR) will issue regulations on implementation, licensing, and supervision of related service providers.

title: Rwanda Welcomes 32 Former Armed Group Members from DRC for Rehabilitation
excerpt: Musanze, February 25, 2026 – Rwanda received 32 former members of armed groups from eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), along with 31 of their family members, as part of the country’s ongoing demobilization and reintegration efforts. The group was handed over by the Unite
title_en: Rwanda Welcomes 32 Former Armed Group Members from DRC for Rehabilitation
excerpt_en: Musanze, February 25, 2026 – Rwanda received 32 former members of armed groups from eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), along with 31 of their family members, as part of the country’s ongoing demobilization and reintegration efforts. The group was handed over by the Unite
body_en:
Musanze, February 25, 2026 – Rwanda received 32 former members of armed groups from eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), along with 31 of their family members, as part of the country’s ongoing demobilization and reintegration efforts.
The group was handed over by the United Nations Peacekeeping Mission in the DRC (MONUSCO), under the Disarmament, Demobilization, Reintegration, and Security (DDR&S) program, and received at the National Demobilization and Rehabilitation Commission (RDRC) facility in Mutobo, Musanze District. They will undergo early training to support their reentry into civilian life and social integration.
The returning fighters include former members of FDLR-FOCA, CNRD, and Nyatura CMC, groups historically linked to the Genocide ideology. Most of the returnees are young adults aged 18 to 30, although the oldest is a 53-year-old woman, Odette, formerly part of the FDLR special forces unit CRAP. The group also includes more than 10 women and one child who had participated in Nyatura CMC operations.
Since 2001, Rwanda has received 12,602 former combatants from armed groups aiming to destabilize the country, reintegrating them into civilian life. Authorities emphasize that Rwanda remains willing to accept individuals who lay down arms, though the DRC government reportedly continues to restrict returns, and the FDLR-FOCA still maintains 7,000 to 10,000 fighters, blending with civilian populations when threatened.
The initiative reflects Rwanda’s ongoing commitment to peacebuilding, rehabilitation, and the reintegration of former combatants, contributing to regional stability and security in the Great Lakes region.

The initiative reflects Rwanda’s ongoing commitment to peacebuilding, rehabilitation, and the reintegration of former combatants, contributing to regional stability and security in the Great Lakes region.

title: Belgian Analyst Says US Misplaced Sanctions Over FDLR Issue in DRC
excerpt: Alain Destexhe, former Belgian Senator and Secretary General of Doctors Without Borders (MSF), has criticized the United States for sanctioning the Rwandan Defence Forces (RDF) instead of holding the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government accountable for its ties to the FD
title_en: Belgian Analyst Says US Misplaced Sanctions Over FDLR Issue in DRC
excerpt_en: Alain Destexhe, former Belgian Senator and Secretary General of Doctors Without Borders (MSF), has criticized the United States for sanctioning the Rwandan Defence Forces (RDF) instead of holding the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government accountable for its ties to the FD
body_en:
Alain Destexhe, former Belgian Senator and Secretary General of Doctors Without Borders (MSF), has criticized the United States for sanctioning the Rwandan Defence Forces (RDF) instead of holding the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government accountable for its ties to the FDLR terrorist group, in remarks made on March 4, 2026.
Destexhe’s comments followed US sanctions imposed on March 2, 2026, targeting RDF and senior Rwandan officers accused of supporting the AFC/M23 coalition and destabilizing eastern DRC. He argued that the DRC government, not Rwanda, is responsible for continuing insecurity in the region.
“The DRC should be punished, not Rwanda. Despite UN Security Council Resolution 2773 and peace agreements, the DRC has refused to distance itself from the FDLR, which remains a major security threat. Meanwhile, Wazalendo extremists’ funds continue to fuel terrorism,” Destexhe wrote on X on March 3.
He further accused the DRC of collaborating with foreign mercenaries and conducting drone attacks on civilians, including in Minembwe, South Kivu, noting that such attacks have persisted for several days.
Destexhe, who has long monitored the Great Lakes region, highlighted that the FDLR’s capabilities doubled after receiving support from the DRC government, making it difficult to dismantle the group entirely. “Their numbers increased after the FDLR received weapons and material support from President Félix Tshisekedi to fight M23,” he said.
UN expert reports estimate the FDLR has between 1,500 and 3,000 fighters, though the group’s military spokesman claimed in November 2025 that their numbers were significantly higher.
Destexhe called on the United States to reassess its approach and hold the DRC government responsible for enabling continued violence in eastern DRC.

title: Government Acknowledges Delays in Civil Servants’ Salaries, Promises Normalization Within a Month
excerpt: KINSHASA March 6, 2026 — The Democratic Republic of Congo government has acknowledged delays in salary payments for civil servants, citing strain on public finances, and pledged a return to regular payments within the month. At a meeting on March 5, the government, led by Prime M
title_en: Government Acknowledges Delays in Civil Servants’ Salaries, Promises Normalization Within a Month
excerpt_en: KINSHASA March 6, 2026 — The Democratic Republic of Congo government has acknowledged delays in salary payments for civil servants, citing strain on public finances, and pledged a return to regular payments within the month. At a meeting on March 5, the government, led by Prime M
body_en:
KINSHASA March 6, 2026 — The Democratic Republic of Congo government has acknowledged delays in salary payments for civil servants, citing strain on public finances, and pledged a return to regular payments within the month.
At a meeting on March 5, the government, led by Prime Minister Judith Suminwa, and the Economic Situation Committee (CCE) reviewed public finances, monetary dynamics, market prices, and the potential effects of the Middle East crisis on the Congolese economy. Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Economy Daniel Mukoko Samba confirmed that delayed salaries result from pressure on the treasury, compounded by security and humanitarian expenditures linked to the ongoing conflict in eastern DRC.
“The delay is due to strain on the treasury,” Mukoko Samba explained. “A few months ago, the Government already emphasized the growing burden of the wage bill. We are taking measures to strengthen revenue collection and better control spending to restore timely salary payments.”
He reassured that steps to improve payroll management and public revenue collection, aligned with President Félix Tshisekedi’s directives, should normalize payments within the month.
The recurring delays have drawn attention from economists, such as Deputy Gode Mpoy, who noted that exchange rate fluctuations contribute to shortfalls when payrolls are calculated in USD but converted to Congolese francs. The government, however, rejects claims of liquidity problems, maintaining that sufficient resources are available.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has also flagged the growing public sector wage bill as a fiscal risk, particularly in education, health, and justice, where recent salary adjustments, recruitment, and administrative regularizations have strained the budget.
President Tshisekedi previously instructed a comprehensive payroll audit, with results expected within 30 days, aimed at ensuring sustainable public finances and regular, reliable salary payments for civil servants.
This move comes as the DRC faces increased expenditures related to security operations, including responses to the AFC/M23 rebellion in North and South Kivu, highlighting the delicate balance between fiscal management and social stability.
