title: Measles and Mpox Cases Threaten Isangi Health Zone
excerpt: Isangi, Tshopo, March 2, 2026 – The Isangi health zone is facing a dual health threat as measles and Mpox cases are confirmed in the district, according to Dr. Charles Koy, chief medical officer. In the Yalosase health area, of 18 samples tested, five were positive for measles an
title_en: Measles and Mpox Cases Threaten Isangi Health Zone
excerpt_en: Isangi, Tshopo, March 2, 2026 – The Isangi health zone is facing a dual health threat as measles and Mpox cases are confirmed in the district, according to Dr. Charles Koy, chief medical officer. In the Yalosase health area, of 18 samples tested, five were positive for measles an
body_en:
Isangi, Tshopo, March 2, 2026 – The Isangi health zone is facing a dual health threat as measles and Mpox cases are confirmed in the district, according to Dr. Charles Koy, chief medical officer.
In the Yalosase health area, of 18 samples tested, five were positive for measles and one for rubella. Mpox cases were also reported. In the Weko health area, all seven samples tested positive for Mpox. As of February 28, at least 23 Mpox cases have been recorded, including two deaths.
A small-scale local response has been organized, but resources remain severely limited, Dr. Koy noted. “We have forwarded the report to our superiors, and today a partner came to investigate and confirm whether there is an outbreak of cases,” he said.
Health facilities in Isangi are inadequate, with some treatment centers destroyed by Congo River flooding. The health zone also lacks essential medications for providing free medical care.
“For now, our SOS is for partners to assist with the medical treatment of Mpox and measles cases,” Dr. Koy pleaded, urging urgent support from government and humanitarian partners.

title_en: FARDC Drone Strikes Target AFC/M23 Positions in Kishusha Near Rubaya
excerpt_en: MASISI, North Kivu February 24, 2026 — The security situation remains highly tense in Masisi territory after the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) carried out drone strikes against AFC/M23 rebel positions early Tuesday morning in Kishusha, a locality locate
body_en:
MASISI, North Kivu February 24, 2026 — The security situation remains highly tense in Masisi territory after the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) carried out drone strikes against AFC/M23 rebel positions early Tuesday morning in Kishusha, a locality located near the strategic mining town of Rubaya.
The operation reportedly took place at around 4:00 a.m., when a military drone launched strikes on positions held by AFC/M23 fighters in the area, which has witnessed intense clashes in recent days.
Residents reported powerful explosions that could be heard as far as Rubaya, triggering panic among the local population. Several families, already living under the strain of ongoing insecurity, spent the early hours of the morning fearing a possible escalation of fighting in the area.
For now, no official casualty figures have been released. Information from the ground indicates that assessments are underway to determine the extent of human and material damage caused by the strikes.
The drone operation comes amid renewed clashes between AFC/M23 rebels and FARDC forces, supported by Wazalendo fighters, around Rubaya and in several other localities of Masisi territory, highlighting the continued volatility of the security situation in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.

title: UN Experts Condemn “Extreme” Violence by M23 Against Human Rights Defenders
excerpt: EASTERN DRC February 26, 2026 — United Nations experts have issued a strong warning over the escalating human rights violations perpetrated by the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 rebellion against human rights defenders in North and South Kivu provinces. The experts cited assassination at
title_en: UN Experts Condemn “Extreme” Violence by M23 Against Human Rights Defenders
excerpt_en: EASTERN DRC February 26, 2026 — United Nations experts have issued a strong warning over the escalating human rights violations perpetrated by the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 rebellion against human rights defenders in North and South Kivu provinces. The experts cited assassination at
body_en:
EASTERN DRC February 26, 2026 — United Nations experts have issued a strong warning over the escalating human rights violations perpetrated by the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 rebellion against human rights defenders in North and South Kivu provinces. The experts cited assassination attempts, repeated kidnappings, torture, sexual violence, and death threats targeting those who document abuses, support communities, or denounce violations.
In a statement released in Geneva during the 61st session of the UN Human Rights Council, the experts emphasized that human rights defenders in eastern DRC are facing unbearable risks, particularly women and members of the LGBT community, who are subjected to heightened threats of sexual violence and torture.
Between November 2025 and February 2026, multiple defenders were reportedly targeted. Two women advocating against forced civilian expulsions in Uvira were abducted and tortured, and their whereabouts remain unknown. Another woman defending LGBT rights suffered repeated abductions and severe torture. A human rights defender in Goma was forced into hiding after threats and attacks on his family, while another defender received death threats and was assaulted at home.
The experts stressed that even when violations are committed by non-state armed groups, the State has a legal obligation under international human rights law to protect all persons under its jurisdiction. They called on authorities to investigate abuses promptly, provide medical and psychosocial support, and ensure that human rights defenders can operate safely.
“Human rights defenders are not combatants. They are essential actors for justice, accountability, and peace. Silencing them through fear and brutality undermines prospects for lasting peace in eastern DRC,” the experts stated.
This warning follows a recent government report documenting 17,015 cases of human rights violations in Goma, North Kivu, and Bukavu, South Kivu, which was presented to Prime Minister Judith Suminwa Tuluka. The government has pledged to intensify international advocacy and ensure accountability for these abuses.
The UN experts’ statement highlights the urgent need for protection, accountability, and respect for the ceasefire, as ongoing attacks on human rights defenders threaten both the humanitarian situation and the peace process in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.

title: Multiple Drone Attacks Target Kisangani Airport, No Casualties, March 1, 2026
excerpt: KISANGANI March 1, 2026 — Kisangani’s Bangboka International Airport in Tshopo province was targeted by a series of drone attacks on Sunday, March 1, but no casualties were reported. Local sources and provincial authorities told that the first drone was intercepted around 3:00 PM
title_en: Multiple Drone Attacks Target Kisangani Airport, No Casualties, March 1, 2026
excerpt_en: KISANGANI March 1, 2026 — Kisangani’s Bangboka International Airport in Tshopo province was targeted by a series of drone attacks on Sunday, March 1, but no casualties were reported. Local sources and provincial authorities told that the first drone was intercepted around 3:00 PM
body_en:
KISANGANI March 1, 2026 — Kisangani’s Bangboka International Airport in Tshopo province was targeted by a series of drone attacks on Sunday, March 1, but no casualties were reported.
Local sources and provincial authorities told that the first drone was intercepted around 3:00 PM local time. Three additional “kamikaze” drones were neutralized by airport security between 5:00 PM and 7:00 PM. Shrapnel caused minor damage to infrastructure, including broken windows, but the control tower remained operational. Some nearby residents temporarily evacuated as a precaution.
The provincial government attributed the attacks to the AFC/M23 rebellion and Rwanda. The group had previously claimed responsibility for a drone attack on Bangboka Airport in late January.
According to the Congolese research institute Ebuteli, the army employs Turkish TAI Anka drones and Chinese CH-4 combat drones. The recent attacks were reportedly carried out using Turkish Baykar Yiha-III drones, with additional drones possibly supplied by Estonian Threod Systems.
This wave of drone incidents follows FARDC airstrikes in Masisi territory on February 24 that killed Willy Ngoma, AFC/M23 military spokesperson, and several other rebel members, underscoring the growing aerial dimension of the conflict in eastern DRC.
The airport remains operational, and authorities continue to monitor the security situation closely.

WALIKALE, North Kivu March 4, 2026 — The security situation in Walikale territory is deteriorating as AFC/M23 rebels consolidate control over Kibati, following three days of intense clashes with FARDC forces and the Wazalendo militia.
Local sources report that after government forces withdrew, rebels secured all positions in the town. On the evening of Tuesday, March 3, additional reinforcements of fighters and ammunition arrived from Masisi territory via the Kashebere axis. This development underscores the persistent volatility in Walikale, where recurring clashes between AFC/M23 rebels and government forces continue to threaten security and disrupt daily life.

On March 4, 2026, the Rwandan Embassy in Qatar announced that all its services would be temporarily moved online due to ongoing security concerns stemming from Iranian attacks in the region.
The embassy explained that the decision was made to ensure safety while continuing assistance to Rwandans and others in need.
“Due to the current security concerns, the Rwandan Embassy in Doha is operating online,” the statement read.

The embassy reassured the public that, despite moving services online, it would continue to provide support remotely.

title: Rwanda Sets New Fuel Prices Amid International Market Volatility

title_en: Rwanda Sets New Fuel Prices Amid International Market Volatility
excerpt_en: The Regulatory Authority for Rwanda (RURA) has announced revised fuel prices, effective March 5, 2026, which will remain in force for the next two months. Petrol: 1,989 Frw per liter Diesel: 1,948 Frw per liter The new pricing, inclusive of Value Added Tax (VAT), reflects fluctua
body_en:
The Regulatory Authority for Rwanda (RURA) has announced revised fuel prices, effective March 5, 2026, which will remain in force for the next two months.
Petrol: 1,989 Frw per liter
Diesel: 1,948 Frw per liter
The new pricing, inclusive of Value Added Tax (VAT), reflects fluctuations in the international oil market, particularly following the US-Iran conflict that temporarily disrupted the Strait of Hormuz, a critical channel for 20% of global oil trade.
Minister of Finance and Economic Planning, Yusuf Murangwa, explained that the government is actively supporting fuel traders through financial facilitation, ensuring sufficient reserves to stabilize domestic supply. He noted that if the conflict is short-lived (up to two weeks), the economic impact on Rwanda will be minimal.
Murangwa emphasized contingency planning, stating, “If the war continues for more than two weeks or a month, additional measures will be taken to assist oil traders and other essential goods suppliers, preventing further disruption to the Rwandan economy.”
The move underscores Rwanda’s proactive approach to energy security and price stability, while mitigating the effects of international geopolitical tensions on domestic markets.

title: Rwanda Welcomes 22 Citizens Returning from Democratic Republic of Congo
excerpt: Rusizi, February 25, 2026 – Rwanda welcomed 22 of its citizens returning from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), including individuals who had lived in exile for over 30 years, expressing regret over the years lost during displacement and the impact on their education and fa
title_en: Rwanda Welcomes 22 Citizens Returning from Democratic Republic of Congo
excerpt_en: Rusizi, February 25, 2026 – Rwanda welcomed 22 of its citizens returning from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), including individuals who had lived in exile for over 30 years, expressing regret over the years lost during displacement and the impact on their education and fa
body_en:
Rusizi, February 25, 2026 – Rwanda welcomed 22 of its citizens returning from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), including individuals who had lived in exile for over 30 years, expressing regret over the years lost during displacement and the impact on their education and family life.
The returnees arrived via the Rusizi I Border on February 24, 2026, marking the second group this year to come back from the DRC. The group includes two men, four women, and 16 children. They were first received at the Nyarushishi temporary camp before being reunited with their families.
Speaking to local media, the returnees described years spent in the DRC as a period of hardship, noting that their children were unable to attend school and grew up under difficult conditions in a war zone. One returnee said, “This is a great loss because we kept running away and our children were unable to study and were always in trouble.” Another added, “My older brother returned first and told me that Rwanda was safe, so we decided to come back.”
The returnees were warmly received by the Rusizi District Administration, UNHCR staff, and security forces. The Mayor of Rusizi District, Sindayiheba Phanuel, described the return as a significant step toward leaving behind a history of conflict and hatred, encouraging others still in exile to consider returning. He said, “Their arrival is good news as they come to join other Rwandans in rebuilding the country. We want to show others that Rwanda is peaceful and encourage them to make their own decision to return.”
The repatriation reflects Rwanda’s ongoing efforts to support displaced citizens, promote reconciliation, and facilitate family reunification.

title: US Sanctions on RDF Criticized as Attack on African Interests, Says Zimbabwean Watchdog
excerpt: Rutendo Matinyarare of Zimbabwe Human Rights Watch has said that recent US sanctions on the Rwandan Defence Forces (RDF) reflect Rwanda’s defense of African interests, rather than wrongdoing, and accused international actors of misrepresenting the situation in eastern DRC. On the
title_en: US Sanctions on RDF Criticized as Attack on African Interests, Says Zimbabwean Watchdog
excerpt_en: Rutendo Matinyarare of Zimbabwe Human Rights Watch has said that recent US sanctions on the Rwandan Defence Forces (RDF) reflect Rwanda’s defense of African interests, rather than wrongdoing, and accused international actors of misrepresenting the situation in eastern DRC. On the
body_en:
Rutendo Matinyarare of Zimbabwe Human Rights Watch has said that recent US sanctions on the Rwandan Defence Forces (RDF) reflect Rwanda’s defense of African interests, rather than wrongdoing, and accused international actors of misrepresenting the situation in eastern DRC.
On the evening of March 2, 2026, the US Treasury Department imposed sanctions on the RDF and several senior military officers, alleging their involvement in security disruptions in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo—claims repeatedly denied by Rwanda.
Matinyarare, who visited Rwanda in February 2025 to make a feature film about the M23 movement, said he initially believed Rwanda was a tool of Western powers. However, his visit revealed a country committed to African pride and self-determination.
“When I arrived in M23-controlled areas, I learned how Belgian colonialists divided Kinyarwanda-speaking communities and how the DRC government sought to displace them. Sharing this truth on platforms like TikTok was censored,” he said.
He argued that the RDF’s actions are aimed at defending African communities, and that sanctions from the West often target countries protecting the continent’s interests, rather than those violating human rights.
“I think as Africans, we know that when the West sanctions you, it is because you are serving Africa, hindering international efforts. Let us congratulate Rwanda for being a revolutionary society,” Matinyarare said.
The Rwandan government condemned the sanctions, calling them biased and contrary to the realities in eastern DRC, and reaffirmed that the RDF remains committed to national and regional security.

title: DRC Signs $155 Million AfDB Loan to Boost Ngandajika Agro-Industrial Park
excerpt: KINSHASA February 26, 2026 — The Government of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has signed a $155 million loan agreement with the African Development Bank (AfDB) to strengthen connectivity for the Ngandajika Agro-Industrial Park. The signing was carried out by Minister of F
title_en: DRC Signs $155 Million AfDB Loan to Boost Ngandajika Agro-Industrial Park
excerpt_en: KINSHASA February 26, 2026 — The Government of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has signed a $155 million loan agreement with the African Development Bank (AfDB) to strengthen connectivity for the Ngandajika Agro-Industrial Park. The signing was carried out by Minister of F
body_en:
KINSHASA February 26, 2026 — The Government of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has signed a $155 million loan agreement with the African Development Bank (AfDB) to strengthen connectivity for the Ngandajika Agro-Industrial Park. The signing was carried out by Minister of Finance Doudou Fwamba Likunde Li-Botayi.
This project forms the third component of the DRC’s Agricultural Transformation Program, aligning with the vision of President Félix Tshisekedi to make agriculture a strategic lever for economic diversification and food security.
Minister Fwamba emphasized that connectivity is central to the success of existing investments in governance and value chain development. “It is essential for the sustainable development of our agricultural potential and the effective integration of producers into local and regional markets,” he said.
The project includes the improvement of the Lukalaba–Ngandajika and Nkuadi–Ngandajika–Park roads, aiming to:
Open up the region sustainably
Reduce transport costs
Facilitate trade
Create jobs, particularly for youth and women
The government underscored that infrastructure development is key to agricultural transformation, food security, and national cohesion, while praising the AfDB partnership as vital for achieving strategic priorities.
Officials noted that this agreement strengthens DRC’s financial credibility with international partners and opens new avenues for integrated and sustainable rural development.

title: Nearly 22,000 Congolese Return to Uvira from Burundi, Kinshasa Engages UNHCR
excerpt: Uvira, March 8, 2026 – Nearly 22,000 Congolese have spontaneously returned to the Democratic Republic of Congo via Uvira in South Kivu, coming from Bujumbura, Burundi, the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of the Interior, Security, Decentralization, and Customary Affairs, Jacqu
title_en: Nearly 22,000 Congolese Return to Uvira from Burundi, Kinshasa Engages UNHCR
excerpt_en: Uvira, March 8, 2026 – Nearly 22,000 Congolese have spontaneously returned to the Democratic Republic of Congo via Uvira in South Kivu, coming from Bujumbura, Burundi, the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of the Interior, Security, Decentralization, and Customary Affairs, Jacqu
body_en:
Uvira, March 8, 2026 – Nearly 22,000 Congolese have spontaneously returned to the Democratic Republic of Congo via Uvira in South Kivu, coming from Bujumbura, Burundi, the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of the Interior, Security, Decentralization, and Customary Affairs, Jacquemain Shabani, reported during the 81st meeting of the Council of Ministers.
Shabani confirmed that the government has already contacted the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) to ensure that the return of displaced persons and refugees complies with international regulations, through a planned tripartite framework.
The mass return follows violent clashes between the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 rebellion and government forces, which had previously led to the fall of Uvira and worsened the humanitarian situation in the region, affecting neighboring countries such as Burundi.
In response, the Congolese government, led by Minister of State for Social Affairs and Humanitarian Action Ève Bazaiba Masudi, conducted a humanitarian mission to Burundi and Tanzania, providing support to returning refugees, coordinating with host countries, and working with partners including the UNHCR.
The return coincides with the reopening of cross-border trade, symbolizing renewed state authority after months of closure due to security tensions linked to AFC/M23 activities. The government delegation presided over the reopening ceremony and continues to monitor measures aimed at restoring order and governance.
Uvira, a strategic city in South Kivu, had been under AFC/M23 control, strengthening the rebel presence in North and South Kivu. The city is considered a key security and economic stronghold, potentially facilitating advances toward the Greater Katanga region, the economic heartland of the DRC.
The developments follow the recent visit of European Commissioner for Crisis Preparedness and Management, Hadja Lahbib, who urged all parties in the Great Lakes region to respect international humanitarian law, reinforcing the message of humanitarian compliance and conflict resolution.

The return coincides with the reopening of cross-border trade, symbolizing renewed state authority after months of closure due to security tensions linked to AFC/M23 activities. The government delegation presided over the reopening ceremony and continues to monitor measures aimed at restoring order and governance.
Uvira, a strategic city in South Kivu, had been under AFC/M23 control, strengthening the rebel presence in North and South Kivu. The city is considered a key security and economic stronghold, potentially facilitating advances toward the Greater Katanga region, the economic heartland of the DRC.
The developments follow the recent visit of European Commissioner for Crisis Preparedness and Management, Hadja Lahbib, who urged all parties in the Great Lakes region to respect international humanitarian law, reinforcing the message of humanitarian compliance and conflict resolution.

title: MONUSCO and ICGLR Deploy Joint Assessment Mission to Uvira to Support Ceasefire Monitoring
excerpt: UVIRA, South Kivu February 24, 2026 — The United Nations Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (MONUSCO) and the International Conference on the Great Lakes Region (ICGLR) have launched a joint exploratory and preliminary assessment mission in
title_en: MONUSCO and ICGLR Deploy Joint Assessment Mission to Uvira to Support Ceasefire Monitoring
excerpt_en: UVIRA, South Kivu February 24, 2026 — The United Nations Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (MONUSCO) and the International Conference on the Great Lakes Region (ICGLR) have launched a joint exploratory and preliminary assessment mission in
body_en:
UVIRA, South Kivu February 24, 2026 — The United Nations Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (MONUSCO) and the International Conference on the Great Lakes Region (ICGLR) have launched a joint exploratory and preliminary assessment mission in Uvira, South Kivu, as part of efforts to support the implementation and monitoring of the ceasefire in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
The mission, scheduled to run from February 23 to 27, 2026, follows consultations with President Félix Tshisekedi, who currently serves as Chair of the ICGLR. According to a joint statement released Tuesday, the deployment represents a crucial preparatory step toward the future establishment of a joint ceasefire monitoring mechanism within the framework of the broader regional ceasefire architecture.
The primary objective of the mission is operational and technical, focusing on ensuring that future monitoring and verification mechanisms are credible, secure, and operationally feasible. Teams on the ground will assess accessibility, security conditions, logistical requirements, and operational needs necessary for the effective functioning of the monitoring system.
During the mission, the joint delegation will conduct a comprehensive evaluation of the political, security, logistical, and socio-environmental environment in and around Uvira, with the goal of facilitating coherent planning for the future deployment of ceasefire monitoring structures.
Officials emphasized that effective monitoring of the ceasefire is essential to reducing violence and creating the conditions necessary for a lasting political solution in the region.
The acting head of MONUSCO, Vivian van de Perre, noted that the mission’s mandate in South Kivu differs from its operations in North Kivu and Ituri, explaining that MONUSCO’s role in the province is focused primarily on monitoring the ceasefire rather than conducting Protection of Civilians operations, in accordance with United Nations Security Council Resolution 2808 (2025).
She stressed that the current deployment represents an exploratory phase, and that the scope and configuration of any future operations will depend on agreed parameters, security guarantees, and operational requirements.
For his part, ICGLR Executive Secretary Dr. Mubita Luwabelwa highlighted the importance of regional cooperation, stating that the Great Lakes region possesses significant potential for peace and prosperity if states work together to address shared security challenges.
Both organizations underscored that credible ceasefire monitoring requires favorable operational conditions, including freedom of movement for monitoring teams and reliable security guarantees, which remain key aspects of the ongoing assessment.
Under UN Security Council Resolution 2808 (2025), MONUSCO is authorized to support the implementation of a permanent ceasefire in the Democratic Republic of Congo. This support includes assistance to the Ceasefire Monitoring and Verification Mechanism as well as the Expanded Joint Verification Mechanism Plus (EJVM+), established following the signing of the Doha Global Peace Framework on November 15, 2025.
The deployment comes amid renewed diplomatic and peacekeeping efforts aimed at stabilizing eastern DRC. It also follows a recent field visit to the region by MONUSCO leadership, during which discussions were held with AFC/M23 representatives, as well as a visit to Kinshasa by United Nations Under-Secretary-General for Peace Operations Jean-Pierre Lacroix, who reaffirmed the UN’s commitment to implementing MONUSCO’s updated mandate and supporting peace efforts in the region.

title: Mobondo Militia Threat Reduced to 10%, Says Minister Eliezer Ntambwe
excerpt: GREATER BANDUNDU February 26, 2026 — Minister Delegate Eliezer Ntambwe, in charge of Veterans Affairs, reported significant progress in the disarmament and reintegration of the Mobondo militia in Greater Bandundu and Kinshasa, marking a major step in reducing insecurity linked to
title_en: Mobondo Militia Threat Reduced to 10%, Says Minister Eliezer Ntambwe
excerpt_en: GREATER BANDUNDU February 26, 2026 — Minister Delegate Eliezer Ntambwe, in charge of Veterans Affairs, reported significant progress in the disarmament and reintegration of the Mobondo militia in Greater Bandundu and Kinshasa, marking a major step in reducing insecurity linked to
body_en:
GREATER BANDUNDU February 26, 2026 — Minister Delegate Eliezer Ntambwe, in charge of Veterans Affairs, reported significant progress in the disarmament and reintegration of the Mobondo militia in Greater Bandundu and Kinshasa, marking a major step in reducing insecurity linked to intercommunal conflict.
Since January 2026, more than 500 Mobondo militiamen have surrendered and been referred to the National Service for professional reintegration, a program designed to equip former combatants with vocational skills. The threat posed by the militia has now been reduced to approximately 10%, according to Ntambwe, who distinguished this internal intercommunal conflict—between the Teke and Yaka communities—from external aggression such as that of AFC/M23 in the east of the DRC.
The Mobondo phenomenon, which emerged in 2022, escalated from a land dispute into armed violence, causing murders, looting, and mass displacement. The militia, originally led by a farmer named Sadam, alias Faux Yaya, spread across Kwilu, Kwango, Mai-Ndombe provinces, and parts of Kinshasa, particularly Maluku, before disarmament operations began.
Ntambwe highlighted that the disarmament strategy focused on awareness-raising, voluntary surrender, and structured reintegration rather than forced integration into military programs. Former militiamen are assessed individually for eligibility in reintegration programs, ensuring that those involved in atrocities are subject to transitional justice measures.
“This does not mean everything will be forgotten,” Ntambwe said. “The transitional justice phase will follow, ensuring truth, reconciliation, and commitments to non-repetition.” He added that while the threat is not completely eliminated, it has been significantly diminished, with only isolated elements remaining in the bush.
On the question of political involvement, Ntambwe partially confirmed that former President Joseph Kabila and PPRD members may have played a role in the conflict, citing testimonies regarding land purchases and insufficient compensation that fueled tensions. Security services continue to investigate these claims, which will be made public once verified.
Despite the progress, Ntambwe emphasized that absolute security does not exist, and while the Mobondo threat has decreased, pockets of insecurity remain. He reiterated the ongoing role of the FARDC and the police (PNC) in pursuing remaining militants and preventing a resurgence of violence.
The humanitarian impact of the Mobondo militia has been severe, with numerous deaths, displaced populations, and significant material losses. The Minister noted that the current phase prioritizes calming the situation and preparing for reintegration, with detailed assessments of displacement and damage planned as pacification advances.
This initiative reflects a structured approach to local militia management, aiming to regulate conflict, reduce harm, and reintegrate combatants into society, contrasting sharply with external armed groups destabilizing other regions of the DRC.

title: Mass Graves Found Following AFC/M23 Withdrawal, Specialized Teams Mobilized
excerpt: UVIRA March 1, 2026 — Two mass graves were discovered in Uvira, the provisional capital of South Kivu province, following the withdrawal of the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 rebellion from the city. The findings were reported by Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of the Interior, Jacque
title_en: Mass Graves Found Following AFC/M23 Withdrawal, Specialized Teams Mobilized
excerpt_en: UVIRA March 1, 2026 — Two mass graves were discovered in Uvira, the provisional capital of South Kivu province, following the withdrawal of the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 rebellion from the city. The findings were reported by Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of the Interior, Jacque
body_en:
UVIRA March 1, 2026 — Two mass graves were discovered in Uvira, the provisional capital of South Kivu province, following the withdrawal of the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 rebellion from the city. The findings were reported by Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of the Interior, Jacquemain Shabani, after a mission to oversee the DRC-Burundi border.
According to the government, the graves were located in the Kavinvira and Kilomoni neighborhoods. Preliminary investigations by provincial authorities indicate a total of 151 civilians were buried, including 121 in Kavinvira and 30 in Kilomoni. These executions reportedly occurred around January 18, 2026, shortly before the forced withdrawal of AFC/M23 forces from the city.
The South Kivu provincial government classified the killings as war crimes under Article 8 of the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court, and as potential crimes against humanity, citing the organized and systematic nature of the executions targeting civilians.
Specialized teams have been deployed to secure the sites, recover the bodies, and conduct further investigations, though no official exhumations have yet taken place. The identities of both victims and perpetrators remain unknown.
Uvira, a strategic city in South Kivu, had been under AFC/M23 control since December 2025. The withdrawal followed international pressure, notably from the United States, after violations of the Washington Agreement were reported. The city’s recapture is considered a key step in DRC’s efforts to reassert control over the region and prevent further rebel advances toward Greater Katanga, the country’s economic heartland.
The discovery underscores the severe humanitarian impact of the AFC/M23 rebellion and highlights the ongoing challenges in securing civilian safety in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.

title: Kibati Remains Under AFC/M23 Control After Three Days of Fighting
excerpt: WALIKALE, North Kivu March 3, 2026 — After three days of intense clashes between AFC/M23 rebels and FARDC forces supported by the Wazalendo local militia, the town of Kibati in the Luberike area of Walikale territory remains under rebel control. Local sources indicate that govern
title_en: Kibati Remains Under AFC/M23 Control After Three Days of Fighting
excerpt_en: WALIKALE, North Kivu March 3, 2026 — After three days of intense clashes between AFC/M23 rebels and FARDC forces supported by the Wazalendo local militia, the town of Kibati in the Luberike area of Walikale territory remains under rebel control. Local sources indicate that govern
body_en:
WALIKALE, North Kivu March 3, 2026 — After three days of intense clashes between AFC/M23 rebels and FARDC forces supported by the Wazalendo local militia, the town of Kibati in the Luberike area of Walikale territory remains under rebel control.
Local sources indicate that government forces, despite having recaptured much of the town during the fighting, ultimately withdrew to the villages of Miba and Mungazi, allowing AFC/M23 fighters to reclaim all lost positions.
The clashes have caused significant disruption to logistics and humanitarian aid, with traffic on the Mungazi-Kashebere road completely suspended. Travelers and transporters remain stranded on both sides, awaiting an improvement in security conditions.
This development comes amid a broader context of insecurity in Walikale, where repeated confrontations between government forces and AFC/M23 rebels continue to severely affect civilians. Fighting in Kibati initially broke out on Saturday, February 28, and has since escalated, reflecting the ongoing volatility in the region.

title: US Senate Urges DRC Forces to Halt Attacks, Return to Negotiating Table
excerpt: The United States Senate has called on the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) forces to cease attacks on AFC/M23 positions in North and South Kivu provinces, emphasizing the need for a return to peace negotiations. The statement was made on March 4, 2026, by Senator Jim Risch, Ch
title_en: US Senate Urges DRC Forces to Halt Attacks, Return to Negotiating Table
excerpt_en: The United States Senate has called on the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) forces to cease attacks on AFC/M23 positions in North and South Kivu provinces, emphasizing the need for a return to peace negotiations. The statement was made on March 4, 2026, by Senator Jim Risch, Ch
body_en:
The United States Senate has called on the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) forces to cease attacks on AFC/M23 positions in North and South Kivu provinces, emphasizing the need for a return to peace negotiations. The statement was made on March 4, 2026, by Senator Jim Risch, Chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.
Senator Risch highlighted that the Washington peace agreement signed between Rwanda and the DRC with US support offers a path to lasting peace and regional development if fully implemented.
“The DRC government and FARDC must stop pursuing a military solution in eastern DRC, respect the ceasefire, and work with partners, including the United States, to build a lasting solution to the security situation in the east of the country,” Risch said.
While AFC/M23 forces are expected to halt the expansion of their positions, the senator stressed that the FARDC and its allies, including Burundian troops, Wazalendo, mercenaries, and the FDLR, must also refrain from military actions and adhere to the ceasefire.
Despite a ceasefire agreement signed in Doha, Qatar, and the establishment of a monitoring mechanism, attacks by the DRC forces continue. AFC/M23 expressed regret that mediators remain silent while its fighters defend themselves and civilians in North and South Kivu, asserting that bias and misinformation persist in statements condemning the group.
On March 2, 2026, AFC/M23 announced it would continue defending its positions and protecting civilians while calling for renewed dialogue and compliance with the ceasefire.

title: IAEA Conducts Assessment to Support Rwanda’s Nuclear Power Ambitions
excerpt: Rwanda is undergoing an International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) assessment to evaluate its readiness to build a nuclear power plant, the agency announced on March 4, 2026. The inspection, conducted by IAEA experts, began on March 2 and will run until March 9, 2026. The assessme
title_en: IAEA Conducts Assessment to Support Rwanda’s Nuclear Power Ambitions
excerpt_en: Rwanda is undergoing an International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) assessment to evaluate its readiness to build a nuclear power plant, the agency announced on March 4, 2026. The inspection, conducted by IAEA experts, began on March 2 and will run until March 9, 2026. The assessme
body_en:
Rwanda is undergoing an International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) assessment to evaluate its readiness to build a nuclear power plant, the agency announced on March 4, 2026. The inspection, conducted by IAEA experts, began on March 2 and will run until March 9, 2026.
The assessment focuses on 19 key areas, including Rwanda’s nuclear energy policy, funding sources, safety measures, and technical capacity to manage potential risks associated with nuclear plants.
Dr. Fidele Ndahayo, Director General of the Rwanda Atomic Energy Agency (RAEB), said the evaluation will identify areas where Rwanda needs to strengthen efforts. “This assessment will help us gain confidence in the international community and attract support to build these plants,” he explained.
The head of the IAEA Expert Group, Aline des Cloizeaux, clarified that the mission is advisory, not a decision-making process. “We are here to provide guidance on what needs improvement so Rwanda can continue its nuclear development plans,” she said.
Rwanda aims to have a nuclear power plant operational by the 2030s and has already invested in training programs, medical nuclear applications, and collaborations with international partners. In 2023, Rwanda signed an agreement with Dual Fluid Energy Inc. (Germany and Canada) to test a nuclear reactor, followed by projects with partners in Russia and the United States focusing on Small Modular Reactors (SMRs).
SMRs are compact plants capable of generating 100 megawatts of electricity, occupying 15–50 hectares, employing up to 230 workers, and being relocatable to remote areas. They are considered environmentally friendly, reducing up to 29 tons of CO₂ per gigawatt-hour (GWh) according to the World Nuclear Association.
The IAEA assessment is a critical step for Rwanda to demonstrate its commitment to safe, sustainable, and internationally compliant nuclear energy development.

title: MONUSCO and ICGLR Assess Security Situation
excerpt: UVIRA, February 24, 2026 — A joint assessment mission by MONUSCO and the International Conference on the Great Lakes Region (ICGLR) has been deployed to Uvira, South Kivu, to evaluate the security situation and the feasibility of future peacekeeping operations. The five-day missi
title_en: MONUSCO and ICGLR Assess Security Situation
excerpt_en: UVIRA, February 24, 2026 — A joint assessment mission by MONUSCO and the International Conference on the Great Lakes Region (ICGLR) has been deployed to Uvira, South Kivu, to evaluate the security situation and the feasibility of future peacekeeping operations. The five-day missi
body_en:
UVIRA, February 24, 2026 — A joint assessment mission by MONUSCO and the International Conference on the Great Lakes Region (ICGLR) has been deployed to Uvira, South Kivu, to evaluate the security situation and the feasibility of future peacekeeping operations.
The five-day mission, running from February 23 to 27, 2026, follows consultations with President Félix Tshisekedi, who currently chairs the ICGLR. The joint team is tasked with assessing the credibility, security conditions, and operational feasibility of potential peacekeeping deployments in the area.
Focus on Ceasefire Monitoring
Officials say the assessment will help determine how ceasefire monitoring mechanisms could contribute to reducing violence and creating conditions for a sustainable political solution in South Kivu.
The acting head of MONUSCO, Vivian van de Perre, emphasized that effective monitoring of the ceasefire could help stabilize the region and support long-term peace efforts.
Limited Mandate in South Kivu
Unlike in North Kivu and Ituri, the MONUSCO mandate in South Kivu does not include civilian protection, according to mission officials. The assessment aims to clarify what role peacekeeping forces could realistically play under the current mandate.
Phased Deployment Planned
Senior United Nations peacekeeping officials have indicated that any future MONUSCO deployment in South Kivu will be carried out in phases.
Before deploying troops, authorities intend to verify the reliability of security arrangements for peacekeepers operating in the region. The plan also includes the use of surveillance drones to gather security intelligence and support operational planning.
The joint mission is expected to provide key recommendations on the future role of MONUSCO and the ICGLR in supporting stability efforts in Uvira and surrounding areas.

excerpt_en: Lt. Col. Willy Ngoma, widely remembered as the founder of “Les Lions de Sarambwe”, led the M23 armed group in defending Congolese Tutsis who faced killings, expulsions, and forced displacement to Rwanda and neighboring countries. Ngoma earned the nickname “Quickly Quickly!”, a ph
body_en:
Lt. Col. Willy Ngoma, widely remembered as the founder of “Les Lions de Sarambwe”, led the M23 armed group in defending Congolese Tutsis who faced killings, expulsions, and forced displacement to Rwanda and neighboring countries.
Ngoma earned the nickname “Quickly Quickly!”, a phrase he famously shouted at mercenaries from Romania in early 2025, during operations that expelled them from DRC territory. His decisive leadership forced these mercenaries to return to Europe, showcasing his courage and tactical skill.
Those familiar with the M23 of 2012–2013 recognized Ngoma as a loyal and capable leader, seen as a worthy successor to Col. Kazarama Vianney. He was respected across all ranks, from junior fighters to senior commanders, for his dedication and commitment to the cause.
Ngoma’s legacy is remembered for his courage, leadership, and sacrifice in the defense of vulnerable communities in eastern Congo, cementing his place as a symbol of resilience and loyalty within the M23 movement.

title: Paul Kagame Denounces Selective Pressure, Calls for Equal Accountability of All Parties
excerpt: KIGALI, Rwanda March 6, 2026 — Rwandan President Paul Kagame has rejected what he describes as selective international pressure on Rwanda over its alleged support for the AFC/M23 rebellion in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), calling instead for equal scrutiny of all pa
title_en: Paul Kagame Denounces Selective Pressure, Calls for Equal Accountability of All Parties
excerpt_en: KIGALI, Rwanda March 6, 2026 — Rwandan President Paul Kagame has rejected what he describes as selective international pressure on Rwanda over its alleged support for the AFC/M23 rebellion in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), calling instead for equal scrutiny of all pa
body_en:
KIGALI, Rwanda March 6, 2026 — Rwandan President Paul Kagame has rejected what he describes as selective international pressure on Rwanda over its alleged support for the AFC/M23 rebellion in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), calling instead for equal scrutiny of all parties to the conflict.
Speaking at a dinner with ambassadors, diplomats, and representatives of international organizations accredited to Kigali, Kagame emphasized that the crisis in eastern DRC is long-standing and rooted in structural issues, including the persistent threat posed by the Forces Démocratiques de Libération du Rwanda (FDLR). He criticized Kinshasa’s view that the FDLR is a residual force, arguing the group continues to pose a significant threat to Rwanda and spreads its ideology to other armed factions in the region.
Kagame highlighted what he sees as a double standard in international expectations: while the Washington Agreements call for a ceasefire and security measures by all parties, he asserts that only Rwanda faces punitive measures and sanctions. He cited military operations and troop buildups by DRC and allied forces in eastern and western DRC, arguing that these actions undermine the ceasefire and shift the burden unfairly onto Rwanda.
“As expected, responsibility has been placed exclusively on Rwanda. This selective pressure has only encouraged the Congolese government and affiliated elements to resume military operations. We are asking for the same rigor to be demanded from all parties,” Kagame said.
The Rwandan President’s remarks come amid U.S. sanctions and visa restrictions targeting Rwandan officials accused of supporting the M23 rebellion. The U.S. State Department insists that all parties, including the DRC, must honor the Washington Agreements, including the neutralization of the FDLR and withdrawal of Rwandan forces from Congolese territory.
Kagame stressed that Rwanda’s actions are driven by legitimate security concerns, defending the country’s right to protect its borders from the continued presence of armed groups and their genocidal ideology. “The choice is clear: tolerate the FDLR and its growing network of militias advancing toward our border, or defend ourselves and bear the consequences. Any other country in our position would do the same,” he concluded.
This statement underscores ongoing tensions between Kinshasa and Kigali, as diplomatic pressure intensifies amid continued clashes in North Kivu and South Kivu provinces, prolonging instability in the Great Lakes region.

title: DRC Signs Memorandum to Institutionalize Gender Equality
excerpt: Kinshasa, March 8, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo has taken a major step toward gender equality with the signing of a memorandum of understanding aimed at structuring and institutionalizing parity. The ceremony followed a workshop organized on March 6 by the Ministry of
title_en: DRC Signs Memorandum to Institutionalize Gender Equality
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, March 8, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo has taken a major step toward gender equality with the signing of a memorandum of understanding aimed at structuring and institutionalizing parity. The ceremony followed a workshop organized on March 6 by the Ministry of
body_en:
Kinshasa, March 8, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo has taken a major step toward gender equality with the signing of a memorandum of understanding aimed at structuring and institutionalizing parity. The ceremony followed a workshop organized on March 6 by the Ministry of Gender, in collaboration with the Friedrich Ebert Foundation (FES), to validate the implementing decree of Law No. 15/013 of 2015 on women's rights and gender parity.
The initiative seeks to strengthen inclusive governance, promote networking among women, and enhance female leadership. The signing was attended by the Ambassador of Germany to the DRC, Ingo Herbert, and representatives of Congolese women’s associations.
Minister of Gender, Chantal Ombae, highlighted the significance of the agreement: “This paradigm shift means moving from symbolic representation to women’s decision-making participation; from political discourse to the structural implementation of parity. Together with civil society, we are building concrete mechanisms to strengthen governance and accelerate the achievement of SDG 5.”
She added that the partnership complements government efforts to build a more just and egalitarian society, amplifying the voices of women and children, “not as an option, but as a necessity for progress.”
During the ceremony, Minister Ombae also inaugurated the headquarters of the Friedrich Ebert Foundation, emphasizing its role as a space for dialogue, cooperation, and empowerment.
The Foundation’s representative, Constantin Grund, said: “By inaugurating this building on the eve of International Women's Day, we are sending a symbolic message: spaces for dialogue must be open to everyone, particularly women. We hope this will be a place for debates, inspiration, and partnerships that promote justice, equality, and democracy.”

title: Catholic Church Says It Was First to Denounce Rwanda’s Support for AFC/M23
excerpt: KINSHASA February 24, 2026 — The Catholic Church in the Democratic Republic of Congo has reiterated that it was among the first institutions to denounce Rwanda’s alleged support for the AFC/M23 rebellion operating in eastern DRC, while also announcing a shift in its pastoral appr
title_en: Catholic Church Says It Was First to Denounce Rwanda’s Support for AFC/M23
excerpt_en: KINSHASA February 24, 2026 — The Catholic Church in the Democratic Republic of Congo has reiterated that it was among the first institutions to denounce Rwanda’s alleged support for the AFC/M23 rebellion operating in eastern DRC, while also announcing a shift in its pastoral appr
body_en:
KINSHASA February 24, 2026 — The Catholic Church in the Democratic Republic of Congo has reiterated that it was among the first institutions to denounce Rwanda’s alleged support for the AFC/M23 rebellion operating in eastern DRC, while also announcing a shift in its pastoral approach to address the ongoing crisis in the Great Lakes region.
In a statement issued Monday, Bishop Donatien Nshole, Secretary General of the Congolese National Episcopal Conference (CENCO), said the Church had already raised concerns about Rwanda’s backing of AFC/M23 rebels in previous official declarations.
Nshole stressed that statements made in the past by Archbishop Fulgence Muteba of Lubumbashi and other members of CENCO had clearly referenced Rwanda’s involvement, rejecting claims that the Church had only recently taken such a position.
“The Catholic Church is not new to this position. If you review CENCO’s documents, you will see that the bishops, including Archbishop Fulgence Muteba, have mentioned Rwanda several times,” Nshole said, emphasizing that the Church had also conducted international advocacy on the issue.

body_en:
MASISI, North Kivu February 26, 2026 — Fighting continued for a second consecutive day on Thursday, February 26, in the village of Kibanda, near Kasopo in the Osso Banyungu sector of Masisi territory. The Wazalendo militia launched an offensive on Wednesday against AFC/M23 positions, aiming to regain control of this strategic town, which has been under rebel occupation for several months.
Since Thursday morning, the sounds of heavy and light weapons fire have reverberated throughout Kibanda and surrounding villages, creating widespread fear among civilians. Residents, already suffering from persistent insecurity in Masisi territory, are attempting to flee to safer areas, while panic spreads to neighboring towns, halting socio-economic activities.
At this stage, no official casualty figures have been released. Sources report an extremely volatile situation, with ongoing fighting and reinforcements reported on both sides.
Masisi territory continues to be one of the epicenters of armed violence in North Kivu, where recurring clashes between local armed groups and AFC/M23 rebels are worsening the already critical humanitarian situation in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.

SHABUNDA March 1, 2026 — Violent clashes erupted in the village of Byangama, Bamukuba Sud area, between two factions of the Wazalendo militia, resulting in the deaths of Ufamando, a local Wazalendo leader, and his brother, Constantin.
Local sources report that the fighting involved Ufamando’s men attacking the forces led by the self-proclaimed General Muswahili. Their bodies were found in the forest the following day.
Several others were injured and evacuated to Shabunda Centre for medical treatment. The clashes sparked panic among residents, highlighting ongoing tensions over control of the region.

excerpt: MASISI, North Kivu March 3, 2026 — The village of Kazinga, in the Nyamaboko 1st group of Masisi territory, fell back under the control of AFC/M23 rebels on Tuesday afternoon following fierce clashes with the FARDC and the Wazalendo local militia. This recapture comes roughly two
title_en: AFC/M23 Rebels Retake Kazinga
excerpt_en: MASISI, North Kivu March 3, 2026 — The village of Kazinga, in the Nyamaboko 1st group of Masisi territory, fell back under the control of AFC/M23 rebels on Tuesday afternoon following fierce clashes with the FARDC and the Wazalendo local militia. This recapture comes roughly two
body_en:
MASISI, North Kivu March 3, 2026 — The village of Kazinga, in the Nyamaboko 1st group of Masisi territory, fell back under the control of AFC/M23 rebels on Tuesday afternoon following fierce clashes with the FARDC and the Wazalendo local militia.
This recapture comes roughly two weeks after government forces had taken the village. Local sources report that AFC/M23 fighters, mainly from the Ndete and Kasopo axes, launched an offensive early Tuesday morning. Exchanges of fire, including heavy weapons, continued throughout the morning.
Kazinga occupies a strategic location in the Osso Banyungu sector, serving as a corridor to Buhimba (Waloa Yungu group, Walikale territory) and the Katoy sector in southern Masisi. With this advance, the rebels are consolidating control over a triangle linking Buhimba, Katoy, and Kazinga, strengthening their capacity to project force into surrounding groups, including Waloa Yungu, Waloa Uroba, and Waloa Loanda in Walikale territory.
The recapture highlights the persistent fragility of security in this part of North Kivu, which has seen a succession of attacks, counter-offensives, and population displacements in recent weeks. Humanitarian concerns continue to mount as civilians face ongoing insecurity amid this renewed escalation of fighting.

body_en:
Ambassador Santa Laker Kinyera, Uganda’s Deputy Ambassador to Rwanda, has died at Mulago Hospital in Kampala on the morning of March 3, 2026, the Ugandan Ministry of Foreign Affairs announced. The cause of death has not been disclosed.
Ambassador Kinyera had a diplomatic career spanning over 30 years, beginning in 1994, serving in various capacities including Minister of Foreign Affairs and representing Uganda in multiple international postings.
He played a key role in restoring and strengthening bilateral relations between Uganda and Rwanda, particularly in areas of trade, security, and cross-border cooperation, including efforts to reopen the border during periods of tension.
In Uganda, Kinyera is remembered as a dedicated diplomat whose work contributed significantly to peaceful and productive relations between the two neighboring countries.

title: Chamber of Deputies Urges MINAGRI to Reduce Agricultural Spoilage
excerpt: The Chamber of Deputies has requested the Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock (MINAGRI) to develop strategies to monitor and reduce post-harvest spoilage, particularly for rice and maize, by March 3, 2026. The decision was taken during the Plenary Session of March 3, 2026, foll
title_en: Chamber of Deputies Urges MINAGRI to Reduce Agricultural Spoilage
excerpt_en: The Chamber of Deputies has requested the Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock (MINAGRI) to develop strategies to monitor and reduce post-harvest spoilage, particularly for rice and maize, by March 3, 2026. The decision was taken during the Plenary Session of March 3, 2026, foll
body_en:
The Chamber of Deputies has requested the Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock (MINAGRI) to develop strategies to monitor and reduce post-harvest spoilage, particularly for rice and maize, by March 3, 2026.
The decision was taken during the Plenary Session of March 3, 2026, following a study to be conducted by the National Institute of Statistics of Rwanda (NISR). MINAGRI has been given three months to implement the measures.
The move comes after an audit by the Auditor General of Government Finance revealed post-harvest losses of 12.4% for rice and 13.8% for maize, exceeding the national target of reducing crop losses to 5% by 2029.
The audit highlighted insufficient and damaged infrastructure, with rice and maize drying facilities operating at 9% and 18% capacity, and storage facilities accommodating only 33% of production, of which 33% were damaged. In some districts, storage facilities were being misused; for example, Nyagatare’s Rwangingo rice cooperative stored hay instead of rice, while in Rusizi, some storage sheds remained unused.
Muzana Alice, Chairperson of the Commission on Land, Agriculture, Livestock and Environment, emphasized challenges such as limited market access, seasonal variations in production, and highly perishable crops, which affect both farmers and consumers. The audit found that of 14 maize cooperatives visited across Nyagatare, Gatsibo, Gisagara, and Rusizi, 12 lacked active markets for stored produce.
The Chamber urged MINAGRI to:
Establish quarterly and annual monitoring mechanisms for perishable crops, supported by NISR research every three years.
Accelerate the implementation of AMIS technology, which will improve the management of agricultural produce and connect farmers to markets.
Develop methods to better link rice and maize production with markets, ensuring farmers can cultivate with confidence even before AMIS technology is fully operational.
AMIS is a forthcoming agricultural information system designed to provide timely and comprehensive data to support farming decisions and market access across Rwanda.

title: Two Ugandan Generals Removed Over Citizenship Document Dispute
excerpt: On 23 February 2026, the Ugandan Army reassigned two senior officers from the Immigration Service following allegations that Rwandan-origin Ugandans were being denied access to citizenship documents and passports. The officers affected are Maj Gen Apollo Kasiita-Gowa, former head
title_en: Two Ugandan Generals Removed Over Citizenship Document Dispute
excerpt_en: On 23 February 2026, the Ugandan Army reassigned two senior officers from the Immigration Service following allegations that Rwandan-origin Ugandans were being denied access to citizenship documents and passports. The officers affected are Maj Gen Apollo Kasiita-Gowa, former head
body_en:
On 23 February 2026, the Ugandan Army reassigned two senior officers from the Immigration Service following allegations that Rwandan-origin Ugandans were being denied access to citizenship documents and passports.
The officers affected are Maj Gen Apollo Kasiita-Gowa, former head of the Citizenship Inspection Service, and Brig Gen Johnson Abaho Namanya, former Commissioner for Passports. Both have been returned to Army Headquarters for reassignment to other military duties.
The decision follows earlier orders by Chief of Defence Forces Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who announced the dismissal of officials accused of obstructing Rwandans living in Uganda from obtaining official documents.
The issue concerns the legal status of Rwandan-origin communities, recognized as a constitutionally protected ethnic group whose presence predates 1926. Many members of the community have long complained about delays and refusals in obtaining national identification and travel documents, despite being born and raised in Uganda.
Authorities have reiterated that the 1995 Constitution guarantees citizenship rights to eligible residents, and efforts are ongoing to review pending cases and facilitate access to official documentation.

body_en:
Rwandan peacekeepers (Rwanbatt-1) serving with the United Nations Mission in South Sudan (UNMISS) were awarded UN medals on March 3, 2026, in recognition of their contribution to peacekeeping operations.
The ceremony took place at UNMISS Tomping headquarters in Juba, the capital of South Sudan, and was led by Major General Robert Yaw Affram, Deputy Force Commander of UNMISS, who described the medals as a symbol of professionalism, dedication, and commitment to duty.
“The UN Medal you received today reflects professionalism, good conduct, dedication, and courage in challenging conditions. It is earned through days of hard work, nights on guard duty, and steadfast commitment to peacekeeping,” Maj Gen Affram said.
He also commended the Government of Rwanda and the Rwanda Defence Forces (RDF) for continuously deploying soldiers of competence and professionalism to the UNMISS mission.
Lt Col Paul Ndushabandi, Commander of Rwanbatt-1, praised his unit for their dedication, perseverance, and courage over ten months of service, encouraging them to maintain this commitment for the remainder of the mission.
The ceremony featured military parades and cultural performances, including traditional Rwandan dances, celebrating the peacekeepers’ achievements and their role in protecting humanity.

title: Félix Tshisekedi Attends Funeral of Civil Rights Leader Reverend Jesse Jackson in Chicago
excerpt: CHICAGO, USA March 6, 2026 — Congolese President Félix Tshisekedi attended the funeral of civil rights icon Reverend Jesse Jackson in Chicago on Friday, paying tribute to the late activist whose lifelong commitment to racial equality and social justice left a profound mark global
title_en: Félix Tshisekedi Attends Funeral of Civil Rights Leader Reverend Jesse Jackson in Chicago
excerpt_en: CHICAGO, USA March 6, 2026 — Congolese President Félix Tshisekedi attended the funeral of civil rights icon Reverend Jesse Jackson in Chicago on Friday, paying tribute to the late activist whose lifelong commitment to racial equality and social justice left a profound mark global
body_en:
CHICAGO, USA March 6, 2026 — Congolese President Félix Tshisekedi attended the funeral of civil rights icon Reverend Jesse Jackson in Chicago on Friday, paying tribute to the late activist whose lifelong commitment to racial equality and social justice left a profound mark globally.
The DRC Presidency noted that Tshisekedi’s presence also honored Jackson’s historic ties to the Democratic Republic of Congo, particularly during its most challenging democratic transitions. Jackson’s work as US Special Envoy for Africa, including meetings with Étienne Tshisekedi, was highlighted as a pivotal moment in DRC-U.S. relations.
Jackson, who passed away on February 17, 2026, at age 84, was a central figure in the American Civil Rights Movement and collaborated closely with Reverend Martin Luther King Jr. His activism and global influence continue to resonate in Africa and beyond.
President Tshisekedi’s attendance at the ceremony underscores both personal respect and the DRC’s recognition of Jackson’s enduring legacy in supporting democratic values and human rights on the African continent.

title_en: Journalist Serge Sindani Detained in Kisangani, Press Freedom Concerns Raised
excerpt_en: Kisangani, March 6, 2026 – Journalist Serge Sindani, director general of the online news outlet KIS24.INFO, has been detained for three days at the National Intelligence Agency (ANR) in Kisangani, Tshopo province, without contact with his family, colleagues, or lawyers. The edito
body_en:
Kisangani, March 6, 2026 – Journalist Serge Sindani, director general of the online news outlet KIS24.INFO, has been detained for three days at the National Intelligence Agency (ANR) in Kisangani, Tshopo province, without contact with his family, colleagues, or lawyers.
The editorial team of KIS24.INFO reports that Sindani has spent his third night in detention without official information regarding the reasons for his arrest or his state of health. The media outlet described the situation as a serious attack on press freedom and the fundamental right to inform, guaranteed by the Constitution of the DRC, calling on journalists, media organizations, and civil society to mobilize.
The Tshopo branch of the National Union of Congolese Press (UNPC) denounced the journalist’s “abduction” in a press release. According to the UNPC, Sindani was arrested on Tuesday, March 3, 2026, around noon at the FIRVAO headquarters by agents claiming to be from the ANR. He was taken away in a vehicle without any official explanation and has not been informed of any charges or questioned formally.
The UNPC considers the detention a flagrant violation of fundamental rights, including the right to defense and due process. The organization demands immediate notification of allegations, access to legal counsel, respect for his legal rights, and calls for his immediate release if no legally substantiated charges are presented.
The UNPC further urges authorities to guarantee the safety and freedom of journalists working in Kisangani and across Tshopo province, emphasizing the importance of protecting press freedom in the region.

title: AFC/M23 Reinforces Positions in Mpety and Mindjendje, Tensions Rise Around Pinga
excerpt: WALIKALE, North Kivu February 23, 2026 — The security situation remains tense in Walikale territory as AFC/M23 rebels reinforced their positions on Sunday, February 22, in the villages of Mpety and Mindjendje, located in the Banakindi area of the Kisimba group. Reports indicate t
title_en: AFC/M23 Reinforces Positions in Mpety and Mindjendje, Tensions Rise Around Pinga
excerpt_en: WALIKALE, North Kivu February 23, 2026 — The security situation remains tense in Walikale territory as AFC/M23 rebels reinforced their positions on Sunday, February 22, in the villages of Mpety and Mindjendje, located in the Banakindi area of the Kisimba group. Reports indicate t
body_en:
WALIKALE, North Kivu February 23, 2026 — The security situation remains tense in Walikale territory as AFC/M23 rebels reinforced their positions on Sunday, February 22, in the villages of Mpety and Mindjendje, located in the Banakindi area of the Kisimba group.
Reports indicate that the reinforcements arrived from the Kitshanga–Kalembe axis, with several witnesses observing columns of heavily armed fighters moving through Kalembe before heading toward Mpety. The movements were also confirmed by security sources in Walikale, raising concerns about a possible military buildup in the area.
Although the exact objective of the deployment remains unclear, local observers believe the repositioning could signal preparations for new offensives against the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) and Wazalendo fighters, particularly around the strategic town of Pinga.
The developments have heightened anxiety among local communities, which are already under pressure following recent clashes reported in several parts of Walikale territory.
Local traditional authorities in the Kisimba group have denounced what they describe as a violation of the current ceasefire, calling on FARDC forces and Wazalendo fighters to remain highly vigilant in the face of the evolving security situation.
Amid a regional context marked by persistent instability, civilians fear that the reinforcement of rebel positions could lead to a renewed escalation of violence, potentially triggering fresh waves of displacement and further worsening the humanitarian situation in this already fragile area of North Kivu.

excerpt: MASISI, North Kivu February 26, 2026 — The villages of Kasenyi and Luke in Masisi territory fell back under AFC/M23 rebel control on Thursday, February 26, following intense fighting with the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) and Wazalendo militias. The cou
title_en: AFC/M23 Retakes Kasenyi and Luke After Fierce Clashes
excerpt_en: MASISI, North Kivu February 26, 2026 — The villages of Kasenyi and Luke in Masisi territory fell back under AFC/M23 rebel control on Thursday, February 26, following intense fighting with the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) and Wazalendo militias. The cou
body_en:
MASISI, North Kivu February 26, 2026 — The villages of Kasenyi and Luke in Masisi territory fell back under AFC/M23 rebel control on Thursday, February 26, following intense fighting with the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) and Wazalendo militias.
The counter-offensive, launched on Wednesday, February 25, came just one day after the rebels had lost both villages. Fighting was concentrated around strategic positions in Kasenyi and Luke, causing panic among local residents.
Reinforcements from Rutshuru territory reportedly bolstered the rebels’ capabilities, facilitating the recapture of the two villages and altering the balance of power on the ground.
The security situation remains volatile, with front lines shifting unpredictably. Local authorities, civil society actors, and community leaders have expressed concerns over a potential escalation of violence in an area already weakened by months of persistent insecurity.
The civilian population, caught between the warring parties, continues to bear the brunt of the clashes. Displacement has been reported, with residents seeking safer areas, though official casualty figures are not yet available.
In a region marked by chronic instability, the recapture of Kasenyi and Luke by AFC/M23 threatens to further complicate stabilization efforts, exacerbating the security and humanitarian crisis in Masisi and greater North Kivu.

body_en:
WALIKALE March 1, 2026 — Fighting resumed on Sunday, March 1, between AFC/M23 rebels and the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC), supported by the Wazalendo militia, in Kibati, Luberike area of Walikale territory, North Kivu.
Local sources reported that heavy and light weapons fire has been heard since 10:00 a.m., with the combat zone remaining highly tense.
As a result, traffic on the Mungazi-Kibati-Kashebere road remains suspended, leaving travelers stranded.
These clashes follow a government offensive launched on Saturday, February 29, targeting rebel positions in the strategic town. Authorities have not yet released a casualty report, and the situation on the ground remains fluid.

body_en:
UPPEMBA NATIONAL PARK March 3, 2026 — An armed group attacked Upemba National Park in Haut-Katanga province on the night of Monday, March 2, to Tuesday, March 3, 2026. The assailants targeted Lusinga, the park headquarters, where several rangers and expatriates were staying, according to local sources.
The attack has been attributed to an unidentified Mai-Mai armed group. No casualties have been reported so far, and authorities are investigating the incident.
Established in 1939 during the colonial era, Upemba National Park spans approximately 1,773,000 hectares and is home to a rich diversity of wildlife, including zebras, roan antelopes, Cape elands, hartebeests, greater kudus, elephants, and buffalo.
Park officials and security forces are reportedly on high alert to prevent further incursions and ensure the safety of staff and visitors.

title: Rwanda and India Sign Cultural Exchange Agreement

title_en: Rwanda and India Sign Cultural Exchange Agreement
excerpt_en: Rwanda and India have signed an agreement on cultural exchange aimed at strengthening bilateral cooperation and deepening people-to-people ties between the two countries. The agreement was signed on March 3, 2026, during the second meeting of the bilateral commission monitoring c
body_en:
Rwanda and India have signed an agreement on cultural exchange aimed at strengthening bilateral cooperation and deepening people-to-people ties between the two countries. The agreement was signed on March 3, 2026, during the second meeting of the bilateral commission monitoring cooperation.
The meeting took place in New Delhi, India, with the Rwandan delegation led by Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation Nduhungirehe Olivier, and the Indian delegation led by Secretary of State for External Affairs Kirti Vardhan Singh.
Officials reviewed the status of cooperation in key sectors, including military, agriculture, trade and investment, education, science and technology, as well as culture and people-to-people exchanges. The cultural exchange agreement will guide initiatives between the two nations until 2030.
Minister Kirti highlighted that the discussions also included global and regional developments that could affect the interests of both countries.
Rwanda-India relations have grown steadily over the years. Rwanda was among the first African countries to open an Indian representative office, part of a plan to open 18 new offices across Africa to boost engagement.
Indian investment in Rwanda has also expanded, making India the second-largest investor in the country in 2024, after China. In that year, China invested $460 million (14.1% of total investment), while India invested $445.1 million (13.6%), reflecting its growing economic partnership with Rwanda.

Rwanda and India have signed an agreement on cultural exchange aimed at strengthening bilateral cooperation and deepening people-to-people ties between the two countries. The agreement was signed on March 3, 2026, during the second meeting of the bilateral commission monitoring cooperation.
The meeting took place in New Delhi, India, with the Rwandan delegation led by Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation Nduhungirehe Olivier, and the Indian delegation led by Secretary of State for External Affairs Kirti Vardhan Singh.
Officials reviewed the status of cooperation in key sectors, including military, agriculture, trade and investment, education, science and technology, as well as culture and people-to-people exchanges. The cultural exchange agreement will guide initiatives between the two nations until 2030.
Minister Kirti highlighted that the discussions also included global and regional developments that could affect the interests of both countries.
Rwanda-India relations have grown steadily over the years. Rwanda was among the first African countries to open an Indian representative office, part of a plan to open 18 new offices across Africa to boost engagement.
Indian investment in Rwanda has also expanded, making India the second-largest investor in the country in 2024, after China. In that year, China invested $460 million (14.1% of total investment), while India invested $445.1 million (13.6%), reflecting its growing economic partnership with Rwanda.

title: 32 Rwandan Industries to Receive Licenses for Pan-African Trade
excerpt: For the first time, 32 Rwandan industries that have met common African standards will be granted trade licenses allowing them to export 72 product types to other African countries without additional requirements or obstacles. The licenses are scheduled to be issued on March 6, 20
title_en: 32 Rwandan Industries to Receive Licenses for Pan-African Trade
excerpt_en: For the first time, 32 Rwandan industries that have met common African standards will be granted trade licenses allowing them to export 72 product types to other African countries without additional requirements or obstacles. The licenses are scheduled to be issued on March 6, 20
body_en:
For the first time, 32 Rwandan industries that have met common African standards will be granted trade licenses allowing them to export 72 product types to other African countries without additional requirements or obstacles. The licenses are scheduled to be issued on March 6, 2026.
The announcement was made on March 3, 2026, during the three-day African Standards Organization (ARSO) meeting held in Kigali. The meeting, attended by 16 countries, focused on establishing 25 continental standards covering textiles, textile materials, and related products.
The licenses will initially cover products in agriculture and value addition, with plans to extend certification to other sectors, including garments and footwear.
Gatera Emmanuel, Director of Regulatory Affairs at the Rwanda Standards Board (RSB), said the certifications will expand markets, accelerate collaboration with exporting countries, and promote the ‘Made in Rwanda’ brand. He added, “If a garment is sewn and tested in Rwanda, it will pass quality checks in the destination country without delays, speeding up shipments.”
Gatera also highlighted the potential to boost intra-African trade, noting that current trade among African countries is only 15–18%, compared with over 60% on continents such as Asia and Europe.
Milagrosa Ntombikasiye, representing the National Standards Institute of Eswatini, said that most of Eswatini’s exports currently go to the European Union due to trade challenges within Africa. She welcomed the new regulations, stating they will facilitate continental trade and economic growth.
Dr. Hermogene Nsengimana, Secretary General of ARSO, explained that the initiative aims to harmonize regulations across Africa, reducing costs for inspections and compliance in different countries.
At the conclusion of the meeting, Rwanda will sign cooperation agreements with Zimbabwe and Congo-Brazzaville to further promote trade and streamline export processes with these countries.
