title: Rwanda to Launch Two New Mediation Centers to Resolve Disputes Outside Courts
excerpt: On March 4, 2026, the Ministry of Justice (MINIJUST) announced the establishment of two new mediation centers in the provinces to complement the existing center in Kigali City. These centers aim to provide out-of-court dispute resolution services and are part of Rwanda’s ongoing
title_en: Rwanda to Launch Two New Mediation Centers to Resolve Disputes Outside Courts
excerpt_en: On March 4, 2026, the Ministry of Justice (MINIJUST) announced the establishment of two new mediation centers in the provinces to complement the existing center in Kigali City. These centers aim to provide out-of-court dispute resolution services and are part of Rwanda’s ongoing
body_en:
On March 4, 2026, the Ministry of Justice (MINIJUST) announced the establishment of two new mediation centers in the provinces to complement the existing center in Kigali City. These centers aim to provide out-of-court dispute resolution services and are part of Rwanda’s ongoing effort to strengthen access to justice.
South Province: Center in Nyanza, opening in May 2026
Eastern Province: Construction expected to be completed by late 2026 or early 2027
The initiative was presented by Permanent Secretary Mbonera Théophile during the annual dialogue on access to justice organized by the Legal Aid Federation (LAF).
The centers will:
Receive clients seeking mediation instead of going directly to court
Provide advice and connect them with trained mediators
Serve as a line of first contact for disputes suitable for mediation
A judicial mechanism now allows judges to recommend mediation before cases enter the court system. According to the Judiciary report for 2024/2025:
Cases resolved through mediation increased by 32%, from 2,395 to 3,166
Cases settled via plea bargains rose by 20%, from 9,851 to 11,846
The non-judicial dispute resolution policy, launched in 2022, aims to reduce court backlogs from 62% at the policy’s start to 25% within five years.
These centers are part of Rwanda’s long-term plan for each province to eventually have at least one mediation facility, promoting faster, fairer, and more accessible justice for all citizens.

title: AFC/M23 Says It Is Not Bound by Washington Peace Accords
excerpt: The AFC/M23 alliance has asserted that it is not bound by the Washington peace agreement signed between Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) in Washington, D.C., on March 3, 2026. The statement was delivered by Bertrand Bisimwa, Deputy Director for Politics, Diplomac
title_en: AFC/M23 Says It Is Not Bound by Washington Peace Accords
excerpt_en: The AFC/M23 alliance has asserted that it is not bound by the Washington peace agreement signed between Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) in Washington, D.C., on March 3, 2026. The statement was delivered by Bertrand Bisimwa, Deputy Director for Politics, Diplomac
body_en:
The AFC/M23 alliance has asserted that it is not bound by the Washington peace agreement signed between Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) in Washington, D.C., on March 3, 2026.
The statement was delivered by Bertrand Bisimwa, Deputy Director for Politics, Diplomacy and Governance of AFC/M23, in response to claims by US Senator Jeanne Shaheen that the group was violating the accords.
Senator Shaheen, a member of the US Senate Foreign Relations Committee, had stated: “After three months of Rwanda-backed M23 violating the Washington Peace Accords, the US has finally imposed sanctions on the RDF and four leaders.”
Bisimwa countered, saying the alliance cannot breach an agreement it did not sign or observe, and urged the senator to familiarize herself with the realities of the conflict in eastern DRC.
“How could M23 violate an agreement it did not sign and does not observe? The real problem lies in the way Washington understands this war,” Bisimwa said, emphasizing that the Washington agreement concerns the DRC and Rwanda, with the DRC tasked to dismantle the FDLR terrorist group and Rwanda required to adjust border security measures.
He added that ongoing talks in Doha, Qatar, are aimed at resolving the conflict permanently, but claimed that the DRC government under President Félix Tshisekedi has sought to shift discussions to Washington, which he suggested misrepresents the nature of the conflict.

title: 25th Summit Opens in Arusha Without DRC’s Tshisekedi or Rwanda’s Kagame
excerpt: ARUSHA, Tanzania March 7, 2026 — The 25th Ordinary Summit of the East African Community (EAC) opened today in Arusha under the theme, “Deepening Integration to Improve the Living Conditions of EAC Citizens,” despite notable absences, including DRC President Félix Tshisekedi and R
title_en: 25th Summit Opens in Arusha Without DRC’s Tshisekedi or Rwanda’s Kagame
excerpt_en: ARUSHA, Tanzania March 7, 2026 — The 25th Ordinary Summit of the East African Community (EAC) opened today in Arusha under the theme, “Deepening Integration to Improve the Living Conditions of EAC Citizens,” despite notable absences, including DRC President Félix Tshisekedi and R
body_en:
ARUSHA, Tanzania March 7, 2026 — The 25th Ordinary Summit of the East African Community (EAC) opened today in Arusha under the theme, “Deepening Integration to Improve the Living Conditions of EAC Citizens,” despite notable absences, including DRC President Félix Tshisekedi and Rwandan President Paul Kagame.
Ahead of the summit, the EAC Council of Ministers met from March 2 to 5 to review progress on previous decisions, prepare key agenda items, and formulate recommendations for the heads of state. The summit agenda includes reviewing the Council’s report covering November 30, 2024, to December 31, 2025, implementing the 24th Summit directive on sustainable financing of the EAC budget, assessing the integration status of partner states admitted between 2016 and 2024, appointing a new Secretary-General, judges to the East African Court of Justice, renewing Deputy Secretaries-General mandates, appointing commissioners to the EAC Competition Authority, and approving draft laws from the East African Legislative Assembly.
Several heads of state were present, including Yoweri Museveni (Uganda), Évariste Ndayishimiye (Burundi and current African Union Chairperson), and William Ruto (Kenya and current EAC Chairperson). South Sudan’s President Salva Kiir was represented by his foreign minister, Semaya Kumba, while Somalia’s Hassan Sheikh Mohamud was expected to arrive later.
Both Tshisekedi and Kagame delegated representatives—DRC’s Minister of Regional Integration Floribert Anzuluni Isiloketshi and Rwanda’s Prime Minister Justin Nsengiyumva, respectively. Tshisekedi’s absence was due to attending the funeral of Reverend Jesse Jackson in the United States. The absence of the two leaders highlights ongoing tensions between Kinshasa and Kigali over accusations of support for armed groups, including Rwanda’s alleged backing of the AFC/M23 rebellion and the DRC’s criticism of Kigali for supporting these rebels.
The summit coincides with escalating security challenges in eastern DRC, where government forces continue to confront the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23. Diplomatic friction between the DRC and Rwanda persists despite efforts under the Washington and Doha frameworks. Observers note a broader sense of unease between Kinshasa and the EAC, fueled by perceptions that the DRC is distanced from regional decision-making and that the bloc is not fully engaged in resolving the eastern DRC security crisis.
The 25th Summit thus opens in a complex regional context, with integration, security, and diplomatic reconciliation as key tests for the EAC and its member states.

title: Families in Uncertainty After Deadly Landslide as Rebels Block Access
excerpt: Rubaya, March 5, 2026 – Two days after a deadly landslide struck the Kasasa coltan mining site in the Rubaya mining area of Masisi territory, North Kivu, the exact death toll remains unclear as search operations continue under challenging conditions. Local sources report that acc
title_en: Families in Uncertainty After Deadly Landslide as Rebels Block Access
excerpt_en: Rubaya, March 5, 2026 – Two days after a deadly landslide struck the Kasasa coltan mining site in the Rubaya mining area of Masisi territory, North Kivu, the exact death toll remains unclear as search operations continue under challenging conditions. Local sources report that acc
body_en:
Rubaya, March 5, 2026 – Two days after a deadly landslide struck the Kasasa coltan mining site in the Rubaya mining area of Masisi territory, North Kivu, the exact death toll remains unclear as search operations continue under challenging conditions.
Local sources report that access to the site has been blocked by AFC/M23 rebels, who currently control this strategic mining area. This restriction prevents families and residents from obtaining information about loved ones who may still be buried under the rubble.
Sources also indicate that anyone attempting to publicly discuss the incident or provide details risks arrest, heightening anxiety and fear among the local population. Residents believe the rebels are deliberately trying to restrict the flow of information regarding the disaster.
Despite these obstacles, search efforts at the site continue, though conditions remain difficult and dangerous, leaving communities in deep uncertainty over the full extent of the tragedy.

title: Wazalendo Offensive Forces AFC/M23 Rebels Out of Three Villages Near Rubaya
excerpt: MASISI, North Kivu February 23, 2026 — Violent clashes erupted in Masisi territory after Wazalendo fighters launched an offensive against AFC/M23 rebel positions, resulting in the loss of three villages previously controlled by the rebels near the strategic mining town of Rubaya.
title_en: Wazalendo Offensive Forces AFC/M23 Rebels Out of Three Villages Near Rubaya
excerpt_en: MASISI, North Kivu February 23, 2026 — Violent clashes erupted in Masisi territory after Wazalendo fighters launched an offensive against AFC/M23 rebel positions, resulting in the loss of three villages previously controlled by the rebels near the strategic mining town of Rubaya.
body_en:
MASISI, North Kivu February 23, 2026 — Violent clashes erupted in Masisi territory after Wazalendo fighters launched an offensive against AFC/M23 rebel positions, resulting in the loss of three villages previously controlled by the rebels near the strategic mining town of Rubaya.
The fighting took place on Sunday, February 22, in the villages of Kasenyi, Chugi, and Kinigi, located in the Bahunde chiefdom. These localities are considered strategically important due to their proximity to Rubaya, an area widely known for its intensive mining activities and its significance in the military and economic dynamics of the region.
After intense exchanges of gunfire, Wazalendo fighters reportedly regained control of the three villages, which had previously served as key positions for AFC/M23 forces in this part of North Kivu. During the clashes, several rebel fighters were reportedly captured, while weapons and ammunition were seized by the Wazalendo.
In response to the loss of these positions, AFC/M23 elements reinforced their presence on the hill known as “Sita,” a strategic location overlooking the contested area. The reinforcements appear aimed at stopping the Wazalendo advance and potentially launching a counteroffensive to retake Chugi and Kinigi.
Amid the escalation, AFC/M23 representatives accused the government coalition of violating the ceasefire, while also reporting drone strikes in several areas of Masisi territory, further highlighting the fragile security environment in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
On Monday, February 23, a fragile calm prevailed along the front line, but the situation remains volatile. body_en:
MASISI, North Kivu February 25, 2026 — Fighting intensified on Wednesday, February 25, in the village of Kasenyi, located in the Kibabi group of Masisi territory, as AFC/M23 rebels launched a counter-offensive against the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) and their Wazalendo allies. The government forces had seized Kasenyi last Sunday following several hours of clashes.
Local sources report that rebels redeployed to Kasenyi with reinforcements in men and ammunition, aiming to retake the village and halt the advance of pro-government forces toward the mining town of Rubaya, a strategic rebel stronghold in the region. Kasenyi is a key crossing point on the road leading to Rubaya, making its control crucial for both sides.
Since midday, heavy and light weapons fire has been reported in and around Kasenyi, causing renewed panic among civilians. Several families have fled their homes, abandoning belongings and seeking safer areas, while the humanitarian situation in Masisi territory, already precarious, faces further strain.
In nearby Rubaya, tensions remain high following FARDC airstrikes that destroyed a rebel position in Kishusha, further exacerbating insecurity. Many residents have reportedly fled Rubaya over fears of reprisals or intensified fighting in the coming days.
The ongoing clashes in Kasenyi reflect the volatile security landscape in Masisi territory, where multi-front fighting between AFC/M23 rebels, government forces, and allied militias continues to displace civilians and disrupt humanitarian operations.

title: AFC/M23 Confirms Death of Military Spokesperson Willy Ngoma
excerpt: NORTH KIVU February 28, 2026 — The AFC/M23 rebel movement officially announced on Saturday, February 28, the death of its military spokesperson, Colonel Willy Ngoma, who was killed on February 24 in a drone strike attributed to the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo
title_en: AFC/M23 Confirms Death of Military Spokesperson Willy Ngoma
excerpt_en: NORTH KIVU February 28, 2026 — The AFC/M23 rebel movement officially announced on Saturday, February 28, the death of its military spokesperson, Colonel Willy Ngoma, who was killed on February 24 in a drone strike attributed to the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo
body_en:
NORTH KIVU February 28, 2026 — The AFC/M23 rebel movement officially announced on Saturday, February 28, the death of its military spokesperson, Colonel Willy Ngoma, who was killed on February 24 in a drone strike attributed to the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC).
In its statement, the movement accused the Kinshasa government of deliberately violating the ceasefire and launching a full-scale offensive in eastern DRC. The rebels said that the strike, and other recent military operations, have made both soldiers and civilians primary targets, even beyond active frontlines.
“These crimes will not go unnoticed or unpunished. Our duty is to guarantee the protection of our people and our soldiers throughout the liberated territory,” the AFC/M23 declared.
The announcement comes amid escalating fighting across North and South Kivu, following repeated FARDC airstrikes and ground offensives by the Wazalendo militia, allies of the government forces. The movement cited multiple localities affected by the conflict, including Kawele, Mweso, Rutigita, Kitazungura, Rugezi, Rubaya, Walikale, Masisi, Kalehe, Gasovu, Minembwe, Kinyumba, and Nyabyondo, among others.
This marks the second significant loss for the group after the death of Magloire Paluku, occurring in the context of slow progress on international peace initiatives under the Washington and Doha processes, supported by the African Union, but with limited impact on the ground. Despite the intensified military pressure, the AFC/M23 maintains control over large areas of North and South Kivu.

title: FARDC and Wazalendo Repel AFC/M23 Attack in Fungura
excerpt: WALIKALE March 3, 2026 — The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC), supported by Wazalendo fighters, successfully repelled an attack by AFC/M23 rebels on Fungura Hill, overlooking Katobi in the Banakindi area of the Kisimba group, on Monday, March 2. According

excerpt_en: WALIKALE March 3, 2026 — The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC), supported by Wazalendo fighters, successfully repelled an attack by AFC/M23 rebels on Fungura Hill, overlooking Katobi in the Banakindi area of the Kisimba group, on Monday, March 2. According
body_en:
WALIKALE March 3, 2026 — The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC), supported by Wazalendo fighters, successfully repelled an attack by AFC/M23 rebels on Fungura Hill, overlooking Katobi in the Banakindi area of the Kisimba group, on Monday, March 2.
According to local traditional sources, the rebels launched their offensive from Mpety, targeting positions held by government forces. Fungura Hill is considered a strategic security stronghold for Pinga, a central town in this part of Walikale territory. Its capture could have provided a corridor to neighboring towns.
Heavy and light weapons fire was reported over several hours, spreading fear among the civilian population. However, the FARDC and Wazalendo forces contained the attack and forced the rebels to retreat to their original positions after failing to break through.
This incident highlights the ongoing volatility in North Kivu, where repeated clashes between AFC/M23 rebels and loyalist forces, often with local allies, continue to destabilize areas including Walikale, Masisi, and Rutshuru. Residents remain on high alert, fearing further hostilities in the coming days.

title: Rwanda’s Ambassador to UN Says DRC Insecurity Stems from Internal Problems
excerpt: Rwanda’s Ambassador to Switzerland and the United Nations in Geneva, Urujeni Bakuramutsa, told the UN Human Rights Council on March 3, 2026, that the ongoing insecurity in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is largely caused by internal governance and institutional problems w
title_en: Rwanda’s Ambassador to UN Says DRC Insecurity Stems from Internal Problems
excerpt_en: Rwanda’s Ambassador to Switzerland and the United Nations in Geneva, Urujeni Bakuramutsa, told the UN Human Rights Council on March 3, 2026, that the ongoing insecurity in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is largely caused by internal governance and institutional problems w
body_en:
Rwanda’s Ambassador to Switzerland and the United Nations in Geneva, Urujeni Bakuramutsa, told the UN Human Rights Council on March 3, 2026, that the ongoing insecurity in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is largely caused by internal governance and institutional problems within the country.
Speaking on the situation in the Great Lakes region, Ambassador Bakuramutsa noted that more than 160 armed groups operate in the DRC, particularly in the eastern provinces, where instability has persisted for over 30 years.
“In eastern DRC, the problem of insecurity has been ongoing for decades, driven by deep-seated internal and institutional issues,” he said. He added that insecurity is not confined to the east but has spread to other areas, including near Kinshasa, where groups such as Mobondo are active, illustrating systemic governance challenges.
Addressing accusations that Rwanda supports the M23 armed group, Ambassador Bakuramutsa emphasized that M23 is composed of Congolese fighters who have taken up arms due to political and security problems in the DRC, and that the primary responsibility to resolve these issues lies with the DRC government through political measures.
He also criticized the DRC government for continuing to support the FDLR terrorist group, formed by members of the defeated army (Ex-FAR) and Interahamwe, who were responsible for the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi. Ambassador Bakuramutsa noted that despite the June 2025 peace agreement, reinforced in December 2025, the DRC has failed to dismantle the FDLR and has even integrated members into its military, contravening UN Security Council resolutions.
Ambassador Bakuramutsa called for a thorough analysis of the root causes of insecurity in the Great Lakes region to determine the responsibilities of each country and to guide solutions for lasting peace.

excerpt: Kayonza, February 25, 2026 – The Government of Rwanda has received a $78.5 million grant from the International Fund for Agriculture and Livestock Development (IFAD) to boost agricultural development and irrigation infrastructure in Kayonza District. The grant agreement was signe
title_en: Rwanda Secures $78.5 Million Grant for Kayonza Irrigation Project
excerpt_en: Kayonza, February 25, 2026 – The Government of Rwanda has received a $78.5 million grant from the International Fund for Agriculture and Livestock Development (IFAD) to boost agricultural development and irrigation infrastructure in Kayonza District. The grant agreement was signe
body_en:
Kayonza, February 25, 2026 – The Government of Rwanda has received a $78.5 million grant from the International Fund for Agriculture and Livestock Development (IFAD) to boost agricultural development and irrigation infrastructure in Kayonza District.
The grant agreement was signed on February 24, 2026, with Rwanda represented by Minister of Finance and Economic Planning Yusuf Murangwa, and IFAD represented by its Country Director in Rwanda, Dagmawi Habte-Selassie.
The funding will support the irrigation of hills currently used for agriculture and the development of value-added small livestock sectors, aiming to reduce poverty, enhance food security, improve climate resilience, and increase rural household incomes.
Kayonza, one of the districts most vulnerable to droughts caused by extreme heat, experienced significant agricultural challenges in late 2025. The grant is expected to complement ongoing projects, including the Gishanda artificial pond, which will help irrigate 200 hectares of farmland.

title: Rwanda Appoints Members of the Appeals Board for Refugees and Asylum Seekers
excerpt: On March 4, 2026, the Rwandan Cabinet appointed the leadership of the Appeals Board for Refugees and Asylum Seekers. Chairpersons: Edda Mukabagwiza and Rusanganwa Jean Damascène Registrars: Mukanyundo Patricie, Nyirinkwaya Immaculée, Rudasingwa Joseph, Mukama Augustin, and Ndabir
title_en: Rwanda Appoints Members of the Appeals Board for Refugees and Asylum Seekers
excerpt_en: On March 4, 2026, the Rwandan Cabinet appointed the leadership of the Appeals Board for Refugees and Asylum Seekers. Chairpersons: Edda Mukabagwiza and Rusanganwa Jean Damascène Registrars: Mukanyundo Patricie, Nyirinkwaya Immaculée, Rudasingwa Joseph, Mukama Augustin, and Ndabir
body_en:
On March 4, 2026, the Rwandan Cabinet appointed the leadership of the Appeals Board for Refugees and Asylum Seekers.
Chairpersons: Edda Mukabagwiza and Rusanganwa Jean Damascène
Registrars: Mukanyundo Patricie, Nyirinkwaya Immaculée, Rudasingwa Joseph, Mukama Augustin, and Ndabirora Kalinda Jean Damascène
The Appeals Board is mandated to review cases of migrants or asylum seekers who are dissatisfied with decisions made by the Immigration and Refugee Service. Appeals must be submitted in writing within 30 days of notification of the initial decision, and the Board is required to issue a ruling within six months. Decisions are communicated in writing within seven days of adoption. Article 15 allows appellants to submit any evidence supporting their case.
Edda Mukabagwiza brings extensive experience to the position:
Served as Minister of Justice and Deputy Speaker of the Chamber of Deputies
Rwanda’s Ambassador to Canada and Cuba (2007–2013)
Member of Parliament 2013–2018
Founder of EM Pathways Legal & Advisory Ltd, admitted to the bar in November 2025
Holds a Master’s in Diplomacy and a Bachelor of Laws
The establishment of this Appeals Board comes as Rwanda prepares to process migrants deported from the UK who will have the opportunity to appeal decisions regarding their refugee or asylum status.
This new structure is designed to strengthen due process and legal oversight in the country’s refugee and asylum system, ensuring that applicants have a formal mechanism to contest decisions fairly.

Registrars: Mukanyundo Patricie, Nyirinkwaya Immaculée, Rudasingwa Joseph, Mukama Augustin, and Ndabirora Kalinda Jean Damascène
The Appeals Board is mandated to review cases of migrants or asylum seekers who are dissatisfied with decisions made by the Immigration and Refugee Service. Appeals must be submitted in writing within 30 days of notification of the initial decision, and the Board is required to issue a ruling within six months. Decisions are communicated in writing within seven days of adoption. Article 15 allows appellants to submit any evidence supporting their case.
Edda Mukabagwiza brings extensive experience to the position:
Served as Minister of Justice and Deputy Speaker of the Chamber of Deputies
Rwanda’s Ambassador to Canada and Cuba (2007–2013)
Member of Parliament 2013–2018
Founder of EM Pathways Legal & Advisory Ltd, admitted to the bar in November 2025
Holds a Master’s in Diplomacy and a Bachelor of Laws
The establishment of this Appeals Board comes as Rwanda prepares to process migrants deported from the UK who will have the opportunity to appeal decisions regarding their refugee or asylum status.
This new structure is designed to strengthen due process and legal oversight in the country’s refugee and asylum system, ensuring that applicants have a formal mechanism to contest decisions fairly.

title: RDF Pledges Partnership with Ethiopian Army on AI and Advanced Technologies

title_en: RDF Pledges Partnership with Ethiopian Army on AI and Advanced Technologies
excerpt_en: The Rwanda Defence Forces (RDF) leadership held high-level talks with the Ethiopian Ministry of Defence on March 2, 2026, to explore cooperation in military and technological areas, including the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI). The RDF delegation, led by Brigadier General Ro
body_en:
The Rwanda Defence Forces (RDF) leadership held high-level talks with the Ethiopian Ministry of Defence on March 2, 2026, to explore cooperation in military and technological areas, including the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI).
The RDF delegation, led by Brigadier General Ronald Rwivanga, RDF Spokesperson, was in Ethiopia to join celebrations marking the 130th anniversary of the Battle of Adwa, a historic victory in 1896 where Ethiopian forces defeated the Italian army, preserving the country’s independence during the reign of Emperor Menelik II. The celebrations ran from February 28 to March 1, 2026.
Following the commemorations, the RDF leaders were received by Ethiopia’s Minister of Defense, Eng. Aisha Muhammed, where they discussed ways to strengthen bilateral military cooperation, particularly in intelligent and advanced technologies.
The RDF emphasized on social media that the discussions aimed to deepen existing collaboration in the military sector and expand it to emerging fields such as AI.
Rwanda and Ethiopia have a history of cooperation spanning more than 20 years, including training of soldiers and police forces, as well as collaboration in security, agriculture, trade, and education.
In March 2025, a military cooperation agreement was signed during a visit by the Chief of Staff of the Rwandan Armed Forces, Gen. Mubarakh Muganga, formalizing joint efforts.
In addition to defense cooperation, both countries recently signed agreements on air travel services, allowing RwandAir and Ethiopian Airlines to operate smoothly between their nations, further strengthening bilateral relations.

title: Senate Petition Targets Modeste Bahati Lukwebo Over Opposition to Constitutional Revision
excerpt: KINSHASA March 5, 2026 — Just a day after publicly opposing a proposed constitutional revision championed by President Félix Tshisekedi and the Sacred Union of the Nation, Modeste Bahati Lukwebo, Second Vice-President of the Senate and head of AFDC-A, has become the target of a f
title_en: Senate Petition Targets Modeste Bahati Lukwebo Over Opposition to Constitutional Revision
excerpt_en: KINSHASA March 5, 2026 — Just a day after publicly opposing a proposed constitutional revision championed by President Félix Tshisekedi and the Sacred Union of the Nation, Modeste Bahati Lukwebo, Second Vice-President of the Senate and head of AFDC-A, has become the target of a f
body_en:
KINSHASA March 5, 2026 — Just a day after publicly opposing a proposed constitutional revision championed by President Félix Tshisekedi and the Sacred Union of the Nation, Modeste Bahati Lukwebo, Second Vice-President of the Senate and head of AFDC-A, has become the target of a formal petition in the upper house of Parliament.
The initiative, led by Senator Dany Kabongo Bondanya, criticizes Bahati Lukwebo’s remarks as “completely inappropriate” and disrespectful to the President, particularly given his prominent role in both the Senate and the Sacred Union presidium. Kabongo emphasized that Bahati Lukwebo should have consulted the President, described as the “moral authority” of the Sacred Union, before expressing his personal opposition.
During a press conference on March 4, Bahati Lukwebo had dismissed the debate over changing the Constitution as false and politically motivated, arguing that the real issue lies in the failure to implement the existing law, not the law itself. He called for political actors to focus on practical governance for the benefit of the Congolese people rather than pursuing constitutional amendments.
The petition reflects growing tensions within the Sacred Union, with high-ranking figures such as Déo Bizibu, Secretary General of the UDPS, publicly criticizing Bahati Lukwebo’s stance as contrary to the coalition’s vision. Kabongo Bondanya promised a detailed statement outlining the grounds for possible removal from office ahead of the March parliamentary session.
This unfolding dispute underscores the heightened political sensitivity in the DRC surrounding potential constitutional reforms and the balancing of authority between the President and senior members of the ruling coalition.

title: Deadly Landslides in Rubaya Highlight Unregulated Mining
excerpt: Rubaya Masisi , March 8, 2026 — The Support Group for Traceability and Transparency in Natural Resource Management (GATT-RN) expressed deep dismay following recent deadly landslides in the Rubaya mining town, Masisi territory, North Kivu. The organization denounced dangerous arti
title_en: Deadly Landslides in Rubaya Highlight Unregulated Mining
excerpt_en: Rubaya Masisi , March 8, 2026 — The Support Group for Traceability and Transparency in Natural Resource Management (GATT-RN) expressed deep dismay following recent deadly landslides in the Rubaya mining town, Masisi territory, North Kivu. The organization denounced dangerous arti
body_en:
Rubaya Masisi , March 8, 2026 — The Support Group for Traceability and Transparency in Natural Resource Management (GATT-RN) expressed deep dismay following recent deadly landslides in the Rubaya mining town, Masisi territory, North Kivu. The organization denounced dangerous artisanal mining practices and called on the government to take urgent action.
The Gakombe site landslide is the latest in a series of recurring tragedies, exacerbated by the rainy season and lack of safety standards. Several mining areas in Rubaya are under AFC/M23 rebel control, facilitating illegal and fraudulent mining. GATT-RN emphasized that Congolese miners risk their lives for minimal wages while some actors profit from strategic minerals, including nearly 15% of global coltan production.
This disaster follows another landslide in the same area less than a month prior, which claimed over 300 lives. GATT-RN stressed that these incidents reflect avoidable failures in mine management and safety.
The organization urged the government to formalize artisanal mining, impose strict safety and labor standards, and open an independent investigation to determine administrative, security, and economic responsibilities. It also called for strengthened mineral traceability, improved certification mechanisms, and a compensation system for families of victims.

title: DRC–Burundi Border Reopens After Two Months of Closure
excerpt: UVIRA, South Kivu – February 23, 2026 — The Gatumba–Kavimvira border crossing between the Democratic Republic of Congo and Burundi officially reopened on Monday, February 23, restoring the movement of travelers and traders after more than two months of closure linked to the AFC/M
title_en: DRC–Burundi Border Reopens After Two Months of Closure
excerpt_en: UVIRA, South Kivu – February 23, 2026 — The Gatumba–Kavimvira border crossing between the Democratic Republic of Congo and Burundi officially reopened on Monday, February 23, restoring the movement of travelers and traders after more than two months of closure linked to the AFC/M
body_en:
UVIRA, South Kivu – February 23, 2026 — The Gatumba–Kavimvira border crossing between the Democratic Republic of Congo and Burundi officially reopened on Monday, February 23, restoring the movement of travelers and traders after more than two months of closure linked to the AFC/M23 conflict in eastern Congo.
The crossing connects the Congolese city of Uvira with Gatumba in Burundi, a strategic point for cross-border trade and daily travel between the two neighboring countries.
The border had been closed by Burundian authorities on December 10, 2025, shortly after AFC/M23 rebels seized control of Uvira, a development that heightened security concerns along the frontier.
Reopening Without Formal Ceremony
The resumption of activities at the border took place without an official ceremony, as authorities on both sides agreed to immediately allow the passage of travelers.
Migration officials confirmed that standard administrative procedures remain in place, requiring travelers to present valid visas and travel documents.
The border post will operate daily from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., according to migration authorities.
Relief Among Border Communities
The reopening sparked relief and renewed hope among residents and traders who depend on the crossing for their livelihoods and daily commerce.
For many small-scale traders, the closure had severely disrupted cross-border economic activities, particularly trade between Uvira and the Burundian capital, Bujumbura.
With the border now open again, traders and travelers began resuming their movements, signaling a gradual return to normal economic life in the region.
Strategic Border for Regional Trade
The Gatumba–Kavimvira crossing is one of the most important border points between the DRC and Burundi, facilitating the movement of goods, traders, and travelers every day.
Its reopening is expected to revive cross-border trade, which plays a crucial role in supporting local economies on both sides of the frontier.
Authorities hope that the reopening will contribute to easing tensions and restoring economic stability, although the security situation in eastern DRC remains fragile amid ongoing armed conflicts in the region.

title: Zambian General Charles Simuyuni Nakeempa Visits Goma as EJVM+ Head Amid Ongoing Clashes
excerpt: GOMA, North Kivu February 25, 2026 — Brigadier General Charles Simuyuni Nakeempa of Zambia, newly appointed head of the Expanded Joint Verification Mechanism Plus (EJVM+), arrived in Goma on Wednesday, February 25, marking his first visit since taking command. He is accompanied b
title_en: Zambian General Charles Simuyuni Nakeempa Visits Goma as EJVM+ Head Amid Ongoing Clashes
excerpt_en: GOMA, North Kivu February 25, 2026 — Brigadier General Charles Simuyuni Nakeempa of Zambia, newly appointed head of the Expanded Joint Verification Mechanism Plus (EJVM+), arrived in Goma on Wednesday, February 25, marking his first visit since taking command. He is accompanied b
body_en:
GOMA, North Kivu February 25, 2026 — Brigadier General Charles Simuyuni Nakeempa of Zambia, newly appointed head of the Expanded Joint Verification Mechanism Plus (EJVM+), arrived in Goma on Wednesday, February 25, marking his first visit since taking command. He is accompanied by a five-member delegation amid ongoing hostilities between government forces and AFC/M23 rebels across North Kivu and South Kivu.
According to MONUSCO, the delegation reaffirmed its support for ongoing peace efforts and indicated that the finalized 2026 action plan will be shared with the UN Mission to guide monitoring and verification operations. This initiative is part of MONUSCO’s mandate under UN Security Council Resolution 2808 (2025), which emphasizes support for peace and stability in eastern DRC, including the implementation of ceasefire monitoring mechanisms.
In parallel, MONUSCO and the International Conference on the Great Lakes Region (ICGLR) have deployed a joint exploratory and preliminary assessment mission to Uvira, South Kivu, running from February 23 to 27, 2026. The mission follows consultations with President Félix Tshisekedi, current Chair of the ICGLR, and serves as a prelude to the future deployment of the joint ceasefire monitoring mechanism.
The primary objective of this exploratory mission is operational, aiming to ensure that future monitoring and verification mechanisms are credible, secure, and operationally feasible. Teams will assess accessibility, security, logistics, and engagement needs to ensure the effective functioning of the mechanism. A thorough evaluation of political, security, logistical, and socio-environmental conditions around Uvira will guide coherent planning for future operations, with final deployment configurations dependent on agreed parameters and operational requirements.
The ceasefire monitoring and verification mechanism, signed in Doha on October 14, 2025, resulted from the sixth round of talks between the Congolese government and AFC/M23, mediated by Qatar. Implementation on the ground has faced challenges due to the reduced operational capacity of the EJVM, and the new command under General Simuyuni Nakeempa is tasked with revitalizing the mechanism to ensure effective monitoring and credible peace processes.
This visit follows recent field trips by MONUSCO leadership to eastern DRC, including meetings with AFC/M23 authorities, and was reinforced by United Nations Under-Secretary-General for Peace Operations Jean-Pierre Lacroix, who reiterated the UN’s commitment to fully execute MONUSCO’s updated mandate.
The deployment of EJVM+ under new leadership is expected to strengthen ceasefire monitoring, facilitate conflict de-escalation, and support ongoing peace initiatives in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.

MASISI February 28, 2026 — Fresh fighting broke out on Saturday, February 28, between AFC/M23 rebels and the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC), supported by Wazalendo militias, in Kinyumba, Masisi territory, North Kivu.
Kinyumba, located approximately 10 km north of Nyabiondo on the road to Pinga, was reportedly attacked by rebels aiming to regain control from the government coalition. As a result, traffic between Nyabiondo and Pinga has been suspended, and fear is spreading among local residents, many of whom have remained indoors.
Heavy and light weapons fire was reported throughout the combat zone, causing panic in surrounding villages. Displacements toward Nyabiondo have been observed, as civilians seek safety from the ongoing violence.
These clashes occur just 24 hours after a FARDC airstrike in Nyabiondo, which injured three civilians, highlighting the intensifying military operations in the Masisi territory.

title: AFC/M23 Claims Drone Attack on Kisangani Airport
excerpt: KISANGANI March 2, 2026 — The Congo River Alliance/March 23 Movement (AFC/M23) has officially claimed responsibility for the drone attacks targeting Kisangani-Bangboka International Airport in Tshopo Province on Sunday, March 1. In a statement, the rebel movement described the op
title_en: AFC/M23 Claims Drone Attack on Kisangani Airport
excerpt_en: KISANGANI March 2, 2026 — The Congo River Alliance/March 23 Movement (AFC/M23) has officially claimed responsibility for the drone attacks targeting Kisangani-Bangboka International Airport in Tshopo Province on Sunday, March 1. In a statement, the rebel movement described the op
body_en:
KISANGANI March 2, 2026 — The Congo River Alliance/March 23 Movement (AFC/M23) has officially claimed responsibility for the drone attacks targeting Kisangani-Bangboka International Airport in Tshopo Province on Sunday, March 1.
In a statement, the rebel movement described the operation as a “targeted mission” to “neutralize and destroy drones” that, according to them, were being prepared to “massacre civilians and attack AFC/M23 positions” near Kisangani. The group emphasized that its actions are part of its “patriotic duty to protect innocent populations.”
Local sources and provincial authorities had reported that four drones were intercepted over the airport on Sunday. The first drone was thwarted around 3:00 PM local time, followed by three additional “kamikaze” drones between 5:00 PM and 7:00 PM. Shrapnel from the drones damaged windows in some buildings, but there were no injuries or disruptions to the airport’s control tower.
The provincial government confirmed that all four drones were neutralized, noting that one crashed as a CAA aircraft announced its landing. Residents in nearby areas temporarily evacuated as a precaution.
The governor of Tshopo Province had previously attributed the attacks to the AFC/M23 and Rwanda. The rebels had also claimed responsibility for a previous drone strike on Bangboka Airport in late January. Local authorities had reported those incidents on January 31 and February 1 before the army declared the situation under control.

title: Rwanda Receives Credentials of Three Newly Appointed Ambassadors
excerpt: The Rwanda Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation (MINAFFET) has received copies of the credentials of three diplomats appointed by their respective governments to serve as Ambassadors to Rwanda. The documents were received on March 2, 2026, by Usta Kayitesi, S
title_en: Rwanda Receives Credentials of Three Newly Appointed Ambassadors
excerpt_en: The Rwanda Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation (MINAFFET) has received copies of the credentials of three diplomats appointed by their respective governments to serve as Ambassadors to Rwanda. The documents were received on March 2, 2026, by Usta Kayitesi, S
body_en:
The Rwanda Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation (MINAFFET) has received copies of the credentials of three diplomats appointed by their respective governments to serve as Ambassadors to Rwanda.
The documents were received on March 2, 2026, by Usta Kayitesi, Secretary of State at MINAFFET, during a formal ceremony in Kigali.
The diplomats who presented their letters of credence copies are Giles Cerutti, appointed as Ambassador of Switzerland to Rwanda, Brigadier General Boubacar Diallo, representing Mali, and Victorino-Nká Obiang Maye, representing Equatorial Guinea.
In international diplomatic practice, a government first appoints an individual to serve as ambassador to another country, after which the receiving state must approve the appointment before the diplomat assumes official duties.
Once approved, the envoy travels to the host country and presents copies of the credentials to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs or an authorized official, confirming their designation.
Within a specified period, the ambassador then presents the original letters of credence to the Head of State, formally completing the process and officially beginning their diplomatic mission in the host country.

title: Rwanda Registers Over 1.8 Million Citizens for Digital e-ID System
excerpt: Kigali, February 25, 2026 – More than 1.8 million citizens have been photographed and registered under Rwanda’s national electronic identity card (e-ID) program, a major digital transformation initiative designed to modernize public services and improve identity verification acro
title_en: Rwanda Registers Over 1.8 Million Citizens for Digital e-ID System
excerpt_en: Kigali, February 25, 2026 – More than 1.8 million citizens have been photographed and registered under Rwanda’s national electronic identity card (e-ID) program, a major digital transformation initiative designed to modernize public services and improve identity verification acro
body_en:
Kigali, February 25, 2026 – More than 1.8 million citizens have been photographed and registered under Rwanda’s national electronic identity card (e-ID) program, a major digital transformation initiative designed to modernize public services and improve identity verification across the country.
The e-ID system will serve as a single permanent identification document, issued to every Rwandan citizen from birth, securely linking interactions between individuals and both government institutions and private services.
Authorities reported that 1,828,763 people have already been registered across nine districts, including the pilot districts of Huye, Nyanza, and Gisagara, as well as Kamonyi, Muhanga, Ruhango, Nyarugenge, Gasabo, and Kicukiro. The project aims to eventually cover at least 15 million people, including citizens living abroad as well as refugees and migrants.
The digital ID project, which has already received more than $50 million in investment, is expected to complete the validation phase by the end of 2026, with the first electronic ID cards scheduled to be issued starting in August 2026.
Integrated Digital Identity System
The e-ID card will integrate multiple services throughout a citizen’s lifetime. For children, the system will be linked to birth registration, school enrollment, vaccinations, and medical care.
For young people, it will support identity verification for education, examinations, driver’s licenses, and employment records.
Among adults, the digital identity will connect services such as taxation, banking, healthcare, land ownership, marriage registration, business activities, and voting systems. It will also support pensions, social services, and asset management.
In the health sector, the system will link insurance coverage, medical records, medications, and vaccination histories. In education, it will provide a continuous identity record from early childhood to adulthood. The system is also expected to improve social protection programs by preventing identity fraud.
Privacy and Data Protection Measures
Officials emphasized that the digital ID system is designed to protect personal data and will not be used for daily surveillance. Access to personal information will require the explicit consent of the citizen.
Only limited information will be shared when verifying identity. For example, a financial institution may confirm that a person is over 18 years old without accessing the full date of birth. Citizens will be able to revoke access rights at any time.
Under data protection regulations, any misuse of information must be reported within 72 hours, and citizens retain the right to correct data and seek compensation if necessary.
Multiple Forms of Digital Identification
The electronic identity system will be available in three formats to ensure accessibility:
A mobile ID card with a QR code containing essential identity data
A secure electronic ID number for official verification
A Token system, allowing users to conduct electronic transactions without revealing their full ID number
These options are intended to ensure that every citizen can verify their identity even if one method is unavailable.
Inclusive Access to Digital Services
Authorities indicated that the system will remain accessible to citizens without smartphones, using mobile SIM cards and USSD services. Local officials will assist residents who lack access to digital technology, ensuring that no one is excluded from essential services.
Officials and lawmakers believe the national e-ID program will accelerate service delivery, simplify administrative procedures, and reduce the need to carry multiple documents.

title: Rwanda’s Ministry of Environment Questioned Over Rwf1.2 Billion Forest Loss
excerpt: The Chamber of Deputies has demanded an explanation from the Ministry of Environment regarding a Rwf1.2 billion loss caused by mismanagement of contracts between the Government of Rwanda and Sawmill East Africa Ltd (SEAL), the issue was raised during a plenary session on March 4,
title_en: Rwanda’s Ministry of Environment Questioned Over Rwf1.2 Billion Forest Loss
excerpt_en: The Chamber of Deputies has demanded an explanation from the Ministry of Environment regarding a Rwf1.2 billion loss caused by mismanagement of contracts between the Government of Rwanda and Sawmill East Africa Ltd (SEAL), the issue was raised during a plenary session on March 4,
body_en:
The Chamber of Deputies has demanded an explanation from the Ministry of Environment regarding a Rwf1.2 billion loss caused by mismanagement of contracts between the Government of Rwanda and Sawmill East Africa Ltd (SEAL), the issue was raised during a plenary session on March 4, 2026.
The concern stems from forest management agreements for the Shariyo and Ntobo I, II, III forests, which were reportedly not respected, leading to significant financial losses. A joint audit by the Ministry of Environment, Rwanda Forestry Authority (RFA), and SEAL, launched on February 17, 2025, revealed total losses of Rwf 1,238,244,838, including over Rwf 1.1 billion in unpaid timber harvests and Rwf 9.08 million in unpaid land leases.
The Ministry confirmed that SEAL has agreed to repay the losses, though payment has not yet been made. The Forest Service informed MPs that termination of the contract is nearly complete, with hopes of full repayment within 30 days.
The chairperson of the Commission on Land, Agriculture, Livestock and Environment, Muzana Alice, stated that measures are being taken to prevent future losses, including requiring contractors to pay 100% of tree costs before harvesting and strengthening contract monitoring.
Parliament also requested that the Ministry establish clear regulations for collaboration between RFA, districts, and Kigali City, ensuring continuous and timely reporting on forest management nationwide. This directive must be implemented within two months.
The case highlights the importance of accountability in state-forest contracts and the need for robust oversight to protect public resources.

title: AFC/M23 Vows Retaliation After Death of Lt. Col. Willy Ngoma
excerpt: The AFC/M23 coalition has vowed to continue attacks on Bangoka Airport in Kisangani and to avenge the death of its former military spokesperson, Lt. Col. Willy Ngoma, amid escalating tensions in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. In a statement issued on March 3, 2026, the coa
title_en: AFC/M23 Vows Retaliation After Death of Lt. Col. Willy Ngoma
excerpt_en: The AFC/M23 coalition has vowed to continue attacks on Bangoka Airport in Kisangani and to avenge the death of its former military spokesperson, Lt. Col. Willy Ngoma, amid escalating tensions in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. In a statement issued on March 3, 2026, the coa
body_en:
The AFC/M23 coalition has vowed to continue attacks on Bangoka Airport in Kisangani and to avenge the death of its former military spokesperson, Lt. Col. Willy Ngoma, amid escalating tensions in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
In a statement issued on March 3, 2026, the coalition confirmed that it carried out a drone strike on Bangoka Airport on March 1, 2026, saying the operation targeted drones allegedly being prepared by the Congolese army to strike AFC/M23 positions and civilian areas.
The group said a similar attack had already been conducted on February 1, 2026, with the same objective of destroying facilities used to coordinate drone operations against its bases.
Bertrand Bisimwa, Deputy Director for Political, Diplomatic and Governance Affairs within the coalition, said the group considers the attacks part of its responsibility to protect civilians, particularly as mediation efforts have not stopped ongoing hostilities.
“While mediators in the peace process have not been able to compel Kinshasa to respect its commitments or stop attacks against innocent people, we must fulfill our duty to protect the population,” he said.
The escalation follows the death of Lt. Col. Willy Ngoma, who was killed on February 24, 2026, during a drone strike attributed to Congolese government forces near Rubaya centre in Masisi territory, North Kivu.
According to the coalition, the strike targeted AFC/M23 fighters engaged on the front line, resulting in several casualties including Ngoma, who served as the movement’s military spokesperson.
Lawrence Kanyuka, the coalition’s political spokesperson, said the deaths of fighters and civilians would not be forgotten and that those responsible must be held accountable.
He stated that the coalition remains determined to seek justice for its members and supporters, including Ngoma.
The developments come despite a ceasefire agreement signed between the DRC government and AFC/M23 during talks in Qatar, which was intended to reduce hostilities in North Kivu and South Kivu provinces.
However, continued military operations and drone strikes in the region have contributed to renewed clashes and heightened tensions, with fighting reported in several areas over recent days.

The escalation follows the death of Lt. Col. Willy Ngoma, who was killed on February 24, 2026, during a drone strike attributed to Congolese government forces near Rubaya centre in Masisi territory, North Kivu.
According to the coalition, the strike targeted AFC/M23 fighters engaged on the front line, resulting in several casualties including Ngoma, who served as the movement’s military spokesperson.
Lawrence Kanyuka, the coalition’s political spokesperson, said the deaths of fighters and civilians would not be forgotten and that those responsible must be held accountable.
He stated that the coalition remains determined to seek justice for its members and supporters, including Ngoma.
The developments come despite a ceasefire agreement signed between the DRC government and AFC/M23 during talks in Qatar, which was intended to reduce hostilities in North Kivu and South Kivu provinces.
However, continued military operations and drone strikes in the region have contributed to renewed clashes and heightened tensions, with fighting reported in several areas over recent days.

excerpt_en: ARUSHA March 2, 2026 — The East African Community (EAC) is set to hold its 25th Ordinary Summit of Heads of State and Government on Saturday, March 7, 2026, in Arusha, Tanzania, under the theme “Deepening Integration to Improve the Living Conditions of EAC Citizens.” The summit a
body_en:
ARUSHA March 2, 2026 — The East African Community (EAC) is set to hold its 25th Ordinary Summit of Heads of State and Government on Saturday, March 7, 2026, in Arusha, Tanzania, under the theme “Deepening Integration to Improve the Living Conditions of EAC Citizens.” The summit aims to advance regional integration, review institutional reports, and launch key initiatives, including the EAC Customs Guarantee and the 7th Development Strategy (2026/27–2030/31).
The meeting will also address governance matters, including the appointment of a new Secretary-General, judges to the East African Court of Justice, renewal of Deputy Secretaries-General, appointments to the EAC Competition Authority, and ratification of draft laws from the East African Legislative Assembly.
However, the summit occurs amid persistent security tensions in eastern DRC, where clashes continue between the Armed Forces of the DRC (FARDC) and AFC/M23 rebels, supported by Rwanda. Diplomatic strains between Kinshasa and Kigali remain high despite the Washington and Doha peace processes, complicating regional stabilization efforts.
Kinshasa also maintains a strained relationship with the EAC, perceiving insufficient engagement or balance from the regional bloc. This tension traces back to the 24th EAC Summit in November 2024, which President Félix Tshisekedi did not attend, and the ineffectiveness of the EAC Regional Force (EACRF), whose mandate expired in December 2023 without renewal. Frustrated by the inability of the EACRF to neutralize armed groups, the DRC has increasingly sought collaboration with SADC forces, following the withdrawal of its troops from Goma amid rebel advances.
Despite these challenges, the EAC remains a central actor in regional stability and integration. Observers are closely watching how the Kenyan presidency under President William Ruto will address the security crisis in eastern DRC and restore confidence in the Community’s role in regional peace and economic integration.

title_en: 15 to 30% of Global Coltan Production under M23 Control, March 7, 2026
excerpt_en: At the UN Security Council debate on energy and critical minerals, France highlighted the role of natural resources in fueling conflict and instability. Eastern DRC, largely controlled by the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 rebellion, produces between 15 and 30% of global coltan, which is
body_en:
At the UN Security Council debate on energy and critical minerals, France highlighted the role of natural resources in fueling conflict and instability. Eastern DRC, largely controlled by the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 rebellion, produces between 15 and 30% of global coltan, which is exploited to finance armed activities and expand territorial control.
This resource grabbing perpetuates violence, prolongs conflicts, and worsens the suffering of civilian populations. France condemned the predatory exploitation model, noting that such practices hinder economic and social development by depriving states of the resources of their own land. Comparisons were also made to Ukraine, where energy infrastructure attacks are used as a weapon of coercion.
The session occurred amid ongoing Rwandan aggression in eastern DRC, with AFC/M23 forces occupying large parts of North and South Kivu. The Congolese government considers these attacks as economic wars aimed at the plundering and illicit exploitation of minerals, while Kigali rejects these claims, citing FDLR threats and denying military support to M23.
Efforts to resolve tensions include the Washington Process, addressing Kinshasa-Kigali relations, and the Doha Process, focusing on the AFC/M23 crisis. Despite these initiatives, hostilities persist, endangering civilian populations and worsening humanitarian conditions, especially as international aid declines.

title: Fragile Calm Returns to Walikale After Two Days of Fighting Between AFC/M23 and Wazalendo
excerpt: WALIKALE, North Kivu February 23, 2026 — A tense and fragile calm returned Monday morning to Mounts Buhaya and Fungura, located near Katobi in the Banakindi area of Kisimba group, Walikale territory, after two days of intense clashes between AFC/M23 rebels and Wazalendo fighters.
title_en: Fragile Calm Returns to Walikale After Two Days of Fighting Between AFC/M23 and Wazalendo
excerpt_en: WALIKALE, North Kivu February 23, 2026 — A tense and fragile calm returned Monday morning to Mounts Buhaya and Fungura, located near Katobi in the Banakindi area of Kisimba group, Walikale territory, after two days of intense clashes between AFC/M23 rebels and Wazalendo fighters.
body_en:
WALIKALE, North Kivu February 23, 2026 — A tense and fragile calm returned Monday morning to Mounts Buhaya and Fungura, located near Katobi in the Banakindi area of Kisimba group, Walikale territory, after two days of intense clashes between AFC/M23 rebels and Wazalendo fighters.
The fighting erupted despite a ceasefire initiative proposed by Angola, part of ongoing regional diplomatic efforts aimed at reducing the persistent insecurity in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
Reports indicate that AFC/M23 combatants launched simultaneous offensives on Wazalendo positions established on the strategic hills of Buhaya and Fungura. These elevated positions dominate the village of Katobi and are considered a critical defensive line for the nearby town of Pinga, an area frequently targeted by armed incursions.
The confrontation led to fierce exchanges of gunfire as both sides attempted to secure control of the strategic high ground. After prolonged fighting, Wazalendo fighters claimed to have halted the rebel advance, forcing AFC/M23 elements to withdraw toward Mpety, described as one of their main operational strongholds in the zone.
The violence triggered panic among civilians in Katobi and surrounding villages. Fearing for their safety, many residents fled into nearby forests, abandoning their homes to escape the clashes.
Although relative calm was reported Monday morning, most displaced residents have not yet returned to their homes, citing fears of a renewed outbreak of fighting.
On the ground, the security situation remains volatile, with local communities living in uncertainty and fear amid a broader context of resurgent armed violence in Walikale territory, one of the areas repeatedly affected by conflict in North Kivu Province.

title_en: AFC/M23 Launches Counter-Offensive in Kazinga Amid Ongoing Clashes
excerpt_en: MASISI, North Kivu February 25, 2026 — Clashes resumed early Wednesday afternoon, February 25, in the village of Kazinga, located in the Nyamaboko 1 group (Masisi territory), as AFC/M23 rebels launched a counter-offensive to try to recapture the town after being expelled earlier
body_en:
MASISI, North Kivu February 25, 2026 — Clashes resumed early Wednesday afternoon, February 25, in the village of Kazinga, located in the Nyamaboko 1 group (Masisi territory), as AFC/M23 rebels launched a counter-offensive to try to recapture the town after being expelled earlier in the day by government forces and Wazalendo fighters.
Local sources report that the rebels simultaneously attacked multiple positions inside and around Kazinga, quickly intensifying the exchange of fire and plunging residents into renewed fear. The sounds of heavy and light weapons fire were reportedly heard for several kilometers.
Kazinga, situated in the Butsike area, has become a major theater of fighting in the southern part of Masisi territory, with front lines shifting rapidly and villages changing hands between government-allied forces and AFC/M23 rebels in recent days.
The AFC/M23 counter-offensive comes amid escalating clashes in neighboring localities, following the loss of other strategic rebel positions. Residents describe a fluid and chaotic situation, as fighting continued into the late afternoon, heightening fears of a further deterioration of security in this part of Masisi territory.

body_en:
WALIKALE February 28, 2026 — Intense fighting erupted on Saturday, February 28, between AFC/M23 rebels and the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC), supported by Wazalendo militias, in Kibati, Luberike area, Walikale territory, North Kivu.
Local security and administrative sources reported that government forces launched an offensive to reclaim the town, which has been under rebel control for nearly a year.
Heavy and light weapons fire were heard across the combat zone. Movement along the Mungazi–Kashebere road has been suspended since the morning, leaving travelers and taxi drivers stranded—those heading from Walikale to Goma are halted in Mungazi, while travelers from Goma to Walikale are waiting in Kashebere.
The clashes come amid a tense security environment, with escalating hostilities in neighboring Masisi territory, despite a ceasefire agreement mediated by Angola on February 18, 2026.

title: Rwanda Condemns U.S. Sanctions, Calls Them Unilateral and One-Sided
excerpt: KIGALI March 2, 2026 — The Rwandan government criticized the recent sanctions imposed by the United States on the Rwanda Defense Force (RDF) and four Rwandan nationals, describing the measures as “unilateral” and unfairly targeting “only one party” involved in the peace process i
title_en: Rwanda Condemns U.S. Sanctions, Calls Them Unilateral and One-Sided
excerpt_en: KIGALI March 2, 2026 — The Rwandan government criticized the recent sanctions imposed by the United States on the Rwanda Defense Force (RDF) and four Rwandan nationals, describing the measures as “unilateral” and unfairly targeting “only one party” involved in the peace process i
body_en:
KIGALI March 2, 2026 — The Rwandan government criticized the recent sanctions imposed by the United States on the Rwanda Defense Force (RDF) and four Rwandan nationals, describing the measures as “unilateral” and unfairly targeting “only one party” involved in the peace process in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).
In an official statement, Kigali argued that the sanctions “distort the reality” of the security situation in eastern Congo and fail to account for alleged violations by the DRC government, including “constant and indiscriminate drone attacks” and ground offensives that have reportedly caused numerous civilian casualties.
The statement also highlights that the DRC’s coalition forces reportedly include foreign mercenaries, state-backed ethnic militias such as the Wazalendo, and the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), described by Kigali as a “genocidal militia” operating alongside the Armed Forces of the DRC (FARDC).
Rwanda asserts that under the Washington Accords, the DRC committed to ending support for the FDLR and allied militias in a verifiable and irreversible manner, but has yet to take any meaningful action. Kigali emphasizes that it remains fully committed to the disengagement of its own forces, in parallel with DRC’s compliance.
Finally, the Rwandan government reaffirmed its commitment to the full implementation of the Washington Agreements, including the regional economic integration framework, and called for a “balanced” approach from international partners through mechanisms such as the Joint Monitoring Committee.
This statement comes shortly after the U.S. Treasury Department sanctioned the RDF and four Rwandan individuals for their role in the ongoing conflict in eastern DRC, citing Rwanda’s support for the AFC/M23 rebel movement.

title_en: Parliament Ratifies Peace and Strategic Partnership Agreements with Rwanda and the United States
excerpt_en: KINSHASA March 7, 2026 — The government of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has adopted bills ratifying the peace agreement with Rwanda and the Strategic Partnership Agreement with the United States, two landmark accords signed under the Trump administration. The adoption w
body_en:
KINSHASA March 7, 2026 — The government of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has adopted bills ratifying the peace agreement with Rwanda and the Strategic Partnership Agreement with the United States, two landmark accords signed under the Trump administration.
The adoption was carried out by Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Noëlla Ayeganato, on behalf of the Minister of Foreign Affairs. The bills come ahead of the March 2026 ordinary parliamentary session, scheduled for March 16, with the government emphasizing alignment with its legislative agenda.
The agreements were originally signed on December 4, 2025, in Washington, D.C., where President Félix Tshisekedi and President Paul Kagame endorsed the instruments in the presence of international dignitaries including Donald Trump, Faure Gnassingbé, João Lourenço, Évariste Ndayishimiye, William Ruto, Jessica Alupo, Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, Mohammed Al Khulaifi, and Shakhboot bin Nahyan Al Nahyan.
The ratified instruments include:
The Washington Agreements for Peace and Prosperity between DRC and Rwanda, reaffirming the June 27, 2025 peace commitments and establishing the Regional Economic Integration Framework (REIF).
The United States–DRC Strategic Partnership Agreement and related Memorandum of Understanding on Enhanced Security Cooperation.
The United States–Rwanda Framework for Shared Economic Prosperity, aiming to strengthen bilateral economic ties.
According to the U.S. State Department, these agreements aim to end decades of conflict, promote economic cooperation, and provide a roadmap for peace, security, and growth in the Great Lakes region. They also open opportunities for the U.S. private sector and reinforce regional integration.
The DRC government described the ratifications as a historic step toward sustainable peace, stability, and shared prosperity, in line with its commitments under the Washington Accords and related frameworks.
Conclusion
The period from February 22 to March 8, 2026, in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) was marked by a complex interplay of persistent conflict, diplomatic tension, and internal governance reforms. While the country demonstrated significant international initiative—notably through the nomination of Juliana Lumumba for the OIF leadership and active participation in global mining forums—the security situation in the East remains its most pressing challenge.
The escalating conflict with the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 rebellion continues to destabilize North and South Kivu, resulting in mass displacements, humanitarian crises, and the discovery of mass graves in recently liberated areas such as Uvira. Despite international efforts under the Washington and Doha frameworks, diplomatic friction between Kinshasa and Kigali remains high, with both sides exchanging accusations regarding support for armed groups and the legitimacy of security concerns.
Domestically, the government is navigating a delicate political landscape, evidenced by internal divisions within the ruling coalition over constitutional reforms and growing opposition demands for a more inclusive and transparent national dialogue. At the same time, the presidency’s emphasis on government performance reviews and addressing fiscal pressures, including civil service salary delays, highlights a commitment to administrative efficiency and accountability.
In parallel, the DRC is making progress in areas such as agricultural transformation, industrial partnerships, and gender equality institutionalization. However, these gains remain fragile, and achieving lasting stability will require not only the effective implementation of regional peace agreements, but also a sustained effort to strengthen governance, ensure mineral traceability, and address the urgent health and humanitarian needs of the population.
In conclusion, while the DRC demonstrates resilience and strategic initiative, its future stability hinges on balancing security, diplomacy, and internal reforms to create a more peaceful, inclusive, and prosperous nation.
By Glad Musema
Jeff Buleli

title: Rwanda and Singapore Strengthen Financial Sector Cooperation
excerpt: Singapore, February 25, 2026 – Rwanda and Singapore are expanding cooperation in the financial sector, focusing on banking, financial technology, and capacity building for government institutions. The Rwandan Ambassador to Singapore, Innocent B. Muhizi, held talks with representa
title_en: Rwanda and Singapore Strengthen Financial Sector Cooperation
excerpt_en: Singapore, February 25, 2026 – Rwanda and Singapore are expanding cooperation in the financial sector, focusing on banking, financial technology, and capacity building for government institutions. The Rwandan Ambassador to Singapore, Innocent B. Muhizi, held talks with representa
body_en:
Singapore, February 25, 2026 – Rwanda and Singapore are expanding cooperation in the financial sector, focusing on banking, financial technology, and capacity building for government institutions.
The Rwandan Ambassador to Singapore, Innocent B. Muhizi, held talks with representatives from Singapore’s banking sector and Ministry of Foreign Affairs, emphasizing opportunities for multi-sectoral collaboration, knowledge sharing, and partnerships to promote growth and innovation.
During a meeting with Ai Boon Ong-Ang, President of the Singapore Bankers Association, discussions centered on banking sector collaboration, particularly in fintech, as Singapore supports Rwanda’s goal of becoming a regional Fintech hub.
Ambassador Muhizi also met with Jolene Tan, Director General for Development Partnerships, to discuss continued cooperation in capacity building programs for civil servants, including knowledge development, institutional strengthening, and creating sustainable cooperation mechanisms.
Rwanda and Singapore already maintain partnerships in technology development, innovation, education, green technology, and capacity building. The countries also collaborate through FOSS, an organization established in 1992 to foster international cooperation.
In September 2023, the two countries signed a cooperation agreement to enhance population welfare and promote economic development, laying the groundwork for ongoing financial and technological collaboration.

title: Rwanda Plans $5 Billion Nuclear Power Plant to Boost Electricity Supply
excerpt: Kigali, February 24, 2026 – The Rwanda government estimates that more than $5 billion will be required to construct the country’s first nuclear power plant, a strategic project aimed at significantly increasing electricity production nationwide. Officials indicated that the plann
title_en: Rwanda Plans $5 Billion Nuclear Power Plant to Boost Electricity Supply
excerpt_en: Kigali, February 24, 2026 – The Rwanda government estimates that more than $5 billion will be required to construct the country’s first nuclear power plant, a strategic project aimed at significantly increasing electricity production nationwide. Officials indicated that the plann
body_en:
Kigali, February 24, 2026 – The Rwanda government estimates that more than $5 billion will be required to construct the country’s first nuclear power plant, a strategic project aimed at significantly increasing electricity production nationwide.
Officials indicated that the planned nuclear energy project is expected to strengthen the country’s energy capacity and support long-term industrial development. The initiative was highlighted during a meeting bringing together public institutions and private-sector stakeholders to discuss the investment opportunities linked to the construction of the facility.
Authorities emphasized that building the nuclear power station will require a major financial commitment, estimated between $5 billion and $6 billion, and stressed the importance of private sector participation. The project is expected to involve local industries, particularly companies producing cement, steel, and construction materials, which are among the country’s largest electricity consumers.
The project is also intended to promote local industrial involvement, with national companies encouraged to meet international quality standards in order to contribute to the construction and supply chain. Officials warned that relying exclusively on foreign contractors would represent a missed opportunity for domestic economic growth.
The future nuclear facility is expected to supply electricity across the country and improve industrial productivity, particularly in energy-intensive sectors.
According to projections, Rwanda’s first nuclear plant could become operational in the 2030s, with a specialized workforce of about 230 employees expected to be ready by 2028.
The installation is planned on a site covering between 15 and 50 square kilometers, located far from residential areas. The design includes advanced safety systems, allowing the plant to automatically shut down in the event of a malfunction, preventing the release of harmful radiation.

title: Complaint Filed at ICC Against Congolese General Over Alleged Anti-Tutsi Remarks
excerpt: A group of Congolese Tutsi organizations has filed a complaint at the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague, accusing former Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (FARDC) spokesperson Sylvain Ekenge of incitement and hate speech targeting the Tutsi commun
title_en: Complaint Filed at ICC Against Congolese General Over Alleged Anti-Tutsi Remarks
excerpt_en: A group of Congolese Tutsi organizations has filed a complaint at the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague, accusing former Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (FARDC) spokesperson Sylvain Ekenge of incitement and hate speech targeting the Tutsi commun
body_en:
A group of Congolese Tutsi organizations has filed a complaint at the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague, accusing former Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (FARDC) spokesperson Sylvain Ekenge of incitement and hate speech targeting the Tutsi community.
The complaint was submitted on February 17, 2026, by Belgian lawyer Bernard Maingain, who represents several Congolese Tutsi families and organizations. According to the filing, statements made by Gen. Maj. Ekenge could fuel discrimination and violence against the Tutsi minority in the Democratic Republic of Congo.
The legal action stems from comments reportedly made by Ekenge in December 2025 during an appearance on the national broadcaster Radio‑Télévision Nationale Congolaise (RTNC). During the broadcast, he allegedly discouraged Congolese Tutsi women from having children with people from other ethnic groups and warned men to be cautious when marrying them.
The remarks sparked strong criticism from human rights groups and members of the Tutsi community, leading to Ekenge’s temporary suspension from his role as military spokesperson.
Lawyer Maingain argued in the complaint that the statements form part of a broader pattern of rhetoric targeting the Tutsi ethnic group in the DRC. He also claimed that certain individuals who promote such rhetoric have received political backing from figures within the government, including government spokesperson Patrick Muyaya.
According to Maingain, the situation creates a legal paradox, where Congolese law criminalizes hate speech, yet authorities have allegedly failed to enforce those provisions consistently.
The lawyer further recalled that Congolese families had previously filed a similar complaint in 2020, warning about the spread of anti-Tutsi rhetoric. He said that case was never fully investigated, despite evidence being submitted to national authorities.
In his letter to the ICC Prosecutor, Maingain urged the court to examine the evidence and determine whether the statements constitute crimes under international law, including incitement to persecution or violence against an ethnic group.
Under ICC procedures, once a complaint is received, the Prosecutor’s Office reviews the allegations and supporting evidence. If the information is considered credible and within the court’s jurisdiction, prosecutors may open a preliminary examination and potentially build a case for formal judicial proceedings.
