title: Over 160 Killed in Armed Attack in South Sudan
excerpt: At least 169 people, including security personnel, were killed when unidentified gunmen attacked the Abiemnom district in Ruweng State, South Sudan, in the early hours of March 1, 2026. According to Ruweng State Information Minister James Monyluak Mijok, the attackers are believe
title_en: Over 160 Killed in Armed Attack in South Sudan
excerpt_en: At least 169 people, including security personnel, were killed when unidentified gunmen attacked the Abiemnom district in Ruweng State, South Sudan, in the early hours of March 1, 2026. According to Ruweng State Information Minister James Monyluak Mijok, the attackers are believe
body_en:
At least 169 people, including security personnel, were killed when unidentified gunmen attacked the Abiemnom district in Ruweng State, South Sudan, in the early hours of March 1, 2026.
According to Ruweng State Information Minister James Monyluak Mijok, the attackers are believed to be fighters linked to the Sudan-based SPLA-IO, who launched a coordinated assault on the area.
Mijok said the militants engaged in intense clashes with local security forces for several hours, with the fighting lasting between four and five hours. During the attack, homes and shops were set on fire, causing widespread destruction.
Among the 169 victims were children, women, elderly civilians and members of the state’s security forces, including police officers, the minister said.
The United Nations Mission in South Sudan (UNMISS) reported that the violence forced around 1,000 civilians to flee their homes, while 23 injured people have been treated following the attack.
UNMISS said that after the fighting subsided, it began working with South Sudanese security forces to help restore stability and security in the Abiemnom area.

title_en: Rwanda’s Warnings Ignored Before Uvira Battle
excerpt_en: Kigali, March 8, 2026 – President Paul Kagame said that Rwanda had repeatedly warned the international community about escalating violence in Uvira, South Kivu, prior to the AFC/M23 coalition capturing parts of the territory in the Democratic Republic of Congo. In a meeting with
body_en:
Kigali, March 8, 2026 – President Paul Kagame said that Rwanda had repeatedly warned the international community about escalating violence in Uvira, South Kivu, prior to the AFC/M23 coalition capturing parts of the territory in the Democratic Republic of Congo.
In a meeting with his counterparts in Rwanda on March 6, 2026, Kagame explained that the Washington peace talks had created a temporary lull and established a framework for resolving security concerns. Despite this, clashes continued between the DRC government, Burundian troops, FDLR, and Wazalendo armed groups, which blocked civilian access and launched ground and air attacks in South Kivu.
“Despite the ongoing talks, forces continued to clash in eastern DRC. Thousands of Burundian troops and pro-government forces remained in line and launched attacks, blocking civilians and striking relentlessly,” Kagame said.
The President stated that these ongoing attacks prompted the AFC/M23 to act against government forces to stop the assaults and reopen civilian access. The period from February 22 to March 8, 2026, was marked by a complex interplay of diplomatic tensions, regional security challenges, and domestic progress for Rwanda. The ongoing conflict in eastern DRC—underscored by the death of AFC/M23 spokesperson Col. Willy Ngoma and heated exchanges at the United Nations—continues to strain regional relations, highlighting the persistent need for adherence to the Washington Peace Accords and inclusive dialogue.
Despite these external pressures, Rwanda has maintained a firm commitment to long-term development and modernization. In addition, Rwanda has strengthened international partnerships, notably with Singapore and India, and expanded trade licenses for domestic industries under Pan-African standards, positioning the country as an emerging hub for innovation and regional commerce.
Looking ahead, the successful implementation of the 7th East African Community (EAC) Development Plan and the resolution of cross-border challenges, particularly with Burundi, will be essential to fostering deeper regional integration and ensuring sustainable peace in the Great Lakes region.
In conclusion, Rwanda’s strategic initiatives and international engagement demonstrate resilience and forward-looking governance, balancing domestic progress with regional stability in a challenging geopolitical environment.

title: President Tshisekedi Orders Review of Council of Ministers Decisions to Strengthen Government Action
excerpt: KINSHASA March 1, 2026 — President Félix Tshisekedi has instructed Prime Minister Judith Suminwa to conduct a comprehensive review of all presidential instructions issued during Council of Ministers meetings, amid concerns over the non-implementation of key decisions. Since takin
title_en: President Tshisekedi Orders Review of Council of Ministers Decisions to Strengthen Government Action
excerpt_en: KINSHASA March 1, 2026 — President Félix Tshisekedi has instructed Prime Minister Judith Suminwa to conduct a comprehensive review of all presidential instructions issued during Council of Ministers meetings, amid concerns over the non-implementation of key decisions. Since takin
body_en:
KINSHASA March 1, 2026 — President Félix Tshisekedi has instructed Prime Minister Judith Suminwa to conduct a comprehensive review of all presidential instructions issued during Council of Ministers meetings, amid concerns over the non-implementation of key decisions.
Since taking office, President Tshisekedi has designated Fridays for Council of Ministers sessions, during which presidential instructions are given, texts adopted, and government members present proposals for their sectors. However, several instructions have reportedly remained unimplemented or inadequately addressed, raising concerns over governmental accountability and efficiency.
At the 80th Council of Ministers meeting held at the African Union City complex, President Tshisekedi emphasized that the proper execution of these instructions is crucial for good governance, the credibility of public action, and state effectiveness. He stressed the need for results that are concrete, measurable, verifiable, and tangible for citizens, warning that failure to implement directives cannot be tolerated.
The comprehensive review, led by Prime Minister Suminwa with support from her office and the Presidency, will systematically assess individual and institutional performance, identify gaps, and propose corrective measures to ensure optimal government functioning aligned with national priorities.
The president cited specific examples, including the creation of 53 institutions during his first five-year term, noted by former Finance Minister Nicolas Kazadi, which require evaluation to determine whether they should be streamlined or restructured for efficiency.
This initiative is seen as a timely effort to reinforce discipline, accountability, and performance within the government, with the objective of delivering tangible improvements for the Congolese population and restoring confidence in public administration.

title: UN Proposes Initiatives to Strengthen Governance and Combat Illicit Flows
excerpt: Critical Minerals March 7, 2026 — At the UN Security Council meeting on Energy, Critical Minerals, and Security, the growing importance of critical minerals in the global economy was highlighted. Minerals such as lithium, cobalt, and nickel are now essential for digital technolog
title_en: UN Proposes Initiatives to Strengthen Governance and Combat Illicit Flows
excerpt_en: Critical Minerals March 7, 2026 — At the UN Security Council meeting on Energy, Critical Minerals, and Security, the growing importance of critical minerals in the global economy was highlighted. Minerals such as lithium, cobalt, and nickel are now essential for digital technolog
body_en:
Critical Minerals March 7, 2026 — At the UN Security Council meeting on Energy, Critical Minerals, and Security, the growing importance of critical minerals in the global economy was highlighted. Minerals such as lithium, cobalt, and nickel are now essential for digital technologies and the energy transition, with trade in raw and semi-processed minerals reaching $2.5 trillion in 2023. Demand is projected to triple by 2030 and quadruple by 2040, creating opportunities for job creation, economic diversification, and sustainable development.
The UN outlined three key priorities to ensure conflict-affected countries benefit responsibly from their natural resources. First, exploitation must lead to fair and equitable outcomes, strengthening national institutions, regulatory frameworks, and processing capacities, while mitigating negative impacts. Second, multilateral and regional action is needed to improve traceability, combat illicit flows, and build resilient supply chains. Third, mediation tools must be deployed to address conflicts related to natural resources, fostering cooperative relationships and enabling parties to share benefits equitably.
The session comes amid ongoing conflict in eastern DRC, where the AFC/M23 rebellion occupies areas in North and South Kivu. The Congolese government frames these attacks as part of an economic war aimed at plundering critical minerals, while providing military support to rebels. Rwanda denies involvement, citing the threat of the FDLR, a group with a genocidal ideology, and framing the situation as linked to Tutsi community security concerns.
Efforts to resolve tensions include the Washington Process, addressing relations between Kinshasa and Kigali, and the Doha Process, focused on the AFC/M23 crisis. Despite these initiatives, hostilities persist, endangering civilian populations and worsening humanitarian conditions amid declining international aid.
The UN emphasized that equitable and responsible management of critical minerals could lift millions out of poverty, promote peace, and support sustainable development, but only if governance, traceability, and diplomacy are effectively enforced.

title: Clashes Between AFC/M23 Rebels and Wazalendo Spread Fear in Kavumu

title_en: Clashes Between AFC/M23 Rebels and Wazalendo Spread Fear in Kavumu
excerpt_en: KAVUMU, South Kivu February 21, 2026 — Residents of Kavumu and surrounding localities in Kabare territory, eastern DRC, spent the day gripped by fear and uncertainty as armed clashes erupted between AFC/M23 rebels and Wazalendo fighters. According to information gathered locally,
body_en:
KAVUMU, South Kivu February 21, 2026 — Residents of Kavumu and surrounding localities in Kabare territory, eastern DRC, spent the day gripped by fear and uncertainty as armed clashes erupted between AFC/M23 rebels and Wazalendo fighters.
According to information gathered locally, the exchange of gunfire began early in the morning before temporarily subsiding, only to resume later in the evening, heightening tensions across the area.
Witnesses reported that the violence broke out shortly after a Wazalendo combatant was evacuated from a health facility, an incident that appeared to trigger the confrontation between the two armed groups. Within hours, heavy gunfire could be heard across several localities, particularly along the Katana–Kavumu axis.
Residents described hearing continuous bursts of gunfire, creating panic among civilians who were forced to seek shelter in their homes throughout the day.
The situation escalated again at around 6:30 p.m., when renewed shooting was reported in Kavumu, signaling a fresh wave of confrontation. Shortly afterward, observers noted a reinforcement of Wazalendo fighters near the Kavumu commercial center, suggesting preparations for further engagement.
The security situation quickly affected daily life and movement in the area. Traffic along the Bukavu–Kavumu road, one of the region’s key routes, was severely disrupted as armed elements positioned weapons along the Katana–Kavumu section.
The presence of combatants and the intensity of the shooting forced many residents to remain indoors, while commercial activities and transport were largely paralyzed.
The latest clashes illustrate the fragile security environment in parts of South Kivu, where confrontations between AFC/M23 forces and local Wazalendo militias continue to threaten civilian safety and regional stability.

title: AFC/M23 Denounces Kinshasa’s “General Offensive” Amid Escalating Fighting
excerpt: MASISI, North Kivu February 25, 2026 — The AFC/M23 rebel movement has accused the Kinshasa government of launching a “general offensive” across multiple frontlines following the death of its military spokesperson, Willy Ngoma, in a drone strike near Rubaya on Tuesday, February 24
title_en: AFC/M23 Denounces Kinshasa’s “General Offensive” Amid Escalating Fighting
excerpt_en: MASISI, North Kivu February 25, 2026 — The AFC/M23 rebel movement has accused the Kinshasa government of launching a “general offensive” across multiple frontlines following the death of its military spokesperson, Willy Ngoma, in a drone strike near Rubaya on Tuesday, February 24
body_en:
MASISI, North Kivu February 25, 2026 — The AFC/M23 rebel movement has accused the Kinshasa government of launching a “general offensive” across multiple frontlines following the death of its military spokesperson, Willy Ngoma, in a drone strike near Rubaya on Tuesday, February 24.
Bertrand Bisimwa, president of M23 and deputy coordinator of AFC/M23, stated on Wednesday that the operation represents a coordinated military campaign, violating the ceasefire and reflecting a deliberate choice to prioritize military action over dialogue. He criticized the absence of any visible initiative to halt the government’s offensive, contrasting it with the swift international reactions observed when the rebels defend themselves.
Lawrence Kanyuka, spokesperson for AFC/M23, reported several attacks on Wednesday: at 9:00 a.m. in Rutigita (Minembwe), 10:30 a.m. in Kitazungura (Kalehe territory), and 12:00 p.m. in Rugezi and its surroundings (Minembwe). The attacks reportedly involved armed drones and heavy artillery, resulting in casualties and population displacements.
Ngoma’s death comes after Magloire Paluku was killed, amid intensifying hostilities in eastern DRC. The escalation follows challenges to the ceasefire proposed by Angola, airstrikes by FARDC, and ground offensives by Wazalendo forces, allies of the government, targeting AFC/M23 positions, a group reportedly supported by Rwanda according to the United Nations. Ngoma had been sanctioned by the United States in 2023 for the group’s role in murders and sexual violence against civilians.
On the ground, fighting has resumed with intensity in Kibanda, approximately two kilometers from Kasopo, in the Nyamaboko 1 group (Osso Banyungu sector). FARDC troops and Wazalendo fighters from Buhimba launched an offensive against rebel positions, with heavy and light weapons fire reported in and around Kibanda. Explosions were also heard in neighboring villages, notably Kashebere in Walikale territory. Residents described the situation as volatile, fearing further escalation. Since the beginning of the week, clashes have spread across Osso Banyungu, Katoy sectors, and the Bahunde chiefdom, reflecting a multi-front offensive in a strategic territory near mining areas and supply routes.
Renewed fighting also erupted in the villages of Lumbishi and Kashovu, where Wazalendo militias launched a counter-offensive early Wednesday to reclaim the localities. The clashes triggered further population displacements, with families fleeing the areas affected by the fighting.
The ongoing conflict has also disrupted communications in Masisi territory, including the mining town of Rubaya, which has been without telephone, internet, and mobile money services since Tuesday, February 24. The outage has directly affected economic activity and financial exchanges, forcing some residents to travel up to ten kilometers or climb hills to regain a signal. The interruption follows drone attacks by the FARDC, including the strike that killed Willy Ngoma, highlighting the broader humanitarian and operational impact of the military escalation.
These developments underscore the fragility of security in Masisi and surrounding areas, with residents bearing the brunt of the ongoing multi-front offensive and population displacements while armed clashes continue to escalate.

Ngoma’s death comes after Magloire Paluku was killed, amid intensifying hostilities in eastern DRC. The escalation follows challenges to the ceasefire proposed by Angola, airstrikes by FARDC, and ground offensives by Wazalendo forces, allies of the government, targeting AFC/M23 positions, a group reportedly supported by Rwanda according to the United Nations. Ngoma had been sanctioned by the United States in 2023 for the group’s role in murders and sexual violence against civilians.
On the ground, fighting has resumed with intensity in Kibanda, approximately two kilometers from Kasopo, in the Nyamaboko 1 group (Osso Banyungu sector). FARDC troops and Wazalendo fighters from Buhimba launched an offensive against rebel positions, with heavy and light weapons fire reported in and around Kibanda. Explosions were also heard in neighboring villages, notably Kashebere in Walikale territory. Residents described the situation as volatile, fearing further escalation. Since the beginning of the week, clashes have spread across Osso Banyungu, Katoy sectors, and the Bahunde chiefdom, reflecting a multi-front offensive in a strategic territory near mining areas and supply routes.
Renewed fighting also erupted in the villages of Lumbishi and Kashovu, where Wazalendo militias launched a counter-offensive early Wednesday to reclaim the localities. The clashes triggered further population displacements, with families fleeing the areas affected by the fighting.
The ongoing conflict has also disrupted communications in Masisi territory, including the mining town of Rubaya, which has been without telephone, internet, and mobile money services since Tuesday, February 24. The outage has directly affected economic activity and financial exchanges, forcing some residents to travel up to ten kilometers or climb hills to regain a signal. The interruption follows drone attacks by the FARDC, including the strike that killed Willy Ngoma, highlighting the broader humanitarian and operational impact of the military escalation.
These developments underscore the fragility of security in Masisi and surrounding areas, with residents bearing the brunt of the ongoing multi-front offensive and population displacements while armed clashes continue to escalate.

RUTSHURU – February 27, 2026 — Two civilians were killed on Thursday, February 26, during clashes between AFC/M23 rebels and an unidentified armed group in the JTN concession near Mwesso, Bwito chiefdom, North Kivu.
Local sources reported that the confrontation erupted in the early evening when AFC/M23 patrols encountered armed men whose affiliation remains unclear. Heavy gunfire ensued across the agricultural and pastoral area, causing panic among nearby residents.
The victims were identified as a young girl and a cattle herder, both struck by stray bullets. The incident also resulted in the death of twelve cows, impacting local herders whose livelihoods depend on livestock.
After several minutes, calm gradually returned, though the situation remains fragile. No official reports have been released regarding casualties among the combatants.
This incident underscores the ongoing insecurity in Bwito chiefdom, where civilians continue to bear the brunt of sporadic clashes and the presence of multiple armed groups.

title: U.S. Imposes Sanctions on Rwandan Army and Four Nationals over DRC Involvement
excerpt: WASHINGTON, D.C. March 2, 2026 — The United States Treasury Department announced Monday that the Rwanda Defense Force (RDF) and four Rwandan nationals have been sanctioned for their involvement in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC)
title_en: U.S. Imposes Sanctions on Rwandan Army and Four Nationals over DRC Involvement
excerpt_en: WASHINGTON, D.C. March 2, 2026 — The United States Treasury Department announced Monday that the Rwanda Defense Force (RDF) and four Rwandan nationals have been sanctioned for their involvement in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC)
body_en:
WASHINGTON, D.C. March 2, 2026 — The United States Treasury Department announced Monday that the Rwanda Defense Force (RDF) and four Rwandan nationals have been sanctioned for their involvement in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).
The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) added the RDF and individuals Stanislas Gashugi, Ruki Karusisi, Mubarakh Muganga (also known as "MK MUBARKH"), and Vincent Nyakarundi to its Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons (SDN) list. Assets of the designated entities and individuals under U.S. jurisdiction are now frozen, and U.S. citizens and companies are prohibited from engaging in transactions with them.
At the same time, OFAC issued General Licence No. 1 under 31 CFR Part 547, authorizing, until April 1, 2026, transactions that are “normally incidental and necessary” to the phased cessation of dealings with the RDF or any entity in which it holds at least 50% ownership. Payments to blocked individuals must be directed to blocked accounts, and the licence does not authorize other prohibited transactions unless explicitly approved.
This move comes amid escalating tensions in eastern DRC, where the RDF has been accused of supporting the AFC/M23 rebel movement, contributing to ongoing clashes in North and South Kivu provinces. The sanctions reflect Washington’s effort to hold Rwandan actors accountable for their involvement in destabilizing operations in the DRC.

title: FARDC Conducts Airstrike on AFC/M23 Position Near Mushaki
excerpt: MASISI March 7, 2026 — An AFC/M23 rebel position in the Mushaki area of Masisi territory, North Kivu, was targeted by an airstrike attributed to the FARDC (Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo) on the morning of Saturday, March 7. Local sources reported that the strik

excerpt_en: MASISI March 7, 2026 — An AFC/M23 rebel position in the Mushaki area of Masisi territory, North Kivu, was targeted by an airstrike attributed to the FARDC (Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo) on the morning of Saturday, March 7. Local sources reported that the strik
body_en:
MASISI March 7, 2026 — An AFC/M23 rebel position in the Mushaki area of Masisi territory, North Kivu, was targeted by an airstrike attributed to the FARDC (Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo) on the morning of Saturday, March 7.
Local sources reported that the strike focused on a rebel position situated on the farm of businessman and former national deputy Edouard Mwangachuchu, a site reportedly used as a logistical base for the rebels. The operation was carried out using a military drone, part of the Congolese army’s ongoing campaign against AFC/M23 positions.
Residents heard a loud explosion followed by unusual activity near the target. While AFC/M23 political spokesperson Lawrence Kanyuka claimed civilian casualties, local sources dispute this, noting no immediate confirmation of civilian injuries. The FARDC has not released an official statement regarding the strike.
This airstrike occurs amid a volatile security situation in Masisi and wider North Kivu, where clashes between government forces and AFC/M23 rebels have persisted for months. Mushaki, strategically located on the axis linking Masisi to Goma, has repeatedly been a focus of military operations.
Local populations continue to live under fear, with concern over further escalation and humanitarian consequences in an already conflict-affected area. Reports indicate ongoing troop movements from both sides near Mushaki, maintaining a tense atmosphere.

title: Bobi Wine Refuses to Negotiate with Uganda Government While in Hiding
excerpt: Uganda, February 25, 2026 – Opposition politician Robert Kyagulanyi Ssentamu, popularly known as Bobi Wine, has rejected calls to negotiate with the Ugandan government while remaining in hiding, nearly six weeks after the country’s presidential elections. Bobi Wine went into hidi
title_en: Bobi Wine Refuses to Negotiate with Uganda Government While in Hiding
excerpt_en: Uganda, February 25, 2026 – Opposition politician Robert Kyagulanyi Ssentamu, popularly known as Bobi Wine, has rejected calls to negotiate with the Ugandan government while remaining in hiding, nearly six weeks after the country’s presidential elections. Bobi Wine went into hidi
body_en:
Uganda, February 25, 2026 – Opposition politician Robert Kyagulanyi Ssentamu, popularly known as Bobi Wine, has rejected calls to negotiate with the Ugandan government while remaining in hiding, nearly six weeks after the country’s presidential elections.
Bobi Wine went into hiding on January 15, 2026, following the controversial re-election of President Yoweri Kaguta Museveni. He has voiced concerns over the conduct of the elections and alleges that security forces are seeking to harm him, which he says is why he remains in seclusion.
In an interview with UK’s Channel 4, Bobi Wine stated that he would only come out of hiding if necessary to avoid being forced into government demands.
Asked about ongoing discussions and calls for him to meet with President Museveni or his son, General Muhoozi Kainerugaba, Bobi Wine said he could not negotiate under coercion. “You cannot negotiate with someone who has a gun to your neck and say ‘let’s talk.’ Only those who are free can truly discuss. That is what meaningful dialogue looks like,” he said.
The Ugandan Electoral Commission reported that President Museveni won with 71.65% of the vote, while Bobi Wine secured 24.72%. Despite the official results, Bobi Wine continues to question the transparency and fairness of the election process.

body_en:
Arusha, March 7, 2026 – Ambassador Stephen Patrick Mbundi has been appointed Secretary-General of the East African Community (EAC), replacing Kenyan diplomat Veronica Nduva, who held the position since 2024.
The appointment was made during the 25th General Assembly of the EAC, where Mbundi was named for a five-year term from 2026 to 2031. The EAC statement highlighted that he is expected to strengthen diplomatic cooperation among member states and enhance the cohesion of the regional community.
Following the announcement, Mbundi was sworn in before the General Assembly of Heads of State and immediately assumed his duties. Prior to this appointment, he served as Permanent Secretary in charge of EAC Affairs at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Tanzania.

title: Over 60 Convicted in Crackdown on Illegal Mining
excerpt: KARONGI, February 24, 2026 — Authorities in Karongi District have intensified efforts against illegal mining, leading to the conviction of more than 60 individuals over the past three months as officials seek to protect legal mining investments and curb environmental damage. Oper
title_en: Over 60 Convicted in Crackdown on Illegal Mining
excerpt_en: KARONGI, February 24, 2026 — Authorities in Karongi District have intensified efforts against illegal mining, leading to the conviction of more than 60 individuals over the past three months as officials seek to protect legal mining investments and curb environmental damage. Oper
body_en:
KARONGI, February 24, 2026 — Authorities in Karongi District have intensified efforts against illegal mining, leading to the conviction of more than 60 individuals over the past three months as officials seek to protect legal mining investments and curb environmental damage.
Operators in the legal mining sector say illegal miners continue to threaten their businesses by selling minerals at lower prices while avoiding tax obligations, creating what they describe as unfair competition.
Illegal mining activities are particularly widespread in the sectors of Rubengera, Rugabano, Gashari, Murambi, Bwishyura, and Mutuntu, where miners operate along several rivers, including Musogoro, Mashyiga, and Nyabahanga.
Environmental and Agricultural Damage
Residents report that illegal mining operations have caused significant environmental degradation, including the destruction of farmland, crop losses, and damage to riverbanks.
The affected waterways — including the Nyabahanga and Musogoro rivers, which flow into Lake Kivu, and the Mashyiga River, a tributary of the Nyabarongo River — play an important role in the region’s ecosystem and agriculture.
Legal Miners Report Economic Losses
Investors in licensed mining operations warn that illegal extraction activities are undermining their financial viability.
One long-time legal mining operator in Karongi District, who has worked in the sector for over 13 years, reported producing five to six tons of minerals per month and employing between 400 and 500 workers. He said illegal traders avoid paying taxes, allowing them to sell minerals at significantly lower prices, which weakens the formal market.
According to the investor, legally mined minerals are sold at approximately 35,000 Rwandan francs per kilogram, while illegally sourced minerals are sold for around 30,000 francs, making it difficult for licensed operators to remain competitive.
Authorities Intensify Enforcement
Local authorities say enforcement measures introduced since late 2025 are beginning to show results.
Officials have held meetings with landowners across the district to warn them about the legal consequences of allowing unauthorized mining on their property. Landowners who fail to report illegal activity risk being treated as accomplices under the law.
As part of the crackdown, more than 60 suspects have been prosecuted and convicted in court, contributing to a decline in illegal mining activities, according to district officials.
Local Official Under Investigation
Authorities have also detained a local administrative leader accused of collaborating with illegal miners.
The official is under investigation for allegedly leaking information to suspects and helping them evade arrest during enforcement operations.
Officials say the ongoing crackdown aims to protect natural resources, support legal mining investors, and reduce the economic and environmental impact of illegal mining in Karongi District.

The AFC/M23 coalition has confirmed the death of Colonel Willy Ngoma, a senior officer and spokesperson of its military wing, the Congolese Revolutionary Army (ARC), who was killed in North Kivu province in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
The announcement was made on the evening of February 28, 2026, by AFC/M23 spokesperson Lawrence Kanyuka, who stated that the officer died on February 24, 2026 during ongoing fighting in the region.
According to Kanyuka, Col. Willy Ngoma was killed at around 9:00 a.m. when a drone strike attributed to the Congolese army targeted positions where he and other fighters were engaged in combat against forces aligned with the DRC government.
Kanyuka accused the government of violating a ceasefire agreement and escalating hostilities, alleging that attacks involving drones and military operations have targeted both AFC/M23 fighters and civilians.
“This violation of the ceasefire has cost us one of our senior officers,” he said, adding that the situation continues to result in casualties among what he described as innocent civilians.
The coalition said clashes have intensified in several conflict-affected areas of North and South Kivu, including Mweso, Rutigita, Kitazungura, Rugezi, Rubaya, Walikale, Masisi, Kalehe, Minembwe and Gasheke, where fighting and drone strikes have been reported in recent weeks.
Particularly heavy fighting has been reported around Rubaya, where armed groups associated with the Wazalendo coalition, including CMC-FDP, Raia Mutomboki and PARECO-FFF, have been involved in clashes with AFC/M23 forces. The coalition said reinforcements were deployed to the area in response to the attacks.
Kanyuka stated that the alliance remains committed to protecting civilians in territories under its control while continuing to participate in peace efforts aimed at ending the conflict.
Colonel Willy Ngoma became widely known as the spokesperson of the M23 movement when the group resumed armed operations in November 2021 following the collapse of negotiations with the DRC government.
During that period, he regularly communicated the movement’s position, arguing that Kinyarwanda-speaking Congolese communities, particularly those of Tutsi origin, were facing violence and displacement.
Ngoma was also among senior commanders who appeared publicly in areas captured by the movement in eastern Congo to reassure local populations during military advances.
At the start of the renewed rebellion, Ngoma held the rank of Major. He was promoted to Colonel in January 2024, a promotion the movement said recognized his leadership and operational performance during the conflict.

body_en:
Rumangabo, North Kivu, March 8, 2026 – The AFC/M23 coalition, engaged in conflict with the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government, announced the handover of more than 5,000 captured Wazalendo fighters and FARDC soldiers to the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC). The handover ceremony took place on March 2, 2026, in Rumangabo, North Kivu, and the prisoners are to be transported to Kinshasa and returned to the DRC government, according to AFC/M23 spokesperson Lawrence Kanyuka.
The coalition described the move as a demonstration of its commitment to humanitarian principles, building trust between warring parties, and reducing hostilities.
However, Kanyuka criticized the Kinshasa government, claiming it has refused to release some fighters and other individuals allegedly detained illegally. “Although AFC/M23 is taking concrete measures to reduce the atmosphere of war, the Kinshasa government remains stubborn. It continues to refuse to release our comrades, arrested simply because of their appearance,” he said.
The coalition accused the government of violating the ceasefire agreement and targeting civilians and their property, urging peace negotiators and domestic and international partners to closely monitor compliance. Kanyu

excerpt_en: KINSHASA February 27, 2026 — The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has officially nominated Juliana Amato Lumumba, daughter of independence hero Patrice Emery Lumumba, as its candidate for Secretary General of the International Organisation of La Francophonie (OIF). A political
body_en:
KINSHASA February 27, 2026 — The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has officially nominated Juliana Amato Lumumba, daughter of independence hero Patrice Emery Lumumba, as its candidate for Secretary General of the International Organisation of La Francophonie (OIF).
A political science graduate from Paris and a prominent figure in Congolese public life, Lumumba brings over 30 years of experience in governance, cultural diplomacy, and international cooperation. She has held key positions in the Congolese government, including Deputy Minister and Minister of Culture (1997–2001), and has extensive entrepreneurial experience in consulting, communications, and international trade. From 2007 to 2015, she served as Secretary General of the Union of African Chambers of Commerce (UACCIAP), contributing to continental economic integration.
According to Crispin Mbadu, Minister Delegate responsible for Francophonie and the Congolese Diaspora, Lumumba’s candidacy reflects the DRC’s desire to promote a modern, inclusive, and people-centered Francophonie, highlighting her leadership, pan-African expertise, cultural diplomacy, commitment to women’s empowerment, and fluency in multiple languages, including French, Arabic, English, Lingala, and Swahili.
Her nomination comes amid a diplomatic contest with Rwanda, as current OIF Secretary General Louise Mushikiwabo seeks a third term. The DRC intends to submit Lumumba’s candidacy before June 2026.
The selection was reinforced by recent diplomatic engagement with France, including the February 2 visit of French Minister Delegate for Francophonie Éléonore Caroit to Kinshasa and the February 25 meeting in Paris between Presidents Emmanuel Macron and Félix Tshisekedi, emphasizing the DRC’s strategic role in the future of the Francophone space in Africa.
The DRC government stated that Lumumba’s vision, combined with her extensive public service and international experience, positions her as a candidate capable of strengthening solidarity, promoting diversity, and fostering development across Francophone countries.

title_en: UK-DRC Chamber of Commerce Launched to Boost Trade and Investment
excerpt_en: KINSHASA March 6, 2026 — The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and the United Kingdom (UK) launched the UK-DRC Chamber of Commerce, a platform aimed at strengthening trade, investment, and sustainable development between the two countries. The launch coincided with a ministerial
body_en:
KINSHASA March 6, 2026 — The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and the United Kingdom (UK) launched the UK-DRC Chamber of Commerce, a platform aimed at strengthening trade, investment, and sustainable development between the two countries. The launch coincided with a ministerial visit from the UK, highlighting the country’s commitment to long-term partnerships and high-quality investments in the DRC.
The Chamber of Commerce aims to bring Congolese and British businesses closer together, fostering partnerships that promote local value addition, skills transfer, and economic growth. Recent initiatives include a $25 million financing agreement to support small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and nearly £3 million to expand agricultural operations and strengthen climate resilience.
The DRC emphasized the importance of local processing of mineral resources to create quality jobs, develop technical skills, and ensure sustainable economic benefits for its population. Key requests made during the launch included establishing a direct London-Kinshasa air route and increasing the presence of British companies to support technology transfer and capacity building. The DRC also highlighted its access to global markets through trade agreements, including AGOA, UAE partnerships, EU Economic Partnership Agreements, the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), and upcoming agreements with China and India.
The Chamber plans to formalize its operational structure, expand membership, launch targeted business forums, and create regular networking opportunities between Congolese and British companies. The UK-DRC Chamber of Commerce is expected to accelerate trade, attract investment, create jobs, develop skills, and reinforce governance standards amid the DRC’s ongoing economic transformation.

title: Attempted Prison Escape Causes Major Damage at Bandundu

title_en: Attempted Prison Escape Causes Major Damage at Bandundu
excerpt_en: Bandundu, March 7, 2026 – Significant property damage was reported Friday evening at the Bandundu Central Prison following a thwarted escape attempt by inmates. The prison’s food store and kitchen were set on fire, while the doors and windows of the police station and several cel
body_en:
Bandundu, March 7, 2026 – Significant property damage was reported Friday evening at the Bandundu Central Prison following a thwarted escape attempt by inmates. The prison’s food store and kitchen were set on fire, while the doors and windows of the police station and several cell block doors were damaged.
Preliminary reports indicate one serious injury and several minor injuries, with warning shots fired by security forces to restore order. While some sources cite prolonged hunger as a possible trigger, provincial authorities suggest the unrest began as a minor incident between inmates that escalated.
Governor of Kwilu, Philippe Akamituna, described the situation: “The final straw was when a prisoner insulted the storekeeper and was punished. Ferre, a convicted hardened criminal, encouraged him and incited everyone to revolt. They burned fresh food and tried to break through the back to escape. They damaged the entrance gate and the window. There’s no famine; the prison had 60 sacks of cassava, but they ransacked and burned the food supplies.”
The incident comes days after civil society organizations in Kwilu condemned conditions at the Cinquantenaire Prison, noting that penitentiary subsidies had not been delivered for three quarters, leaving inmates in particularly difficult living conditions.

title_en: Intense Fighting in Kibanda as Government Forces Target AFC/M23 Positions
excerpt_en: MASISI, North Kivu February 25, 2026 — Clashes intensified on Wednesday, February 25, in Kibanda village, located approximately two kilometers from Kasopo in the Nyamaboko 1 group of the Osso Banyungu sector, as government forces and local fighters from Buhimba launched an offens
body_en:
MASISI, North Kivu February 25, 2026 — Clashes intensified on Wednesday, February 25, in Kibanda village, located approximately two kilometers from Kasopo in the Nyamaboko 1 group of the Osso Banyungu sector, as government forces and local fighters from Buhimba launched an offensive against AFC/M23 rebel positions that have controlled the area for several months.
The objective of the operation is reportedly to regain control of Kibanda and expel the rebels from this strategic locality. Heavy and light weapons fire has been reported since the morning, with explosions heard in nearby villages, including Kashebere in Walikale territory, spreading fear among civilians.
Residents described a volatile situation and expressed concern over a potential escalation of fighting throughout the day. The renewed hostilities in Kibanda coincide with a broader resurgence of clashes across Masisi territory, including the Osso Banyungu and Katoy sectors and the Bahunde chiefdom, reflecting an offensive strategy on multiple fronts in an area critical for mining operations and supply routes.
The persistent insecurity has prompted many families to abandon their homes, seeking safety in less exposed areas. The resulting population movements are aggravating an already fragile humanitarian situation in the region, highlighting the ongoing vulnerability of civilians amid repeated clashes between AFC/M23 rebels and government-allied forces.

body_en:
MASISI February 27, 2026 — Three civilians were seriously injured on Thursday evening, February 26, during an army drone strike targeting an AFC/M23 rebel position in the Isiro neighborhood of Nyabiondo, Masisi territory, North Kivu.
Local sources reported that the explosion sent shrapnel into nearby homes, injuring three residents from the same neighborhood, who were urgently evacuated to a medical facility for treatment.
No official figures have been released regarding casualties among the rebels. Access to the targeted site remains restricted, preventing independent verification of the damage.
The strike is part of resurgent military operations in Masisi, where clashes between government forces (FARDC) and AFC/M23 rebels have intensified in recent weeks. Nyabiondo continues to be a strategic focal point in the ongoing conflict.

title: Katoy Falls to AFC/M23 Amid Escalating Clashes

excerpt_en: MASISI March 2, 2026 — The AFC/M23 rebels have seized control of Katoy, the main town of the Katoy sector in southern Masisi, following intense clashes with the Armed Forces of the DRC (FARDC), supported by the Wazalendo militia. According to local security sources, the offensive
body_en:
MASISI March 2, 2026 — The AFC/M23 rebels have seized control of Katoy, the main town of the Katoy sector in southern Masisi, following intense clashes with the Armed Forces of the DRC (FARDC), supported by the Wazalendo militia.
According to local security sources, the offensive began early Sunday morning when the rebels attacked FARDC positions. Heavy exchanges of fire continued throughout the day, and by early evening, the town had fallen entirely under rebel control, marking a significant setback for government forces in this strategic area of southern Masisi.
The capture of Katoy has triggered a wave of population displacement. Residents, primarily women and children, fled to the bush and neighboring villages, abandoning homes and belongings. Many spent the night outdoors, exposed to harsh conditions and without immediate humanitarian aid, local sources reported.
This development underscores the ongoing volatility in southern Masisi, where positions continue to shift between the AFC/M23 and government forces. The resurgence of fighting in the region has further deepened the humanitarian crisis, compounding insecurity and instability for civilians in North Kivu.

excerpt_en: MASISI March 6, 2026 — AFC/M23 rebels have withdrawn without engaging in clashes from the villages of Buabo and Ndete in the Osso Banyungu sector of Masisi territory, North Kivu. Local sources reported the rebels’ absence early Thursday morning, March 5, after several days of occ
body_en:
MASISI March 6, 2026 — AFC/M23 rebels have withdrawn without engaging in clashes from the villages of Buabo and Ndete in the Osso Banyungu sector of Masisi territory, North Kivu.
Local sources reported the rebels’ absence early Thursday morning, March 5, after several days of occupation following previous fighting with the FARDC (Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo) and their Wazalendo allies.
Following the withdrawal, the Wazalendo forces reoccupied Buabo and Ndete on the morning of Friday, March 6, according to security sources. The reasons behind the rebels’ departure remain unclear, though some observers suggest that military pressure and encirclement strategies by government forces may have influenced the decision.
The security situation in Masisi territory remains volatile, with continued troop movements and sporadic clashes reported in surrounding villages. These ongoing hostilities are causing further civilian displacement, aggravating the already fragile humanitarian conditions in the region.

title: Rwandan Peacekeepers Provide Free Medical Care to Prisoners in Central African Republic
excerpt: Bria, February 25, 2026 – Rwandan peacekeepers deployed in the Central African Republic have provided free medical treatment to detainees at the Bria prison camp, as part of ongoing humanitarian assistance efforts under the United Nations peacekeeping mission. The operation was c
title_en: Rwandan Peacekeepers Provide Free Medical Care to Prisoners in Central African Republic
excerpt_en: Bria, February 25, 2026 – Rwandan peacekeepers deployed in the Central African Republic have provided free medical treatment to detainees at the Bria prison camp, as part of ongoing humanitarian assistance efforts under the United Nations peacekeeping mission. The operation was c
body_en:
Bria, February 25, 2026 – Rwandan peacekeepers deployed in the Central African Republic have provided free medical treatment to detainees at the Bria prison camp, as part of ongoing humanitarian assistance efforts under the United Nations peacekeeping mission.
The operation was carried out by members of the Rwandan Battle Group 8, supported by a Level II military hospital team, and aimed at addressing urgent healthcare needs among prisoners. Services included treatment for internal diseases, women’s health services, dental care, and other essential medical support.
Officials present during the operation included the Bria camp commander, the head of the Rwandan military hospital, and the commander of Rwandan Battle Group 8.
Local authorities welcomed the initiative, highlighting the longstanding cooperation between peacekeeping forces and local institutions. They emphasized that detainees often face serious challenges in accessing medical services, particularly due to shortages of medicines and limited healthcare resources.
The medical outreach was presented as part of the broader peacekeeping mandate, which focuses not only on security operations but also on the protection of civilians and the promotion of human dignity.
Peacekeeping officials stressed that access to healthcare remains a fundamental right and that humanitarian activities such as these contribute to improving living conditions for vulnerable populations, including detainees.
The initiative reflects the expanding role of peacekeeping missions, which increasingly combine security responsibilities with humanitarian support, reinforcing commitments to human rights, solidarity, and civilian protection in conflict-affected areas.

title: Rwanda’s Foreign Minister Criticizes DRC Ex-Minister Over US Statement on Peace in Great Lakes
excerpt: Kinshasa, March 8, 2026 – Rwandan Minister of Foreign Affairs, Amb. Olivier Nduhungirehe, criticized former DRC Minister of Foreign Affairs and Deputy Prime Minister Léonard She Okitundu Lundula for distorting the US position on peace efforts in the Great Lakes Region. Okitundu L
title_en: Rwanda’s Foreign Minister Criticizes DRC Ex-Minister Over US Statement on Peace in Great Lakes
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, March 8, 2026 – Rwandan Minister of Foreign Affairs, Amb. Olivier Nduhungirehe, criticized former DRC Minister of Foreign Affairs and Deputy Prime Minister Léonard She Okitundu Lundula for distorting the US position on peace efforts in the Great Lakes Region. Okitundu L
body_en:
Kinshasa, March 8, 2026 – Rwandan Minister of Foreign Affairs, Amb. Olivier Nduhungirehe, criticized former DRC Minister of Foreign Affairs and Deputy Prime Minister Léonard She Okitundu Lundula for distorting the US position on peace efforts in the Great Lakes Region.
Okitundu Lundula, who served from December 2016 to 2019, claimed on social media that the United States had imposed sanctions on Rwandan troops supporting the AFC/M23, and urged Rwanda to withdraw its forces from DRC territory, suggesting this would restore peace.
Ambassador Nduhungirehe responded, emphasizing that the primary threat to peace in eastern DRC is not Rwandan troop presence but the FDLR terrorist group, composed of Rwandans involved in the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi, some of whom were incorporated into the FARDC.
“You are misrepresenting the US Department of State statement,” Nduhungirehe said. “You have overlooked the most important directive: the United States asked the DRC to destroy the FDLR group as soon as possible.”
He noted that this directive is not new. During ministerial peace talks in Luanda, Angola, the then DRC Foreign Minister Christophe Lutundula presented a plan to dismantle the FDLR on June 21, 2024, which was agreed upon by Rwanda and Angola. The plan was signed by the ministers on November 25, 2025, and ratified in Washington on June 27, 2025, during the Washington Peace Accords, attended by President Félix Tshisekedi, President Paul Kagame, and Donald Trump.
Ambassador Nduhungirehe expressed regret that nearly two years later, the DRC has yet to implement its commitments, while mediators continue to urge compliance. He highlighted that the government has not dismantled the FDLR, and in some cases continues to provide the group with weapons, food, and funding, which it uses in the ongoing conflict with AFC/M23 forces controlling parts of North and South Kivu.

title: Over Rwf 900 Million Invested in Rwanda’s Good Governance Program
excerpt: Trōcaire, the Irish Catholic organization supporting community development, has launched a good governance program in Rwanda aimed at promoting participatory and inclusive governance, prioritizing citizens’ needs, and improving service delivery. The program was officially launche
title_en: Over Rwf 900 Million Invested in Rwanda’s Good Governance Program
excerpt_en: Trōcaire, the Irish Catholic organization supporting community development, has launched a good governance program in Rwanda aimed at promoting participatory and inclusive governance, prioritizing citizens’ needs, and improving service delivery. The program was officially launche
body_en:
Trōcaire, the Irish Catholic organization supporting community development, has launched a good governance program in Rwanda aimed at promoting participatory and inclusive governance, prioritizing citizens’ needs, and improving service delivery. The program was officially launched on February 27, 2026, with a total investment of over Rwf 900 million.
The initiative, named the “Twiyubakire Programme”, is supported by the British Government’s Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) and focuses on education, agriculture, and citizen collaboration with government institutions.
The program had been piloted over the past nine months in eight districts: Rusizi, Gisagara, Kamonyi, Muhanga, Nyaruguru, Nyamagabe, Gatsibo, and Bugesera.
Marleen Levina Masclee, Director of Trōcaire in Rwanda, said the program’s main objective is to strengthen cooperation between citizens and government while prioritizing women, youth, and people with disabilities.
“The aim of this program is to promote collaboration in agriculture, education, and national unity, placing citizens at the forefront of development,” Masclee said.
The Director of Development at the British Embassy in Rwanda, Billy Stewart, commended the Rwandan Government’s commitment to good governance and its continued focus on people-centered initiatives.
The Twiyubakire Programme will run for one year, ending in March 2027, and will be implemented in partnership with the Rwandan Coalition of Community-Based Development Organizations (CCOAIB).
Trōcaire has been operating in Rwanda since 1994, following the Genocide against the Tutsi, contributing to poverty reduction, justice, and community development across the country.
According to the 2025 Rwanda Governance Scorecard conducted by the Rwanda Governance Board (RGB), Rwanda’s participatory and inclusive governance pillar scored 86.31%, highlighting the country’s long-standing commitment to good governance over the past 30 years.

title: Rwandan Author Richard Hategekimana Launches Book on the Diversity and Values of the RDF
excerpt: On February 28, 2026, Rwandan author and President of the Rwanda Writers' Guild, Richard Hategekimana, officially launched a new book examining the diversity, history, and values of the Rwanda Defence Force (RDF). The publication highlights the role of the Rwandan military in the
title_en: Rwandan Author Richard Hategekimana Launches Book on the Diversity and Values of the RDF
excerpt_en: On February 28, 2026, Rwandan author and President of the Rwanda Writers' Guild, Richard Hategekimana, officially launched a new book examining the diversity, history, and values of the Rwanda Defence Force (RDF). The publication highlights the role of the Rwandan military in the
body_en:
On February 28, 2026, Rwandan author and President of the Rwanda Writers' Guild, Richard Hategekimana, officially launched a new book examining the diversity, history, and values of the Rwanda Defence Force (RDF). The publication highlights the role of the Rwandan military in the country’s security, unity, and development agenda.
Titled “The Force Behind the Vision: RDF and Rwanda’s Development Agenda,” the 400-page book explores the evolution of the Rwandan armed forces from the Rwandan Patriotic Army (RPA)—the movement credited with liberating the country and ending the Genocide against the Tutsi—to the modern RDF.
In the book, Hategekimana revisits not only the wars fought by the RPA and RDF, but also the core values that have shaped the force, including patriotism, courage, discipline, and vision. He argues that these principles have contributed significantly to Rwanda’s governance, economic development, social welfare, and justice systems.
According to the author, the book was written to preserve the history of the Rwandan armed forces while also sharing lessons that could inspire leadership and professionalism across other sectors of society.
Hategekimana emphasized that the diversity and institutional culture of the RDF serve as an example that could be adopted in government institutions, ministries, and public administration. He describes the RDF as an army guided by a mindset of “I know, I do, and I strive for,” reflecting a commitment to discipline and achieving objectives.
The author also explained that he chose to write the book in English to allow international readers to better understand the structure, diversity, and achievements of the Rwandan military.
He noted that the work aims to highlight Rwanda’s positive experiences, particularly the strong public trust in the RDF, which surveys have shown to be among the most respected national institutions in the country. By sharing these lessons globally, Hategekimana believes other countries can learn from Rwanda’s approach to security, leadership, and national unity.
Looking ahead, the author revealed plans to translate the book into Kinyarwanda, French, and Swahili to ensure that its contents are accessible to a broader audience across Rwanda and the wider African region.
During the launch event, Tito Rutaremara, Chairman of the Rwandan Armed Forces Advisory Board, praised the initiative, describing the book as an important contribution to preserving the historical record of the RDF.
Rutaremara also highlighted the importance of leadership in shaping the armed forces, pointing to President Paul Kagame, the Commander-in-Chief of the RDF, as a central figure in guiding the institution and contributing to the country’s broader development.
He further encouraged Rwandans to cultivate a culture of reading, stressing that support for literature and scholarship helps encourage authors to continue documenting national history and achievements.
Hategekimana dedicated the book to President Paul Kagame, Tito Rutaremara, and the Rwanda Defence Force, acknowledging their role in shaping the institution that the book seeks to document.
Participants at the launch described the RDF as a pillar of Rwanda’s development, welcoming the publication as an important effort to record and share the history and values of the country’s armed forces.
body_fr:
On February 28, 2026, Rwandan author and President of the Rwanda Writers' Guild, Richard Hategekimana, officially launched a new book examining the diversity, history, and values of the Rwanda Defence Force (RDF). Titled “The Force Behind the Vision: RDF and Rwanda’s Development Agenda,” the 400-page book explores the evolution of the Rwandan armed forces from the Rwandan Patriotic Army (RPA)—the movement credited with liberating the country and ending the Genocide against the Tutsi—to the modern RDF.
In the book, Hategekimana revisits not only the wars fought by the RPA and RDF, but also the core values that have shaped the force, including patriotism, courage, discipline, and vision. He argues that these principles have contributed significantly to Rwanda’s governance, economic development, social welfare, and justice systems.
According to the author, the book was written to preserve the history of the Rwandan armed forces while also sharing lessons that could inspire leadership and professionalism across other sectors of society.

He describes the RDF as an army guided by a mindset of “I know, I do, and I strive for,” reflecting a commitment to discipline and achieving objectives.

He further encouraged Rwandans to cultivate a culture of reading, stressing that support for literature and scholarship helps encourage authors to continue documenting national history and achievements.
Hategekimana dedicated the book to President Paul Kagame, Tito Rutaremara, and the Rwanda Defence Force, acknowledging their role in shaping the institution that the book seeks to document.

title: Museveni Rejects US and UK Military Bases in Uganda

title_en: Museveni Rejects US and UK Military Bases in Uganda
excerpt_en: On March 5, 2026, Ugandan President Yoweri Kaguta Museveni stated that he rejected proposals by the United States and the United Kingdom to establish military bases in Uganda, despite offers to strengthen military cooperation. Museveni explained that Uganda’s army is already well
body_en:
On March 5, 2026, Ugandan President Yoweri Kaguta Museveni stated that he rejected proposals by the United States and the United Kingdom to establish military bases in Uganda, despite offers to strengthen military cooperation.
Museveni explained that Uganda’s army is already well-built and capable of defending the country independently. He referenced Uganda’s military history, highlighting the army’s success in defeating Milton Obote’s forces in 1986, as a foundation for self-reliance.
“Foreign troops? What? We can defend ourselves, we don’t need help from others. If we want knowledge, we can come, learn, and come back,” Museveni said.
He also emphasized concerns over legal accountability, noting that agreements in other countries often require foreign soldiers accused of crimes to be tried in their home countries, which he would not accept for Ugandans.
The announcement comes amid Iranian attacks on US military bases in the Middle East, showing vulnerabilities for countries hosting foreign bases. Museveni highlighted that security in West African nations with foreign bases like Niger, Burkina Faso, and Mali has improved, but Uganda prefers self-reliance and national control over military matters.
Currently, the US maintains bases in African countries including Djibouti, Somalia, Cameroon, Seychelles, and Kenya, while the UK has a base in Nanyuki, Laikipia Region.
This decision reinforces Uganda’s stance on sovereignty and independent defense capabilities.

title: Seth Kikuni Rejects Dialogue Without Preconditions
excerpt: KINSHASA February 26, 2026 — In exile since mid-January, opposition leader Seth Kikuni stressed that any national dialogue in the Democratic Republic of Congo cannot be credible in a context of repression. Responding to Martin Fayulu, who had proposed topics for discussion, Kikun
title_en: Seth Kikuni Rejects Dialogue Without Preconditions
excerpt_en: KINSHASA February 26, 2026 — In exile since mid-January, opposition leader Seth Kikuni stressed that any national dialogue in the Democratic Republic of Congo cannot be credible in a context of repression. Responding to Martin Fayulu, who had proposed topics for discussion, Kikun
body_en:
KINSHASA February 26, 2026 — In exile since mid-January, opposition leader Seth Kikuni stressed that any national dialogue in the Democratic Republic of Congo cannot be credible in a context of repression. Responding to Martin Fayulu, who had proposed topics for discussion, Kikuni called for clear prerequisites, including a ceasefire and the cessation of all forms of political repression.
“The opposition will not engage in dialogue unless it is based on clear, credible, and verifiable preconditions,” wrote Kikuni on X, emphasizing that dialogue in a context of injustice, intimidation, and deprivation of fundamental rights risks legitimizing the status quo.
Among Kikuni’s preconditions for an inclusive dialogue are:
Release of political prisoners and prisoners of conscience
Lifting of politically motivated convictions
Restoration of civil and political rights, including the return of passports and freedom of movement for political actors
Annulment of politically motivated legal proceedings and lifting of arrest warrants
Reparations for damages suffered
Martin Fayulu, meanwhile, has called for a dialogue giving voice to all segments of society, including armed groups, outlining seven essential discussion points:
Preservation of DRC sovereignty and army/security reforms
Promotion of ethical governance, public finance reform, and anti-corruption measures
Strengthening justice, human rights, and equality before the law
Electoral reforms to ensure transparency for the 2028 elections
Peaceful coexistence among Congolese ethnic groups
Regional stability in the Great Lakes region
Review and analysis of past national dialogue resolutions since 1958 to develop a coherent governance doctrine
Kikuni and other opposition leaders insist that participation criteria must ensure tangible benefits for the Congolese people, rejecting any dialogue reduced to a mere political exercise.

title: DRC Showcases Mining Strategy on Global Stage
excerpt: TORONTO March 3, 2026 — The Democratic Republic of Congo presented its mining strategy at the annual Prospectors & Developers Association of Canada (PDAC 2026) convention, highlighting investment opportunities and sustainable development in the sector. Led by Minister of Mines Lo
title_en: DRC Showcases Mining Strategy on Global Stage
excerpt_en: TORONTO March 3, 2026 — The Democratic Republic of Congo presented its mining strategy at the annual Prospectors & Developers Association of Canada (PDAC 2026) convention, highlighting investment opportunities and sustainable development in the sector. Led by Minister of Mines Lo
body_en:
TORONTO March 3, 2026 — The Democratic Republic of Congo presented its mining strategy at the annual Prospectors & Developers Association of Canada (PDAC 2026) convention, highlighting investment opportunities and sustainable development in the sector.
Led by Minister of Mines Louis Watum Kabamba, the DRC delegation emphasized reforms in governance, transparency, traceability, and local transformation through special economic zones. These initiatives reflect the vision of President Félix Tshisekedi and coordination by Prime Minister Judith Suminwa Tuluka to position the DRC as a responsible, strategic player in the global mining industry.
Minister Watum Kabamba stressed: “It’s not enough to have critical minerals. We must create the conditions necessary for investment to transform this potential into tangible wealth. Our laws and administration are the investor’s best allies.” He underscored fiscal stability, streamlined administrative procedures, and a modernized regulatory framework as tools to attract responsible investors.
The delegation showcased the DRC’s mining potential through booths representing the Ministry of Mines and Lualaba Province, reinforcing the country’s international visibility and the modernization of its sector.
In addition, the minister participated in the 11th International Summit of Mining Ministers, focusing on aligning strategies between producing and consuming countries, securing supply chains, and financing energy-transition projects.
The DRC’s presence at PDAC 2026 aims to stimulate new investments in local exploration and processing, foster strategic partnerships with global developers and financiers, and strengthen its recognition as a critical player in global mineral security, while advancing the country’s economic transformation and contribution to the global energy transition.

title_en: 14 Twiraneho Fighters Released to Banyamulenge Community
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, March 6, 2026 – The Minister of Justice and Keeper of the Seals, Guillaume Ngefa, formally handed over 14 Twiraneho fighters to the Banyamulenge community in Kinshasa on Thursday, March 5, 2026. These fighters, affiliated with the AFC/M23, had voluntarily surrendered to
body_en:
Kinshasa, March 6, 2026 – The Minister of Justice and Keeper of the Seals, Guillaume Ngefa, formally handed over 14 Twiraneho fighters to the Banyamulenge community in Kinshasa on Thursday, March 5, 2026. These fighters, affiliated with the AFC/M23, had voluntarily surrendered to the Congolese army during last December’s fighting for control of Uvira in South Kivu.
According to the Ministry of Justice, all necessary checks were conducted to determine whether the individuals were personally involved in any acts warranting criminal charges, in line with the principles of the rule of law. “No individual charges have been brought against them at this stage,” the Ministry reported.
The release, carried out in the presence of military justice officials and representatives of the Disarmament, Demobilization and Community Reintegration Program (P-DDR-CS), was welcomed by the Kinshasa Banyamulenge community, who praised the Head of State for his “relentless fight against tribal hate speech.”
The Ministry highlighted that the ceremony reflects President Félix Antoine Tshisekedi’s commitment to encouraging all Congolese involved in armed groups to abandon violence and reintegrate into civil life.
Twirwaneho, a self-defense militia formed in the late 2000s to protect the Banyamulenge community, is led by Michel Rukunda, alias Makanika. The group, allied with the M23 and AFC, has been accused of human rights violations, including child recruitment, and remains a significant actor in the ongoing Kivu conflicts.

excerpt_en: MASISI, North Kivu – February 25, 2026 — Violent clashes erupted on Wednesday, February 25, between AFC/M23 rebels and Wazalendo militias in the villages of Lumbishi and Kashovu, located in the Katoy sector, southern Masisi territory, North Kivu province. The fighting began early
body_en:
MASISI, North Kivu – February 25, 2026 — Violent clashes erupted on Wednesday, February 25, between AFC/M23 rebels and Wazalendo militias in the villages of Lumbishi and Kashovu, located in the Katoy sector, southern Masisi territory, North Kivu province.
The fighting began early Wednesday as Wazalendo forces launched a counter-offensive aimed at retaking the two villages from rebel control. The exchanges of heavy and light weapon fire were reported across the area, triggering widespread panic among local residents.
The renewed confrontations have caused significant population displacement, with families fleeing the affected villages. Many sought shelter in the surrounding bush, while others moved toward the town of Ngungu in search of safety.
Masisi territory remains one of the most unstable regions in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, frequently affected by clashes between local armed groups and AFC/M23 rebels. Observers note that the security situation remains fluid, with ongoing movements of both government-allied militias and rebel forces contributing to persistent civilian insecurity.

These villages, strategically located to control access to the mining town of Rubaya, had been seized by Wazalendo last Monday. After four days of occupation, the militia withdrew in the face of a reinforced counter-offensive by AFC/M23, according to local administrative and security sources.
The recapture underscores the intensifying violence in Masisi, which has been a focal point of recurrent clashes between Wazalendo and AFC/M23 over the past week. Reports indicate troop movements and reinforcements on both sides as each seeks to consolidate territorial control.
Residents reported heavy exchanges of fire and bombings, generating widespread fear among civilians. No official casualty or damage figures have been released.
Humanitarian concerns are mounting as repeated displacement is forcing families to abandon homes, crops, and livelihoods. If hostilities continue or spread, the population may face new waves of displacement toward Rubaya, Nyabiondo, or other safer areas, further worsening an already fragile socio-economic situation in the territory.

title: FARDC Retakes Strategic Villages in Fizi and Mwenga
excerpt: FIZI/MWENGA March 2, 2026 — The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC), supported by the Wazalendo and elements of the Burundian army, have recaptured more than five villages in the Fizi and Mwenga territories of South Kivu following operations against the Twirw
title_en: FARDC Retakes Strategic Villages in Fizi and Mwenga
excerpt_en: FIZI/MWENGA March 2, 2026 — The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC), supported by the Wazalendo and elements of the Burundian army, have recaptured more than five villages in the Fizi and Mwenga territories of South Kivu following operations against the Twirw
body_en:
FIZI/MWENGA March 2, 2026 — The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC), supported by the Wazalendo and elements of the Burundian army, have recaptured more than five villages in the Fizi and Mwenga territories of South Kivu following operations against the Twirweneho militia, an ally of the AFC/M23 rebels.
Local sources report that clashes intensified since Sunday, March 1, culminating in the retaking of Mikenge, a town held by rebel forces since March 2025, along with other strategic villages including Kakenge, Bilalombili, Bidegu 1, Madegu, and parts of Kalinga.
According to Pacifique Kararuka, president of the New Congolese Civil Society in Kipupu, “It was on Sunday that the FARDC, supported by the Wazalendo, recaptured Mikenge and other areas. The operations are being led from Kakobanya.”
The army reports that the counteroffensive resulted in significant rebel losses: several were killed, five captured, 17 surrendered, and 11 bodies were recovered, including a brigade commander of the AFC/M23 and a logistics officer of the Twirweneho militia with their escorts. Military equipment, including anti-drone lasers, was also recovered.
These operations have caused displacement, with some residents fleeing to Uvira for safety. Lieutenant Reagan Mbuyi Kalonji, the army spokesperson, stressed that the counterattack aims to neutralize AFC/M23 influence in the area and restore government control over strategic towns and villages.
Fighting in this region remains ongoing, as clashes continue between the Twirweneho-Red Tabara-FNL coalition allied with AFC/M23 and FARDC forces supported by Wazalendo and Burundian troops.

title: FARDC Seizes CRP/Zaire Coalition Ammunition Stockpile
excerpt: DJUGU March 5, 2026 — The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) have announced the seizure of a significant ammunition stockpile belonging to the CRP/Zaire coalition, a rebel alliance led by Thomas Lubanga in Ituri province. Lieutenant Jules Ngongo, spokesperso
title_en: FARDC Seizes CRP/Zaire Coalition Ammunition Stockpile
excerpt_en: DJUGU March 5, 2026 — The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) have announced the seizure of a significant ammunition stockpile belonging to the CRP/Zaire coalition, a rebel alliance led by Thomas Lubanga in Ituri province. Lieutenant Jules Ngongo, spokesperso
body_en:
DJUGU March 5, 2026 — The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) have announced the seizure of a significant ammunition stockpile belonging to the CRP/Zaire coalition, a rebel alliance led by Thomas Lubanga in Ituri province.
Lieutenant Jules Ngongo, spokesperson for the provincial government, said the stockpile included ammunition of all calibers, RPG-7 rockets, AK-47s, PKM machine guns, and Castor bombs, previously hidden at the coalition’s headquarters in Jingo, Mambisa chiefdom, Djugu territory. He described the operation as a “fatal blow” to the coalition’s logistical capabilities and credited local populations for their collaboration with the army.
“The Armed Forces will continue to search everywhere weapons and ammunition have been hidden. This is a major military achievement. Credit goes to the Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces for deploying the necessary resources to progressively pacify Ituri, area by area,” Lieutenant Ngongo said.
The CRP/Zaire coalition has been responsible for escalating violence in Djugu territory since last year, targeting both FARDC positions and civilians, leading to mass displacements and numerous deaths. The FARDC said it intends to continue operations to fully restore security and state authority across the province, which remains under a state of siege since 2021.
Authorities maintain that military interventions have achieved some progress, though pacification efforts in Ituri are ongoing, and the humanitarian situation remains precarious, with a high number of displaced persons and civilian victims.

title: Catholic Church Says Condemning Rwanda Will Not Resolve DRC Crisis
excerpt: KINSHASA, February 24, 2026 — The Catholic Church in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has stated that repeatedly condemning Rwanda is not a solution to the country’s ongoing security and political crisis, emphasizing instead the need for inclusive national dialogue among Co
title_en: Catholic Church Says Condemning Rwanda Will Not Resolve DRC Crisis
excerpt_en: KINSHASA, February 24, 2026 — The Catholic Church in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has stated that repeatedly condemning Rwanda is not a solution to the country’s ongoing security and political crisis, emphasizing instead the need for inclusive national dialogue among Co
body_en:
KINSHASA, February 24, 2026 — The Catholic Church in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has stated that repeatedly condemning Rwanda is not a solution to the country’s ongoing security and political crisis, emphasizing instead the need for inclusive national dialogue among Congolese stakeholders.
Church leaders say their current priority is to promote peace talks and national reconciliation, rather than focusing on accusations against Rwanda, which has frequently been blamed by authorities for its alleged support to the AFC/M23 rebellion operating in North Kivu and South Kivu provinces.
Shift in Approach
The Catholic Bishops' Conference (CENCO) acknowledged that it had previously raised concerns about Rwanda’s alleged role in the conflict but concluded that continued condemnation would not help resolve the country’s internal challenges.
The Secretary General of CENCO, Bishop Donatien Nshole, explained that Church leaders had mentioned Rwanda in past statements but later decided to adopt a different strategy centered on national unity and dialogue.
According to Church officials, the new approach focuses on creating space for peace negotiations involving all Congolese actors, seen as a more effective path toward resolving the crisis.
Peace Dialogue Initiative
Since early 2025, the Catholic Church and the Anglican Church have been working on a joint initiative aimed at promoting inclusive peace talks between Congolese parties.
Church leaders argue that broad national dialogue, without excluding any stakeholders, offers the best chance for lasting stability in the country.
Government Opposition
The DRC government has expressed reservations about the initiative, maintaining that armed groups should not be included in political discussions.
Authorities insist that individuals who have taken up arms against the state must first lay down their weapons before being considered for participation in political negotiations.
The debate highlights continuing differences between the Catholic Church and the government over the best approach to resolving the ongoing conflict in eastern DRC, where insecurity linked to armed groups continues to affect civilian populations.
