title: Humanitarian Access Severely Restricted as 78,500 Displaced People Face Multi-Sectoral Needs
excerpt: February 19, 2026 – Djugu, Ituri, DRC – The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) reports that humanitarian access remains severely limited in Bule and surrounding villages in the Djugu territory, where repeated armed clashes continue to disrup
title_en: Humanitarian Access Severely Restricted as 78,500 Displaced People Face Multi-Sectoral Needs
excerpt_en: February 19, 2026 – Djugu, Ituri, DRC – The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) reports that humanitarian access remains severely limited in Bule and surrounding villages in the Djugu territory, where repeated armed clashes continue to disrup
body_en:
February 19, 2026 – Djugu, Ituri, DRC – The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) reports that humanitarian access remains severely limited in Bule and surrounding villages in the Djugu territory, where repeated armed clashes continue to disrupt civilian life.
Over 78,500 displaced persons, along with host communities, face urgent needs across multiple sectors, including food, education, water, sanitation, hygiene, and shelter, according to a rapid multi-sectoral assessment conducted by the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC) in January 2026.
The report highlights that the use of school buildings as emergency shelters has left more than 60 schools non-functional since December 2025, depriving over 24,000 children of education.
Many displaced individuals have sought refuge in neighboring territories of Mahagi and Irumu, including the Plaine Savo displacement site, placing significant pressure on already limited social services. Since December 2025, approximately 37,000 displaced people from Djugu have arrived in the Logo, Rimba, and Kambala health zones in Mahagi, primarily hosted by local families.
Protection concerns are mounting, with reports of arbitrary arrests, illegal fines, thefts, and kidnappings. On January 21, at least ten children were abducted in the Rabu health area by members of an armed group.
The humanitarian crisis in Ituri is exacerbated by persistent insecurity, massive population displacement, epidemics such as measles and Mpox, and the impact of natural disasters. Armed groups, including the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) and the Convention for the People’s Revolution (CRP) led by Thomas Lubanga, continue to operate in the region. The ADF, active for nearly three decades and pledged to the Islamic State, has forced thousands to flee despite joint Congolese-Ugandan military operations.
OCHA warns that the combination of armed violence, intercommunal tensions, and displacement has created a protracted humanitarian crisis in Ituri, requiring urgent international and local support to meet the basic needs of affected populations.

The report highlights that the use of school buildings as emergency shelters has left more than 60 schools non-functional since December 2025, depriving over 24,000 children of education.
Many displaced individuals have sought refuge in neighboring territories of Mahagi and Irumu, including the Plaine Savo displacement site, placing significant pressure on already limited social services. Since December 2025, approximately 37,000 displaced people from Djugu have arrived in the Logo, Rimba, and Kambala health zones in Mahagi, primarily hosted by local families.
Protection concerns are mounting, with reports of arbitrary arrests, illegal fines, thefts, and kidnappings. On January 21, at least ten children were abducted in the Rabu health area by members of an armed group.
The humanitarian crisis in Ituri is exacerbated by persistent insecurity, massive population displacement, epidemics such as measles and Mpox, and the impact of natural disasters. Armed groups, including the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) and the Convention for the People’s Revolution (CRP) led by Thomas Lubanga, continue to operate in the region. The ADF, active for nearly three decades and pledged to the Islamic State, has forced thousands to flee despite joint Congolese-Ugandan military operations.
OCHA warns that the combination of armed violence, intercommunal tensions, and displacement has created a protracted humanitarian crisis in Ituri, requiring urgent international and local support to meet the basic needs of affected populations.

title: DRC Government Acts Against MTN Rwanda for Illegal Use of Frequencies
excerpt: Kinshasa, February 11, 2026 – Prime Minister Judith Suminwa Tuluka has instructed the DRC government to take immediate technical action against MTN Rwanda for its illegal use of Congolese frequencies. The decision follows a meeting with Minister of Posts and Telecommunications Jo
title_en: DRC Government Acts Against MTN Rwanda for Illegal Use of Frequencies
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, February 11, 2026 – Prime Minister Judith Suminwa Tuluka has instructed the DRC government to take immediate technical action against MTN Rwanda for its illegal use of Congolese frequencies. The decision follows a meeting with Minister of Posts and Telecommunications Jo
body_en:
Kinshasa, February 11, 2026 – Prime Minister Judith Suminwa Tuluka has instructed the DRC government to take immediate technical action against MTN Rwanda for its illegal use of Congolese frequencies.
The decision follows a meeting with Minister of Posts and Telecommunications José Mpanda Kabangu, the President of the Postal and Telecommunications Regulatory Authority (ARPTC), and representatives from major mobile operators in the DRC, including Airtel, Orange, and Vodacom.
The discussions focused on MTN Rwanda’s unauthorized occupation of national frequencies, which Minister Mpanda described as a strategic and sovereign issue. The Prime Minister instructed the ARPTC to take the lead in technical communications regarding the matter, with political bodies to intervene once the technical aspects are clarified.
“The issue remains technical. Technical communication will be conducted, and political bodies will come afterward. The Prime Minister has given precise instructions for ARPTC experts to communicate and contact international bodies,” stated José Mpanda.
The DRC intends to defend its frequencies and prevent any malicious foreign intrusion, a concern heightened by the ongoing M23/AFC rebellion in eastern DRC, which reportedly receives support from Rwanda.

title: OCC Director General Suspended Over Alleged Fraudulent Import-Export System
excerpt: Kinshasa, February 17, 2026 – The Director General of the Congolese Office of Control (OCC), Étienne Tshimanga Mutombo, has been suspended from his duties by the Minister of Foreign Trade, Julien Paluku, following allegations of serious mismanagement. The suspension, decreed on F
title_en: OCC Director General Suspended Over Alleged Fraudulent Import-Export System
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, February 17, 2026 – The Director General of the Congolese Office of Control (OCC), Étienne Tshimanga Mutombo, has been suspended from his duties by the Minister of Foreign Trade, Julien Paluku, following allegations of serious mismanagement. The suspension, decreed on F
body_en:
Kinshasa, February 17, 2026 – The Director General of the Congolese Office of Control (OCC), Étienne Tshimanga Mutombo, has been suspended from his duties by the Minister of Foreign Trade, Julien Paluku, following allegations of serious mismanagement.
The suspension, decreed on February 16, 2026, aims to protect the institution from further administrative and technical misconduct.
Allegations against Mutombo include:
Installing a parallel computer system for import and export control, reportedly facilitating the use of fraudulent Verification Certificates (VCs).
Mismanagement of human and financial resources.
Acts of insubordination.
These irregularities are said to have caused significant financial losses, estimated at thousands of US dollars.
A reform commission for the OCC has been established, with its composition and mission to be defined by a separate ministerial decree. The Deputy Director General, Christelle Muabilu, has been appointed interim director during the investigation.
According to the Minister’s office, disciplinary proceedings against Mutombo had begun in late January, and his responses were deemed unsatisfactory, prompting the suspension. Additional administrative and extra-administrative measures will target any OCC agents complicit in the alleged acts.

title: Despite Ceasefire Calls, AFC/M23 Announces Reinforcement of 7,532 Fighters
excerpt: February 10, 2026 – While diplomatic pressure mounts for a ceasefire in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, the AFC/M23 rebellion has announced a significant reinforcement of its military forces, signaling continued tensions on the ground. In a statement released Tuesday, the m
title_en: Despite Ceasefire Calls, AFC/M23 Announces Reinforcement of 7,532 Fighters
excerpt_en: February 10, 2026 – While diplomatic pressure mounts for a ceasefire in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, the AFC/M23 rebellion has announced a significant reinforcement of its military forces, signaling continued tensions on the ground. In a statement released Tuesday, the m
body_en:
February 10, 2026 – While diplomatic pressure mounts for a ceasefire in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, the AFC/M23 rebellion has announced a significant reinforcement of its military forces, signaling continued tensions on the ground.
In a statement released Tuesday, the movement confirmed the completion of a training cycle for new recruits within its armed wing, the Congolese Revolutionary Army (ARC). The ceremony reportedly took place in Tshanzu, where, according to the group, 7,532 commandos were officially integrated into its operational units. The figure, however, could not be independently verified.
The AFC/M23, which has been accused by Kinshasa and several international partners of receiving support from Rwanda, said the newly trained fighters would be deployed on missions aimed at securing and defending strategic positions, controlling key axes and operational zones, and maintaining what it described as “tactical superiority.”
The announcement comes at a time when diplomatic initiatives are intensifying. African leaders meeting in Luanda recently urged both the Congolese government and the AFC/M23 to commit to an immediate ceasefire, while the United Nations reiterated that MONUSCO stands ready to support its implementation.
Simultaneously, representatives of the Congolese government and the armed group reaffirmed their commitment to the ceasefire framework agreement signed in November 2025 in Doha, during a session of the monitoring and verification mechanism held under the auspices of Qatar. The meeting brought together delegates from the African Union, the United States, and the International Conference on the Great Lakes Region.
Despite these diplomatic engagements, the armed movement maintained a firm tone.
“If the Kinshasa regime wants peace, we are ready; if it chooses war, we are too,” the AFC/M23 declared in its communiqué.
The latest development underscores the fragile nature of ongoing peace efforts, as military posturing continues alongside high-level diplomatic negotiations.

body_en:
February 11, 2026 – The Republic of Angola has proposed a ceasefire between the government of the Democratic Republic of Congo and the M23 armed group, set to take effect at noon on February 18, the Angolan presidency announced Tuesday.
The proposal follows a high-level meeting in Luanda on Monday, attended by Angolan President João Lourenço, Congolese President Félix Tshisekedi, Togolese President Faure Gnassingbé, the African Union mediator, and former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo, representing the AU-designated facilitators of the DRC peace process.
According to the announcement, the proposed ceasefire date is conditional upon a public declaration of acceptance by both parties. Angola also indicated that the start of the preparatory phase for the inter-Congolese dialogue, scheduled to be held in Luanda, will be announced at a later date.
The initiative underscores regional efforts to stabilize eastern DRC and curb ongoing hostilities involving the M23 rebellion.

title_en: Kinshasa and Luanda Establish Joint Defense and Security Commission
excerpt_en: February 15, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and Angola signed an agreement in Luanda establishing a Joint Defense and Security Commission, following two days of meetings between security and defense experts from both countries. The agreement, signed by the respecti
body_en:
February 15, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and Angola signed an agreement in Luanda establishing a Joint Defense and Security Commission, following two days of meetings between security and defense experts from both countries.
The agreement, signed by the respective Ministers of the Interior and Security, aims to enhance bilateral security cooperation and strengthen coordination along the shared border. Both countries emphasized the importance of regular information sharing and scheduled meetings between military and police commands to address cross-border threats.
Deputy Prime Minister Jacquemain Shabani and his Angolan counterpart, Manuel Gomes, also addressed the issue of Rwandan aggression in eastern DRC, condemning the use of force to seize power and highlighting the need to respect democratic principles for regional stability.
Experts from both nations praised the political commitment of President Félix Tshisekedi and the Angolan President in reinforcing fraternal ties and fostering cooperation between their peoples.
This joint commission marks a strategic step in addressing security challenges and reinforcing peace and stability along the DRC-Angola border.

title_en: Wazalendo Militiamen Imposing Illegal Taxes on Displaced Populations in Musienene
excerpt_en: February 19, 2026 – Musienene, Lubero, North Kivu, DRC – Civil society organizations in Musienene, the main town of the Baswagha chiefdom, are sounding the alarm over the harassment of displaced populations by Wazalendo militiamen. Residents report being forced to pay illegal tax
body_en:
February 19, 2026 – Musienene, Lubero, North Kivu, DRC – Civil society organizations in Musienene, the main town of the Baswagha chiefdom, are sounding the alarm over the harassment of displaced populations by Wazalendo militiamen.
Residents report being forced to pay illegal taxes for activities such as charcoal production, with amounts ranging from 5,000 Congolese francs to 10 US dollars per batch. Affected communities include Vikindwe, Vulimira, Kirirya, Mutiri, and surrounding areas.
Kambale Maboko Fanuel, president of Musienene civil society, highlighted that these demands hinder the livelihoods of displaced people and even impact host families. He urged political and administrative authorities to intervene to halt these abusive practices.
Similar illegal taxation reportedly targets sawyers and timber traders, further disrupting local economic activity.
Civil society notes that displaced residents had previously issued a 48-hour ultimatum to Wazalendo fighters to leave their areas of origin, citing the militia’s actions as the main cause of their displacement. The appeal was delivered during a meeting at the ESCO field in Butembo, led by representatives from the Mwenye civil society and the New Congolese Civil Society (NSCC).
Abuses by Wazalendo-affiliated militiamen in the region reportedly include looting, harassment, sexual violence, arbitrary arrests, unauthorized roadblocks, and the illegal collection of taxes, which have become recurrent in the Baswagha chiefdom and Musienene.
Civil society continues to call for exclusive control by the Armed Forces of the DRC (FARDC) to restore peace and security in the area.

excerpt: Walikale, North Kivu, February 23, 2026 – The security situation in the Walikale territory remains worrying as AFC/M23 rebels reinforced their positions on Sunday, February 22, in the villages of Mpety and Mindjendje, located in the Banakindi area (Kisimba group). According to lo
title_en: AFC/M23 Reinforces Positions in Mpety and Mindjendje, Raising Concerns Around Pinga
excerpt_en: Walikale, North Kivu, February 23, 2026 – The security situation in the Walikale territory remains worrying as AFC/M23 rebels reinforced their positions on Sunday, February 22, in the villages of Mpety and Mindjendje, located in the Banakindi area (Kisimba group). According to lo
body_en:
Walikale, North Kivu, February 23, 2026 – The security situation in the Walikale territory remains worrying as AFC/M23 rebels reinforced their positions on Sunday, February 22, in the villages of Mpety and Mindjendje, located in the Banakindi area (Kisimba group).
According to local authorities, the reinforcements came from the Kitshanga-Kalembe axis, with columns of heavily armed men moving through Kalembe toward Mpety, a development confirmed by security sources in Walikale.
While the exact objective of these movements is unclear, observers suggest that the rebels could be preparing offensives against FARDC and Wazalendo positions, particularly near the strategic town of Pinga.
The situation has alarmed local communities, already strained by recent clashes in the area. Traditional authorities of the Kisimba group denounce what they describe as a violation of the ceasefire and urge the Armed Forces of the DRC (FARDC) and Wazalendo fighters to remain vigilant.
Amid a regional context of persistent instability, the civilian population fears a further escalation of violence, which could trigger more displacement and worsen the humanitarian situation in this already fragile part of Walikale territory.
Conclusion
The period from February 8 to 23, 2026, underscores the Democratic Republic of Congo’s position at a critical juncture, marked by a delicate balance between diplomatic engagement, economic ambition, and persistent humanitarian and security challenges.
Diplomatically and politically, the DRC is actively engaging regional and continental partners to stabilize its eastern provinces. President Félix Tshisekedi’s discussions in Luanda with Angolan and African Union leaders, alongside the acceptance of a regional ceasefire scheduled for February 18, signal a commitment to dialogue. Yet, the process remains fragile: the AFC/M23 continues to denounce what it sees as “diplomatic fragmentation” and alleges ongoing government offensives, highlighting the tenuous nature of peace efforts.
Economically, progress is visible in the formalization of the extractive sector. The first legal artisanal gold exports from Haut-Katanga and the inaugural copper and cobalt shipment via the Lobito Atlantic Railway demonstrate tangible steps toward transparency, traceability, and integration into global markets. At the same time, structural challenges persist. The IMF identifies the public wage bill as a major fiscal risk, while institutional weaknesses and entrenched corruption—as reflected in the DRC’s continued low ranking on the Corruption Perceptions Index—threaten to undermine these gains.

title: “Congo First” Advocates for International Criminal Tribunal to Address Decades of Crimes in DRC
excerpt: Kinshasa, February 12, 2026 – The political platform “Congo First” (Le Congo d’Abord) has called for the establishment of an International Criminal Tribunal in the DRC to ensure that perpetrators of unlawful acts are held accountable. During the official presentation of the polit
title_en: “Congo First” Advocates for International Criminal Tribunal to Address Decades of Crimes in DRC
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, February 12, 2026 – The political platform “Congo First” (Le Congo d’Abord) has called for the establishment of an International Criminal Tribunal in the DRC to ensure that perpetrators of unlawful acts are held accountable. During the official presentation of the polit
body_en:
Kinshasa, February 12, 2026 – The political platform “Congo First” (Le Congo d’Abord) has called for the establishment of an International Criminal Tribunal in the DRC to ensure that perpetrators of unlawful acts are held accountable.
During the official presentation of the political group on Thursday, coordinator Toussaint Alonga emphasized the need to try those responsible for crimes committed over the past 30 years in the country.
The platform aims to promote values such as goodness, truth, justice, and good governance, while encouraging the exchange of ideas and empowering proposals for the development of the Democratic Republic of Congo.
Alonga noted that the tribunal would help end the cycle of violence that has characterized the DRC’s political life, including elections, disputes, rebellions, dialogues, and governments of national unity.
He further stated that the Head of State’s openness to inclusive dialogue continues existing peace efforts, aiming to reach a consensus on governance reforms, restore national cohesion, and strengthen national unity.
“National cohesion and national unity secure the strategic partnership between the DRC and the USA. Inclusive dialogue, being an extra-constitutional political process, can only be achieved through consensus among actors to reach a lasting solution,” Alonga added.

title: IMF Warns of Rising Public Wage Bill as Major Fiscal Risk in DRC
excerpt: Kinshasa, February 15, 2026 – The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has identified the public wage bill as a major fiscal risk for the Democratic Republic of Congo under the Extended Credit Facility (ECF) program. According to the IMF’s second review, rapidly increasing salaries
title_en: IMF Warns of Rising Public Wage Bill as Major Fiscal Risk in DRC
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, February 15, 2026 – The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has identified the public wage bill as a major fiscal risk for the Democratic Republic of Congo under the Extended Credit Facility (ECF) program. According to the IMF’s second review, rapidly increasing salaries
body_en:
Kinshasa, February 15, 2026 – The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has identified the public wage bill as a major fiscal risk for the Democratic Republic of Congo under the Extended Credit Facility (ECF) program.
According to the IMF’s second review, rapidly increasing salaries in the education, health, and justice sectors are straining budget execution and reducing available fiscal space, particularly in a context already burdened by security expenditures.
The report highlights that the growth of the wage bill stems from salary adjustments, recruitment, administrative regularization, and the continuation of previously undertaken commitments by authorities. This increase has placed pressure on current expenditures in 2024–2025, exceeding initially projected levels.
The IMF warns that the public wage bill is consuming a growing share of budgetary resources, limiting the government’s capacity to fund public investment and social spending, which are priorities under the program. Rising security expenditures further exacerbate this fiscal strain.
For 2025 and 2026, the IMF notes that the widening deficit is partly explained by increased compensation in social and judicial sectors. The fund underscores that this trend, coupled with limited revenue mobilization, heightens the risk of reduced macro-budgetary flexibility.
The IMF calls on the Congolese authorities to:
Contain the growth of the public sector wage bill.
Develop and implement a coherent wage policy.
Strengthen control over civil service size.
Integrate these measures into broader public financial management reforms.
While the IMF did not provide specific timelines or instruments for these reforms, it emphasized that controlling the wage bill is critical for the credibility of the medium-term program and the pursuit of stabilization and development objectives.
Without corrective action, the rigidity of current expenditures could further reduce fiscal space, complicating efforts to maintain macroeconomic stability and support growth.

title: UN Peacekeeping Chief Begins Visit for Ceasefire Consultations
excerpt: Kinshasa DRC February 9, 2026 – The Under-Secretary-General for Peace Operations, Jean-Pierre Lacroix, begins a three-day official visit to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) on Monday, as efforts intensify to implement a ceasefire in the eastern region of the country. Ac
title_en: UN Peacekeeping Chief Begins Visit for Ceasefire Consultations
excerpt_en: Kinshasa DRC February 9, 2026 – The Under-Secretary-General for Peace Operations, Jean-Pierre Lacroix, begins a three-day official visit to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) on Monday, as efforts intensify to implement a ceasefire in the eastern region of the country. Ac
body_en:
Kinshasa DRC February 9, 2026 – The Under-Secretary-General for Peace Operations, Jean-Pierre Lacroix, begins a three-day official visit to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) on Monday, as efforts intensify to implement a ceasefire in the eastern region of the country.
According to the United Nations (UN), the visit will include consultations with national and provincial authorities, as well as meetings with members of the political class, civil society, and religious organizations. Discussions are expected to focus on the evolving security situation and the progress of the ceasefire process.
In line with UN Security Council Resolution 2808 (2025), the United Nations Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is mandated to support the implementation of a permanent ceasefire. The mission’s support includes technical and logistical assistance to the International Conference on the Great Lakes Region within the framework of the Expanded Joint Verification Mechanism Plus.
As part of this mechanism, an initial team of peacekeepers is set to deploy to Uvira, in South Kivu, to assist in monitoring the ceasefire. MONUSCO clarified that the deployment does not signal a permanent redeployment to the province, but rather constitutes limited and targeted support strictly confined to the verification framework.
Currently, MONUSCO forces remain deployed in Ituri and North Kivu provinces. The mission officially completed its withdrawal from South Kivu in June 2024, as part of its phased disengagement plan agreed upon with the Congolese government.

title: FARDC Launches Drone Strikes on AFC/M23 Positions in Mpety
excerpt: Walikale February 11, 2026 – The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) carried out drone airstrikes on AFC/M23 rebel positions around Mpety, in the Kisimba area of Walikale territory, North Kivu, on Wednesday. Local administrative and traditional sources report
title_en: FARDC Launches Drone Strikes on AFC/M23 Positions in Mpety
excerpt_en: Walikale February 11, 2026 – The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) carried out drone airstrikes on AFC/M23 rebel positions around Mpety, in the Kisimba area of Walikale territory, North Kivu, on Wednesday. Local administrative and traditional sources report
body_en:
Walikale February 11, 2026 – The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) carried out drone airstrikes on AFC/M23 rebel positions around Mpety, in the Kisimba area of Walikale territory, North Kivu, on Wednesday.
Local administrative and traditional sources reported that the first explosions were heard around 1 p.m., triggering panic among villagers and prompting several families to flee into the bush.
These strikes come just 48 hours after drone operations targeting rebel positions in Mindjendje, near Mpety in the Banakindi area, which reportedly caused multiple injuries among AFC/M23 fighters, according to local sources. The casualty figures from Wednesday’s strikes remain unknown.
The Pinga-Mpety-Mindjendje axis has been a flashpoint for violent clashes between the FARDC, supported by Wazalendo forces, and the AFC/M23 rebels over the past several months. The area’s strategic importance has made it a key target for both sides, fueling ongoing instability.
According to military sources, the current operations are part of the FARDC’s broader strategy to weaken AFC/M23 military capabilities and regain control of key positions around Pinga, a locality considered a security stronghold in this part of Walikale territory.

title: Explosive Devices Found in Residents’ Fields in Ruwenzori
excerpt: Ruwenzori Beni February 14, 2026 – Two explosive devices were discovered in Manzembe and Mwenda, areas within the Beni territory of North Kivu, reportedly left behind by Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) rebels during their retreat, according to Kalungo Mambo of the Civil Protection
title_en: Explosive Devices Found in Residents’ Fields in Ruwenzori
excerpt_en: Ruwenzori Beni February 14, 2026 – Two explosive devices were discovered in Manzembe and Mwenda, areas within the Beni territory of North Kivu, reportedly left behind by Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) rebels during their retreat, according to Kalungo Mambo of the Civil Protection
body_en:
Ruwenzori Beni February 14, 2026 – Two explosive devices were discovered in Manzembe and Mwenda, areas within the Beni territory of North Kivu, reportedly left behind by Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) rebels during their retreat, according to Kalungo Mambo of the Civil Protection service in the Ruwenzori sector.
Experts from the United Nations Mine Action Service (UNMAS) intervened in Manzembe to defuse a bomb discovered by residents last Saturday. Civil Protection authorities urged locals to exercise caution in areas near former ADF strongholds, highlighting the risks posed by abandoned explosive devices.
“The bomb discovered in Manzembe posed a danger near a busy road leading to the population's fields. We urge everyone to be careful when working in the fields, because after the attackers passed through, several explosive devices were left behind,” Mambo said.
In Mwenda, another device was located by FARDC forces, buried in the sand and awaiting demining to allow safe access for residents.
The discovery of such explosive hazards has become increasingly frequent following the recapture of several ADF strongholds by the Congolese army in the Ruwenzori sector. Authorities continue to call for heightened vigilance among civilians in these high-risk areas.

excerpt_en: February 18, 2026 – Shabunda, South Kivu, DRC – Armed assailants targeted a convoy transporting teachers’ salaries for multiple schools in the Shabunda 8 subdivision, specifically in the village of Mungole, on the Shabunda–Centre–Makese road, stealing funds and other valuables. L
body_en:
February 18, 2026 – Shabunda, South Kivu, DRC – Armed assailants targeted a convoy transporting teachers’ salaries for multiple schools in the Shabunda 8 subdivision, specifically in the village of Mungole, on the Shabunda–Centre–Makese road, stealing funds and other valuables.
Local civil society sources reported that the attack occurred about one kilometer from Shabunda Centre, with a school principal among the victims. Salaries for teachers at Kigulube Primary School, Un Point Primary School, Kamika Primary School, and Kiseku Primary School were taken, totaling approximately 13 million Congolese francs.
In addition to teachers’ salaries, the assailants also seized money belonging to a businessman, as well as cell phones and personal belongings of other residents traveling with the convoy.
The administrator of Shabunda territory, Raphaël Konga Konga, confirmed the incident and called on security services to apprehend the perpetrators and ensure they face justice.
This robbery highlights the ongoing insecurity in South Kivu, disrupting the delivery of essential public services and threatening education in the region.

title_en: Wazalendo Recapture Three Villages Near Rubaya After AFC/M23 Clashes
excerpt_en: Masisi, North Kivu, February 23, 2026 – Violent fighting erupted on Sunday, February 22, between AFC/M23 rebels and Wazalendo fighters in the villages of Kasenyi, Chugi, and Kinigi, located in the Bahunde chiefdom of Masisi territory, near the mining town of Rubaya. The Wazalendo
body_en:
Masisi, North Kivu, February 23, 2026 – Violent fighting erupted on Sunday, February 22, between AFC/M23 rebels and Wazalendo fighters in the villages of Kasenyi, Chugi, and Kinigi, located in the Bahunde chiefdom of Masisi territory, near the mining town of Rubaya.
The Wazalendo successfully regained control of the three villages, which had been considered strategic positions for the AFC/M23 rebels due to the economic and security significance of the area. The proximity to Rubaya, known for its mining activities, underscores the importance of these localities in the military strategy of the warring parties.
During the clashes, several rebel fighters were reportedly captured, and weapons and ammunition were recovered by the Wazalendo. In response, the AFC/M23 reinforced their positions on the Sita hill, aiming to contain the advance and attempt to retake Chugi and Kinigi.
The AFC/M23 denounced the government coalition’s violation of the ceasefire and reported drone strikes in several areas of the Masisi territory.
On Monday, February 23, a fragile calm prevailed along the front line, but the situation remains volatile, with residents fearing a resumption of fighting in a region already weakened by months of insecurity.

body_en:
Cape Town, South Africa, February 10, 2026 – At Mining Indaba 2026, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) reaffirmed its commitment to using its natural resources to promote peace, stability, and prosperity for its people.
During the “DRC Breakfast” conference, held under the theme “Global Value Chains: The Economic Case for Upstream and Downstream Investments in the DRC”, Minister of Mines Louis Watum presented the government’s vision to position the DRC as a major industrial player in the global energy transition.
Watum emphasized the shift from a reliance on raw material exports toward a model focused on:
Local value creation
Development of battery value chains
Industrialization of critical minerals
Integration of artisanal mining within a formal, structured, and sustainable framework
He also highlighted key government priorities, including strengthening legal security, alignment with international ESG standards, improved governance, and a strengthened fight against fraud and illicit activities. The goal is to offer investors a predictable, transparent, and competitive environment.
The DRC aims to become a major mining transformation hub and a strategic partner in global value chains, benefiting investors, local communities, and the nation.
The event brought together parliamentarians, diplomats, investors, and mining sector partners, along with the Minister of Mines, to discuss the country’s path toward sustainable industrial growth.

title: EGC and Trafigura Launch First Copper and Cobalt Shipment via Lobito Atlantic Railway
excerpt: Kinshasa, February 13, 2026 – Entreprise Générale du Cobalt (EGC) and Trafigura announced their first shipment of copper and cobalt to international markets through the Lobito Atlantic Railway (LAR), marking a major step in creating a fast, efficient, and traceable mining supply
title_en: EGC and Trafigura Launch First Copper and Cobalt Shipment via Lobito Atlantic Railway
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, February 13, 2026 – Entreprise Générale du Cobalt (EGC) and Trafigura announced their first shipment of copper and cobalt to international markets through the Lobito Atlantic Railway (LAR), marking a major step in creating a fast, efficient, and traceable mining supply
body_en:
Kinshasa, February 13, 2026 – Entreprise Générale du Cobalt (EGC) and Trafigura announced their first shipment of copper and cobalt to international markets through the Lobito Atlantic Railway (LAR), marking a major step in creating a fast, efficient, and traceable mining supply chain from the DRC.
The rail corridor, spanning 1,300 kilometers from the deep-water port of Lobito in Angola to the Congolese border at Luau, with an additional 450 kilometers to Kolwezi in the Copperbelt, is now the shortest route from Kolwezi to an African port, reducing inland transit time to approximately seven days.
Eric Kalala, CEO of EGC, said the shipment reflects progress toward an ethical, traceable, and transparent supply of large-scale artisanal cobalt and copper, facilitated by ARECOMS and the Congolese Ministry of Mines. “The copper shipment is initially destined for the United States, reflecting the strategic partnership between the DRC and the U.S., supported by Gécamines and FOMIN,” he added.
Franck Rogozin, Trafigura’s Head of Metals and Minerals in Africa, emphasized that the partnership strengthens the resilience of the global supply of critical metals. “This collaboration facilitates the responsible transport of copper and cobalt to global markets via the most efficient route, highlighting the importance of strong producer-trader partnerships,” he stated.
Nicholas Fournier, CEO of LAR, described the railway as a regional asset and a catalyst for positioning Angola and the DRC as key suppliers of metals and minerals vital for decarbonization, digitalization, and industrialization.
Owned by Trafigura, Mota-Engil, and Vecturis, LAR recently secured $753 million in financing from the International Development Finance Corporation (DFC) and the Development Bank of Southern Africa (DBSA) for rehabilitation and expansion of the network.
Under existing agreements, Trafigura handles the marketing of cobalt supplied by EGC, which purchases minerals from artisanal producers across the DRC.
About the partners:
Trafigura: A leading employee-owned commodities group operating in over 150 countries, with 14,500 employees. Its portfolio spans metals, minerals, oil, gas, electricity, and renewable energy projects.
EGC: A subsidiary of Gécamines, established in 2019, with an exclusive mandate to purchase, process, and market strategic minerals like cobalt, coltan, and germanium from artisanal mining.
Lobito Atlantic Railway (LAR): Operates a 1,300 km line connecting Lobito port to Luau, plus a 450 km section to Kolwezi, under a 30-year concession. It collaborates with the DRC’s SNCC to modernize and operate the railway section within the DRC.
This milestone positions the DRC as a strategic supplier of critical metals, reinforcing ethical mining standards and enhancing regional export infrastructure.

title: DRC Trains 2,500 New Magistrates, Emphasizes Integrity and Rule of Law
excerpt: Kinshasa, February 23, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo has completed the initial training of 2,500 new magistrates, the second wave of appointees under a presidential decree from March 28, 2025. The training, conducted from November 2025 to February 2026, focused on ethic
title_en: DRC Trains 2,500 New Magistrates, Emphasizes Integrity and Rule of Law
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, February 23, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo has completed the initial training of 2,500 new magistrates, the second wave of appointees under a presidential decree from March 28, 2025. The training, conducted from November 2025 to February 2026, focused on ethic
body_en:
Kinshasa, February 23, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo has completed the initial training of 2,500 new magistrates, the second wave of appointees under a presidential decree from March 28, 2025. The training, conducted from November 2025 to February 2026, focused on ethics, professional conduct, and technical competence for both civilian and military magistrates.
Dieudonné Kamuleta Badibanga, President of the High Council of the Judiciary (CSM) and the Constitutional Court, urged the new magistrates to “resist pressure of all kinds, refuse unethical concessions, and remain steadfast in the face of corruption.” He stressed that true greatness is measured by integrity, conscience, and sense of justice, not rank or power.
Kamuleta emphasized that magistrates are servants of the Republic, entrusted with upholding the Constitution and safeguarding fundamental freedoms. He described the robes worn by magistrates as symbols of responsibility, not privilege, reminding them of their duty to the Congolese people.
Minister of Justice Guillaume Ngefa highlighted that this new cohort strengthens the judiciary, ensures adequate numbers for effective law enforcement, and supports the rule of law, judicial reform, and anti-impunity efforts. The program included 86 instructors across 31 modules, conducted in Kinshasa and Lubumbashi (Haut-Katanga).
This latest recruitment brings the total number of magistrates appointed since 2022 to 5,000, addressing a previous shortage of approximately 3,000 magistrates. The initiative aims to improve access to justice for over 100 million Congolese citizens, modernize the judiciary, and enhance ethical and professional standards.

title: Kinshasa and Brazzaville Strengthen Military Cooperation for Joint Border Security
excerpt: February 11, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and the Republic of Congo are consolidating bilateral military cooperation to enhance security along their shared border, as Deputy Prime Minister of National Defense Guy Kabombo visited Brazzaville to meet with Congolese
title_en: Kinshasa and Brazzaville Strengthen Military Cooperation for Joint Border Security
excerpt_en: February 11, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and the Republic of Congo are consolidating bilateral military cooperation to enhance security along their shared border, as Deputy Prime Minister of National Defense Guy Kabombo visited Brazzaville to meet with Congolese
body_en:
February 11, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and the Republic of Congo are consolidating bilateral military cooperation to enhance security along their shared border, as Deputy Prime Minister of National Defense Guy Kabombo visited Brazzaville to meet with Congolese counterparts.
According to Kabombo’s office, the visit aims to fortify mutual trust and promote a strategic rapprochement between the two neighboring countries. Charles Richard Mondjo, Minister of National Defense of the Republic of Congo, emphasized that the discussions are designed to strengthen diplomatic ties and address common security challenges, while ensuring that the Republic of Congo will not serve as a rear base to undermine regional stability.
“I want to clearly reiterate that the Republic of Congo will not undertake any action that could jeopardize the collective security and stability of our region,” Mondjo stated.
“Our shared concern is to make these areas safe and controlled, facilitating the smooth flow of traffic to support trade and the development of our countries. Incidents along the 1,200 km river border must be addressed through dialogue and in accordance with national interests, while respecting the bonds of fraternity between our peoples and heads of state.”
Both officials highlighted the importance of military training programs, describing them as a platform for dynamic South-South cooperation that contributes to regional stability. Kabombo underscored that the DRC expects neighboring countries to support ongoing diplomatic initiatives, including the Expanded Joint Verification Mechanism Plus, and to resist manipulations based on old pretexts.
“We aim to transform the eastern part of our country into a reservoir of supported resources,” Kabombo said, stressing the need for practical collaboration to secure national territory.
The visit comes amid ongoing Rwandan aggression through the AFC/M23 rebellion, which continues to control large areas in North Kivu and South Kivu, and amid slow progress on diplomatic initiatives in Washington and Doha.
Historically, rapprochement between Brazzaville and Kigali has been viewed skeptically in Kinshasa due to Rwanda’s perceived role in destabilizing eastern DRC. Despite these concerns, leaders in Brazzaville and Kinshasa have consistently reaffirmed their commitment to joint security efforts and broader regional cooperation. President Félix Tshisekedi of the DRC maintains regular engagements with his Congolese counterpart, Denis Sassou Nguesso, to address security challenges and other pressing international issues affecting the sub-region.

Charles Richard Mondjo, Minister of National Defense of the Republic of Congo, emphasized that the discussions are designed to strengthen diplomatic ties and address common security challenges, while ensuring that the Republic of Congo will not serve as a rear base to undermine regional stability.

title: Tshisekedi Urges MONUSCO’s “Credible Technical” Support for Ceasefire
excerpt: February 14, 2026 – On the sidelines of the 39th African Union Summit in Addis Ababa, Congolese President Félix Tshisekedi called on UN Secretary-General António Guterres for “urgent and credible technical support” from MONUSCO to operationalize the ceasefire monitoring and verif
title_en: Tshisekedi Urges MONUSCO’s “Credible Technical” Support for Ceasefire
excerpt_en: February 14, 2026 – On the sidelines of the 39th African Union Summit in Addis Ababa, Congolese President Félix Tshisekedi called on UN Secretary-General António Guterres for “urgent and credible technical support” from MONUSCO to operationalize the ceasefire monitoring and verif
body_en:
February 14, 2026 – On the sidelines of the 39th African Union Summit in Addis Ababa, Congolese President Félix Tshisekedi called on UN Secretary-General António Guterres for “urgent and credible technical support” from MONUSCO to operationalize the ceasefire monitoring and verification mechanism in eastern DRC.
The meeting focused on the security situation in the Great Lakes region, strengthening multilateral cooperation, and the DRC’s role as a non-permanent member of the UN Security Council. President Tshisekedi reaffirmed the DRC’s commitment to consolidating peace efforts and emphasized the need to move from exhortations to action to ensure compliance with international law and agreements under regional and international frameworks.
“We need credible technical support from MONUSCO to guarantee the operationalization of the ceasefire monitoring and verification mechanism,” Tshisekedi stated, citing UN Security Council resolution 2808 (2025).
Secretary-General Guterres pledged the UN’s support for the implementation of the established ceasefire architecture, welcoming the DRC’s engagement in fair and effective multilateralism.
On the ground, the acting head of MONUSCO, Vivian van de Perre, traveled to Goma on Thursday to support preparations for monitoring and verifying the ceasefire. Arriving by air—marking the first flight access to Goma since January 2025—she is scheduled to meet with stakeholders to advance the practical arrangements for the mechanism.
“I am going to Goma to support preparations for monitoring and verifying the ceasefire, in close coordination with the established ceasefire architecture, including the EJVM+,” van de Perre said.
MONUSCO is authorized under resolution 2808 (2025) to provide technical and logistical support to the International Conference on the Great Lakes Region (ICGLR) through the Expanded Joint Verification Mechanism Plus (EJVM+). An initial team of peacekeepers will be deployed to Uvira, South Kivu, to assist the ceasefire monitoring mechanism. This deployment is limited and technical, not constituting a permanent return to the province, from which MONUSCO withdrew in June 2024.
Peacekeepers remain actively deployed in Ituri and North Kivu, continuing their support for security and monitoring operations in eastern DRC.

title: Over Fifty Civilians Killed in Rutshuru and Surrounding Villages, January 2026 – OCHA
excerpt: February 18, 2026 – North Kivu, DRC – The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) reported that armed clashes in Masisi, Rutshuru, and Walikale territories in January 2026 claimed nearly 100 civilian lives, left many wounded, and caused large-scale populatio
title_en: Over Fifty Civilians Killed in Rutshuru and Surrounding Villages, January 2026 – OCHA
excerpt_en: February 18, 2026 – North Kivu, DRC – The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) reported that armed clashes in Masisi, Rutshuru, and Walikale territories in January 2026 claimed nearly 100 civilian lives, left many wounded, and caused large-scale populatio
body_en:
February 18, 2026 – North Kivu, DRC – The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) reported that armed clashes in Masisi, Rutshuru, and Walikale territories in January 2026 claimed nearly 100 civilian lives, left many wounded, and caused large-scale population displacement. The violence involved AFC/M23 rebels and Wazalendo militias aligned with the Congolese army.
Between January 12 and 16, fighting engulfed over a dozen villages in the Bukombo, Kihondo, Mutanda, Bambo, and Tongo groups within the Bwito chiefdom (Rutshuru territory), killing approximately 50 civilians. Displaced populations fled to Bukombo-centre, Ihula, Nyanzale, Kikuku-centre, and Katsiru, while others sought refuge in Mweso and Kitchanga (Masisi territory).
OCHA also noted renewed clashes in Nyamaboko 1 and 2 villages in Masisi and Katoyi Health Zones, further displacing civilians. An army airstrike on January 2 in Masisi-Centre reportedly killed 11 people, injured around 40 others, and destroyed the office of an international NGO.
In Walikale, drone strikes between January 19 and 30 targeted hills overlooking Kasopo, Buleusa (Ikobo group), Mpety, Mindjenje, and Chanjikiro (Kisimba group), leading to mass displacement. Residents of Mpombi and Iteya were forced to flee on January 21 due to escalating clashes, while healthcare access deteriorated as several health facilities were looted or damaged. The Pinga General Referral Hospital reported critical shortages of medicines, equipment, and medical staff.
Adding to the humanitarian toll, a landslide in Burutsi killed at least 30 people, buried homes, and severed the Kashebere Mungazi–Kibua road, the only link to central Walikale.
OCHA’s report underscores the ongoing insecurity, displacement, and disruption of essential services in eastern DRC, emphasizing the urgent need for humanitarian assistance and civilian protection in North Kivu.

title: Gatumba-Kavimvira Border Crossing Reopens After Two Months
excerpt: Uvira–Gatumba, February 23, 2026 – The border crossing between Uvira in the Democratic Republic of Congo and Gatumba in Burundi officially reopened this Monday, more than two months after being closed due to the AFC/M23 conflict. The closure, imposed by Burundi following the occu
title_en: Gatumba-Kavimvira Border Crossing Reopens After Two Months
excerpt_en: Uvira–Gatumba, February 23, 2026 – The border crossing between Uvira in the Democratic Republic of Congo and Gatumba in Burundi officially reopened this Monday, more than two months after being closed due to the AFC/M23 conflict. The closure, imposed by Burundi following the occu
body_en:
Uvira–Gatumba, February 23, 2026 – The border crossing between Uvira in the Democratic Republic of Congo and Gatumba in Burundi officially reopened this Monday, more than two months after being closed due to the AFC/M23 conflict.
The closure, imposed by Burundi following the occupation of Uvira by AFC/M23 rebels, disrupted trade and travel between the two countries. No official ceremony marked the reopening, but both sides agreed to allow free passage for travelers.
The head of migration services in Kavimvira (DRC), after discussions with the Burundian Commissioner General of Migration, Maurice Mbonimpa, emphasized that standard migration formalities—including visas and necessary documents—remain mandatory. The border will operate daily from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.
The reopening brought relief to residents and traders on both sides. A Congolese trader said, “I do small-scale trading in Uvira, go to Luvumera in Bujumbura to buy goods, and today I can return as usual. We thank our authorities and those of Burundi for listening to our pleas.”
Burundian citizens expressed similar satisfaction. One resident commented, “The reopening of the border is a huge relief for most of us. Our lives depend on our brotherly and friendly countries.”
The reopening was announced in Uvira on Sunday by the Governor of South Kivu, Jean-Jacques Purusi Sadiki, signaling a step toward restoring normalcy after the recent conflict-induced disruptions.

excerpt_en: Kinshasa, February 11, 2026 – The United Nations has welcomed Angola’s willingness to help organize an inclusive national dialogue among the people of the Democratic Republic of Congo. The announcement was made in Kinshasa by Jean-Pierre Lacroix, UN Under-Secretary-General for Pe
body_en:
Kinshasa, February 11, 2026 – The United Nations has welcomed Angola’s willingness to help organize an inclusive national dialogue among the people of the Democratic Republic of Congo.
The announcement was made in Kinshasa by Jean-Pierre Lacroix, UN Under-Secretary-General for Peacekeeping Operations, following consultations with social and political forces in the DRC and national authorities.
“Regarding dialogue efforts, we noted with great interest Angola’s willingness to support the organization of an inclusive dialogue. Many political groups have high expectations, and the contribution of a third party, such as Angola, is essential to achieving this objective,” said Lacroix.
He emphasized that MONUSCO will continue to support all progress, particularly in verifying compliance with the ceasefire.
“The crucial importance is that diplomatic efforts intensify to implement commitments, especially regarding the ceasefire. MONUSCO must remain ready, available, and proactive to support these advances, focusing on efficiency in line with the Security Council mandate,” Lacroix added.

title: Mercuria Purchases First Copper and Cobalt Lot from EGC
excerpt: Kinshasa, February 13, 2026 – Mercuria Energy Trading SA, a Swiss commodity trading company, has completed its first copper and cobalt transaction with the Entreprise Générale du Cobalt (EGC), marking a significant step for the DRC’s strategic metals sector. This operation follow
title_en: Mercuria Purchases First Copper and Cobalt Lot from EGC
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, February 13, 2026 – Mercuria Energy Trading SA, a Swiss commodity trading company, has completed its first copper and cobalt transaction with the Entreprise Générale du Cobalt (EGC), marking a significant step for the DRC’s strategic metals sector. This operation follow
body_en:
Kinshasa, February 13, 2026 – Mercuria Energy Trading SA, a Swiss commodity trading company, has completed its first copper and cobalt transaction with the Entreprise Générale du Cobalt (EGC), marking a significant step for the DRC’s strategic metals sector.
This operation follows the implementation of a cobalt export quota system in the Democratic Republic of Congo, established by the Regulatory and Control Authority for the Strategic Mineral Substances Market (ARECOMS) in 2025.
The transaction adheres to EGC’s supply chain management standards and emphasizes responsible practices in the artisanal and small-scale mining sector.
According to the press release, the copper cathodes are destined for markets in the United States, United Arab Emirates, and Saudi Arabia.
This first export of copper and cobalt strengthens the DRC’s position as a key player in the global critical metals market. It also builds on the creation of a joint venture between Gécamines and Mercuria announced in 2025.

excerpt: February 20, 2026 – The Kinshasa/Gombe Military Court has scheduled the first hearing in the case between Claudien Likulia, son of former Human Rights Minister Marie-Ange Mushobekwa, and Philémon Mambabwa Zebo, a senior official at the National Intelligence Agency (ANR). The hear
title_en: Kinshasa Military Court to Hear Case of Alleged ANR Abduction and Torture
excerpt_en: February 20, 2026 – The Kinshasa/Gombe Military Court has scheduled the first hearing in the case between Claudien Likulia, son of former Human Rights Minister Marie-Ange Mushobekwa, and Philémon Mambabwa Zebo, a senior official at the National Intelligence Agency (ANR). The hear
body_en:
February 20, 2026 – The Kinshasa/Gombe Military Court has scheduled the first hearing in the case between Claudien Likulia, son of former Human Rights Minister Marie-Ange Mushobekwa, and Philémon Mambabwa Zebo, a senior official at the National Intelligence Agency (ANR). The hearing is set for Thursday, February 26, at the court’s premises on 46 Lubefu Avenue, Gombe, Kinshasa.
Marie-Ange Mushobekwa alleges that on December 21, 2025, her two minor children, Claudien (18) and Christopher Likulia (17), along with a 17-year-old friend, were abducted, tied up, beaten, and tortured at the private residence of the ANR official. She claims the attack was carried out by seven police officers and soldiers acting on Mambabwa’s orders.
Describing the incident as “arbitrary, brutal, and disproportionate”, Mushobekwa emphasized that her children were unarmed, not wanted by the police, and present by invitation, yet suffered serious physical and psychological trauma, including visible bruises, difficulty sitting, and functional impairment of one hand.
Mushobekwa denounced the incident as an abuse of personal power and a state affair, criticizing the absence of administrative or judicial sanctions nearly three weeks after the event. She called for a fair and impartial trial, stating, “This is not a political matter; it is a moral test for the state,” and urged the authorities to take responsibility.
The upcoming hearing will test the Congolese justice system’s ability to address alleged abuses by state security agents and deliver accountability for serious human rights violations.

title: ADF Attack in Mangadu Claims Five Lives
excerpt: Mangadu Beni February 11, 2026 – Violence continues to escalate in the Beni-Mbau area, as an attack by Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) fighters on Tuesday, February 10, left at least five civilians dead in Mangadu-Upende, located 7 kilometers from Mbau town in Beni territory, Nort
title_en: ADF Attack in Mangadu Claims Five Lives
excerpt_en: Mangadu Beni February 11, 2026 – Violence continues to escalate in the Beni-Mbau area, as an attack by Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) fighters on Tuesday, February 10, left at least five civilians dead in Mangadu-Upende, located 7 kilometers from Mbau town in Beni territory, Nort
body_en:
Mangadu Beni February 11, 2026 – Violence continues to escalate in the Beni-Mbau area, as an attack by Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) fighters on Tuesday, February 10, left at least five civilians dead in Mangadu-Upende, located 7 kilometers from Mbau town in Beni territory, North Kivu.
According to Kisaki Luis, president of the local civil society organization in the Batangi Mbau group, the victims’ bodies were recovered early Wednesday morning.
“We found five bodies lying on the ground, four men and one woman. The victims were killed with firearms. Before withdrawing, the attackers placed an explosive device on one of the bodies, which is why we recovered four bodies. There is also one missing person and material damage,” Luis reported.
Civil society actors warn that attacks continue to occur despite prior warnings about ADF movements. Local leaders expressed frustration at what they describe as the inaction of security forces, noting that the armed group has carried out numerous killings since the beginning of the year.
“Right now, the population is moving towards areas considered safe, and we are tired of what is happening. Our armed forces must pursue the assailants to their strongholds. From Otomabere to here, they are carrying out a series of killings, and we don't understand this lethargy on the part of the armed forces,” lamented Kisaki Luis.
The latest attack adds to a rising climate of fear in Beni and surrounding areas, where more than 60 civilians have reportedly been killed since the start of 2026 due to ADF insurgency.

title: FARDC Accuses AFC/M23 of Burning Houses Ahead of Ceasefire
excerpt: Fizi-Uvira February 14, 2026 – Four days before the scheduled ceasefire between the Congolese government and the M23, the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) accused the AFC/M23-RDF coalition of burning civilian homes on February 11 in the Rusankuku area of t
title_en: FARDC Accuses AFC/M23 of Burning Houses Ahead of Ceasefire
excerpt_en: Fizi-Uvira February 14, 2026 – Four days before the scheduled ceasefire between the Congolese government and the M23, the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) accused the AFC/M23-RDF coalition of burning civilian homes on February 11 in the Rusankuku area of t
body_en:
Fizi-Uvira February 14, 2026 – Four days before the scheduled ceasefire between the Congolese government and the M23, the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) accused the AFC/M23-RDF coalition of burning civilian homes on February 11 in the Rusankuku area of the Fizi-Uvira highlands, citing a military statement.
The statement, signed by acting spokesperson Lieutenant Colonel Mongba Hazukay Mak, described the actions as “serious violations of International Humanitarian Law and Human Rights.” According to the FARDC, the operation was intended to punish local populations who refused to comply with the rebels’ demands. The army condemned the acts as terrorist attacks, emphasizing that they demonstrate the cruelty and determination of the Rwandan army and its proxies to undermine the ongoing peace process.
This comes as Kinshasa announced acceptance of an Angolan ceasefire proposal, set to take effect at noon on February 18, 2026. The Presidency emphasized that this decision reflects responsibility, appeasement, and the search for a peaceful solution, while commending Angola for its efforts toward a lasting return to peace in the Great Lakes region.
The ceasefire falls under the monitoring and verification mechanism signed in Doha on October 14, 2025, which stipulates:
Immediate freeze on military positions
Halt to all reinforcements and offensive rotations
No modification of the status quo on the ground
End of external support for armed groups
Protection of civilians and respect for international humanitarian law
Kinshasa warned that any unilateral military consolidation during the ceasefire would seriously undermine the credibility of the process.
The Angolan proposal followed a Luanda meeting involving Angolan President João Lourenço, DRC President Félix Tshisekedi, Togolese President Faure Gnassingbé (AU mediator), and former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo, designated by the AU as facilitator. This diplomatic momentum was preceded by a high-level meeting in Lomé on January 17, 2026, which defined the AU mediation structure for the DRC peace process, led by Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé, supported by five co-facilitators and a joint secretariat.
For its part, the AFC/M23 confirmed readiness to implement the Doha mechanism in good faith, but political coordinator Corneille Nangaa criticized Kinshasa for a “strategy of diplomatic fragmentation”, calling the government’s ceasefire acceptance a public relations maneuver. He also accused the authorities of continuing belligerent acts, including offensives on populated areas, the use of mercenaries, and indiscriminate bombings affecting civilians.

title: EU Commissioner Hadja Lahbib Launches Humanitarian Mission in DRC Amid Escalating Crisis
excerpt: Great Lakes Region February 17, 2026 – Kinshasa, DRC – The European Commissioner for Crisis Preparedness, Management, and Equality, Hadja Lahbib, has begun a humanitarian mission to the Great Lakes region, starting in the Democratic Republic of Congo. The visit comes amid persist
title_en: EU Commissioner Hadja Lahbib Launches Humanitarian Mission in DRC Amid Escalating Crisis
excerpt_en: Great Lakes Region February 17, 2026 – Kinshasa, DRC – The European Commissioner for Crisis Preparedness, Management, and Equality, Hadja Lahbib, has begun a humanitarian mission to the Great Lakes region, starting in the Democratic Republic of Congo. The visit comes amid persist
body_en:
Great Lakes Region February 17, 2026 – Kinshasa, DRC – The European Commissioner for Crisis Preparedness, Management, and Equality, Hadja Lahbib, has begun a humanitarian mission to the Great Lakes region, starting in the Democratic Republic of Congo. The visit comes amid persistent violence in eastern DRC, fueled by the activities of Rwandan-backed ADF/M23 rebels, which has caused massive displacement across South Kivu and neighboring countries.
During her mission, Lahbib plans to meet all parties to the conflict to advocate for improved humanitarian access, ensure the opening of safe corridors, and maintain essential services, including health care, even in areas controlled by armed groups. She will also visit refugee camps, including the largest Congolese camp in Bujumbura, Burundi, which hosts over 70,000 people.
“I have just arrived in the Democratic Republic of Congo, the first stop on my mission to the Great Lakes region. My absolute priority is to negotiate access and humanitarian deliveries. In the East, the situation is critical, with a dramatic humanitarian crisis. Lives must be saved,” Lahbib stated on her Twitter account.
The visit highlights a critical funding shortfall for humanitarian operations in DRC, forcing aid agencies to prioritize resources for only 7.3 million people out of nearly 15 million in urgent need. The European Union, alongside its member states, remains a key donor, providing emergency aid to save lives, prevent suffering, and preserve dignity in areas affected by conflict or disaster.
This humanitarian mission follows government-led efforts by Minister of State Ève Bazaiba Masudi, who recently visited Burundi and Tanzania to support Congolese refugees, coordinate aid, and assess conditions in collaboration with UNHCR and other partners. Lahbib’s mission underscores the urgency of international solidarity to address one of the world’s longest-running and most neglected humanitarian crises, exacerbated by continued rebel activity and recent territorial gains by AFC/M23 in Uvira and surrounding towns.

excerpt: Walikale, North Kivu, February 23, 2026 – A relative calm has returned to the Buhaya and Fungura mountains, near Katobi in the Banakindi area of Walikale territory, following two days of intense fighting between AFC/M23 rebels and the Wazalendo. The hostilities erupted despite a
title_en: Fragile Calm After Clashes Between AFC/M23 Rebels and Wazalendo in Buhaya and Fungura
excerpt_en: Walikale, North Kivu, February 23, 2026 – A relative calm has returned to the Buhaya and Fungura mountains, near Katobi in the Banakindi area of Walikale territory, following two days of intense fighting between AFC/M23 rebels and the Wazalendo. The hostilities erupted despite a
body_en:
Walikale, North Kivu, February 23, 2026 – A relative calm has returned to the Buhaya and Fungura mountains, near Katobi in the Banakindi area of Walikale territory, following two days of intense fighting between AFC/M23 rebels and the Wazalendo.
The hostilities erupted despite a ceasefire proposed by Angola as part of regional efforts to curb persistent insecurity in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
The rebels launched simultaneous offensives on the strategic heights of Buhaya and Fungura, which overlook Katobi village and serve as key security positions for Pinga, a town frequently targeted by armed incursions.
After fierce exchanges of fire, the Wazalendo reportedly contained the rebel advance, forcing AFC/M23 fighters to retreat toward Mpety, considered their main stronghold in the area.
Many residents of Katobi fled into surrounding forests for safety. Despite the lull observed on Monday morning, the displaced population has yet to return, fearing a resumption of fighting.
The situation on the ground remains volatile, with local communities living in uncertainty amid a resurgence of armed violence in Walikale territory.

title: President Félix Tshisekedi in Luanda for Mediation Talks on Eastern DRC
excerpt: Luanda, Angola, February 9, 2026 – President Félix-Antoine Tshisekedi of the Democratic Republic of Congo is in Luanda as part of ongoing mediation efforts aimed at restoring peace in eastern DRC, a region facing tensions linked to Rwanda. During his visit, President Tshisekedi i
title_en: President Félix Tshisekedi in Luanda for Mediation Talks on Eastern DRC
excerpt_en: Luanda, Angola, February 9, 2026 – President Félix-Antoine Tshisekedi of the Democratic Republic of Congo is in Luanda as part of ongoing mediation efforts aimed at restoring peace in eastern DRC, a region facing tensions linked to Rwanda. During his visit, President Tshisekedi i
body_en:
Luanda, Angola, February 9, 2026 – President Félix-Antoine Tshisekedi of the Democratic Republic of Congo is in Luanda as part of ongoing mediation efforts aimed at restoring peace in eastern DRC, a region facing tensions linked to Rwanda.
During his visit, President Tshisekedi is scheduled to meet with his Angolan counterpart, João Lourenço, who currently serves as Chairperson of the African Union (AU). Togolese President Faure Gnassingbé and former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo are also participating in the discussions.
“At the invitation of the President of Angola and current AU Chairperson, João Lourenço, President Tshisekedi is undertaking a working visit to discuss ongoing mediation initiatives aimed at restoring peace to eastern DRC,” said Tina Salama, spokesperson for the Congolese president.
This is President Tshisekedi’s second visit to Luanda in 2026; he previously met with João Lourenço on January 5 to address the security situation in eastern DRC.

excerpt_en: Kinshasa, February 10, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has officially exported its first legal artisanal gold from Haut-Katanga, following the opening of a provincial branch of DRC Gold Trading S.A.A. in Lubumbashi. In just a few days, over 20 kilograms of gold were
body_en:
Kinshasa, February 10, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has officially exported its first legal artisanal gold from Haut-Katanga, following the opening of a provincial branch of DRC Gold Trading S.A.A. in Lubumbashi.
In just a few days, over 20 kilograms of gold were collected, traced, and exported—a historic first for a region traditionally known for copper and cobalt, where no artisanal gold had previously been legally exported.
The government has also expanded its presence in Haut-Uele, opening another DRC Gold Trading S.A.A. office in Durba to improve production traceability and bring administrative support closer to artisanal miners.
Authorities emphasize that this effort aims to formalize the gold sector, replacing the informal market with official channels to strengthen transparency and economic sovereignty.

title_en: Justice at a Standstill in Bulungu – 93 Detainees, Only 25 Convicted
excerpt_en: February 12, 2026 – The justice system in Bulungu, Kwilu province, is facing a critical impasse, leaving detainees to die without knowing their fate. Local sources report that at least five detainees have died since January while awaiting trial, due to a severe shortage of magist
body_en:
February 12, 2026 – The justice system in Bulungu, Kwilu province, is facing a critical impasse, leaving detainees to die without knowing their fate.
Local sources report that at least five detainees have died since January while awaiting trial, due to a severe shortage of magistrates and the closure of the Bulungu High Court since December 15, 2025.
Currently, the central prison houses 93 detainees, of whom only 25 have been convicted. The remaining 68 detainees await hearings that have not taken place, including appeals from five territories across Kwilu Province.
Attorney Dirigeant Munzende, president of the Bulungu civil society organization, condemned the situation as a violation of the right to justice. He explained that the court is functioning with only the presiding judge and a single judge, relying on a legal aid lawyer to fill the panel.
“The last hearings were on December 15, 2025. Since then, no case has been heard, and several detainees have died during proceedings, while others remain in indefinite limbo,” Munzende stated.
The situation highlights the urgent need to reinforce judicial capacity in Kwilu to prevent further deaths and ensure timely access to justice for all detainees.

title: Calm Returns to Kilama After Three Days of Clashes Between AFC/M23 and Wazalendo
excerpt: Kilama Rutshuru February 11, 2026 – A gradual return to calm has been reported in Kilama, part of the Bambo group in Rutshuru territory, North Kivu, following three days of intense clashes between AFC/M23 rebels and Wazalendo fighters of the Collective of Movements for Change/Peo
title_en: Calm Returns to Kilama After Three Days of Clashes Between AFC/M23 and Wazalendo
excerpt_en: Kilama Rutshuru February 11, 2026 – A gradual return to calm has been reported in Kilama, part of the Bambo group in Rutshuru territory, North Kivu, following three days of intense clashes between AFC/M23 rebels and Wazalendo fighters of the Collective of Movements for Change/Peo
body_en:
Kilama Rutshuru February 11, 2026 – A gradual return to calm has been reported in Kilama, part of the Bambo group in Rutshuru territory, North Kivu, following three days of intense clashes between AFC/M23 rebels and Wazalendo fighters of the Collective of Movements for Change/People’s Defense Forces (CMC/FDP).
Local sources indicate that the fighting erupted on February 8, when AFC/M23 forces launched simultaneous attacks on Wazalendo positions in the villages of Mayengo and Bugabo, as well as in areas near Domaine in Kilama.
The assaults reportedly involved the use of kamikaze drones, heavy artillery, and aerial bombardment, followed by attempted ground advances. After several hours of intense combat, Wazalendo forces successfully repelled the rebels on all fronts, according to local reports.
The clashes prompted population movements, as residents sought safety in areas considered more secure. The return of calm comes as authorities and local communities monitor the situation to prevent renewed violence.

title: AFC/M23 Denounces Kinshasa’s “Diplomatic Fragmentation” Despite Angolan Ceasefire Proposal
excerpt: February 14, 2026 – Following renewed calls for a ceasefire, the AFC/M23 rebellion reaffirmed its commitment to implementing the mechanism agreed upon in the Doha peace process. In a statement released on Friday, February 13, political coordinator Corneille Nangaa emphasized that
title_en: AFC/M23 Denounces Kinshasa’s “Diplomatic Fragmentation” Despite Angolan Ceasefire Proposal
excerpt_en: February 14, 2026 – Following renewed calls for a ceasefire, the AFC/M23 rebellion reaffirmed its commitment to implementing the mechanism agreed upon in the Doha peace process. In a statement released on Friday, February 13, political coordinator Corneille Nangaa emphasized that
body_en:
February 14, 2026 – Following renewed calls for a ceasefire, the AFC/M23 rebellion reaffirmed its commitment to implementing the mechanism agreed upon in the Doha peace process. In a statement released on Friday, February 13, political coordinator Corneille Nangaa emphasized that this stance reflects a sense of political responsibility and a desire for a negotiated, lasting, and inclusive settlement of the conflict.
“However, the AFC/M23 denounces the strategy of diplomatic fragmentation employed by the illegitimate and corrupt regime in Kinshasa, characterized by the proliferation of parallel frameworks and initiatives outside a centralized and consensual process. Such an approach compromises mediation efforts, weakens credibility, and risks delaying a serious political settlement,” Nangaa stated.
He also accused the Kinshasa government of continuing belligerent acts, including offensives against populated areas, use of mercenaries, and indiscriminate bombings, despite its public support for the ceasefire. Nangaa described the government’s acceptance of the ceasefire principle as a public relations maneuver, aimed at deceiving national and international opinion while continuing a militaristic strategy.
This statement follows an Angolan ceasefire proposal, announced after a meeting in Luanda with Angolan President João Lourenço, Congolese President Félix Tshisekedi, Togolese President Faure Gnassingbé (AU mediator), and former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo, representing AU-designated facilitators for the DRC peace process.
The diplomatic momentum was preceded by a high-level meeting in Lomé, Togo, on January 17, 2026, aimed at consolidating the peace process in the DRC and the Great Lakes region. Initiated by Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé, AU lead mediator for eastern DRC, the meeting reinforced coordination with the United States and Qatar to encourage parties to honor their commitments.
Following Lomé, the African Union outlined its mediation structure, under Gnassingbé’s authority, supported by five co-facilitators with specific responsibilities and a joint secretariat comprising the AU and regional organizations, tasked with steering the peace process in eastern DRC.

title: Washington Warns of Potential Sanctions Against Kigali
excerpt: DRC-Rwanda February 17, 2026 – The United States has indicated that the agreement between Rwanda and the DRC signed in Washington “is only a starting point” and not the ultimate solution, according to Massad Boulos, Africa advisor to former President Donald Trump. His remarks cam
title_en: Washington Warns of Potential Sanctions Against Kigali
excerpt_en: DRC-Rwanda February 17, 2026 – The United States has indicated that the agreement between Rwanda and the DRC signed in Washington “is only a starting point” and not the ultimate solution, according to Massad Boulos, Africa advisor to former President Donald Trump. His remarks cam
body_en:
DRC-Rwanda February 17, 2026 – The United States has indicated that the agreement between Rwanda and the DRC signed in Washington “is only a starting point” and not the ultimate solution, according to Massad Boulos, Africa advisor to former President Donald Trump. His remarks came during a February 16 interview on France 24, amid renewed fighting on the ground.
Boulos stressed that the Washington agreement is complementary to the Doha process, led by Qatar with US and EU support, which focuses specifically on the M23-DRC conflict. He acknowledged a “serious violation” of the Washington agreement following the capture of Uvira by M23 rebels, reportedly backed by Rwanda. While fighters withdrew, some positions around the city remain under rebel control.
Regarding sanctions, the US official indicated that Washington has “a number of tools” available and could implement measures against President Paul Kagame or other actors. Targeted sanctions have previously been applied to individuals, including James Kabarebe, for conflict-related activities.
Speaking in Kigali at the opening of the “Umushyikirano” national dialogue, Kagame blamed tensions on Rwandan Hutu rebels from the FDLR operating in Congolese territory and denied involvement in M23 operations, mineral exploitation, or territorial ambitions.
UN and US reports, however, continue to allege Rwandan military support to M23, with the UN Security Council calling on Kigali to cease all support and withdraw troops from the DRC. Washington continues to engage Kigali, awaiting “concrete measures on the battlefield” to verify compliance with commitments.
