title: DRC and South Africa Discuss Revision of 2004 Military Agreement
excerpt: Kinshasa–Pretoria, February 22, 2026 – The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defense and Veterans Affairs of the Democratic Republic of Congo, Guy Kabombo Muadiamvita, is on an official mission to South Africa to strengthen military cooperation between the two countr
title_en: DRC and South Africa Discuss Revision of 2004 Military Agreement
excerpt_en: Kinshasa–Pretoria, February 22, 2026 – The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defense and Veterans Affairs of the Democratic Republic of Congo, Guy Kabombo Muadiamvita, is on an official mission to South Africa to strengthen military cooperation between the two countr
body_en:
Kinshasa–Pretoria, February 22, 2026 – The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defense and Veterans Affairs of the Democratic Republic of Congo, Guy Kabombo Muadiamvita, is on an official mission to South Africa to strengthen military cooperation between the two countries.
During his participation in the 71st anniversary of the South African Army on February 21, 2026, he met with his South African counterpart, Angie Motshekga, to discuss the revision of the 2004 military agreement that governs bilateral defense collaboration. Both ministers agreed to adopt resolutions based on the work of sectoral experts from each country.
This diplomatic engagement follows South Africa's decision to withdraw its troop contribution from the United Nations Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (MONUSCO). With over 700 soldiers deployed, South Africa has been among the top ten troop-contributing countries to the mission.
According to the South African Presidency, President Cyril Ramaphosa stated that the withdrawal aims to reorient resources of the South African National Defence Force after 27 years of support for peacekeeping in the DRC. The process of withdrawal is expected to be completed by the end of 2026, in collaboration with the UN.
Bilateral cooperation between Kinshasa and Pretoria has intensified in recent years. In July 2023, Presidents Félix Tshisekedi and Cyril Ramaphosa reaffirmed their commitment to strengthen security, economic development, infrastructure, agriculture, and other sectors. On the military front, South Africa deployed 2,900 troops to the DRC from December 2023 to December 2024 under Operation SAMIDRC, investing over 2 billion rand (≈ US$134 million) to support peace and security in the eastern provinces.
The 2004 General Cooperation Agreement remains the framework guiding bilateral relations, providing a foundation for enhanced military and strategic collaboration along the Kinshasa-Pretoria axis.

title: DRC Signals It Could Seek New Mining Partner if U.S. Deal Falters
excerpt: CAPE TOWN, February 11, 2026 — Louis Watum Kabamba, Minister of Mineral Resources of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, said Kinshasa may look for another mining partner if its agreement with the United States fails to deliver benefits. He made the remarks at the Mining Indaba
title_en: DRC Signals It Could Seek New Mining Partner if U.S. Deal Falters
excerpt_en: CAPE TOWN, February 11, 2026 — Louis Watum Kabamba, Minister of Mineral Resources of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, said Kinshasa may look for another mining partner if its agreement with the United States fails to deliver benefits. He made the remarks at the Mining Indaba
body_en:
CAPE TOWN, February 11, 2026 — Louis Watum Kabamba, Minister of Mineral Resources of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, said Kinshasa may look for another mining partner if its agreement with the United States fails to deliver benefits. He made the remarks at the Mining Indaba in Cape Town.
The agreement, signed on December 4, 2025, allows American investors access to several mining sites in exchange for U.S. support in strengthening the DRC’s security systems. Kabamba stressed the deal remains at a preliminary stage and has not transferred ownership of resources.
“It could result in a good and big project, or another that is not very profitable. We will continue because there are many partners to discuss,” he said, adding:“We have not sold anything and we will not sell anything if we do not profit.”
Despite its vast resources, the minister noted that only about 10% of the country’s minerals are currently exploited. He also downplayed the geopolitical competition between Washington and Beijing, saying the DRC would prioritize its own national interests.
Earlier in January 2026, Kinshasa reportedly sent Washington a list of targeted resources including manganese, gold, lithium, copper, and cobalt, key materials for electric vehicle batteries and electronics manufacturing. Potential sites include Kisenge and Mutoshi (Lualaba), Moto (Haut-Uélé), Kilo (Ituri), as well as deposits in North Kivu, South Kivu, and Maniema.

“It could result in a good and big project, or another that is not very profitable. We will continue because there are many partners to discuss,” he said, adding:“We have not sold anything and we will not sell anything if we do not profit.”
Despite its vast resources, the minister noted that only about 10% of the country’s minerals are currently exploited. He also downplayed the geopolitical competition between Washington and Beijing, saying the DRC would prioritize its own national interests.
Earlier in January 2026, Kinshasa reportedly sent Washington a list of targeted resources including manganese, gold, lithium, copper, and cobalt, key materials for electric vehicle batteries and electronics manufacturing. Potential sites include Kisenge and Mutoshi (Lualaba), Moto (Haut-Uélé), Kilo (Ituri), as well as deposits in North Kivu, South Kivu, and Maniema.

title: Belgium Declines to Share Colonial-Era DRC Mineral Records with U.S. Firm
excerpt: February 16, 2026 — The Belgian government has refused to grant U.S.-based mining company KoBold Metals access to colonial-era archives detailing mineral deposits in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Belgium, which ruled the DRC from 1885 to 1960, gathered extensive geologica
title_en: Belgium Declines to Share Colonial-Era DRC Mineral Records with U.S. Firm
excerpt_en: February 16, 2026 — The Belgian government has refused to grant U.S.-based mining company KoBold Metals access to colonial-era archives detailing mineral deposits in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Belgium, which ruled the DRC from 1885 to 1960, gathered extensive geologica
body_en:
February 16, 2026 — The Belgian government has refused to grant U.S.-based mining company KoBold Metals access to colonial-era archives detailing mineral deposits in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
Belgium, which ruled the DRC from 1885 to 1960, gathered extensive geological data during the colonial period to support mining operations. Much of that information has since been preserved in museums and state archives.
Two years ago, following an agreement with the European Union, Belgian authorities began compiling these historical records into a digital platform intended to be accessible, under certain conditions, to researchers, private entities, and the Congolese government.
Agreements with Kinshasa
In July 2025, KoBold’s DRC representative, Benjamin Katabuka, and Congo’s Minister of Mineral Resources, Kizito Pakabomba, signed an agreement authorizing a company delegation to travel to Brussels to request copies of the documents.
A month later, in August 2025, the DRC government and KoBold concluded another agreement granting the company rights to explore and mine lithium, cobalt, and copper across a 1,600-square-kilometer area.
Seeking to better pinpoint mineral locations, KoBold requested participation in Belgium’s digitization process. However, Belgian authorities rejected the request.
Legal and Policy Constraints
Officials at the Royal Museum for Central Africa in Tervuren — which houses many Africa-related archives — stated that private companies cannot be granted privileged access to the records.
“We cannot give all the ancient documents to a private sector,” said museum director Bart Ouvry.
Belgium’s Minister for Science Policy, Vanessa Matz, argued that granting exclusive access to a foreign company would contravene Belgian and European legal frameworks.
Strategic Minerals at Stake
KoBold Metals is pursuing mining operations in the DRC under broader U.S.–Congo cooperation initiatives. The targeted minerals — particularly lithium, cobalt, and copper — are critical components in the production of electric vehicle batteries and advanced electronic devices, placing the dispute within the wider geopolitical competition over strategic resources.
Social and Health

title: Gen Mbala to Testify in Trial of Lt Gen Yav Over Alleged Rwanda Collaboration
excerpt: Kinshasa, February 21, 2026 – Gen Célestin Mbala Munsense, former Commander-in-Chief of the FARDC (2018–2022), is set to testify in the trial of Lt Gen Philemon Yav Irung, who faces accusations of collaborating with the Rwandan government while commanding the 3rd Military Region.
title_en: Gen Mbala to Testify in Trial of Lt Gen Yav Over Alleged Rwanda Collaboration
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, February 21, 2026 – Gen Célestin Mbala Munsense, former Commander-in-Chief of the FARDC (2018–2022), is set to testify in the trial of Lt Gen Philemon Yav Irung, who faces accusations of collaborating with the Rwandan government while commanding the 3rd Military Region.
body_en:
Kinshasa, February 21, 2026 – Gen Célestin Mbala Munsense, former Commander-in-Chief of the FARDC (2018–2022), is set to testify in the trial of Lt Gen Philemon Yav Irung, who faces accusations of collaborating with the Rwandan government while commanding the 3rd Military Region.
The Military High Court heard that Lt Gen Yav allegedly communicated with Rwandan officials to undermine FARDC troops. The general denied the accusations, stating that he had never engaged with Rwandan authorities, and that he only received a phone message from an unknown sender alleging FARDC collusion with the FDLR.
The prosecution acknowledged the difficulty in accessing the phone messages. The court subsequently requested the National Cyber Security Agency (CNC) to investigate any potential communications.
Lt Gen Yav requested that Gen Mbala be summoned to clarify the issues and testify on his conduct while serving in the national army. The judges approved this request, scheduling Gen Mbala to appear at the next hearing on March 2, 2026.
Additionally, Lt Gen Yav asked for the re-summoning of other military officials, including Lt Gen Constant Ndima (former Governor of North Kivu Province), Brig Gen Mwehu Lumbu (former FARDC Spokesperson), and Gen Maj Sylvain Ekenge (former National Army Spokesperson), to provide further testimony. Previous statements from these officials had been contradictory regarding messages allegedly received from Rwandan authorities.
Lt Gen Yav was arrested in September 2022 following the capture of Rutshuru territory, including Bunagana, by the M23 armed group. His trial began in January 2026, amid growing scrutiny of alleged military collusion with neighboring countries.

title: Foreign Contractors Linked to Erik Prince Involved in Uvira Offensive
excerpt: KINSHASA, February 11, 2026 — Foreign military contractors linked to American security entrepreneur Erik Prince were deployed in South Kivu to assist the national army of the Democratic Republic of the Congo during operations aimed at retaking the city of Uvira from the M23/AFC c
title_en: Foreign Contractors Linked to Erik Prince Involved in Uvira Offensive
excerpt_en: KINSHASA, February 11, 2026 — Foreign military contractors linked to American security entrepreneur Erik Prince were deployed in South Kivu to assist the national army of the Democratic Republic of the Congo during operations aimed at retaking the city of Uvira from the M23/AFC c
body_en:
KINSHASA, February 11, 2026 — Foreign military contractors linked to American security entrepreneur Erik Prince were deployed in South Kivu to assist the national army of the Democratic Republic of the Congo during operations aimed at retaking the city of Uvira from the M23/AFC coalition, according to security and diplomatic sources.
The coalition seized Uvira on December 9, 2025, and advanced toward Makobola, prompting heavy counter-offensives by Congolese special forces units known as the Hiboux and Cheetah groups. The army used heavy weapons, warplanes, and drones as it attempted to push the fighters toward the South Kivu highlands. Foreign contractors were reportedly brought in to operate drone systems, while Israeli advisers focused on training two Congolese special units to conduct operations both day and night.
On January 17–18, the AFC/M23 withdrew its fighters from the city following a request from the United States, which had pledged the resumption of peace talks in Doha, Qatar, if the movement complied. Government troops and allied Wazalendo fighters re-entered Uvira on the morning of January 18 without major clashes, ending the immediate need for the contractors on the battlefield.
After the withdrawal, the personnel returned to their initial assignment — helping authorities monitor mining revenues and combat embezzlement linked to the country’s mineral sector. One official indicated they had been mobilized to support the recapture of the city using all available resources before resuming financial oversight activities.
Security officials say the government may again rely on the contractors if hostilities resume, suggesting their role could shift back to combat support depending on developments on the ground.

title: AFC/M23 to Release 230 DRC Soldiers and Former Child Fighters
excerpt: Goma, February 20, 2026 – The AFC/M23 coalition announced plans to release 230 DRC soldiers captured in Goma last year, along with former Wazalendo fighters and child soldiers, signaling a gesture toward peace and reconciliation. The announcement was made by AFC/M23 Director-Gene
title_en: AFC/M23 to Release 230 DRC Soldiers and Former Child Fighters
excerpt_en: Goma, February 20, 2026 – The AFC/M23 coalition announced plans to release 230 DRC soldiers captured in Goma last year, along with former Wazalendo fighters and child soldiers, signaling a gesture toward peace and reconciliation. The announcement was made by AFC/M23 Director-Gene
body_en:
Goma, February 20, 2026 – The AFC/M23 coalition announced plans to release 230 DRC soldiers captured in Goma last year, along with former Wazalendo fighters and child soldiers, signaling a gesture toward peace and reconciliation.
The announcement was made by AFC/M23 Director-General Corneille Nangaa Yobeluo following talks with EU Commissioner for Conflict Resolution and Humanitarian Aid, Hadja Lahbib, who visited Goma on February 20.
Details of the Release
41 former child soldiers from FARDC and Wazalendo will be released.
About 100 women from FARDC and Wazalendo captured in Rumangabo will also be freed.
230 FARDC soldiers held at the Katindo military camp will be released as a gesture of goodwill.
Nangaa emphasized, “We are not war mongers. We are prioritizing political talks because that is what will bring peace. If the DRC government does not respect them and wants to continue the war, we will defend ourselves as we usually do.”
Background
In April 2025, 1,359 DRC soldiers and police officers who had sought refuge in camps under MONUSCO, the UN peacekeeping mission, were repatriated to Kinshasa after negotiations between the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) and AFC/M23.
The release underlines AFC/M23’s focus on dialogue and political solutions as a path to peace, while maintaining the group’s readiness to defend its positions if hostilities persist.

title: Rwanda’s Nduhungirehe Questions DRC’s Commitment to Angola-Proposed Ceasefire
excerpt: KIGALI, February 12, 2026 — Ambassador Olivier Nduhungirehe, Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation, expressed doubt over the Democratic Republic of Congo’s willingness to respect a new ceasefire proposed by João Lourenço. He cited the lack of political will demonstrated by
title_en: Rwanda’s Nduhungirehe Questions DRC’s Commitment to Angola-Proposed Ceasefire
excerpt_en: KIGALI, February 12, 2026 — Ambassador Olivier Nduhungirehe, Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation, expressed doubt over the Democratic Republic of Congo’s willingness to respect a new ceasefire proposed by João Lourenço. He cited the lack of political will demonstrated by
body_en:
KIGALI, February 12, 2026 — Ambassador Olivier Nduhungirehe, Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation, expressed doubt over the Democratic Republic of Congo’s willingness to respect a new ceasefire proposed by João Lourenço. He cited the lack of political will demonstrated by Kinshasa since previous agreements.
The Angolan government, acting on Lourenço’s authority as Chairperson of the African Union, requested that the ceasefire begin on February 18, 2026, while inter-Congolese peace talks are being prepared. Nduhungirehe recalled that in 2024, two ceasefires were declared, and in 2025, six peace or ceasefire agreements were signed, none of which the DRC government fully respected.
He stated:
“We can always negotiate peace agreements or ceasefires, but as long as Kinshasa does not stop airstrikes and heavy artillery, and President Tshisekedi insists on an impossible military solution, while the international community ignores these violations, it will be futile.”
The ceasefire request followed a meeting on February 9, 2026, between President Félix Tshisekedi, AU-appointed mediator Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé, and Olusegun Obasanjo, appointed by the East African Community (EAC) and Southern African Development Community (SADC).
The mediators emphasized that an AU-led inter-Congolese dialogue remains the only way to address the root causes of DRC’s conflict.

title: Goma Connected to High-Speed Fiber Network via Kenya, Uganda and Rwanda
excerpt: GOMA, February 10, 2026 — The city of Goma in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo has begun receiving high-speed fiber optic internet through a new regional network linking Kenya, Uganda, and Rwanda, according to the Paratus Group. The company announced the launch of a 2
title_en: Goma Connected to High-Speed Fiber Network via Kenya, Uganda and Rwanda
excerpt_en: GOMA, February 10, 2026 — The city of Goma in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo has begun receiving high-speed fiber optic internet through a new regional network linking Kenya, Uganda, and Rwanda, according to the Paratus Group. The company announced the launch of a 2
body_en:
GOMA, February 10, 2026 — The city of Goma in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo has begun receiving high-speed fiber optic internet through a new regional network linking Kenya, Uganda, and Rwanda, according to the Paratus Group.
The company announced the launch of a 2,000-kilometer fiber optic corridor stretching from the Port of Mombasa in Kenya to Goma, passing through major hubs in East Africa. The infrastructure includes data centers in Kigali, Kampala, and Nairobi, aimed at strengthening regional connectivity.
Paratus said the network will provide high-speed and secure internet access to traditional internet service providers as well as corporate clients operating across multiple locations.
The company’s Chief Commercial Officer, Martin Cox, stated that the new connection is expected to boost the digital economy in the region.
“The establishment of a secure network from the port to Goma is an opportunity for internet service providers and businesses to access the international market. It will enhance stability and efficiency and open up new business opportunities in Kenya, Uganda, Rwanda and the DRC,” he said.

title: DRC and AS Monaco Face French Court Over Alleged Embezzlement
excerpt: Paris, February 19, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and French football club AS Monaco have been taken to court in France over allegations of embezzlement and corruption related to a cooperation agreement signed in June 2025. The agreement aimed to promote the DRC i
title_en: DRC and AS Monaco Face French Court Over Alleged Embezzlement
excerpt_en: Paris, February 19, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and French football club AS Monaco have been taken to court in France over allegations of embezzlement and corruption related to a cooperation agreement signed in June 2025. The agreement aimed to promote the DRC i
body_en:
Paris, February 19, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and French football club AS Monaco have been taken to court in France over allegations of embezzlement and corruption related to a cooperation agreement signed in June 2025.
The agreement aimed to promote the DRC internationally, develop football talent, and advance the sport in the country. However, concerns quickly arose among Congolese citizens over the legality and transparency of the deal.
Legal Action Initiated by Congolese Residents in France
Two Congolese residents in France, requesting anonymity, filed a lawsuit with the help of lawyer Hervé Diakiese, prompting the French Public Prosecutor’s Office (PNF) to review the case. The complaint alleges that the agreement involved corruption, misuse of public funds, and bribery.
The complaint specifically cites irregularities linked to the DRC Minister of Sports and Recreation, Didier Budimbu, in relation to the payment of €4.8 million (≈8.3 billion Rwandan francs) over three years.
Although the complaint was initially addressed to the Attorney General of Monaco, Stéphane Thibault, the PNF noted that it lacks jurisdiction to prosecute certain international crimes, prompting Diakiese to consider escalating the case to other courts.
AS Monaco and Other Clubs Respond
AS Monaco has stated that it will defend itself vigorously, emphasizing that due diligence and legal compliance were followed before signing the contract. Other European clubs involved in similar agreements with the DRC, including FC Barcelona and AC Milan, are also part of the investigation.
The case has drawn attention to the governance and oversight of public funds in international sports partnerships, raising questions about accountability in agreements involving government and private entities.
The proceedings are ongoing, and the next steps could set a precedent for cross-border accountability in sports and public funding.

title: UN Plans Aerial Reconnaissance Before Peacekeepers Deploy to Uvira
excerpt: KINSHASA, February 11, 2026 — The United Nations will deploy reconnaissance aircraft before sending peacekeepers to Uvira Territory in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, as part of a phased plan to monitor a ceasefire in the volatile border region. The announcement was made by
title_en: UN Plans Aerial Reconnaissance Before Peacekeepers Deploy to Uvira
excerpt_en: KINSHASA, February 11, 2026 — The United Nations will deploy reconnaissance aircraft before sending peacekeepers to Uvira Territory in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, as part of a phased plan to monitor a ceasefire in the volatile border region. The announcement was made by
body_en:
KINSHASA, February 11, 2026 — The United Nations will deploy reconnaissance aircraft before sending peacekeepers to Uvira Territory in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, as part of a phased plan to monitor a ceasefire in the volatile border region.
The announcement was made by Jean-Pierre Lacroix, Under-Secretary-General for Peacekeeping Operations, during his working visit to the country on February 10.
Mandate Backed by the UN Security Council
The move follows the January 2026 withdrawal of fighters from the city of Uvira by the M23/AFC coalition, which requested the deployment of neutral forces to prevent reprisals against civilians by government troops.
The United Nations Security Council has mandated the UN mission MONUSCO to oversee implementation of the peace arrangement — a framework accepted by both the Congolese authorities and the armed group.
Phased Deployment for Security Reasons
According to Lacroix, troops will not be deployed immediately. Instead, reconnaissance aircraft will first collect intelligence on security conditions before personnel are transported.
He warned that sending helicopters without prior assessment could expose peacekeepers to attack.
“We will not send helicopters to take our personnel into areas where there are dangers or where drones are present,” Lacroix said, adding that security guarantees are required before the mission proceeds.
He also called on international partners and the parties involved to ensure the safety of peacekeepers as they begin monitoring the ceasefire.
Flights from Goma
The reconnaissance aircraft are expected to operate from Goma International Airport, currently under the control of the AFC/M23 coalition. The airport has remained closed since January 2025, and UN officials did not confirm whether reopening is imminent.
Gradual Arrival of Peacekeepers
Once aerial surveillance is completed, a small contingent of troops will be deployed to Uvira, with numbers increasing progressively depending on developments on the ground.
The UN says the cautious rollout is intended to prevent incidents and build confidence while stabilizing the region after months of fighting.

title: DRC Seeks US Military Training and Intelligence Cooperation in Exchange for Minerals
excerpt: Kinshasa, February 20, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is seeking military training, equipment, and intelligence cooperation from the United States under a growing security and economic partnership. The DRC aims to exchange access to strategic mineral deposits for e
title_en: DRC Seeks US Military Training and Intelligence Cooperation in Exchange for Minerals
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, February 20, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is seeking military training, equipment, and intelligence cooperation from the United States under a growing security and economic partnership. The DRC aims to exchange access to strategic mineral deposits for e
body_en:
Kinshasa, February 20, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is seeking military training, equipment, and intelligence cooperation from the United States under a growing security and economic partnership.
The DRC aims to exchange access to strategic mineral deposits for enhanced US military support, building on a cooperation agreement signed on December 4, 2025, which allows American investors to mine and process key minerals.
Minerals Linked to Technology and Defense
On February 5, 2026, the DRC provided the US with a list of specific mineral deposits, including those essential for electric car batteries, electronics, and military equipment.
Security Cooperation Plans
Reports indicate that a classified security clause is part of the December agreement, potentially enabling the US to:
Train DRC military personnel
Provide advanced military equipment
Exchange intelligence to strengthen regional security
The initiative was outlined in a document prepared by the DRC President’s security advisor, Désiré Cashmir Eberande Kolongele, and signed by DRC Foreign Minister Thérèse Kayikwamba Wagner and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Ongoing US Engagement
In January 2026, a US military delegation led by Col. Michael Gacheru visited the DRC to discuss bilateral cooperation on peace and security, building on existing US support that includes financial aid, technical assistance, and police equipment.
The DRC government has indicated it seeks expanded military assistance, aiming to strengthen its armed forces while ensuring continued access to strategic minerals for industrial and defense applications.

title: United States Urges DRC to Respect Upcoming Ceasefire
excerpt: KINSHASA, February 15, 2026 — Massad Boulos, Senior Advisor on African Affairs to the U.S. President, has called on the government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo to fully respect the ceasefire agreed on February 13 and expected to take effect on February 18. The presiden
title_en: United States Urges DRC to Respect Upcoming Ceasefire
excerpt_en: KINSHASA, February 15, 2026 — Massad Boulos, Senior Advisor on African Affairs to the U.S. President, has called on the government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo to fully respect the ceasefire agreed on February 13 and expected to take effect on February 18. The presiden
body_en:
KINSHASA, February 15, 2026 — Massad Boulos, Senior Advisor on African Affairs to the U.S. President, has called on the government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo to fully respect the ceasefire agreed on February 13 and expected to take effect on February 18.
The presidency confirmed that Félix Tshisekedi accepted the truce proposed by Angola, current chair of the African Union (AU). Authorities, however, stressed that the government would not allow the rebel coalition AFC/M23 to expand positions, reinforce fighters, or receive foreign support during the ceasefire period.
Rebels Dispute Government Position
AFC/M23 leader Corneille Nangaa accused government forces of continuing attacks on civilians and rebel positions, describing the ceasefire announcement as an attempt to mislead the international community.
The group stated it had not been invited to the negotiations that preceded the Angolan proposal but said it supports the peace process and would respect the truce framework emerging from the Doha talks in Qatar.
Washington Calls for Concrete Action
Boulos welcomed Kinshasa’s acceptance of the ceasefire but emphasized that it must translate into real actions on the ground.
He urged all parties to immediately halt hostilities, including drone strikes, warning that civilians continue to be killed despite diplomatic commitments.
Implementation on the Ground
The Angolan initiative comes as the MONUSCO peacekeeping mission prepares to implement additional arrangements linked to the Doha discussions, particularly in Uvira territory in eastern DRC.
Diplomatic efforts are ongoing to stabilize the region amid persistent fighting and humanitarian concerns, with international actors pushing for the ceasefire to become a first step toward broader negotiations.

title: Rwandan Embassy in UK Launches ‘Nshuti’ Online Platform for Citizens Abroad
excerpt: London, February 19, 2026 – The Rwandan Embassy in the United Kingdom has launched a new digital platform called ‘Nshuti’, designed to provide 24/7 services and support to Rwandans living abroad and others seeking information about Rwanda. The platform, part of the Embassy’s broa
title_en: Rwandan Embassy in UK Launches ‘Nshuti’ Online Platform for Citizens Abroad
excerpt_en: London, February 19, 2026 – The Rwandan Embassy in the United Kingdom has launched a new digital platform called ‘Nshuti’, designed to provide 24/7 services and support to Rwandans living abroad and others seeking information about Rwanda. The platform, part of the Embassy’s broa
body_en:
London, February 19, 2026 – The Rwandan Embassy in the United Kingdom has launched a new digital platform called ‘Nshuti’, designed to provide 24/7 services and support to Rwandans living abroad and others seeking information about Rwanda.
The platform, part of the Embassy’s broader digital innovation strategy, allows users to access a wide range of services instantly via WhatsApp or the embassy’s website.
Key Features of Nshuti
Immediate assistance and answers to frequently asked questions
Support for passport applications, identity card registration, document authentication, and appointment requests
Guidance for accessing other consular services
Information on embassy activities, national holidays, and Rwandan organizations abroad
Contact details for Rwandan representatives in countries served by the embassy
Users can interact with the platform by sending a WhatsApp message to +44 7427 941212 or starting a chat via the embassy website.
Ambassador Emphasizes Innovation
In a statement, Rwanda’s Ambassador to the UK, Johnston Busingye, highlighted that Nshuti reflects the embassy’s commitment to leveraging technology to simplify processes, reduce waiting times, and provide reliable, up-to-date information to Rwandans abroad.
The launch of Nshuti marks a significant step toward modernizing consular services, improving accessibility, and enhancing engagement with Rwanda’s diaspora community in the UK and beyond.

Paris, February 18, 2026 – A witness convicted of involvement in the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi testified before the Appeals Chamber of the Paris People’s Court, alleging that Claude Muhayimana’s representative attempted to influence him to give misleading testimony to protect Muhayimana from conviction.
The witness, a former teacher who admitted participating in Interahamwe patrols and attacks against Tutsi, explained that he was sentenced by a Gacaca Court in 2006 or 2007 to 12 years in prison for his role in the killings.
Witness Details Muhayimana’s Involvement
The witness recounted seeing Muhayimana drive a blue Daihatsu transporting Interahamwe members, armed men, and gendarmes to the Bisesero hills in Kibuye Prefecture, where Tutsi civilians were attacked.
“From April, when the genocide began, until July, the vehicles were used across all communes of Kibuye Prefecture, hunting Tutsi in the mountains,” the witness told the court.
During the investigation, Muhayimana, through his lawyer, contacted the witness asking about life in Rwanda and the progress of the case. The witness provided information but later said the lawyer instructed him to give less incriminating testimony, claiming foreign judges would not distinguish truth from falsehood.
“He asked me to give a less incriminating testimony so that the judges would not be able to understand the truth,” the witness said, describing how he provided a confusing statement on October 16, 2013.
Document Controversy
The witness also testified about a search of Muhayimana’s home, where authorities found a document listing witnesses, their families, and staff of the French Office for the Fight against Crimes against Humanity (OCLCH). The witness denied providing the names of French personnel and said Muhayimana had lied about his access to this information.
When Muhayimana claimed that the Rwandan government had trained witnesses to lie against him, the witness rejected the allegation, stating that his testimony was truthful and based on firsthand knowledge of the events.
Conviction and Appeal
In December 2021, the Paris International Criminal Court convicted Muhayimana of genocide and crimes against humanity, sentencing him to 14 years in prison. The court determined that he had led the Interahamwe militia responsible for killing Tutsi, a charge Muhayimana has consistently denied.
The appeal hearing, which began on February 3, 2026, is focused on Muhayimana’s efforts to overturn his convictions and secure release. The testimony presented by the witness highlights allegations of witness tampering and attempts to mislead the court, central to the appeal proceedings.

title: Former Women Combatants Urged to Safeguard National Unity

title_en: Former Women Combatants Urged to Safeguard National Unity
excerpt_en: KIGALI, February 14, 2026 — Former female fighters from different armed groups in Rwanda have been called upon to strengthen reconciliation and preserve national unity during the General Assembly of the Ndabaga Community, held on Saturday. The community brings together women who
body_en:
KIGALI, February 14, 2026 — Former female fighters from different armed groups in Rwanda have been called upon to strengthen reconciliation and preserve national unity during the General Assembly of the Ndabaga Community, held on Saturday.
The community brings together women who participated in the country’s liberation struggle — including members of the Rwandan Patriotic Front (RPF-Inkotanyi), former soldiers of the RPF, and ex-combatants from the defeated Forces armées rwandaises (EX-FAR). Participants were encouraged to share experiences and develop initiatives that promote cohesion and social progress.
The name Ndabaga refers to a historical symbol meaning “a girl who became a warrior and went to battle,” reflecting the members’ military service while recognizing their identity as women.
Promoting Skills and Self-Reliance
The head of the community, retired Lieutenant Mbabazi Diane, urged members to prioritize mutual learning and development projects aimed at improving their living conditions.
“Our objective as Ndabaga members is to strengthen our skills so we can improve our daily lives,” she said.
To support economic empowerment, the community is partnering with Airtel Rwanda Communications on a 30-million-Rwandan-franc tailoring project. The initiative will begin with a pilot group before expanding nationwide if successful.
According to organizers, tailoring was chosen because many members had limited access to formal education, and the project offers a practical pathway toward financial independence.
Unity and Reconciliation Emphasized
Leaders reminded participants that, despite ongoing development efforts, they must remain ambassadors of reconciliation and unity and guide others away from division.
“As people who contributed to the country’s liberation, we must lead by example and demonstrate the value of Rwandan unity,” Mbabazi added.
Personal Transformation
Member Umurungi Musiime Florence, who joined the Ndabaga Community in 2004, said participation helped her regain confidence and rebuild her life.
She explained that being surrounded by peers encouraged her to return to school, continue contributing to society, and pursue personal development.
The Ndabaga Community says its activities aim not only at economic empowerment but also at reinforcing long-term social cohesion and post-conflict healing in Rwanda.

excerpt: South Kivu, February 20, 2026 – The AFC/M23 coalition has criticized the international community for remaining silent as DRC government forces and allied groups continue to target civilians in South Kivu Province. According to AFC/M23 spokesman Lawrence Kanyuka, forces from the D
title_en: AFC/M23 Condemns International Silence Amid Ongoing Civilian Killings in South Kivu
excerpt_en: South Kivu, February 20, 2026 – The AFC/M23 coalition has criticized the international community for remaining silent as DRC government forces and allied groups continue to target civilians in South Kivu Province. According to AFC/M23 spokesman Lawrence Kanyuka, forces from the D
body_en:
South Kivu, February 20, 2026 – The AFC/M23 coalition has criticized the international community for remaining silent as DRC government forces and allied groups continue to target civilians in South Kivu Province.
According to AFC/M23 spokesman Lawrence Kanyuka, forces from the DRC, Burundi, FDLR, Wazalendo, and foreign mercenaries have carried out killings in the communes of Minembwe, Mikenge, Karingi, and other parts of the highlands.
“These intolerable acts of cruelty against humanity are being carried out with the appalling and unjustified silence of aid workers, human rights organizations, and diplomatic institutions,” Kanyuka said.
Targeting Vulnerable Populations
He emphasized that the attacks disproportionately affect women, children, and the elderly, and are intended to inflict massive harm on the civilian population, in clear violation of international humanitarian law.
Ceasefire Violations
The coalition reiterated that the DRC government continues to violate the ceasefire agreement signed in Doha, Qatar, as well as other peace resolutions adopted in Washington, United States.
“This belligerent behavior threatens to reverse the progress made toward lasting peace and stability in the region,” Kanyuka warned.
The statement underscores the growing tensions in South Kivu and calls for urgent international attention to prevent further humanitarian crises.

title: Mia Amor Mottley Reaffirms Commitment to Rwanda After Re-Election
excerpt: BRIDGETOWN, February 15, 2026 — Mia Amor Mottley, re-elected for a third term as Prime Minister of Barbados, has reaffirmed her commitment to strengthening bilateral ties with Rwanda following her decisive electoral victory. After securing a landslide win in the parliamentary ele
title_en: Mia Amor Mottley Reaffirms Commitment to Rwanda After Re-Election
excerpt_en: BRIDGETOWN, February 15, 2026 — Mia Amor Mottley, re-elected for a third term as Prime Minister of Barbados, has reaffirmed her commitment to strengthening bilateral ties with Rwanda following her decisive electoral victory. After securing a landslide win in the parliamentary ele
body_en:
BRIDGETOWN, February 15, 2026 — Mia Amor Mottley, re-elected for a third term as Prime Minister of Barbados, has reaffirmed her commitment to strengthening bilateral ties with Rwanda following her decisive electoral victory.
After securing a landslide win in the parliamentary elections — with her party, the Barbados Labour Party, winning all 30 seats — Mottley thanked Paul Kagame for his congratulatory message and underscored the importance of continued cooperation between the two nations.
President Kagame had earlier congratulated her, calling the victory well deserved.
In response, Mottley expressed appreciation for what she described as a friendship rooted in mutual respect and shared development goals. She emphasized that Barbados places great value on its relationship with Rwanda and looks forward to deepening collaboration aimed at protecting dignity, expanding opportunities, and advancing prosperity for their respective populations.
Growing Strategic Partnership
Relations between Rwanda and Barbados have strengthened in recent years through agreements in areas including air transport and sports cooperation. A key component of this partnership has involved collaboration with RwandAir to enhance air connectivity.
In November 2022, Prime Minister Mottley inaugurated Barbados’ embassy in Kigali during an official working visit — a move that followed President Kagame’s visit to Barbados earlier the same year. Those engagements led to the signing of multiple cooperation agreements.
Barbados, a Caribbean island known for its thriving tourism sector and investor-friendly climate, has increasingly sought to expand its diplomatic and economic partnerships beyond the region.
The renewed mandate for Prime Minister Mottley is expected to further consolidate ties between Bridgetown and Kigali as both countries pursue expanded South–South cooperation.

title: Rwandans in Europe to Gather for Dialogue on Unity and Solidarity
excerpt: Paris, February 19, 2026 – The Rwandan Ministry of National Unity and Civic Engagement (MINUC) has announced a dialogue aimed at strengthening unity and solidarity among Rwandans living in Europe. The event is scheduled for February 21, 2026, in Paris, France. The dialogue will b
title_en: Rwandans in Europe to Gather for Dialogue on Unity and Solidarity
excerpt_en: Paris, February 19, 2026 – The Rwandan Ministry of National Unity and Civic Engagement (MINUC) has announced a dialogue aimed at strengthening unity and solidarity among Rwandans living in Europe. The event is scheduled for February 21, 2026, in Paris, France. The dialogue will b
body_en:
Paris, February 19, 2026 – The Rwandan Ministry of National Unity and Civic Engagement (MINUC) has announced a dialogue aimed at strengthening unity and solidarity among Rwandans living in Europe. The event is scheduled for February 21, 2026, in Paris, France.
The dialogue will bring together Rwandans, particularly young people born abroad or who left the country during the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi, as well as representatives of Rwandan communities from across Europe.
Purpose and Focus
The event is designed as a platform for sharing ideas and experiences, providing participants with a better understanding of Rwanda’s journey toward national unity and the challenges that have arisen over the years. It will also highlight opportunities for those living abroad to engage with and contribute to their homeland.
Topics of discussion will include:
The role of youth in preserving Rwandan culture
How various community forums maintain unity
The community’s role in sharing accurate information and promoting social cohesion
Event Format
The dialogue will feature a combination of speeches, expert panels, testimonies, and interactive discussions, aiming to strengthen connections among Rwandans abroad.
Officials expect the event to:
Foster a stronger sense of community and shared values
Promote a culture of support, respect, and non-violence
Encourage young Rwandans abroad to uphold Rwandan traditions and cultural identity
The initiative reflects Rwanda’s ongoing commitment to unity, reconciliation, and the active participation of its diaspora in national development.

title: Family of Former President Edgar Lungu Denies Poisoning Claims
excerpt: Lusaka, February 18, 2026 – Lawyers representing the family of former Zambian President Edgar Lungu have dismissed claims that his death was the result of poisoning. Edgar Lungu passed away in South Africa in June 2025, but his body has yet to be buried. South African authorities
title_en: Family of Former President Edgar Lungu Denies Poisoning Claims
excerpt_en: Lusaka, February 18, 2026 – Lawyers representing the family of former Zambian President Edgar Lungu have dismissed claims that his death was the result of poisoning. Edgar Lungu passed away in South Africa in June 2025, but his body has yet to be buried. South African authorities
body_en:
Lusaka, February 18, 2026 – Lawyers representing the family of former Zambian President Edgar Lungu have dismissed claims that his death was the result of poisoning.
Edgar Lungu passed away in South Africa in June 2025, but his body has yet to be buried. South African authorities have stated that his remains are still needed for an autopsy.
According to legal representatives, including Neo Mashele, the allegations of poisoning are unfounded. Lungu’s family is reportedly cooperating with security agencies to investigate the circumstances of his death.
His body remains in a South African morgue while legal disputes continue over the location of his burial. The African Union described the situation as “a serious matter that cannot be discussed publicly.”
Lungu’s family has expressed a desire for him to be buried in South Africa, in part to ensure that President Hakainde Hichilema would not miss the funeral.
This ongoing situation continues to attract attention in Zambia and across the region, as legal and diplomatic considerations surrounding the former president’s burial remain unresolved.

KAMPALA/KIGALI, February 14, 2026 — The Chief of Staff of the Uganda People's Defence Force, Gen. Muhoozi Kainerugaba, has once again declared his affection for Rwanda and its people, confirming that he will soon travel to Kigali for an official visit.
In a message posted in the early hours of February 14, 2026, on the social media platform X, Gen. Muhoozi expressed his deep admiration in Kinyarwanda, stating: “I love Rwanda and Rwandans very much. I will soon be visiting my Uncle Afande Paul.”
The Ugandan army chief was referring to Paul Kagame, whom he has frequently described as both a mentor and a family figure. Gen. Muhoozi has often publicly referred to President Kagame as his “uncle” and a role model.
Earlier this week, Gen. Muhoozi first announced his intention to visit Rwanda and revealed plans to meet President Kagame during his stay in Kigali. His latest statement reinforces growing expectations of renewed high-level engagement between the two neighboring nations.
On several occasions, Gen. Muhoozi has emphasized the historic ties and long-standing friendship between Uganda and Rwanda, highlighting their shared political and military history as the foundation of bilateral cooperation.
The anticipated visit comes amid continued efforts to strengthen diplomatic and security relations between the two countries, which share deep historical, cultural, and strategic links in the Great Lakes region.

title: Ugandan General Says DRC No Longer a Haven for Rwandan Armed Groups
excerpt: Musanze, Rwanda, February 20, 2026 – Gen. Maj. Paul Muhanguzi, Commander of the 2nd Division of the Ugandan Army, stated that the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is no longer a safe haven for armed groups targeting Rwanda’s security, despite both countries being members of the
title_en: Ugandan General Says DRC No Longer a Haven for Rwandan Armed Groups
excerpt_en: Musanze, Rwanda, February 20, 2026 – Gen. Maj. Paul Muhanguzi, Commander of the 2nd Division of the Ugandan Army, stated that the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is no longer a safe haven for armed groups targeting Rwanda’s security, despite both countries being members of the
body_en:
Musanze, Rwanda, February 20, 2026 – Gen. Maj. Paul Muhanguzi, Commander of the 2nd Division of the Ugandan Army, stated that the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is no longer a safe haven for armed groups targeting Rwanda’s security, despite both countries being members of the East African Community (EAC).
Gen. Maj. Muhanguzi led a Ugandan military delegation to Rwanda, starting at the Rwandan Demobilization and Rehabilitation Commission (RDRC) headquarters in Mutobo, Musanze District, on February 19, 2026. The mission focused on understanding programs that support the reintegration of former armed group members, including FDLR fighters, and their families from the DRC.
Commitment to Regional Security
He emphasized that the DRC’s inclusion in the EAC should mean the elimination of armed threats:
“Congo also requested to join East Africa. After joining, we should not have criminals in Congo. Rwanda would not have an enemy from Uganda, and Uganda would not have an enemy from Rwanda. However, we also want Congo not to have enemies who attack Uganda, who attack Rwanda,” Gen. Maj. Muhanguzi said.
Reintegration of Former Fighters
The General praised FDLR fighters who have returned to Rwanda, acknowledging their potential to contribute positively to the country:
“A country is not built by one person, it is built by all the people. I also congratulate President Kagame for being able to lead Rwanda, and you too, when the time comes, will know the truth and return home,” he added.
Since 2001, the RDRC has repatriated 12,602 former armed group members, though reports indicate that some, particularly from the FDLR, remain in DRC forests.
The visit highlights ongoing regional cooperation between Rwanda and Uganda to enhance security, reintegration programs, and peace-building efforts in the Great Lakes region.

title_en: Rwanda Presents Political Perspective at Munich Security Conference 2026
excerpt_en: MUNICH, February 14, 2026 — A Rwandan government delegation led by Vincent Biruta, Minister of Security, and Juvenal Marizamunda, Minister of Defence, is participating in the Munich Security Conference 2026 (MSC 2026), which opened on February 13 and runs through February 15 in M
body_en:
MUNICH, February 14, 2026 — A Rwandan government delegation led by Vincent Biruta, Minister of Security, and Juvenal Marizamunda, Minister of Defence, is participating in the Munich Security Conference 2026 (MSC 2026), which opened on February 13 and runs through February 15 in Munich, Germany.
According to Rwanda’s Ministry of Defence, the delegation took part in a series of high-level discussions, presenting Rwanda’s perspective on the current international political and security landscape. The meetings brought together heads of state and government, senior policymakers, and global security experts from multiple continents.
The delegation also held bilateral talks with representatives of friendly nations, focusing on advancing shared interests and strategic cooperation.
The Munich Security Conference, now in its 62nd edition, is being hosted at the Hotel Bayerischer Hof and Rosewood Munich. Approximately 50 heads of state and government, alongside key international decision-makers, are expected to attend.
The annual gathering serves as a major platform for debating global security challenges, including geopolitical tensions, armed conflicts, and emerging threats to international stability.

title: Rwanda Urges UN to Act Against Rising Hate Speech
excerpt: New York, February 19, 2026 – Rwanda has called on the United Nations to take urgent action against the growing spread of hate speech, warning that inaction amounts to complicity. Speaking at the UN Special Committee on Peacekeeping Operations on February 18, 2026, Col. Deo Mutab
title_en: Rwanda Urges UN to Act Against Rising Hate Speech
excerpt_en: New York, February 19, 2026 – Rwanda has called on the United Nations to take urgent action against the growing spread of hate speech, warning that inaction amounts to complicity. Speaking at the UN Special Committee on Peacekeeping Operations on February 18, 2026, Col. Deo Mutab
body_en:
New York, February 19, 2026 – Rwanda has called on the United Nations to take urgent action against the growing spread of hate speech, warning that inaction amounts to complicity.
Speaking at the UN Special Committee on Peacekeeping Operations on February 18, 2026, Col. Deo Mutabazi, Military Adviser at the Rwandan Embassy to the UN, described hate speech as a deliberate, government-led project that often precedes mass atrocities and genocide.
“Hate speech is a government project, and it precedes mass atrocities, crimes of genocide and stems from a genocide ideology that has been planted in a well-planned manner,” Col. Mutabazi said.
Hate Speech as a Precursor to Genocide
Col. Mutabazi reminded UN member states that hate speech was a key factor leading to the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi, where acts of dehumanization were used to justify mass killings. He emphasized that such rhetoric should not be mistaken for freedom of expression, and silence in the face of it can be seen as support or complicity.
“I would like to emphasize that hate speech should not be confused with freedom of speech, and the UN’s continued silence on these increasing crimes is seen as supporting and complicity in the violation of the rights of a group of people and the deprivation of their identity,” he said.
Current Situation in the DRC
Col. Mutabazi’s warning comes amid escalating hate speech targeting Kinyarwanda-speaking Congolese, particularly the Tutsi ethnic group, reportedly spread by elements within the DRC government.
Politicians and former military officials have made inflammatory statements, including MP Justin Bitakwira, who referred to the Tutsi as “the worst creature that ever lived,” and former military spokesman Gen. Maj. Sylvain Ekenge, who claimed on national television that Tutsi women cannot have children with spouses from other ethnic groups.
These statements coincide with airstrikes and drone attacks in areas predominantly inhabited by Tutsi-Congolese, including Minembwe Commune in South Kivu Province.
Call to Action
Rwanda reiterated its commitment to combating hate speech and called on UN member states to protect fundamental rights and the right to life, urging the international community to act before the situation escalates further.
“Rwanda is committed to combating hate speech and calls on member states to not tolerate those who deny others their fundamental right to life,” Col. Mutabazi said.
The appeal highlights the urgent need for international intervention as rising hate speech continues to fuel violence and ethnic targeting in the eastern DRC.

title: Rwandan Woman Testifies to Being Raped by FARDC Soldiers in DRC
excerpt: RUBAVU, February 12, 2026 — Nyiramana, 36, is one of 161 Rwandans recently repatriated from the Democratic Republic of Congo, who has spoken out about being raped twice by FARDC soldiers because she is Rwandan. Nyiramana returned on February 10 from the Masisi area, describing ye
title_en: Rwandan Woman Testifies to Being Raped by FARDC Soldiers in DRC
excerpt_en: RUBAVU, February 12, 2026 — Nyiramana, 36, is one of 161 Rwandans recently repatriated from the Democratic Republic of Congo, who has spoken out about being raped twice by FARDC soldiers because she is Rwandan. Nyiramana returned on February 10 from the Masisi area, describing ye
body_en:
RUBAVU, February 12, 2026 — Nyiramana, 36, is one of 161 Rwandans recently repatriated from the Democratic Republic of Congo, who has spoken out about being raped twice by FARDC soldiers because she is Rwandan. Nyiramana returned on February 10 from the Masisi area, describing years of persecution since her parents fled in 1994 from the former Rutongo commune.
She recounted her first assault in 2020:
“My parents separated me, we became Gatoyi, later I married Kamuronzi. Life was not good because when they found out that you are a refugee, they treat you like someone who came to rob them… I went to collect firewood in the forest and met men dressed badly like shepherds but wearing FARDC military uniforms. They raped me and I kept quiet to protect my home.”
Nyiramana explained that the soldiers targeted her for being Rwandan and even tried to coerce her into marriage:
“I saw that they could even kill me, so I decided to agree by force. I kept quiet because I had a husband and did not want the family to fall apart. Now I can speak because he has returned.”
Her second assault occurred in 2024 after leaving the market:
“I came back late and found them waiting near my house, not in military uniforms. They said we asked you many times and you refused, so we decided to rape you. It was dark, and I decided to accept. I kept quiet to avoid being hurt, but now I am happy to have returned to Rwanda.”
Nyiramana returned to Rwanda with her seven children, the survivors of her late husband, and expressed her readiness to work and rebuild her life. She also encouraged others still in the Congolese jungle to return, highlighting the opportunities and development available in Rwanda.
The repatriation was based on resolutions adopted at a meeting between Rwanda, the DRC, and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees in Addis Ababa on July 24, 2025.
Mulindwa Prosper, Mayor of Rubavu District, addressed the returning Rwandans, saying:
“There is no reason for any Rwandan to still be called a refugee. You were misled in the forest. You are now witnessing the truth… You are in the hands of a country that loves you, and you must call those left behind to return home.”

excerpt: GOMA, February 13, 2026 — Corneille Nangaa, Chairman of the AFC/M23 Alliance, has denounced the announcement by the Office of the President of the Democratic Republic of Congo that President Félix Tshisekedi has “accepted” a ceasefire requested by the Angola government, calling i

excerpt_en: GOMA, February 13, 2026 — Corneille Nangaa, Chairman of the AFC/M23 Alliance, has denounced the announcement by the Office of the President of the Democratic Republic of Congo that President Félix Tshisekedi has “accepted” a ceasefire requested by the Angola government, calling i
body_en:
GOMA, February 13, 2026 — Corneille Nangaa, Chairman of the AFC/M23 Alliance, has denounced the announcement by the Office of the President of the Democratic Republic of Congo that President Félix Tshisekedi has “accepted” a ceasefire requested by the Angola government, calling it misleading as attacks by the DRC army continue.
On February 13, the Presidential Office stated that acceptance of the ceasefire would include no expansion of military bases, no reinforcement of forces in conflict areas, and halting foreign support. Nangaa, however, emphasized that AFC/M23 remains committed to the Doha peace process, which is grounded in respecting political obligations and achieving peace through dialogue.
Nangaa accused the DRC government of attempting to launch new negotiations while existing talks are still ongoing, warning that this approach risks undermining earlier progress and delaying solutions to urgent issues. He said:
“Contrary to the declaration of acceptance of the ceasefire, the Kinshasa government has demonstrated through verified actions the continuation of the war. Attacks in densely populated areas, the use of mercenaries, and indiscriminate shootings affecting civilians demonstrate its choice to continue the war, violating its commitments.”
He added that the Kinshasa government’s declaration is propaganda aimed at misleading the population and the international community, while concealing the continuation of its military operations.
Meanwhile, Benjamin Mbonimpa, Permanent Secretary of AFC/M23, told journalists in Goma that DRC government forces launched further attacks on the morning of February 13.

title: DRC Hands Over Rubaya Mines Controlled by AFC/M23 to US Investors
excerpt: Kinshasa, February 19, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government has handed over mines in the Rubaya area of Masisi Territory, long controlled by the AFC/M23 group, to US investors, officials confirmed. A government document listing Rubaya and other mining sites wa
title_en: DRC Hands Over Rubaya Mines Controlled by AFC/M23 to US Investors
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, February 19, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government has handed over mines in the Rubaya area of Masisi Territory, long controlled by the AFC/M23 group, to US investors, officials confirmed. A government document listing Rubaya and other mining sites wa
body_en:
Kinshasa, February 19, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government has handed over mines in the Rubaya area of Masisi Territory, long controlled by the AFC/M23 group, to US investors, officials confirmed.
A government document listing Rubaya and other mining sites was submitted to US representatives on February 5, 2026, during the inaugural meeting of the Joint Cooperation Committee in Washington. The committee was established under a cooperation agreement signed in December 2025, focusing on the mining and processing of precious metals.
The list of mines provided by the DRC was intended for review by US investors to confirm the presence of essential minerals and identify any potential obstacles to extraction.
Government Perspective
DRC Minister of Economy, Daniel Mukoko Samba, emphasized that the government remains responsible for mines, even those not under its direct control.
“The fact that the Rubaya site is not under the control of government forces today does not mean that we, the DRC government, will not hand them over to our partners,” he said.
AFC/M23 Reaction
Bertrand Bisimwa, Deputy Director for Political, Diplomatic, and Governance Affairs of AFC/M23, criticized the handover, calling it a sign of government weakness.
“Selling publicly assets that one does not own or does not control is a way of fighting and surviving,” Bisimwa said.
The Rubaya mines, under AFC/M23 control since May 2024, are highly strategic, containing up to 15% of the world’s Coltan, making them a key resource in the global minerals market.
The handover marks a significant development in the DRC-US mining partnership, even as the DRC government grapples with limited control over territories in the east.

title: Tshisekedi ‘Agrees’ to Respect Angola-Requested Ceasefire, But Violations Continue
excerpt: KINSHASA, February 13, 2026 — President Félix Tshisekedi has announced that DRC government forces will respect a ceasefire called for by his João Lourenço, in coordination with the African Union. According to the Presidential Office, the ceasefire requires both the government and
title_en: Tshisekedi ‘Agrees’ to Respect Angola-Requested Ceasefire, But Violations Continue
excerpt_en: KINSHASA, February 13, 2026 — President Félix Tshisekedi has announced that DRC government forces will respect a ceasefire called for by his João Lourenço, in coordination with the African Union. According to the Presidential Office, the ceasefire requires both the government and
body_en:
KINSHASA, February 13, 2026 — President Félix Tshisekedi has announced that DRC government forces will respect a ceasefire called for by his João Lourenço, in coordination with the African Union. According to the Presidential Office, the ceasefire requires both the government and the AFC/M23 coalition to remain in current positions, stop reinforcing fighting areas, refrain from repositioning to launch attacks, and halt external assistance.
The agreement, based on the Doha peace process signed on October 15, 2025, also establishes a monitoring body to track compliance. The Angolan government had requested the ceasefire to begin on February 18, following consultations with Tshisekedi and mediators including Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé and Olusegun Obasanjo.
Despite Tshisekedi’s announcement, ceasefire violations by the DRC government have persisted. AFC/M23 forces have repeatedly responded, citing the principle of “destroying evil at its source”, and have seized key areas including Goma and Bukavu.
On February 12, Olivier Nduhungirehe, Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, expressed skepticism over the DRC’s commitment, saying:
“We can always negotiate peace agreements or ceasefire declarations, but as long as Kinshasa does not stop airstrikes and heavy artillery, and President Tshisekedi insists on a military solution, while the international community overlooks these violations, it will be futile.”
On February 13, Benjamin Mbonimpa, Permanent Secretary of AFC/M23, stated that Angola had not formally informed the alliance of the ceasefire request, reaffirming that AFC/M23 continues to respect the Doha process. He added:
“We were not invited, we do not know its contents. We have always respected the ceasefire and many times announced it ourselves.”
Mbonimpa also accused the DRC government of further violating the ceasefire on February 13 and expressed confidence that MONUSCO troops will properly monitor compliance.

title: Rwanda Holds Talks with Russian Nuclear Watchdog on Future Cooperation
excerpt: Moscow, February 18, 2026 – The Government of Rwanda is in discussions with the Russian nuclear regulatory agency, Rostekhnadzor, exploring potential cooperation on nuclear energy development. The talks took place on February 16, 2026, between Rwandan Ambassador to Russia Maj. Ge
title_en: Rwanda Holds Talks with Russian Nuclear Watchdog on Future Cooperation
excerpt_en: Moscow, February 18, 2026 – The Government of Rwanda is in discussions with the Russian nuclear regulatory agency, Rostekhnadzor, exploring potential cooperation on nuclear energy development. The talks took place on February 16, 2026, between Rwandan Ambassador to Russia Maj. Ge
body_en:
Moscow, February 18, 2026 – The Government of Rwanda is in discussions with the Russian nuclear regulatory agency, Rostekhnadzor, exploring potential cooperation on nuclear energy development.
The talks took place on February 16, 2026, between Rwandan Ambassador to Russia Maj. Gen. Joseph Nzabamwita and Rostekhnadzor Director Alexander Trembitsky in Moscow. During the meeting, Trembitsky explained the agency’s functions and expressed readiness to collaborate with Rwanda on nuclear facility supervision, technology transfer, and related areas.
Maj. Gen. Nzabamwita thanked Russia and President Vladimir Putin for supporting Rwanda and other African countries, while also acknowledging Rostekhnadzor’s willingness to cooperate. The discussions led to preparations for a cooperation agreement between Rostekhnadzor and Rwanda’s Public Utilities Regulatory Authority (RURA).
Rwanda’s Nuclear Ambitions
Rwanda aims to increase its electricity generation from the current 447 megawatts to over 3,000 megawatts, with plans to construct small nuclear power plants. These plants are designed to produce high energy output while minimizing environmental impact compared to conventional power facilities.
In November 2025, Rwanda’s Minister of Infrastructure Dr. Gasore Jimmy informed the Senate that the first feasibility study had been completed, approved, and site selection was underway. A second impact assessment is currently ongoing.
“The goal is that between 2030 and 2032 we will have our first nuclear power plant. We have chosen small nuclear plants because they require less land, reduce accident risks, and are suitable for our country, which has limited space,” Minister Gasore explained.
Rwanda is also engaging with other international partners, including the United States and several European countries, to advance its nuclear energy program, signaling a strategic push toward sustainable and high-capacity electricity generation.

title: Banyamulenge Organizations Sue Burundi at EAC Court Over Alleged Atrocities in South Kivu
excerpt: ARUSHA, February 14, 2026 — Two organizations representing Banyamulenge communities in South Kivu Province have filed a lawsuit against the Burundi before the East African Court of Justice (EACJ), accusing Burundian forces of committing war crimes and crimes against humanity in e
title_en: Banyamulenge Organizations Sue Burundi at EAC Court Over Alleged Atrocities in South Kivu
excerpt_en: ARUSHA, February 14, 2026 — Two organizations representing Banyamulenge communities in South Kivu Province have filed a lawsuit against the Burundi before the East African Court of Justice (EACJ), accusing Burundian forces of committing war crimes and crimes against humanity in e
body_en:
ARUSHA, February 14, 2026 — Two organizations representing Banyamulenge communities in South Kivu Province have filed a lawsuit against the Burundi before the East African Court of Justice (EACJ), accusing Burundian forces of committing war crimes and crimes against humanity in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo.
The groups — ADEPAE and Mutualité Shikama — allege that since October 2025, Burundian troops deployed in South Kivu have blocked all major roads linking the Banyamulenge population in Minembwe commune to surrounding areas, including access to markets, health centers, and humanitarian assistance.
According to the complaint, the road closures were allegedly intended to isolate the community and expose it to life-threatening conditions.
Allegations of Abuses
One of the lawyers representing the plaintiffs, Me Innocent Nteziryayo, stated that beyond restricting movement, Burundian troops are accused of abductions, torture, destruction of property, and undermining the community’s livelihoods.
On November 11, 2025, the spokesperson of the Burundian army, Brig. Gen. Gaspard Baratuza, confirmed that troops had sealed off roads leading to Minembwe. He said the measure was aimed at protecting the town of Uvira, which Burundian forces continue to control.
Baratuza argued that securing Uvira required broader territorial control, adding that individuals suspected of collaborating with armed groups would not be allowed to cross.
Humanitarian Concerns Raised
On November 24, 2025, the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) reported that humanitarian access to Minembwe and surrounding border areas had become impossible due to the road closures.
OCHA warned that the restrictions had contributed to a sharp rise in deaths, particularly among children under five, and had triggered significant price increases for basic goods as supply routes remained cut off.
Burundi Rejects Allegations
While Brig. Gen. Baratuza acknowledged the closure of the roads, Burundi’s Minister of Justice reportedly told the regional court that the government does not accept responsibility for the full range of alleged crimes in South Kivu.
The complainants maintain that they possess documented evidence and witness testimonies to substantiate their claims and say they are prepared to present their case before the EACJ in pursuit of justice.
The case is expected to test regional legal mechanisms at a time of heightened tensions in eastern DRC, where multiple armed actors and foreign forces remain active.

The donated vehicle, a MAN Model TGS 31,400 truck, comes equipped with modern firefighting equipment suitable for residential and high-rise buildings, valued at €759,100 (over Rwf 1.3 billion).
Eric Mpayimana, CEO of RPC Ltd, said the donation is part of broader community initiatives beyond electricity provision:
“We chose to donate firefighting vehicles to the countries where our hydroelectric power plant—Burundi, Tanzania, and now Rwanda—operates, to provide assistance in the event of a fire and to build local firefighting capacity.”
Mpayimana noted that RPC’s activities also include building markets, youth centers, and health centers, contributing to regional unity across the three countries.
ACP Rutikanga Boniface, spokesperson for the Rwanda Police, described the vehicle as a major boost for protecting people and property, noting that current resources are insufficient for fire emergencies:
“Infrastructure is growing, cities and businesses are expanding, and rescue operations are increasingly necessary. This vehicle will enhance our capacity, and we plan to deploy similar vehicles in other areas.”
Boniface added that the donation also reflects awareness of fire risks linked to electricity usage:
“RPC provides electricity to heat homes, but misuse can cause fires. Receiving this vehicle shows consideration for the safety of those using electricity in the event of an accident.”
Rangira Bruno, Mayor of Kirehe District, where the power plant is located, described the donation as an important step in community care initiatives that RPC Ltd is implementing in partnership with the government.

excerpt_en: South Kivu, February 18, 2026 – The armed group MRDP-Twirwaneho has accused the DRC military coalition, including FARDC troops and allied FDLR forces, of burning Banyamulenge homes in several villages of South Kivu Province during recent clashes. The statement, issued on February
body_en:
South Kivu, February 18, 2026 – The armed group MRDP-Twirwaneho has accused the DRC military coalition, including FARDC troops and allied FDLR forces, of burning Banyamulenge homes in several villages of South Kivu Province during recent clashes.
The statement, issued on February 18, 2026, was a response to claims made by acting DRC military spokesperson Lt. Col. Mak Hazukay, who had accused Twirwaneho of the destruction. Twirwaneho rejected these allegations, calling them “baseless and shameless.”
“Contrary to what the FARDC announced, soldiers of the government coalition—including the DRC army, allied groups, and foreign forces—during their operations and so-called ‘strategic response’ were the ones who burned the houses of Banyamulenge civilians in Kalingi, Gakenke, and Kalongi,” the group said.
Impact on Civilians
A local resident reported that airstrikes by government forces have targeted communities in Minembwe Commune and surrounding areas for nearly two weeks.
“This is the second week that planes have been shooting at the population. They started at Point-Zéro, then moved to Bidegu, and finally Kalongi, where houses were burned and residents fled to Ilundu. Villages were destroyed,” the resident said.
The witness condemned the attacks, questioning how government forces could claim to be fighting Twirwaneho while targeting civilian homes and infrastructure, including hospitals.
Allegations of Cover-Up
Twirwaneho further alleged that while criminal activities continue in Minembwe and border areas, the DRC government is conducting a campaign to conceal these actions, allowing destruction and attacks to remain undetected.
The accusations underscore escalating tensions in South Kivu, where civilians continue to bear the brunt of military operations in a complex and volatile security environment.

title: EU Parliament Calls on Uganda to Release Opposition Members
excerpt: BRUSSELS, February 13, 2026 — The European Union Parliament has adopted a resolution condemning violence and the detention of opposition members before and after the January 15, 2026 elections in Uganda. The resolution highlights human rights violations, including internet shutdo
title_en: EU Parliament Calls on Uganda to Release Opposition Members
excerpt_en: BRUSSELS, February 13, 2026 — The European Union Parliament has adopted a resolution condemning violence and the detention of opposition members before and after the January 15, 2026 elections in Uganda. The resolution highlights human rights violations, including internet shutdo
body_en:
BRUSSELS, February 13, 2026 — The European Union Parliament has adopted a resolution condemning violence and the detention of opposition members before and after the January 15, 2026 elections in Uganda.
The resolution highlights human rights violations, including internet shutdowns, political violence, and the detention of members of the National Unity Platform, led by Robert Kyagulanyi. Following the elections, President Yoweri Museveni secured 71.6% of the vote, while Kyagulanyi went into exile, alleging that the Ugandan military besieged his home and attempted to arrest him.
In its February 12, 2026 resolution, the EU Parliament called for the release of all unlawfully detained individuals and urged Uganda to stop trying civilians in military courts and reveal the whereabouts of missing persons.
The resolution notes that detained opposition figures include Dr. Kiiza Besigye, held for over a year, and Robert Kyagulanyi, who fled into exile in January 2026.
