title: Nduhungirehe Criticizes Journalist Over Interview on Rwanda–DRC Peace Deal
excerpt: Kigali, 17 February 2026 – Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, Amb. Olivier Nduhungirehe, has criticized what he described as bias in an interview conducted by a France 24 journalist with Massad Boulos, Senior Advisor to the President of the United
title_en: Nduhungirehe Criticizes Journalist Over Interview on Rwanda–DRC Peace Deal
excerpt_en: Kigali, 17 February 2026 – Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, Amb. Olivier Nduhungirehe, has criticized what he described as bias in an interview conducted by a France 24 journalist with Massad Boulos, Senior Advisor to the President of the United
body_en:
Kigali, 17 February 2026 – Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, Amb. Olivier Nduhungirehe, has criticized what he described as bias in an interview conducted by a France 24 journalist with Massad Boulos, Senior Advisor to the President of the United States for African Affairs.
Speaking on February 17, 2026, Nduhungirehe reacted to an interview published on social media in which Marc Perelman of France 24 questioned Boulos on issues concerning Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).
“You will remember me to tell you how I feel when there is an impartial interview by a France 24 journalist. I am not interested in the way journalists or evaluators try to present themselves who always think about Rwanda,” Nduhungirehe said.
Debate Over the Washington Peace Agreement
The remarks come amid renewed debate over the Washington peace agreement signed on December 4, 2025, between Rwanda and Democratic Republic of the Congo with facilitation from the United States. The accord reinforced a previous agreement reached on June 27, 2025, but tensions have persisted since its signing.
In the February 16 interview, Perelman asked Boulos whether the agreement had failed to deliver tangible results. Boulos responded that the deal marked the beginning of a longer process toward regional stability.
“From the beginning, we said that the Washington peace agreement is not the end but the beginning. Eventually, there will be complete peace and security in the region. But that is a journey that will take time,” Boulos said.
He added that the agreement’s strength lies in its multi-track approach to addressing different aspects of the conflict. According to Boulos, the Washington accord—focused specifically on relations between Rwanda and the DRC—will be complemented by the Doha process, which seeks to facilitate dialogue between the Congolese government and the AFC/M23 rebellion, with backing from the United States and the African Union.
Tensions After Uvira’s Capture
The peace deal came under strain after AFC/M23 fighters captured the city of Uvira on December 9, 2025. Following the takeover, the Congolese government accused Rwanda of violating the Washington agreement and called on Washington to impose sanctions.
When asked whether the United States still had confidence in President Paul Kagame, Boulos replied, “We believe we do. We are talking.”
Allegations of Selective Questioning
Rwandan officials argue that the interview sought to portray Rwanda as the primary source of instability in eastern DRC, and that the journalist pressed Boulos on potential sanctions against Kigali while refraining from addressing other contentious issues.
Among them is the presence of the FDLR (Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda), an armed group operating in eastern DRC. The Congolese government has maintained that dismantling the group is complicated because many of its fighters are allegedly in areas controlled by AFC/M23.
However, Minister Nduhungirehe recently reiterated Rwanda’s position that numerous FDLR fighters have been integrated into the Congolese army and are operating in government-controlled zones.
The latest exchange highlights the ongoing diplomatic friction surrounding implementation of the Washington peace agreement, as regional and international actors continue efforts to stabilize eastern DRC.

title: “We Are Beginning to See Changes” — Minister Bizimana Highlights Impact of Reintegration Training for Genocide Convicts
excerpt: NYAMASHEKE, February 13, 2026 — Jean-Damascene Bizimana, Rwanda’s Minister of National Unity and Civic Engagement, says authorities are observing positive behavioral changes among prisoners convicted for their role in the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi who underwent pre-release
title_en: “We Are Beginning to See Changes” — Minister Bizimana Highlights Impact of Reintegration Training for Genocide Convicts
excerpt_en: NYAMASHEKE, February 13, 2026 — Jean-Damascene Bizimana, Rwanda’s Minister of National Unity and Civic Engagement, says authorities are observing positive behavioral changes among prisoners convicted for their role in the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi who underwent pre-release
body_en:
NYAMASHEKE, February 13, 2026 — Jean-Damascene Bizimana, Rwanda’s Minister of National Unity and Civic Engagement, says authorities are observing positive behavioral changes among prisoners convicted for their role in the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi who underwent pre-release civic training.
He made the remarks in Nyamasheke District during the closing ceremony of the sixth phase of a reintegration program targeting inmates with less than six months remaining on their sentences for genocide-related crimes.
According to Minister Bizimana, individuals who received the training demonstrated improved reintegration outcomes upon returning to their families, while some who did not participate showed signs of social isolation, divisionism, and adherence to genocide ideology.
Call for Accountability and Unity
Addressing the participants, Minister Bizimana emphasized the importance of acknowledging responsibility for past crimes committed during the Genocide against the Tutsi. He reminded them that their convictions stemmed from choices made under a regime that promoted persecution and mass violence against the Tutsi population.
“The message we give them,” he said, “is to accept that they have completed their sentence, that they have received the lessons provided, and that they are rejoining the Rwandan community to build ‘Ndi Umunyarwanda’ — a Rwanda free from ethnic division, discrimination, and genocide ideology.”
He stressed the importance of telling the truth about history, underscoring that national unity depends on confronting the realities of the past.
Low Recidivism Among Trained Inmates
Minister Bizimana noted that cases of reoffending remain rare among those who completed the training. In contrast, some individuals who did not undergo the program have reportedly exhibited signs associated with genocide ideology.
Also speaking at the ceremony, the Commissioner General of the National Service for the Prevention of Crime, CG Evariste Murenzi, urged participants to avoid reoffending and to become responsible members of society.
Families Participate in Reintegration
For the first time, families attended the closing ceremony, which included the awarding of completion certificates. Officials say the move aims to strengthen family reconciliation and community reintegration.
Iyakaremye Pacifique, a resident of Nyamasheke whose father was sentenced to 19 years for genocide crimes, shared the emotional toll of growing up with that legacy. He said he once felt ashamed but now hopes for positive change and responsible parental guidance moving forward.
Twagiramungu Jean Baptiste, who completed a 30-year sentence, thanked the government for establishing the program and pledged to uphold national unity. “The days we have spent here will not be in vain,” he said, adding that the rebuilding of unity under the ‘Ndi Umunyarwanda’ framework must be preserved.
Another participant, Musabyimana Jean, said he intends to promote what he described as historical truth and defend Rwanda’s leadership, including Paul Kagame.
654 Participants in Sixth Cohort
The sixth phase of the program brought together 654 inmates, including 165 individuals who were released immediately after completing both their sentences and the training.
Rwandan authorities say the initiative forms part of broader efforts to reinforce national reconciliation, civic responsibility, and long-term social cohesion more than three decades after the 1994 genocide.

Low Recidivism Among Trained Inmates
Minister Bizimana noted that cases of reoffending remain rare among those who completed the training. In contrast, some individuals who did not undergo the program have reportedly exhibited signs associated with genocide ideology.
Also speaking at the ceremony, the Commissioner General of the National Service for the Prevention of Crime, CG Evariste Murenzi, urged participants to avoid reoffending and to become responsible members of society.
Families Participate in Reintegration
For the first time, families attended the closing ceremony, which included the awarding of completion certificates. Officials say the move aims to strengthen family reconciliation and community reintegration.
Iyakaremye Pacifique, a resident of Nyamasheke whose father was sentenced to 19 years for genocide crimes, shared the emotional toll of growing up with that legacy. He said he once felt ashamed but now hopes for positive change and responsible parental guidance moving forward.
Twagiramungu Jean Baptiste, who completed a 30-year sentence, thanked the government for establishing the program and pledged to uphold national unity. “The days we have spent here will not be in vain,” he said, adding that the rebuilding of unity under the ‘Ndi Umunyarwanda’ framework must be preserved.
Another participant, Musabyimana Jean, said he intends to promote what he described as historical truth and defend Rwanda’s leadership, including Paul Kagame.
654 Participants in Sixth Cohort
The sixth phase of the program brought together 654 inmates, including 165 individuals who were released immediately after completing both their sentences and the training.
Rwandan authorities say the initiative forms part of broader efforts to reinforce national reconciliation, civic responsibility, and long-term social cohesion more than three decades after the 1994 genocide.

excerpt_en: GOMA, February 13, 2026 — Leaders of the AFC/M23 coalition and the MONUSCO met in Goma on February 13 to discuss the implementation of the ceasefire. On the AFC/M23 side, the meeting included Corneille Nangaa, the coalition’s General Director, and military officials such as Col N
body_en:
GOMA, February 13, 2026 — Leaders of the AFC/M23 coalition and the MONUSCO met in Goma on February 13 to discuss the implementation of the ceasefire.
On the AFC/M23 side, the meeting included Corneille Nangaa, the coalition’s General Director, and military officials such as Col Nzenze Imani John, head of intelligence. Representing MONUSCO was its Acting Director, Vivian van de Perre, who arrived in Goma on February 12. Her plane landed at the local airport, the first operational flight since late January 2025, when AFC/M23 took control of the facility.
Upon arrival, van de Perre stated that discussions would focus on partners responsible for monitoring the ceasefire, and proposed that the airport be reopened in phases to facilitate the mission.
The UN Security Council has mandated MONUSCO to monitor the ceasefire in areas from which AFC/M23 withdrew in Uvira Territory, an agreement reached with the DRC government during the Doha peace talks in Qatar.
Jean-Pierre Lacroix, UN Under-Secretary-General for Peacekeeping Operations, said on February 12 that MONUSCO troop deployment will be phased, beginning with reconnaissance aircraft to ensure security. The reconnaissance flights to Uvira will depart from Goma airport, suggesting that AFC/M23 may need to facilitate access for the mission.

title: Kenya Foils Al-Shabaab Attack, Seizes Weapons in Nairobi
excerpt: Nairobi, February 18, 2026 – The Kenyan military, led by soldiers from the Counter-Terrorism Service (CTS), successfully thwarted a planned attack by suspected Al-Shabaab operatives, authorities announced. The operation, carried out on February 18, 2026, followed careful monitori
title_en: Kenya Foils Al-Shabaab Attack, Seizes Weapons in Nairobi
excerpt_en: Nairobi, February 18, 2026 – The Kenyan military, led by soldiers from the Counter-Terrorism Service (CTS), successfully thwarted a planned attack by suspected Al-Shabaab operatives, authorities announced. The operation, carried out on February 18, 2026, followed careful monitori
body_en:
Nairobi, February 18, 2026 – The Kenyan military, led by soldiers from the Counter-Terrorism Service (CTS), successfully thwarted a planned attack by suspected Al-Shabaab operatives, authorities announced.
The operation, carried out on February 18, 2026, followed careful monitoring of the suspects’ movements, communication networks, and other links. Acting on intelligence reports, CTS personnel intercepted a large cache of weapons, including 600 rounds of ammunition, small and large firearms, and explosives, intended for use in various parts of Nairobi City.
“The plans of the Al-Shabaab terrorist group to kill many Kenyans have been foiled by the intelligence service,” the CTS statement said.
Planned Attacks During Ramadan
Initial investigations indicated that the group had planned attacks during the fasting month of Ramadan. Officials also revealed that the suspects had considered kidnapping foreigners as part of their operation.
Kenyan security agencies emphasized that ongoing investigations aim to uncover additional activities linked to the planned attacks.
Crackdown on Funding Networks
Over the past two weeks, intelligence services identified 13 accounts used to fund terrorist activities, involving citizens from Kenya, Uganda, and Tanzania. All accounts were subsequently closed, disrupting the financial networks supporting the planned operations.
The successful intervention highlights Kenya’s continued vigilance against terrorism and its commitment to protecting civilians from potential threats.

body_en:
ADDIS ABABA, February 13, 2026 — Justin Nsengiyumva represented Paul Kagame at the Africa–Italy Summit held in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, ahead of the 39th Ordinary Session of the African Union Heads of State and Government.
Arriving on the afternoon of February 13, the Prime Minister immediately joined the high-level proceedings, which focused on sustainable access to clean water, sanitation, and hygiene, in line with Africa’s long-term development framework, Agenda 2063. Participants also assessed progress in political and economic cooperation between Italy and African nations under the Mattei Plan.
The summit marked the second edition of the Africa–Italy meeting, following the inaugural gathering in Rome in 2024. Rwanda and Italy maintain longstanding diplomatic relations, further strengthened in 2024 through a €50 million agreement supporting environmental protection projects in Rwanda.
The Addis Ababa engagement highlights Kigali’s sustained multilateral diplomacy, reinforcing partnerships aimed at economic growth, sustainable development, and continental integration.

title: Danish Foreign Minister Visits Rwanda to Officially Open Embassy in Kigali
excerpt: Kigali, 16 February 2026 – Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen is in Rwanda for an official visit marked by the formal inauguration of Denmark’s embassy in Kigali, underscoring Copenhagen’s growing engagement with African countries. Lars Løkke Rasmussen arrived in Rwanda
title_en: Danish Foreign Minister Visits Rwanda to Officially Open Embassy in Kigali
excerpt_en: Kigali, 16 February 2026 – Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen is in Rwanda for an official visit marked by the formal inauguration of Denmark’s embassy in Kigali, underscoring Copenhagen’s growing engagement with African countries. Lars Løkke Rasmussen arrived in Rwanda
body_en:
Kigali, 16 February 2026 – Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen is in Rwanda for an official visit marked by the formal inauguration of Denmark’s embassy in Kigali, underscoring Copenhagen’s growing engagement with African countries.
Lars Løkke Rasmussen arrived in Rwanda on Sunday, 15 February 2026, as part of Denmark’s broader strategy to strengthen bilateral cooperation and deepen diplomatic and economic ties across the continent.
On Monday, the Danish minister and his delegation visited the Kigali Genocide Memorial in Gisozi, Gasabo District, where they were briefed on the history of the Genocide against the Tutsi. The delegation paid tribute to the victims laid to rest at the memorial site.
During his stay, the Danish top diplomat is expected to hold talks with his Rwandan counterpart, Amb. Olivier Nduhungirehe, focusing on enhancing partnerships, expanding economic cooperation, and exploring new avenues of collaboration between the two countries.
The minister will also engage with Danish entrepreneurs operating in Rwanda, discussing both the investment opportunities and challenges facing European businesses in the country. In addition, he is scheduled to visit the University of Rwanda, where he will meet with students to discuss opportunities for pursuing further studies in Europe.
Ahead of the visit, Lars Løkke Rasmussen described the opening of the embassy as part of Denmark’s expanding focus on Africa and its commitment to strengthening engagement with African nations. He highlighted Rwanda’s rapid development, particularly its ambitions in innovation, technology, and green solutions, noting that Danish expertise could contribute meaningfully to these sectors.
A key milestone of the visit is the official opening of the Danish Embassy in Rwanda, which began operations in August 2025. Denmark appointed Casper Stenger Jensen as its first resident ambassador to Rwanda. Based in Kigali, Ambassador Jensen has emphasized Denmark’s intention to further broaden and deepen its relations with Rwanda and other countries in the region.
The visit signals a new chapter in Denmark–Rwanda relations, anchored in diplomacy, trade, education, and sustainable development cooperation.

title: Rwanda Seeks Extradition of “Prince Kid” From the United States
excerpt: KIGALI, February 9, 2026 — Rwanda’s prosecution authorities say they are working with the United States to extradite Ishimwe Dieudonne, widely known as Prince Kid, to face justice after his conviction in a high-profile sexual assault case linked to the Miss Rwanda beauty pageant.
title_en: Rwanda Seeks Extradition of “Prince Kid” From the United States
excerpt_en: KIGALI, February 9, 2026 — Rwanda’s prosecution authorities say they are working with the United States to extradite Ishimwe Dieudonne, widely known as Prince Kid, to face justice after his conviction in a high-profile sexual assault case linked to the Miss Rwanda beauty pageant.
body_en:
KIGALI, February 9, 2026 — Rwanda’s prosecution authorities say they are working with the United States to extradite Ishimwe Dieudonne, widely known as Prince Kid, to face justice after his conviction in a high-profile sexual assault case linked to the Miss Rwanda beauty pageant.
Prosecutor General Angelique Habyarimana announced that Kigali issued an international arrest warrant after confirming he was in the United States and submitted the necessary legal documents for his return.
Prince Kid rose to national prominence as the organizer of the pageant through his company Rwanda Inspiration Backup. In October 2023, Rwanda’s High Court sentenced him to five years in prison for sexual assault and solicitation of sexual favors involving contestants.
Court proceedings were held in his absence, as he had already fled the country.
On March 3, 2025, the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrested him in Fort Worth, Texas. Authorities stated he had entered the United States legally but later violated immigration rules and now faces separate legal proceedings there.
Speaking during Anti-Corruption Week activities, Habyarimana said Rwanda formally transmitted the conviction record and requested extradition.
“The verdict is final and without further appeal. We submitted arrest warrants and his full profile to the relevant authorities and cooperation is ongoing,” she said.
She added that extradition could occur once U.S. proceedings conclude.
The charges against Prince Kid stem from allegations that he abused participants in the pageant over several years, prompting a major public scandal in Rwanda’s entertainment industry.
Rwandan officials say they will continue legal cooperation with U.S. authorities until the case is resolved and the sentence enforced.

title: Wazalendo Groups Clash Over Batakirwa Control
excerpt: WALIKALE, February 13, 2026 — Armed groups of the Wazalendo Alliance, backed by the Democratic Republic of Congo government, are clashing for control of the Batakirwa area in the Bafuna group, Walikale Territory. The confrontation pits the NDC-R, led by Guidon Shimiray Mwissa, ag
title_en: Wazalendo Groups Clash Over Batakirwa Control
excerpt_en: WALIKALE, February 13, 2026 — Armed groups of the Wazalendo Alliance, backed by the Democratic Republic of Congo government, are clashing for control of the Batakirwa area in the Bafuna group, Walikale Territory. The confrontation pits the NDC-R, led by Guidon Shimiray Mwissa, ag
body_en:
WALIKALE, February 13, 2026 — Armed groups of the Wazalendo Alliance, backed by the Democratic Republic of Congo government, are clashing for control of the Batakirwa area in the Bafuna group, Walikale Territory.
The confrontation pits the NDC-R, led by Guidon Shimiray Mwissa, against Uhuru-RDC, commanded by Mashite Kashira. On February 11, 2026, Mashite deployed fighters to three mineral-rich villages in Batakirwa, warning the NDC-R that any attempt to enter would trigger fighting.
Local leader Kibaki reported that Uhuru-RDC fighters have been intimidating civilians, accusing them of supporting the NDC-R, forcing him to flee to Walikale town. He told Actualite newspaper:
“The population is in great danger. The armed groups are terrorizing civilians, associating them with their enemies.”
Kibaki urged the DRC government to take action against these armed groups, which are already engaged against the AFC/M23 alliance, warning that failure to intervene could escalate the conflict.

title_en: France Clarifies Presence of Troops in Kisangani Amid Social Media Speculation
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, February 17, 2026 – The Embassy of France in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has dismissed claims of a secret deployment of French troops to Kisangani, stating that the personnel seen in the city are part of an ongoing military training partnership with the Democra
body_en:
Kinshasa, February 17, 2026 – The Embassy of France in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has dismissed claims of a secret deployment of French troops to Kisangani, stating that the personnel seen in the city are part of an ongoing military training partnership with the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
Since February 15, 2026, photos circulating on social media have shown French soldiers in Kisangani, the capital of Tshopo Province, prompting speculation about their possible involvement in the conflict in eastern DRC.
The speculation intensified amid claims that Kisangani serves as a strategic hub where the Congolese army and foreign mercenaries prepare air operations targeting positions held by the AFC/M23 armed group, including areas where civilians are present.
“No Secret Deployment”
In response, the French Embassy emphasized that the presence of French troops is part of a transparent and longstanding bilateral military cooperation program.
“The French military is training the DRC military, at the request of the DRC government. It is a normal bilateral partnership; it will not be sent there in secret. We have openly announced the activities based on our partnership,” the Embassy said in a statement.
According to French officials, the cooperation includes training Congolese soldiers in jungle warfare techniques. The Embassy shared images of training sessions conducted in Kisangani in 2022 as well as more recent sessions from February 2026, underscoring the continuity of the program.
The clarification comes as tensions remain high in eastern DRC, where fighting between government forces and AFC/M23 rebels continues to shape regional security dynamics.

title: Rwanda Grants Citizenship to 1,500 Foreigners Since 2009
excerpt: KIGALI, February 12, 2026 — The Rwanda Immigration Service announced that since 2009, Rwanda has granted citizenship to 1,500 foreigners, drawn to the country for its security, peace, cleanliness, and ease of investment. Rusanganwa Jean Damascène, Director of Citizenship Services
title_en: Rwanda Grants Citizenship to 1,500 Foreigners Since 2009
excerpt_en: KIGALI, February 12, 2026 — The Rwanda Immigration Service announced that since 2009, Rwanda has granted citizenship to 1,500 foreigners, drawn to the country for its security, peace, cleanliness, and ease of investment. Rusanganwa Jean Damascène, Director of Citizenship Services
body_en:
KIGALI, February 12, 2026 — The Rwanda Immigration Service announced that since 2009, Rwanda has granted citizenship to 1,500 foreigners, drawn to the country for its security, peace, cleanliness, and ease of investment.
Rusanganwa Jean Damascène, Director of Citizenship Services, told RBA that the latest round included 101 individuals, with 80 residing in Rwanda and 21 in Rwandan embassies abroad, who will gradually receive their citizenship.
Citizenship is granted based on criteria such as birth in Rwanda, adoption on Rwandan soil, marriage, national interests, special knowledge or talents, large investments, residence in Rwanda, or honorary recognition. Rusanganwa emphasized that naturalized citizens have the same rights and obligations as all Rwandans, without distinctions by ethnic group, noting that the previous categories of Hutu, Tutsi, Twa, and Naturalized no longer apply.
Regarding revocation, Organic Law No. 002/2021.OL of July 16, 2021, allows citizenship to be revoked under four circumstances: use of fraudulent documents, betrayal of the Republic, marriages intended solely to gain citizenship, or behavior contrary to Rwandan values. To date, no naturalized citizen has had their Rwandan citizenship revoked.
The authority to grant Rwandan citizenship lies with the Cabinet, while citizenship granted on the basis of merit is under the discretion of the President of the Republic of Rwanda.

title: Burundian Team Poised to Support Ndayishimiye’s AU Leadership
excerpt: Addis Ababa February 16, 2026 — Burundian President Évariste Ndayishimiye is assembling a team of trusted officials and diplomats to support his one-year tenure at the helm of the African Union (AU), with a focus on advancing the bloc’s economic and security agenda. Ndayishimiye
title_en: Burundian Team Poised to Support Ndayishimiye’s AU Leadership
excerpt_en: Addis Ababa February 16, 2026 — Burundian President Évariste Ndayishimiye is assembling a team of trusted officials and diplomats to support his one-year tenure at the helm of the African Union (AU), with a focus on advancing the bloc’s economic and security agenda. Ndayishimiye
body_en:
Addis Ababa February 16, 2026 — Burundian President Évariste Ndayishimiye is assembling a team of trusted officials and diplomats to support his one-year tenure at the helm of the African Union (AU), with a focus on advancing the bloc’s economic and security agenda.
Ndayishimiye officially assumed the rotating presidency of the AU on February 14, 2026, succeeding Angolan President João Lourenço. In line with the organization’s rotational principles, he is expected to hand over leadership next year to the President of Ghana.
Key Figures in the Inner Circle
Among the prominent figures expected to play a central role is Burundi’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, Dr. Édouard Bizimana. A seasoned diplomat, Bizimana previously served under former President Pierre Nkurunziza before being appointed special advisor to Ndayishimiye in August 2022. In August 2025, he was named Foreign Minister, replacing Albert Shingiro, who had held the post since June 2020.
Ndayishimiye and Bizimana share longstanding ties, having both originated from Gitega province and studied at the University of Burundi — a relationship seen as reinforcing political trust at the highest level of government.
Diplomatic and Security Support
Burundi’s Ambassador to Ethiopia and the AU, Willy Nyamitwe, is also viewed as a key asset, given his experience in Addis Ababa, where the AU is headquartered. Though he is nearing the end of his current posting, he is expected to remain influential in supporting the AU presidency.
Other diplomats who may join the presidential support team include Ambassador Ferdinand Bashikako, former Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs; Gaudence Sindayigaya, former Ambassador to the United States; Ambassador Thérence Ntahiraja in Belgium; and Jean Bosco Bare in Washington.
On security matters, former customs chief Joseph Ndarishikanye and Adolphe Hasabindero, known for his expertise in reintegration and rehabilitation of former soldiers, are among those being considered to provide technical backing.
Formation of a Strategic Taskforce
President Ndayishimiye is reportedly preparing to establish a core team of around ten members to coordinate his AU leadership, with five already confirmed. In parallel, a national committee dubbed “Cap2026” is set to be formed in Burundi to support strategic planning efforts tied to his continental mandate. Among those expected to contribute is Ambassador Adolphe Nahayo, Director-General for Cooperation in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
With a trusted circle of diplomats and technocrats, Ndayishimiye appears intent on consolidating Burundi’s diplomatic footprint while steering the African Union through a year marked by pressing economic and security challenges.

title: 46% of People with Disabilities in Rwanda Lack Access to Bank Loans
excerpt: Kigali, February 20, 2026 – A recent consultative meeting organized by Access to Finance Rwanda (AFR) revealed that 46% of people with disabilities in Rwanda do not have access to bank and financial services, highlighting persistent barriers to financial inclusion. The meeting, h
title_en: 46% of People with Disabilities in Rwanda Lack Access to Bank Loans
excerpt_en: Kigali, February 20, 2026 – A recent consultative meeting organized by Access to Finance Rwanda (AFR) revealed that 46% of people with disabilities in Rwanda do not have access to bank and financial services, highlighting persistent barriers to financial inclusion. The meeting, h
body_en:
Kigali, February 20, 2026 – A recent consultative meeting organized by Access to Finance Rwanda (AFR) revealed that 46% of people with disabilities in Rwanda do not have access to bank and financial services, highlighting persistent barriers to financial inclusion.
The meeting, held on February 19, 2026, brought together government agencies, financial institutions, development partners, non-profits, civil society, and disability associations to discuss findings from an AFR survey on financial accessibility for people with disabilities.
Key Findings
The proportion of people with disabilities unable to apply for bank loans rose from 36.3% in 2020 to 46.6% in 2024.
Overall access to financial services has decreased, despite 92.9% of those surveyed reportedly being reached by some services.
Key obstacles include lack of collateral, limited trust from banks, and insufficient staff trained to communicate with people with hearing or visual impairments.
Voices from the Community
Ingabire Mukamurenzi Francine, a blind entrepreneur, shared her experience:
“Banks generally do not trust people with disabilities, and there are no special programs for us like there are for youth or women. I had to approach Urwego Finance to secure a loan to expand my business, and they have supported me ever since.”
Dr. Mukarwego Beth Nasiforo, head of the Rwandan Network of People with Disabilities (NUDOR), emphasized that perceptions and lack of awareness among financial institution employees hinder access for people with disabilities.
Emmanuel Ndayisaba, Executive Secretary of the National Council for Persons with Disabilities (NCPD), highlighted the broader impact:
“When people with disabilities are given access to financial services, they contribute to business development, employment creation, innovation, and national development.”
The meeting underscored the urgent need for targeted financial programs and inclusive policies to ensure that people with disabilities can fully participate in Rwanda’s economic growth.

title: AFC/M23 Accuses Burundi’s President of Role in Attacks on Banyamulenge
excerpt: GOMA, February 13, 2026 — Corneille Nangaa, leader of the opposition coalition AFC/M23, has condemned Évariste Ndayishimiye over what he described as the continued targeting of Banyamulenge civilians in South Kivu province, eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo. In a statement
title_en: AFC/M23 Accuses Burundi’s President of Role in Attacks on Banyamulenge
excerpt_en: GOMA, February 13, 2026 — Corneille Nangaa, leader of the opposition coalition AFC/M23, has condemned Évariste Ndayishimiye over what he described as the continued targeting of Banyamulenge civilians in South Kivu province, eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo. In a statement
body_en:
GOMA, February 13, 2026 — Corneille Nangaa, leader of the opposition coalition AFC/M23, has condemned Évariste Ndayishimiye over what he described as the continued targeting of Banyamulenge civilians in South Kivu province, eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo.
In a statement released February 13, Nangaa denounced ongoing military operations allegedly carried out by Congolese government forces alongside Burundian troops against both civilians and AFC/M23 positions.
He also criticized the Burundian leader, who is expected to assume a senior continental role, accusing him of contributing to crimes against the Banyamulenge population.
Call for International Intervention
Nangaa urged the international community and African institutions to act quickly to prevent wider ethnic tensions in the Great Lakes region and to assist affected civilians.
Background to Burundian Deployment
The Burundi deployed troops to the DRC under a bilateral agreement aimed at fighting armed groups operating in the region, including RED Tabara, FNL-Nzabampema, and FOREBU.
According to the AFC/M23, the mission later expanded, with Burundian forces allegedly participating in operations in Banyamulenge-inhabited areas across the territories of Uvira, Fizi, and Mwenga, particularly in Minembwe commune.
Road Closures and Humanitarian Impact
For several months, roads linking Minembwe residents to markets and health facilities have reportedly been closed. Burundian army spokesperson Brig. Gen. Gaspard Baratuza previously stated the restrictions were imposed because some residents were suspected of collaborating with hostile armed groups.
The accusations come amid escalating tensions in eastern DRC, where multiple armed actors and foreign forces remain engaged in a complex conflict with significant humanitarian consequences.

title: AFC/M23 Announces Plans to Establish Telecommunications Company in Areas Under Its Control
excerpt: Masisi, February 16, 2026 – The AFC/M23 coalition, which is fighting against the Democratic Republic of the Congo, has announced plans to establish a telecommunications company in territories under its control, aiming to restore communication services for local populations. The a
title_en: AFC/M23 Announces Plans to Establish Telecommunications Company in Areas Under Its Control
excerpt_en: Masisi, February 16, 2026 – The AFC/M23 coalition, which is fighting against the Democratic Republic of the Congo, has announced plans to establish a telecommunications company in territories under its control, aiming to restore communication services for local populations. The a
body_en:
Masisi, February 16, 2026 – The AFC/M23 coalition, which is fighting against the Democratic Republic of the Congo, has announced plans to establish a telecommunications company in territories under its control, aiming to restore communication services for local populations.
The announcement was made on February 16, 2026, by Bahati Musanga Erasto, the governor of North Kivu appointed by AFC/M23, during a visit to residents in the town center of Kitshanga, located in Masisi Territory.
Accusations Against Kinshasa
Addressing residents, Governor Bahati accused the government in Kinshasa of deliberately cutting off telecommunications services in areas controlled by the coalition, alleging that the move was intended to harm civilians living in those areas.
“It is the government of Kinshasa that interrupted the transmission. We are working to ensure this does not happen again. We are putting in place an alternative transmission system; no one will interrupt it because it belongs to us. It will reach Goma, Kitshanga, and everywhere else. No one will touch these antennas again to disrupt transmission,” he said.
According to Bahati, only the cities of Goma and Bukavu currently have functioning telephone services, while other localities remain cut off, depriving residents of access to modern communication technologies.
Uncertainty Surrounding the Project
Details about how the project will be implemented remain unclear. It is not known whether AFC/M23 intends to launch a new telecommunications company or partner with an existing operator already active in other countries.
The announcement comes amid ongoing tensions in eastern DRC, where control over territory, public services, and strategic infrastructure remains a central issue in the broader conflict.
body_fr:

title_en: U.S. Lawmakers Urge DRC to Dismantle FDLR as Condition for Rwanda Security Withdrawal
excerpt_en: WASHINGTON, February 11, 2026 — Members of the U.S. House of Representatives Africa Subcommittee have reminded the government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo that Rwanda is expected to lift its security measures only after the dismantling of the FDLR. In a statement issue
body_en:
WASHINGTON, February 11, 2026 — Members of the U.S. House of Representatives Africa Subcommittee have reminded the government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo that Rwanda is expected to lift its security measures only after the dismantling of the FDLR.
In a statement issued on February 10, Congresswoman Sara Jacobs said that despite a U.S.-brokered peace arrangement between Kigali and Kinshasa, reports indicate elements of the Congolese army continue cooperating with the armed group.
“On the part of the DRC military, in violation of the peace agreement, it is said to continue working with the FDLR, a group founded by leaders who organized the 1994 genocide in Rwanda,” she said.
Subcommittee chairman Chris Smith emphasized that Rwanda’s commitment to remove defensive measures depends on full implementation of the agreement’s provisions, particularly the neutralization of the militia.
“The Washington Peace Agreement includes a four-stage action plan agreed to by both parties. This is essential for Rwanda to withdraw its forces, but only if the DRC follows through on a comprehensive plan to dismantle the FDLR,” he said.
Lawmakers also warned that the genocidal ideology associated with the group remains a security concern for Rwanda and areas under control of the AFC/M23, urging efforts to mobilize combatants to disarm.
Kigali has already launched reintegration initiatives through the Rwanda Demobilization and Reintegration Commission, including the Isange mu Banyu program encouraging Rwandan fighters in eastern Congo to return home.
Authorities, local residents and former rebels have continued awareness campaigns in the forests of eastern Congo, particularly targeting fighters originating from Rubavu District, which officials say accounts for a majority of returnees.
In November 2025, the commission’s vice president Jacques Nziza noted that about 70 percent of former FDLR members who repatriated came from that region, explaining why the area remains central to demobilization efforts.

title: Ruto and Nsengiyumva Agree to Strengthen Rwanda–Kenya Ties
excerpt: Addis Ababa February 15, 2026 — Kenyan President William Ruto and Rwandan Prime Minister Justin Nsengiyumva have agreed to further reinforce diplomatic and economic relations between their two countries. The talks took place on the sidelines of the 39th Ordinary Session of the Af
title_en: Ruto and Nsengiyumva Agree to Strengthen Rwanda–Kenya Ties
excerpt_en: Addis Ababa February 15, 2026 — Kenyan President William Ruto and Rwandan Prime Minister Justin Nsengiyumva have agreed to further reinforce diplomatic and economic relations between their two countries. The talks took place on the sidelines of the 39th Ordinary Session of the Af
body_en:
Addis Ababa February 15, 2026 — Kenyan President William Ruto and Rwandan Prime Minister Justin Nsengiyumva have agreed to further reinforce diplomatic and economic relations between their two countries.
The talks took place on the sidelines of the 39th Ordinary Session of the African Union Summit in Addis Ababa, where Nsengiyumva represented President Paul Kagame.
In a message posted on X, President Ruto said the discussions focused on strengthening bilateral cooperation.
“I met with the Prime Minister of Rwanda, Mr. Justin Nsengiyumva, following the 39th Ordinary Summit of the Heads of State and Government of the African Union in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. We agreed to strengthen our diplomatic relations and partnerships with other countries, in our common interest, to contribute to the development of Africa and the world,” Ruto stated.
The Prime Minister’s Office also confirmed that Nsengiyumva held talks with Namibian President Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah during the summit.
Strong and Expanding Economic Links
Rwanda and Kenya maintain long-standing and robust ties, particularly in trade and investment.
Kenyan banks — including Equity Bank, KCB Bank, I&M Bank, and NCBA Bank — have established a strong presence in Rwanda’s financial sector.
In higher education, Kenyan institutions such as Mount Kigali University operate in Rwanda.
Air connectivity also remains strong, with Kenya Airways and Jambojet serving the Rwandan market.
The renewed commitment announced in Addis Ababa signals continued momentum in Rwanda–Kenya cooperation, with both governments positioning their partnership as a driver of regional integration and African development.

title: Rwanda Signs Firm to Develop Nationwide Housing Plans Aligned with 2050 Vision
excerpt: Kigali, February 17, 2026 – The Rwandan Ministry of Infrastructure has signed a long-term contract with Dar Al-Handasah Consultants (Shair & Partners) S.A.L to develop and prepare housing plans across the country, in line with the Kigali City Master Plan and other regional land-u
title_en: Rwanda Signs Firm to Develop Nationwide Housing Plans Aligned with 2050 Vision
excerpt_en: Kigali, February 17, 2026 – The Rwandan Ministry of Infrastructure has signed a long-term contract with Dar Al-Handasah Consultants (Shair & Partners) S.A.L to develop and prepare housing plans across the country, in line with the Kigali City Master Plan and other regional land-u
body_en:
Kigali, February 17, 2026 – The Rwandan Ministry of Infrastructure has signed a long-term contract with Dar Al-Handasah Consultants (Shair & Partners) S.A.L to develop and prepare housing plans across the country, in line with the Kigali City Master Plan and other regional land-use plans extending to 2050.
The agreement aims to produce comprehensive urban designs covering housing sites, infrastructure, government service centers, stormwater drainage, roads, commercial areas, recreational facilities, and other public amenities. Without an approved physical plan, developers cannot obtain building permits.
The contract, signed at the national level, allows government agencies and regional authorities to collaborate directly with Dar Al-Handasah Consultants (Shair & Partners) S.A.L without issuing separate tenders, reducing both time and cost in preparing urban studies.
Dar Al-Handasah Consultants (Shair & Partners) S.A.L is an international firm specializing in construction, civil engineering, and environmental project management. In Rwanda, it has contributed to major infrastructure projects, including the new Kigali International Airport in Bugesera and updates to the national transport master plan.
Streamlining Urban Development
Jack Ngarambe, Director General of Urban Development and Housing at MININFRA, explained that using ministerial-level contracts will accelerate the procurement process for housing projects and ensure high-quality designs tailored to each area.
“The biggest challenge has been integrating accurate information into the design and aligning it with the local planning system,” Ngarambe said. He emphasized that housing projects must reflect a comprehensive vision, including stormwater and sewage systems, domestic water supply, transportation links, and public infrastructure such as schools, sports facilities, and conservation areas.
The initiative is intended to allow different institutions to carry out high-level urban planning whenever capacity is available. Ngarambe noted that the main obstacle has been the high cost of preparing housing designs, which limits the simultaneous development of multiple projects, especially when incorporating community preferences.
The national land-use master plan remains aligned with Rwanda’s 2050 vision, and authorities believe that contracting a single firm for nationwide planning will improve quality, even if it may raise service costs and affect opportunities for local surveyors and planners.
This move reflects Rwanda’s commitment to systematic, long-term urban development, balancing population growth, infrastructure needs, and sustainable land use across the country.

title_en: Rwanda Replaces 160 Police Officers in South Sudan Peacekeeping Mission
excerpt_en: KIGALI, January 12, 2026 — Rwanda National Police has rotated 160 police officers from the RWAFPU3-7 team, who returned to Kigali after a one-year deployment in South Sudan under the United Nations Peacekeeping Mission in South Sudan. The outgoing team, led by SSP Devotha Nyinawu
body_en:
KIGALI, January 12, 2026 — Rwanda National Police has rotated 160 police officers from the RWAFPU3-7 team, who returned to Kigali after a one-year deployment in South Sudan under the United Nations Peacekeeping Mission in South Sudan. The outgoing team, led by SSP Devotha Nyinawumuntu, was based in Juba and immediately replaced by the RWAFPU3-8 team, commanded by SSP Donatha Iribagiza.
The police officers’ duties in South Sudan included restoring peace and security, protecting civilians, safeguarding United Nations personnel and operations, and promoting the well-being of local populations.
At Kigali International Airport, the incoming team was received by CP Yahaya Kamunuga, Commissioner of Police, who thanked the returning officers for their dedication and professionalism. He said:
“You have returned to Rwanda to continue serving your country. You may find that things have changed. But your integrity and dedication must remain the same.”
On behalf of the outgoing team, SP Vincent Mwine Rubimbura, deputy leader of RWAFPU3-7, highlighted key community engagement initiatives carried out during their deployment. In addition to protecting civilians and UN personnel, the team worked to strengthen relations with the local population through activities such as community service, school renovations, distribution of mosquito nets and school supplies, and providing medical care and clean water to vulnerable families.
SP Rubimbura noted that these efforts have enhanced trust and cooperation between the police and local communities, reinforcing the overall peacekeeping mission.

title_en: AFC/M23 Announces Arrival of More Than 7,500 New Commandos
excerpt_en: NORTH KIVU, February 10, 2026 — The M23/AFC coalition, fighting the government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, says it has added 7,532 newly trained commandos to its ranks following training at the Tshanzu military center in Rutshuru Territory. According to the movement,
body_en:
NORTH KIVU, February 10, 2026 — The M23/AFC coalition, fighting the government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, says it has added 7,532 newly trained commandos to its ranks following training at the Tshanzu military center in Rutshuru Territory.
According to the movement, the recruits underwent extended preparation that included combat techniques and physical engagement training before being deployed toward active front lines in eastern Congo.
The group’s military chief, Sultani Makenga, told the new fighters that their predecessors had already defeated coalition forces aligned with the Congolese army, which he claimed included foreign troops, militias and mercenaries.
“Your comrades have done a great job on the battlefields. The enemy brought different groups — Burundians, the FDLR and foreign mercenaries — but they were defeated,” he said during the address.
Makenga urged the recruits to join ongoing operations and support fighters already engaged in combat, instructing them to maintain discipline and avoid harming civilians or engaging in looting and drug use.
“Your comrades are waiting for you. Help liberate people who have suffered for a long time and do not become a burden to them,” he added.
The announcement comes as the movement continues expanding its manpower after capturing Goma in January 2025. The group says that in September and October 2025, more than 16,000 fighters graduated from the Tshanzu and Rumangabo camps and were subsequently deployed to combat zones.
The reported increase in fighters highlights ongoing militarization in eastern Congo despite repeated diplomatic initiatives aimed at restoring stability in the region.

Makenga urged the recruits to join ongoing operations and support fighters already engaged in combat, instructing them to maintain discipline and avoid harming civilians or engaging in looting and drug use.
“Your comrades are waiting for you. Help liberate people who have suffered for a long time and do not become a burden to them,” he added.
The announcement comes as the movement continues expanding its manpower after capturing Goma in January 2025. The group says that in September and October 2025, more than 16,000 fighters graduated from the Tshanzu and Rumangabo camps and were subsequently deployed to combat zones.
The reported increase in fighters highlights ongoing militarization in eastern Congo despite repeated diplomatic initiatives aimed at restoring stability in the region.

title: Nduhungirehe Questions UN and AU Over Alleged Use of Mercenaries in DRC
excerpt: Kigali February 11, 2026 - Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation, Olivier Nduhungirehe, has called on the United Nations Security Council and the African Union to clarify whether they will continue to remain silent over what he described as the unlawful use of merc
title_en: Nduhungirehe Questions UN and AU Over Alleged Use of Mercenaries in DRC
excerpt_en: Kigali February 11, 2026 - Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation, Olivier Nduhungirehe, has called on the United Nations Security Council and the African Union to clarify whether they will continue to remain silent over what he described as the unlawful use of merc
body_en:
Kigali February 11, 2026 - Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation, Olivier Nduhungirehe, has called on the United Nations Security Council and the African Union to clarify whether they will continue to remain silent over what he described as the unlawful use of mercenaries by the government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
His remarks follow reports that American security contractor Erik Prince deployed personnel to South Kivu to assist Congolese forces in efforts to retake Uvira from the M23/AFC coalition. The contractors were reportedly involved in operating drone systems during military operations.
In a statement released by his ministry, Nduhungirehe argued that the recruitment and use of mercenaries constitute a violation of international law. He cited the 1977 OAU Convention for the Elimination of Mercenarism in Africa, adopted in Libreville, and the 1989 International Convention against the Recruitment, Use, Financing and Training of Mercenaries, adopted by the UN General Assembly, both of which prohibit such practices.
“Through the repeated use of foreign mercenaries, the DRC government is violating the norms of the international community,” the minister said, accusing Kinshasa of disregarding binding continental and international legal frameworks.
He further questioned whether international institutions would continue to observe what he described as ongoing violations. “Will the UN Security Council, the African Union and the international community in general continue to remain silent while these international laws are being violated?” he asked.
The Congolese government has previously faced allegations of relying on foreign fighters in its conflict with the AFC/M23. Such accusations intensified after the armed group captured Goma, where European contractors — reportedly including Romanian nationals — were seen withdrawing before returning to their home countries.
Following those developments, Kinshasa is said to have turned to Erik Prince for additional security support, a move that has further heightened regional diplomatic tensions amid the ongoing crisis in eastern Congo.

title: Rwanda Criticizes Belgian MP Over Meeting With Paul Rusesabagina
excerpt: Kigali Rwanda February 10, 2026 - Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation, Olivier Nduhungirehe, has condemned Belgian lawmaker Lydia Mutyebele Ngoi after she publicly expressed support for Paul Rusesabagina, who was convicted in Rwanda on terrorism-related charges.
title_en: Rwanda Criticizes Belgian MP Over Meeting With Paul Rusesabagina
excerpt_en: Kigali Rwanda February 10, 2026 - Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation, Olivier Nduhungirehe, has condemned Belgian lawmaker Lydia Mutyebele Ngoi after she publicly expressed support for Paul Rusesabagina, who was convicted in Rwanda on terrorism-related charges.
body_en:
Kigali Rwanda February 10, 2026 - Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation, Olivier Nduhungirehe, has condemned Belgian lawmaker Lydia Mutyebele Ngoi after she publicly expressed support for Paul Rusesabagina, who was convicted in Rwanda on terrorism-related charges.
On February 9, Mutyebele announced she had received Rusesabagina at the Belgian Parliament in Brussels, describing him as “a powerful voice for human rights” and thanking him for supporting the Democratic Republic of the Congo in its fight against the M23/AFC alliance, which she accused of seeking control of mineral resources.
In response, Nduhungirehe posted a list of civilians killed by the FLN, the armed group linked to Rusesabagina, arguing that praising him disregards victims of attacks carried out in southwestern Rwanda.
“Fighting for dignity clearly means supporting criminals convicted of terrorism,” the minister wrote, criticizing what he described as indifference toward victims of the FLN’s violence.
Rusesabagina — a former head of the MRCD coalition — was arrested in Kigali in August 2020 and later convicted by Rwanda’s High Court chamber for international crimes for terrorism-related offenses, including backing attacks in 2018 and 2019. He was sentenced to 25 years in prison.
On March 24, 2023, he was released following a presidential pardon granted by President Paul Kagame, after requesting specialized medical treatment. He currently resides in San Antonio, Texas, and holds permanent U.S. residency as well as Belgian citizenship.
The exchange underscores ongoing diplomatic tensions surrounding Rusesabagina’s case, which continues to draw sharply divided reactions among political figures internationally.

excerpt_en: ADDIS ABABA, February 14, 2026 — Justin Nsengiyumva held high-level talks with Richard Hatchett, Director-General of the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI), focusing on strengthening pandemic preparedness and response capacity in Rwanda and across Africa. The
body_en:
ADDIS ABABA, February 14, 2026 — Justin Nsengiyumva held high-level talks with Richard Hatchett, Director-General of the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI), focusing on strengthening pandemic preparedness and response capacity in Rwanda and across Africa.
The meeting took place on the sidelines of the Ordinary Session of the Assembly of Heads of State and Government of the African Union, held on February 14–15, 2026, in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.
Discussions centered on deepening cooperation to enhance the continent’s ability to anticipate and respond to health emergencies, including boosting medical research, strengthening legislative frameworks, and accelerating the production and equitable distribution of vaccines in the event of unexpected outbreaks.
Rwanda has positioned itself as an emerging hub for biomedical innovation and vaccine manufacturing, aligning with broader continental efforts to reduce reliance on external supply chains during global health crises.
On February 15, Prime Minister Nsengiyumva is also expected to participate in a session of the African Union High-Level Ad Hoc Committee on South Sudan, a body established to promote political dialogue, unity, and lasting peace in South Sudan.
The Prime Minister’s engagements in Addis Ababa reflect Rwanda’s continued commitment to continental solidarity, health security, and regional stability.

title: MONUSCO Chief Urges Reopening of Goma Airport
excerpt: GOMA, February 12, 2026 — Vivian van de Perre, Acting Head of the United Nations Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, visited Goma for the first time in over a year to call for the reopening of Goma airport. She arrived by helicopter on the morning of February 12, mar
title_en: MONUSCO Chief Urges Reopening of Goma Airport
excerpt_en: GOMA, February 12, 2026 — Vivian van de Perre, Acting Head of the United Nations Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, visited Goma for the first time in over a year to call for the reopening of Goma airport. She arrived by helicopter on the morning of February 12, mar
body_en:
GOMA, February 12, 2026 — Vivian van de Perre, Acting Head of the United Nations Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, visited Goma for the first time in over a year to call for the reopening of Goma airport. She arrived by helicopter on the morning of February 12, marking the first use of the airport since the AFC/M23 coalition took control of the city in late January 2025.
The visit aimed to coordinate with stakeholders, including members of the Great Lakes region community, in preparation for ceasefire monitoring operations in Uvira Territory. The UN Security Council has mandated MONUSCO to monitor the ceasefire between the DRC Government and AFC/M23, in collaboration with the regional EJVM.
Van de Perre said:
“I would like to remind you that more than a year ago, on January 26, 2025, I was on the last plane to land at Goma airport. Today, I was on the first helicopter to land here. I hope this marks the gradual reopening of the airport for the benefit of the population.”
On February 10, 2026, Jean-Pierre Lacroix, UN Under-Secretary-General for Peacekeeping Operations, announced that MONUSCO would use Goma airport for ceasefire monitoring operations, adding that surveillance drones would first be deployed from the airport to assess the security situation in Uvira before troops arrive.

title: Rwanda Receives 161 Returnees from DRC
excerpt: RUBAVU Rwanda, February 10, 2026 — Rwanda on Tuesday welcomed 161 citizens repatriated from the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where they had been living in displacement after reportedly being held by the FDLR. The returnees — 110 children, 38 women, and 13 men — crossed into
title_en: Rwanda Receives 161 Returnees from DRC
excerpt_en: RUBAVU Rwanda, February 10, 2026 — Rwanda on Tuesday welcomed 161 citizens repatriated from the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where they had been living in displacement after reportedly being held by the FDLR. The returnees — 110 children, 38 women, and 13 men — crossed into
body_en:
RUBAVU Rwanda, February 10, 2026 — Rwanda on Tuesday welcomed 161 citizens repatriated from the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where they had been living in displacement after reportedly being held by the FDLR.
The returnees — 110 children, 38 women, and 13 men — crossed into Rwanda through the La Corniche main border post, linking Rubavu with Goma. Upon arrival, they were received by local officials, including Prosper Mulindwa, Mayor of Rubavu District.
They were immediately transported to a temporary transit center in Kijote, located in Nyabihu District, where they are undergoing short-term orientation and reintegration support.
The repatriation followed resolutions adopted during a tripartite meeting between Rwanda, the DRC and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees held in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, on July 24, 2025. Prior to their return, the group had been residing in a temporary camp in Goma, after fleeing various parts of eastern Congo.
Addressing the returnees, Mayor Mulindwa questioned why any Rwandan should still consider themselves refugees, stating that Rwanda has abolished refugee status for its nationals and guarantees protection to its citizens.
“A person who remains outside the country believing they are a refugee is pursuing a losing cause,” he said, urging them to contact others still in eastern Congo and encourage them to return home.
Among the returnees was Nyiransabimana Ancille, 64, who said she fled Rwanda in 1994 and has now returned to the former Mutura Commune, expressing readiness to contribute to local development.
Authorities stated that once the returnees receive their national identity documents, they will receive government reintegration assistance. Adults over 18 are to be granted $188, minors under 18 will receive $113, and each individual will also be provided with essential food supplies valued at 45,000 Rwandan Francs to support their transition back into normal life.
The repatriation marks another step in ongoing regional efforts to facilitate voluntary returns and reduce the presence of Rwandan nationals in armed groups operating in eastern Congo.

title: DRC Distributes Cash to Soldiers and Wazalendo Amid Ongoing Battles
excerpt: South Kivu, DRC – February 21, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government has begun distributing cash payments to its national army soldiers and Wazalendo fighters actively engaged against the AFC/M23 coalition in South Kivu province. The distribution started on 11
title_en: DRC Distributes Cash to Soldiers and Wazalendo Amid Ongoing Battles
excerpt_en: South Kivu, DRC – February 21, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government has begun distributing cash payments to its national army soldiers and Wazalendo fighters actively engaged against the AFC/M23 coalition in South Kivu province. The distribution started on 11
body_en:
South Kivu, DRC – February 21, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government has begun distributing cash payments to its national army soldiers and Wazalendo fighters actively engaged against the AFC/M23 coalition in South Kivu province.
The distribution started on 11 February 2026, following a visit by a Ministry of Defense team to Uvira on February 10. According to reports, each DRC soldier received $400, while Wazalendo fighters were given $200 each.
The Ministry’s team was reportedly divided into six groups to monitor payments in Uvira, the Rusizi Valley, Baraka, Fizi, Minembwe, and Makobola.
The cash distribution follows AFC/M23’s withdrawal from Uvira in January and coincides with the DRC government’s intensified efforts to reclaim lost territory. Governor Jean-Jacques Purusi Sadiki, appointed to South Kivu province, reiterated that President Félix Tshisekedi intends to retake Kamanyola, Bukavu, Goma, and Bunagana, emphasizing that the army would advance in the coming days.
Since late January, clashes have escalated across South Kivu, including Sange, Mukoko, Gakenke, Point-Zéro, Rugezi, Biziba, Kundondo, Mitamba, and Kirungwa. On 17 February, DRC and Wazalendo forces attacked AFC/M23 positions in the Mulenge and Lemera highlands, supported by Burundian troops. On 18 February, coalition forces targeted MRDP-Twirwaneho positions in Minembwe commune, while AFC/M23 positions near the Lemera football stadium were also attacked.
These operations have involved heavy weaponry, warplanes, and drones, despite ongoing regional and international diplomatic efforts to halt fighting.
Although President Tshisekedi accepted the principle of a ceasefire proposed by Angola on 13 February, attacks on AFC/M23, Twirwaneho positions, and civilian homes continued before and after the proposed date.
Political analysts suggest that Tshisekedi’s strategy—simultaneously escalating military operations while showing readiness for dialogue—is aimed at consolidating the DRC government’s leverage ahead of potential peace talks. They urge regional and international mediators to take concrete steps to curb violence rather than relying on declarations alone.
CONCLUSION
This period was marked by a complex interplay of escalating military operations and high-stakes diplomacy in the Great Lakes region. Although President Félix Tshisekedi of the DRC publicly accepted an Angola-brokered ceasefire scheduled for 18 February 2026, its effectiveness remained uncertain as military actions—including drone strikes and airstrikes—continued against AFC/M23 and Twirwaneho positions. Rwanda expressed skepticism about Kinshasa’s commitment to peace, citing the DRC’s ongoing use of heavy artillery, airstrikes, and foreign mercenaries.
Security concerns remained deep-rooted. Rwanda, supported by members of the U.S. Congress, highlighted the DRC’s alleged continued cooperation with the FDLR, a group linked to the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi. title: Nyarugabo Warns Tshisekedi and Ndayishimiye Over Civilian Deaths in Minembwe
excerpt: February 9, 2026 – Lawyer and former Minister of Economy and Senator Moïse Nyarugabo has issued a stark warning to President Félix Tshisekedi of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and his Burundian counterpart Evariste Ndayishimiye, declaring that they will be held accountable
title_en: Nyarugabo Warns Tshisekedi and Ndayishimiye Over Civilian Deaths in Minembwe
excerpt_en: February 9, 2026 – Lawyer and former Minister of Economy and Senator Moïse Nyarugabo has issued a stark warning to President Félix Tshisekedi of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and his Burundian counterpart Evariste Ndayishimiye, declaring that they will be held accountable
body_en:
February 9, 2026 – Lawyer and former Minister of Economy and Senator Moïse Nyarugabo has issued a stark warning to President Félix Tshisekedi of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and his Burundian counterpart Evariste Ndayishimiye, declaring that they will be held accountable for the blood of innocent civilians.
According to Nyarugabo, since the early hours of February 8, 2026, multiple drones deployed by the DRC and Burundi have targeted villages of the Banyamulenge in the Minembwe commune while residents were asleep, causing deaths and injuries.
“These drones have returned repeatedly, firing during both day and night. Their bombs and long-range gunfire have caused casualties in villages including Bicumbi, Mutunda, Ruhemba, and Karongi,” Nyarugabo said.
He added that these attacks are part of a series of assaults by the DRC-Burundi military alliance, which have occurred in areas such as Rugezi, Rwitsankuku, Baruta, Point-Zéro, Mukoko, Gakenke, Biziba, and Runundu over the past days.
“I condemn these acts of genocide in Minembwe and against the Banyamulenge, carried out by Mr. Tshisekedi and the Kinshasa government, alongside his accomplice Mr. Evariste Ndayishimiye and the Burundian government. You will be held accountable for the blood of these innocents, one way or another,” he warned.
The Chairperson of the African Union Commission (AU), Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, recently condemned a drone attack by the AFC/M23 alliance on the DRC military base at Bangoka Airport in Kisangani. The AFC/M23 stated that the base was being used by the DRC army to plan drone attacks on their positions and civilian areas.
Nyarugabo urged AU Chairperson Mahmoud Ali Youssouf to remain impartial and to condemn the crimes committed by the DRC government, including the use of mercenaries, which he described as violations of AU principles.

title: Before U.S. Congress, Byamungu Says DRC Must Address Internal Failures Instead of Blaming Rwanda
excerpt: WASHINGTON, D.C., February 11, 2026 — Appearing before members of the U.S. Congress, Umunye-Congo researcher Christian-Géraud Neema Byamungu argued that the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) should not place primary blame on Rwanda for its persistent instability, warning that su
title_en: Before U.S. Congress, Byamungu Says DRC Must Address Internal Failures Instead of Blaming Rwanda
excerpt_en: WASHINGTON, D.C., February 11, 2026 — Appearing before members of the U.S. Congress, Umunye-Congo researcher Christian-Géraud Neema Byamungu argued that the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) should not place primary blame on Rwanda for its persistent instability, warning that su
body_en:
WASHINGTON, D.C., February 11, 2026 — Appearing before members of the U.S. Congress, Umunye-Congo researcher Christian-Géraud Neema Byamungu argued that the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) should not place primary blame on Rwanda for its persistent instability, warning that such an approach risks overlooking the country’s deeper structural problems.
Byamungu told lawmakers that focusing solely on Kigali would be “like treating a disease with the wrong medicine.” While acknowledging accusations that Rwanda has undermined security in eastern Congo, he stressed that multiple armed groups operating within the DRC are major drivers of violence.
“Stopping Rwanda alone will not solve the problem of armed groups in the DRC such as the ADF,” he said, referring to the Allied Democratic Forces, which has been blamed for deadly attacks in the east. “The ADF kills hundreds of people almost every week, but there is little mention of CODECO, Red Tabara, the Wazalendo, or the Mobondo militia near Kinshasa.”
Byamungu further emphasized that externalizing responsibility would not address what he described as chronic poor governance, misappropriation of resources, and weak state institutions. According to him, these longstanding deficiencies have enabled armed groups to flourish for more than two decades.
“It will not solve the problem of poor governance, incompetent institutions, and the systemic weaknesses that allow these groups to grow,” he stated. “If these root causes remain unaddressed, insecurity will return, as it has repeatedly over the past 20 years.”
The researcher also challenged the widely held assumption that precious minerals are the principal driver of violence in the DRC. While acknowledging their role in criminal networks, he argued that many conflicts stem from communal tensions, disputes over traditional leadership, and the rise of self-defense groups formed in response to state failures.
“For many years, insecurity in the DRC has been caused by reasons other than precious metals,” Byamungu said. “Resources are sometimes used for criminal activities, but they are not the primary cause of the crisis.”
He concluded by urging U.S. policymakers to adopt a more comprehensive approach to the Congolese crisis—one that not only seeks to end current conflicts but also prevents future ones. Key stakeholders, he noted, must include civil society organizations, religious institutions, and church leaders, whose involvement he described as essential for sustainable peace.
Byamungu’s remarks come amid heightened diplomatic attention on the Great Lakes region, as Washington reassesses its engagement strategy in Central Africa.

title: First Epilepsy Surgery Successfully Performed in Rwanda
excerpt: KIGALI, February 9, 2026 — Doctors at Kigali University Teaching Hospital have carried out Rwanda’s first epilepsy surgery, marking a major step forward in specialized neurological care in the country. The procedure began on Monday with the operation of a 39-year-old patient who
title_en: First Epilepsy Surgery Successfully Performed in Rwanda
excerpt_en: KIGALI, February 9, 2026 — Doctors at Kigali University Teaching Hospital have carried out Rwanda’s first epilepsy surgery, marking a major step forward in specialized neurological care in the country. The procedure began on Monday with the operation of a 39-year-old patient who
body_en:
KIGALI, February 9, 2026 — Doctors at Kigali University Teaching Hospital have carried out Rwanda’s first epilepsy surgery, marking a major step forward in specialized neurological care in the country.
The procedure began on Monday with the operation of a 39-year-old patient who had suffered from epilepsy for 15 years despite continuous medication. The intervention was performed by a local medical team working alongside visiting foreign specialists.
Until now, patients requiring this type of treatment were often referred abroad — mainly to India — due to the lack of local surgical capacity.
The operation was led by neurosurgeon Sylvie Musoni Inyange, who explained that scans showed the seizures originated from a specific area on the left side of the brain.
“We removed a small part of the brain where the MRI indicated the source of the epilepsy,” she said.
Doctors reported the patient had been collapsing about twice a week and had become physically weakened. Following surgery, the treatment offers roughly an 85% chance of recovery, with the possibility of reducing or completely stopping medication.
Medical specialists describe epilepsy as abnormal brain activity causing symptoms such as loss of consciousness, repeated falls, involuntary movements, temporary paralysis and sometimes loss of bladder control.
Health professionals say the new capability represents a significant breakthrough for Rwanda’s healthcare system, as some patients could not be effectively treated with medication alone and traveling abroad was financially and logistically difficult.
Family members welcomed the development, saying the condition had affected the patient since childhood and required frequent travel to Kigali for care.
The hospital indicated that expanding specialized surgery locally will reduce medical evacuation costs and improve long-term treatment access for patients across the country.

title: Rwanda Police Wins Bronze at Dubai Counter-Terrorism Competition
excerpt: DUBAI, February 11, 2026 — The Rwanda National Police SWAT Team I secured a bronze medal at the UAE SWAT Challenge, an international counter-terrorism competition held in Dubai, bringing together 109 police and military teams from around the world. The event tested tactical skill
title_en: Rwanda Police Wins Bronze at Dubai Counter-Terrorism Competition
excerpt_en: DUBAI, February 11, 2026 — The Rwanda National Police SWAT Team I secured a bronze medal at the UAE SWAT Challenge, an international counter-terrorism competition held in Dubai, bringing together 109 police and military teams from around the world. The event tested tactical skill
body_en:
DUBAI, February 11, 2026 — The Rwanda National Police SWAT Team I secured a bronze medal at the UAE SWAT Challenge, an international counter-terrorism competition held in Dubai, bringing together 109 police and military teams from around the world.
The event tested tactical skills across five categories, including obstacle courses requiring strength, teamwork, wall-climbing, and navigation through complex terrain. During the final on February 11, teams from 48 countries tackled 19 demanding obstacles in coordinated five-member formations.
RNP SWAT Team I completed the course in 3 minutes 40 seconds, earning third place in the final challenge and ultimately finishing sixth overall with 484 points.
Rwanda fielded two additional teams:
RNP SWAT Team II placed 14th in the final and 29th overall with 386 points.
The Rwanda Defence Force SOF Team finished 15th in the final and 37th overall with 361 points.
In the overall standings, Kazakhstan Police Team C won the gold medal with 536 points, followed by Kazakhstan A with silver, while China Police Team C also placed on the podium.
The competition showcased Rwanda’s growing capacity in specialized counter-terrorism operations and its expanding presence in international security exercises.
