title: South Africa Announces Withdrawal of Troops from Eastern DRC
excerpt: KINSHASA, February 10, 2026 — South Africa has announced it will withdraw its troops from the UN peacekeeping mission in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, citing the need to consolidate its military forces, financial constraints, limited operational results, and a renewed
title_en: South Africa Announces Withdrawal of Troops from Eastern DRC
excerpt_en: KINSHASA, February 10, 2026 — South Africa has announced it will withdraw its troops from the UN peacekeeping mission in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, citing the need to consolidate its military forces, financial constraints, limited operational results, and a renewed
body_en:
KINSHASA, February 10, 2026 — South Africa has announced it will withdraw its troops from the UN peacekeeping mission in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, citing the need to consolidate its military forces, financial constraints, limited operational results, and a renewed focus on domestic priorities.
The troops are part of MONUSCO, where South Africa has maintained between 700 and 800 soldiers, primarily within the Force Intervention Brigade (FIB) — a unit authorized to conduct offensive operations against armed groups.
The withdrawal, announced on February 8, is scheduled to take place gradually from the first quarter of 2026 through December 2026.
While Pretoria has officially framed the move as strategic and financial, critics argue the decision is also influenced by broader political and economic interests, particularly in mineral-rich regions of eastern Congo. South African deployments have largely been concentrated in North Kivu, South Kivu, and Ituri — provinces known for deposits of gold, coltan, gas, and copper.
Since the 1990s, South Africa has publicly justified its military engagements across the continent as part of efforts to restore peace and stability. However, observers note that troop deployments have frequently coincided with areas of significant natural resource wealth.
Allegations have also surfaced over the years accusing certain elements within the mission of involvement in illegal mining activities, including the illicit trade of gold and coltan. Some reports claim that military-controlled airports were used in mineral transactions and that intermediaries facilitated cross-border trading networks. These allegations have not led to formal international prosecutions but continue to fuel debate over the economic dimensions of foreign troop deployments.
South Africa remains one of the largest contributors to MONUSCO’s Force Intervention Brigade, whose mandate differs from traditional UN peacekeeping contingents by allowing proactive combat operations against armed groups.
The gradual withdrawal marks a significant shift in regional security dynamics, raising questions about the future balance of forces in eastern Congo and the long-term sustainability of international stabilization efforts.

title: RDF and UPDF Strengthen Border Security to Boost Regional Stability
excerpt: Musanze, Rwanda, February 20, 2026 – The Rwanda Defence Forces (RDF) and Uganda People’s Defence Forces (UPDF) concluded the seventh meeting of the Heads of Defence Forces along the shared border, reaffirming their commitment to enhance border security and promote regional stabil
title_en: RDF and UPDF Strengthen Border Security to Boost Regional Stability
excerpt_en: Musanze, Rwanda, February 20, 2026 – The Rwanda Defence Forces (RDF) and Uganda People’s Defence Forces (UPDF) concluded the seventh meeting of the Heads of Defence Forces along the shared border, reaffirming their commitment to enhance border security and promote regional stabil
body_en:
Musanze, Rwanda, February 20, 2026 – The Rwanda Defence Forces (RDF) and Uganda People’s Defence Forces (UPDF) concluded the seventh meeting of the Heads of Defence Forces along the shared border, reaffirming their commitment to enhance border security and promote regional stability.
The three-day talks, held in Musanze District, reviewed progress on decisions from the sixth meeting in Kabale, Uganda (September 30 – October 2, 2025), and addressed ongoing challenges along the border.
Key Focus Areas
Strengthening border security measures
Combating illegal crossings, human trafficking, illicit trade, livestock theft, fraud, and impersonation
Coordinating import and export monitoring, including illicit liquor control
Both militaries emphasized the importance of continued dialogue, joint activities, and public participation through Civil-Military Interaction (CIMIC) programs, environmental protection initiatives, and joint exercises.
Statements from Military Leaders
Maj. Gen. Ruki Karusisi, Commander of the RDF 5th Division, praised the professionalism, trust, and constructive atmosphere, noting that the discussions strengthened the resolve of both sides to maintain peace and security along the border.
Maj. Gen. Paul Muhanguzi, Commander of the UPDF 2nd Land Division, affirmed Uganda’s commitment to implement the meeting’s decisions and to continue addressing emerging border issues. He also thanked the leadership of both countries for their guidance in enhancing bilateral military cooperation.
The meeting underscores the strong partnership between Rwanda and Uganda, highlighting continued efforts to secure borders, foster regional stability, and prevent cross-border crimes.

title: Massive Human Rights Violations Reported in Azawad and Central Mali – 2025
excerpt: Bamako, February 5, 2026 – The 2025 annual report of a leading human rights monitoring organization reveals a disturbing surge in human rights violations in Azawad (northern Mali) and parts of central Mali, documenting 374 serious incidents committed amid a non-international arme
title_en: Massive Human Rights Violations Reported in Azawad and Central Mali – 2025
excerpt_en: Bamako, February 5, 2026 – The 2025 annual report of a leading human rights monitoring organization reveals a disturbing surge in human rights violations in Azawad (northern Mali) and parts of central Mali, documenting 374 serious incidents committed amid a non-international arme
body_en:
Bamako, February 5, 2026 – The 2025 annual report of a leading human rights monitoring organization reveals a disturbing surge in human rights violations in Azawad (northern Mali) and parts of central Mali, documenting 374 serious incidents committed amid a non-international armed conflict.
The report attributes most violations to the Malian Armed Forces (FAMa) operating alongside foreign armed actors, including Wagner Group and later Africa Corps. Documented abuses include:
Extrajudicial killings, enforced disappearances, and arbitrary arrests.
Torture and the destruction and looting of civilian property.
Drone strikes causing hundreds of casualties, including women and children, contributing to a reported 553 deaths.
The economic, social, and environmental impact is equally alarming: over 2,600 civilian properties have been destroyed or looted, and deliberate forest fires have further endangered vulnerable communities. While sexual violence remains under-documented due to security challenges, the report classifies it as a war crime, highlighting the gravity of the abuses.
In response to these systematic violations of international humanitarian law, the organization calls for:
Independent investigations.
Immediate cessation of attacks on civilians.
A strong fight against impunity.
The report urges both Malian authorities and the international community to take urgent action to protect civilians, ensure justice, and restore prospects for lasting peace in Mali.

excerpt: Mopti, February 15, 2026 – The Jama'at Nasr al-Islam wal Muslimin (JNIM) announced that it ambushed a patrol of pro-government militias affiliated with the Malian army on the morning of February 15, 2026, between Sofara and Kouli in the Mopti region. The incident highlights the c
title_en: JNIM Ambushes Pro-Government Militias in Mopti
excerpt_en: Mopti, February 15, 2026 – The Jama'at Nasr al-Islam wal Muslimin (JNIM) announced that it ambushed a patrol of pro-government militias affiliated with the Malian army on the morning of February 15, 2026, between Sofara and Kouli in the Mopti region. The incident highlights the c
body_en:
Mopti, February 15, 2026 – The Jama'at Nasr al-Islam wal Muslimin (JNIM) announced that it ambushed a patrol of pro-government militias affiliated with the Malian army on the morning of February 15, 2026, between Sofara and Kouli in the Mopti region.
The incident highlights the continuing insecurity in central Mali and the persistent operational capabilities of armed extremist groups targeting government-aligned forces.
Conclusion
The period from February 2 to 15, 2026, underscores a Mali defined by a stark tension between diplomatic assertiveness and internal fragility. While the transitional government under General Assimi Goïta continues to promote a vision of sovereign diplomacy and national ownership, the realities on the ground reveal an escalating security crisis and mounting humanitarian challenges.
Key Takeaways
Diplomatic Recalibration: Mali is actively diversifying its international partnerships, consolidating relations with Saudi Arabia, Iran, China, and Japan. At the same time, ties with traditional Western partners, notably the United States, remain contingent on compliance with constitutional benchmarks and clarity regarding foreign military presence.
Security & Humanitarian Crisis: Despite ongoing efforts to neutralize terrorist cells, insurgent groups such as JNIM and ISIS-Sahel continue to display high operational mobility, launching deadly ambushes across the north, center, and even previously stable western and southern regions. The abduction of senior officials and reports of severe food shortages within the military highlight systemic vulnerabilities in national defense structures.
Economic Sovereignty vs. Fragility: The government has undertaken strategic initiatives to secure economic independence, including the launch of a Tier III Data Center and the renewal of gold mining permits. However, these efforts are undermined by a persistent fuel crisis and the ongoing extortion of rural populations through "zakat" and ransom demands by armed groups.
Human Rights Challenges: Reports from 2025 and January 2026 depict a grim situation of systematic violations, including extrajudicial killings and drone strikes. While judicial reforms have been pursued, the detention of journalists and allegations of military-involved massacres reveal a complex road toward accountability and rule of law.
Ultimately, Mali stands at a crossroads. The government’s pursuit of absolute sovereignty is being rigorously tested by a resilient insurgency and a worsening humanitarian landscape. The success of the “Mali Kura” vision will hinge on the state’s ability to translate diplomatic ambition into concrete security and economic stability for its citizens.
By Maïga Sidi Bonkana
(Boukari Zankey Sidi)
Jeff Buleli

body_en:
Bamako, February 5, 2026 – Youssouf Sissoko, editor-in-chief of the daily newspaper L’Alternance, was placed in pretrial detention on Thursday in Bamako, facing prosecution for “spreading false information,” “damaging the reputation of the state,” and “insulting a foreign head of state.”
According to the Association of Private Press Publishers (ASSEP), the arrest follows the publication of an article in the February 2 edition of the newspaper.
The journalist’s hearing is scheduled for March 9, 2026, while the charges against him continue to raise concerns over freedom of expression and press freedom in Mali.
In a statement, ASSEP said it is closely monitoring the case and reaffirmed its commitment to the constitutional protections for freedom of the press enshrined in the July 22, 2023 Constitution.

title_en: Assimi Goïta Reaffirms Mali’s Sovereign Diplomacy During New Year’s Diplomatic Ceremony
excerpt_en: Koulouba, February 10, 2026 – President of the Transition, General Assimi Goïta, received the Diplomatic Corps accredited to Mali on Tuesday, February 10, 2026, at the Koulouba Palace for the traditional New Year’s greetings ceremony. In his address, President Goïta reaffirmed th
body_en:
Koulouba, February 10, 2026 – President of the Transition, General Assimi Goïta, received the Diplomatic Corps accredited to Mali on Tuesday, February 10, 2026, at the Koulouba Palace for the traditional New Year’s greetings ceremony.
In his address, President Goïta reaffirmed the principles of sovereign diplomacy, emphasizing mutual respect, freedom of strategic choice, and responsibility. He declared 2026 a year of constructive dialogue and sincere partnerships, welcoming the strengthening of political dialogue and new diplomatic accreditations, which highlight growing interest in Mali and the Confederation of Sahel States (CESA).
On security, the Head of State commended the Defense and Security Forces for confronting the asymmetric threat, stressing that territorial security is essential for the restoration of state authority and essential social services. He also denounced disinformation targeting the countries of the Economic and Social Affairs Group (ESA) and reaffirmed Mali’s adherence to UN principles, including non-interference and respect for territorial integrity.
Domestically, President Goïta reiterated ongoing state reforms under the Vision “Mali Kura ɲɛtaasira ka bɛn san 2063 ma” and the National Strategy for Emergence and Sustainable Development 2024-2033. He announced that 2026-2027 would focus on education and culture, while emphasizing endogenous solutions, energy sovereignty, and structuring investments to support sustainable development and shared progress.

Kayes, January 29, 2026 – The JNIM (Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims) claimed responsibility for an ambush on a Malian army convoy escorting tanker trucks between Diboli and Kayes in the Kayes region on Thursday, January 29, 2026.
According to the group, the attack resulted in:
2 Malian soldiers killed.
Four military vehicles set on fire.
Seizure of a motorcycle, various weapons, and a large quantity of ammunition.
Approximately 50 tanker trucks burned, aggravating the country’s energy crisis.
15 drivers killed in the ambush.
The incident underscores the intense security threats facing both military personnel and civilians in western Mali.

title_en: Mali Co-Chairs National Steering Committee for Peacebuilding Investments
excerpt_en: Bamako, February 12, 2026 – Abdoulaye Diop, Malian Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, and Lieutenant General Ismaël Wagué, Minister of State for Reconciliation, Peace, and National Cohesion, co-chaired the National Steering Committee for Peacebuilding Inve
body_en:
Bamako, February 12, 2026 – Abdoulaye Diop, Malian Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, and Lieutenant General Ismaël Wagué, Minister of State for Reconciliation, Peace, and National Cohesion, co-chaired the National Steering Committee for Peacebuilding Investment Mechanisms in Mali on Thursday, February 12, 2026, in Bamako, with the UN Resident Coordinator in Mali in attendance.
The session reviewed projects under the Peacebuilding Fund and the Women’s Peace and Humanitarian Action Fund, bringing together technical and financial partners, including the Chargé d’affaires of Canada, representatives of UN Women, the United Nations Population Fund, and members of civil society.
Minister Diop highlighted the importance of aligning all projects with national priorities and the country’s strategic development vision, in line with new principles guiding public action. The UN Resident Coordinator praised the government’s leadership in peacebuilding, noting the structured and inclusive nature of Mali’s framework.
Minister Wagué welcomed progress in project implementation, while Committee members recommended intensifying government-led interventions, with strengthened operational monitoring and field visits, to sustainably improve the living conditions of the population.

title: Ministry of National Entrepreneurship Signs MoU with UNHCR to Support Refugees and Displaced Persons
excerpt: Bamako, February 6, 2026 – Minister Oumou Sall Seck, head of the Ministry of National Entrepreneurship, Employment and Vocational Training (MENEFP), presided over the signing of a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), fo
title_en: Ministry of National Entrepreneurship Signs MoU with UNHCR to Support Refugees and Displaced Persons
excerpt_en: Bamako, February 6, 2026 – Minister Oumou Sall Seck, head of the Ministry of National Entrepreneurship, Employment and Vocational Training (MENEFP), presided over the signing of a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), fo
body_en:
Bamako, February 6, 2026 – Minister Oumou Sall Seck, head of the Ministry of National Entrepreneurship, Employment and Vocational Training (MENEFP), presided over the signing of a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), focusing on the socio-professional integration and capacity building of refugees, internally displaced persons (IDPs), and stateless persons in Mali.
The ceremony brought together UNHCR Resident Representative Pierre Camara, Ministry staff, and UNHCR personnel.
Supporting Vulnerable Populations
UNHCR highlighted that over 280,000 refugees reside in Mali, 58% of whom are women, and contribute to national development. The organization emphasized the importance of vocational training, micro-enterprise creation, and socio-professional integration in empowering displaced populations.
Minister Oumou Sall Seck commended UNHCR’s pragmatism and recalled Mali’s commitment, under President Assimi Goïta and Prime Minister Abdoulaye Maïga, to protect displaced persons while creating conditions for voluntary return or integration. She underscored the need for coordinated action with national and international stakeholders to deliver effective and sustainable solutions.
Key Areas of Cooperation
The MoU will guide three years of collaborative initiatives, including:
Institutional support for state structures in entrepreneurship, employment, and vocational training;
Inclusion of refugees, IDPs, and stateless persons in national vocational training and employability programs;
Enhanced cooperation to mobilize funding from development partners and financial institutions.
The Minister emphasized that this partnership is rooted in Mali’s cultural concepts of “Maya” and “Diatiguiya”, reflecting collective responsibility toward vulnerable populations. She described the MoU as the foundation for future programs aimed at empowering displaced persons and integrating them into Mali’s socio-economic fabric.
The memorandum is renewable every three years by mutual agreement, establishing a long-term framework for sustainable cooperation.

Mopti, February 4, 2026 – The JNIM (Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims) claimed responsibility for an attack on a pro-army militia post near Kéngué, in the Mopti region, resulting in 5 fighters killed and the seizure of weapons, including machine guns and hunting rifles.

title: Mali Celebrates Emperor Naruhito’s Birthday, Highlights Strengthening Ties with Japan
excerpt: Bamako, February 12, 2026 – Abdoulaye Diop, Malian Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, participated in celebrations marking the birthday of His Majesty Emperor Naruhito of Japan on Thursday, February 12, 2026, in Bamako, at the invitation of Japanese Ambass
title_en: Mali Celebrates Emperor Naruhito’s Birthday, Highlights Strengthening Ties with Japan
excerpt_en: Bamako, February 12, 2026 – Abdoulaye Diop, Malian Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, participated in celebrations marking the birthday of His Majesty Emperor Naruhito of Japan on Thursday, February 12, 2026, in Bamako, at the invitation of Japanese Ambass
body_en:
Bamako, February 12, 2026 – Abdoulaye Diop, Malian Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, participated in celebrations marking the birthday of His Majesty Emperor Naruhito of Japan on Thursday, February 12, 2026, in Bamako, at the invitation of Japanese Ambassador Yukuo Murata. The event was also attended by the President of the Economic, Social, Environmental and Cultural Council.
On behalf of Mali’s highest authorities, Minister Diop conveyed wishes for health, happiness, and prosperity to His Majesty, the Imperial Family, and the Government and People of Japan. He praised the Japanese model, noting its harmonious integration of culture, technology, and modernity, and its focus on human capital development, particularly as Mali marks 2026-2027 as the Years of Education and Culture.
Both countries also highlighted the achievements of Professor Abdoulaye Djimdé, recipient of the Hideyo Noguchi Prize for Africa in medical research, recognizing his contribution to the fight against malaria.
The event further underscored the strengthening of bilateral cooperation between Mali and Japan, with ongoing projects in security, agriculture, health, education, access to drinking water, justice, and infrastructure. Minister Diop concluded by commending the resilience of the Malian people amid ongoing complex challenges.

Bamako, February 4, 2026 – Mali’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, Abdoulaye Diop, received the newly appointed Country Director of the African Development Bank (AfDB) in Mali, Cédric Achille Mbeng Mezui, and the new Resident Coordinator of the United Nations system in Mali, Hanaa Fikry Ahmed Singer, during an official audience on Wednesday in Bamako.
The two officials were present to submit their letters of accreditation.
Focus on Multilateral Cooperation
Following formalities, discussions centered on the evolving national context and the prospects for strengthened multilateral cooperation. Minister Diop highlighted what he described as a paradigm shift in Mali’s governance, marked by renewed national ownership and revised principles guiding public action and partnerships.
He outlined Mali’s strategic development vision, which prioritizes structural transformation of the economy and enhanced mobilization of domestic resources to finance sustainable and integrated development.
Alignment with National Priorities
The minister emphasized the importance of multilateral cooperation that is better aligned with national priorities, conducted in a spirit of mutual respect, ongoing consultation, and under Malian leadership.
For their part, the AfDB Country Director and the UN Resident Coordinator reaffirmed their commitment to supporting Mali’s development agenda, in line with their respective cooperation frameworks, with the objective of improving the living conditions of the Malian population.
Social and Health

title_en: Minister Kassogué Visits Victims of Human Trafficking and Launches Fourth Edition
excerpt_en: Bamako, February 12, 2026 – As part of the 4th annual Justice Week, Minister of Justice and Human Rights Mamoudou Kassogué visited the Enda Mali reception center in Boulkassoumbougou-Kouloubléni on Thursday, February 12, 2026, to show the State’s solidarity with victims of human
body_en:
Bamako, February 12, 2026 – As part of the 4th annual Justice Week, Minister of Justice and Human Rights Mamoudou Kassogué visited the Enda Mali reception center in Boulkassoumbougou-Kouloubléni on Thursday, February 12, 2026, to show the State’s solidarity with victims of human trafficking.
During the visit, the Minister toured facilities, including dormitories, restrooms, staff offices, and the courtyard, and listened to poignant testimonies from residents. Deeply moved by accounts of sexual exploitation and fraud, he condemned this “silent tragedy” and promised rigorous sanctions against perpetrators, while commending the remarkable work of partner organizations. He also urged stakeholders to guarantee respect for human dignity in Mali.
Earlier the same day, Minister Kassogué officially launched the fourth edition of Justice Week at the Bamako International Conference Center (CICB). The event brought together government members, technical and financial partners, judicial stakeholders, and other prominent figures, under the theme “Justice in the Era of Implementing and Strengthening Reforms.”
Dr. Aboubacar Sidiki Diarrah, chairman of the organizing committee, highlighted that “there is no growth without reforms, nor reforms without growth.” Established in 2022 by the transitional government, Justice Week aims to bring justice closer to citizens, promote a more efficient public justice system, and restore public trust.
In his address, Minister Kassogué emphasized that justice is no longer a silent institution, underscoring the importance of transparency and accessibility. He added that legal professionals must not lecture citizens if they themselves openly break the law, reaffirming the commitment to a more accessible and reliable justice system for all Malians.

body_en:
Bla, February 4, 2026 – Local sources report a serious cross-border incident in the village of Tourdou, near Bla, in Malian territory, in which ten Mauritanian nationals were reportedly killed in gruesome circumstances.
According to multiple accounts, the victims, from Hassi Alak (Djiguenni district), were grazing livestock when they were allegedly attacked. Witnesses suggest that a unit of the Malian army may be involved. The bodies were reportedly burned and concealed under branches.
Witnesses have identified the herd owner, Cheikhen Ould Embeyarik, and nine of his herders, all from the same village, among the victims. The incident raises serious concerns about security, accountability, and cross-border violence in the region.

Bamako, February 13, 2026 – Abdoulaye Diop, Malian Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, participated in celebrations marking the 47th anniversary of the Islamic Revolution of the Islamic Republic of Iran in Bamako on Friday, February 13, 2026.
On behalf of Mali’s highest authorities, Minister Diop conveyed congratulations and wishes for peace, prosperity, and progress to the President, Government, and people of Iran.
Speaking on Mali’s current challenges in its pursuit of freedom and dignity, he highlighted the shared commitment of both countries to the inalienable right of peoples to preserve national sovereignty and define their development paths without external interference.
Minister Diop also praised Mali-Iran cooperation on major international issues, including:
Respect for territorial integrity
Rejection of the instrumentalization of human rights for political ends
Defense of non-interference
Promotion of a democratic, inclusive, and multipolar multilateral order
Both sides condemned unilateral coercive measures and economic sanctions, labeling them unjustified and counterproductive, and welcomed the strengthening of bilateral cooperation since the first Mali-Iran Joint Commission in Bamako, August 2022.

title: Mali Targets CFA 1.45 Trillion in Government Bond Issuances for 2026
excerpt: Bamako, January 6, 2026 – Mali has unveiled its 2026 government securities issuance calendar, aiming to mobilize 1.45 trillion CFA francs on the regional financial market of the West African Economic and Monetary Union (WAEMU). The program forms part of the government’s strategy
title_en: Mali Targets CFA 1.45 Trillion in Government Bond Issuances for 2026
excerpt_en: Bamako, January 6, 2026 – Mali has unveiled its 2026 government securities issuance calendar, aiming to mobilize 1.45 trillion CFA francs on the regional financial market of the West African Economic and Monetary Union (WAEMU). The program forms part of the government’s strategy
body_en:
Bamako, January 6, 2026 – Mali has unveiled its 2026 government securities issuance calendar, aiming to mobilize 1.45 trillion CFA francs on the regional financial market of the West African Economic and Monetary Union (WAEMU).
The program forms part of the government’s strategy to meet its financing needs through structured, market-based instruments.
According to details presented at the launch ceremony, the annual target is distributed as follows:
340 billion CFA francs in the first quarter
400 billion CFA francs in the second quarter
430 billion CFA francs in the third quarter
280 billion CFA francs in the fourth quarter
Authorities stated that this quarterly allocation is intended to enhance market transparency and allow investors to better plan their participation throughout the year.
Mali Inaugurates Tier III Data Center, Advances Digital Sovereignty
As part of the third edition of Mali’s Digital Week, Minister of Communication, Digital Economy and Administrative Modernization Alhamdou Ag Ilyène officially inaugurated a Tier III Data Center, a strategic infrastructure aimed at strengthening national and regional digital sovereignty.
The ceremony was attended by digital ministers from Niger and Burkina Faso, members of the Confederation of Sahel States (AES).
Designed to meet high international standards, the facility guarantees 99.982% service availability, full redundancy of critical systems, uninterrupted operations during maintenance, and advanced physical and cybersecurity safeguards.
The data center will provide secure hosting for:
Government databases and critical applications
National e-government platforms and public digital services
Future shared digital infrastructure within the AES region
Officials emphasized that the infrastructure will reduce dependence on foreign hosting services, enhance cybersecurity, and create a foundation for the development of artificial intelligence, digital financial services, and sovereign digital platforms.
According to participating ministers, control over national data hosting and processing is essential for protecting sensitive state information and reinforcing independent public decision-making.

title: First Class Graduates from Mali’s New School of Penitentiary Administration
excerpt: Koulikoro, February 13, 2026 – As part of Justice Week, Minister of Justice Mamoudou Kassogué presided over the graduation ceremony for the first class of the Koulikoro School of Penitentiary Administration and Juvenile Detention on Friday, February 13, 2026, marking a historic m

excerpt_en: Koulikoro, February 13, 2026 – As part of Justice Week, Minister of Justice Mamoudou Kassogué presided over the graduation ceremony for the first class of the Koulikoro School of Penitentiary Administration and Juvenile Detention on Friday, February 13, 2026, marking a historic m
body_en:
Koulikoro, February 13, 2026 – As part of Justice Week, Minister of Justice Mamoudou Kassogué presided over the graduation ceremony for the first class of the Koulikoro School of Penitentiary Administration and Juvenile Detention on Friday, February 13, 2026, marking a historic milestone for Mali since independence.
Established in 2023, the school aims to strengthen the staffing and operational capacities of prison personnel, ensuring a balance between security imperatives and respect for human rights.
The inaugural graduating class included 124 recruits, among them 32 women, and was named in honor of Lieutenant Colonel Tiémoko Keïta, an officer who died in the line of duty in Gao in 2021.
After six months of rigorous training combining military discipline and legal instruction, the new officers, under Commander Cheick Ibrahim Cissouma, were officially appointed, symbolizing a commitment to integrity, dedication, and service in the prison administration.

body_en:
Bamako, February 5, 2026 – Strengthening bilateral cooperation in the transport and infrastructure sector was at the center of discussions between Mali’s Minister of Transport and Infrastructure, Dembélé Madina Sissoko, and Li Xiang, Ambassador of the People’s Republic of China to Mali.
The meeting, held Thursday in Bamako, marked the first official exchange between the two officials. Ambassador Li paid a courtesy visit to Minister Sissoko shortly after presenting his credentials to General Assimi Goïta, President of the Transition and Head of State.
Discussions focused on reinforcing the Sino-Malian partnership in key infrastructure projects and exploring avenues to deepen collaboration in transport development, a strategic sector for Mali’s economic growth and regional connectivity.
The engagement reflects the continued dynamism of relations between Mali and China, particularly in infrastructure development and public works.

The luncheon provided a forum for discussion, allowing the Minister of Justice to review the week’s activities and highlight the Ministry’s key achievements over the past year. The opening ceremony included the screening of a documentary showcasing the Ministry’s initiatives for 2025.

Minister Kassogué praised the event’s success, congratulated the national organizing committee, and highlighted ongoing reforms and ambitious prospects for 2026.

Ségou, February 8, 2026 – The Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims (JNIM) announced that it targeted a Malian army armored vehicle with an improvised explosive device (IED) on Sunday morning along the Markala–Ké-Macina road in the Ségou region.
According to the group, the explosion destroyed the military vehicle, marking the second attack in the same area in a short period and highlighting the ongoing threat to this strategic route.

The attack comes amid escalating operations by armed groups in central Mali, particularly in the Ségou region, where Malian forces remain frequently targeted by IED attacks.

title: Mali Launches Steering Committee for EU Technical Cooperation Unit
excerpt: Bamako, February 5, 2026 – Mali officially launched the inaugural session of the Steering Committee of the Technical Cooperation Unit with the European Union (CTC-EU) on Thursday in Bamako. The meeting was chaired by Abdoulaye Diop, Minister of Foreign Affairs and International C
title_en: Mali Launches Steering Committee for EU Technical Cooperation Unit
excerpt_en: Bamako, February 5, 2026 – Mali officially launched the inaugural session of the Steering Committee of the Technical Cooperation Unit with the European Union (CTC-EU) on Thursday in Bamako. The meeting was chaired by Abdoulaye Diop, Minister of Foreign Affairs and International C
body_en:
Bamako, February 5, 2026 – Mali officially launched the inaugural session of the Steering Committee of the Technical Cooperation Unit with the European Union (CTC-EU) on Thursday in Bamako. The meeting was chaired by Abdoulaye Diop, Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, in the presence of the European Union Representative in Mali.
Strengthening National Ownership
Minister Diop emphasized that the establishment of the CTC-EU, financed through the national budget, reflects the commitment of Mali’s highest authorities to ensuring strong national ownership and leadership in the management of cooperation programs with the European Union.
According to the minister, the initiative seeks to enhance coordination, improve oversight of ongoing projects, and maximize the impact of EU-funded programs, particularly in a context requiring greater efficiency in public action.
Reinforcing Institutional Capacity
Diop welcomed the role of the CTC-EU in strengthening the operational capacities of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, enabling it to effectively manage, coordinate, and oversee the full cycle of EU-financed projects and programs in Mali.
He also reaffirmed the Malian government’s commitment to maintaining a constructive and collaborative partnership with the European Union and its Member States, aimed at improving the well-being of the population.
During the session, members of the Steering Committee were tasked with reviewing the draft annual report of the CTC-EU, assessing project implementation, identifying constraints, and outlining prospects to enhance the impact of future interventions.

title_en: WAEMU Grants CFA 100 Million to Mali to Combat Desert Locust Resurgence
excerpt_en: Bamako, February 5, 2026 – Mali has received an exceptional financial contribution of 100 million CFA francs from the Commission of the West African Economic and Monetary Union (WAEMU) to strengthen efforts against the resurgence of the desert locust in the western part of the co
body_en:
Bamako, February 5, 2026 – Mali has received an exceptional financial contribution of 100 million CFA francs from the Commission of the West African Economic and Monetary Union (WAEMU) to strengthen efforts against the resurgence of the desert locust in the western part of the country.
The symbolic check was presented on Thursday at the Ministry of Agriculture by Roberto Alexandre Vieira, WAEMU Commission Representative in Mali, to the Minister of Agriculture, Daniel Siméon Kelema. The funds were subsequently handed over to the National Locust Control Center (CNLCP) during the ceremony.
According to WAEMU’s representative, the special contribution is intended to support the implementation of Mali’s National Locust Risk Response Plan, reinforcing prevention, monitoring, and rapid intervention activities to protect agricultural production.
The initiative reflects regional solidarity within WAEMU and aims to mitigate potential threats to food security posed by desert locust infestations.

February 12, 2026 –The 2025 annual report by the CD-DPA reveals a deteriorating human rights situation in Azawad and parts of central Mali, documenting 374 incidents of serious violations against civilian populations amid a non-international armed conflict.
The report notes a heavy death toll of 553, including many women and children, and attributes the abuses primarily to the Malian Armed Forces (FAMa) operating alongside foreign armed actors, notably Wagner and later the Africa Corps.
Documented violations include torture, arbitrary arrests, enforced disappearances, and the widespread destruction of civilian property, illustrating a systematic pattern of violence in flagrant violation of international humanitarian law.

title_en: Mali Faces Security Collapse Amid Military Junta Rule
excerpt_en: Mali, February 2, 2026 – The military junta in Mali is facing a severe security crisis, with jihadist groups reportedly taking advantage of the government’s inability to protect civilians in the south and west of the country. According to local reports, these armed groups have es
body_en:
Mali, February 2, 2026 – The military junta in Mali is facing a severe security crisis, with jihadist groups reportedly taking advantage of the government’s inability to protect civilians in the south and west of the country.
According to local reports, these armed groups have established agreements with hundreds of villages across the Ségou, Mopti, and Kita regions, while the army struggles to ensure safety even on the outskirts of the capital.

Ségou, February 5, 2026 – Mali’s Minister of Industry and Trade, Moussa Alassane Diallo, officially launched the 2025–2026 sugar campaign on Thursday at the Séribala and Bewani sugar complexes in the Ségou region.
The minister was accompanied by senior officials from his department, including the National Director of Industry and a representative of the National Transitional Council (CNT), alongside regional and local authorities.
Repairs Completed After August Attacks
During a tour of the Séribala industrial facilities, Minister Diallo confirmed that repairs following the attacks last August had been successfully completed. He stated that restoration work was carried out efficiently through the joint mobilization of Malian and Chinese technical teams, underscoring the strength of the bilateral technical partnership.
Assurance on Sugar Availability
The official launch of the campaign comes amid concerns about production disruptions. Authorities reassured the public that industrial operations have resumed normally and that sugar supply will be maintained throughout the campaign.
The event signals the government’s commitment to ensuring continuity in strategic agro-industrial production despite security and logistical challenges.

body_en:
Bamako, February 9, 2026 – As part of the 4th annual Justice Week, Minister of Justice and Human Rights Mamoudou Kassogué presented a consignment of solar equipment and office furniture to the National Human Rights Directorate (DNDH) on Monday, February 9, 2026.
Valued at 33 million CFA francs and funded by the European Union’s Sahel-Mali mission (EUCAP), the support aims to provide the DNDH with energy independence, addressing frequent power outages that have hampered operations since its commissioning in September 2024.

title: U.S. Envoy Raises Conditions for Security Cooperation During Bamako Visit
excerpt: February 3, 2026 – Twenty-four hours after the visit to Bamako by Nick Checker, Director of the Bureau of African Affairs at the U.S. State Department, details have emerged regarding discussions between American officials and Malian authorities. According to diplomatic sources, t
title_en: U.S. Envoy Raises Conditions for Security Cooperation During Bamako Visit
excerpt_en: February 3, 2026 – Twenty-four hours after the visit to Bamako by Nick Checker, Director of the Bureau of African Affairs at the U.S. State Department, details have emerged regarding discussions between American officials and Malian authorities. According to diplomatic sources, t
body_en:
February 3, 2026 – Twenty-four hours after the visit to Bamako by Nick Checker, Director of the Bureau of African Affairs at the U.S. State Department, details have emerged regarding discussions between American officials and Malian authorities.
According to diplomatic sources, the talks focused primarily on security cooperation and intelligence sharing in the Sahel region. In recent months, Mali—alongside Burkina Faso and Niger—has reportedly sought closer engagement with Washington on military and intelligence matters amid persistent insecurity.
During a separate visit to Abuja, a senior official from the U.S. Africa Command (AFRICOM) indicated that intelligence collaboration with Sahelian armed forces could continue under certain conditions.
U.S. Conditions for Cooperation
During his discussions in Bamako, Nick Checker reportedly conveyed that the United States is open to strengthening cooperation with Mali and other Sahelian states. However, American support would be contingent upon specific political and security benchmarks.
Among the key conditions mentioned were:
Progress toward a return to constitutional order
Clarification regarding the presence of foreign military actors in Mali
The visit comes amid evolving geopolitical dynamics in the Sahel, where transitional authorities have diversified partnerships in response to mounting security challenges.
Observers note that intelligence cooperation remains a strategic priority for all parties, as armed groups continue to operate across the region.
The discussions in Bamako highlight the broader recalibration of international partnerships in the Sahel and underscore the linkage between security cooperation, governance reforms, and diplomatic alignment.

title: Upper Niger Valley Office Opens 34th Session, Highlights Agricultural Gains
excerpt: Ségou, February 12, 2026 – Daniel Siméon Kelema, Minister of Agriculture, presided over the opening of the 34th ordinary session of the Upper Niger Valley Office (OHVN) for the 2025 agricultural campaign on Thursday, February 12, 2026, in Ségou. The campaign has shown promising r
title_en: Upper Niger Valley Office Opens 34th Session, Highlights Agricultural Gains
excerpt_en: Ségou, February 12, 2026 – Daniel Siméon Kelema, Minister of Agriculture, presided over the opening of the 34th ordinary session of the Upper Niger Valley Office (OHVN) for the 2025 agricultural campaign on Thursday, February 12, 2026, in Ségou. The campaign has shown promising r
body_en:
Ségou, February 12, 2026 – Daniel Siméon Kelema, Minister of Agriculture, presided over the opening of the 34th ordinary session of the Upper Niger Valley Office (OHVN) for the 2025 agricultural campaign on Thursday, February 12, 2026, in Ségou.
The campaign has shown promising results, with production targets largely met:
Cereals: 347,964 tons (82% of target)
Seed cotton: 19,200 tons (70%)
Pulses: 54,351 tons (79%)
Sesame: 4,859 tons (72%)
Vegetables: 134,035 tons (91%)
The campaign has resulted in a cereal surplus of approximately 7,388 tons.
As part of agricultural modernization efforts, equipment was provided to 25 family farms, three input storage warehouses were renovated, and two organic sesame storage warehouses were constructed. Additionally, 6,025 tons of mineral fertilizers were made available to farmers in the OHVN zone to support continued growth.

body_en:
Bamako, February 7, 2026 – The Minister of Justice and Human Rights, Keeper of the Seals, Mamoudou Kassogué, officially launched the first phase of the recruitment examination for prison and juvenile justice officers at the Faculty of Private Law (FDPRI) in Badalabougou, known as the hill of knowledge.
This session saw 4,403 candidates registered for 200 available positions, highlighting the growing appeal of careers in the judicial and correctional system.
The examination began with a general knowledge test, personally administered by the Minister. The test focused on the importance of work in achieving independence, a theme reflecting both civic values and the country’s current socio-economic challenges.
Addressing the candidates, Minister Kassogué assured them of the transparency, fairness, and credibility of the recruitment process, stressing that the competition would be based solely on merit, skills, and equal opportunity.
The recruitment drive forms part of a broader initiative to strengthen the prison service and juvenile justice system, aimed at improving security, prison management, and the social reintegration of individuals under judicial supervision, in line with directives from the transitional authorities.

He highlighted the quality of cooperation between Mali and UNAIDS, noting tangible progress in prevention efforts, treatment access, and care for people living with HIV.

The farewell meeting underscored the continued partnership between Mali and UNAIDS in addressing public health challenges and consolidating gains in the fight against HIV/AIDS.

title: Council of Ministers Focuses on Mines, Sugar Industry, and Economic Reforms
excerpt: Bamako, February 13, 2026 – In an ordinary session at the Koulouba Palace chaired by President Assimi Goïta, the Council of Ministers adopted several measures with significant economic impact, particularly in the mining, industrial, and commercial sectors. Under the Ministry of M
title_en: Council of Ministers Focuses on Mines, Sugar Industry, and Economic Reforms
excerpt_en: Bamako, February 13, 2026 – In an ordinary session at the Koulouba Palace chaired by President Assimi Goïta, the Council of Ministers adopted several measures with significant economic impact, particularly in the mining, industrial, and commercial sectors. Under the Ministry of M
body_en:
Bamako, February 13, 2026 – In an ordinary session at the Koulouba Palace chaired by President Assimi Goïta, the Council of Ministers adopted several measures with significant economic impact, particularly in the mining, industrial, and commercial sectors.
Under the Ministry of Mines, the Council approved a draft decree renewing the gold mining permit for the Loulo Mining Company (SOMILO S.A.). Originally granted in 1996 for the exploitation of the Loulo gold mine in the Kéniéba district, the permit is renewed for ten years. Feasibility studies by Barrick Mining Corporation indicate that exploitable reserves could support substantial production, boosting the mining sector’s contribution to the national economy.
In the industrial and commercial sector, the Council noted the official launch of the 2025-2026 sugar campaign for SUKALA and N-SUKALA, with an anticipated combined production of approximately 120,000 tons, meeting nearly 34% of Mali’s annual sugar needs. Measures have been implemented to ensure domestic supply ahead of Ramadan 2026.
These decisions reflect the authorities’ commitment to strengthening Mali’s economic sovereignty through the development of natural resources, support for local production, and securing essential goods, amid ongoing economic and geopolitical challenges.

title: Alarming Human Rights Violations Reported in Azawad – January 2026
excerpt: Bamako, February 6, 2026 –The security and humanitarian situation in Azawad has sharply deteriorated, with a surge in human rights violations against civilians in January 2026, according to a new report by a local human rights organization. The report documents multiple forms of
title_en: Alarming Human Rights Violations Reported in Azawad – January 2026
excerpt_en: Bamako, February 6, 2026 –The security and humanitarian situation in Azawad has sharply deteriorated, with a surge in human rights violations against civilians in January 2026, according to a new report by a local human rights organization. The report documents multiple forms of
body_en:
Bamako, February 6, 2026 –The security and humanitarian situation in Azawad has sharply deteriorated, with a surge in human rights violations against civilians in January 2026, according to a new report by a local human rights organization.
The report documents multiple forms of abuse, highlighting a troubling trend of violence and lawlessness:
10 cases of abduction, enforced disappearance, and torture, primarily targeting civilians.
8 cases of summary executions and airstrikes, resulting in loss of life.
11 cases of looting, destruction, and ransacking of civilian property, affecting homes, businesses, and livelihoods.
Over 10 humanitarian and environmental consequences, including forced displacement, food insecurity, and deteriorating living conditions.
8 cases of environmental damage, linked to bombings, fires, and infrastructure destruction.
Notably, no cases of rape or sexual violence were officially recorded this month, though the report cautions this may reflect limitations in documentation rather than absence of the crime.
The findings underscore a systematic violation of international humanitarian law and a pressing need for action. The organization calls for the urgent protection of civilians, the initiation of independent investigations, and the prosecution of perpetrators.
The situation in Azawad remains critical, with both human and environmental consequences intensifying as the month progresses.

excerpt_en: Niamey, January 31, 2026 – The Confederation of Sahel States (AES) strongly condemned the barbaric and cowardly attack carried out on the night of January 28-29, 2026, targeting Air Base 101 and Diori Hamani International Airport in Niamey, Niger. The AES described the assault as
body_en:
Niamey, January 31, 2026 – The Confederation of Sahel States (AES) strongly condemned the barbaric and cowardly attack carried out on the night of January 28-29, 2026, targeting Air Base 101 and Diori Hamani International Airport in Niamey, Niger.
The AES described the assault as a premeditated, coordinated, and indiscriminate attack, endangering both strategic infrastructure and civilian facilities, and posing serious risks to innocent civilians and property.
In a statement, the AES emphasized that the violence is part of a broader destabilization strategy, fueled by support networks, including foreign actors, whose moral and political responsibility is called into question.
The Confederation reaffirmed that:
Perpetrators, along with anyone who finances, arms, informs, or politically supports them, will be held accountable.
Member states remain united, vigilant, and committed to a coordinated and sovereign fight against terrorism.
The AES expresses full solidarity with the people and government of Niger, praising the courage of its defense and security forces.
The Confederation concluded by reaffirming the determination of the Sahelian peoples to defend sovereignty, protect populations, and pursue a future of peace, justice, and independence.

title: United States Renews AGOA, Opening Major Export Opportunities for the DRC
excerpt: Kinshasa, February 4, 2026 – The United States Congress has officially renewed the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) until December 31, 2026, allowing the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) to continue exporting over 6,000 products duty-free to the American market. Govern
title_en: United States Renews AGOA, Opening Major Export Opportunities for the DRC
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, February 4, 2026 – The United States Congress has officially renewed the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) until December 31, 2026, allowing the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) to continue exporting over 6,000 products duty-free to the American market. Govern
body_en:
Kinshasa, February 4, 2026 – The United States Congress has officially renewed the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) until December 31, 2026, allowing the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) to continue exporting over 6,000 products duty-free to the American market.
Government Welcomes Renewal The Minister of Foreign Trade, Julien Paluku Kahongya, hailed the decision on Wednesday, February 4, describing it as a “strong signal” for the diversification of the national economy. He emphasized that the renewal reflects international recognition of Kinshasa’s economic reform efforts.
The DRC has identified 26 priority products eligible for U.S. trade preferences, and Minister Paluku urged economic operators, particularly in agribusiness, to seize the opportunity.
“We are calling on our economic operators: cocoa, coffee, palm oil, and many other products are included. This allows our people to return to their roots, to cultivate more. Today, the American market is available to Congolese people to sell their products,” the minister declared.
Banana Port: Key Infrastructure Boost In parallel with the AGOA renewal, the minister provided an update on the deep-water port of Banana, crucial for shipping Congolese exports. During his mission to Dubai, he met executives of DP World, the concessionaire of the port.
Key updates include:
Deadline: Completion of the first phase by the end of 2026
Impact: Arrival of the first cargoes and improved trade flow between the DRC and global markets
Goal: Reduce reliance on neighboring countries’ ports and enhance export competitiveness
AGOA Forum in Kinshasa The renewal of AGOA coincides with preparations for the next AGOA Forum in Kinshasa. Experts suggest that the combination of preferential access to the U.S. market and the upcoming Banana port commissioning could transform the country’s trade balance, traditionally dominated by mining exports.

title: Kongo Central Assembly Authorizes Judicial Investigation Against Governor Grâce Bilolo
excerpt: The Bureau of the Kongo Central Provincial Assembly authorized, on Wednesday, January 28, the opening of a judicial investigation against the provincial governor, Grâce Nkuanga Masuangi Bilolo. This decision follows a request from the Attorney General at the Court of Cassation, w
title_en: Kongo Central Assembly Authorizes Judicial Investigation Against Governor Grâce Bilolo
excerpt_en: The Bureau of the Kongo Central Provincial Assembly authorized, on Wednesday, January 28, the opening of a judicial investigation against the provincial governor, Grâce Nkuanga Masuangi Bilolo. This decision follows a request from the Attorney General at the Court of Cassation, w
body_en:
The Bureau of the Kongo Central Provincial Assembly authorized, on Wednesday, January 28, the opening of a judicial investigation against the provincial governor, Grâce Nkuanga Masuangi Bilolo.
This decision follows a request from the Attorney General at the Court of Cassation, who submitted an indictment seeking authorization. The governor met with members of the Bureau prior to their deliberations.
The five members of the Bureau stated that they reviewed the relevant legal texts, including the Constitution, the organic law on the Court of Cassation, laws governing the provinces, and the rules of procedure of the Provincial Assembly. They also considered the facts outlined in the indictment, the urgency of the case, and their discussions with the governor.
While reaffirming the importance of the presumption of innocence, the Bureau granted the Attorney General’s request. This decision requires the Governor of Kongo Central to appear before the competent court to present his defense.
Since last week, the Attorney General had sought this authorization following a damning report from the General Inspectorate of Finance (IGF), which revealed the embezzlement of more than one million US dollars.

title: Looting of Health Facilities Leaves Over 44,600 People Without Access to Care
excerpt: Uvira, South Kivu – January 27, 2026 — The ongoing conflict in Uvira has significantly worsened the humanitarian situation, with the looting of health facilities affecting more than 44,600 people, including 19,287 internally displaced persons and 25,313 returnees, severely limiti
title_en: Looting of Health Facilities Leaves Over 44,600 People Without Access to Care
excerpt_en: Uvira, South Kivu – January 27, 2026 — The ongoing conflict in Uvira has significantly worsened the humanitarian situation, with the looting of health facilities affecting more than 44,600 people, including 19,287 internally displaced persons and 25,313 returnees, severely limiti
body_en:
Uvira, South Kivu – January 27, 2026 — The ongoing conflict in Uvira has significantly worsened the humanitarian situation, with the looting of health facilities affecting more than 44,600 people, including 19,287 internally displaced persons and 25,313 returnees, severely limiting their access to essential healthcare.
A security and humanitarian overview for South Kivu province covering December 2025 reveals that the intensification of armed clashes in Uvira has caused widespread displacement, disrupted livelihoods, and halted critical humanitarian operations. Thousands of people have fled within the city and territory, while others have crossed into Burundi seeking refuge.
Assessments in the Ruzizi Health Zone indicate tens of thousands living in precarious conditions across multiple health areas, including Kiliba, Runigu, Kabunambo, Sange État, Sange CEPAC, Nazareni, Rusabagi, Ndunda, Kigurwe, and Kimuka. Many displaced families are sheltered in collective centers, such as schools and churches, while more than eight health facilities have been looted, drastically reducing or entirely halting operations.
The Kalehe territory also experienced massive displacements and disruption of socio-economic activities. Fighting along the Katasomwa–Ramba and Bushaku–Chambombo axes displaced nearly 2,900 households, now housed in Lemera, Luzira, Kasheke, Kalehe Centre, Bushushu, Nyamukubi, and Tchofi. These populations face severe vulnerabilities, including food insecurity, lack of shelter, limited access to healthcare, clean water, and sanitation.
In the Walungu territory, armed clashes led to population displacements, the suspension of socio-economic activities, and the destruction of numerous schools, churches, and health facilities in health zones such as Kaziba, Nyangezi, and Mubumbano. Assessments in Kamanyola and Kashenyi health zones indicate thousands of returnees and displaced persons facing acute food insecurity, malnutrition, and limited access to safe water and healthcare.
Since early 2025, the escalation of the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 rebellion in North and South Kivu has displaced hundreds of thousands, resulting in hundreds of deaths, thousands of injuries, and blocked access for humanitarian aid. Despite these challenges, humanitarian actors continue to provide emergency medical care, food aid, and essential services, negotiating access to affected areas wherever possible.
Humanitarian experts emphasize the urgent need for safe and unimpeded access to vulnerable populations. Meanwhile, progress in regional mediation initiatives, including the US-led Washington process and Qatar-facilitated talks, has yet to produce tangible improvements on the ground. Many voices are now calling on all stakeholders to honor commitments, silence the guns, and provide a chance for lasting peace after nearly three decades of conflict.

title: Violent Clashes Between AFC/M23 and FARDC in Chanjikiro
excerpt: Walikale North Kivu, January 30, 2026 — Violent fighting erupted on Thursday, January 29, 2026, between AFC/M23 rebels and the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC), supported by the Wazalendo and the Armed Reserve of the Defense (RAD), in Chanjikiro, within th

excerpt_en: Walikale North Kivu, January 30, 2026 — Violent fighting erupted on Thursday, January 29, 2026, between AFC/M23 rebels and the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC), supported by the Wazalendo and the Armed Reserve of the Defense (RAD), in Chanjikiro, within th
body_en:
Walikale North Kivu, January 30, 2026 — Violent fighting erupted on Thursday, January 29, 2026, between AFC/M23 rebels and the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC), supported by the Wazalendo and the Armed Reserve of the Defense (RAD), in Chanjikiro, within the Kisimba group of Walikale territory, North Kivu province.
According to local administrative authorities, the attackers advanced from Mpety and launched an offensive against government positions at around 2:00 p.m. local time.
Heavy and light weapon fire was reported, with loud explosions heard across the area, triggering widespread panic among civilians.
After nearly two hours of fighting, FARDC forces and their allies repelled the assault, forcing the rebels to retreat toward Mpety in the Banakindi area.
Local sources in Kisimba report a mass displacement of residents into surrounding bush areas, where civilians are now exposed to harsh weather conditions and heightened vulnerability.
The security situation remains tense in this part of Walikale, which has faced persistent insecurity for several months, further deepening the humanitarian crisis.

title: New Ceasefire Monitoring and Verification Mechanism Explained
excerpt: DRC–AFC/M23 February 3, 2026 — The Congolese government and AFC/M23 have adopted the terms of reference for a joint mechanism to monitor and verify the ceasefire agreement, reached on Monday in Doha. The mechanism consists of two complementary components: Ceasefire Monitoring and
title_en: New Ceasefire Monitoring and Verification Mechanism Explained
excerpt_en: DRC–AFC/M23 February 3, 2026 — The Congolese government and AFC/M23 have adopted the terms of reference for a joint mechanism to monitor and verify the ceasefire agreement, reached on Monday in Doha. The mechanism consists of two complementary components: Ceasefire Monitoring and
body_en:
DRC–AFC/M23 February 3, 2026 — The Congolese government and AFC/M23 have adopted the terms of reference for a joint mechanism to monitor and verify the ceasefire agreement, reached on Monday in Doha.
The mechanism consists of two complementary components:
Ceasefire Monitoring and Verification Mechanism (CMVM) – the supervisory and decision-making body.
Extended Joint Verification Mechanism Plus (EJVM+) – responsible for technical activities and on-the-ground verifications.
The CMVM is composed equally of government and rebel representatives, with observers from the African Union, Qatar, the United States, and the ICGLR. MONUSCO also participates. Decisions are made by consensus, requiring both parties to establish a quorum. Meetings are conducted primarily virtually, on a monthly or ad hoc basis.
The Joint Monitoring and Verification Committee+ (JMVC+) serves as the operational arm, tasked with:
Monitoring, verifying, and reporting on the implementation of the permanent ceasefire under the Doha Framework Agreement.
Investigating alleged violations and reporting observed breaches.
Monitoring the security and humanitarian situation in affected areas.
Promoting compliance with agreed security measures and building confidence between parties.
Joint verification teams, appointed by the JMVC Commander, include an equal number of representatives from both sides, with observers where possible. They operate in areas of reported violations, with unrestricted front-line access. MONUSCO facilitates logistics, including transportation and communications.
The reporting framework ensures weekly incident summaries, monthly analytical reports, and, where appropriate, public statements on major developments. All information is shared among mechanism members according to impartiality, transparency, and confidentiality principles.
The mechanism operates within the framework of commitments to a permanent ceasefire and a comprehensive peace process, remaining active until its mandate is fulfilled or the parties decide to terminate it jointly.

title: Kagame Defies Sanctions Threats and Rejects Any Involvement in Congo
excerpt: DRC–Rwanda, February 5, 2026 – Rwandan President Paul Kagame attributed ongoing tensions with the DRC to the presence of Rwandan Hutu rebels from the FDLR on Congolese territory, rejecting any claims of Kigali’s involvement in mineral exploitation during the opening of the “Umush
title_en: Kagame Defies Sanctions Threats and Rejects Any Involvement in Congo
excerpt_en: DRC–Rwanda, February 5, 2026 – Rwandan President Paul Kagame attributed ongoing tensions with the DRC to the presence of Rwandan Hutu rebels from the FDLR on Congolese territory, rejecting any claims of Kigali’s involvement in mineral exploitation during the opening of the “Umush
body_en:
DRC–Rwanda, February 5, 2026 – Rwandan President Paul Kagame attributed ongoing tensions with the DRC to the presence of Rwandan Hutu rebels from the FDLR on Congolese territory, rejecting any claims of Kigali’s involvement in mineral exploitation during the opening of the “Umushyikirano” national dialogue in Kigali.
Kagame stated:
“The problem Rwanda has with the DRC mainly concerns the FDLR present there, as well as their genocidal ideology,” asserting that these fighters threaten Rwanda. He dismissed accusations that Kigali is motivated by exploitation of Congolese resources or seeks to seize territory, calling them “pretensions.”
According to the Rwandan head of state,
“The war in the DRC was not started by Rwanda, nor did it originate in Rwanda,”adding that Rwanda’s defensive measures are unrelated to Congolese minerals, but are a response to persistent security threats since 1994.
Kagame further accused Congolese authorities of harboring and arming FDLR members, asserting that some had been integrated into the Congolese army, while others were collaborating with it. He noted that the transmission of ideology to new generations made the issue “not insignificant.”
On international sanctions threats, Kagame emphasized that Rwanda would not be “stifled”, adding:
“If we were truly in the DRC for minerals, Rwanda would be a hundred times richer than we are today.”
Background:
UN and US reports accuse Rwanda of supporting the M23 armed group, escalating the conflict and regional instability.
UN experts claim the rebels receive instructions and support from Kigali, and the UN Security Council has demanded Rwanda cease support and withdraw troops.
The US has accused Kigali of provoking war through training, logistics, equipment, and fighters for M23, despite the Washington Peace Agreement.
Targeted sanctions have been imposed on Rwandan officials for their alleged role in the Congolese crisis.
Kigali rejects these accusations, denying any support for AFC/M23 and reaffirming its commitment to peace.

title: U.S. Government Offices Close in Burundi Amid Federal Shutdown
excerpt: Bujumbura — February 2, 2026 — The United States Embassy in Burundi announced that several U.S. government offices in the country will be closed due to the ongoing federal government shutdown in Washington. In a statement published on February 2, the embassy said: “U.S. offices w
title_en: U.S. Government Offices Close in Burundi Amid Federal Shutdown
excerpt_en: Bujumbura — February 2, 2026 — The United States Embassy in Burundi announced that several U.S. government offices in the country will be closed due to the ongoing federal government shutdown in Washington. In a statement published on February 2, the embassy said: “U.S. offices w
body_en:
Bujumbura — February 2, 2026 — The United States Embassy in Burundi announced that several U.S. government offices in the country will be closed due to the ongoing federal government shutdown in Washington.
In a statement published on February 2, the embassy said: “U.S. offices will be closed starting February 3, 2026, until further notice regarding the government shutdown.”
The closure does not affect the U.S. Embassy, which will continue to operate normally. However, the shutdown impacts U.S.-run libraries, cultural centers, and other affiliated facilities.
The embassy also indicated that routine announcements on its social media platforms will be reduced to essential updates only, in line with guidance issued to U.S. diplomatic missions across Africa.
The shutdown stems from a failure in Congress to pass the budget for several federal departments, amid disputes over immigration policy and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).
The standoff intensified following protests in Minneapolis after two civilians were killed by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents.
Democrats have called for ICE reform, while Republicans argue existing immigration laws should remain in force. The budget impasse resulted in funding lapses, forcing some departments to suspend operations.
This follows the end-of-2025 shutdown, which halted government operations for 43 days, the longest shutdown in U.S. history.

Dubai, January 29, 2026 — Rwanda participated in the Gulfood Exhibition, the world’s largest annual trade fair for vegetables, fruits, and flowers, bringing together more than 8,500 exhibitors from 195 countries across 280,000 square meters in Dubai.
The country was represented by the National Agricultural Export Promotion Board (NAEB) alongside Rwandan farmers engaged in export-oriented production. NAEB described the event as a strategic opportunity to expand Rwanda’s access to markets in the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries.
While in Dubai, NAEB CEO Claude Bizimana met with Mussab Aboud, CEO of Grandiose, a major UAE food retailer operating 47 stores. The discussions focused on strengthening a long-term partnership to supply Rwandan products such as coffee, flowers, avocados, and fresh produce to the UAE market.
NAEB reported that 90% of Rwanda’s avocado exports currently go to the UAE, with overall fruit exports continuing to rise. Trade between Rwanda and the UAE is expanding steadily, with bilateral trade value projected to reach $1.1 billion.
Export volumes have grown significantly over the past decade. In 2017, Rwanda exported about 40 tons per month of fruits, vegetables, and flowers; today, that figure exceeds 1,000 tons per month. From July 2023 to February 2024, Rwanda exported agricultural products worth $46 million.
The 31st edition of Gulfood was held for the first time across two venues — the Dubai World Trade Centre and the Dubai Exhibition Centre — reflecting the growing scale of the event.

title: Appeal Trial of Claude Muhayimana Convicted of Genocide Begins
excerpt: France February 3, 2026 -- The Appeals Chamber of the Court of Cassation in France is set to hear the appeal of Claude Muhayimana, who is contesting his 14-year prison sentence for his role in the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi. On February 2, 2026, the list of participants in t
title_en: Appeal Trial of Claude Muhayimana Convicted of Genocide Begins
excerpt_en: France February 3, 2026 -- The Appeals Chamber of the Court of Cassation in France is set to hear the appeal of Claude Muhayimana, who is contesting his 14-year prison sentence for his role in the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi. On February 2, 2026, the list of participants in t
body_en:
France February 3, 2026 -- The Appeals Chamber of the Court of Cassation in France is set to hear the appeal of Claude Muhayimana, who is contesting his 14-year prison sentence for his role in the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi. On February 2, 2026, the list of participants in the appeal proceedings was updated.
On February 3, 2026, the Inyangamugayo Bench expected to hear the case is to be confirmed, along with a list of at least 50 witnesses and experts, about 20 of whom will testify in Kigali. The defendant is also expected to be questioned, along with the investigator who assessed his background, behavior, and lifestyle.
On November 19, 2025, the President of the Paris Criminal Court met with lawyers to prepare the appeal, reviewing the list of witnesses.
Muhayimana is seeking to be cleared of the charges and declared innocent of crimes for which he was convicted nearly four years ago.
Born in 1961 in the former Kibuye Prefecture, western Rwanda, Muhayimana was a guest house driver during the genocide. He later fled to France, where he obtained citizenship in 2010 and resides in Rouen.
He was arrested on April 9, 2014, following a complaint by the CPCR, an organization pursuing genocide suspects. He was released under house arrest on April 10, 2015, while under investigation. His trial, initially scheduled for September 2020, was postponed due to the COVID-19 pandemic.
At his trial, which began on November 22, 2021, Muhayimana was accused of leading Interahamwe militias involved in killings of Tutsi in Kibuye between April and July 1994.
Prosecutors also alleged his involvement in massacres at the Kibuye Parish Church on April 17, 1994, at Gatwaro Stadium, and at Home St Jean the following day.
Defended by Me Philippe Meilhac and Françoise Marthe, Muhayimana pleaded not guilty, claiming he was a member of the RNC, an opposition group to the Rwandan government.
On December 16, 2021, the court found him guilty of complicity in genocide and crimes against humanity, sentencing him to 14 years in prison, confirming that he had led Interahamwe members.
However, the court did not find that he directly participated in the Kibuye town massacre, accepting his claim that he was transporting the body of a gendarme, Mwafrika, from Bisesero to Ruhengeri at the time.
The IBUKA organization, which represents survivors of the genocide, said the sentence was lenient compared to the crimes committed.

title: Tshisekedi Rejects AFC/M23 Participation in National Peace Talks
excerpt: Kinshasa, January 31, 2026 — President Félix Tshisekedi has signaled that members of the AFC/M23 alliance will not be allowed to participate in planned national peace talks aimed at uniting the Congolese people. Since December 2025, the Congolese government, with support from Ang
title_en: Tshisekedi Rejects AFC/M23 Participation in National Peace Talks
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, January 31, 2026 — President Félix Tshisekedi has signaled that members of the AFC/M23 alliance will not be allowed to participate in planned national peace talks aimed at uniting the Congolese people. Since December 2025, the Congolese government, with support from Ang
body_en:
Kinshasa, January 31, 2026 — President Félix Tshisekedi has signaled that members of the AFC/M23 alliance will not be allowed to participate in planned national peace talks aimed at uniting the Congolese people.
Since December 2025, the Congolese government, with support from Angolan President and African Union Chair João Lourenço, has been preparing a dialogue process initially expected to take place in Kinshasa. Early reports suggested that opposition groups, including AFC/M23, could be invited. However, the venue is now reportedly under consideration in Luanda, Angola, or Lomé, Togo.
AFC/M23 leader Corneille Nangaa confirmed that Angolan authorities had invited him to attend the talks, but he questioned how this forum would differ from the ongoing Doha process, warning that achievements made there should not be undermined.
In an interview conducted in Goma on January 26, Nangaa stated that the Doha talks should continue, as they are, in his view, the only framework capable of resolving differences between AFC/M23 and the Congolese government, before broader national dialogue can take place.
On January 31, Tshisekedi briefed diplomatic representatives in Kinshasa on the security situation in eastern DRC, insisting that any Congolese dialogue must be held on national territory and led by state institutions.
“If these talks take place, they will take place on national territory, led and organized by national institutions, based on the Constitution, national laws and democratic principles,” Tshisekedi said.
He further stressed that dialogue would not include those he accuses of committing crimes against civilians. “Talks, yes. But we will not do it with those who committed crimes against our population,” he added.
The DRC government has long accused the AFC/M23 of serious abuses, including killings, in areas under its control in North Kivu and South Kivu, particularly Goma and Bukavu, a matter discussed during a cabinet meeting on January 30.
AFC/M23 rejects these accusations, instead blaming government forces for most abuses and claiming that security has improved and living conditions are better in areas it controls.
