excerpt_en: Beni, North Kivu, February 7, 2026 – On Saturday, religious leaders urged the army’s civic and patriotic education service and the FARDC Grand North operational sector command to strengthen civil-military relations, seen as a guarantee of lasting peace, in Beni, North Kivu. The a
body_en:
Beni, North Kivu, February 7, 2026 – On Saturday, religious leaders urged the army’s civic and patriotic education service and the FARDC Grand North operational sector command to strengthen civil-military relations, seen as a guarantee of lasting peace, in Beni, North Kivu.
The appeal came during a working session attended by nearly 100 religious leaders and FARDC Deputy Chief of Staff in charge of operations and intelligence, General Jacques Kyaligonza Nduru.
During his mission in Beni, General Nduru emphasized the need to involve all segments of the population, including the religious community, in efforts to find lasting solutions to restore peace in the region.
The area remains affected by the activities of the ADF rebels. According to a report by the Congolese Institute for Research on Politics, Governance and Violence (Ebuteli), this rebel group is responsible for some of the most atrocious acts of violence in the Democratic Republic of Congo.
The report notes that the ADF perpetrates massacres not only to recruit new fighters, but also to undermine the legitimacy of governments combating them.

title: When Diplomacy Failed: The Weeks Leading to the Fall of Goma
excerpt: Goma, January 26, 2026 — One year ago, the city of Goma, the provincial capital of North Kivu and the main urban center of eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), fell under the control of the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 movement. The battle that preceded its capture was of unprec
title_en: When Diplomacy Failed: The Weeks Leading to the Fall of Goma
excerpt_en: Goma, January 26, 2026 — One year ago, the city of Goma, the provincial capital of North Kivu and the main urban center of eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), fell under the control of the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 movement. The battle that preceded its capture was of unprec
body_en:
Goma, January 26, 2026 — One year ago, the city of Goma, the provincial capital of North Kivu and the main urban center of eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), fell under the control of the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 movement. The battle that preceded its capture was of unprecedented intensity, marking a major turning point in the conflict in eastern Congo.
One year later, with the movement still administering the city, this report revisits the political, diplomatic, and military events that paved the way for the Battle of Goma.
December 2024: The Failure of Angolan Mediation
On December 15, 2024, in Luanda, hopes were high. Angola was on the verge of brokering a peace agreement between Kinshasa and Kigali. Both delegations had nearly finalized a text, including a Concept of Operations (CONOPS) detailing military commitments and an implementation timeline.
However, negotiations collapsed over one key issue: Kinshasa’s categorical refusal to negotiate with the AFC/M23, a condition set by Rwanda for signing the agreement. On December 16, President Paul Kagame did not travel to Luanda. President Félix Tshisekedi arrived alone. The agreement was never signed.
Following this diplomatic failure, military pressure rapidly intensified on the ground.
A Military Escalation Documented by the United Nations
In the days that followed, the United Nations documented the deployment of sophisticated weaponry by Rwandan forces in M23-controlled areas, including surface-to-air missiles and GPS jamming systems. These capabilities severely restricted the use of aircraft and drones by Congolese forces and their allies.
In response, President Félix Tshisekedi sought regional support. On December 21, he traveled to Brazzaville, followed by Bujumbura on December 22. Domestically, he initiated sweeping changes within the military command. Four days later, several senior officers were replaced, including the commander of the Third Defense Zone, responsible for North Kivu. The FARDC Chief of Staff had already been replaced ten days earlier.
January 2025: The M23 Advance Toward Goma
The conflict soon shifted decisively to the battlefield. On Friday, January 3, the AFC/M23 captured Katale. The next day, Masisi-centre fell, bringing rebel forces within 80 kilometers of Goma. On January 7, fighting was reported around Saké, a strategic town about 30 kilometers west of Goma.
At the same time, UN experts stated that Rwandan Defense Forces had “continued to provide systematic support to the M23 and effectively controlled its operations.” According to these reports, General Sultani Makenga, the movement’s military leader, continued to “receive instructions and support from Rwandan forces and intelligence services.”
During the first two weeks of January, multiple fronts became active simultaneously — in Masisi, southern Lubero, Rutshuru, and Nyiragongo. Fighting was intense, prolonged, and steadily advanced toward Goma.
The Final Week Before the Fall
On January 18, 2025, President Tshisekedi addressed ambassadors accredited in Kinshasa, calling on Western countries to impose targeted sanctions against Rwanda, which he accused of backing the M23.
Five days later, fighting around Saké escalated further. On January 23, Major General Peter Cirimwami, military governor of North Kivu, was shot and seriously wounded while traveling to the front line west of Goma. He later succumbed to his injuries.
On Saturday, January 25, clashes reached the immediate outskirts of Goma. The Congolese army and its allies faced the M23, backed by Rwanda. Thirteen soldiers — from South Africa, Malawi, and Uruguay, deployed with the SADC regional force or the UN mission in the DRC (MONUSCO) — were killed.
In response, Kinshasa recalled its diplomats from Kigali and gave Rwanda 48 hours to cease all diplomatic activity on Congolese soil.
Goma Plunged Into Chaos
The impact on the city was immediate. High-voltage power lines were cut during the fighting, plunging Goma into darkness and soon cutting off water supplies. M23 fighters and Rwandan soldiers entered the city.
On Monday, January 27, gunfire was heard in the city center, and M23 elements and Rwandan special forces were reported in several neighborhoods. The day before, UN Secretary-General António Guterres had directly blamed Kigali after another day of fighting.
Clashes continued, particularly around the southern part of Goma airport. On the Rwandan side, a spokesperson for the Rwandan Defense Forces reported at least five dead and 24 seriously wounded in a border locality.
That same day, a mass escape occurred at Munzenze prison, which held around 3,000 inmates. On Tuesday, January 28, Goma awoke to heavy detonations and exchanges of fire, while in Kinshasa, protests erupted in several districts, including Limete, Kitambo, and the administrative area of Gombe.
Hospitals in Goma were overwhelmed, unable to cope with the influx of wounded.
On Wednesday, January 29, several hundred Romanian nationals — described by Kinshasa as military instructors with the FARDC and by Kigali as mercenaries — crossed into Gisenyi, Rwanda, before being evacuated to Romania.

On December 15, 2024, in Luanda, hopes were high. Angola was on the verge of brokering a peace agreement between Kinshasa and Kigali. Both delegations had nearly finalized a text, including a Concept of Operations (CONOPS) detailing military commitments and an implementation timeline.
However, negotiations collapsed over one key issue: Kinshasa’s categorical refusal to negotiate with the AFC/M23, a condition set by Rwanda for signing the agreement. On December 16, President Paul Kagame did not travel to Luanda. President Félix Tshisekedi arrived alone. The agreement was never signed.
Following this diplomatic failure, military pressure rapidly intensified on the ground.
A Military Escalation Documented by the United Nations
In the days that followed, the United Nations documented the deployment of sophisticated weaponry by Rwandan forces in M23-controlled areas, including surface-to-air missiles and GPS jamming systems. These capabilities severely restricted the use of aircraft and drones by Congolese forces and their allies.
In response, President Félix Tshisekedi sought regional support. On December 21, he traveled to Brazzaville, followed by Bujumbura on December 22. Domestically, he initiated sweeping changes within the military command. Four days later, several senior officers were replaced, including the commander of the Third Defense Zone, responsible for North Kivu. The FARDC Chief of Staff had already been replaced ten days earlier.
January 2025: The M23 Advance Toward Goma
The conflict soon shifted decisively to the battlefield. On Friday, January 3, the AFC/M23 captured Katale. The next day, Masisi-centre fell, bringing rebel forces within 80 kilometers of Goma. On January 7, fighting was reported around Saké, a strategic town about 30 kilometers west of Goma.
At the same time, UN experts stated that Rwandan Defense Forces had “continued to provide systematic support to the M23 and effectively controlled its operations.” According to these reports, General Sultani Makenga, the movement’s military leader, continued to “receive instructions and support from Rwandan forces and intelligence services.”
During the first two weeks of January, multiple fronts became active simultaneously — in Masisi, southern Lubero, Rutshuru, and Nyiragongo. Fighting was intense, prolonged, and steadily advanced toward Goma.
The Final Week Before the Fall
On January 18, 2025, President Tshisekedi addressed ambassadors accredited in Kinshasa, calling on Western countries to impose targeted sanctions against Rwanda, which he accused of backing the M23.
Five days later, fighting around Saké escalated further. On January 23, Major General Peter Cirimwami, military governor of North Kivu, was shot and seriously wounded while traveling to the front line west of Goma. He later succumbed to his injuries.
On Saturday, January 25, clashes reached the immediate outskirts of Goma. The Congolese army and its allies faced the M23, backed by Rwanda. Thirteen soldiers — from South Africa, Malawi, and Uruguay, deployed with the SADC regional force or the UN mission in the DRC (MONUSCO) — were killed.
In response, Kinshasa recalled its diplomats from Kigali and gave Rwanda 48 hours to cease all diplomatic activity on Congolese soil.
Goma Plunged Into Chaos
The impact on the city was immediate. High-voltage power lines were cut during the fighting, plunging Goma into darkness and soon cutting off water supplies. M23 fighters and Rwandan soldiers entered the city.
On Monday, January 27, gunfire was heard in the city center, and M23 elements and Rwandan special forces were reported in several neighborhoods. The day before, UN Secretary-General António Guterres had directly blamed Kigali after another day of fighting.
Clashes continued, particularly around the southern part of Goma airport. On the Rwandan side, a spokesperson for the Rwandan Defense Forces reported at least five dead and 24 seriously wounded in a border locality.
That same day, a mass escape occurred at Munzenze prison, which held around 3,000 inmates. On Tuesday, January 28, Goma awoke to heavy detonations and exchanges of fire, while in Kinshasa, protests erupted in several districts, including Limete, Kitambo, and the administrative area of Gombe.
Hospitals in Goma were overwhelmed, unable to cope with the influx of wounded.
On Wednesday, January 29, several hundred Romanian nationals — described by Kinshasa as military instructors with the FARDC and by Kigali as mercenaries — crossed into Gisenyi, Rwanda, before being evacuated to Romania.

title: General Strike Paralyzes Shabunda as Residents Demand End to Insecurity and Wazalendo Abuses
excerpt: Shabunda, South Kivu January 29, 2026 — The town of Shabunda has been paralyzed since the beginning of the week by a general strike, as residents protest rising insecurity, alleged abuses by the “wazalendo”, and demand the withdrawal of these armed groups from the town. The strik
title_en: General Strike Paralyzes Shabunda as Residents Demand End to Insecurity and Wazalendo Abuses
excerpt_en: Shabunda, South Kivu January 29, 2026 — The town of Shabunda has been paralyzed since the beginning of the week by a general strike, as residents protest rising insecurity, alleged abuses by the “wazalendo”, and demand the withdrawal of these armed groups from the town. The strik
body_en:
Shabunda, South Kivu January 29, 2026 — The town of Shabunda has been paralyzed since the beginning of the week by a general strike, as residents protest rising insecurity, alleged abuses by the “wazalendo”, and demand the withdrawal of these armed groups from the town.
The strike, launched by civil society on Tuesday, January 27, follows a series of incidents attributed to certain wazalendo elements. Since Monday, schools, markets, and most commercial activities have been shut down, while vehicle traffic has come to a standstill.
“Shops, stores, markets… are not operating. Traffic is suspended,” said a local resident. Another added, “Schools have been closed for four days, which is seriously disrupting classes, especially during first-session exams for secondary students.”
According to Isaac Rashidi, president of Shabunda territory’s civil society, the “ghost town” operation was declared in response to repeated acts of insecurity. He cited the proliferation of illegal roadblocks, extortion of money from civilians, and repeated killings allegedly committed by some wazalendo fighters.
Mr. Rashidi further reported that an altercation last Friday between wazalendo and residents left four people dead, including three civilians, and several others wounded.
“We are asking the security council and the provincial government to order all wazalendo in the central zone to go to the front lines,” he said. “Only the FARDC, the police, and the official security services should remain in Shabunda.”
Civil society has also called on officials of the Armed Reserve for Defense (RAD) to restore order in the management and deployment of wazalendo in this part of South Kivu.

title: Police Arrest 39 Suspected Armed Bandits, Including Those Who Murdered a Security Agent
excerpt: Lubumbashi DRC February 2, 2026 — The Congolese National Police (PNC) conducted a major security operation in Haut-Katanga province. In Lubumbashi, thirty-nine (39) suspected criminals were presented on Monday, including individuals believed responsible for the murder of an agent
title_en: Police Arrest 39 Suspected Armed Bandits, Including Those Who Murdered a Security Agent
excerpt_en: Lubumbashi DRC February 2, 2026 — The Congolese National Police (PNC) conducted a major security operation in Haut-Katanga province. In Lubumbashi, thirty-nine (39) suspected criminals were presented on Monday, including individuals believed responsible for the murder of an agent
body_en:
Lubumbashi DRC February 2, 2026 — The Congolese National Police (PNC) conducted a major security operation in Haut-Katanga province. In Lubumbashi, thirty-nine (39) suspected criminals were presented on Monday, including individuals believed responsible for the murder of an agent of the National Intelligence Agency (ANR).
According to Deputy Divisional Commissioner Blaise Kilimbalimba, provincial commissioner of the PNC in Haut-Katanga, this operation was possible due to close collaboration between the police and the public. The suspects were presented at the provincial police headquarters.
“They were carrying a loaded AK-47 assault rifle, ammunition, bladed weapons, and dozens of stolen cell phones,” stated Deputy Divisional Commissioner Kilimbalimba.
These arrests are the result of operations conducted in several sensitive neighborhoods, including the Mzee market on Sendwe Avenue, Usines Avenue, Mama Yemo, and the Likasi road.
“The group apprehended is heterogeneous but considered particularly dangerous. Thirteen (13) of them are believed to specialize in armed robbery, and the network involved in the recent assassination of an ANR agent has been dismantled,” said police intelligence services in Haut-Katanga.
Deputy Divisional Commissioner Kilimbalimba commended the public for their role in reporting criminals:
“I commend the courage of the population in reporting criminals. We reiterate our unwavering commitment to apprehending all these criminals who disturb the peace. Vigilance must remain paramount,” he declared.
All suspected criminals will be transferred to the competent judicial authorities to face legal proceedings.

title: 4 Dead and Several Injured After Clashes Between Police and Bandits in Panu
excerpt: Panu Kwilu, February 4, 2026 — Four people were killed and several others injured during clashes between police and a group of bandits (Kuluna) in Panu, Idiofa territory, Kwilu province. Among the deceased were two police officers and two civilians. The bandits attacked in retali
title_en: 4 Dead and Several Injured After Clashes Between Police and Bandits in Panu
excerpt_en: Panu Kwilu, February 4, 2026 — Four people were killed and several others injured during clashes between police and a group of bandits (Kuluna) in Panu, Idiofa territory, Kwilu province. Among the deceased were two police officers and two civilians. The bandits attacked in retali
body_en:
Panu Kwilu, February 4, 2026 — Four people were killed and several others injured during clashes between police and a group of bandits (Kuluna) in Panu, Idiofa territory, Kwilu province. Among the deceased were two police officers and two civilians. The bandits attacked in retaliation after the arrest of their leaders, plunging the town into total panic.
Many residents spent the night in the forest, while others sought refuge along the border between Idiofa territory and Maï-Ndombe province.
Nico Mbuka, a provincial deputy from Idiofa, demanded a thorough investigation to hold perpetrators accountable and called for police reinforcements.
“They arrested one of their leaders, and the bandits, in turn, attacked the police. The clashes resulted in four deaths, two police officers and two civilians. As of now, the population is not calm. Some spent the night in the forest. Others went to the river, to the border with Maï-Ndombe, to the sandbars. There is no peace in Panu at this time.” — Nico Mbuka, provincial deputy
The territory administrator, Adelar Kintolo, confirmed the incident but noted a gradual return to calm.
These clashes have disrupted daily life in the area: markets were deserted, and activities in hospitals and schools were paralyzed.

title: Gnassingbé Arrives in Rwanda to Advance Mediation Efforts in DRC Conflict
excerpt: Kigali, January 30, 2026 — The Prime Minister of Togo, Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé, arrived in Rwanda on the night of January 29, 2026, for an official visit. He was received by Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, Olivier Nduhungirehe. Gnassingbé, who has visited Rwanda on sever
title_en: Gnassingbé Arrives in Rwanda to Advance Mediation Efforts in DRC Conflict
excerpt_en: Kigali, January 30, 2026 — The Prime Minister of Togo, Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé, arrived in Rwanda on the night of January 29, 2026, for an official visit. He was received by Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, Olivier Nduhungirehe. Gnassingbé, who has visited Rwanda on sever
body_en:
Kigali, January 30, 2026 — The Prime Minister of Togo, Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé, arrived in Rwanda on the night of January 29, 2026, for an official visit. He was received by Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, Olivier Nduhungirehe.
Gnassingbé, who has visited Rwanda on several occasions, last met with President Paul Kagame in April 2025, shortly after being appointed by the African Union (AU) as mediator in the conflict between Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).
The visit aims to reinforce his commitment to working with regional and international stakeholders to achieve a lasting solution to the crisis in eastern DRC. Discussions focused on the progress of regional peace talks and efforts to stabilize the region.
On March 24, 2025, Angola announced that President João Lourenço would step down as mediator in the DRC–Rwanda conflict to concentrate on continental initiatives. He subsequently proposed Gnassingbé as his successor, a move later endorsed by the African Union.
In early April 2025, the AU supported the proposal, and on April 12, 2025, the AU General Assembly unanimously appointed Gnassingbé as mediator between Rwanda and the DRC.
Gnassingbé has since made several visits to Rwanda to discuss security, regional stability, and African cooperation. He also traveled to Kigali in January 2025 for a two-day working visit, during which both countries agreed to deepen bilateral cooperation.
Relations between Rwanda and the DRC have deteriorated in recent years due to the ongoing conflict in eastern DRC. Kinshasa accuses Rwanda of supporting the AFC/M23 alliance, while Rwanda accuses the DRC of backing the FDLR, a group linked to perpetrators of the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi.
Recently, the African Union reduced the mandate of mediators in the eastern DRC conflict. This decision followed a security meeting held in Lomé, Togo, from January 16 to 17, 2026.
The mediation process is currently led by Prime Minister Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé, supported by a team from Togo’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and his office.

title: President Kagame Criticizes Burundi at Umushyikirano Conference
excerpt: Kigali, Rwanda – February 5, 2026 – President Paul Kagame opened the 20th Umushyikirano Conference, a national forum aimed at sharing ideas, solving problems, and guiding Rwandans. In his address, Kagame called on leaders to fulfill their responsibilities and warned that those wh
title_en: President Kagame Criticizes Burundi at Umushyikirano Conference
excerpt_en: Kigali, Rwanda – February 5, 2026 – President Paul Kagame opened the 20th Umushyikirano Conference, a national forum aimed at sharing ideas, solving problems, and guiding Rwandans. In his address, Kagame called on leaders to fulfill their responsibilities and warned that those wh
body_en:
Kigali, Rwanda – February 5, 2026 – President Paul Kagame opened the 20th Umushyikirano Conference, a national forum aimed at sharing ideas, solving problems, and guiding Rwandans. In his address, Kagame called on leaders to fulfill their responsibilities and warned that those who exceed their authority should be held accountable.
Turning to regional relations, Kagame criticized Burundi, saying that the country has broken the brotherhood traditionally shared with Rwanda by aligning itself with the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).
He said: "As far as I knew, Rwandans and Burundians are twins, but Burundians chose to say, ‘No, we don’t want you to be twins anymore, we want to be twins with Congolese.’ I have no problem with it if someone chooses who they are born with or who they live with as a twin. I have nothing to do with that, I accept it."
Kagame added: "But being twins especially involves bad politics, a politics of self-denial and hatred of others, which they share. This is not a secret because they themselves, the leaders of those countries, are saying it. I am not inventing anything new."
He also addressed the international situation, refuting claims that Rwanda is responsible for insecurity in eastern DRC, and reaffirmed the country’s position on regional stability.
The speech comes amid growing tensions between Rwanda, Burundi, and the DRC, highlighting Kigali’s firm stance on regional diplomacy and security issues.

title: Plea Bargaining Releases Over 600 Inmates in One Month
excerpt: Muhanga, January 26, 2026 — The Rwanda Correctional Service (RCS) announced that 644 prisoners were released in one month through the plea bargaining program, according to CSP Hillary Sengabo, spokesperson for RCS. The announcement was made during the launch of Plea Bargaining We
title_en: Plea Bargaining Releases Over 600 Inmates in One Month
excerpt_en: Muhanga, January 26, 2026 — The Rwanda Correctional Service (RCS) announced that 644 prisoners were released in one month through the plea bargaining program, according to CSP Hillary Sengabo, spokesperson for RCS. The announcement was made during the launch of Plea Bargaining We
body_en:
Muhanga, January 26, 2026 — The Rwanda Correctional Service (RCS) announced that 644 prisoners were released in one month through the plea bargaining program, according to CSP Hillary Sengabo, spokesperson for RCS. The announcement was made during the launch of Plea Bargaining Week at Muhanga Prison.
CSP Sengabo highlighted that the program has significantly reduced overcrowding in Rwandan prisons, noting that the overcrowding rate decreased from 143% to 101% since the program’s implementation.
He explained that the program allows the Criminal Investigation Department to connect perpetrators with victims or enable offenders to pay compensation for damages caused. In the first month alone, 337 prisoners remained incarcerated while 664 were released after completing sentences under the plea bargaining framework.
Vice President of the Supreme Court, Hitiyaremye Alphonse, confirmed that the program applies to all crimes, but emphasized that it does not remove the discretion of prosecutors or the courts.
Judiciary reports show that in the 2024/2025 judicial year, cases concluded through mediation increased by 32%, reaching 3,166 cases, up from 2,395 in the previous year. Meanwhile, 11,846 cases were settled through plea bargains, a rise from 9,851 cases in 2023/2024, representing a 20% increase.
The program is seen as a key measure in reducing prison congestion while maintaining legal oversight and promoting justice through reconciliation and compensation.

title_en: FARDC, Allies Recapture Point Zero from Twirwaneho in South Kivu
excerpt_en: South Kivu, January 30, 2026 — The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC), alongside Burundian forces and Wazalendo fighters, have recaptured Point Zero from the MRDP-Twirwaneho group following intense fighting supported by drone strikes. The area had been seize
body_en:
South Kivu, January 30, 2026 — The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC), alongside Burundian forces and Wazalendo fighters, have recaptured Point Zero from the MRDP-Twirwaneho group following intense fighting supported by drone strikes.
The area had been seized by Twirwaneho on January 17, 2026. Its recapture is considered a major victory, as government forces had been preparing operations in zones inhabited by the Banyamulenge community in the Minembwe commune.
According to reports, in the early hours of January 29, FARDC forces — reportedly accompanied by FDLR fighters and mercenaries — deployed large numbers of troops and heavy weapons to retake the strategic position.
“They were supported in the air by six drones, in groups of three,” said Moïse Nyarugabo, a politician from Minembwe. “When one group of three drones was shot down, the other returned and bombed the compound. These drones fired 34 bombs in one day.”
Following the operation, Twirwaneho fighters were forced to withdraw from Point Zero and Bikyaka, retreating toward the Tuwetuwe area.
The fighting triggered the displacement of thousands of residents, many of whom had previously fled to the area when Twirwaneho first captured it.
The recapture of Point Zero has restored freedom of movement along key routes in Fizi Territory, including access to Baraka and areas leading to Uvira, where the location serves as a critical crossroads.

title: UK and DRC Reach Agreement on Repatriation of Illegal Migrants
excerpt: London / Kinshasa – 06/02/2026 – The United Kingdom and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) have reached an agreement to repatriate Congolese nationals who entered the UK illegally or have criminal convictions. The accord also allows Congolese citizens to legally enter the UK.
title_en: UK and DRC Reach Agreement on Repatriation of Illegal Migrants
excerpt_en: London / Kinshasa – 06/02/2026 – The United Kingdom and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) have reached an agreement to repatriate Congolese nationals who entered the UK illegally or have criminal convictions. The accord also allows Congolese citizens to legally enter the UK.
body_en:
London / Kinshasa – 06/02/2026 – The United Kingdom and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) have reached an agreement to repatriate Congolese nationals who entered the UK illegally or have criminal convictions. The accord also allows Congolese citizens to legally enter the UK.
UK Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood welcomed the partnership, stating that illegal entrants and criminals from the DRC will be repatriated swiftly. She added that similar arrangements are expected for citizens of Namibia and Angola.
The agreement follows Britain’s warning to countries that refuse to accept their citizens, which could face consequences under UK immigration policy.
“My message is clear. If governments in these countries refuse to take in their citizens, they will bear the consequences,” Mahmood said.
The UK continues to grapple with illegal immigration, with the Home Office reporting 41,472 illegal arrivals by boat in 2025, the second-highest number since 2018, following 45,774 arrivals in 2022.
AFC/M23 Accuses African Union Commission of Supporting Crimes in DRC
Kisangani, Tshopo February 6, 2026 – The AFC/M23 alliance has accused the African Union (AU) Commission of supporting crimes committed by the FARDC. Between the night of 31 January and 1 February 2026, the alliance carried out a drone attack against a military facility at Bangoka Airport in Kisangani, Tshopo province.
The AFC/M23 said the attack targeted the installation because the FARDC allegedly use it to strike their bases and civilian populations in North Kivu and South Kivu.
On 6 February, AU Commission President Mahmoud Ali Youssouf condemned the operation, expressing concern that the attack on a facility in a major city could endanger civilians and violate international law. Mahmoud noted that, despite no evidence of the airport’s military use, the attack was considered an assault on a civilian base, labeling it an act of terrorism.
In response, AFC/M23 Secretary General Benjamin Mbonimpa reminded the AU that DRC government forces have conducted drone strikes against their positions and civilians in areas including Minembwe, Kalehe, Masisi, and Rutshuru.
“The drone operation was strictly military, no civilians were involved, and it aimed to protect innocent civilians, in line with the Doha ceasefire,’’ Mbonimpa said.
The alliance criticized the AU for condemning the security operation without investigation, arguing that this shows bias and raises questions about its ability to conduct peace talks in the DRC.
“By siding with a government that has committed serious violations against its population, rather than supporting the victims, the AU undermines its credibility. Labeling an operation that saved lives as terrorism represents a step back for the African Union,” the AFC/M23 statement said.
According to sources, the AFC/M23 deployed eight drones against Bangoka Airport, while the DRC government claims to have destroyed most of them.

title: DRC, Zambia, and Angola Launch Strategic Coordination Meeting in Luanda
excerpt: Luanda, February 5, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Zambia, and Angola kicked off an inaugural coordination meeting in Luanda on Thursday, February 5, focusing on the implementation of the strategic Lobito Corridor project. The two-day session, held in partnership
title_en: DRC, Zambia, and Angola Launch Strategic Coordination Meeting in Luanda
excerpt_en: Luanda, February 5, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Zambia, and Angola kicked off an inaugural coordination meeting in Luanda on Thursday, February 5, focusing on the implementation of the strategic Lobito Corridor project. The two-day session, held in partnership
body_en:
Luanda, February 5, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Zambia, and Angola kicked off an inaugural coordination meeting in Luanda on Thursday, February 5, focusing on the implementation of the strategic Lobito Corridor project. The two-day session, held in partnership with the World Bank, gathers the Ministers of Transport, Finance, and Foreign Trade from the three countries to align policies, coordinate investments, and mobilize public and private partners.
A Regional Driver of Growth The Lobito Corridor is positioned as a key driver of economic growth, intra-African trade, and job creation, linking Southern and Central Africa to global markets. During the opening, Angolan President João Lourenço urged the participating states and financial partners to adopt a pragmatic approach to accelerate implementation.
DRC Prioritizes an Integrated Approach Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Transport Jean-Pierre Bemba emphasized that the DRC is pursuing a comprehensive strategy, combining transport, logistics, energy, trade, and industrial development. The initial priority focuses on the Dilolo-Kolwezi-Tenge section.
“We have different phases that we are currently addressing. The priority has been to stabilize the road between Dilolo and Kolwezi. It’s an old railway line we are rehabilitating with private sector support. We have obtained $110 million in funding to work on 80 kilometers of this section,” Bemba explained.
A Lever for Development Minister of Foreign Trade Julien Paluku Kahongya highlighted the need for country ownership of the corridor to make it a genuine development lever for local populations.
“The Lobito corridor was often perceived as a project driven by others. I am pleased that Angola, the DRC, and Zambia are now working together with partners to consider its impact on our populations. If we continue to view it solely as transport infrastructure, the people will remain in the same situation the corridor found them in,” he said.
Reforms to Boost Investment Finance Minister Doudou Fwamba stressed that the DRC is undertaking reforms to improve the business climate, a crucial step to attract investment and ensure the success of the corridor project.

title: PDDRCS Seen as Key to Strengthening Peace Efforts in Ituri
excerpt: Djugu, Ituri, February 7, 2026 – The administrator of Djugu territory, Chief Commissioner Ruffin Mapela, has emphasized that the Disarmament, Demobilization, Community Recovery and Stabilization Program (PDDRCS) could play a critical role in strengthening peace efforts in Ituri.
title_en: PDDRCS Seen as Key to Strengthening Peace Efforts in Ituri
excerpt_en: Djugu, Ituri, February 7, 2026 – The administrator of Djugu territory, Chief Commissioner Ruffin Mapela, has emphasized that the Disarmament, Demobilization, Community Recovery and Stabilization Program (PDDRCS) could play a critical role in strengthening peace efforts in Ituri.
body_en:
Djugu, Ituri, February 7, 2026 – The administrator of Djugu territory, Chief Commissioner Ruffin Mapela, has emphasized that the Disarmament, Demobilization, Community Recovery and Stabilization Program (PDDRCS) could play a critical role in strengthening peace efforts in Ituri.
Speaking on Saturday, February 7, the Congolese National Police officer praised armed groups that are implementing recommendations from the Aru 1 and Aru 2 talks.
“It is already a first step for us to see these young armed men agree to meet and seek solutions for peace. We know that there is a program, the disarmament and demobilization program, which should support these young people who participated in the Aru 1 and Aru 2 dialogues so that they can implement the resolutions from these meetings,” said Mapela.
The administrator also acknowledged that one armed group continues to disrupt the situation. He pledged to take all necessary steps to involve this faction in the peace program.
“There are always difficulties that require solutions. Since other armed groups have agreed to join this program and surrender their weapons, we will continue to build on this momentum so that peace is fully restored throughout the country,” Mapela concluded.

title: AFC/M23 Withdrawal from Uvira: Government Says “Chaos Envisioned by the Enemy Did Not Occur”
excerpt: Kinshasa, January 25, 2026 — The withdrawal of the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 rebellion from the city of Uvira, in South Kivu province, was discussed for the first time during the Council of Ministers meeting held on Friday, January 23, at the African Union City complex, under the ch
title_en: AFC/M23 Withdrawal from Uvira: Government Says “Chaos Envisioned by the Enemy Did Not Occur”
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, January 25, 2026 — The withdrawal of the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 rebellion from the city of Uvira, in South Kivu province, was discussed for the first time during the Council of Ministers meeting held on Friday, January 23, at the African Union City complex, under the ch
body_en:
Kinshasa, January 25, 2026 — The withdrawal of the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 rebellion from the city of Uvira, in South Kivu province, was discussed for the first time during the Council of Ministers meeting held on Friday, January 23, at the African Union City complex, under the chairmanship of Prime Minister Judith Suminwa.
Presenting the operational situation across the country, particularly in North Kivu and South Kivu, the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defense and Veterans Affairs, Guy Kabombo Muadiamvita, reported the return of security forces to Uvira to ensure public order and the protection of civilians.
He said the chaos scenario predicted by the rebellion following its withdrawal had been thwarted, thanks to measures taken with various military commands to guarantee the safety of all communities.
“Following the withdrawal of RDF/M23 coalition troops from the city of Uvira, units of the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo resumed their initial positions to ensure the firm defense of the city and the protection of the population, particularly members of the Banyamulenge community. The chaos envisioned by the enemy, through the manipulation of local communities, did not materialize, thanks to the firm instructions given to the commanders of operations as well as to the military justice authorities, with a view to punishing any transgressions,” read the minutes of the Council of Ministers.
This development comes amid controversy surrounding the AFC/M23 announcement of its withdrawal from Uvira, which Congolese authorities believe was intended to divert attention and ease international pressure, particularly from the United States, on Kigali, which the United Nations considers the rebellion’s main supporter.

title: DRC Humanitarian Response Refocused on 7.3 Million People Amid $1.4 Billion Funding Appeal for 2026
excerpt: Kinshasa, January 28, 2026 — Facing a severe funding shortfall, the humanitarian community in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has announced a major reprioritization of its 2026 response, targeting 7.3 million people—less than half of the nearly 15 million in critical need.
title_en: DRC Humanitarian Response Refocused on 7.3 Million People Amid $1.4 Billion Funding Appeal for 2026
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, January 28, 2026 — Facing a severe funding shortfall, the humanitarian community in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has announced a major reprioritization of its 2026 response, targeting 7.3 million people—less than half of the nearly 15 million in critical need.
body_en:
Kinshasa, January 28, 2026 — Facing a severe funding shortfall, the humanitarian community in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has announced a major reprioritization of its 2026 response, targeting 7.3 million people—less than half of the nearly 15 million in critical need. The government and its humanitarian partners launched an urgent appeal on Wednesday for USD 1.4 billion to address the country’s most pressing humanitarian needs.
The revised plan reflects a sharp reduction from 2025, when 11 million people were targeted. According to humanitarian officials, this shift represents a strict prioritization of populations facing the most immediate threats to survival, as the country grapples with ongoing armed conflict, mass displacement, climate shocks, and recurring epidemics.
The impact of underfunding has already been severe. In 2025, reduced operational capacity led to the closure of more than 1,000 nutrition centers, leaving over 390,000 children suffering from severe acute malnutrition without essential care. An estimated 1.5 million people lost access to primary healthcare due to facility closures, medicine shortages, and weakened epidemic response. Monthly food assistance targets were reduced by up to 73%, exposing vulnerable communities to heightened hunger and deprivation.
“The combination of immense needs and limited resources forces us to make extremely difficult, sometimes impossible, choices,” said Bruno Lemarquis, Humanitarian Coordinator in the DRC. “We call for renewed and strengthened financial commitments to preserve lives, dignity, and prevent millions from being deprived of vital support.”
The 2026 plan comes amid a deeply disrupted humanitarian environment, particularly in North Kivu, South Kivu, and Ituri, where intensified fighting since January 2025 has reshaped needs, disrupted supply chains, and imposed growing administrative and security constraints. Access to affected populations has become increasingly dangerous and complex.
Mr. Lemarquis called for a paradigm shift in the humanitarian approach. “Humanitarian assistance saves lives, but it does not resolve the root causes of crises,” he said. “Peace must be at the center of our efforts. Solutions are primarily political. We must move beyond constant reaction and establish a culture of anticipation and prevention, while strengthening the Humanitarian–Development–Peace Nexus for real, lasting impact.”
He also praised the resilience and solidarity of Congolese communities, particularly host families who share scarce resources with displaced people, describing them as the country’s first line of humanitarian defense. He emphasized the central role of the government in facilitating humanitarian operations on the ground.
Despite its scale and duration, the humanitarian crisis in the DRC remains one of the world’s most protracted and underfunded. The 2025 Humanitarian Response Plan, budgeted at USD 2.54 billion, was funded at only 22%, even as needs continued to rise. International funding shortages—compounded by recent reductions in humanitarian assistance from key donors—have had particularly severe consequences in eastern DRC.
At the global level, the United Nations’ 2026 humanitarian plan targets 87 million people worldwide and requires USD 23 billion. While major pledges have been announced, humanitarian officials warn that without sustained and predictable financing, millions of vulnerable people in the DRC will remain without life-saving assistance.

excerpt_en: Butembo, February 2, 2026 — A passenger convoy traveling from Rutshuru territory to the city of Butembo was targeted in an armed attack on Sunday, February 1, along the Rwindi-Kanyabayonga road. According to local sources, the incident occurred around 3:00 PM, when several vehicl
body_en:
Butembo, February 2, 2026 — A passenger convoy traveling from Rutshuru territory to the city of Butembo was targeted in an armed attack on Sunday, February 1, along the Rwindi-Kanyabayonga road.
According to local sources, the incident occurred around 3:00 PM, when several vehicles and motorcycles were ambushed by unidentified armed men in an area under AFC/M23 rebel control.
The attackers opened fire and used bladed weapons against the passengers, causing several injuries, though no fatalities were reported. Victims were transported to medical facilities in Kanyabayonga for treatment.
In addition to the physical assault, all passengers’ valuables were looted, including money, cell phones, and merchandise, leaving many stripped of personal belongings.
Civil society actors in Rutshuru noted that such incidents are becoming increasingly frequent on this strategic route. They called on the authorities and security forces to strengthen protection, secure the road, and ensure the free movement of people and goods.
This attack highlights the persistent insecurity in parts of North Kivu, despite repeated warnings and calls for urgent intervention to safeguard civilians.

title: Fighting Intensifies, Thousands Displaced Without Humanitarian Assistance in Fizi
excerpt: South Kivu February 4, 2026 — Thousands of displaced people in Fizi, South Kivu, are living in inhumane conditions, lacking water, food, and healthcare, as ongoing fighting between the Congolese army (FARDC) and allies against AFC/M23 rebels worsens the humanitarian crisis. Autho
title_en: Fighting Intensifies, Thousands Displaced Without Humanitarian Assistance in Fizi
excerpt_en: South Kivu February 4, 2026 — Thousands of displaced people in Fizi, South Kivu, are living in inhumane conditions, lacking water, food, and healthcare, as ongoing fighting between the Congolese army (FARDC) and allies against AFC/M23 rebels worsens the humanitarian crisis. Autho
body_en:
South Kivu February 4, 2026 — Thousands of displaced people in Fizi, South Kivu, are living in inhumane conditions, lacking water, food, and healthcare, as ongoing fighting between the Congolese army (FARDC) and allies against AFC/M23 rebels worsens the humanitarian crisis. Authorities report that at least one million inhabitants have fled their homes along various routes within the territory.
On the orders of armed groups, no displacement camps have been established, forcing people to stay with host families and struggle daily for survival.
In Ekengya village, located dozens of kilometers from Fizi town, nearly two thousand displaced people face severe hardships. Angela Mauwa Ndone, a mother of eight who fled Point Zero, described her plight:
“I am suffering greatly. Since I arrived here, my children have stopped going to school. You might find me pounding this small amount of corn; it’s today’s ration, and I don’t know where to find the rest for tomorrow. I am appealing to the Congolese government and its partners for assistance.”
Malyani Makambe, chief of Ekengya, emphasized that displaced people are exposed to disease and unable to afford healthcare fees.
“We have 1,883 displaced people from Point Zero, Rugezi, Kavanja, Kitumba, and other areas. They fled, leaving everything behind. Here, they have no access to drinking water or healthcare, and cannot pay the 50,000 to 100,000 Congolese francs required for treatment.”
Residents remain at risk from ongoing gunfire. Local observer Maurice Musema explained that with each battle in Point Zero or the Mitumba mountains, fear grips the population, who dread further escalation.
The displaced communities are calling for government intervention and comprehensive strategies to end the conflict, which is seen as the only way to stop uncontrolled displacement.
Children are out of school, some are malnourished, and adults remain uncertain about the future, highlighting the scale of the humanitarian crisis in Fizi.
The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) is working to address immediate needs, though the complexity of the crisis continues to grow daily due to ongoing fighting.

body_en:
January 29, 2026 — Rwanda and Mexico celebrated the 50th anniversary of their diplomatic ties at a ceremony in Nairobi, Kenya, attended by Mexican Ambassador Gisele Fernández Ludlow and Rwandan Ambassador to Kenya Ernest Rwamucyo.
Ambassador Fernández Ludlow said the two countries have built a strong partnership through financial and international cooperation, adding that future efforts will focus on expanding collaboration, particularly in tourism and international events.
Ambassador Rwamucyo подчеркнул that Rwanda values its long-standing ties with Mexico, citing decades of dialogue, cooperation, and support for international law.
Diplomatic relations between the two countries began on January 21, 1976.

title: Gen Muhoozi Clashes with Ugandan Communications Minister
excerpt: Kampala, Uganda – February 5, 2026 – Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, Chief of Defence Staff and son of President Yoweri Museveni, has publicly criticized the country’s Communications Minister, Dr. Chris Baryomunsi, over remarks about his social media activity. The dispute erupted after
title_en: Gen Muhoozi Clashes with Ugandan Communications Minister
excerpt_en: Kampala, Uganda – February 5, 2026 – Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, Chief of Defence Staff and son of President Yoweri Museveni, has publicly criticized the country’s Communications Minister, Dr. Chris Baryomunsi, over remarks about his social media activity. The dispute erupted after
body_en:
Kampala, Uganda – February 5, 2026 – Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, Chief of Defence Staff and son of President Yoweri Museveni, has publicly criticized the country’s Communications Minister, Dr. Chris Baryomunsi, over remarks about his social media activity.
The dispute erupted after Dr. Baryomunsi revealed that he had informed President Museveni that Gen Muhoozi’s posts on X (formerly Twitter) were interfering with his duties as Government Spokesperson.
Baryomunsi defended his stance, explaining that Gen Muhoozi’s social media posts are often jokes, not official statements, saying: "The Chief of Defence Staff does not speak on behalf of the Government of Uganda, but he likes to use X. He writes messages, deletes them, and I hope Ugandans have already made up their minds about what he writes."
The statement reportedly angered Gen Muhoozi, who responded publicly on X:"Baryomunsi, you traitor, I will never be a Minister again."
Baryomunsi replied firmly: "I have come a long way to where I am because of my own abilities, not because of anyone’s gifts. I am a self-made man. Being a Minister is not the best thing in life. My goals are much higher than that. Let’s serve Uganda. Thank you."
The feud continued online, with Gen Muhoozi demanding an apology and reconciliation, while Baryomunsi defended his independence and work ethic, stating: "My father taught me to believe in myself. title: UN Women Rwanda Launches $6 Million Plan to Empower Women
excerpt: Kigali 5 February 2026 – UN Women Rwanda has unveiled a new strategic plan for 2026-2029, allocating up to $6.3 million (over 9.17 billion Frw) to promote women’s empowerment, particularly in rural areas, and address gaps across multiple sectors. Of the planned budget, $3.5 milli
title_en: UN Women Rwanda Launches $6 Million Plan to Empower Women
excerpt_en: Kigali 5 February 2026 – UN Women Rwanda has unveiled a new strategic plan for 2026-2029, allocating up to $6.3 million (over 9.17 billion Frw) to promote women’s empowerment, particularly in rural areas, and address gaps across multiple sectors. Of the planned budget, $3.5 milli
body_en:
Kigali 5 February 2026 – UN Women Rwanda has unveiled a new strategic plan for 2026-2029, allocating up to $6.3 million (over 9.17 billion Frw) to promote women’s empowerment, particularly in rural areas, and address gaps across multiple sectors.
Of the planned budget, $3.5 million (55%) has already been secured. The remaining funds will be mobilized through partnerships with banks and financial institutions, including the National Bank of Rwanda (BNR), Equity Bank, I&M Bank, and government agencies.
The Director of UN Women Rwanda, Jennet Kem, emphasized collaboration with financial and governmental partners to expand opportunities for women, stating:"The fact that the government is here alone means that we have the strength, it will help us to see in its capacity how we can work together to continue to develop women."
The Minister of Gender and Family Development, Uwimana Consolée, highlighted the importance of partnerships for advancing women's programs, noting:"In these times when the world seems to not have enough money, there are ways we can collaborate and work together, and these activities are for Rwandans."
UN Women Rwanda provides training in governance, self-development, and combating violence, among other initiatives. Between 2020-2025, the agency trained over 85,000 people on gender-based violence, assisted 35,000 individuals (26,570 women and 8,876 men), helped 9,000 women access loans, and supported 3,000 women in starting small and medium-sized enterprises.
The UN Country Coordinator in Rwanda, Ozonnia Ojielo, praised Rwanda’s progress in women’s development, emphasizing the importance of sustaining economic growth to ensure women are not left behind. She said:"Rwanda now needs a better way to help it grow its economy… it needs to have a stable economy itself, which will help it go far."
UN Women first arrived in Rwanda in 1996 as UNIFEM and was rebranded in 2010. Its core mission remains the promotion of gender equality, women’s development, and the fight against violence.

title: Ethiopian Airlines Suspends Flights to Tigray Amid Rising Tensions
excerpt: January 29, 2026 — Ethiopian Airlines has suspended passenger flights between Addis Ababa and towns in Tigray, citing unforeseen circumstances, amid fears of renewed fighting between government forces and the TPLF. Neither the airline nor the government has officially commented.
title_en: Ethiopian Airlines Suspends Flights to Tigray Amid Rising Tensions
excerpt_en: January 29, 2026 — Ethiopian Airlines has suspended passenger flights between Addis Ababa and towns in Tigray, citing unforeseen circumstances, amid fears of renewed fighting between government forces and the TPLF. Neither the airline nor the government has officially commented.
body_en:
January 29, 2026 — Ethiopian Airlines has suspended passenger flights between Addis Ababa and towns in Tigray, citing unforeseen circumstances, amid fears of renewed fighting between government forces and the TPLF.
Neither the airline nor the government has officially commented. Tigray’s transport chief, Tadele Mengistu, confirmed the suspension, while BBC reporters in Mekelle said airport staff were told not to report to work. Bus transport between Addis Ababa and Tigray continues.
The 2022 peace deal remains unimplemented, as land disputes, June 2026 elections, and reports of clashes in Mai Degusha fuel tensions. The conflict centers on the Amhara region’s control of land in western Tigray, which the government says will be resolved by referendum, though up to one million displaced people may be unable to vote.
The war that began in November 2020 between the government and the TPLF caused massive destruction, with the African Union reporting over 600,000 deaths.

title: Boulos: Peace Will Take Time
excerpt: Great Lakes Region, 4 February 2026 – Massad Boulos, Special Advisor to the US President for African Affairs, stated that achieving peace in the Great Lakes region will be a long-term process. He emphasized that stability will not come immediately, noting that the region faces on
title_en: Boulos: Peace Will Take Time
excerpt_en: Great Lakes Region, 4 February 2026 – Massad Boulos, Special Advisor to the US President for African Affairs, stated that achieving peace in the Great Lakes region will be a long-term process. He emphasized that stability will not come immediately, noting that the region faces on
body_en:
Great Lakes Region, 4 February 2026 – Massad Boulos, Special Advisor to the US President for African Affairs, stated that achieving peace in the Great Lakes region will be a long-term process. He emphasized that stability will not come immediately, noting that the region faces ongoing challenges and obstacles.
Boulos recalled that on 4 December 2025, Rwanda and the DRC signed a peace agreement with US support, backing the Doha talks aimed at ending the war in North Kivu and South Kivu.
He noted that when AFC/M23 captured Uvira on 9 December 2025, the US condemned the action, although the group explained it was intended to stop attacks by DRC, Burundian, Wazalendo, FDLR forces, and mercenaries against civilians in Minembwe.
During a briefing on humanitarian operations in the DRC and Sudan on 3 February 2026, Boulos said the US remains concerned about Uvira and that AFC/M23 was asked to withdraw its fighters, which they did.
He highlighted the Doha peace talks and the ceasefire monitoring agreement with MONUSCO, signed on 2 February 2026 with Qatar’s support, as major steps toward stability.
Boulos stated, “Peace is a journey and it will take time. Here and there we will encounter obstacles. There will be challenges, but we must be firm and we are very firm. President Trump is firm. He signed as a witness, he is firm.”
Meanwhile, AFC/M23 continues to accuse the DRC government of violating the ceasefire and targeting civilians, pledging on 3 February to combat these violations directly.

title: Citizens Launch Petition to Dissolve Equateur Provincial Assembly
excerpt: Mbandaka, February 5, 2026 – A collective of citizens, calling themselves the “Rebellious Citizens,” has launched a petition demanding the dissolution of the Equateur Provincial Assembly, intensifying political tensions in the provincial capital. Accusations of Interference and P
title_en: Citizens Launch Petition to Dissolve Equateur Provincial Assembly
excerpt_en: Mbandaka, February 5, 2026 – A collective of citizens, calling themselves the “Rebellious Citizens,” has launched a petition demanding the dissolution of the Equateur Provincial Assembly, intensifying political tensions in the provincial capital. Accusations of Interference and P
body_en:
Mbandaka, February 5, 2026 – A collective of citizens, calling themselves the “Rebellious Citizens,” has launched a petition demanding the dissolution of the Equateur Provincial Assembly, intensifying political tensions in the provincial capital.
Accusations of Interference and Patronage The group accuses members of the provincial assembly of paralyzing the executive branch through untimely interference and patronage practices. According to the petitioners, the deliberative body has overstepped its constitutional oversight role, interfering in the day-to-day management of the provincial government.
“The members of parliament are behaving like managers. They are blocking important files and interfering in the executive branch's responsibilities. We say enough is enough; this assembly must be dissolved to allow the province to breathe,” said Papy Ekate Ekofo, spokesperson for the “Rebellious Citizens” collective.
The collective has begun a large-scale signature campaign across Mbandaka, aiming for 25,000 signatures to appeal directly to President Félix Tshisekedi, the only authority empowered to order the dissolution of a provincial assembly in cases of persistent crisis.
Allegations of Bribery Rumors circulating in Mbandaka suggest that some assembly members are engaged in bribery, allegedly pressuring public institutions to hire relatives, disadvantaging local talent.
Assembly Responds The Equateur Provincial Assembly has rejected the petition. Rapporteur Ézéchiel Ambokani emphasized that the initiative lacks legal standing, stating:
“This petition has no legal standing to dissolve our institution. The mechanisms for dissolution are strictly defined by the Constitution and do not depend on collecting signatures in the street.”
Implications for Governance Observers warn that this standoff comes at a time when Équateur Province is struggling with infrastructure and social development. If unresolved, the conflict between citizens and elected officials could further weaken state authority in the region.

title: Awareness Campaigns Promote Peaceful Coexistence in Djugu
excerpt: Djugu, Ituri February 6, 2026 – Public gatherings are being regularly organized in the Walendu Djatsi sector of Djugu territory to promote peace and social cohesion, a Radio Okapi reporter observed on Friday, February 6. Initiated by traditional authorities and security forces, t
title_en: Awareness Campaigns Promote Peaceful Coexistence in Djugu
excerpt_en: Djugu, Ituri February 6, 2026 – Public gatherings are being regularly organized in the Walendu Djatsi sector of Djugu territory to promote peace and social cohesion, a Radio Okapi reporter observed on Friday, February 6. Initiated by traditional authorities and security forces, t
body_en:
Djugu, Ituri February 6, 2026 – Public gatherings are being regularly organized in the Walendu Djatsi sector of Djugu territory to promote peace and social cohesion, a Radio Okapi reporter observed on Friday, February 6.
Initiated by traditional authorities and security forces, these awareness campaigns aim to foster peaceful coexistence among local communities. The initiatives have been welcomed by civil society, which calls for greater involvement of young people in the process.
According to Justin Gudza, head of the Walendu Djatsi sector, all segments of society are engaged, including youth, religious leaders, educators, and military and police authorities.
“Markets and places of worship are frequented by all communities. Traffic flows smoothly. People need to interact, speak the same language, and consider each other as brothers,” Gudza explained.
Youth Called Upon to Get Involved
Germain Mapasa, local civil society coordinator, stressed that lasting peace depends on the active involvement of young people.
“We ask all the communities of Djugu to accept one another and forget the past. We call on our youth to support all initiatives likely to bring about lasting peace. Before, we didn’t question who was Mulendu or Muhema. We must not let manipulators divide us,” he emphasized.
During the campaigns, local authorities also highlight the importance of good civil-military relations to ensure the effective protection of the population.

excerpt: Walikale, North Kivu – January 25, 2026 — The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) have intensified military pressure on the AFC/M23 rebels in Walikale territory, launching targeted airstrikes on what are described as their main strongholds. Late on Saturday e
title_en: FARDC Airstrikes Hit AFC/M23 Strongholds Mpety and Mindjendje in Walikale
excerpt_en: Walikale, North Kivu – January 25, 2026 — The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) have intensified military pressure on the AFC/M23 rebels in Walikale territory, launching targeted airstrikes on what are described as their main strongholds. Late on Saturday e
body_en:
Walikale, North Kivu – January 25, 2026 — The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) have intensified military pressure on the AFC/M23 rebels in Walikale territory, launching targeted airstrikes on what are described as their main strongholds.
Late on Saturday evening, January 24, an FARDC attack drone bombed rebel positions in Mpety and Mindjendje, located in the Banakindi area of the Kisimba group. These two sites are considered the principal logistics and operational bases of the rebels around the strategic town of Pinga.
According to local sources, the drone flew over the Banakindi airspace at around 6:00 p.m. local time before dropping several bombs on the targeted positions. Mpety, situated just 18 kilometers from Pinga, reportedly housed a major logistical hub for the AFC/M23.
The information was confirmed by Lavie Changwi, administrative secretary of the Kisimba group, who said the explosions triggered widespread panic among residents.
“The population was caught off guard by the loud detonations. People stayed indoors, fearing reprisals or an escalation of the fighting,” he said.
While the official human and material toll remains unknown, multiple sources in the area report the destruction of several rebel positions, with significant loss of life and heavy material damage.
Local leaders say Mpety and Mindjendje served as regrouping and supply centers for the rebels, who had recently received reinforcements from Kitshanga, Mwesso, and Kalembe in Masisi territory. These reinforcements were reportedly intended to prepare a large-scale offensive against Pinga, a key strategic stronghold in this part of North Kivu.
The latest airstrikes come just 24 hours after the bombing of Buleusa, in the Ikobo area, where another AFC/M23 position was reportedly completely destroyed. Walikale, North Kivu – January 25, 2026 — The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) have intensified military pressure on the AFC/M23 rebels in Walikale territory, launching targeted airstrikes on what are described as their main strongholds.
Late on Saturday evening, January 24, an FARDC attack drone bombed rebel positions in Mpety and Mindjendje, located in the Banakindi area of the Kisimba group. These two sites are considered the principal logistics and operational bases of the rebels around the strategic town of Pinga.
According to local sources, the drone flew over the Banakindi airspace at around 6:00 p.m. local time before dropping several bombs on the targeted positions. Mpety, situated just 18 kilometers from Pinga, reportedly housed a major logistical hub for the AFC/M23.
The information was confirmed by Lavie Changwi, administrative secretary of the Kisimba group, who said the explosions triggered widespread panic among residents.
“The population was caught off guard by the loud detonations. People stayed indoors, fearing reprisals or an escalation of the fighting,” he said.
While the official human and material toll remains unknown, multiple sources in the area report the destruction of several rebel positions, with significant loss of life and heavy material damage.
Local leaders say Mpety and Mindjendje served as regrouping and supply centers for the rebels, who had recently received reinforcements from Kitshanga, Mwesso, and Kalembe in Masisi territory. These reinforcements were reportedly intended to prepare a large-scale offensive against Pinga, a key strategic stronghold in this part of North Kivu.
The latest airstrikes come just 24 hours after the bombing of Buleusa, in the Ikobo area, where another AFC/M23 position was reportedly completely destroyed. Through these successive air operations, the FARDC appears determined to degrade the rebels’ operational capacity and prevent any advance toward other strategic locations in Walikale territory.

title: Manguredjipa Paralyzed After Deadly Protest Against Insecurity in Lubero

title_en: Manguredjipa Paralyzed After Deadly Protest Against Insecurity in Lubero
excerpt_en: Manguredjipa, January 28, 2026 — Socio-economic activities slowed sharply in Manguredjipa, the main town of the Bapere sector in Lubero territory, on Wednesday, January 28, 2026, marking the second day of unrest triggered by a protest against rising insecurity linked to Allied De
body_en:
Manguredjipa, January 28, 2026 — Socio-economic activities slowed sharply in Manguredjipa, the main town of the Bapere sector in Lubero territory, on Wednesday, January 28, 2026, marking the second day of unrest triggered by a protest against rising insecurity linked to Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) attacks.
Shops remained closed, agricultural work was suspended, and traffic was severely disrupted. On the previous day, local women had erected barricades at the main entry and exit points of the town. Some protesters marched barefoot, while others demonstrated topless, a traditional sign of indignation in the face of persistent violence.
The demonstration, organized on Tuesday, January 27, turned violent, leaving two people dead and three others seriously injured. The victims, all young boys, were reportedly killed by gunfire attributed to security forces during the protest. Among the injured were a woman, a six-month-old infant, and another young boy, all evacuated to medical facilities for urgent treatment.
The unrest also caused significant material damage. The residence of the sector chief was vandalized, a motorcycle was set on fire, and several household appliances were destroyed. These incidents led to the closure of the local market, further paralyzing economic life.
The protest came just 72 hours after an ADF attack in the village of Musenge, in the Baswagha chiefdom, during which several houses, a health center, and a Catholic church were burned down. The attack also caused mass displacement and the deaths of two FARDC soldiers.

title: Implementation Struggles Seven Months After Signing, Overall Rate Stagnates at 23.3%
excerpt: Washington Agreement February 2, 2026 — Seven months after the signing of the Washington Agreement between the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and Rwanda, implementation continues to face serious challenges, with an overall implementation rate remaining unchanged at 23.3%, acc
title_en: Implementation Struggles Seven Months After Signing, Overall Rate Stagnates at 23.3%
excerpt_en: Washington Agreement February 2, 2026 — Seven months after the signing of the Washington Agreement between the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and Rwanda, implementation continues to face serious challenges, with an overall implementation rate remaining unchanged at 23.3%, acc
body_en:
Washington Agreement February 2, 2026 — Seven months after the signing of the Washington Agreement between the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and Rwanda, implementation continues to face serious challenges, with an overall implementation rate remaining unchanged at 23.3%, according to a recent report by the African Peace Agreements Barometer.
The agreement, signed under the auspices of the Trump administration, was intended to address the ongoing conflict in eastern DRC and the activities of the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 rebellion, which continues territorial operations in North Kivu and South Kivu.
The report highlights that the main positive developments between January 1 and 31, 2026, include:
High-level meeting in Lomé (January 16-17) to consolidate peace processes in the DRC and the Great Lakes region and adopt a new AU mediation architecture.
Regional tour of the AU Mediator and the Panel of Facilitators, operationalizing the new mediation framework.
Extraordinary meeting of ICGLR defense experts in Livingstone (January 8-10) to review the deteriorating security situation in eastern DRC.
President João Lourenço’s consultations with Congolese political, military, and religious actors to relaunch inclusive political dialogue.
U.S. Congressional hearings (January 22) to assess the Washington Agreement’s implementation.
Withdrawal of AFC/M23 from Uvira.
Despite these steps, the report identifies persistent challenges, including:
Intensification of hostilities in eastern DRC.
Failure to neutralize the FDLR.
Continued Rwandan defensive measures.
Obstacles to effective humanitarian aid delivery.
Recommendations were made to key stakeholders:
To the U.S. Government:
Maintain and strengthen coordinated diplomatic and political pressure on DRC and Rwanda.
Use targeted coercive measures against actors obstructing implementation, if necessary.
To the Congolese Government:
Accelerate operations to neutralize the FDLR.
Consider MONUSCO involvement in areas under AFC/M23 control.
Provide assurances that no FDLR members are integrated into FARDC.
Promote structured and inclusive political dialogue beyond security issues.
To the Rwandan Government:
Implement disengagement and lifting of defensive measures.
Provide credible security/legal guarantees to FDLR members for voluntary repatriation.
Encourage AFC/M23 not to obstruct MONUSCO operations targeting FDLR.
To the Qatari Government:
Resume the Doha peace process, currently stalled since mid-November 2025.
To the African Union and AU mediator:
Adopt a formal framework linking Washington and Doha commitments.
Finalize methodological instruments and operational tools for the Panel of Facilitators.
Clarify the relationship between President Lourenço’s consultations and the Washington/Doha processes.
Ensure independent funding for the Panel of Facilitators and Joint Secretariat.
Despite the involvement of US President Donald Trump, progress on the ground remains slow. Kinshasa and Kigali are struggling to coordinate effectively, while Doha talks with the AFC/M23, under Qatari mediation, have yet to produce concrete results, particularly regarding the restoration of state authority and reintegration of armed groups.
The report underscores that, seven months post-signing, the Washington Agreement faces persistent implementation gaps, leaving the eastern DRC security situation fragile and the population exposed to ongoing violence.

title: AFC/M23 Claims Attack on Army Drone Command Center
excerpt: Kisangani Airport February 4, 2026 — The AFC/M23 rebel group claimed responsibility Tuesday for the weekend attack on Bangboka Airport, located 17 kilometers from Kisangani, capital of Tshopo province. This airport, a key site within the national security apparatus and home to th
title_en: AFC/M23 Claims Attack on Army Drone Command Center
excerpt_en: Kisangani Airport February 4, 2026 — The AFC/M23 rebel group claimed responsibility Tuesday for the weekend attack on Bangboka Airport, located 17 kilometers from Kisangani, capital of Tshopo province. This airport, a key site within the national security apparatus and home to th
body_en:
Kisangani Airport February 4, 2026 — The AFC/M23 rebel group claimed responsibility Tuesday for the weekend attack on Bangboka Airport, located 17 kilometers from Kisangani, capital of Tshopo province. This airport, a key site within the national security apparatus and home to the Third Defense Zone headquarters, was targeted between Saturday, January 31, and Sunday, February 1, 2026, using “kamikaze drones.”
The rebel movement claims to have destroyed the drone command center at Kisangani airport, from which the Armed Forces of the DRC (FARDC) launch operations in Masisi, Walikale, Rutshuru, Lubero, Kalehe, Mwenga, and Minembwe.
Provincial authorities had previously accused the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 rebels of the attacks.
Corneille Nangaa, political coordinator of AFC/M23, justified the operation, accusing the Kinshasa government of orchestrating a “surge of violence” using Sukhoi-23 aircraft, combat drones, and coalition forces. He warned:
“The monopoly on technological terror is definitively broken. The air superiority upon which Tshisekedi's strategy was based is now obsolete. From now on, any air force deployed against the populations of the liberated zones will be neutralized at its source.”
Nangaa added that the attack marks the end of Kisangani as a rear base for the FARDC, stating:
“The doctrine of preemptive defense is activated: every threat will be struck at its point of origin… If Tshisekedi wants dialogue, we are open to it, but if he wants war, let him accept all the consequences.”
While the AFC/M23 claims to have destroyed the drone command center, authorities confirmed that, thanks to the vigilance of the FARDC and security partners, eight drones were neutralized before reaching their target. No casualties or major material damage were reported. The Tshopo provincial government reiterated that “this attack demonstrates, once again, Rwanda’s intention to undermine the Washington peace agreement.”
These attacks caused spontaneous displacement of residents near Bangboka Airport.
This escalation coincides with the February 2, 2026 signing in Doha of the ICGLR-backed mandate between the DRC government and AFC/M23, following a meeting of the ceasefire monitoring and verification mechanism, organized by Qatar as part of ongoing mediation efforts to resolve the conflict in eastern DRC.
