title: Ministry of Finance Defends New Secure License Plates, Denies Opacity and High Costs
excerpt: Kinshasa DRC January 11, 2026 – The Ministry of Finance has rejected allegations surrounding the reform of the vehicle registration system and the introduction of new secure license plates in the Democratic Republic of Congo, insisting that the process is transparent, lawful, and
title_en: Ministry of Finance Defends New Secure License Plates, Denies Opacity and High Costs
excerpt_en: Kinshasa DRC January 11, 2026 – The Ministry of Finance has rejected allegations surrounding the reform of the vehicle registration system and the introduction of new secure license plates in the Democratic Republic of Congo, insisting that the process is transparent, lawful, and
body_en:
Kinshasa DRC January 11, 2026 – The Ministry of Finance has rejected allegations surrounding the reform of the vehicle registration system and the introduction of new secure license plates in the Democratic Republic of Congo, insisting that the process is transparent, lawful, and financially justified.
In a statement, the ministry said it sought to “set the record straight” and counter what it described as confusion and unfounded accusations, reaffirming its commitment to good governance and transparency.
A Reform to Restore Order and Security
According to the ministry, the reform aims to correct serious security flaws and the absence of a clear contractual framework, which had enabled a parallel market to flourish. Authorities reported the circulation of duplicate license plate numbers and the sale of Congolese plates on foreign online platforms.
“Allowing such a situation to continue would have been a grave mistake,” the ministry said, stressing that the reform is intended to restore state authority, strengthen vehicle identification, and protect public finances.
A Relaunched Process After the 2022 Failure
The ministry acknowledged that an earlier project launched in 2022 failed due to technical and legal shortcomings, notably the absence of a required feasibility study and disagreements among potential partners.
The process was subsequently suspended and relaunched under a new legal framework, with approval from the Public Procurement Regulatory Authority (ARMP). Authorities insist this decision was made solely in the public interest.
No Irregular Technical Changes, Government Says
Responding to claims of last-minute technical changes, the ministry said the tender dossier received a no-objection opinion from the Directorate General for Public Procurement Control (DGCMP).
It added that the technical specifications are largely identical to those of the 2022 project and that all three shortlisted companies were invited to submit bids, ensuring equal treatment.
Contract Awarded in Line with Procurement Rules
The ministry denied any opacity or conflict of interest, emphasizing that the project was included in an approved procurement plan and validated by the Prime Minister.
Contrary to some reports, authorities said the contract was awarded through a restricted tender authorized by the DGCMP, not a negotiated procedure. They also noted that the winning bidders were selected before the current Minister of Finance took office.
Clarifying the Cost of License Plates
The ministry rejected claims that the plates cost only $30 to produce, stating that the official price of $65 includes manufacturing, logistics, transport, supplier margins, and system security services.
It also said no private intermediaries are involved in financing and that the share allocated to the public treasury has increased by 14.3%.
The price of license plates, unchanged for more than a decade, has been reduced from $120 to $115, with a further cut to $105 planned for 2027, a move the government says will increase state revenue.
Transition Period and Call for Transparency
Authorities clarified that replacement of old plates is not immediately mandatory and that a one-year transition period is предусмотр, during which old plates remain valid.
The Ministry of Finance said it remains open to audits and dialogue and urged citizens to consult official documents. It called on the public to remain calm and rely on official sources, stating that “access to facts and documents is the best foundation for responsible public debate.”

title: Étienne Davignon Faces Hearing in Patrice Lumumba Assassination Case
excerpt: Brussels Belgium, January 20, 2026 – The Brussels Criminal Court held a crucial hearing on Tuesday in the long-standing case surrounding the assassination of Patrice Lumumba, the first Prime Minister of independent Congo. The hearing involved Étienne Davignon, the 93-year-old for
title_en: Étienne Davignon Faces Hearing in Patrice Lumumba Assassination Case
excerpt_en: Brussels Belgium, January 20, 2026 – The Brussels Criminal Court held a crucial hearing on Tuesday in the long-standing case surrounding the assassination of Patrice Lumumba, the first Prime Minister of independent Congo. The hearing involved Étienne Davignon, the 93-year-old for
body_en:
Brussels Belgium, January 20, 2026 – The Brussels Criminal Court held a crucial hearing on Tuesday in the long-standing case surrounding the assassination of Patrice Lumumba, the first Prime Minister of independent Congo. The hearing involved Étienne Davignon, the 93-year-old former Belgian diplomat and industrial strategist, though he was absent from the proceedings.
The hearing marks the first session since the Belgian federal prosecutor requested on June 17—after over a decade of investigation—that Davignon be sent to trial. He faces charges including illegal detention and transfer, violation of the right to a fair trial, and inhuman and degrading treatment inflicted on Lumumba. Charges of attempted murder have not yet been upheld.
Six grandchildren of Patrice Lumumba attended the hearing as civil parties, joining the proceedings to seek accountability for the 1961 assassination of Lumumba, along with Maurice M’Polo and Joseph Okito, in Katanga amidst Cold War tensions and regional secessions.
Davignon, a prominent figure in Belgian diplomacy and politics who later became a European Commissioner and industrial strategist, was stationed in Kinshasa and Brazzaville in the early 1960s. According to prosecutors, his diplomatic position provided him with information regarding Lumumba’s arrest and the conditions of his transfer.
“This is an important step toward redressing a colonial crime,” said Christophe Marchand, lawyer for the Lumumba family, describing the hearing as a “crucial step.”
The reopening of the case follows extensive historical research, particularly by historian Ludo De Witte, who documented Belgian civilian and military involvement in Lumumba’s execution. Davignon is now the last surviving Belgian among the ten individuals named in the 2011 complaint filed by Lumumba’s family for war crimes, torture, and inhumane treatment.
Judicial sources indicate that the case is expected to be adjourned for deliberation, with no decision anticipated for several weeks.

title: AFC/M23 Defends Achievements and Calls for Preservation of Gains
excerpt: Doha, January 13, 2026 – The AFC/M23 has reaffirmed its commitment to a peaceful resolution of the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), highlighting the progress achieved under the Doha peace process and urging that these gains be preserved. In correspondence a
title_en: AFC/M23 Defends Achievements and Calls for Preservation of Gains
excerpt_en: Doha, January 13, 2026 – The AFC/M23 has reaffirmed its commitment to a peaceful resolution of the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), highlighting the progress achieved under the Doha peace process and urging that these gains be preserved. In correspondence a
body_en:
Doha, January 13, 2026 – The AFC/M23 has reaffirmed its commitment to a peaceful resolution of the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), highlighting the progress achieved under the Doha peace process and urging that these gains be preserved.
In correspondence addressed to the Chairperson of the African Union, Corneille Nangaa Yobeluo, Political Coordinator of the AFC/M23, acknowledged messages conveyed through Angola under the leadership of João Lourenço. He praised Angola’s mediation efforts and underscored the importance of the negotiations conducted in Doha, under the auspices of Qatar, with the active involvement of the African Union, the United States, and other partners.
Nangaa recalled that since March 30, 2024, both the Congolese government and the AFC/M23 have been fully engaged in a negotiation process aimed at addressing the root causes of the conflict through political dialogue.
Five Major Agreements Cited
According to Nangaa, the Doha framework has enabled the signing of five major instruments, described as “structuring and irreversible” milestones in the peace process:
Joint Communiqué – April 24, 2025
Declaration of Principles – July 19, 2025
Mechanism for the Release of Detainees – September 10, 2025

title: South Kivu Government Condemns Looting and Violations by AFC/M23
excerpt: Uvira, South Kivu, DRC, January 17, 2026 — The South Kivu provincial government has denounced the systematic looting, destruction of property, and serious violations of international humanitarian law committed by the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 rebellion in Uvira. In a statement relea
title_en: South Kivu Government Condemns Looting and Violations by AFC/M23
excerpt_en: Uvira, South Kivu, DRC, January 17, 2026 — The South Kivu provincial government has denounced the systematic looting, destruction of property, and serious violations of international humanitarian law committed by the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 rebellion in Uvira. In a statement relea
body_en:
Uvira, South Kivu, DRC, January 17, 2026 — The South Kivu provincial government has denounced the systematic looting, destruction of property, and serious violations of international humanitarian law committed by the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 rebellion in Uvira. In a statement released Friday, January 16, 2026, Governor Jean-Jacques Purusi Sadiki described these acts as extremely serious and indicative of the rebels’ bad faith.
Contrary to the AFC/M23’s correspondence to the UN on January 15, 2026, the government asserts that the rebels organized coordinated operations of looting in Uvira and surrounding areas, demonstrating a flagrant disregard for international humanitarian law and human rights.
“The South Kivu provincial government condemns these criminal acts in the strongest possible terms; it calls upon the international community, the United Nations, the African Union, the ICC, and human rights organizations to document these events and initiate immediate legal proceedings against the perpetrators,” stated the provincial government.
The government emphasized that these acts violate:
Article 33 of the Fourth Geneva Convention (prohibition of pillage)
Article 52 of Additional Protocol I (protection of civilian property)
Article 8 of the Rome Statute of the ICC (pillaging as a war crime)
Various international instruments on property rights and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights
The provincial government warned that these crimes deliberately exacerbate the severe food crisis, raise the cost of living, and deprive the population—mainly dependent on agriculture and livestock—of access to their land and herds, amounting to collective punishment, strictly prohibited under international law.
The statement further revealed that 49 Wowo trucks and 113 Ben trucks were transported from Bukavu under the pretext of moving withdrawn soldiers to the Ruzizi Plain, but were instead used to illegally transport state and private goods to Rwanda. On the night of January 15, 34 Wowo trucks loaded with tar and trucks carrying tricycles essential for livelihoods were seized and moved across the border. Remaining goods were evacuated via Kamanyola, and livestock from the highlands and midlands was driven to Bwegera, depriving locals of essential resources.
Despite the announcement of withdrawal, the AFC/M23 remained in Uvira on January 16, reinforcing positions at Kigongo, 5 km from the city towards Makobola, confirming continued military presence and control.
In a letter to UN Secretary-General António Guterres on January 15, 2026, the AFC/M23 political coordinator, Corneille Nangaa, claimed that Uvira is now under the responsibility of the international community, following their withdrawal announced on December 15, 2025, and dismantled their "observation and surveillance unit", declining future responsibility for the city’s security.
This situation underscores ongoing instability in South Kivu, the continuing humanitarian crisis, and the urgent need for international attention.

title: AFC/M23 Rebels Launch Attacks on FARDC in Mpombi and Iteya
excerpt: Pinga, Walikale January 21, 2026 - Violent clashes erupted on Wednesday morning, January 21, between AFC/M23 rebels and the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC), supported by the Wazalendo, in the localities of Mpombi and Iteya, part of the Kisimba group in Wa
title_en: AFC/M23 Rebels Launch Attacks on FARDC in Mpombi and Iteya
excerpt_en: Pinga, Walikale January 21, 2026 - Violent clashes erupted on Wednesday morning, January 21, between AFC/M23 rebels and the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC), supported by the Wazalendo, in the localities of Mpombi and Iteya, part of the Kisimba group in Wa
body_en:
Pinga, Walikale January 21, 2026 - Violent clashes erupted on Wednesday morning, January 21, between AFC/M23 rebels and the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC), supported by the Wazalendo, in the localities of Mpombi and Iteya, part of the Kisimba group in Walikale territory, North Kivu.
The rebels launched simultaneous attacks against army positions starting around 10:00 a.m., with heavy and light weapons fire reported, plunging the local population into widespread fear.
The administrative secretary of the Kisimba group, Lavie Changwi, confirmed the clashes and said that civilians were forced to flee their homes, seeking refuge in the surrounding forests.
“Mpombi and Iteya are key strongholds for the protection of Pinga. The situation is very worrying due to the intensity of the fighting,” he stated.
These towns, held by FARDC and Wazalendo forces, occupy a mountainous area overlooking Pinga and are considered crucial for the town’s defense.
This attack comes amid an already fragile security context. In December 2025, authorities were alerted to the strengthening of rebel positions in Mpety, considered the main AFC/M23 stronghold in the Pinga region. Reports indicated that rebels were preparing offensives targeting Pinga.
In early January 2026, the rebels attempted to seize Mpombi and Iteya but were repelled by FARDC forces, retreating to their rear base in Mpety.
Following Wednesday's assaults, no official casualty figures have been released. The situation remains tense and unpredictable in the combat zones around Pinga.

title: Prof. Tombola Says Lomé Talks Allow Tshisekedi to Evade Previous Agreements
excerpt: Kinshasa, January 19, 2026 – Researcher and university lecturer Prof. Tombola Gustave has criticized the launch of new peace talks on insecurity in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), arguing that they serve as a way for President Félix Tshisekedi to avoid implementin
title_en: Prof. Tombola Says Lomé Talks Allow Tshisekedi to Evade Previous Agreements
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, January 19, 2026 – Researcher and university lecturer Prof. Tombola Gustave has criticized the launch of new peace talks on insecurity in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), arguing that they serve as a way for President Félix Tshisekedi to avoid implementin
body_en:
Kinshasa, January 19, 2026 – Researcher and university lecturer Prof. Tombola Gustave has criticized the launch of new peace talks on insecurity in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), arguing that they serve as a way for President Félix Tshisekedi to avoid implementing previously signed agreements.
The talks, held in Lomé, the capital of Togo, on January 17, 2026, aimed to strengthen African responses to insecurity in the DRC and the Great Lakes Region.
They brought together former heads of state from five African countries and were led by President Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé, who currently chairs the African Union (AU), alongside representatives of the East African Community (EAC), the Southern African Development Community (SADC), and the Chairperson of the AU Commission, Mahmoud Ali Youssouf.
In an interview on National Television, Prof. Tombola acknowledged that the involvement of the AU Chairperson could be seen as an African approach to conflict resolution.
However, he noted that the AU already had an established framework addressing insecurity in eastern DRC, and pointed out that President Tshisekedi personally traveled to Togo, indicating that he had requested the talks.
“Tshisekedi went to Lomé, although no one knows exactly what he said there. That is when it was announced that the DRC issue was now in the hands of the AU and that President Faure was the mediator,” Tombola said. “He went and told him, ‘You have taken matters into your own hands.’”
The researcher recalled that peace efforts under Tshisekedi have followed a long and complex trajectory. He said the president initially attempted dialogue with the AFC/M23, which the group rejected, before turning to the EAC and SADC, which deployed troops and launched other initiatives.
He added, “The time came for the EAC and SADC to come together, but Tshisekedi placed Rwanda at the center of the issue, arguing that the problem was not AFC/M23 but Rwanda. This led to two tracks: the AFC/M23 talks in Nairobi and the Rwanda-DRC talks in Luanda, which were later handed over to the AU.”
According to Prof. Tombola, the United States and Qatar later joined the process, culminating in the Washington Agreement, but he said the DRC has implemented it only partially.
“In all this, you wonder whether those who sit at the table truly ignore the problem,” he said. “Is it necessary to move from city to city when the issue is already well known and no decisions are being implemented?”
He argued that the DRC continues to disregard agreements reached in Nairobi, Luanda, and Washington, adding that had they been respected, the crisis would have been resolved. He therefore described the Lomé initiative as “another Tshisekedi maneuver.”
“Tshisekedi is not implementing what was agreed in Washington and Doha, but is instead launching another process to keep people busy,” he said. “It is not because he believes Lomé will bring a solution, but because he is delaying what needs to be implemented.”
Meanwhile, Rwandan Minister of Foreign Affairs Olivier Nduhungirehe stated that peace talks in the Great Lakes Region should build on the steps taken in 2025, when the Rwanda-DRC agreement was signed in Washington.

Kinshasa, DRC – January 21, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has sent a list of minerals to the United States, detailing those it is authorized to mine and process under the December 2025 peace and economic cooperation agreement involving Rwanda and supported by Washington.
Two DRC officials, speaking on condition of anonymity, confirmed that the list was sent to Washington, D.C., last week.
The agreement includes the establishment of a joint DRC-U.S. committee tasked with overseeing the mineral exploration and investment process. Congolese members include representatives from the economy, foreign affairs, and finance ministries, along with the head of the mining regulator, ARECOMS.
A DRC official explained that the list, which includes manganese, gold, lithium, copper, and cobalt, was prepared after an in-depth analysis of the country’s strategic resources and the U.S. demand for these minerals, especially for electric vehicle batteries and electronic devices.
The list designates specific mining sites where U.S. investors can operate, including Kisenge and Mutoshi mines in Lualaba Province, Moto in Haut-Uélé, Kilo in Ituri, as well as locations in the two Kivus and Maniema.
Following the submission, the United States is expected to review the list, after which the joint committee will begin discussions to plan the implementation of the agreement.

title_en: DRC: Family of AFC/M23 Leader Faces Arrests, Death Sentences Amid Anti-Rebel Operations
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, January 22, 2026 – Several members of Corneille Nangaa Yobeluo’s family, the leader of the AFC/M23 rebel group, have been detained, while others have fled the Democratic Republic of Congo. Among the first arrested was Nangaa’s younger brother, Baseane Nangaa Putters, cu
body_en:
Kinshasa, January 22, 2026 – Several members of Corneille Nangaa Yobeluo’s family, the leader of the AFC/M23 rebel group, have been detained, while others have fled the Democratic Republic of Congo.
Among the first arrested was Nangaa’s younger brother, Baseane Nangaa Putters, currently held at Ndolo Military Prison. Several family members, including Nangaa’s wife, Yvette Lubanda, and his brother-in-law, Fabrice Lubala, have reportedly been sentenced to death.
The latest arrest involves another younger brother, Didier Ilaani Nangaa, who spent over ten days in an intelligence facility in Isiro, Haut-Uélé province, suspected of supporting the AFC/M23 through mining operations.
Another brother, Christophe Baseane Nangaa, a former Governor of Haut-Uélé and senator, fled to Dubai after learning security forces were searching for him. The government subsequently seized all his assets, accusing him of collaborating with the rebel group, despite his claims of loyalty to President Félix Tshisekedi’s administration.
Family members indicate that around ten other relatives remain imprisoned in separate facilities on accusations of supporting AFC/M23, while others have sought refuge in various countries in Africa and the Americas over the past two years.
The arrests and escapes are part of ongoing security operations in the Wamba area of Haut-Uélé, where authorities suspect hidden weapons caches linked to the rebel group.

title: Wazalendo Takes Control of Uvira After M23 Withdrawal
excerpt: Uvira, January 18, 2026 — Wazalendo fighters have begun taking control of Uvira town following the withdrawal of the AFC/M23 in compliance with ongoing peace talks in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Residents confirmed that Wazalendo forces entered the town on Sunday morning, a
title_en: Wazalendo Takes Control of Uvira After M23 Withdrawal
excerpt_en: Uvira, January 18, 2026 — Wazalendo fighters have begun taking control of Uvira town following the withdrawal of the AFC/M23 in compliance with ongoing peace talks in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Residents confirmed that Wazalendo forces entered the town on Sunday morning, a
body_en:
Uvira, January 18, 2026 — Wazalendo fighters have begun taking control of Uvira town following the withdrawal of the AFC/M23 in compliance with ongoing peace talks in the Democratic Republic of Congo.
Residents confirmed that Wazalendo forces entered the town on Sunday morning, a day after AFC/M23 announced it had fully withdrawn. Videos circulating online show fighters abusing civilians and looting property.
A former South Kivu commander, now based in Kalemie, confirmed the return of Wazalendo fighters, saying they were awaiting instructions from their superiors.
“We must be very careful. Our leaders must first verify that what M23 is saying is true,” he said.
Despite their presence, AFC/M23 stated that it had left Uvira under the responsibility of the international community, urging it to ensure the safety of residents.
In a letter dated January 15, 2026, AFC/M23 informed the United Nations Secretary-General that it had requested MONUSCO to protect the city’s population.
“Our organization, AFC/M23, has decided to place the city of Uvira under the full responsibility of the international community,” said Corneille Nangaa, leader of the group.
He added that a small AFC/M23 monitoring unit had remained temporarily in the town while awaiting the deployment of neutral forces, but that this unit also withdrew on January 15.
AFC/M23 warned the UN that the Burundian army, the FDLR terrorist group, Wazalendo groups, and the Cancuro pose serious security threats to Uvira’s residents.
“Their presence and activities not only threaten the security of civilians, but also the peace process and the security of the region,” the group said.
The coalition called for the urgent deployment of neutral forces to prevent a return to the violence experienced when the city was under DRC government control.
AFC/M23 captured Uvira on December 9, 2025, after a week-long battle in parts of the Ruzizi Valley in South Kivu Province. It said the withdrawal followed a request from the United States to allow peace talks to continue. The group was asked to return to positions within 75 kilometers of the city to enable the international community to ensure civilian protection.
Residents had reported a period of relative calm under M23 control, with people resuming daily activities without violence, theft, or looting.
However, concerns remain high, with fears that following the M23 withdrawal, supporters of the group could face reprisals or targeted killings.

title: Security Measures to Remain Until FDLR Dismantled, Ambassador Tells US Lawmakers
excerpt: Washington, January 22, 2026 – Rwanda has reaffirmed that its security measures will remain in effect until the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) dismantles the FDLR terrorist group, according to a statement by Rwandan Ambassador to the United States, Mathilde Mukantabana, befor
title_en: Security Measures to Remain Until FDLR Dismantled, Ambassador Tells US Lawmakers
excerpt_en: Washington, January 22, 2026 – Rwanda has reaffirmed that its security measures will remain in effect until the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) dismantles the FDLR terrorist group, according to a statement by Rwandan Ambassador to the United States, Mathilde Mukantabana, befor
body_en:
Washington, January 22, 2026 – Rwanda has reaffirmed that its security measures will remain in effect until the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) dismantles the FDLR terrorist group, according to a statement by Rwandan Ambassador to the United States, Mathilde Mukantabana, before the US House of Representatives Subcommittee on Foreign Affairs.
Addressing lawmakers responsible for monitoring developments in Africa, Ambassador Mukantabana traced the origins of the FDLR, noting that its members have committed crimes for over 31 years. She highlighted that the US State Department designated the ALiR/FDLR as a terrorist organization in 2001 following attacks on tourists, including Americans, in Uganda's Bwindi Impenetrable National Park in May 1999.
“Today, the FDLR remains active in eastern DRC, integrated into the operations of the DRC military. UN experts continue to document its activities. This genocidal group, which has existed since 1994, has not been defeated, has been preserved, protected, and supported by successive DRC governments,” Ambassador Mukantabana said.
The ambassador stressed that the DRC’s cooperation with the FDLR, particularly in military operations against the AFC/M23, poses a direct threat to Rwanda. She cited a recent incident in late January 2025, when the group bombed the town of Rubavu, only to be repelled by Rwandan forces.
“Our operations are solely aimed at protecting the Rwandan population by preventing cross-border threats. These measures are not related to seeking political advantage in the DRC or supporting any specific group,” she explained.
Ambassador Mukantabana underlined that Rwanda’s security measures are temporary and will be lifted once the DRC complies with its obligations under the Washington Accords signed on June 27, 2025, and ratified on December 4, 2025. These accords require the DRC to dismantle the FDLR and repatriate its fighters.
“Rwanda’s security measures will be reviewed as the level of threat decreases. Once a review confirms that the DRC government has acted to dismantle the FDLR, these measures will be lifted,” the ambassador assured US lawmakers.
The statement reinforces Rwanda’s long-standing position that cross-border threats from armed groups in eastern DRC directly impact regional security and that responsibility lies with the DRC to neutralize such threats.

title: After AFC/M23 Withdrawal, Governor Purusi Calls for Peaceful Coexistence in Uvira

title_en: After AFC/M23 Withdrawal, Governor Purusi Calls for Peaceful Coexistence in Uvira
excerpt_en: Uvira DRC January 23, 2026 – Jean Jacques Purusi, governor of South Kivu province, returned to Uvira, the provisional provincial capital, on Friday following the withdrawal of the AFC/M23. On his first day back in the city, which he had left more than 40 days earlier, the governo
body_en:
Uvira DRC January 23, 2026 – Jean Jacques Purusi, governor of South Kivu province, returned to Uvira, the provisional provincial capital, on Friday following the withdrawal of the AFC/M23.
On his first day back in the city, which he had left more than 40 days earlier, the governor delivered a strong message calling for peace, unity, and peaceful coexistence among communities.
“To achieve peace, we must not fall into the enemy’s trap. We must live united; we are all children of the same mother and father,” Governor Purusi declared during a public gathering.
He specifically urged an end to hostile rhetoric against the Banyamulenge and other communities, warning against hate speech and collective punishment.
“Do not fall into the trap of saying, ‘We are going to attack the Banyamulenge, kill them, wound them, or destroy their homes.’ That is the enemy’s strategy. We will find those Banyamulenge families who fled because the enemy contributed to their displacement, because they are our brothers,” he stressed.
The AFC/M23 withdrew from Uvira less than a week ago. Following their departure, the Congolese army and its Wazalendo allies reoccupied the city, allowing state institutions to gradually resume operations.
In addition to the governor, the mayor and several other government officials have also returned to Uvira, marking a step toward the restoration of public administration and stability in the city.

title: DRC Ministry of Human Rights Reaffirms Presumption of Innocence in Ilemo Mosengo Nzuzi Case

title_en: DRC Ministry of Human Rights Reaffirms Presumption of Innocence in Ilemo Mosengo Nzuzi Case
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, January 17, 2026 – The Ministry of Human Rights has issued a statement emphasizing the principle of presumption of innocence in the ongoing case of Ilemo Mosengo Nzuzi, which has recently sparked controversy on social media. According to the Ministry, the case has been
body_en:
Kinshasa, January 17, 2026 – The Ministry of Human Rights has issued a statement emphasizing the principle of presumption of innocence in the ongoing case of Ilemo Mosengo Nzuzi, which has recently sparked controversy on social media.
According to the Ministry, the case has been under monitoring by its services since December 20, 2025, and the viral video that circulated on January 14, 2026 is not the trigger for any renewed investigation.
“The liberty of the accused remains a fundamental principle, in accordance with the Constitution, applicable laws, and international human rights standards. Any infringement of this principle constitutes a violation of fundamental rights and freedoms,” the Ministry said in a press release sent to Actualite.CD.
The video in question shows Mosengo Nzuzi appearing weakened while detained in police custody, reigniting public debate over judicial guarantees and the treatment of individuals during criminal proceedings.
The Ministry reminded judicial authorities to rigorously apply the presumption of innocence and uphold the right to liberty during criminal proceedings, except where deprivation of liberty is strictly justified by law.
“Deprivation of liberty is an exception that must be strictly regulated,” the Ministry stressed, underscoring the government’s commitment to protecting human rights throughout the justice system.

title: DRC Government Humanitarian Mission Moves to Tanzania
excerpt: Dar es Salaam, January 12, 2026 – The humanitarian mission of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) arrived in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, on Sunday, January 11, marking the second leg of its regional tour after Burundi. The delegation is led by Ève Bazaiba Masudi, Minister of Stat
title_en: DRC Government Humanitarian Mission Moves to Tanzania
excerpt_en: Dar es Salaam, January 12, 2026 – The humanitarian mission of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) arrived in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, on Sunday, January 11, marking the second leg of its regional tour after Burundi. The delegation is led by Ève Bazaiba Masudi, Minister of Stat
body_en:
Dar es Salaam, January 12, 2026 – The humanitarian mission of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) arrived in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, on Sunday, January 11, marking the second leg of its regional tour after Burundi. The delegation is led by Ève Bazaiba Masudi, Minister of State in charge of Social Affairs, Humanitarian Action and National Solidarity, and Crispin Mbadu Phanzu, Minister Delegate for Francophonie and the Diaspora.
The mission follows decisions of the Council of Ministers after the occupation of Uvira in South Kivu by the AFC/M23, supported by Rwanda. Its objectives include delivering humanitarian assistance to Congolese refugees in Kigoma, strengthening coordination with Tanzanian and Burundian authorities, and mobilizing international partners in response to the regional humanitarian crisis.
Ève Bazaiba noted that more than 67,000 Congolese had already received assistance at the Busuma site in Burundi, calling it an act of national solidarity. She emphasized that the delegation’s mission is to bring comfort, hope, and moral support to displaced compatriots in Burundi and Tanzania, while working for the return of peace.
Despite the difficult living conditions in displacement camps, she stressed that the Congolese government will spare no effort to support its citizens and remains fully committed to the Doha and Washington peace processes. “Every minute that passes worsens the suffering, not only for Congolese people but also for host communities, the region, and the world,” she said.
The humanitarian situation in Burundi continues to deteriorate following intensified fighting between the AFC/M23 and Congolese government forces in eastern DRC, particularly after the fall of Uvira. These clashes have caused mass displacement, despite the rebels’ announced withdrawal.
The situation has reached a critical threshold, with a massive influx of refugees and asylum seekers fleeing violence in South Kivu. Since early December, more than 84,000 people have crossed into Burundi, bringing the total number of Congolese refugees and asylum seekers there to over 200,000. Transit centers and informal settlements are severely overcrowded, some reaching nearly 200% capacity, plunging hundreds of families into extreme vulnerability. Shortages of clean water, sanitation, shelter, food, and medicine heighten the risk of cholera and other life-threatening diseases.
To ease pressure, the Burundian government has designated a new reception site in Bweru, in Ruyigi Buhumuza province, where nearly 21,000 refugees have been transferred. However, conditions remain harsh, with many families still sleeping outdoors due to a lack of adequate shelter.
Across the border in South Kivu, ongoing violence, drone strikes, and bombings have forced more than 500,000 people to flee their homes, many of them multiple times this year. Dozens of schools have been turned into overcrowded shelters, and the first cholera cases have been reported. Persistent insecurity continues to restrict humanitarian access, limiting the ability of aid workers to reach populations in acute distress.
This humanitarian deterioration comes amid controversy surrounding the announced AFC/M23 withdrawal from Uvira, which Congolese authorities view as an attempt to divert attention and reduce international pressure, particularly on Kigali, considered the main supporter of the rebellion. On the ground, the AFC/M23 continues to consolidate its control, establishing a parallel administration beyond the authority of Kinshasa.
The fall of Uvira, a strategic city in South Kivu, has strengthened the rebellion’s grip on both North and South Kivu, raising fears of a potential advance toward Greater Katanga, regarded as the economic heartland of the DRC.

title: AFC/M23 Rebels Capture "Point Zero," Opening Way to Fizi-Centre
excerpt: Mitumba, DRC, January 17, 2026 — The village of "Point Zero", located on the border between the territories of Fizi and Mwenga, on the Mitumba massif, fell to Twirwaneho fighters, allies of the AFC/M23 rebels, on Friday morning, January 16, 2026, after two days of fierce fighting
title_en: AFC/M23 Rebels Capture "Point Zero," Opening Way to Fizi-Centre
excerpt_en: Mitumba, DRC, January 17, 2026 — The village of "Point Zero", located on the border between the territories of Fizi and Mwenga, on the Mitumba massif, fell to Twirwaneho fighters, allies of the AFC/M23 rebels, on Friday morning, January 16, 2026, after two days of fierce fighting
body_en:
Mitumba, DRC, January 17, 2026 — The village of "Point Zero", located on the border between the territories of Fizi and Mwenga, on the Mitumba massif, fell to Twirwaneho fighters, allies of the AFC/M23 rebels, on Friday morning, January 16, 2026, after two days of fierce fighting against the FARDC, supported by the Wazalendo.
Since Thursday, January 15, heavy fighting had been reported in Tuwetuwe, about 15 km from the Mikenge displaced persons camp in the Itombwe sector, where Twirwaneho fighters pushed the army back towards Point Zero.
According to local sources, the FARDC position was attacked on Friday morning, forcing soldiers to retreat to Mulima in the Basiloca group (Tanganyika sector, Fizi territory).
“We were attacked at 5:00 a.m., and by 9:00 a.m., all FARDC soldiers had left the front and were heading towards Mulima. We found ourselves alone on the battlefield. That is why we were forced to retreat when the enemy occupied the village around 10:00 a.m.,” a security source reported.
Point Zero, built in 2018 by displaced people fleeing intercommunal conflicts in Fizi, Mwenga, and Uvira, was a FARDC stronghold. Its occupation by rebels forced residents to flee in torrential rains to Bilende, Kanguli, Nakiele, Mulima, and Lusuku, where their living conditions remain extremely precarious, with no assistance after abandoning their homes.
The fall of Point Zero, the army’s last stronghold in the area, opens the path for the rebels along the Mulima-Mukera axis towards Fizi-centre, enabling further advances toward Tanganyika province via Misisi, bypassing Baraka.
This development marks a significant strategic gain for the AFC/M23 and allied forces, intensifying the humanitarian and security crisis in the region.

title: Eight Suspects Presented to Authorities After Deadly Customary Conflict
excerpt: Bagata, Kwilu January 20, 2026 -- Eight suspects accused of murder and arson that destroyed 34 houses in the village of Lunkuni, located in the Manzasay sector of Bagata territory, were presented to the Governor of Kwilu by the police on Tuesday. They were arrested in connection
title_en: Eight Suspects Presented to Authorities After Deadly Customary Conflict
excerpt_en: Bagata, Kwilu January 20, 2026 -- Eight suspects accused of murder and arson that destroyed 34 houses in the village of Lunkuni, located in the Manzasay sector of Bagata territory, were presented to the Governor of Kwilu by the police on Tuesday. They were arrested in connection
body_en:
Bagata, Kwilu January 20, 2026 -- Eight suspects accused of murder and arson that destroyed 34 houses in the village of Lunkuni, located in the Manzasay sector of Bagata territory, were presented to the Governor of Kwilu by the police on Tuesday.
They were arrested in connection with a customary conflict that led to the assassination of the chief of the Bamenga Lokwa group on January 5 in Lunkuni.
In addition to the local chief, three other deaths were reported on January 7, including two people who were beheaded.
Police also handed over several 12-gauge shotguns recovered from the suspects.
Two weeks after the violence, a large portion of the population remains displaced, hiding in the forest. Authorities confirmed the deployment of the Northern Mobile Intervention Group to stabilize the area and facilitate the return of residents to their homes.
“This was a poorly managed customary conflict that resulted in the assassination of Chief Bamenga. In retaliation, the deceased’s brothers burned down 34 houses. Police were immediately deployed to restore public order. Many residents have not yet returned home and remain in the bush. A special intervention unit is being sent to enable their safe return,” stated Chief Commissioner Camille Atungale, police spokesperson.
Authorities also indicated that additional bodies may not yet have been recovered due to ongoing tensions between rival families competing for customary authority.

title: Museveni Addresses Supporters After Seventh-Term Victory
excerpt: Kampala, January 18, 2026 — After being re-elected to a seventh term, President Yoweri Kaguta Museveni told his rivals that they were fortunate that over 10 million of his supporters did not vote, suggesting that otherwise they would have been deeply ashamed. Uganda’s presidentia
title_en: Museveni Addresses Supporters After Seventh-Term Victory
excerpt_en: Kampala, January 18, 2026 — After being re-elected to a seventh term, President Yoweri Kaguta Museveni told his rivals that they were fortunate that over 10 million of his supporters did not vote, suggesting that otherwise they would have been deeply ashamed. Uganda’s presidentia
body_en:
Kampala, January 18, 2026 — After being re-elected to a seventh term, President Yoweri Kaguta Museveni told his rivals that they were fortunate that over 10 million of his supporters did not vote, suggesting that otherwise they would have been deeply ashamed.
Uganda’s presidential election, held on January 15, 2026, saw Museveni win with 71.6% of the vote, defeating seven other candidates.
Robert Kyagulanyi Ssentamu, popularly known as Bobi Wine, came second with 24.72%.
The Electoral Commission reported that out of 21.6 million registered voters, 52.5% participated.
A total of 11,090,848 votes were counted from 50,739 polling stations nationwide. Museveni received 7,946,772 votes, Bobi Wine 2,741,238, and Mafabi 209,039.
Speaking on his victory, Museveni said, “10 million of my people did not vote. If they had, you would have been deeply ashamed. We got eight million votes, but remember that when we checked the membership, we had 21 million members, over 18 million of whom were eligible to vote.”
Museveni accused the opposition of exploiting the population, alleging that they received foreign money to bribe voters.
“You know that bribe — 10,000 Ugandan shillings for each person. What can 10,000 buy? A fish? A chicken? This is an insult,” he said.
He added that such practices reflect poverty, which must be eradicated to prevent such behavior.
Museveni also praised the Ugandan people, including members of the opposition NUP party led by Bobi Wine, for refusing to join protests.
“There are many NUP members among them. I thank Ugandans. Many came to me and said, ‘We do not want our country to be like Libya. To all you traitors, this is my free advice: stop what you are doing. We know all about you. No matter what, we will fight for peace in Uganda by all means,’” he said.
The 2026 elections differed from those of 2021, as Museveni’s vote total increased, while the number of registered voters also rose by over three million, with a turnout of 59.35%.
In 2021, Museveni received 6,042,898 votes (58.38%), while Bobi Wine came second with 35.08%. Out of 11 candidates, the last received 0.15%.

body_en:
Kigali, Rwanda – January 20, 2026 – Rwanda is aiming to capitalize on participation in the World Economic Forum (WEF) Annual Meeting, currently taking place in Davos, Switzerland from January 19–23, 2026. The event marks the 56th edition of the forum and brings together over 3,000 participants from 130 countries, including 65 heads of state, 400 senior officials, business leaders, civil society actors, and researchers.
Rwanda’s delegation is led by Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation Amb. Nduhungirehe Olivier, alongside Minister of Technology and Innovation Ingabire Paula and Director General of the National Development Agency Jean-Guy Afrika.
The theme of this year’s summit focuses on promoting dialogue in problem-solving, offering a platform to explore solutions to global challenges without resorting to conflict.
Minister Nduhungirehe emphasized Rwanda’s unique contributions, citing the country’s achievements in economy and technology. “Rwanda has a Center for the Fourth Industrial Revolution (C4IR) that promotes advanced technologies,” he said, highlighting the country’s growing technological expertise.
He added that the summit presents opportunities to engage with world leaders on development cooperation and to discuss how Africa can leverage its population of 1.4 billion, predominantly young people, for economic growth.
“This meeting is a chance to study how long-standing global conflicts can be resolved through dialogue and to exchange ideas on economic development and population well-being,” Nduhungirehe said.
The World Economic Forum provides Rwanda and Africa a platform to explore collaboration on economic development, technology, and innovation. Since 2022, Rwanda has been one of the few countries to host a C4IR center, affiliated with WEF, promoting artificial intelligence, digital governance, and data management in Africa.
Rwanda previously hosted the WEF Africa Summit in 2016, becoming the fifth African country to do so, reinforcing its position as a hub for innovation and economic dialogue on the continent.

title_en: Civilian Concerns Mount in Uvira Following AFC/M23 Withdrawal
excerpt_en: Uvira, South Kivu DRC, January 21, 2026 – After the AFC/M23 rebel group withdrew its fighters from the city of Uvira, civilians remain on edge amid reports of looting and violence. Human Rights Watch (HRW) highlighted that some residents have been targeted by Congolese army (FARD
body_en:
Uvira, South Kivu DRC, January 21, 2026 – After the AFC/M23 rebel group withdrew its fighters from the city of Uvira, civilians remain on edge amid reports of looting and violence. Human Rights Watch (HRW) highlighted that some residents have been targeted by Congolese army (FARDC) and Wazalendo militias allegedly demanding valuables, including mobile phones, and in some cases firing on the population.
Starting the morning of January 18, pro-government forces, including FARDC and Wazalendo units, entered the city to restore state authority. However, HRW reports indicate that despite the military presence, residents are facing intimidation and theft, raising concerns about their safety.
“The community fears for its security. Soldiers and Wazalendo are going door to door, demanding phones and firing shots,” a local resident told HRW.
The organization further noted that homes, shops, and places of worship belonging to Banyamulenge residents were heavily looted following the rebel withdrawal, and several civilians sustained injuries. Wazalendo forces reportedly blocked residents from seeking refuge in the surrounding highland areas connecting Uvira, Fizi, and Mwenga territories.
Clémentine de Montjoye, HRW’s Great Lakes researcher, emphasized that the presence of FARDC troops alone is insufficient to protect civilians while Wazalendo continue to operate with impunity.
HRW called on the Congolese government to deploy well-trained forces to disarm Wazalendo and hold accountable those responsible for crimes against civilians, ensuring the safety of the population.

title: DRC Army Accused of Supplying Ammunition to FDLR and Allied Armed Groups
excerpt: January 17, 2026 ; The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) are accused of providing additional tons of ammunition to the FDLR and other allied armed groups to support their fight against the AFC/M23 coalition. Reports from North Kivu Province indicate that on
title_en: DRC Army Accused of Supplying Ammunition to FDLR and Allied Armed Groups
excerpt_en: January 17, 2026 ; The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) are accused of providing additional tons of ammunition to the FDLR and other allied armed groups to support their fight against the AFC/M23 coalition. Reports from North Kivu Province indicate that on
body_en:
January 17, 2026 ; The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) are accused of providing additional tons of ammunition to the FDLR and other allied armed groups to support their fight against the AFC/M23 coalition.
Reports from North Kivu Province indicate that on January 14, 2026, weapons, ammunition, and funds were delivered to leaders of the FDLR, CMC/Domi, and ANCDH/Nyatura Abazungu.
The operation reportedly took place at the DRC military base of Pinga in Walikale Territory and involved several Abanye-Congolese officers. Among those present were Col. Mokoko, responsible for operations in the 34th Military Region; Col. Salomon Tokolonga, commander of the 3402nd Regiment and acting head of forces in Pinga; and the North Kivu Wazalendo coordinator, Col. Cyprien Semivumbi.
Although the DRC government maintains that any collaboration between its soldiers and the FDLR is carried out on an individual basis, the organization and execution of the operation in Pinga suggest a coordinated effort within a broader state program.
Following the delivery, the FDLR and allied groups reportedly transported the weapons and ammunition to active conflict zones, including Bashali-Mokoto, Malemo, and Buhimba in Masisi Territory, as well as Jardin Théicole de Ngeri (JTN) and Katsiro in Rutshuru Territory.
Additional reports indicate that on January 13, more than 50 Blackwater mercenaries were deployed to Pinga to assist the DRC army and allied groups in operations along the Masisi–Walikale border.
Previously, on November 28, 2025, the DRC government reportedly delivered three tons of ammunition to Pinga, intended for the FDLR, NDC-R, and other Nyatura groups, following instructions from Col. Tokolonga.
The continued support for the FDLR and other armed groups, as well as the alleged use of mercenaries, raises questions about the DRC government’s commitment to the peace agreement signed with Rwanda on June 27, 2025, brokered by the United States. Under the agreement, the DRC had pledged to dismantle the FDLR, but the reported actions suggest that implementation remains uncertain.

title: Five RDF Officers Graduate from Four-Year Military Training in Qatar
excerpt: Qatar, January 22, 2026 – Five junior officers of the Rwandan Defence Forces (RDF) successfully completed a four-year training program at various military schools in Qatar, in a ceremony attended by Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al-Thani, Emir of Qatar. Representing the RDF, Col. Bernar
title_en: Five RDF Officers Graduate from Four-Year Military Training in Qatar
excerpt_en: Qatar, January 22, 2026 – Five junior officers of the Rwandan Defence Forces (RDF) successfully completed a four-year training program at various military schools in Qatar, in a ceremony attended by Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al-Thani, Emir of Qatar. Representing the RDF, Col. Bernar
body_en:
Qatar, January 22, 2026 – Five junior officers of the Rwandan Defence Forces (RDF) successfully completed a four-year training program at various military schools in Qatar, in a ceremony attended by Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al-Thani, Emir of Qatar.
Representing the RDF, Col. Bernard Niyomugabo, Defence Attaché at the Rwandan Embassy in Qatar, praised the officers’ dedication and highlighted the importance of the training for enhancing Rwanda’s military capabilities.
This milestone continues a long-standing partnership between Rwanda and Qatar in defense and security cooperation. In January 2025, nine RDF soldiers completed similar training programs in Qatar, demonstrating the ongoing commitment of both countries to strengthen military skills and safeguard national sovereignty.
The ceremony was also attended by Rwandan officials, including Brig. Gen. Franco Rutagengwa, Director of the Gako Military Academy, who emphasized the strategic significance of international military training in preparing Rwanda’s officers for modern security challenges.
Broader Rwanda-Qatar Cooperation
Military training is just one aspect of the growing partnership between Rwanda and Qatar. The two countries have collaborated in several sectors, including:
Security: At the end of 2024, the Rwandan Police and the Qatari Internal Security Service signed a cooperation agreement on security and crime prevention.
Air Transport: Qatar Airways is expected to acquire a 49% stake in RwandAir, while Qatar holds a 60% share in the Bugesera Airport project, which is designed to handle 14 million passengers per year upon completion.
Investment and Strategic Cooperation: The partnership spans multiple sectors, reflecting strong diplomatic ties between Kigali and Doha.
“Training in Qatar equips our officers with advanced skills, enabling them to protect Rwanda’s sovereignty effectively,” Col. Niyomugabo said.
This latest graduation underscores the strengthening bilateral relations and Rwanda’s commitment to professionalizing its armed forces through international partnerships.

title: Rwanda Warns Against “Uncontrollable Actors” and Reaffirms Commitment to Regional Stability
excerpt: Washington Accords January 23, 2026 – In response to renewed clashes in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, Rwanda has reaffirmed its commitment to the Washington Accords signed with the DRC under U.S. auspices, while calling for the strict implementation of security measures t
title_en: Rwanda Warns Against “Uncontrollable Actors” and Reaffirms Commitment to Regional Stability
excerpt_en: Washington Accords January 23, 2026 – In response to renewed clashes in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, Rwanda has reaffirmed its commitment to the Washington Accords signed with the DRC under U.S. auspices, while calling for the strict implementation of security measures t
body_en:
Washington Accords January 23, 2026 – In response to renewed clashes in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, Rwanda has reaffirmed its commitment to the Washington Accords signed with the DRC under U.S. auspices, while calling for the strict implementation of security measures to prevent escalation and protect civilians.
In an official statement issued on Thursday, January 22, Rwanda’s ambassador to the United States, Mathilde Mukantabana, outlined Kigali’s position on the implementation and implications of the accords.
Rwanda expressed its gratitude to the United States for prioritizing the peace process between Rwanda and the DRC, in coordination with Qatar’s mediation efforts, describing the Washington Accords as a major step toward lasting stability, security, and prosperity in the Great Lakes region.
However, the Rwandan diplomat warned of continued violence in eastern DRC, attributing it to “uncontrollable actors,” including mercenaries, militias supported by certain governments, and elements within the Congolese state. According to her, these actors attempted to undermine the Washington Accords by orchestrating violence in November and December 2025 and shifting blame onto Rwanda.
She also stated that the AFC/M23 rebels had unilaterally withdrawn from Uvira in South Kivu, a move Kigali described as a sign of commitment to de-escalation.
The statement recalls the historical insecurity in the region, particularly linked to the FDLR, which Rwanda accuses of responsibility for atrocities committed since 1994.
Rwanda emphasized that it continues to maintain defensive measures to protect its population against any resurgence of genocidal violence.
“The memory of the genocide survivors, the graves of a million victims, and the documented history of the Abacengezi insurgency compel us to maintain our defense capabilities until credible security guarantees are established and the threat disappears permanently,” the statement said.
On the political and economic front, Rwanda stressed that the Washington Accords are not intended to influence the internal affairs of the DRC, but rather to serve as a framework for regional development.
“The Regional Investment Framework for Peace (REIF) identifies key areas for economic cooperation between Rwanda and the DRC, demonstrating the tangible benefits of peace and creating investment and growth opportunities that directly benefit regional populations,” the statement added.
Rwanda reaffirmed its willingness to continue security coordination, contingent upon the disarmament and neutralization of the FDLR, while also supporting cross-border economic development.
Kigali concluded by reiterating its readiness to work with the DRC, the United States, Qatar, the African Union, and other partners to transform the Washington Accords into lasting peace and inclusive regional development.

title: Aubin Minaku, Vice-President of the PPRD, Arrested at His Home
excerpt: Kinshasa, January 18, 2026 – Congolese security forces arrested Aubin Minaku, Vice-President of the People’s Party for Reconstruction and Democracy (PPRD), in the early hours of Sunday morning at his private residence in Kinshasa. The operation was confirmed by several sources cl
title_en: Aubin Minaku, Vice-President of the PPRD, Arrested at His Home
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, January 18, 2026 – Congolese security forces arrested Aubin Minaku, Vice-President of the People’s Party for Reconstruction and Democracy (PPRD), in the early hours of Sunday morning at his private residence in Kinshasa. The operation was confirmed by several sources cl
body_en:
Kinshasa, January 18, 2026 – Congolese security forces arrested Aubin Minaku, Vice-President of the People’s Party for Reconstruction and Democracy (PPRD), in the early hours of Sunday morning at his private residence in Kinshasa.
The operation was confirmed by several sources close to the case, including members of his political entourage and eyewitnesses. The exact reasons for the arrest have not yet been officially disclosed, but the move comes amid rising tensions surrounding figures linked to the former regime of Joseph Kabila.
Mr. Minaku, a former Speaker of the National Assembly and a close ally of the ex-president, was taken to an undisclosed location shortly after midnight. Security sources said the operation proceeded without violence, although the residence was reportedly cordoned off by special forces.
The PPRD has not yet issued an official statement. The arrest follows a series of legal actions targeting former Kabila associates. In recent weeks, Emmanuel Ramazani Shadary, the party’s permanent secretary and unsuccessful candidate in the 2018 presidential election, was also arrested and remains detained at an undisclosed location.
These developments come in the wake of the military court conviction of Joseph Kabila several months ago. The former head of state, now living in exile, was tried in absentia for his alleged role in supporting the AFC/M23 rebellion, which Kinshasa accuses of being backed by Rwanda. Mr. Kabila has been sentenced to death, a verdict his supporters strongly denounce as politically motivated.

title_en: Another Boat Intercepted on Lake Tanganyika
excerpt_en: Fizi, Monday, January 12, 2026 – Another boat navigating Lake Tanganyika was intercepted on Sunday, January 11, by the FARDC and the Wazalendo in Fizi, South Kivu. The vessel, Super Bus, was reportedly en route to Bujumbura for repairs. A patrol stopped the boat shortly after it
body_en:
Fizi, Monday, January 12, 2026 – Another boat navigating Lake Tanganyika was intercepted on Sunday, January 11, by the FARDC and the Wazalendo in Fizi, South Kivu. The vessel, Super Bus, was reportedly en route to Bujumbura for repairs.
A patrol stopped the boat shortly after it departed from the private port of Kivovo, with 12 crew members on board. It was intercepted by army maritime services and the Wazalendo while patrolling near Makobola.
This interception comes just days after another vessel, Okako 2, was stopped in the village of Mizimu, also in Fizi territory.
Since the capture of Uvira by AFC/M23 rebels, several measures have been implemented to restrict movement in the region, including a ban on traffic between South Kivu and Tanganyika Province via Lake Tanganyika.
In the context of the ongoing conflict between AFC/M23 rebels and the Congolese army, any vessel operating on Lake Tanganyika is now treated with heightened suspicion.

title: Persistent Insecurity Escalates

title_en: Persistent Insecurity Escalates
excerpt_en: Kibua, Walikale, January 17, 2026 — The security situation remains precarious in Kibua and its surroundings, in the Ihana group (Walikale territory), North Kivu, with several serious incidents reported on Thursday, January 15. According to the head of the Ihana group, Mwami Kitwa
body_en:
Kibua, Walikale, January 17, 2026 — The security situation remains precarious in Kibua and its surroundings, in the Ihana group (Walikale territory), North Kivu, with several serious incidents reported on Thursday, January 15.
According to the head of the Ihana group, Mwami Kitwana Ngulu Séraphin, the first incident involved a member of the FARDC (Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo) who was shot in the left foot. The exact circumstances are unclear, but local sources suggest it occurred following a heated argument with superiors.
Later the same day, another FARDC soldier stabbed a young boy in the hand and attempted to shoot him moments later, sparking outrage and fear among residents already traumatized by the recurring insecurity in the region.
The situation worsened further with the intervention of a militiaman from the NDC-Renovated armed group, who carried out armed robberies on Kalonge/Mubea Hill. Vehicles, particularly motorcycle taxis, were looted, temporarily paralyzing traffic and intensifying the sense of insecurity among road users.
In response to this resurgence of violence, Mwami Kitwana Ngulu Séraphin called on military and administrative authorities to take urgent measures to restore order and protect the civilian population.
Meanwhile, the residents of Kibua continue to live in constant fear, urging the State to strengthen discipline within the regular forces and the wazalendo operating in this volatile part of North Kivu.

title: FARDC Post Set on Fire by Wazalendo Militiamen
excerpt: Misevere, Lubero January 20, 2026 — A post belonging to the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) was set on fire overnight from Monday to Tuesday in Misevere, a village near Musienene, close to the Musienene primary school, in the Baswagha chiefdom of Lubero t
title_en: FARDC Post Set on Fire by Wazalendo Militiamen
excerpt_en: Misevere, Lubero January 20, 2026 — A post belonging to the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) was set on fire overnight from Monday to Tuesday in Misevere, a village near Musienene, close to the Musienene primary school, in the Baswagha chiefdom of Lubero t
body_en:
Misevere, Lubero January 20, 2026 — A post belonging to the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) was set on fire overnight from Monday to Tuesday in Misevere, a village near Musienene, close to the Musienene primary school, in the Baswagha chiefdom of Lubero territory, North Kivu.
The fire is attributed to Wazalendo militiamen. The incident reportedly occurred while the FARDC soldiers who normally occupy the post were absent, having reportedly left on a mission to Beni territory, leaving the position undefended. A local civil society leader described the act as a serious offense.
The military administrator of Lubero territory confirmed the incident but did not provide details on the circumstances or measures taken.
This attack comes just days after a similar incident in the same region. On January 8, 2026, an abandoned FARDC position was set on fire in Vusigha, in the Musienene-Katholo area, Ngulo group, also within the Baswagha chiefdom. The soldiers had left the site on January 6, 2026, to return to Beni, after which all barracks built by loyalist forces were burned to the ground by unidentified individuals.

title: Rwanda Urges Regional Talks to Uphold Washington Accords
excerpt: Kigali, January 17, 2026 — Rwanda has called for regional security talks to build on the Washington Accords, emphasizing that ongoing peace efforts in the Great Lakes Region should not ignore the diplomatic progress achieved in 2025. Foreign Minister Olivier Nduhungirehe made the
title_en: Rwanda Urges Regional Talks to Uphold Washington Accords
excerpt_en: Kigali, January 17, 2026 — Rwanda has called for regional security talks to build on the Washington Accords, emphasizing that ongoing peace efforts in the Great Lakes Region should not ignore the diplomatic progress achieved in 2025. Foreign Minister Olivier Nduhungirehe made the
body_en:
Kigali, January 17, 2026 — Rwanda has called for regional security talks to build on the Washington Accords, emphasizing that ongoing peace efforts in the Great Lakes Region should not ignore the diplomatic progress achieved in 2025.
Foreign Minister Olivier Nduhungirehe made the remarks during a high-level dialogue aimed at strengthening African responses to insecurity in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and the wider Great Lakes Region. The meeting was held in Togo and chaired by President Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé.
Minister Nduhungirehe stressed that future negotiations must respect the steps taken in 2025, including the peace agreement signed on December 4 in Washington.
“At the beginning of 2026, it is important to emphasize that the diplomatic achievements of 2025 must not be undermined and should be preserved. Rwanda hopes that today’s talks will help strengthen the African Union’s coordination mechanism, and support the actions of Washington and Doha,” he said.
The peace agreement between Rwanda and the DRC focuses on dismantling the FDLR terrorist group, which has threatened regional security for years, removing Rwanda’s security measures, and facilitating the repatriation of refugees.
It also includes cooperation in infrastructure, park conservation, healthcare, mining, and other development sectors.

title: Senator Murigande: “It Is Incomprehensible That People Are Dying of Hunger in Rwanda”
excerpt: Kigali, January 19, 2026 – Senator Dr. Charles Murigande has expressed concern that people are dying of hunger in Rwanda, a country with favorable rainfall and strong agricultural potential, calling for intensified research to boost food production. He made the remarks on January
title_en: Senator Murigande: “It Is Incomprehensible That People Are Dying of Hunger in Rwanda”
excerpt_en: Kigali, January 19, 2026 – Senator Dr. Charles Murigande has expressed concern that people are dying of hunger in Rwanda, a country with favorable rainfall and strong agricultural potential, calling for intensified research to boost food production. He made the remarks on January
body_en:
Kigali, January 19, 2026 – Senator Dr. Charles Murigande has expressed concern that people are dying of hunger in Rwanda, a country with favorable rainfall and strong agricultural potential, calling for intensified research to boost food production.
He made the remarks on January 19, 2026, during a session of the Rwandan Senate with the Minister of Agriculture and Livestock, who presented the current state of the sector.
Dr. Murigande stressed that greater investment in agricultural research is essential to determine which crops are best suited to Rwanda, how yields can be increased, and how the sector can be modernized.
He noted that Rwanda has a limited land area for farming, making research the main driver of growth in both agriculture and livestock.
“Rwanda’s land is small and we cannot expand it. What will save us is putting more effort into research,” he said.
Drawing a comparison with Israel, Dr. Murigande said it was unacceptable that people in Rwanda face hunger despite having more favorable natural conditions.
“Israel has little land, much of it sandy, yet it produces a great deal because of research. It is incomprehensible that in Rwanda we would starve,” he said.
He added that even when rainfall is uneven, it remains sufficient nationwide and should be better harnessed through scientific methods.
Dr. Murigande also emphasized that research could improve animal feed, seed quality, and overall agricultural productivity.
“Everything will come from sustained research. I want the Minister to tell us about the plans to strengthen research in collaboration with other institutions,” he said.
He further urged the government to leverage the country’s skilled graduates, suggesting that individuals with master’s degrees and advanced training be employed to conduct research, develop suitable seeds, and promote food self-sufficiency.
His remarks come amid ongoing drought in parts of Kayonza District, where residents in the sectors of Ndego, Mwiri, Kabare, and Rwinkwavu continue to face severe food shortages. The crisis contributed to the dismissal of district leaders late last year.
Responding to the concerns, Minister of Agriculture and Livestock Dr. Ndabamenye Telesphore said the government is prioritizing research to guide investment and technology adoption.
He warned that if current farming practices continue, Rwanda will struggle to achieve food self-sufficiency by 2050, when the population is projected to reach 22 million. Under traditional methods, the country would need 10.3 million hectares of arable land—an impossible target.
However, with improved agricultural methods, only 3.4 million hectares would be required, and with international best practices, just 1.4 million hectares would suffice—an achievable goal given that Rwanda currently has more than 1.3 million hectares of arable land.

excerpt_en: Kigali, Rwanda – January 21, 2026 – The Rwandan Ministry of Justice has submitted a comprehensive report to the United Nations Human Rights Office, detailing the country’s progress on 160 recommendations regarding the protection of human rights. These recommendations, drawn from
body_en:

These recommendations, drawn from a broader set of 260 proposals received in 2021, have been implemented at an estimated rate of 97%, according to Minister of Justice and Attorney General Dr. Ugirashebuja Emmanuel.

Rwanda has hosted refugees from countries such as Afghanistan and Sudan, and advanced environmental protection through the Green Fund, investing over $277 million in 64 projects that created over 100,000 jobs and launching a Carbon Market to mitigate climate change.
Countries including Mexico, Mauritius, Montenegro, Morocco, Mozambique, Nepal, the Netherlands, Niger, Nigeria, Norway, Oman, Paraguay, the Philippines, Portugal, Qatar, Korea, Russia, Senegal, Sierra Leone, Singapore, Somalia, South Africa, South Sudan, Spain, Sudan, Sweden, Togo, and many others recognized Rwanda’s achievements and offered recommendations on NGOs, freedom of expression, and press freedom.

title: 47 Officers Complete Training at Police College

title_en: 47 Officers Complete Training at Police College
excerpt_en: Musanze District, January 16, 2026 — Forty-seven police officers and other security personnel at the level of junior officers have successfully completed a five-month training course on leadership and conflict resolution at the Police College (NPC) in Musanze District. The 13th P
body_en:
Musanze District, January 16, 2026 — Forty-seven police officers and other security personnel at the level of junior officers have successfully completed a five-month training course on leadership and conflict resolution at the Police College (NPC) in Musanze District.
The 13th Police Junior Command and Staff Course (PJCSC) included 36 Rwanda National Police officers, five officers from the National Correctional Service (RCS), five officers from the National Bureau of Investigation (RBI), and one officer from the National Intelligence and Security Service (NISS).
The Deputy Inspector General of Police (DIGP) for Administration and Personnel, DCG Jeanne Chantal Ujeneza, highlighted the purpose of the training, describing it as a foundation for developing leadership and professionalism among junior officers.
“This training aims to enhance leadership skills in junior officers. In today’s world, security challenges are evolving due to technological developments, not just job experience. Effective leadership requires forward-thinking, planning, coordination, and decision-making that provide solutions to current challenges,” she said.
She added, “We hope that the knowledge and skills gained from this training will help you address security threats, both conventional and technological.”
DIGP Ujeneza emphasized that leadership is not defined solely by rank, but also by integrity, responsibility, fairness, and the ability to make decisions that protect the public, uphold the law, and promote national interests. She reminded graduates to exercise their authority professionally and responsibly.
The Commissioner of Police (CP) Rafiki Mujiji, head of the Police Academy, said the course focused on professional conduct and ethics, reinforced through practical exercises, collaboration, teamwork, and field trips that helped students apply knowledge in real-world contexts.
CP Mujiji encouraged graduates to make full use of the skills gained in their work assignments, noting that their role extends beyond following instructions. Officers are expected to think strategically, provide sound advice, lead effectively, uphold ethics and values, and utilize modern methods and tools to improve performance and deliver efficient and timely services.

excerpt_en: Bukavu DRC, January 22, 2026 – During a meeting of AFC/M23 members in Bukavu on January 21, leader Corneille Nangaa explained that the rebel group’s decision to withdraw from Uvira was made to demonstrate willingness for peace talks. Nangaa stated that while AFC/M23 previously ca
body_en:
Bukavu DRC, January 22, 2026 – During a meeting of AFC/M23 members in Bukavu on January 21, leader Corneille Nangaa explained that the rebel group’s decision to withdraw from Uvira was made to demonstrate willingness for peace talks.
Nangaa stated that while AFC/M23 previously captured Uvira, the withdrawal was intended to build trust in ongoing negotiations.
“In recent days you’ve heard calls for ‘Uvira, Uvira, Uvira.’ We left Uvira to show goodwill, as we have been repeatedly asked to vacate the city, demonstrating that AFC/M23 does not seek war,” Nangaa said.
He emphasized that the group maintains capable forces, noting that the decision to return to Uvira was operationally feasible, but not the ultimate goal.
“There is no doubt you have forces. Today we say we could go back to Uvira if needed. We have all the capabilities, but that is not our objective,” Nangaa added.
The rebels entered Uvira on December 9, 2025. A week later, the group announced it would withdraw at the request of the United States, which assured the continuation of peace talks. By January 17, 2026, AFC/M23 had partially left the city, awaiting the arrival of neutral forces, after which Congolese troops and Wazalendo militias re-entered Uvira.

title: 13th Governors’ Conference in Kwilu: New Dates Pending, Airport Rehabilitation Contract Reassigned
excerpt: Kinshasa, January 22, 2026 – Preparations for the 13th session of the Governors’ Conference, scheduled to take place in Kwilu Province, were reviewed on Wednesday during a working meeting at the Prime Minister’s Office. The meeting, chaired by the Deputy Chief of Staff to the Pri
title_en: 13th Governors’ Conference in Kwilu: New Dates Pending, Airport Rehabilitation Contract Reassigned
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, January 22, 2026 – Preparations for the 13th session of the Governors’ Conference, scheduled to take place in Kwilu Province, were reviewed on Wednesday during a working meeting at the Prime Minister’s Office. The meeting, chaired by the Deputy Chief of Staff to the Pri
body_en:
Kinshasa, January 22, 2026 – Preparations for the 13th session of the Governors’ Conference, scheduled to take place in Kwilu Province, were reviewed on Wednesday during a working meeting at the Prime Minister’s Office.
The meeting, chaired by the Deputy Chief of Staff to the Prime Minister, brought together the Permanent Secretary of the Governors’ Conference, the Vice-Governor of Kwilu, the Director General of the Congolese Agency for Major Works (ACGT), and the Director General of Safrimex.
Discussions focused primarily on the progress of rehabilitation works at the Bandundu and Kikwit airports, particularly the runways and aprons, as well as on urban road projects, pending the announcement of new conference dates by the Head of State.
The Permanent Secretary, currently on mission in Bandundu, reported that urban road works are progressing normally. However, rehabilitation of the Bandundu airport runway and tarmac has been suspended following the termination of the contract between the Roads Authority and the Civil Aviation Authority. The initial contractor reportedly failed to demonstrate sufficient technical and financial capacity to complete the project within the required timeframe.
The contract has now been awarded to Safrimex, while feasibility studies continue under the coordination of the Congolese Agency for Major Works. Authorities emphasized the need to accelerate the process to ensure the mobility of conference participants. Priority will be given to reinforcing the runway and tarmac to allow the conference to proceed, while full airport construction will continue under the same company.
“The studies are complete. It is now up to the government to support Safrimex, the company in charge of the work in Bandundu. The government demands quality work so that Bandundu can have an airport worthy of its status and capable of supporting air traffic development,” said Jean-Rigobert Tshimanga, Permanent Secretary of the Governors’ Conference.
Kwilu Vice-Governor Professor Espoir Masamanki assured the public that preparations on the ground are continuing, particularly in terms of accommodation and site development, and that mobilization remains strong ahead of the announcement of new dates.
“We have explored several options to accelerate the Bandundu airport project so that, during the next visit, the Head of State and his guests can land under optimal conditions. In both Bandundu and Kikwit, the population is highly motivated and eagerly awaiting the new date,” he said.
Construction work at the Bandundu and Kikwit airports has been suspended since December 10, 2025. According to the Roads Authority, completion rates currently stand at 23% in Bandundu and 15% in Kikwit. Meanwhile, concrete work continues on Kwango Avenue near the Central Bank of Congo, along with the construction of drainage ditches, although temporary structures have yet to be installed.
