title: Jamaica Welcomes Rwandan Army Team to Support Disaster Recovery Efforts
excerpt: Kingston, January 15, 2026 — The Government of Jamaica has officially welcomed a team of Rwandan Army construction personnel deployed to assist in the recovery and rehabilitation of infrastructure damaged by the disaster. The welcoming ceremony took place at the Royal Jamaican Mi
title_en: Jamaica Welcomes Rwandan Army Team to Support Disaster Recovery Efforts
excerpt_en: Kingston, January 15, 2026 — The Government of Jamaica has officially welcomed a team of Rwandan Army construction personnel deployed to assist in the recovery and rehabilitation of infrastructure damaged by the disaster. The welcoming ceremony took place at the Royal Jamaican Mi
body_en:
Kingston, January 15, 2026 — The Government of Jamaica has officially welcomed a team of Rwandan Army construction personnel deployed to assist in the recovery and rehabilitation of infrastructure damaged by the disaster.
The welcoming ceremony took place at the Royal Jamaican Military Academy in Kingston on 15 January 2026, and was presided over by the Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Trade, Senator Kamina Johnson Smith.
Senator Johnson Smith expressed gratitude to the Government of Rwanda, particularly President Paul Kagame and the people of Rwanda, for their support. She noted that the team’s experience would make a significant contribution to Jamaica’s recovery efforts and praised Rwanda’s partnership and brotherhood in responding to the increasing impacts of climate change-related disasters.
Speaking on behalf of the Rwanda Defence Forces (RDF), Col. Claudien Bizimungu conveyed Rwanda’s solidarity with the Government and people of Jamaica. He delivered a message from the RDF leadership, emphasizing Rwanda’s commitment to standing with Jamaica throughout its rebuilding and repair process.
Col. Bizimungu also highlighted that the deployment reflects Rwanda’s broader vision in international cooperation and relief efforts, underscoring the RDF’s experience in reconstruction and community-based activities.
The Commander of the RDF Reconstruction Team, Col. Moses Kayigamba, stated that the team will work closely with the Jamaican Armed Forces and other government agencies as part of the cooperation agreement between the two countries. He added that the deployment aligns with President Paul Kagame’s decision to cooperate with the Republic of Jamaica, announced during his visit in April 2022.

Uvira, DRC – January 21, 2026 – The AFC/M23 coalition, which has been fighting the DRC government, explained the reasons behind its withdrawal from Uvira town before the arrival of neutral forces.
Spokesperson Lawrence Kanyuka told researcher Dr. Bojana Coulibaly that the coalition had planned to leave a monitoring group in the city to maintain security, but mediators refused, demanding a full withdrawal. “There was politics behind it. We explained that we were not leaving Uvira to abandon residents, but they did not allow our group to stay,” Kanyuka said.
The coalition emphasized that it complied with all requirements, taking serious measures to ensure safety, and dissociated itself from any violence that occurred after its departure. Kanyuka expressed regret over atrocities committed by Wazalendo groups and DRC forces, including looting, destruction of homes and churches, and torture since January 18, 2026.
The withdrawal plan had initially been announced on December 16, 2025, with the coalition leaving by January 17, 2026, after waiting for the neutral forces to arrive.

title: Opposition Leader Seth Kikuni Goes Into Exile

title_en: Opposition Leader Seth Kikuni Goes Into Exile
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, January 19, 2026 – Opposition leader Seth Kikuni has left the country and is now in exile, following what his political allies describe as a discreet, coordinated, and courageous operation that ensured his safety and preserved his physical and moral integrity. In a stat
body_en:
Kinshasa, January 19, 2026 – Opposition leader Seth Kikuni has left the country and is now in exile, following what his political allies describe as a discreet, coordinated, and courageous operation that ensured his safety and preserved his physical and moral integrity.
In a statement released Monday, the Consultation Framework for Political and Social Forces said the former 2023 presidential candidate faced an imminent arbitrary political procedure, linked to a letter dated December 15, 2025, from the Auditor General of the Supreme Military Court to the Prosecutor General of the Court of Cassation.
The coalition expressed its deep gratitude to all individuals and organizations involved in what it called a delicate rescue operation, carried out amid serious threats and flagrant violations of fundamental freedoms. It also announced that Mr. Kikuni would address national and international audiences in the coming days to clarify the circumstances of his departure.
Mr. Kikuni was released from Makala Prison on March 1, 2025, after six months of detention, having been sentenced in September 2024 to one year in prison for “incitement to civil disobedience” and “spreading false rumors.”
Upon his return to Kinshasa on October 18, 2025, after attending an opposition summit in Nairobi, he was re-arrested at Ndjili International Airport by individuals presenting themselves as members of the National Intelligence Agency (ANR). His passport, confiscated by the Directorate General of Migration, has not been returned.
On Monday, the opposition leader also strongly criticized the president’s trip to Davos, Switzerland, where he is attending the 56th World Economic Forum.

body_en:
Goma, January 20, 2026 – Virunga National Park announced the birth of a male mountain gorilla to Sebutimbiri, a female in the Mapuwa family. This marks the second birth recorded in the park this year.
With this addition, the Mapuwa family now numbers 28 individuals. The birth occurred in the Mikeno sector, one of the key habitats for mountain gorillas within the park.
The park highlighted the significance of the birth for both social dynamics within gorilla groups and broader conservation programs aimed at supporting this endangered species. International partners, including the European Union and UNESCO, continue to support efforts to protect these primates.
Earlier in January, Virunga National Park reported another milestone: the first twin birth of the year, which occurred on January 3, bringing attention to the park’s ongoing successes in conservation despite challenges.
Virunga National Park, established in 1925 on the border between Rwanda and Uganda, is Africa’s oldest national park and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Covering 7,800 km² in North Kivu province, the park hosts exceptional biodiversity.
The global population of mountain gorillas is estimated at 1,063, with around 350 individuals residing in Virunga, according to 2021 estimates. However, the park faces continued threats from armed clashes between FARDC and AFC/M23 rebels, which endanger both ecosystems and conservation teams.

Masisi, North Kivu – January 11, 2026 – Clashes broke out today between AFC/M23 rebels and Wazalendo forces in Kazinga, located in the Osso Banyungue sector of Masisi territory.
Local sources reported that the Wazalendo attacked rebel positions beginning at 6:00 a.m., with heavy and light weapons fire heard throughout the area. Observers suggest the attack may be intended to preempt a rebel offensive on positions held by government forces and Wazalendo in the Nyamaboko 1 and 2 groups.
This confrontation comes just two days after AFC/M23 reinforced positions in Kazinga and Kasopo, a move previously denounced by local traditional authorities. The situation remains tense, according to local sources.

Walikale, January 15, 2026 —Nine fighters from the AFC/M23 rebellion surrendered to the Wazalendo of the FPP/AP (Patriotic Forces for Peace/People's Army) on Monday, January 12, 2026, in Fatua, in the Munzoa area (Kisimba group), Walikale territory, North Kivu.
According to security sources, the fighters came from the Lubero territory and said they were fleeing the suffering they endured within the rebellion.
The fighters surrendered with five weapons. They are reportedly former FARDC soldiers captured during the fall of Goma.
Military authorities, confirming the surrender, called on other compatriots still within rebel ranks to break away and continue to honor their oath to the nation.
The surrendered fighters were handed over by the Wazalendo to the FARDC (Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo) in Fatua and are reportedly en route to Pinga.

Kasopo, Walikale, DRC January 19, 2026 — The AFC/M23 rebel position located on Mount Kasopo, on the border between the Kisimba and Ikobo groups in Walikale territory (North Kivu), was targeted early Monday morning, January 19, by FARDC airstrikes.
According to local accounts, a Congolese army drone flew over the area throughout the night from Sunday to Monday. Around 4:00 a.m., residents of surrounding villages were awakened by bomb explosions dropped by the drone on the position.

Since the beginning of 2026, this is the first rebel position targeted by FARDC airstrikes in the Walikale territory.

body_en:
Buleusa, Walikale, DRC January 23, 2026 - A rebel position of the AFC/M23 was destroyed by airstrikes conducted by the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) on Friday, January 23, in Buleusa, located in the Ikobo region of Walikale territory, North Kivu.
The operation reportedly took place around 1:00 p.m., when an FARDC drone targeted the rebel camp, a strategic site in the area. Local sources reported that the position was completely destroyed, with flames and thick smoke visible from afar, causing panic among the population.
Witnesses said the rebels fled after the bombing, seeking refuge in nearby parts of the town. “We saw flames and thick smoke rising from the camp. The rebels ran immediately,” one resident said.
Military sources confirmed that the strike is part of ongoing operations in Walikale, where the AFC/M23 has been attempting to consolidate its positions in recent weeks. The FARDC has increasingly deployed drones to locate and neutralize rebel bases, a strategy that appears to be yielding results on the ground.
Despite this success, the security situation remains fragile, with residents of Buleusa and surrounding villages fearing reprisals or renewed clashes. No official figures on rebel casualties have been released, but the strike reportedly inflicted significant material losses and dealt a major blow to the operational capacity of the AFC/M23 in the area.

title: EAC Deploys Observers to Monitor Uganda Elections, Led by Edda Mukabagwiza
excerpt: Kigali/Kampala, January 13, 2026 — Rwandan lawyer and diplomat Edda Mukabagwiza has been appointed to lead the East African Community (EAC) observer mission for Uganda’s upcoming presidential and parliamentary elections scheduled for January 15, 2026. On January 13, the EAC deplo
title_en: EAC Deploys Observers to Monitor Uganda Elections, Led by Edda Mukabagwiza
excerpt_en: Kigali/Kampala, January 13, 2026 — Rwandan lawyer and diplomat Edda Mukabagwiza has been appointed to lead the East African Community (EAC) observer mission for Uganda’s upcoming presidential and parliamentary elections scheduled for January 15, 2026. On January 13, the EAC deplo
body_en:
Kigali/Kampala, January 13, 2026 — Rwandan lawyer and diplomat Edda Mukabagwiza has been appointed to lead the East African Community (EAC) observer mission for Uganda’s upcoming presidential and parliamentary elections scheduled for January 15, 2026.
On January 13, the EAC deployed 61 observers from across its member states to monitor the electoral process. The team includes members of the EAC Assembly, national electoral commissions, foreign affairs ministries, human rights commissions, civil society organizations, and the EAC Secretariat.
Mukabagwiza, whose extensive experience includes serving as Deputy Speaker of the Rwandan Parliament, Minister of Justice, ambassador to multiple countries, and a practicing lawyer, emphasized the mission’s independence and impartiality.
“We are not here to interfere in the electoral process, approve political outcomes, or announce results,” Mukabagwiza said. “Our mission is to observe objectively, collect accurate information, and report impartially.”
Observers will be stationed across Uganda, engaging with the Electoral Commission, political parties, candidates, civil society, media, security agencies, and other stakeholders to monitor the elections comprehensively.
Following the polls, the EAC team is expected to issue an interim report on the conduct of the elections, followed by a final report submitted to the EAC Council of Ministers, the Ugandan government, and other stakeholders. The reports will include recommendations to strengthen future electoral processes and ensure transparency and fairness.

Kigali/Kampala, January 13, 2026 — Rwandan lawyer and diplomat Edda Mukabagwiza has been appointed to lead the East African Community (EAC) observer mission for Uganda’s upcoming presidential and parliamentary elections scheduled for January 15, 2026.
On January 13, the EAC deployed 61 observers from across its member states to monitor the electoral process. The team includes members of the EAC Assembly, national electoral commissions, foreign affairs ministries, human rights commissions, civil society organizations, and the EAC Secretariat.
Mukabagwiza, whose extensive experience includes serving as Deputy Speaker of the Rwandan Parliament, Minister of Justice, ambassador to multiple countries, and a practicing lawyer, emphasized the mission’s independence and impartiality.
“We are not here to interfere in the electoral process, approve political outcomes, or announce results,” Mukabagwiza said. “Our mission is to observe objectively, collect accurate information, and report impartially.”
Observers will be stationed across Uganda, engaging with the Electoral Commission, political parties, candidates, civil society, media, security agencies, and other stakeholders to monitor the elections comprehensively.
Following the polls, the EAC team is expected to issue an interim report on the conduct of the elections, followed by a final report submitted to the EAC Council of Ministers, the Ugandan government, and other stakeholders. The reports will include recommendations to strengthen future electoral processes and ensure transparency and fairness.

title: Zero Tolerance for Corruption Drives Indian Investment in Rwanda

title_en: Zero Tolerance for Corruption Drives Indian Investment in Rwanda
excerpt_en: New Delhi/Kigali, January 13, 2026 — Rwanda’s strong stance against corruption and its business-friendly environment are key factors behind the surge in Indian investment, according to Rwanda’s Ambassador to India, Jacqueline Mukangira. Speaking to the Indian news agency IANS on
body_en:
New Delhi/Kigali, January 13, 2026 — Rwanda’s strong stance against corruption and its business-friendly environment are key factors behind the surge in Indian investment, according to Rwanda’s Ambassador to India, Jacqueline Mukangira.
Speaking to the Indian news agency IANS on January 11, 2026, during the Vibrant Gujarat Regional Conference, Ambassador Mukangira said Rwanda’s stable legal framework, ease of doing business, and strict anti-corruption policies continue to attract investors from India, particularly from the state of Gujarat.
“Rwanda is a good place to invest because investors are facilitated in many ways, including tax incentives and other business-friendly measures,” she said. “Another important factor is that both local and foreign investors operate in an environment of zero tolerance for corruption.”
She noted that Rwanda and India maintain strong diplomatic and economic relations, with Indian businesses playing a major role in Rwanda’s economy.
“Rwanda and India have excellent relations, and many Indians are doing business in Rwanda, especially from Gujarat,” Mukangira said. “India is the second-largest investor in Rwanda and also ranks second in terms of trade.”
Rwanda imports a wide range of goods from India, including medicines, technological equipment, clothing, rice, and sugar, much of which originates from Gujarat.
According to the Rwanda Development Board (RDB), India was Rwanda’s second-largest investor in 2024, after China. That year, China invested $460 million (14.1% of total investment), while India invested $445.1 million (13.6%).
Diplomatic ties between the two countries have deepened in recent years. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi paid his first official visit to Rwanda in 2018, following visits by President Paul Kagame in 2017 and 2018. During Prime Minister Modi’s visit, several agreements were signed, including a $200 million grant and support for Rwanda’s Girinka Munyarwanda program, through which he donated 200 cows.

title: UN Court Rejects Alfred Musema’s Request for Early Release
excerpt: The International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals (IRMCT) has rejected a request for early release filed by Alfred Musema, a former Rwandan tea factory director convicted for his role in the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi. Musema, 76, was arrested in Switzerland on Feb
title_en: UN Court Rejects Alfred Musema’s Request for Early Release
excerpt_en: The International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals (IRMCT) has rejected a request for early release filed by Alfred Musema, a former Rwandan tea factory director convicted for his role in the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi. Musema, 76, was arrested in Switzerland on Feb
body_en:
The International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals (IRMCT) has rejected a request for early release filed by Alfred Musema, a former Rwandan tea factory director convicted for his role in the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi.
Musema, 76, was arrested in Switzerland on February 11, 1995, and later transferred to the custody of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR). He was found responsible for leading and participating in multiple massacres in Kibuye Prefecture between April and May 1994, including attacks on Gitwa Hill, Muyira, Rwirambo Hill, Mataba, and the Nyakavumu Cave, where more than 300 Tutsis were killed and burned.
On January 27, 2000, the ICTR convicted Musema of genocide, extermination, and rape, sentencing him to life imprisonment. Although the Appeals Chamber later overturned the rape conviction in November 2001, it upheld his life sentence for other crimes against humanity.
After serving part of his sentence in Mali and later in Benin, Musema has made several attempts to secure early release. His first request in August 2019 was rejected because he had not yet served two-thirds of his sentence, based on international standards that equate a life sentence with 45 years of imprisonment. A subsequent appeal was dismissed in January 2020.
In January 2025, Musema again petitioned for early release, citing more than 30 years of detention, good conduct in prison, positive relations with fellow inmates, and acknowledgment that the genocide occurred. He also indicated that he intended to live with his family in Switzerland if released.
In a decision dated January 12, 2026, IRMCT President Graciela Gatti Santana acknowledged Musema’s good behavior and recognition of the genocide but ruled that these factors were insufficient given the gravity of his crimes. The court noted that Musema has neither confessed nor expressed remorse, a key requirement for early release.
The judge further emphasized that Musema was a powerful figure in Kibuye who could have prevented the killings but instead stood by and, in many cases, actively participated. Medical reports also indicated that he is in good health, eliminating humanitarian grounds for release.
As a result, Musema will remain in prison.

title: DRC Army Accused of Drone Strike on Kalundu Bridge in Uvira
excerpt: The AFC/M23 coalition has accused the Democratic Republic of Congo’s army of carrying out a major drone attack in Uvira, South Kivu province, on the afternoon of January 14, 2026. According to AFC/M23 spokesperson Lawrence Kanyuka, the Congolese armed forces used unmanned aerial
title_en: DRC Army Accused of Drone Strike on Kalundu Bridge in Uvira
excerpt_en: The AFC/M23 coalition has accused the Democratic Republic of Congo’s army of carrying out a major drone attack in Uvira, South Kivu province, on the afternoon of January 14, 2026. According to AFC/M23 spokesperson Lawrence Kanyuka, the Congolese armed forces used unmanned aerial
body_en:
The AFC/M23 coalition has accused the Democratic Republic of Congo’s army of carrying out a major drone attack in Uvira, South Kivu province, on the afternoon of January 14, 2026.
According to AFC/M23 spokesperson Lawrence Kanyuka, the Congolese armed forces used unmanned aerial vehicles to bomb the Kalundu bridge in Uvira territory, causing extensive damage and putting civilian lives at risk. Photographs shared by Kanyuka on social media show a large residential building severely damaged by the strike.
“In the face of these serious acts, AFC/M23 calls on citizens and the international community to bear witness to the actions of the Kinshasa government that ignore its commitments, especially the Doha principles,” Kanyuka said.
The alleged strike follows another drone attack attributed to the Congolese army on January 12 in the Mukoko area of Minembwe commune and other border zones, which reportedly claimed the lives of several civilians.
These developments come amid ongoing peace talks in Doha between the Congolese government and AFC/M23. The coalition accuses the government of undermining the negotiations through continued military operations.
Meanwhile, President Félix Tshisekedi is reportedly working to launch a new national dialogue in Kinshasa, bringing together Congolese from all ethnic groups—a move that critics say could sideline the Doha process and its outcomes.

title: Burundi Reinforces Military Presence in Kalemie Amid Tensions in Eastern DRC
excerpt: Kalemie, DRC – January 20, 2026 – Burundi has significantly increased its military presence in the town of Kalemie, capital of Tanganyika Province, amid concerns that the AFC/M23 coalition could resume fighting in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). According to s
title_en: Burundi Reinforces Military Presence in Kalemie Amid Tensions in Eastern DRC
excerpt_en: Kalemie, DRC – January 20, 2026 – Burundi has significantly increased its military presence in the town of Kalemie, capital of Tanganyika Province, amid concerns that the AFC/M23 coalition could resume fighting in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). According to s
body_en:
Kalemie, DRC – January 20, 2026 – Burundi has significantly increased its military presence in the town of Kalemie, capital of Tanganyika Province, amid concerns that the AFC/M23 coalition could resume fighting in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).
According to security sources, the Burundian government has deployed up to 29,000 soldiers, along with members of the Imbonerakure, to protect the city from a possible takeover by AFC/M23 forces. In Kalemie, Burundian troops have reportedly coordinated with the DRC army, Wazalendo militias, the FDLR, as well as foreign contractors and personnel.
On January 13, two ships carrying hundreds of Burundian soldiers arrived at the Port of Kalemie from Bujumbura via Rumonge, according to eyewitnesses. Three days earlier, two aircraft had transported approximately 400 DRC soldiers into the city.
Analysts note that the current troop buildup resembles the situation in Goma at the end of 2024, when more than 60,000 troops were deployed to prevent AFC/M23 from capturing the city—an effort that ultimately failed when Goma fell on January 27, 2025.
In Kalemie, however, there is currently no confirmed evidence that AFC/M23 intends to advance on the city. The group previously captured Uvira on December 9, 2025, before withdrawing all fighters by January 17, 2026, moving toward Kamanyola.
The joint actions of the Burundian army, DRC forces, and allied groups suggest preparations for renewed military operations against AFC/M23 positions in South Kivu Province.
Sources in South Kivu report that since January 7, Burundian and DRC forces have been conducting surveillance operations on Lake Tanganyika, primarily from Kalemie, extending to Baraka and Makobola in Fizi Territory.
On that date, approximately 2,000 troops arrived aboard three ships at the Port of Baraka. Both in Baraka and Kalemie, heavy and light weapons, as well as other military equipment, have continued to be delivered.
The DRC government’s arsenal reportedly includes five surveillance drones, four CH-4 combat drones, two Sukhoi-25 fighter jets, three Mi-24 attack helicopters, and four Mi-8 transport helicopters, operated in part by foreign contractors.
On January 9, a boat carrying more than 150 Burundian commandos, reportedly in disguise, was spotted at the Port of Baraka en route to Makobola. A Burundian soldier with the rank of sergeant said their mission was to attack AFC/M23 positions.
Leaders of Wazalendo militias, including William Yakutumba, who styles himself as “General,” also confirmed their intention to launch operations aimed at removing AFC/M23 from eastern DRC following its withdrawal from Uvira.
On January 18, the Permanent Secretary of AFC/M23, Benjamin Mbonimpa, warned that if DRC government forces continued to attack their positions, they would be defeated, adding that international support for the government would not be unconditional.

title: France Calls for Reopening of Goma Airport, Confirms Full Disbursement of €850 Million in Emergency Humanitarian Aid - January 20, 2026
excerpt: France has raised the issue of the reopening of Goma International Airport and confirmed that the entire €850 million in emergency humanitarian aid pledged for the Great Lakes region has already been fully disbursed. France took part in a high-level meeting on the coherence and c
title_en: France Calls for Reopening of Goma Airport, Confirms Full Disbursement of €850 Million in Emergency Humanitarian Aid - January 20, 2026
excerpt_en: France has raised the issue of the reopening of Goma International Airport and confirmed that the entire €850 million in emergency humanitarian aid pledged for the Great Lakes region has already been fully disbursed. France took part in a high-level meeting on the coherence and c
body_en:
France has raised the issue of the reopening of Goma International Airport and confirmed that the entire €850 million in emergency humanitarian aid pledged for the Great Lakes region has already been fully disbursed.
France took part in a high-level meeting on the coherence and consolidation of the peace process in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and the Great Lakes region, held on January 17, 2026, in Lomé, Togo. The meeting brought together facilitators, including former heads of state, leaders of the East African Community (EAC) and the Southern African Development Community (SADC), alongside several international partners. It was convened at the initiative of Faure Gnassingbé, African Union mediator for the crisis in eastern DRC.
During the discussions, France presented an initial progress assessment on the implementation of financial commitments made at the Paris Conference for Peace and Prosperity in the Great Lakes Region, held on October 30, 2025. Of the €1.5 billion pledged by 70 states and international organizations, all emergency humanitarian funding, amounting to €850 million, has already been released.
France reiterated the severity of the humanitarian crisis in eastern DRC, stressing that the funds are intended to meet urgent needs, ensure essential services, and strengthen civilian protection, particularly in areas affected by violence and forced displacement. It also encouraged remaining donors to accelerate their disbursements in the coming weeks.
The French authorities further underlined the urgent need to remove humanitarian obstacles, recalling the commitments made in Paris regarding the humanitarian reopening of Goma airport. France expressed its readiness to contribute, alongside its partners and in coordination with the United Nations, to the logistical and coordination efforts required to reopen the airport for humanitarian flights.
The Paris Conference aimed to mobilize international support to address the humanitarian emergency in the Great Lakes region while backing mediation efforts led by the United States, Qatar, and the African Union. On the margins of the event, discussions also focused on regional economic integration, described as a key pillar for sustainable peace after decades of instability.
At the conclusion of the Paris meetings, two major announcements were made: the mobilization of €1.5 billion in humanitarian aid for the region, and the intention to reopen Goma International Airport, the capital of North Kivu. French President Emmanuel Macron described the reopening of the airport as a concrete and essential signal for the population of North Kivu, calling for swift implementation with the support of international mediators.
However, the announcement sparked strong opposition from the AFC/M23 rebel movement. The group rejected any decision by the Kinshasa authorities to reopen the airport, claiming that the infrastructure lies within what it describes as “liberated territory.” The movement accused Congolese authorities of having looted and sabotaged the facility and insisted that only the AFC/M23 could authorize its reopening.
In the same statement, the group maintained that the dispute between Kinshasa and Kigali does not concern it, asserting that the Congolese government alone bears responsibility for its relations with neighboring states and should resolve its disputes without involving the movement.
body_fr:
France has raised the issue of the reopening of Goma International Airport and confirmed that the entire €850 million in emergency humanitarian aid pledged for the Great Lakes region has already been fully disbursed.
France took part in a high-level meeting on the coherence and consolidation of the peace process in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and the Great Lakes region, held on January 17, 2026, in Lomé, Togo. The meeting brought together facilitators, including former heads of state, leaders of the East African Community (EAC) and the Southern African Development Community (SADC), alongside several international partners. It was convened at the initiative of Faure Gnassingbé, African Union mediator for the crisis in eastern DRC.
During the discussions, France presented an initial progress assessment on the implementation of financial commitments made at the Paris Conference for Peace and Prosperity in the Great Lakes Region, held on October 30, 2025. Of the €1.5 billion pledged by 70 states and international organizations, all emergency humanitarian funding, amounting to €850 million, has already been released.
France reiterated the severity of the humanitarian crisis in eastern DRC, stressing that the funds are intended to meet urgent needs, ensure essential services, and strengthen civilian protection, particularly in areas affected by violence and forced displacement. It also encouraged remaining donors to accelerate their disbursements in the coming weeks.
The French authorities further underlined the urgent need to remove humanitarian obstacles, recalling the commitments made in Paris regarding the humanitarian reopening of Goma airport. France expressed its readiness to contribute, alongside its partners and in coordination with the United Nations, to the logistical and coordination efforts required to reopen the airport for humanitarian flights.
The Paris Conference aimed to mobilize international support to address the humanitarian emergency in the Great Lakes region while backing mediation efforts led by the United States, Qatar, and the African Union. title: Civil Society Gathers to Strengthen Oversight of Mining Revenues
excerpt: Lubumbashi Haut-Katanga, January 24, 2026 – Civil society organizations in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) are stepping up efforts to improve financial governance and transparency in the mining sector. A two-day workshop, held from January 23–24, 2026, brings together memb
title_en: Civil Society Gathers to Strengthen Oversight of Mining Revenues
excerpt_en: Lubumbashi Haut-Katanga, January 24, 2026 – Civil society organizations in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) are stepping up efforts to improve financial governance and transparency in the mining sector. A two-day workshop, held from January 23–24, 2026, brings together memb
body_en:
Lubumbashi Haut-Katanga, January 24, 2026 – Civil society organizations in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) are stepping up efforts to improve financial governance and transparency in the mining sector. A two-day workshop, held from January 23–24, 2026, brings together members of the “Congo Is Not For Sale” (CNPAV) platform and other stakeholders to share best practices in citizen oversight of public fund management.
The workshop focuses on the allocation and management of mining revenues in the provinces of Lualaba, Haut-Uele, and Haut-Katanga, key regions for the DRC’s mineral production. According to Fabien Mayani, a CNPAV steering committee member, the initiative aims to strengthen the ability of civil society to analyze, research, and interact with public authorities, ensuring effective citizen oversight.
“Despite reforms to the mining code and increased revenues from rising mineral prices, poverty remains a pressing reality. Our goal is to ensure that revenues collected by provinces are transparently and effectively managed,” said Mayani.
The workshop highlighted persistent challenges in mining revenue management, including non-compliance with governance rules, lack of transparency, and weak oversight by public bodies. Participants cited EITI data showing that the DRC mobilized over $20 billion in mining revenues between 2018 and 2023, yet questioned how these funds are allocated locally.
“If Haut-Katanga receives $20 million in mining royalties, how are these funds used?” asked Mayani, emphasizing the need for clear reporting and public accountability.
Recommendations emerging from the workshop include:
Strengthening the Court of Auditors and other oversight bodies.
Increasing transparency and public access to financial reports.
Enhancing local authorities’ capacity to mobilize and manage revenue.
Collaborating with the General Inspectorate of Finance (IGF) for better supervision.
Encouraging public accountability, including sanctions for mismanagement.
The CNPAV workshop continues through Saturday, January 24, with organizers aiming to create a structured and effective framework for citizen monitoring of public funds derived from the mining sector.
Social and Health

title: DRC Moves to Establish Steering Committee for Washington Accords Implementation
excerpt: Kinshasa, DRC – January 11, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is taking steps to implement the Washington Accords, signed under the auspices of the Trump administration on December 4, 2025. Prime Minister Judith Suminwa announced at the Council of Ministers meeting on
title_en: DRC Moves to Establish Steering Committee for Washington Accords Implementation
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, DRC – January 11, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is taking steps to implement the Washington Accords, signed under the auspices of the Trump administration on December 4, 2025. Prime Minister Judith Suminwa announced at the Council of Ministers meeting on
body_en:
Kinshasa, DRC – January 11, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is taking steps to implement the Washington Accords, signed under the auspices of the Trump administration on December 4, 2025. Prime Minister Judith Suminwa announced at the Council of Ministers meeting on January 9, 2026, that she had convened a working session on January 8 with ministers responsible for executing these accords.
The session aimed to establish a government-level framework to streamline projects and ensure implementation in line with the President’s policy. A steering committee will be created to develop a roadmap to coordinate government actions and monitor commitments under the accords.
Prime Minister Suminwa also plans to meet with the expanded Economic Situation Committee on January 13, 2026, to harmonize actions and clarify clauses in the agreements.
The Washington Accords, described as historic, reaffirm the DRC-Rwanda peace agreement of June 27, 2025, and aim to foster economic cooperation, regional integration, and lasting peace. They include the Regional Economic Integration Framework (REIF) and multiple bilateral instruments with the United States, including the Strategic Partnership Agreement, the Enhanced Security Partnership, and the US-Rwanda Framework for Shared Economic Prosperity.
Despite government support, the accords face criticism within the DRC. Archbishop Fulgence Muteba Mugalu of Lubumbashi criticized the agreements as a potential “sell-off”, warning that they could sacrifice national development and compromise the future of the Congolese people.

excerpt_en: Walikale, January 14, 2026 —AFC/M23 rebels launched coordinated attacks on Tuesday afternoon, January 13, targeting the villages of Buma, Mpombi, and Iteya in the Kisimba group, Walikale territory, North Kivu. After nearly three hours of fighting, the attackers were repelled by t
body_en:
Walikale, January 14, 2026 —AFC/M23 rebels launched coordinated attacks on Tuesday afternoon, January 13, targeting the villages of Buma, Mpombi, and Iteya in the Kisimba group, Walikale territory, North Kivu.
After nearly three hours of fighting, the attackers were repelled by the Wazalendo, forcing the rebels to withdraw toward Mpety, in the Banakindi area, according to sources on the ground.
The human toll from the clashes has not yet been established. However, the fighting triggered a mass displacement of residents into surrounding bush areas. Local administrative authorities report that displaced families began gradually returning to their villages on Wednesday.
As of now, Buma, Mpombi, and Iteya remain under Wazalendo control, while the security situation in the area remains fragile.

title: Looting and Chaos Force Several Parishes to Cancel Masses
excerpt: Uvira, South Kivu, DRC January 18, 2026 — Looting was reported Sunday in several neighborhoods of Uvira, in South Kivu province, where young people broke into buildings and stole various items, according to witnesses. The morning was marked by repeated gunfire, creating a climate
title_en: Looting and Chaos Force Several Parishes to Cancel Masses
excerpt_en: Uvira, South Kivu, DRC January 18, 2026 — Looting was reported Sunday in several neighborhoods of Uvira, in South Kivu province, where young people broke into buildings and stole various items, according to witnesses. The morning was marked by repeated gunfire, creating a climate
body_en:
Uvira, South Kivu, DRC January 18, 2026 — Looting was reported Sunday in several neighborhoods of Uvira, in South Kivu province, where young people broke into buildings and stole various items, according to witnesses.
The morning was marked by repeated gunfire, creating a climate of insecurity and triggering looting across different parts of the city. Administrative buildings were among the targets.
Due to this deteriorating security situation, several Catholic parishes, including the Uvira Cathedral, were forced to cancel Sunday masses.
At this stage, it remains unclear who controls the situation on the ground. Youths claiming affiliation with the Wazalendo group were seen in some neighborhoods, while the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) were reportedly absent from the city.
These events occurred the day after a column of AFC/M23 fighters left Uvira on Saturday, January 17. Armed men in fatigues and helmets were seen departing the city, some on foot and others in trucks, with their number estimated at at least 200.
The AFC/M23 claims this group was its “observation and surveillance unit” and states that their departure marks the completion of its withdrawal from Uvira, announced on January 15, while declaring that it now disclaims all responsibility for the security of the city and its inhabitants.
Gunfire had already been heard around Uvira on Saturday, and anxiety remained high among residents by the end of the day.

title: Clashes Erupt Between FARDC and AFC/M23 Rebels in Strategic Pinga Area
excerpt: Buma, Walikale, DRC - Violent clashes erupted on Friday, January 23, between AFC/M23 rebels and the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC), supported by the Wazalendo militia, in Buma and the Ciprès Mountains, along the border between Baljnda and Banakindi in th
title_en: Clashes Erupt Between FARDC and AFC/M23 Rebels in Strategic Pinga Area
excerpt_en: Buma, Walikale, DRC - Violent clashes erupted on Friday, January 23, between AFC/M23 rebels and the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC), supported by the Wazalendo militia, in Buma and the Ciprès Mountains, along the border between Baljnda and Banakindi in th
body_en:
Buma, Walikale, DRC - Violent clashes erupted on Friday, January 23, between AFC/M23 rebels and the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC), supported by the Wazalendo militia, in Buma and the Ciprès Mountains, along the border between Baljnda and Banakindi in the Pinga region of Walikale territory, North Kivu.
Fighting reportedly began around 5:00 a.m., when rebel elements launched attacks on FARDC positions. The clashes occurred along the road linking Balinda and Banakindi, in the Kisimba region, a strategic mountainous area overlooking Munsanga, considered a key security stronghold for Pinga.
Heavy and light weapons fire reverberated for hours, sending residents fleeing into nearby forests in fear for their safety. Many villagers from Munsanga, Buma, and surrounding communities remain displaced as a result of the attacks.
By midday, military authorities had not released official figures on casualties or material damage. However, local sources indicate that the FARDC mounted a resolute defense, attempting to contain the rebels’ advance and protect Pinga, an important administrative and humanitarian center in the region.
These clashes come amid a fragile security situation in Walikale, characterized by repeated armed attacks, population displacement, and a worsening humanitarian crisis. Civil society groups in the region have urged the government and loyalist forces to reinforce security measures to prevent the fall of Pinga, which could have serious consequences for thousands of civilians already living in precarious conditions.

Bujumbura, January 14, 2026 — Burundi is witnessing a renewed struggle for political power between President Évariste Ndayishimiye and Révérien Ndikuriyo, Secretary General of the ruling CNDD-FDD party. Recent statements by Ndikuriyo have fueled speculation over who truly holds authority in the country.
At a press conference on January 2, Ndikuriyo suggested that his influence in Burundi rivals, or even surpasses, that of the president, signaling a shift in internal party dynamics. Observers note that Ndikuriyo has increasingly criticized senior government officials, refuted economic claims, and asserted control over key national decisions, including border management with the Democratic Republic of Congo and Rwanda.
He publicly challenged the Minister of Finance, Alain Ndikumana, over alleged security threats involving a fertilizer company, and contradicted government assurances on petroleum shortages, stating the problem would persist until at least 2029. These statements contrast with President Ndayishimiye’s assurances that mining and other resources would strengthen the economy.
Political analysts highlight that tension escalated over control of the National Assembly leadership. Ndayishimiye opposed Daniel Gélase Ndabirabe continuing as head of deputies, while Ndikuriyo and CNDD-FDD leaders insisted he remain. This disagreement extended to cabinet formation, with Ndayishimiye appointing ministers loyal to him, including in defense, security, justice, foreign affairs, and finance. Ndikuriyo publicly rejects the legitimacy of this government, further demonstrating the power divide.
The ongoing military challenges in eastern DRC have also weakened Ndayishimiye’s perceived authority, bolstering Ndikuriyo’s position within the party. Analysts note that while both leaders share ideological goals—opposing foreign exploitation and criticizing government institutions—their methods and influence are sharply contested.
Historically, the CNDD-FDD has experienced recurring internal conflicts, including power struggles under former President Pierre Nkurunziza between 2005 and 2010. Ndikuriyo’s assertiveness reflects a continuation of this pattern, where political authority is often enforced through loyalty, intimidation, or the marginalization of rivals.
Despite Ndayishimiye’s public warnings to government staff about dual allegiances, observers question his ultimate ability to enforce authority over CNDD-FDD’s powerful party structures. The current power struggle underscores the fragility of institutional governance in Burundi and the enduring influence of party leadership over state affairs.

title: I&M Bank Partners with Toyota Rwanda to Expand Access to Vehicle Ownership
excerpt: Kigali, January 8, 2026 — I&M Bank Rwanda has entered into a strategic partnership with Toyota Rwanda Ltd to help customers acquire vehicles through affordable financing and exclusive price concessions. The partnership agreement was signed on January 8, 2026, at Toyota Rwanda’s h
title_en: I&M Bank Partners with Toyota Rwanda to Expand Access to Vehicle Ownership
excerpt_en: Kigali, January 8, 2026 — I&M Bank Rwanda has entered into a strategic partnership with Toyota Rwanda Ltd to help customers acquire vehicles through affordable financing and exclusive price concessions. The partnership agreement was signed on January 8, 2026, at Toyota Rwanda’s h
body_en:
Kigali, January 8, 2026 — I&M Bank Rwanda has entered into a strategic partnership with Toyota Rwanda Ltd to help customers acquire vehicles through affordable financing and exclusive price concessions.
The partnership agreement was signed on January 8, 2026, at Toyota Rwanda’s headquarters in Karuruma, Kigali City. Toyota Rwanda is the authorized distributor of Toyota vehicles and accessories in the country.
Under the agreement, I&M Bank customers — as well as prospective clients — will be able to purchase Toyota vehicles through soft loans and preferential pricing, making car ownership more accessible, particularly for individuals with limited financial resources.
Speaking at the signing ceremony, the Head of Retail Banking and Branches at I&M Bank Rwanda, Yves Kayihura, said the initiative aims to remove financial barriers and promote broader access to reliable transportation.
“This partnership will enable our customers to access quality vehicles while the bank uses the car itself as collateral, eliminating the need for additional assets,” Kayihura said. “We are also providing insurance services, allowing customers to complete the entire process through one institution in a short time.”
He added that I&M Bank has a dedicated car lending department and an integrated insurance system to ensure a seamless customer experience.
Toyota Rwanda’s Chief Operating Officer, Patrick Kanyandekwe, said the agreement reflects the company’s commitment to improving customer service and strengthening its collaboration with financial institutions.
“This partnership will make it easier for customers to receive discounts on the vehicles they want and obtain them quickly,” Kanyandekwe said. “It also demonstrates our desire to continue enhancing our services while maintaining a strong relationship with I&M Bank.”
He further noted that Toyota Rwanda remains responsible for post-sale vehicle servicing and currently offers a range of 13 different vehicle models to meet diverse customer needs.

title: Rwanda Hosts African Handball Championship, Focuses on Winning and National Pride
excerpt: Kigali, January 22, 2026 – Rwanda has demonstrated its ability to host major sports competitions while also prioritizing victory, according to Minister of Sports Nelly Mukazayire. Speaking to RBA on January 21, the day the African Handball Championship began in Rwanda, Minister M
title_en: Rwanda Hosts African Handball Championship, Focuses on Winning and National Pride
excerpt_en: Kigali, January 22, 2026 – Rwanda has demonstrated its ability to host major sports competitions while also prioritizing victory, according to Minister of Sports Nelly Mukazayire. Speaking to RBA on January 21, the day the African Handball Championship began in Rwanda, Minister M
body_en:
Kigali, January 22, 2026 – Rwanda has demonstrated its ability to host major sports competitions while also prioritizing victory, according to Minister of Sports Nelly Mukazayire. Speaking to RBA on January 21, the day the African Handball Championship began in Rwanda, Minister Mukazayire emphasized that the country is not only preparing to organize events but also to field competitive teams that make the nation proud.
The tournament, held from January 21 to 31, 2026, brought together 16 teams from across the continent, including Algeria, Angola, Benin, Cameroon, Cape Verde, the Republic of Congo, Egypt, Gabon, Guinea, Kenya, Morocco, Nigeria, Rwanda, Tunisia, Uganda, and Zambia. Rwanda faced Zambia in the opening match, winning decisively 30–19.
Minister Mukazayire highlighted that hosting international competitions enhances the country’s image while also contributing to the development of Rwanda’s tourism sector, a key source of foreign exchange. She stated:
“We are preparing our teams not only to host but to play and to win. We no longer want to be mere hosts; we want to compete at the highest level and bring victory home.”
The championship provided a platform for Rwanda to showcase organizational capacity, national talent, and the growing competitiveness of its athletes, reinforcing the country’s ambition to become a prominent hub for sports in Africa.

title: Brig. Gen. Charles Simuyuni Nakeempa Appointed Head of Great Lakes Regional Border Security Mechanism
excerpt: Livingstone, Zambia, January 13, 2026 — Brigadier General Charles Simuyuni Nakeempa of the Zambian army has been appointed as the new head of the Great Lakes Africa Regional Joint Border Security Mechanism (MCVE/EJVM). The decision was made during a meeting of regional defense mi
title_en: Brig. Gen. Charles Simuyuni Nakeempa Appointed Head of Great Lakes Regional Border Security Mechanism
excerpt_en: Livingstone, Zambia, January 13, 2026 — Brigadier General Charles Simuyuni Nakeempa of the Zambian army has been appointed as the new head of the Great Lakes Africa Regional Joint Border Security Mechanism (MCVE/EJVM). The decision was made during a meeting of regional defense mi
body_en:
Livingstone, Zambia, January 13, 2026 — Brigadier General Charles Simuyuni Nakeempa of the Zambian army has been appointed as the new head of the Great Lakes Africa Regional Joint Border Security Mechanism (MCVE/EJVM). The decision was made during a meeting of regional defense ministers held on January 10, 2026, in Livingstone, Zambia. Rwanda’s Defence Minister Juvenal Marizamunda attended the meeting.
The regional council also announced that Colonel Arlindo Sebastiao Vandunem Fernandes from Angola will serve as deputy head of the EJVM.
Established in September 2012, the EJVM was created to manage and resolve border security disputes between member countries through investigation and military expertise. The body is headquartered in Goma and has played a key role in de-escalating regional conflicts and assisting in operations involving cross-border security incidents.
The EJVM has been involved in numerous border security interventions, including the July 20, 2021 operation when Rwanda handed over 19 fighters of the RED Tabara armed group captured in Nyungwe Park to Burundi, with EJVM personnel participating in the process.

title: Tensions Escalate in Uganda as Gen. Muhoozi Targets Bobi Wine
excerpt: Kampala, Uganda – January 20, 2026 – Political tensions in Uganda have intensified following statements by Army Chief of Staff Gen. Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who announced that 22 members of the National Unity Platform (NUP) were killed in a single week and appeared to threaten opposi
title_en: Tensions Escalate in Uganda as Gen. Muhoozi Targets Bobi Wine
excerpt_en: Kampala, Uganda – January 20, 2026 – Political tensions in Uganda have intensified following statements by Army Chief of Staff Gen. Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who announced that 22 members of the National Unity Platform (NUP) were killed in a single week and appeared to threaten opposi
body_en:
Kampala, Uganda – January 20, 2026 – Political tensions in Uganda have intensified following statements by Army Chief of Staff Gen. Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who announced that 22 members of the National Unity Platform (NUP) were killed in a single week and appeared to threaten opposition leader Bobi Wine, the popular name of Robert Kyagulanyi.
The conflict has deep roots, but political hostilities had largely subsided during the recent campaign period.
On January 15, during the Ugandan general elections, Bobi Wine, who secured 24.7% of the vote, second to President Yoweri Museveni, reported that his home was attacked by soldiers and police, forcing him to go into hiding.
That night, Ugandan authorities said that opposition supporters attempted to force their way into a vote counting center, resulting in more than 10 people killed.
Gen. Muhoozi issued several statements online threatening NUP members. In one post, he declared, “We have killed 22 NUP terrorists. I pray that the 23rd will be Bobi Wine.” He warned that opposition figures would be targeted wherever found unless President Museveni intervened.
He also reportedly gave Bobi Wine 48 hours to surrender to authorities, warning that failure to do so would result in him being treated as a rebel.
Responding to the threats, Bobi Wine stated that he had secured a safe location and would reveal himself on his own terms, criticizing the regime for attacking his home. He said: “You ordered an attack on my house to harm me; I defeated them, and they escaped. I will show myself when I want, and then you and your father can do whatever you want.”
The situation has sparked widespread concern, as some of Gen. Muhoozi’s messages included graphic threats against the opposition leader.
Following the elections, Bobi Wine and NUP party members denounced the provisional results, alleging they were rigged.
President Museveni was declared the winner, securing a seventh term with 71.6% of the vote, further fueling tensions between the ruling party and opposition forces.

title: Luanda Consults Congolese Religious Leaders
excerpt: The meeting brought together bishops from the National Episcopal Conference of Congo (CENCO) and pastors from the Church of Christ in Congo (ECC). It followed two visits within a week by President Félix Tshisekedi to Luanda for consultations with his Angolan counterpart. The dipl
title_en: Luanda Consults Congolese Religious Leaders
excerpt_en: The meeting brought together bishops from the National Episcopal Conference of Congo (CENCO) and pastors from the Church of Christ in Congo (ECC). It followed two visits within a week by President Félix Tshisekedi to Luanda for consultations with his Angolan counterpart. The dipl
body_en:
The meeting brought together bishops from the National Episcopal Conference of Congo (CENCO) and pastors from the Church of Christ in Congo (ECC). It followed two visits within a week by President Félix Tshisekedi to Luanda for consultations with his Angolan counterpart.
The diplomatic momentum around the eastern DRC crisis has intensified in recent weeks. A telephone exchange reportedly took place between Qatari Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani and Angolan Foreign Minister Tete António, focusing on a peaceful solution between the DRC and Rwanda. Doha reiterated its commitment to dialogue.
These talks come as negotiations on the six protocols meant to complement the first two of the framework agreement between the Congolese government and the AFC/M23 remain stalled, according to informed sources.
Since the start of 2026, Félix Tshisekedi has traveled to Luanda twice in less than a month — an unusual pace in bilateral relations. According to sources within the Congolese presidency, João Lourenço has submitted several proposals, but no immediate decision or new peace process has been officially announced.
After announcing its withdrawal from mediation in the Congolese crisis in March 2025, Angola has made a gradual and discreet return, multiplying consultations with key stakeholders. In this context, former President Joseph Kabila was received in Luanda at the end of December, followed by a visit from a delegation from his camp.
Angolan diplomacy has also engaged with the AFC/M23 political-military movement. Its coordinator, Corneille Nangaa, reportedly sent a letter to President João Lourenço seeking clarification on the nature of Angola’s initiative, particularly regarding a possible new process.
The diplomatic push has expanded to Togo. President Félix Tshisekedi traveled to Lomé for a working session on peace and stabilization in eastern DRC, at the invitation of Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé, President of the Council of the Republic of Togo and AU-appointed mediator. The visit was described as brief.
Togo plans to host a high-level meeting on January 17 aimed at strengthening coordination of peace initiatives in the DRC and the Great Lakes region. This builds on recent international efforts, including the Paris Peace Conference of October 30, 2025, which mobilized more than €1.5 billion for vulnerable populations and supported negotiations led by the United States, Qatar, and the African Union.
Faure Gnassingbé succeeded João Lourenço as the AU-designated mediator for the eastern DRC conflict, following decisions of the joint virtual summit of the East African Community (EAC) and the Southern African Development Community (SADC) held on March 24, 2025.

excerpt_en: Davos, Switzerland January 18, 2026 – President Félix Tshisekedi of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) will participate as a guest of honor in the 56th annual meeting of the World Economic Forum (WEF), scheduled from January 19 to 23, 2026. The WEF in Davos, one of the world’
body_en:
Davos, Switzerland January 18, 2026 – President Félix Tshisekedi of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) will participate as a guest of honor in the 56th annual meeting of the World Economic Forum (WEF), scheduled from January 19 to 23, 2026.
The WEF in Davos, one of the world’s foremost platforms for public-private cooperation, brings together heads of state, business leaders, and civil society representatives to discuss global challenges under the theme: “A Spirit of Dialogue.” This year’s edition expects participation from over 50 world leaders.
According to Tina Salama, spokesperson for President Tshisekedi, the DRC will present itself as a “country of solutions” for Africa and the world. Key areas highlighted include:
Climate solutions, leveraging the DRC’s rich forests and peatlands.
Energy transition, through critical mineral resources and hydroelectric potential.
Human capital, driven by a youthful population of nearly 70%, forming a strategic workforce for AI, technology, and innovation sectors.
The presentation also addresses the security challenges facing the DRC, including Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 rebel occupation in parts of North Kivu and South Kivu, emphasizing mutually beneficial partnerships that respect the country’s sovereignty and contribute to lasting peace.
Organizers of the Forum underscore that the 2026 program will focus on five major global challenges, emphasizing inclusive dialogue, collaboration, and innovation as essential for progress.
Since 1971, the World Economic Forum has served as a platform for geopolitical and economic cooperation, fostering relationships across regions, sectors, and generations to address pressing global issues. Its permanent initiatives continue year-round, translating dialogue into concrete actions.
The WEF is headquartered in Geneva, Switzerland, with offices in New York, San Francisco, Beijing, and Tokyo, providing an independent and trusted platform for dialogue and collaboration.

title_en: Concerns Rise as AFC/M23 Rebels Receive Reinforcements
excerpt_en: Masisi-Walikale, DRC – January 11, 2026 – AFC/M23 rebels have reinforced their positions with fighters and ammunition in Kasopo and Kazinga, located in the Osso Banyungu chiefdom, Masisi territory, North Kivu, on January 9, 2026. Local sources report that these reinforcements cam
body_en:
Masisi-Walikale, DRC – January 11, 2026 – AFC/M23 rebels have reinforced their positions with fighters and ammunition in Kasopo and Kazinga, located in the Osso Banyungu chiefdom, Masisi territory, North Kivu, on January 9, 2026.
Local sources report that these reinforcements came from Nyabiondo and Masisi town, following a regrouping in Kaandja village, a strategic crossroads between Kasopo, Kazinga, and Kashebere.
The move comes one week after clashes resumed between rebel forces and government troops, supported by Wazalendo, in the Katoy sector, where rebels lost several villages.
Traditional leaders of Nyamabiko 1 and 2 (Masisi) and Waloa Yungu (Walikale) have expressed concern over a potential rebel offensive, urging FARDC and Wazalendo forces to remain vigilant.
The reinforcements, particularly in areas hosting displaced populations, indicate that the rebels may be preparing to retake lost territories, intensifying insecurity in North Kivu.

title_en: Rusamambu and Buleusa Receive New Displaced Families After Fighting in Kalonge
excerpt_en: Walikale, January 14, 2026 —Fresh waves of displacement have been reported in Walikale territory, North Kivu, as residents flee renewed clashes between AFC/M23 rebels and Wazalendo fighters of the Coalition of Movements for Change (CMC). Since Monday, January 12, population movem
body_en:
Walikale, January 14, 2026 —Fresh waves of displacement have been reported in Walikale territory, North Kivu, as residents flee renewed clashes between AFC/M23 rebels and Wazalendo fighters of the Coalition of Movements for Change (CMC).
Since Monday, January 12, population movements have intensified following fighting in Mulema locality, within the Kisimba group. As a result, residents of Kalonge have sought refuge in Rusamambu and Buleusa, both located in the neighboring Ikobo group, while Kalonge itself remains under AFC/M23 control.
This new displacement wave further deepens the humanitarian crisis in the area, where communities have already been severely affected by prolonged insecurity since the occupation of parts of the Wanianga sector by the rebels.
Local authorities have issued urgent appeals to humanitarian organizations to provide emergency assistance to the displaced families, many of whom fled without belongings, food, or shelter.
Meanwhile, the local population movement monitoring committee has begun registering newly displaced households, adding to those who have been living in the area without aid since February 2025, highlighting the growing strain on host communities and already limited resources.

title: “Human Tragedy” and “Desolation” of Congolese Refugees in Burundi and Tanzania: Government Issues Urgent Appeal for National Solidarity — January 18, 2026
excerpt: Burundi and Tanzania, neighboring countries of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), are hosting hundreds of thousands of Congolese refugees fleeing clashes between government forces and the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 rebellion. These hostilities have led to the fall of Uvira and o
title_en: “Human Tragedy” and “Desolation” of Congolese Refugees in Burundi and Tanzania: Government Issues Urgent Appeal for National Solidarity — January 18, 2026
excerpt_en: Burundi and Tanzania, neighboring countries of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), are hosting hundreds of thousands of Congolese refugees fleeing clashes between government forces and the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 rebellion. These hostilities have led to the fall of Uvira and o
body_en:
Burundi and Tanzania, neighboring countries of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), are hosting hundreds of thousands of Congolese refugees fleeing clashes between government forces and the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 rebellion. These hostilities have led to the fall of Uvira and other localities, expanding rebel influence across North Kivu and South Kivu in eastern DRC.
In response, the Congolese government, led by the Minister of State for Social Affairs and Humanitarian Action, Ève Bazaiba Masudi, conducted a humanitarian mission to both countries to support refugees, deliver assistance, strengthen coordination with host governments, and assess needs alongside international partners.
Following the mission, the minister described the situation as one of “human tragedy” and “desolation.” Speaking at a press conference in Kinshasa on Saturday, January 17, she declared:
“This is a devastating human tragedy. Our compatriots did not flee because of poverty or climate change, but because of the hostilities and the aggression carried out through AFC/M23 proxies.”
Alarming Figures
Burundi currently hosts approximately 250,000 Congolese refugees, spread across seven sites.
The largest site, Busuma, shelters 67,000 people, including 30,000 children and 2,200 unaccompanied minors.
Tanzania is hosting around 87,000 Congolese refugees, including 50,000 children under 18.
Recent arrivals include nearly 10,000 people, and 28 births were recorded on the day of the Congolese delegation’s visit.
Humanitarian Crisis and Funding Shortfalls
The minister warned of a severe shortage of international humanitarian funding, noting that many major donors have reduced or withdrawn support, forcing host countries to shoulder an increasing burden.
Despite its own challenges, the DRC government has become the main donor supporting its refugees, an exceptional step under international humanitarian law.
“Under normal circumstances, the country of origin does not intervene directly. But exceptional circumstances require exceptional measures,” Ève Bazaiba emphasized.
Humanitarian aid delivered included food and non-food items, supported by a special memorandum of understanding between the Congolese government, UNHCR, and Burundi, allowing direct intervention.
Appeal for National Solidarity
Commending the resilience and patriotism of the refugees, who expressed a strong desire to return home once peace is restored, Ève Bazaiba issued a national call to action:
“I appeal to the national solidarity of all Congolese, at home and abroad, to come to the aid of our compatriots in distress. Let us be true soldiers of the digital army and of the nation.”
She urged citizens to mobilize, especially through digital platforms, to defend the national cause and support vulnerable populations.
Security Context
This humanitarian emergency unfolds amid continued territorial gains by the AFC/M23, despite its controversial announcement of withdrawal from Uvira. Congolese authorities believe this declaration is aimed at reducing international pressure, particularly on Kigali, while the rebels continue to consolidate control and establish parallel administrations.
Once a strategic security hub in South Kivu, the fall of Uvira has significantly strengthened the rebellion’s grip on eastern DRC and is viewed as a potential gateway toward the Greater Katanga region, the economic heart of the country.
The Congolese government insists that only sustained international pressure, national solidarity, and concrete humanitarian action can prevent further suffering and restore dignity to displaced populations.

title: Surge in Injuries Strains Hospital Capacity Amid Ongoing Violence
excerpt: Fizi, South Kivu January 23, 2026 - The escalation of armed violence in Fizi territory, South Kivu, since late December 2025, has led to a dramatic rise in gunshot wounds and severely limited access to healthcare. The Fizi General Referral Hospital (HGR), supported by the Interna
title_en: Surge in Injuries Strains Hospital Capacity Amid Ongoing Violence
excerpt_en: Fizi, South Kivu January 23, 2026 - The escalation of armed violence in Fizi territory, South Kivu, since late December 2025, has led to a dramatic rise in gunshot wounds and severely limited access to healthcare. The Fizi General Referral Hospital (HGR), supported by the Interna
body_en:
Fizi, South Kivu January 23, 2026 - The escalation of armed violence in Fizi territory, South Kivu, since late December 2025, has led to a dramatic rise in gunshot wounds and severely limited access to healthcare. The Fizi General Referral Hospital (HGR), supported by the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), is now facing critical overcrowding.
According to ICRC reports, the number of wounded patients has quadrupled in just a few weeks. As of January 18, 2026, the hospital was treating 115 wounded patients, far exceeding its official capacity of 25 beds.
Medical staff report that many patients arrive too late for timely care, often with infected or complicated injuries, due to delays in treatment at peripheral health centers. “Most of the new patients had infected wounds from lack of adequate care. Many were unable to receive proper stabilization in the local facilities they passed through,” explained one hospital physician.
To respond to the crisis, the ICRC established additional tents to expand treatment capacity and deployed an emergency surgical team on January 10, 2026 to support local staff.
The ICRC highlights that these late arrivals reflect the collapse of frontline healthcare facilities near the conflict zones. Persistent insecurity, looting, shortages of medicines, and the departure of medical personnel have left several health centers paralyzed, leaving civilians and combatants alike without access to timely care.
The situation in Fizi underscores the humanitarian toll of the ongoing conflict in South Kivu and the urgent need for support to restore healthcare services for affected populations.

body_en:
Kinshasa/Luanda, January 13, 2026 — The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government has been placed on high alert following the entry of AFC/M23 fighters into the city of Uvira on December 10, 2025, amid fears that Kalemie in Tanganyika Province could also fall.
In response to the situation, Kinshasa sought military assistance from several countries to counter the rebel advance. In mid-December, the DRC formally requested support from Angola, citing Luanda’s role as a guarantor of President Félix Tshisekedi’s political stability.
However, Angolan authorities rejected the request to deploy troops, recalling that Angola had not intervened militarily even when regional forces were previously deployed to North Kivu Province.
On December 14, 2025, President Tshisekedi traveled to Luanda, where Angolan President and African Union Chairperson João Lourenço expressed support for a political solution rather than a military one.
Tshisekedi returned to Luanda on January 5, 2026, where both leaders agreed on the need for inclusive dialogue involving Congolese stakeholders from different sectors, including opposition figures and armed groups such as the AFC/M23. The Congolese president proposed that the talks be held in Kinshasa.
At Tshisekedi’s request, President Lourenço has continued consultations with potential participants. Former President Joseph Kabila and his close associates, including Moïse Nyarugabo and Raymond Tshibanda, were recently reported to be in Luanda as part of these discussions.
Despite clear signs that a new peace process is underway, both the Congolese and Angolan governments have avoided formally labeling the initiative as “new peace talks.”
AFC/M23 leader Corneille Nangaa has asked President Lourenço to clarify how the proposed process differs from the previous Doha talks, particularly after the group was invited to Luanda to prepare for discussions scheduled in Kinshasa.
On January 8, 2026, President Tshisekedi returned once again to Luanda to continue talks with Lourenço after agreeing on a list of potential participants for the upcoming dialogue.

title: US Congressman Advocates Regional Sharing of Eastern DRC Mineral Wealth
excerpt: Washington, January 23, 2026 – Representative Ronny Jackson, a member of the United States House Foreign Affairs Committee, called for regional cooperation in managing minerals from eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), arguing that neighboring countries should share in the
title_en: US Congressman Advocates Regional Sharing of Eastern DRC Mineral Wealth
excerpt_en: Washington, January 23, 2026 – Representative Ronny Jackson, a member of the United States House Foreign Affairs Committee, called for regional cooperation in managing minerals from eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), arguing that neighboring countries should share in the
body_en:
Washington, January 23, 2026 – Representative Ronny Jackson, a member of the United States House Foreign Affairs Committee, called for regional cooperation in managing minerals from eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), arguing that neighboring countries should share in the benefits to promote stability and security.
Jackson, who visited Rwanda, Burundi, Uganda, and other regional countries in 2025 to investigate the roots of the conflict between Rwanda and the DRC, presented his findings to US lawmakers on January 22, 2026.
“I have repeatedly suggested that there should be an agreement between countries—not only Rwanda, but also Burundi, Uganda, and other neighbors—so that everyone can benefit from the thousands of billions of dollars from minerals in eastern DRC,” Jackson said.
The congressman emphasized that processing the minerals in neighboring countries could foster shared responsibility for regional security.
“If these minerals are mined in the DRC and processed in neighboring countries, everyone will have an interest in maintaining peace in the region,” he explained.
Jackson also highlighted the importance of investing the revenue from these resources in eastern DRC to improve infrastructure, enhance living standards, and support local communities, framing economic development as a key factor in long-term stability.
His comments come amid ongoing tensions in eastern DRC, where armed groups, including the AFC/M23 coalition, have repeatedly clashed with government forces, and control of mineral-rich areas remains contested.

body_en:
Goma, January 12, 2026 — The AFC/M23 coalition says the city of Goma has seen a significant reduction in violence after one year under its control. Corneille Nangaa, coordinator of the coalition, made the announcement during a meeting with representatives from Lubero, Walikale, Masisi, Nyiragongo, Rutshuru, and South Kivu.
“A year has passed since this city was liberated from the clutches of murderers,” Nangaa said. “Now, by the grace of God and the dedication of our troops, but especially by the contribution of everyone, we now sleep and sleep. The so-called 40 bandits are no longer there. The endless killings and shootings are now history.”
He praised the coalition’s security forces for maintaining order and protecting residents and their property, despite what he described as interference from the Kinshasa government, including salary suspensions, bank closures, and disruptions to electricity and communications.
“Kinshasa has stopped our salaries, closed banks, stolen our savings, and continues to seize resources. Yet we have shown that we are citizens who can find solutions and are committed to fighting for change until it is complete,” Nangaa said.
The AFC/M23 captured Goma and Bukavu at the end of January 2025 and has maintained control over the cities since then. The coalition emphasizes that security has improved for residents, marking a shift from the widespread violence reported before their takeover.
