excerpt_en: Kinshasa, Tuesday, January 6, 2026 — The majority of newspapers published in Kinshasa this Tuesday focused on the private meeting held in Luanda between Congolese President Félix Tshisekedi and his Angolan counterpart João Lourenço, who also serves as Chairperson of the African U
body_en:
Kinshasa, Tuesday, January 6, 2026 — The majority of newspapers published in Kinshasa this Tuesday focused on the private meeting held in Luanda between Congolese President Félix Tshisekedi and his Angolan counterpart João Lourenço, who also serves as Chairperson of the African Union.
According to press reports, the talks took place against a backdrop of a rapidly deteriorating security situation in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo. Before departing for Luanda, President Félix Tshisekedi indicated that the primary objective of his visit was to advance peace efforts in eastern DRC. During the meeting, João Lourenço reportedly presented several proposals that the Congolese head of state described as constructive and capable of contributing significantly to a peaceful resolution of the conflict. Despite these discussions, President Tshisekedi emphasized that the situation on the ground remains “a war imposed upon us.”
The meeting occurred one day after the ratification of the Washington Accords between Kinshasa and Kigali, carried out in the presence of US President Donald Trump, and at a time when fighting continues to intensify in the eastern part of the country.
During his brief stay in Luanda, President Tshisekedi reiterated his determination to accelerate the search for peace through African-led diplomacy. As Chairperson of the African Union, João Lourenço is viewed as a central figure in efforts to revitalize continental mechanisms for conflict prevention and resolution. The discussions in Luanda are presented as complementary to existing diplomatic initiatives, notably those undertaken in Washington and Doha.
For several months, the Congolese authorities have sought to internationalize the crisis in eastern DRC and rally greater political support, denouncing what they describe as a persistent violation of national sovereignty. The repeated reference to an “imposed war” reflects a desire to shift the narrative from chronic internal insecurity to broader regional responsibility.
During the meeting, President Félix Tshisekedi also expressed his gratitude to João Lourenço for his commitment to peace in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, as diplomatic efforts continue amid ongoing instability in the east.

title: Insecurity Paralyzes Schools in Masisi I During First Term
excerpt: Masisi, North Kivu, January 3, 2026 — Several schools in the Masisi I subdivision of North Kivu faced serious operational disruptions during the first term of the 2025–2026 school year, as persistent insecurity severely affected teaching and learning conditions. While some school
title_en: Insecurity Paralyzes Schools in Masisi I During First Term
excerpt_en: Masisi, North Kivu, January 3, 2026 — Several schools in the Masisi I subdivision of North Kivu faced serious operational disruptions during the first term of the 2025–2026 school year, as persistent insecurity severely affected teaching and learning conditions. While some school
body_en:
Masisi, North Kivu, January 3, 2026 — Several schools in the Masisi I subdivision of North Kivu faced serious operational disruptions during the first term of the 2025–2026 school year, as persistent insecurity severely affected teaching and learning conditions.
While some schools managed to relocate in order to continue their activities, others saw their operations completely paralyzed. Luc Nyamulinduka, head of the Masisi I subdivision of the Ministry of Primary, Secondary, and Technical Education (EPST), paid tribute to the resilience and courage of both students and teachers amid the ongoing violence.
“Having to interrupt classes at the slightest sound of gunfire, or even move entire schools in an attempt to continue activities elsewhere—this has been the ordeal faced by students in Masisi during this first term,” he said.
According to Nyamulinduka, several schools located along the Buabo road were transferred to Masisi-Centre, a relatively safer area, where they were able to complete the term without major difficulties.
However, the situation remained precarious in other localities. In Nyabiondo, classes were repeatedly interrupted by gunfire, forcing schools to suspend and later resume activities. Along the Burora road, disruptions were more severe: although classes initially started, they could not be completed due to ongoing insecurity.
The education official indicated that in areas where calm has returned, particularly in Buabo, schools are expected to resume classes in their usual locations. He also announced the deployment of school inspectors to assist teachers in recovering lost learning time.
Despite these measures, families continue to hope for a lasting return to peace, which remains the only guarantee of a normal school year. The head of the subdivision expressed concern over the incomplete school calendar and the mass displacement of students caused by the fighting, warning of its long-term impact on education in the region.

title: Police Commander Lynched by Angry Youths in Ilebo, Kasai Province
excerpt: Ilebo, DRC – January 1, 2026 A police commander was brutally killed by angry youths at the Lumbundi camp in the Ilebo territory of Kasai province on Thursday, January 1. The victim, Commander Djuma of the Mapangu police station, was reportedly beaten to death after being accused
title_en: Police Commander Lynched by Angry Youths in Ilebo, Kasai Province
excerpt_en: Ilebo, DRC – January 1, 2026 A police commander was brutally killed by angry youths at the Lumbundi camp in the Ilebo territory of Kasai province on Thursday, January 1. The victim, Commander Djuma of the Mapangu police station, was reportedly beaten to death after being accused
body_en:
Ilebo, DRC – January 1, 2026
A police commander was brutally killed by angry youths at the Lumbundi camp in the Ilebo territory of Kasai province on Thursday, January 1. The victim, Commander Djuma of the Mapangu police station, was reportedly beaten to death after being accused of assaulting a woman in police custody, according to local sources.
Eyewitnesses say the incident began when a woman was arrested and allegedly assaulted by Commander Djuma. In response, a group of youths from the Lumbundi camp intervened, violently attacking the commander.
Following the lynching, the Mapangu police station, with support from the Masongo police station, rushed to the scene to investigate and attempt to restore calm. However, residents of the camp fled into the surrounding bush, fearing reprisals.
Authorities have confirmed that Commander Djuma’s body has been buried in the center of Mapangu. One young man implicated in the attack has already been detained by police.
In the wake of the tragedy, François Malepo, coordinator of the New Civil Society of the Ilebo territory, called on judicial authorities to conduct a thorough investigation. He urged that all individuals responsible for the murder be arrested and prosecuted, emphasizing the need for accountability.
Malepo also denounced acts of looting reportedly committed by some security forces during their intervention at the Lumbundi camp, highlighting concerns over law enforcement conduct in the area.
This incident underscores the growing tensions and challenges facing law enforcement in Kasai province, where community-police relations remain fragile and allegations of abuse can quickly escalate into deadly confrontations.

excerpt: Kinzau-Mvuete, Kongo-Central Province, January 3, 2026 — A wave of criminal attacks has shaken the town of Kinzau-Mvuete, in Sekebanza territory, Kongo-Central province, after several homes and businesses were targeted by bandits locally known as “Kulunas.” According to police so

excerpt_en: Kinzau-Mvuete, Kongo-Central Province, January 3, 2026 — A wave of criminal attacks has shaken the town of Kinzau-Mvuete, in Sekebanza territory, Kongo-Central province, after several homes and businesses were targeted by bandits locally known as “Kulunas.” According to police so
body_en:
Kinzau-Mvuete, Kongo-Central Province, January 3, 2026 — A wave of criminal attacks has shaken the town of Kinzau-Mvuete, in Sekebanza territory, Kongo-Central province, after several homes and businesses were targeted by bandits locally known as “Kulunas.”
According to police sources, the attacks occurred between December 31, 2025, and the evening of Friday, January 3, 2026, spreading fear and panic among the local population. The assailants reportedly looted valuables and cash, leaving several victims injured.
Sylvain Bakulu, Police Commander of Kinzau-Mvuete, confirmed the incidents and called on the population to cooperate with the police in order to facilitate the arrest of the perpetrators.
Victims reported that the masked and armed attackers operated in groups during the night of December 31 to January 1, mainly targeting the Mobutu and Mbenza Thubi neighborhoods. According to testimonies, the assailants threatened residents with death before ransacking their homes.
In total, around fifteen houses were attacked, and several people were seriously injured, some suffering machete wounds during the assaults.
The police commander noted that the attacks came after a long period of relative calm in the area. He attributed the resurgence of violence to the recent release of several suspected bandits by the prosecutor’s office of the Kinzau-Mvuete Court of First Instance, citing a lack of formal complaints as the reason for their release.
Security forces say investigations are ongoing as authorities seek to restore order and safety in the town.

excerpt: Lubero–Butembo, January 10, 2026 — The North Kivu provincial security committee has recommended the cantonment of FARDC soldiers and Wazalendo fighters to demilitarize Lubero commune, reduce tensions, and better protect civilians. The decision was made during a meeting held on Th
title_en: North Kivu Authorities Recommend Cantonment of FARDC and Wazalendo to Reduce Insecurity in Lubero and Butembo
excerpt_en: Lubero–Butembo, January 10, 2026 — The North Kivu provincial security committee has recommended the cantonment of FARDC soldiers and Wazalendo fighters to demilitarize Lubero commune, reduce tensions, and better protect civilians. The decision was made during a meeting held on Th
body_en:
Lubero–Butembo, January 10, 2026 — The North Kivu provincial security committee has recommended the cantonment of FARDC soldiers and Wazalendo fighters to demilitarize Lubero commune, reduce tensions, and better protect civilians. The decision was made during a meeting held on Thursday, January 8, in Butembo with representatives from both Lubero commune and Butembo city.
The meeting addressed concerns from local communities regarding a recent surge in crime, including urban banditry, looting, and murders. In Lubero, about twenty cases of criminal activity were recorded within a few days, prompting civil society-led general strikes to pressure authorities into action.
In Butembo, insecurity has also resulted in the murder of two people and the theft of several motorcycles by armed bandits.
The provincial security committee, led by Governor Évariste Kakule Somo, met with local representatives to discuss measures aimed at restoring law and order. Jackson Mumbere, a civil society representative in Lubero commune, emphasized the community’s expectations:“Murders, extortion, and looting have been reported, along with numerous other incidents. We met with the provincial governor, who responded favorably to our requests. We will monitor how the proposed solutions are implemented upon returning to Lubero-Centre.”
Authorities also announced that they would cover funeral expenses for the victim murdered on Wednesday evening in Butembo, signaling immediate steps to address the consequences of escalating insecurity.

title: Tshisekedi Turns Away from Doha Mediation, Pushes for New Luanda Talks
excerpt: President Félix Tshisekedi of the Democratic Republic of the Congo is seeking to relaunch peace talks in Luanda, while continuing to distance himself from the Qatari-led mediation process initiated in early 2025. Tshisekedi last traveled to Luanda on December 14, 2025, where he h
title_en: Tshisekedi Turns Away from Doha Mediation, Pushes for New Luanda Talks
excerpt_en: President Félix Tshisekedi of the Democratic Republic of the Congo is seeking to relaunch peace talks in Luanda, while continuing to distance himself from the Qatari-led mediation process initiated in early 2025. Tshisekedi last traveled to Luanda on December 14, 2025, where he h
body_en:
President Félix Tshisekedi of the Democratic Republic of the Congo is seeking to relaunch peace talks in Luanda, while continuing to distance himself from the Qatari-led mediation process initiated in early 2025.
Tshisekedi last traveled to Luanda on December 14, 2025, where he held brief discussions with Angolan President João Lourenço on efforts to restore peace in eastern DRC. The Luanda framework, led by Lourenço, has been stalled since October 2024, when the Congolese government delegation refused to engage in direct dialogue with the AFC/M23 coalition.
The paralysis of the Luanda process coincided with President Lourenço assuming the chairmanship of the African Union (AU). During this period, mediation efforts shifted toward Washington and Doha, though with limited progress. Lourenço is expected to step down from the AU presidency during the AU General Assembly on February 15, 2026, to be replaced by Burundi’s President Évariste Ndayishimiye, potentially freeing him to re-engage fully in mediation efforts.
On January 5, 2026, President Tshisekedi again visited Angola to discuss security developments in eastern DRC. However, the agenda reportedly mirrored discussions already held under the Doha and Washington initiatives.
Although the Congolese presidency maintains that Tshisekedi still formally supports the Doha process, his actions suggest otherwise. The DRC recently declined to send representatives to two meetings organized by Qatar, which were aimed at assessing the implementation of the ceasefire agreement.
Meanwhile, regional tensions around mediation have intensified. Burundi’s foreign minister has publicly accused Qatar of using its diplomatic influence to block potential international sanctions against Rwanda—claims that have been repeatedly denied.
Sources in Kinshasa indicate that Tshisekedi has formally asked President Lourenço to initiate a new round of talks in Luanda, a request the Angolan leader has reportedly accepted. The proposed talks would involve a broad range of Congolese stakeholders, including members of the ruling coalition, political opposition figures, armed groups such as AFC/M23, religious leaders, and civil society representatives.
If launched, the new Luanda talks are expected to resemble the inclusive national dialogue formats previously held in Nairobi, as well as those advocated by religious leaders, particularly the Catholic and Anglican churches.
However, for the AFC/M23, the Luanda framework may lack the leverage of the Doha process. The group argues that broader national dialogues tend to overlook specific issues directly affecting them, such as the release of hundreds of their detained members, which they consider central to any lasting agreement.
As diplomatic maneuvering continues, uncertainty remains over which mediation track—Luanda, Doha, or another format—will ultimately shape the future of peace efforts in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo.

title: GTBank Rwanda Launches ‘M-Pay’ Technology to Offer Collateral-Free Loans to Traders
excerpt: Kigali, 9 January 2026: GTBank (Rwanda) Plc, in partnership with Rswitch, has introduced a new technology platform designed to make it easier for traders to access loans without collateral, supporting Rwanda’s ongoing push for digital payments and cashless transactions. The new s
title_en: GTBank Rwanda Launches ‘M-Pay’ Technology to Offer Collateral-Free Loans to Traders
excerpt_en: Kigali, 9 January 2026: GTBank (Rwanda) Plc, in partnership with Rswitch, has introduced a new technology platform designed to make it easier for traders to access loans without collateral, supporting Rwanda’s ongoing push for digital payments and cashless transactions. The new s
body_en:
Kigali, 9 January 2026: GTBank (Rwanda) Plc, in partnership with Rswitch, has introduced a new technology platform designed to make it easier for traders to access loans without collateral, supporting Rwanda’s ongoing push for digital payments and cashless transactions.
The new system, called ‘M-Pay’, enables merchants to receive payments directly into their GTBank accounts without any fees, while also providing collateral-free loans of up to 2 million Rwandan francs. Repayment is structured over 12 months at an interest rate of 3.99%.
Through the M-Pay system:
Customers can pay merchants using a USSD code (18212USSD Code#) with the payment going directly to the merchant’s account.
Merchants, such as hotel owners, can set up multiple payment methods without risking theft.
Customers do not need a GTBank account to make payments.
GTBank account holders can pay via 6005#, sending money directly to the merchant’s M-Pay code without deductions for either party.
GTBank says the platform aligns with Rwanda’s national direction to promote digital payments, reduce reliance on cash, and provide financial services to small and medium-sized traders more efficiently.
This innovation is expected to empower businesses, facilitate safer transactions, and improve access to credit across the country.
Social and Health

title: DRC – AFC/M23 Accuses Kinshasa of Breaching Peace Agreements
excerpt: Kinshasa/Uvira, January 1, 2026 Corneille Nangaa, coordinator of the AFC/M23, has accused the government of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) of failing to honor agreements signed in 2025 aimed at stabilizing the eastern region and ensuring the security of Abanye-Congophone
title_en: DRC – AFC/M23 Accuses Kinshasa of Breaching Peace Agreements
excerpt_en: Kinshasa/Uvira, January 1, 2026 Corneille Nangaa, coordinator of the AFC/M23, has accused the government of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) of failing to honor agreements signed in 2025 aimed at stabilizing the eastern region and ensuring the security of Abanye-Congophone
body_en:
Kinshasa/Uvira, January 1, 2026
Corneille Nangaa, coordinator of the AFC/M23, has accused the government of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) of failing to honor agreements signed in 2025 aimed at stabilizing the eastern region and ensuring the security of Abanye-Congophone communities.
The agreements, signed in July 2025 under Qatari mediation, included a Declaration of Principles, a prisoner release mechanism, a ceasefire and monitoring mechanism, and a basic framework for peace.
In a recent statement, Nangaa criticized Kinshasa for betraying the trust of the AFC/M23. “The regime of Kinshasa has shown its inability to uphold its commitments and its own word. This is a regime built on lies and outdated agreements. To date, no prisoners have been released, in clear violation of the signed accords,” he said.
He also accused the DRC of ceasefire violations through repeated attacks against AFC/M23 positions.
While acknowledging the peace agreement between Rwanda and the DRC signed in Washington as a positive development, Nangaa emphasized that negotiations in Doha between Kinshasa and AFC/M23 have not yielded concrete results. Several agreements from these talks remain unimplemented.
Despite these setbacks, Nangaa reaffirmed that the AFC/M23 withdrew its forces from the city of Uvira as requested by the mediators, demonstrating continued commitment to peace efforts.

title: Martin Fayulu Renewes Call for Inclusive Dialogue Amid Deepening Crisis in the DRC
excerpt: Kinshasa | December 31, 2025 — Congolese opposition leader Martin Fayulu has reiterated his call for an inclusive national dialogue, warning that the Democratic Republic of Congo is facing what he described as “one of the most serious crises in its history.” Fayulu made the remar
title_en: Martin Fayulu Renewes Call for Inclusive Dialogue Amid Deepening Crisis in the DRC
excerpt_en: Kinshasa | December 31, 2025 — Congolese opposition leader Martin Fayulu has reiterated his call for an inclusive national dialogue, warning that the Democratic Republic of Congo is facing what he described as “one of the most serious crises in its history.” Fayulu made the remar
body_en:
Kinshasa | December 31, 2025 — Congolese opposition leader Martin Fayulu has reiterated his call for an inclusive national dialogue, warning that the Democratic Republic of Congo is facing what he described as “one of the most serious crises in its history.”
Fayulu made the remarks in a New Year’s message to the Congolese people, published on social media on Wednesday, December 31, 2025. In the message, he urged political leaders to engage in open discussions aimed at restoring stability and national cohesion.
The opposition figure sharply criticized the agreements signed on December 4 in Washington, arguing that they commit the future of the DRC without national debate, transparency, or popular consent. “These agreements are opaque. The people do not know. The people have not decided,” Fayulu said.
According to him, rejecting inclusive dialogue would amount to rejecting peace, stressing that only a broad-based political process can provide a sustainable solution to the country’s ongoing political and security challenges.
DRC Joins UN Security Council, Says Entry Is “a Mission, Not a Reward”
Kinshasa, January 2, 2026 — The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) officially takes its seat on the United Nations Security Council this Friday as a non-permanent member, marking a significant milestone in the country’s diplomatic engagement on the global stage.
Foreign Affairs Minister Thérèse Kayikwamba Wagner underscored the gravity of the moment, stressing that the DRC’s entry into the Council should not be seen as a symbolic achievement, but as a serious responsibility. “By officially joining the United Nations Security Council, our country assumes a major responsibility in the service of international peace and security,” she said. “It is a moment of dignity, but above all, a moment of commitment.”
Drawing on the DRC’s own history, the minister highlighted the country’s understanding of the human cost of conflict and instability. She noted that the Congolese experience gives the nation a unique perspective on the expectations of civilian populations who look to the United Nations in times of war and insecurity.
Thérèse Kayikwamba Wagner outlined the DRC’s mandate on the Council around three core priorities: defending respect for international law, reaffirming the non-negotiable principle of state sovereignty, and amplifying the voices of populations affected by conflict, particularly in Africa.
According to the minister, the DRC approaches its role on the Security Council with a message shaped by lived experience—one rooted in truth, responsibility, and a firm commitment to contributing to lasting solutions to international crises.

title: Over 450 Measles Cases Reported in Kasai-Oriental in Two Weeks
excerpt: Kasai-Oriental, January 3, 2026 — More than 450 cases of measles have been recorded in Kasai-Oriental province over the past two weeks, raising serious public health concerns. According to health authorities, at least 456 cases have been registered since December 15. Dr. Jean-Pie
title_en: Over 450 Measles Cases Reported in Kasai-Oriental in Two Weeks
excerpt_en: Kasai-Oriental, January 3, 2026 — More than 450 cases of measles have been recorded in Kasai-Oriental province over the past two weeks, raising serious public health concerns. According to health authorities, at least 456 cases have been registered since December 15. Dr. Jean-Pie
body_en:
Kasai-Oriental, January 3, 2026 — More than 450 cases of measles have been recorded in Kasai-Oriental province over the past two weeks, raising serious public health concerns. According to health authorities, at least 456 cases have been registered since December 15.
Dr. Jean-Pierre Sumba, the physician in charge of the measles response, reported that all 19 health zones in the province have been affected. He noted that children aged 0 to 59 months are the most impacted, although no deaths have been recorded so far.
Health officials are urging parents to promptly take any children with fever to the nearest health center for early diagnosis and treatment.
“Cases of measles are present throughout the province. It even resembles an epidemic,” Dr. Sumba warned. “However, we are awaiting an official declaration by the competent authority, namely the provincial governor. Some cases have already been confirmed by laboratory tests at the national level, and we have exceeded the alert thresholds.”
According to Dr. Sumba, the province is preparing to roll out a measles response plan, while also expressing concern over vaccine hesitancy among some parents, which could complicate containment efforts.
“At present, patients are being treated in the various health facilities where they are received. Our intervention plan is already operational,” he said. “In the meantime, targeted and small-scale vaccination campaigns are being organized in certain areas to prevent rapid spread of the disease.”
Health authorities continue to monitor the situation closely as preventive measures are intensified across the province.

According to Dr. Sumba, the province is preparing to roll out a measles response plan, while also expressing concern over vaccine hesitancy among some parents, which could complicate containment efforts.
“At present, patients are being treated in the various health facilities where they are received. Our intervention plan is already operational,” he said. “In the meantime, targeted and small-scale vaccination campaigns are being organized in certain areas to prevent rapid spread of the disease.”
Health authorities continue to monitor the situation closely as preventive measures are intensified across the province.

title: FARDC Accuses AFC/M23 Rebels of Abducting 42 Women in Rutshuru, North Kivu
excerpt: Rutshuru, North Kivu, DRC | December 28, 2025 The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) have accused AFC/M23 rebels of abducting at least 42 women in the Bukombo Centre area of Rutshuru territory, North Kivu. According to Dieudonné Kasereka, communications offi
title_en: FARDC Accuses AFC/M23 Rebels of Abducting 42 Women in Rutshuru, North Kivu
excerpt_en: Rutshuru, North Kivu, DRC | December 28, 2025 The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) have accused AFC/M23 rebels of abducting at least 42 women in the Bukombo Centre area of Rutshuru territory, North Kivu. According to Dieudonné Kasereka, communications offi
body_en:
Rutshuru, North Kivu, DRC | December 28, 2025
The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) have accused AFC/M23 rebels of abducting at least 42 women in the Bukombo Centre area of Rutshuru territory, North Kivu.
According to Dieudonné Kasereka, communications officer for the 34th Military Region, the abductions occurred on Sunday, December 28, in the Bwito chiefdom. The army reports that the victims were tortured prior to their abduction, citing testimonies from local residents.
“The exact destination or whereabouts of the women remain unclear,” Kasereka added.
The FARDC noted that this is not the first violent act attributed to the AFC/M23 rebels, who have previously targeted civilians in Mushoro (Bwito chiefdom), Pitango and Musinde (Batangi chiefdom), and Kahongole (Katsiru locality).
The Bukombo area remains a high-risk zone, marked by skirmishes between Wazalendo forces of the CMC group and M23 rebels, alongside human rights violations against civilians.
Mass Displacement
Hundreds of families displaced by the clashes are currently living in Mweso, in the Bashali Mokoto area, Masisi territory. According to local sources, these people are housed in schools and churches under precarious conditions, receiving little to no humanitarian aid.
Displaced families are forced to move their belongings each morning to allow classes to resume, often in the rain. This situation is especially dangerous for breastfeeding women and children, who are exposed to the elements.
Local residents are appealing to the humanitarian community for decent shelter and support to enable them to return safely to their home villages.

title: Police Officers’ Homes Set Ablaze by Angry Youths in Ango
excerpt: Ango, Bas-Uele Province, January 3, 2026 — Tensions escalated in Ango territory, Bas-Uele province, after the burial of two victims of police violence, leading to acts of retaliation by angry youths who set fire to dozens of homes belonging to police officers. According to local
title_en: Police Officers’ Homes Set Ablaze by Angry Youths in Ango
excerpt_en: Ango, Bas-Uele Province, January 3, 2026 — Tensions escalated in Ango territory, Bas-Uele province, after the burial of two victims of police violence, leading to acts of retaliation by angry youths who set fire to dozens of homes belonging to police officers. According to local
body_en:
Ango, Bas-Uele Province, January 3, 2026 — Tensions escalated in Ango territory, Bas-Uele province, after the burial of two victims of police violence, leading to acts of retaliation by angry youths who set fire to dozens of homes belonging to police officers.
According to local authorities, 38 houses owned by police officers were burned down in one of Ango’s two neighborhoods, following the funerals of the victims, who were shot and killed by police on New Year’s Eve.
After an emergency meeting convened on Saturday, January 3, 2026, the Deputy Territorial Administrator, Alfred Kipa, announced that measures had been taken to prevent a recurrence of such violence.
Calm reportedly returned to the area after the funerals, which the deputy administrator described as dignified. He also confirmed that financial assistance was provided to the bereaved families, following his intervention with the provincial governor.
Despite this, Alfred Kipa strongly condemned the destruction caused by what he described as unemployed youths, noting that nearly all police housing in the affected area had been targeted, including the residence of the group leader.
“Five houses were burned down, including that of the leader, as well as others belonging to police officers who were absent,” he said. “We have decided to reinforce patrols to put an end to these barbaric acts carried out by a handful of unemployed youths.”
Left without shelter, the affected police officers have taken refuge in a building previously donated to the territorial administration by an NGO. Authorities have pledged to allocate land to enable them to rebuild their homes.
The unrest follows the fatal shooting of two civilians by police on the evening of January 1, as residents were celebrating the New Year, an incident that has deeply shaken the local community.

title_en: Six CRP Militiamen Surrender Amid Fighting with FARDC in Djugu
excerpt_en: Djugu, Ituri, January 9, 2026 — Six militiamen from the Convention for the Popular Revolution (CRP) surrendered on Friday, January 9, during clashes with the Armed Forces of the DRC (FARDC) in the Nyaka and Lodha localities of Djugu territory. The surrender followed an attack by
body_en:
Djugu, Ituri, January 9, 2026 — Six militiamen from the Convention for the Popular Revolution (CRP) surrendered on Friday, January 9, during clashes with the Armed Forces of the DRC (FARDC) in the Nyaka and Lodha localities of Djugu territory.
The surrender followed an attack by CRP fighters on a FARDC position in the area. Sporadic gunfire had been reported since last Monday around Fataki, where Thomas Lubanga’s CRP militia had unsuccessfully tried to establish a foothold following an incursion into Bule, approximately 15 kilometers away.
These attempts were repeatedly repelled by MONUSCO soldiers, stationed in Djaiba, who maintain regular patrols in the region.
On the morning of Friday, January 9, the CRP attacked a FARDC position near Lodha, which also hosts a camp for internally displaced persons. The FARDC, reinforced in the area, responded vigorously, leading to clashes that continued until mid-afternoon.
MONUSCO peacekeepers intensified patrols along the Fataki–Lodha and Fataki–Sanduku roads to protect civilians, many of whom fled to nearby FARDC positions and the MONUSCO base due to ongoing threats from the militia.
The incident underscores the persistent insecurity in Djugu and the continued efforts by FARDC and MONUSCO to safeguard civilians.

title: DRC Agriculture Minister Criticizes FARDC and Intelligence Services Over War and Media Influence
excerpt: The Minister of Agriculture and Food Security of the Democratic Republic of Congo, Muhindo Nzangi Butondo, has strongly criticized the FARDC and military intelligence services, accusing them of being intimidated by narratives circulating on social media amid the ongoing conflict.
title_en: DRC Agriculture Minister Criticizes FARDC and Intelligence Services Over War and Media Influence
excerpt_en: The Minister of Agriculture and Food Security of the Democratic Republic of Congo, Muhindo Nzangi Butondo, has strongly criticized the FARDC and military intelligence services, accusing them of being intimidated by narratives circulating on social media amid the ongoing conflict.
body_en:
The Minister of Agriculture and Food Security of the Democratic Republic of Congo, Muhindo Nzangi Butondo, has strongly criticized the FARDC and military intelligence services, accusing them of being intimidated by narratives circulating on social media amid the ongoing conflict.
Speaking in an interview on January 5, 2026, the minister argued that the DRC government is losing not only the war on the ground but also the information battle. He said the situation surrounding the fall of Uvira illustrates how misinformation and panic contributed to military failure.
“Take the example of Uvira. They announced its capture while M23 fighters were still in Luvungi, about 30 kilometers away. Once the news spread online, everyone believed Uvira had fallen, and the national army fled the city before the enemy even arrived,” he said.
On December 9, 2025, AFC/M23 fighters entered Uvira, before withdrawing about a week later following international pressure, particularly from the United States, which had assured that peace talks would continue.
According to Minister Muhindo, the AFC/M23 coalition maintains significant military strength, to the extent that, without external intervention, it could have advanced far beyond Uvira.
“I must be honest: if it had not been for a message from Marco Rubio saying, ‘We are not happy! We are not happy!’, they would likely be in Kalemie, in Tanganyika Province, because there was practically nothing stopping them. That message gave us time to prepare,” he stated.
The minister emphasized that the absence of further territorial advances by AFC/M23 should not be interpreted as a lack of military capability, but rather as the result of diplomatic intervention, mainly by the United States.
He concluded by asserting that the only real leverage the DRC government still retains is diplomatic, not military, underscoring the fragility of the country’s security apparatus in the face of organized armed groups.

title: Aterian Plc Posts Rwf210.5 Million Profit from Rwanda Operations in Q4 2025
excerpt: British mining company Aterian Plc has reported a profit of Rwf210.5 million (approximately USD 145,000) from its mining operations in Rwanda for the fourth quarter ended December 31, 2025. In a statement released on January 5, 2026, the company said its business in Rwanda contin
title_en: Aterian Plc Posts Rwf210.5 Million Profit from Rwanda Operations in Q4 2025
excerpt_en: British mining company Aterian Plc has reported a profit of Rwf210.5 million (approximately USD 145,000) from its mining operations in Rwanda for the fourth quarter ended December 31, 2025. In a statement released on January 5, 2026, the company said its business in Rwanda contin
body_en:
British mining company Aterian Plc has reported a profit of Rwf210.5 million (approximately USD 145,000) from its mining operations in Rwanda for the fourth quarter ended December 31, 2025.
In a statement released on January 5, 2026, the company said its business in Rwanda continues to grow, alongside ongoing mineral exploration and research activities in the country.
Aterian noted that the volume of minerals traded fell short of government targets, explaining that the company prioritized compliance with international standards over production volumes.
Commenting on the results, Aterian CEO Charles Bray said the fourth-quarter performance reflects the company’s solid business position and expressed confidence in continued growth in 2026.
“We believe that the results achieved in the fourth quarter of 2025 demonstrate the opportunities in the company’s business and provide a foundation for what can be done in 2026, depending on the available capital and the market situation,” Bray said.
He added that the company will remain focused on meeting international regulatory requirements governing the trade of precious metals, as well as the expectations of global buyers and regulators.
Aterian Plc also confirmed that it identified lithium deposits in Rwanda following exploration activities that began in 2023. This discovery led Rio Tinto and Mining Exploration, in partnership with Aterian, to commit USD 7.5 million to lithium mining projects.
According to national data, Rwanda’s mining sector generated USD 1.6 billion in revenue in the 2024/2025 period, driven by strong exports of tin, tungsten, tantalum, and gold to international markets.

title: Burundi Tightens Airport Controls to Stop Military Desertions Linked to DRC Conflict
excerpt: Bujumbura, December 29, 2025 The Government of Burundi has introduced new measures to block the escape route used by soldiers fleeing abroad, amid growing concern that military desertions could increase due to the country’s involvement in the conflict in eastern Democratic Republ
title_en: Burundi Tightens Airport Controls to Stop Military Desertions Linked to DRC Conflict
excerpt_en: Bujumbura, December 29, 2025 The Government of Burundi has introduced new measures to block the escape route used by soldiers fleeing abroad, amid growing concern that military desertions could increase due to the country’s involvement in the conflict in eastern Democratic Republ
body_en:
Bujumbura, December 29, 2025
The Government of Burundi has introduced new measures to block the escape route used by soldiers fleeing abroad, amid growing concern that military desertions could increase due to the country’s involvement in the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).
According to the Burundian presidency, between 2023 and August 2025, at least 14 senior military officers deserted the national army and fled abroad after Burundi’s forces became engaged in fighting against the AFC/M23. Those officers include nine colonels and five majors, alongside numerous soldiers of lower rank.
The most recent confirmed defection is that of Lt. Irambona Désiré, whose desertion was officially recognized through a presidential decree signed on December 22, 2025, by President Évariste Ndayishimiye.
Sources in Bujumbura indicate that deserters come from various ranks, though the majority are lieutenants and captains. Many reportedly travel to European countries, Canada, or Dubai in the United Arab Emirates, where they seek civilian employment.
Several soldiers who have fled say they do not understand why they were deployed to fight in the war in eastern DRC, describing fear of prolonged involvement in a foreign conflict as a major reason for desertion.
Until recently, desertion through legal travel channels was reportedly facilitated by corruption. Officers from the Special Police Service responsible for issuing passports (PAFE) allegedly demanded bribes and instructed soldiers to obtain identity cards under false names, which were then used to secure travel documents.
Following the defeat of AFC/M23 forces in several areas of South Kivu Province, including Katogota, Lubarika, Sange, Kiliba, and the city of Uvira, Burundian authorities grew increasingly concerned that more soldiers would attempt to flee with the assistance of corrupt officials.
On December 29, Pacifique Nininahazwe, head of the human rights organization FOCODE, announced that several soldiers had recently been arrested at Bujumbura International Airport while attempting to travel to Dubai in search of work. Some of the arrests reportedly involved PAFE officers suspected of facilitating illegal departures.
Earlier, on December 22, Burundi’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, Dr. Édouard Bizimana, issued a decree introducing stricter requirements for Burundians seeking employment abroad. While officially applicable to all citizens, multiple sources say the measure primarily targets military personnel attempting to desert.
Under the new rules, any Burundian departing for work abroad must present an identity card issued by the competent ministry, a signed contract from the employer, and authorization from a family member. For soldiers, this effectively requires documentation from the Ministry of Defense and Veterans Affairs, which is not issued to active-duty personnel.
Previously, Burundi’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs only monitored labor migration to countries that had formal worker-exchange agreements with Burundi. The new directive expands oversight to all destination countries, including those without bilateral agreements.
The move signals a significant tightening of controls as Burundi seeks to curb military desertions amid growing domestic unease over its role in the DRC conflict.

Officers from the Special Police Service responsible for issuing passports (PAFE) allegedly demanded bribes and instructed soldiers to obtain identity cards under false names, which were then used to secure travel documents.

On December 29, Pacifique Nininahazwe, head of the human rights organization FOCODE, announced that several soldiers had recently been arrested at Bujumbura International Airport while attempting to travel to Dubai in search of work. Some of the arrests reportedly involved PAFE officers suspected of facilitating illegal departures.

title: DRC: 73rd Ordinary Cabinet Meeting Focuses on Security and Economic Priorities for 2026
excerpt: Kinshasa, January 2, 2026 Amid persistent tensions in the eastern provinces and as the Democratic Republic of the Congo begins its term on the United Nations Security Council, President Félix Antoine Tshisekedi Tshilombo on Friday chaired the 73rd ordinary meeting of the Council
title_en: DRC: 73rd Ordinary Cabinet Meeting Focuses on Security and Economic Priorities for 2026
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, January 2, 2026 Amid persistent tensions in the eastern provinces and as the Democratic Republic of the Congo begins its term on the United Nations Security Council, President Félix Antoine Tshisekedi Tshilombo on Friday chaired the 73rd ordinary meeting of the Council
body_en:
Kinshasa, January 2, 2026
Amid persistent tensions in the eastern provinces and as the Democratic Republic of the Congo begins its term on the United Nations Security Council, President Félix Antoine Tshisekedi Tshilombo on Friday chaired the 73rd ordinary meeting of the Council of Ministers at the African Union City in Kinshasa.
The government briefing, delivered by the Minister of Communication and Media and government spokesperson Patrick Muyaya Katembwe, outlined the main discussions of the session, which centered on security challenges, economic recovery, and institutional reforms expected to shape the country’s agenda in 2026.
Presidential address: security vigilance and diplomatic engagement
Opening the meeting, President Tshisekedi focused on national sovereignty and the deteriorating security situation in eastern DRC. He strongly condemned repeated ceasefire violations attributed to various armed coalitions, including national forces, militias, and external actors, echoing recent accusations made by the AFC/M23.
The Head of State warned of serious risks facing civilian populations, including Congolese Tutsi communities, and called for urgent international action. He also welcomed the DRC’s new mandate as a non-permanent member of the UN Security Council for 2026–2027, describing it as a strategic opportunity to influence regional security dynamics, particularly ongoing diplomatic efforts involving Rwanda under international facilitation.
President Tshisekedi further stressed the need for deep state reforms in 2026, with priority given to strengthening the justice system, consolidating institutions, and intensifying the fight against corruption in response to governance shortcomings observed in 2025.
Prime Minister’s intervention: assessment and outlook of government action
Prime Minister Judith Suminwa Tuluka presented an update on the implementation of the Government Action Program (2024–2028). She announced that a comprehensive evaluation of government performance would begin in January 2026, with the aim of adjusting priorities to improve effectiveness.
Key highlights included:
Industrialization and economic transformation: Particular emphasis was placed on the Maluku Special Economic Zone, where recent assessments have helped define an industrial roadmap focused on large-scale job creation and economic diversification through local processing of natural resources.
Rural and social development: The government plans to reinforce support for farmers, expand access to low-interest loans for young people and women, and allocate 10% of locally generated revenues to programs targeting these groups.
The Prime Minister also pointed to improved fiscal performance, with tax pressure nearing the African average, while calling for a broader tax base to finance critical infrastructure in roads, energy, and transport.
Information briefings: security, health, and the economy
Several sectoral updates were presented to the Council:
Security: The Minister of Defense reported ongoing military operations against armed groups in Ituri, North Kivu, and South Kivu, including air strikes and actions targeting rebel coalitions. Authorities raised concerns over continued massacres and population displacement, reaffirming the government’s commitment to restoring state authority in occupied areas.
Health and environment: Ministers reviewed the response to ongoing epidemics, including cholera and measles, and urged continued vigilance in the post-Covid context. Discussions also covered cybersecurity and data protection, with plans for the establishment of a national agency.

title: FARDC Pays Tribute to Colonel Mamadou Ndala Twelve Years After His Assassination
excerpt: Kinshasa, January 3, 2026 — The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (FARDC) on Friday paid tribute to Colonel Mamadou Ndala, marking twelve years since his assassination in an ambush on his convoy while he was traveling to Eringeti, in North Kivu. On this day of

excerpt_en: Kinshasa, January 3, 2026 — The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (FARDC) on Friday paid tribute to Colonel Mamadou Ndala, marking twelve years since his assassination in an ambush on his convoy while he was traveling to Eringeti, in North Kivu. On this day of
body_en:
Kinshasa, January 3, 2026 — The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (FARDC) on Friday paid tribute to Colonel Mamadou Ndala, marking twelve years since his assassination in an ambush on his convoy while he was traveling to Eringeti, in North Kivu.
On this day of remembrance, the Congolese army reaffirmed its determination to pursue the struggle for which Mamadou Ndala gave his life: the defense of a united, sovereign, and peaceful Democratic Republic of the Congo.
“Honor and glory to General Mamadou Ndala. The grateful nation will never forget you. Long live the FARDC, long live the Democratic Republic of Congo!” the army declared in an official message.
At the time of his death, Colonel Mamadou Ndala was leading military operations against the Ugandan Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) rebels and other armed groups operating in the Beni region.
Widely regarded as a national hero, Mamadou Ndala remains an emblematic figure of courage, loyalty, and supreme sacrifice in the defense of the homeland. A respected commander and exceptional officer, he distinguished himself through his unwavering commitment to the fight for peace, security, and the territorial integrity of the DRC.
According to the FARDC, his leadership on the ground, his close connection with the troops, and his determination in the face of the enemy have left a lasting mark on the history of the Congolese army. His legacy, the military emphasized, remains alive in the hearts of Congolese soldiers and the entire nation.
The commemoration of the 12th anniversary of Colonel Mamadou Ndala’s assassination comes at a time when the FARDC is engaged in ongoing confrontations with AFC/M23 rebels, reportedly supported by the Rwandan army, in the eastern part of the country.

title: Around 850 Congolese Refugees Receive Humanitarian Aid in Rumonge, Burundi
excerpt: Rumonge, Burundi | December 2025 A total of 846 Congolese refugees residing in the Rumonge camp in Burundi received humanitarian aid, including food and non-food items, on Thursday. Most of the refugees originate from Uvira, while others fled from Fizi and Baraka, according to ca
title_en: Around 850 Congolese Refugees Receive Humanitarian Aid in Rumonge, Burundi
excerpt_en: Rumonge, Burundi | December 2025 A total of 846 Congolese refugees residing in the Rumonge camp in Burundi received humanitarian aid, including food and non-food items, on Thursday. Most of the refugees originate from Uvira, while others fled from Fizi and Baraka, according to ca
body_en:
Rumonge, Burundi | December 2025
A total of 846 Congolese refugees residing in the Rumonge camp in Burundi received humanitarian aid, including food and non-food items, on Thursday. Most of the refugees originate from Uvira, while others fled from Fizi and Baraka, according to camp officials.
The aid, provided by private donors, is described by recipients as a lifeline amid difficult living conditions. Mapenzi Manyebwa, president of the Congolese refugees in Rumonge, expressed gratitude to the benefactors and called on the DRC government to emulate such support.
“We have been here in Rumonge for two weeks, after leaving the territories and cities of Uvira, Fizi, and Baraka. Here, we are starting to receive assistance from local associations and some national members of parliament,” Manyebwa said.
He specifically mentioned MP Justin Bitawira, who donated 140 bags of cornmeal, 1,740 kg of beans, 10 jerrycans of palm oil, 100 tarpaulins, and soap to the camp. The distribution reached 846 registered households, providing essential relief to the refugee population.
“We thank these leaders who continue to think about our difficulties, because we live in such challenging conditions here in Rumonge,” Manyebwa added.

title: Over 2,000 Displaced People Struggle to Survive at Katanika Site
excerpt: Kalemie, Tanganyika Province, January 3, 2026 — More than 2,000 displaced people, who fled the conflict involving the AFC and M23 in North and South Kivu, are living in extremely precarious conditions at the Katanika displacement site in the city of Kalemie, according to local so
title_en: Over 2,000 Displaced People Struggle to Survive at Katanika Site
excerpt_en: Kalemie, Tanganyika Province, January 3, 2026 — More than 2,000 displaced people, who fled the conflict involving the AFC and M23 in North and South Kivu, are living in extremely precarious conditions at the Katanika displacement site in the city of Kalemie, according to local so
body_en:
Kalemie, Tanganyika Province, January 3, 2026 — More than 2,000 displaced people, who fled the conflict involving the AFC and M23 in North and South Kivu, are living in extremely precarious conditions at the Katanika displacement site in the city of Kalemie, according to local sources.
The displaced families reportedly lack access to medical care, clean water, and other basic necessities, prompting the site management to issue an urgent appeal for humanitarian assistance.
“There is no medical center or pharmacy at the site,” the site manager said. “These displaced people, whose total number is estimated at more than 11,000, are living in very poor shelter conditions, particularly during the rainy season, and are also facing severe shortages of water and food.”
According to the site management, displaced persons who fall ill are often forced to cope on their own, as access to healthcare remains extremely limited. Those who seek treatment at the Kifungo hospital are reportedly turned away, further worsening the humanitarian situation.
One displaced woman described the daily hardships faced by families at the site. “I have seven children. There is no pharmacy or hospital here. We receive no assistance. Malaria is widespread among the displaced. We have neither mosquito nets nor proper shelter. If someone of goodwill could help us…” she said.
The displaced people began settling at the Katanika site in February 2025. According to the site’s leadership, a humanitarian organization has provided tarpaulins and limited financial assistance, but these efforts remain insufficient to meet the growing needs of the population.
As conditions continue to deteriorate, calls are mounting for a scaled-up humanitarian response to prevent further suffering among the displaced communities in Kalemie.

title_en: Motorcycle Taxi Drivers Denounce Illegal Roadblocks on Goma–Masisi–Walikale Road
excerpt_en: Goma, January 8, 2026 — Motorcycle taxi drivers using the Goma–Masisi–Walikale road are raising alarms over repeated looting and the proliferation of illegal roadblocks set up by armed groups along the route. The road passes through a buffer zone, with one portion controlled by t
body_en:
Goma, January 8, 2026 — Motorcycle taxi drivers using the Goma–Masisi–Walikale road are raising alarms over repeated looting and the proliferation of illegal roadblocks set up by armed groups along the route.
The road passes through a buffer zone, with one portion controlled by the FARDC (Armed Forces of the DRC) and the Wazalendo militia, and another portion occupied by AFC-M23 rebels. Drivers report that these conditions have made travel dangerous and costly.
Lucien Amani Bitaha, spokesperson for the motorcyclists, said that motorcyclists now have to budget at least 200,000 Congolese francs (around 90 US dollars) to transport a single package from Goma to Walikale. He also described repeated looting incidents along the stretch between Kashebere and Miba, controlled by M23 rebels, and in the buffer zone between Kibati and Mikumbi, while the Miba area is under government and Wazalendo control.
“The road is completely dilapidated, with reeds growing in abundance, which only exacerbates the insecurity. Passengers, package owners, and motorcyclists alike continue to suffer these losses,” he added.
A local traditional leader from the Ihana group confirmed that authorities have been informed through official reports, but there has been no visible intervention to date to improve security or remove the illegal roadblocks.

title: Togo Moves to Revive Peace Talks Between DRC Government and AFC/M23
excerpt: January 5, 2026 — The government of Togo has initiated efforts to revive peace talks between the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and the AFC/M23 movement, amid renewed violence in eastern DRC. According to diplomatic sources, Lomé was expected to host a high-level mediation me
title_en: Togo Moves to Revive Peace Talks Between DRC Government and AFC/M23
excerpt_en: January 5, 2026 — The government of Togo has initiated efforts to revive peace talks between the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and the AFC/M23 movement, amid renewed violence in eastern DRC. According to diplomatic sources, Lomé was expected to host a high-level mediation me
body_en:
January 5, 2026 — The government of Togo has initiated efforts to revive peace talks between the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and the AFC/M23 movement, amid renewed violence in eastern DRC.
According to diplomatic sources, Lomé was expected to host a high-level mediation meeting on January 17, 2026, aimed at restoring dialogue between the two sides. The initiative was intended to rebuild mutual trust and restart negotiations that have stalled in recent weeks. Other international mediators, including the United States and Qatar, were expected to take part in the meeting.
Relations between the DRC government and the AFC/M23 deteriorated sharply in early December 2025, following intense fighting in South Kivu province, particularly in the Rusizi Valley.
Tensions further escalated when AFC/M23 fighters entered the city of Uvira, claiming they were responding to continued attacks by Congolese government forces on their positions. On December 16, the AFC/M23 announced its decision to withdraw from Uvira, a move that was carried out two days later. However, the DRC government rejected the withdrawal, and its forces reportedly launched fresh attacks from the Fizi area.
In his end-of-year address, AFC/M23 leader Corneille Nangaa Yobeluo disclosed that Qatar had convened two meetings aimed at discussing the implementation of a ceasefire agreement, but said the DRC government declined to attend.
According to Nangaa, Kinshasa deliberately chose to sabotage the peace process, favoring a military option, as it had done in previous conflicts. He reaffirmed that the AFC/M23 remains committed to a genuine and lasting peace, and said the movement continues to place its trust in Qatar’s mediation efforts.

title: Rwanda’s Jet Fuel Storage Reaches 12 Million Liters
excerpt: On January 5, 2026, the Rwanda Energy Corporation (REG) announced that Rwanda’s jet fuel storage capacity now stands at 12 million liters, a figure that reflects the country’s broader position in terms of petroleum storage capacity. Overall, Rwanda has petroleum storage facilitie
title_en: Rwanda’s Jet Fuel Storage Reaches 12 Million Liters
excerpt_en: On January 5, 2026, the Rwanda Energy Corporation (REG) announced that Rwanda’s jet fuel storage capacity now stands at 12 million liters, a figure that reflects the country’s broader position in terms of petroleum storage capacity. Overall, Rwanda has petroleum storage facilitie
body_en:
On January 5, 2026, the Rwanda Energy Corporation (REG) announced that Rwanda’s jet fuel storage capacity now stands at 12 million liters, a figure that reflects the country’s broader position in terms of petroleum storage capacity.
Overall, Rwanda has petroleum storage facilities totaling 118 million liters, combining both government-owned and private storage facilities across the country.
The government’s oil storage facilities in Gatsata have a capacity of 7,200,000 liters, while private oil storage facilities in Kabuye (Kigali City) can store 3,100,000 liters. In Rwabuye (Huye District), government tanks hold 1,900,000 liters, and in Bigogwe (Nyabihu District), government facilities store 3,000,000 liters.
Additional private fuel tanks in Jabana (Kigali City) have a capacity of 10,000,000 liters, while government-owned tanks in Rusororo can store up to 20,000,000 liters. Altogether, Rwanda’s fuel tanks have a combined storage capacity of 45,200,000 liters.
Rwanda’s fuel storage infrastructure includes government-owned tanks in Gatsata with a capacity of 6,700,000 liters and private tanks in Kabuye holding 2,700,000 liters. There are also government fuel oil tanks in Rwabuye with a capacity of 1,900,000 liters, fuel oil tanks in Bigogwe holding 2,000,000 liters, and private fuel oil tanks in Jabana with a capacity of 10,000,000 liters.
In addition, the government operates fuel oil tanks in Rusororo with a capacity of 36,000,000 liters, bringing the total fuel oil storage capacity to 59,300,000 liters. There are also government-owned kerosene tanks in Gatsata with a capacity of 1,500,000 liters.
Regarding aviation fuel, Rwanda operates government-owned jet fuel storage facilities in Rusororo with a capacity of 10,000,000 liters, as well as another facility in Kanombe holding 2,000,000 liters, for a total jet fuel storage capacity of 12 million liters.
By location, Gatsata has a total capacity of 15,400,000 liters of petroleum products, Kabuye holds 5,800,000 liters, Rwabuye stores 3,800,000 liters, and Bigogwe has 5,000,000 liters. Jabana accounts for 20,000,000 liters, Rusororo for 66,000,000 liters, and Kanombe for 2,000,000 liters, together reaching a national storage capacity of 118,000,000 liters.
In March 2025, the Minister of Trade and Industry, Prudence Sebahizi, stated that Rwanda’s petroleum storage capacity exceeded 110 million liters, with plans to expand it to 320 million liters within two years.
He recalled that in 2017, Rwanda consumed around 600,000 liters of petroleum products per day, while storage capacity stood at 111 million liters, enough to last six months. Today, however, due to the increase in vehicles and industrial activity, daily consumption has risen to at least two million liters, meaning current reserves can last no more than two months.
He warned that this situation could become critical in the event of disruptions along regional supply routes, which is why the government is pursuing a strategy to expand national fuel reserves.
Rwanda sources its petroleum products primarily from Arab countries, while also importing from East Africa, with Tanzania as the main regional supplier, and smaller volumes coming from Kenya.

title: Trial of Sheikh Bahame Hassan Continues in Closed Session
excerpt: Nyamata, Bugesera District – 8 January 2026: The Nyamata Primary Court has ordered that the trial of Sheikh Bahame Hassan, Coordinator of the Gitagata Ngororamuco Center, suspected of sexually abusing some beneficiaries of the center, continue behind closed doors. Bahame was arre
title_en: Trial of Sheikh Bahame Hassan Continues in Closed Session
excerpt_en: Nyamata, Bugesera District – 8 January 2026: The Nyamata Primary Court has ordered that the trial of Sheikh Bahame Hassan, Coordinator of the Gitagata Ngororamuco Center, suspected of sexually abusing some beneficiaries of the center, continue behind closed doors. Bahame was arre
body_en:
Nyamata, Bugesera District – 8 January 2026: The Nyamata Primary Court has ordered that the trial of Sheikh Bahame Hassan, Coordinator of the Gitagata Ngororamuco Center, suspected of sexually abusing some beneficiaries of the center, continue behind closed doors.
Bahame was arrested on 16 December 2025 following a multi-day investigation into allegations that he exploited female victims at the center for sexual purposes, under the pretense of helping them or connecting them with families.
The Rwanda Investigation Bureau (RIB) charged him with abusing his legal authority for personal gain and soliciting or performing sexual acts.
The hearing on detention and provisional release, initially scheduled for 6 January 2026, was postponed to 8 January after the Prosecution presented evidence of its participation in the investigation. During the hearing, Bahame’s lawyer, Me Nyembo Emeline, requested that the trial continue in camera due to the sensitive nature of the case. The court granted this request, clearing the courtroom while proceedings continued.
Although the trial is being held privately, the judgment will be read publicly, in accordance with Rwandan criminal law. The court’s decision is expected to be announced on 13 January 2026.
The investigation revealed that Bahame allegedly provided illegal benefits to individuals for personal sexual gratification. Under Article 6 of Rwanda’s Anti-Corruption Law, soliciting, accepting, or promising sexual favors for personal or unlawful gain is a punishable offense, carrying prison terms from 5 to 10 years and fines ranging from 1,000,000 to 10,000,000 Rwf, depending on the nature of the offense.
Sheikh Bahame Hassan was appointed Director of the Gitagata Cultural Center in 2021 and previously gained public recognition while leading the Rubavu District. The RIB continues its investigation into his alleged crimes.

title: DRC Government Denounces Repression Ahead of Planned Goma Protest
excerpt: Goma, DRC — January 2, 2026 On the eve of a planned citizens’ march in Goma, scheduled for Friday, January 2, 2026, the Congolese government has denounced what it describes as a climate of repression and intimidation in areas under occupation. In a statement, Patrick Muyaya, Gove
title_en: DRC Government Denounces Repression Ahead of Planned Goma Protest
excerpt_en: Goma, DRC — January 2, 2026 On the eve of a planned citizens’ march in Goma, scheduled for Friday, January 2, 2026, the Congolese government has denounced what it describes as a climate of repression and intimidation in areas under occupation. In a statement, Patrick Muyaya, Gove
body_en:
Goma, DRC — January 2, 2026
On the eve of a planned citizens’ march in Goma, scheduled for Friday, January 2, 2026, the Congolese government has denounced what it describes as a climate of repression and intimidation in areas under occupation.
In a statement, Patrick Muyaya, Government Spokesperson and Minister of Communication and Media, said residents of Goma are facing arbitrary arrests, intimidation, and preventive repression, measures he claims are aimed at preventing any peaceful expression of dissent. According to the minister, these actions have created what he called a “climate of terror.”
Muyaya also pointed to similar incidents in Sake, where several young people reportedly disappeared after participating in demonstrations last December against what he described as Rwandan occupation.
“These events confirm the Congolese people’s total rejection of the occupation,” Muyaya said, adding that civilians are exhausted by what he described as abuses, torture, and massacres. He expressed the government’s solidarity with the victims of repression and with civilian populations living in affected areas.
Despite the reported crackdown, the government spokesperson said the population continues to resist and voice opposition, pledging that such resistance will persist until the withdrawal of all foreign forces from Congolese territory.
Muyaya further accused Rwanda and the M23 of attempting to export methods of repression, intimidation, imprisonment, and the suppression of freedoms into the DRC, stressing that “coercion can generate neither legitimacy nor popular support.”

title: DRC Reports Decline in Monkeypox Cases, Around 300 New Infections Weekly

title_en: DRC Reports Decline in Monkeypox Cases, Around 300 New Infections Weekly
excerpt_en: Kinshasa | January 1, 2026 — Health authorities in the Democratic Republic of Congo report a notable decline in monkeypox cases, with approximately 250 to 300 new infections recorded each week, according to officials from the National Institute of Public Health (INSP). Speaking a
body_en:
Kinshasa | January 1, 2026 — Health authorities in the Democratic Republic of Congo report a notable decline in monkeypox cases, with approximately 250 to 300 new infections recorded each week, according to officials from the National Institute of Public Health (INSP).
Speaking at a press conference held on Wednesday, December 31, 2025, the coordinator of the Public Health Emergency Operations Center (PHOOC), Christian Ngandu, said that only 19 health zones reported monkeypox cases in December 2025, compared to much higher figures earlier in the outbreak.

excerpt_en: Kalehe Territory, South Kivu | December 30, 2025 Tensions remained high on Tuesday in the village of Tushunguti, located in the Ziralo group, Kalehe Territory, following the killing of a local resident allegedly carried out by an armed individual affiliated with the Wazalendo Kir
body_en:
Kalehe Territory, South Kivu | December 30, 2025
Tensions remained high on Tuesday in the village of Tushunguti, located in the Ziralo group, Kalehe Territory, following the killing of a local resident allegedly carried out by an armed individual affiliated with the Wazalendo Kirikicho group, according to local sources.
Early Tuesday morning, angry residents surrounded the residence of the Ziralo group chief, expressing frustration over what they described as persistent insecurity in the area. Demonstrators denounced the silence of the authorities in response to repeated abuses allegedly committed by armed men linked to the Wazalendo, particularly those from the Mai-Mai Kirikicho faction.
A civil society representative reported that these armed elements are frequently accused of theft, violence, and killings. He stated that the victim of Monday evening’s attack was a security guard assigned to protect a depot belonging to the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC).
According to the same source, following the murder, local residents pursued the suspected assailant, who was later killed during the chase. This account was confirmed by notable figures in the region.
Community leaders have since urged South Kivu provincial authorities to take urgent measures to curb the activities of armed groups operating in the area. They called for strict control of weapons and tighter oversight of fighters associated with the Mai-Mai Kirikicho group, warning that continued inaction could further destabilize the region.

title: FARDC Presents Seven Rwandan Soldiers to the Press in Kinshasa
excerpt: Kinshasa, January 3, 2026 — The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (FARDC) on Saturday presented to the press seven Rwandan soldiers alongside eight civilians from neighboring countries, whom they say were captured during military operations in eastern Congo. Ac
title_en: FARDC Presents Seven Rwandan Soldiers to the Press in Kinshasa
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, January 3, 2026 — The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (FARDC) on Saturday presented to the press seven Rwandan soldiers alongside eight civilians from neighboring countries, whom they say were captured during military operations in eastern Congo. Ac
body_en:
Kinshasa, January 3, 2026 — The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (FARDC) on Saturday presented to the press seven Rwandan soldiers alongside eight civilians from neighboring countries, whom they say were captured during military operations in eastern Congo.
According to Lieutenant Colonel Mak Hazukay, Deputy Commander of the FARDC’s Command and Information Service, the arrest of these individuals provides clear evidence of the presence of the Rwandan army on Congolese territory. He strongly criticized what he described as Kigali’s continued and deliberate violation of the Washington Agreement and United Nations Security Council Resolution 2773.
Lieutenant Colonel Mak Hazukay specified that the suspects were apprehended far from the border areas, during operations conducted in North Kivu and South Kivu, undermining claims that Rwanda’s actions are defensive in nature.
“Since the beginning of this war, the DRC has consistently maintained, with supporting evidence, that it is under attack by Rwanda,” he stated. “The FARDC presented seven Rwandan soldiers and eight civilians, nationals of countries in the sub-region, captured during military operations in North and South Kivu. The current occupation of Uvira, located far from the borders, proves that the justification invoked by Kigali is a blatant lie,” he added.
The FARDC official further accused the Kigali regime of manipulating nationals from countries in the sub-region, as well as collaborating with other armed groups, including RED Tabala, in an effort to regionalize the armed conflict.
The presentation of these captives comes amid a renewed security escalation in eastern DRC, as AFC/M23 rebels have launched an offensive to retake control of Katoyi, the main town of the Katoyi sector in Masisi territory, North Kivu.

excerpt: Djugu, Ituri, January 9, 2026 — In the past month, MONUSCO has evacuated 152 vulnerable people from the Bule region of Djugu territory to Bunia amid ongoing clashes between the FARDC (Armed Forces of the DRC) and militias of the Convention for the Popular Revolution (CRP) led by
title_en: MONUSCO Evacuates Over 150 Civilians from Djugu Conflict Zone
excerpt_en: Djugu, Ituri, January 9, 2026 — In the past month, MONUSCO has evacuated 152 vulnerable people from the Bule region of Djugu territory to Bunia amid ongoing clashes between the FARDC (Armed Forces of the DRC) and militias of the Convention for the Popular Revolution (CRP) led by
body_en:
Djugu, Ituri, January 9, 2026 — In the past month, MONUSCO has evacuated 152 vulnerable people from the Bule region of Djugu territory to Bunia amid ongoing clashes between the FARDC (Armed Forces of the DRC) and militias of the Convention for the Popular Revolution (CRP) led by Thomas Lubanga.
The commander of the Bangladeshi peacekeepers deployed with MONUSCO reported the operations on Thursday, January 8, during a meeting with a UN mission delegation in Bayo. The evacuated individuals include wounded soldiers, humanitarian workers, priests, medical personnel, teachers, and other at-risk civilians. Evacuations were carried out via vehicle, helicopter, and armored tank.
To strengthen civilian protection, Bangladeshi peacekeepers conducted 152 combat patrols over the past month in the Savo Plain, where thousands of families have been displaced by the conflict.
The fighting, ongoing since December 5, 2025, has severely impacted Bule-Centre in the Badjere chiefdom, which has been largely reduced to a ghost town as FARDC and CRP militias contest control.
Through these operations, MONUSCO reaffirms its support for the FARDC in efforts to restore peace in the region and highlights the continued intensification of patrols to protect civilians in accordance with its mandate.
